name: UKMLA
description: UK Medical Licensing Assessment - Comprehensive curriculum covering all medical specialties.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Definition
concepts.content: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is an umbrella term covering a number of acute presentations of ischaemic heart disease.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Included presentations
concepts.content: ACS includes ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and unstable angina.

concepts.title: Unstable angina – Definition and diagnosis
concepts.content: Unstable angina is considered present in patients with ischaemic symptoms suggestive of ACS and no elevation in troponins, with or without ECG changes indicative of ischaemia.

concepts.title: Unstable angina and NSTEMI – Initial indistinguishability
concepts.content: Because troponin elevation may take hours to appear, unstable angina may be initially indistinguishable from NSTEMI and is treated the same until troponin results are available.

concepts.title: Ischaemic heart disease – Synonyms
concepts.content: Ischaemic heart disease is synonymous with coronary heart disease and coronary artery disease.

concepts.title: Ischaemic heart disease – Pathophysiology overview
concepts.content: Ischaemic heart disease describes the gradual buildup of fatty plaques within the walls of coronary arteries.

concepts.title: Ischaemic heart disease – Consequences of plaque buildup
concepts.content: Plaque buildup causes gradual narrowing of coronary arteries leading to reduced blood and oxygen supply to myocardium during increased demand, causing angina.

concepts.title: Ischaemic heart disease – Risk of plaque rupture
concepts.content: Fatty plaques in the coronary artery endothelium may rupture suddenly, causing artery occlusion and complete loss of blood and oxygen supply to myocardium.

concepts.title: Ischaemic heart disease – Unmodifiable risk factors
concepts.content: Unmodifiable risk factors for ischaemic heart disease include increasing age, male gender, and family history.

concepts.title: Ischaemic heart disease – Modifiable risk factors
concepts.content: Modifiable risk factors for ischaemic heart disease include smoking, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, and obesity.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Chest pain location
concepts.content: Chest pain in acute coronary syndromes is classically located on the left side of the chest.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Chest pain radiation
concepts.content: Chest pain in acute coronary syndromes may radiate to the left arm or neck.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Atypical chest pain presentation
concepts.content: Chest pain may not always be present in acute coronary syndromes; elderly, diabetic, or female patients are more likely to have atypical presentations.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Dyspnoea
concepts.content: Dyspnoea is a clinical feature of acute coronary syndromes.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Nausea and vomiting
concepts.content: Nausea and vomiting can occur as clinical features in acute coronary syndromes.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Sweating
concepts.content: Sweating is a common clinical feature of acute coronary syndromes.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Palpitations
concepts.content: Palpitations may be experienced as a clinical feature in acute coronary syndromes.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Definition
concepts.content: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is a common and important medical presentation involving a spectrum of conditions caused by acute myocardial ischemia.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Classification
concepts.content: ACS is classified into ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), non ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and unstable angina.

concepts.title: ST-elevation myocardial infarction – Definition
concepts.content: STEMI is defined by ST-segment elevation on ECG and elevated biomarkers of myocardial damage.

concepts.title: Non ST-elevation myocardial infarction – Definition
concepts.content: NSTEMI is characterized by ECG changes without ST-segment elevation and elevated biomarkers of myocardial damage.

concepts.title: Unstable angina – Definition
concepts.content: Unstable angina is a form of ACS characterized by ischemic chest pain without elevated biomarkers of myocardial damage.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Initial management grouping
concepts.content: NICE guidelines group ACS patients into two management categories: STEMI and NSTEMI/unstable angina.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Aspirin initial therapy
concepts.content: Aspirin 300 mg is recommended as initial drug therapy for all patients with suspected ACS.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Oxygen therapy indication
concepts.content: Oxygen should be administered only if the patient has oxygen saturations below 94%, according to British Thoracic Society guidelines.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Morphine use criteria
concepts.content: Morphine should be given only to patients with severe chest pain; routine intravenous morphine use is no longer recommended due to potential adverse outcomes.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Nitrate administration
concepts.content: Nitrates can be administered sublingually or intravenously for ongoing chest pain or hypertension but should be used cautiously in hypotensive patients.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – STEMI ECG diagnostic criteria
concepts.content: STEMI diagnosis requires clinical symptoms consistent with ACS lasting ≥ 20 minutes and persistent ST elevation > 20 minutes in at least two contiguous leads.

concepts.title: ST-elevation myocardial infarction – ST elevation threshold in leads V2-V3
concepts.content: ST elevation of ≥ 2.5 mm (2.5 small squares) in leads V2-V3 is diagnostic for STEMI in appropriate clinical context.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Prognostic model source
concepts.content: The 2006 Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events (GRACE) study was used to derive regression models predicting in-hospital and post-discharge death in patients with acute coronary syndrome.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Age as poor prognostic factor
concepts.content: Advanced age is associated with a poorer prognosis in patients with acute coronary syndrome.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Heart failure history as poor prognostic factor
concepts.content: Development or history of heart failure predicts worse outcomes in acute coronary syndrome patients.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Peripheral vascular disease as poor prognostic factor
concepts.content: Presence of peripheral vascular disease is associated with a poorer prognosis in acute coronary syndrome.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Reduced systolic blood pressure as poor prognostic factor
concepts.content: Lower systolic blood pressure at presentation predicts worse outcomes in acute coronary syndrome patients.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Killip classification system
concepts.content: The Killip classification stratifies risk after myocardial infarction based on clinical signs of heart failure.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Killip class I features and mortality
concepts.content: Killip class I is defined by no clinical signs of heart failure and is associated with a 6% 30-day mortality.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Killip class II features and mortality
concepts.content: Killip class II is characterized by lung crackles and S3 heart sound, with a 17% 30-day mortality.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Killip class III features and mortality
concepts.content: Killip class III involves frank pulmonary oedema and carries a 38% 30-day mortality risk.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Killip class IV features and mortality
concepts.content: Killip class IV is defined by cardiogenic shock and is associated with an 81% 30-day mortality.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Initial serum creatinine concentration as poor prognostic factor
concepts.content: Elevated initial serum creatinine concentration predicts worse prognosis in acute coronary syndrome patients.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Elevated initial cardiac markers as poor prognostic factor
concepts.content: Elevated initial cardiac biomarkers indicate a worse prognosis in patients with acute coronary syndrome.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Cardiac arrest on admission as poor prognostic factor
concepts.content: Cardiac arrest occurring on admission is associated with a poor prognosis in acute coronary syndrome patients.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – ST segment deviation as poor prognostic factor
concepts.content: ST segment deviation on ECG at presentation predicts worse outcomes in acute coronary syndrome.

concepts.title: Adenosine – Definition and Clinical Use
concepts.content: Adenosine is a medication most commonly used to terminate supraventricular tachycardias.

concepts.title: Adenosine – Mechanism of Action
concepts.content: Adenosine acts as an agonist of the A1 receptor in the atrioventricular (AV) node, causing transient heart block by inhibiting adenylyl cyclase, reducing cAMP, and causing hyperpolarization through increased outward potassium flux.

concepts.title: Adenosine – Pharmacokinetics
concepts.content: Adenosine has a very short half-life of approximately 8 to 10 seconds.

concepts.title: Adenosine – Administration Considerations
concepts.content: Due to its short half-life, adenosine should ideally be infused via a large-calibre cannula to ensure rapid delivery.

concepts.title: Adenosine – Drug Interactions
concepts.content: The effects of adenosine are enhanced by dipyridamole and blocked by theophyllines.

concepts.title: Adenosine – Contraindications
concepts.content: Adenosine should be avoided in patients with asthma due to the risk of bronchospasm.

concepts.title: Adenosine – Adverse Effect: Chest Pain
concepts.content: Adenosine administration can cause chest pain as an adverse effect.

concepts.title: Adenosine – Adverse Effect: Bronchospasm
concepts.content: Adenosine can cause bronchospasm as an adverse effect, particularly in susceptible individuals.

concepts.title: Adenosine – Adverse Effect: Transient Flushing
concepts.content: Transient flushing is a common adverse effect following adenosine administration.

concepts.title: Adenosine – Risk in Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome
concepts.content: Adenosine can enhance conduction down accessory pathways, potentially increasing ventricular rate in patients with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Definition
concepts.content: Adrenaline is a sympathomimetic amine with both alpha and beta adrenergic stimulating properties.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Indications
concepts.content: Adrenaline is indicated for the treatment of anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Adult Life Support Dose for Anaphylaxis
concepts.content: The recommended adult dose of adrenaline for anaphylaxis is 0.5 ml of 1:1,000 concentration administered intramuscularly (IM).

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Adult Life Support Dose for Cardiac Arrest
concepts.content: The recommended adult dose of adrenaline for cardiac arrest is 10 ml of 1:10,000 concentration intravenously (IV) or alternatively 1 ml of 1:1,000 concentration IV.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Management of Accidental Injection
concepts.content: Accidental injection of adrenaline causing digital ischaemia is managed by local infiltration of phentolamine.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Background Physiology
concepts.content: Adrenaline is responsible for the fight or flight response and is released by the adrenal glands.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Receptor Targets
concepts.content: Adrenaline acts on alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, and beta-2 adrenergic receptors.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Vascular Effects on Skeletal Muscle
concepts.content: Adrenaline acts on beta-2 receptors in skeletal muscle vessels causing vasodilation.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Cardiovascular Effects
concepts.content: Adrenaline increases cardiac output and total peripheral resistance.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Vasoconstriction Effects
concepts.content: Adrenaline causes vasoconstriction in the skin and kidneys, resulting in a narrow pulse pressure.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Actions on Alpha Adrenergic Receptors: Insulin Secretion
concepts.content: Adrenaline inhibits insulin secretion by the pancreas via alpha adrenergic receptor stimulation.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Actions on Alpha Adrenergic Receptors: Glycogenolysis
concepts.content: Adrenaline stimulates glycogenolysis in the liver and muscle via alpha adrenergic receptor activation.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Actions on Alpha Adrenergic Receptors: Glycolysis
concepts.content: Adrenaline stimulates glycolysis in muscle via alpha adrenergic receptor activation.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Actions on Beta Adrenergic Receptors: Glucagon Secretion
concepts.content: Adrenaline stimulates glucagon secretion in the pancreas via beta adrenergic receptor activation.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Actions on Beta Adrenergic Receptors: ACTH Stimulation
concepts.content: Adrenaline stimulates adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion via beta adrenergic receptor activation.

concepts.title: Adrenaline – Actions on Beta Adrenergic Receptors: Lipolysis
concepts.content: Adrenaline stimulates lipolysis in adipose tissue via beta adrenergic receptor activation.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Definition
concepts.content: Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic agent used in the treatment of atrial, nodal, and ventricular tachycardias.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Mechanism of action
concepts.content: Amiodarone primarily blocks potassium channels, inhibiting repolarisation and prolonging the cardiac action potential; it also blocks sodium channels, exhibiting a class I antiarrhythmic effect.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Half-life and dosing implications
concepts.content: Amiodarone has a very long half-life ranging from 20 to 100 days, necessitating the use of loading doses to achieve therapeutic levels.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Administration route considerations
concepts.content: Amiodarone should ideally be administered via central veins to reduce the risk of thrombophlebitis.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Proarrhythmic effects
concepts.content: Amiodarone can cause proarrhythmic effects by lengthening the QT interval, which may predispose to arrhythmias.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Drug interactions
concepts.content: Amiodarone is a cytochrome P450 inhibitor and can decrease the metabolism of concurrently used drugs such as warfarin.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Baseline monitoring before treatment
concepts.content: Before starting amiodarone, thyroid function tests (TFT), liver function tests (LFT), urea and electrolytes (U&E), and chest X-ray (CXR) should be performed.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Ongoing monitoring during treatment
concepts.content: During amiodarone therapy, thyroid function tests and liver function tests should be repeated every 6 months.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Thyroid dysfunction adverse effects
concepts.content: Amiodarone can cause thyroid dysfunction, including both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Corneal deposits adverse effect
concepts.content: Long-term use of amiodarone may lead to corneal deposits.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Pulmonary toxicity adverse effects
concepts.content: Amiodarone can cause pulmonary fibrosis and pneumonitis as long-term adverse effects.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Hepatic toxicity adverse effects
concepts.content: Amiodarone may cause liver fibrosis and hepatitis as adverse effects.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Neuromuscular adverse effects
concepts.content: Amiodarone use can lead to peripheral neuropathy and myopathy.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Photosensitivity adverse effect
concepts.content: Amiodarone can cause photosensitivity reactions in patients.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Skin discoloration adverse effect
concepts.content: Chronic amiodarone use may cause a 'slate-grey' skin discoloration.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Injection site adverse effects
concepts.content: Amiodarone administration can cause thrombophlebitis and other injection site reactions.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – Bradycardia adverse effect
concepts.content: Amiodarone therapy can cause bradycardia as an adverse effect.

concepts.title: Amiodarone – QT interval prolongation adverse effect
concepts.content: Amiodarone lengthens the QT interval, which can predispose to arrhythmias.

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – Overview of management
concepts.content: Management of stable angina includes lifestyle changes, medication, percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), and surgery.

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – NICE guidelines for stable angina management
concepts.content: NICE guidelines published in 2011 provide recommendations for the management of stable angina.

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – Aspirin and statin use
concepts.content: All patients with stable angina should receive aspirin and a statin unless contraindicated.

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – Use of sublingual glyceryl trinitrate
concepts.content: Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate is used to abort angina attacks.

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – First-line antianginal therapy choice
concepts.content: NICE recommends using either a beta-blocker or a calcium channel blocker first-line based on comorbidities, contraindications, and patient preference.

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – Calcium channel blocker monotherapy selection
concepts.content: If a calcium channel blocker is used as monotherapy, a rate-limiting agent such as verapamil or diltiazem should be chosen.

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – Combination therapy with beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker
concepts.content: When combining with a beta-blocker, use a longer-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine or modified-release nifedipine.

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – Contraindication of beta-blockers with verapamil
concepts.content: Beta-blockers should not be prescribed concurrently with verapamil due to the risk of complete heart block.

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – Dose escalation for poor response to initial treatment
concepts.content: If there is a poor response to initial treatment, medication should be increased to the maximum tolerated dose, e.g., atenolol up to 100 mg once daily.

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – Addition of second-line agent after monotherapy failure
concepts.content: If a patient remains symptomatic after monotherapy with a beta-blocker, add a calcium channel blocker, and vice versa.

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – Alternative drugs when combination therapy not tolerated
concepts.content: If a patient on monotherapy cannot tolerate adding a calcium channel blocker or beta-blocker, consider long-acting nitrates, ivabradine, nicorandil, or ranolazine.

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – Addition of third drug during PCI or CABG assessment
concepts.content: If a patient is taking both a beta-blocker and a calcium channel blocker, only add a third drug while awaiting assessment for PCI or coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG).

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – Nitrate tolerance development
concepts.content: Many patients taking nitrates develop tolerance, leading to reduced efficacy of the medication.

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – Asymmetric dosing to prevent nitrate tolerance
concepts.content: Patients taking standard-release isosorbide mononitrate should use an asymmetric dosing interval to maintain a daily nitrate-free period of 10-14 hours to minimize nitrate tolerance.

concepts.title: Angina pectoris – Modified-release isosorbide mononitrate and nitrate tolerance
concepts.content: Once-daily modified-release isosorbide mononitrate does not cause nitrate tolerance due to its dosing profile.

concepts.title: Angiotensin II receptor blockers – Definition
concepts.content: Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) are medications that block the effects of angiotensin II at the AT1 receptor.

concepts.title: Angiotensin II receptor blockers – Indication after ACE inhibitor intolerance
concepts.content: ARBs are generally used in patients who have not tolerated ACE inhibitors, usually due to the development of a cough.

concepts.title: Angiotensin II receptor blockers – Examples
concepts.content: Examples of ARBs include candesartan, losartan, and irbesartan.

concepts.title: Angiotensin II receptor blockers – Caution in renovascular disease
concepts.content: ARBs should be used with caution in patients with renovascular disease, similar to ACE inhibitors.

concepts.title: Angiotensin II receptor blockers – Side effects
concepts.content: Common side effects of ARBs include hypotension and hyperkalaemia.

concepts.title: Angiotensin II receptor blockers – Mechanism of action
concepts.content: ARBs block the effects of angiotensin II at the AT1 receptor, preventing vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion.

concepts.title: Angiotensin II receptor blockers – Evidence in diabetic nephropathy
concepts.content: ARBs have been shown to reduce progression of renal disease in patients with diabetic nephropathy.

concepts.title: Losartan – Evidence in cardiovascular mortality reduction
concepts.content: Losartan has evidence supporting reduction of cerebrovascular accident (CVA) and ischaemic heart disease (IHD) mortality in hypertensive patients.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – First-line antiplatelet therapy
concepts.content: For medically treated acute coronary syndrome, first-line antiplatelet therapy consists of lifelong aspirin combined with ticagrelor for 12 months.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Second-line antiplatelet therapy
concepts.content: If aspirin is contraindicated in medically treated acute coronary syndrome, lifelong clopidogrel is recommended as second-line antiplatelet therapy.

concepts.title: Percutaneous coronary intervention – First-line antiplatelet therapy
concepts.content: Following percutaneous coronary intervention, first-line antiplatelet therapy includes lifelong aspirin combined with prasugrel or ticagrelor for 12 months.

concepts.title: Percutaneous coronary intervention – Second-line antiplatelet therapy
concepts.content: If aspirin is contraindicated after percutaneous coronary intervention, lifelong clopidogrel is recommended as second-line antiplatelet therapy.

concepts.title: Transient ischaemic attack – First-line antiplatelet therapy
concepts.content: Clopidogrel lifelong is the first-line antiplatelet therapy for patients with transient ischaemic attack.

concepts.title: Transient ischaemic attack – Second-line antiplatelet therapy
concepts.content: If clopidogrel is not used, aspirin combined with dipyridamole lifelong is recommended as second-line antiplatelet therapy for transient ischaemic attack.

concepts.title: Ischaemic stroke – First-line antiplatelet therapy
concepts.content: Lifelong clopidogrel is the first-line antiplatelet therapy for ischaemic stroke.

concepts.title: Ischaemic stroke – Second-line antiplatelet therapy
concepts.content: If clopidogrel is not used, aspirin combined with dipyridamole lifelong is recommended as second-line antiplatelet therapy for ischaemic stroke.

concepts.title: Peripheral arterial disease – First-line antiplatelet therapy
concepts.content: Clopidogrel lifelong is the first-line antiplatelet therapy for peripheral arterial disease.

concepts.title: Peripheral arterial disease – Second-line antiplatelet therapy
concepts.content: Aspirin lifelong is recommended as second-line antiplatelet therapy for peripheral arterial disease.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Definition
concepts.content: Aortic regurgitation (AR) is the leaking of the aortic valve of the heart that causes blood to flow in the reverse direction during ventricular diastole.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Aortic regurgitation occurs due to leaking of the aortic valve causing reverse blood flow into the left ventricle during ventricular diastole.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Causes due to valve disease (chronic)
concepts.content: Chronic causes of aortic regurgitation due to valve disease include rheumatic fever, calcific valve disease, connective tissue diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus, and bicuspid aortic valve.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Causes due to aortic root disease (chronic)
concepts.content: Chronic causes of aortic regurgitation due to aortic root disease include bicuspid aortic valve, spondylarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis, hypertension, syphilis, Marfan's syndrome, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Causes due to valve disease (acute)
concepts.content: Acute causes of aortic regurgitation due to valve disease include infective endocarditis.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Causes due to aortic root disease (acute)
concepts.content: Acute causes of aortic regurgitation due to aortic root disease include aortic dissection.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Clinical feature: Early diastolic murmur
concepts.content: Aortic regurgitation presents with an early diastolic murmur whose intensity is increased by the handgrip manoeuvre.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Clinical feature: Collapsing pulse
concepts.content: A collapsing pulse is a clinical feature of aortic regurgitation.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Clinical feature: Wide pulse pressure
concepts.content: Wide pulse pressure is a clinical feature of aortic regurgitation.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Clinical feature: Quincke's sign
concepts.content: Quincke's sign, which is nailbed pulsation, is a clinical feature of aortic regurgitation.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Clinical feature: De Musset's sign
concepts.content: De Musset's sign, which is head bobbing, is a clinical feature of aortic regurgitation.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Clinical feature: Austin-Flint murmur
concepts.content: A mid-diastolic Austin-Flint murmur occurs in severe aortic regurgitation due to partial closure of the anterior mitral valve cusps caused by regurgitation streams.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Investigation
concepts.content: Suspected aortic regurgitation should be investigated with echocardiography.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Management: Medical
concepts.content: Medical management of aortic regurgitation includes treatment of any associated heart failure.

concepts.title: Aortic regurgitation – Management: Surgical indications
concepts.content: Surgical aortic valve replacement is indicated in symptomatic patients with severe aortic regurgitation and in asymptomatic patients with severe aortic regurgitation who have left ventricular systolic dysfunction.

concepts.title: Aspirin – Mechanism of action
concepts.content: Aspirin blocks the action of cyclooxygenase-1 and cyclooxygenase-2 enzymes, which are responsible for the synthesis of prostaglandins, prostacyclin, and thromboxane.

concepts.title: Aspirin – Effect on platelet aggregation
concepts.content: By blocking thromboxane A2 formation in platelets, aspirin reduces platelet aggregation, which helps prevent thrombosis in cardiovascular disease.

concepts.title: Aspirin – Use in secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease
concepts.content: Low-dose aspirin has been widely used for secondary prevention in patients with established cardiovascular disease unless contraindicated.

concepts.title: Aspirin – Changes in guidelines after 2010 technology appraisal of clopidogrel
concepts.content: Following the 2010 technology appraisal of clopidogrel, aspirin is no longer universally recommended for all patients with established cardiovascular disease.

concepts.title: Aspirin – Role in primary prevention of cardiovascular disease
concepts.content: Recent trials (Aspirin for Asymptomatic Atherosclerosis and Antithrombotic Trialists Collaboration) have questioned the benefit of aspirin in primary prevention of cardiovascular disease.

concepts.title: Aspirin – Regulatory status for primary prevention
concepts.content: The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) issued a drug safety update in January 2010 stating aspirin is not licensed for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease.

concepts.title: Aspirin – Current guideline recommendation for ischaemic heart disease
concepts.content: Aspirin is recommended as first-line antiplatelet therapy for patients with ischaemic heart disease.

concepts.title: Aspirin – Drug interactions
concepts.content: Aspirin potentiates the effects of oral hypoglycaemics, warfarin, and steroids.

concepts.title: Aspirin – Contraindication in children under 16 years
concepts.content: Aspirin should not be used in children under 16 years due to the risk of Reye's syndrome, except in Kawasaki disease where benefits outweigh risks.

concepts.title: Clopidogrel – Guideline recommendation after ischaemic stroke and peripheral arterial disease
concepts.content: NICE recommends clopidogrel as first-line antiplatelet therapy following ischaemic stroke and for peripheral arterial disease, replacing aspirin.

concepts.title: Transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs) – Antiplatelet therapy guideline complexity
concepts.content: For TIAs, Royal College of Physicians guidelines support clopidogrel use, whereas older NICE guidelines recommend aspirin plus dipyridamole; the RCP considers the older NICE position illogical.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Need for anticoagulation
concepts.content: Anticoagulation should be considered in patients with any history of atrial fibrillation, including symptomatic or asymptomatic paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent AF, atrial flutter, and those with a continuing risk of arrhythmia recurrence after cardioversion or catheter ablation.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – CHA2DS2-VASc score for anticoagulation decision
concepts.content: The CHA2DS2-VASc score is recommended by NICE to determine the need for anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation patients, replacing the older CHADS2 score.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – CHA2DS2-VASc score components
concepts.content: CHA2DS2-VASc score components and points: Congestive heart failure (1), Hypertension (1), Age ≥75 years (2), Age 65-74 years (1), Diabetes (1), Prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2), Vascular disease (1), Female sex (1).

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Anticoagulation strategy based on CHA2DS2-VASc score
concepts.content: Anticoagulation recommendations: Score 0 - no treatment; Score 1 - males consider anticoagulation, females no treatment (score 1 due to sex only); Score ≥2 - offer anticoagulation.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Exclusion of valvular heart disease before withholding anticoagulation
concepts.content: If CHA2DS2-VASc score suggests no anticoagulation, a transthoracic echocardiogram should be performed to exclude valvular heart disease, which combined with AF is an absolute indication for anticoagulation.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Bleeding risk assessment before anticoagulation
concepts.content: Bleeding risk factors include history of falls, old age, alcohol excess, and previous bleeding; however, anticoagulation should not be withheld solely due to age or fall risk.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Use of ORBIT score for bleeding risk assessment
concepts.content: NICE recommends formalizing bleeding risk assessment before anticoagulation using the ORBIT score.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Indications for cardioversion
concepts.content: Cardioversion in atrial fibrillation is used in two scenarios: as an emergency electrical cardioversion if the patient is haemodynamically unstable, and as an elective procedure (electrical or pharmacological) when a rhythm control strategy is preferred.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Electrical cardioversion synchronization
concepts.content: Electrical cardioversion is synchronized to the R wave to avoid delivering a shock during the vulnerable period of cardiac repolarisation, which can induce ventricular fibrillation.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – NICE guideline recommendation for rate or rhythm control
concepts.content: NICE guidelines recommend offering rate or rhythm control if atrial fibrillation onset is less than 48 hours, and starting rate control if onset is more than 48 hours or uncertain.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Anticoagulation if onset less than 48 hours
concepts.content: Patients with atrial fibrillation of less than 48 hours onset should be heparinised; those with risk factors for ischaemic stroke require lifelong oral anticoagulation.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Cardioversion options if onset less than 48 hours
concepts.content: For atrial fibrillation less than 48 hours onset, cardioversion may be electrical (DC cardioversion) or pharmacological using amiodarone if structural heart disease is present, or flecainide or amiodarone if absent.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Anticoagulation after electrical cardioversion if onset less than 48 hours
concepts.content: If atrial fibrillation is confirmed to be less than 48 hours duration after electrical cardioversion, further anticoagulation is unnecessary.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Anticoagulation before cardioversion if onset more than 48 hours
concepts.content: If atrial fibrillation duration exceeds 48 hours, anticoagulation should be administered for at least 3 weeks prior to cardioversion.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Use of transoesophageal echocardiography before cardioversion
concepts.content: Transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE) can be performed to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus, allowing immediate heparinisation and cardioversion if no thrombus is detected.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Preferred cardioversion method if onset more than 48 hours
concepts.content: NICE recommends electrical cardioversion rather than pharmacological cardioversion for atrial fibrillation lasting more than 48 hours.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Pre-treatment before cardioversion in high risk of failure
concepts.content: In patients at high risk of cardioversion failure or atrial fibrillation recurrence, at least 4 weeks of amiodarone or sotalol is recommended prior to electrical cardioversion.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Pharmacological cardioversion guidelines
concepts.content: NICE guidelines (2014) and joint AHA, ACC, ESC guidelines (2016) provide recommendations for the pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Amiodarone efficacy in pharmacological cardioversion
concepts.content: Amiodarone is an agent with proven efficacy for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Flecainide use in pharmacological cardioversion without structural heart disease
concepts.content: Flecainide is effective for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation in patients without structural heart disease.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Less commonly used pharmacological cardioversion agents in the UK
concepts.content: Quinidine, dofetilide, ibutilide, and propafenone are less commonly used agents for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation in the UK.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Beta-blockers are less effective for pharmacological cardioversion
concepts.content: Beta-blockers, including sotalol, are less effective agents for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Calcium channel blockers are less effective for pharmacological cardioversion
concepts.content: Calcium channel blockers are less effective agents for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Digoxin is less effective for pharmacological cardioversion
concepts.content: Digoxin is a less effective agent for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Disopyramide is less effective for pharmacological cardioversion
concepts.content: Disopyramide is a less effective agent for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Procainamide is less effective for pharmacological cardioversion
concepts.content: Procainamide is a less effective agent for pharmacological cardioversion of atrial fibrillation.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Risk factor for ischaemic stroke
concepts.content: Atrial fibrillation is a key risk factor for ischaemic stroke.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Importance of recognition post-stroke or TIA
concepts.content: Recognising and treating atrial fibrillation after a stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA) is crucial for secondary stroke prevention.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Exclusion of haemorrhage before anticoagulation post-stroke or TIA
concepts.content: Before starting anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy following a stroke or TIA, it is essential to exclude cerebral haemorrhage via imaging.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Long-term stroke prevention anticoagulants
concepts.content: For long-term stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation, NICE recommends warfarin or direct thrombin or factor Xa inhibitors.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Timing of anticoagulation initiation after TIA
concepts.content: Anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation should be started immediately after a TIA once haemorrhage has been excluded by imaging.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Timing of anticoagulation initiation after acute ischaemic stroke
concepts.content: In acute ischaemic stroke patients without haemorrhage, anticoagulation therapy should be started after 2 weeks.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Use of antiplatelet therapy between stroke and anticoagulation
concepts.content: Antiplatelet therapy should be administered in the period between acute stroke and the initiation of anticoagulation therapy.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Delay of anticoagulation initiation after large cerebral infarction
concepts.content: If imaging shows a very large cerebral infarction, initiation of anticoagulation therapy should be delayed beyond the usual 2-week period.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Guideline sources
concepts.content: Management of atrial fibrillation is guided by NICE 2021 guidelines and the joint 2012 guidelines from the American Heart Association (AHA), American College of Cardiology (ACC), and European Society of Cardiology (ESC).

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Haemodynamic instability indication for electrical cardioversion
concepts.content: Patients with atrial fibrillation presenting with signs of haemodynamic instability such as hypotension or heart failure should undergo electrical cardioversion according to peri-arrest tachycardia guidelines.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Acute management based on duration of arrhythmia
concepts.content: In haemodynamically stable patients with atrial fibrillation, if the arrhythmia duration is less than 48 hours, either rate or rhythm control can be offered; if 48 hours or more, or if onset is uncertain, rate control is preferred.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Anticoagulation requirement in new-onset AF
concepts.content: All patients with new-onset atrial fibrillation require anticoagulation regardless of the time of onset.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Long-term anticoagulation guided by CHA2DS2-VASc score
concepts.content: Long-term anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation is determined based on the patient's CHA2DS2-VASc score to assess stroke risk.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Delay of cardioversion with anticoagulation in long-term rhythm control
concepts.content: If long-term rhythm control is planned, cardioversion should be delayed until the patient has been on therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Rate control as first-line treatment strategy
concepts.content: Rate control should be offered as the first-line treatment strategy for atrial fibrillation except in specific patient groups.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Exceptions to first-line rate control strategy
concepts.content: Rate control is not first-line in patients whose atrial fibrillation has a reversible cause, those with heart failure primarily caused by AF, new-onset AF less than 48 hours, atrial flutter suitable for ablation, or when rhythm control is clinically preferred.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Beta-blockers for rate control
concepts.content: Beta-blockers are commonly used agents for rate control in atrial fibrillation but are contraindicated in patients with asthma.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Calcium channel blockers for rate control
concepts.content: Calcium channel blockers are used as rate control agents in atrial fibrillation management.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Digoxin use in rate control
concepts.content: Digoxin is no longer considered first-line for rate control in atrial fibrillation due to less effectiveness during exercise and is reserved for patients with minimal physical activity or when other rate-limiting drugs are contraindicated.

concepts.title: Atrial flutter – Definition
concepts.content: Atrial flutter is a form of supraventricular tachycardia characterised by a succession of rapid atrial depolarisation waves.

concepts.title: Atrial flutter – Pathophysiology: Re-entry loop location
concepts.content: A large, stable re-entry loop develops in the right atrium in atrial flutter.

concepts.title: Atrial flutter – Pathophysiology: Circuit re-excitation
concepts.content: The re-entry circuit continuously re-excites atrial tissue in atrial flutter.

concepts.title: Atrial flutter – Pathophysiology: Circuit anatomical path
concepts.content: The re-entry circuit circles around the tricuspid annulus in atrial flutter.

concepts.title: Atrial flutter – Pathophysiology: Cavotricuspid isthmus role
concepts.content: The cavotricuspid isthmus, located between the tricuspid valve and inferior vena cava, is a critical slow-conduction zone in atrial flutter.

concepts.title: Atrial flutter – Pathophysiology: Anatomical fixation and rhythm regularity
concepts.content: Because the re-entry circuit is anatomically fixed, the atrial flutter rhythm is highly regular.

concepts.title: Atrial flutter – Pathophysiology: Anatomical dependence and ablation efficacy
concepts.content: The anatomical dependence of the re-entry circuit explains why catheter ablation is very effective in atrial flutter.

concepts.title: Atrial flutter – ECG findings: Sawtooth pattern
concepts.content: The ECG in atrial flutter shows a characteristic 'sawtooth' appearance of flutter waves.

concepts.title: Atrial flutter – ECG findings: Atrial and ventricular rates
concepts.content: The underlying atrial rate in atrial flutter is often around 300/min; the ventricular rate depends on the degree of AV block, e.g., 2:1 block results in a ventricular rate of 150/min.

concepts.title: Atrial flutter – ECG findings: Flutter waves visibility after maneuvers
concepts.content: Flutter waves may become visible on ECG following carotid sinus massage or administration of adenosine.

concepts.title: Atrial flutter – Management: Similarity to atrial fibrillation treatment
concepts.content: Management of atrial flutter is similar to that of atrial fibrillation, although medication may be less effective.

concepts.title: Atrial flutter – Management: Sensitivity to cardioversion
concepts.content: Atrial flutter is more sensitive to cardioversion than atrial fibrillation, allowing use of lower energy levels.

concepts.title: Atrial flutter – Management: Radiofrequency ablation
concepts.content: Radiofrequency ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus is curative for most patients with atrial flutter.

concepts.title: Atrial myxoma – Definition
concepts.content: Atrial myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumour.

concepts.title: Atrial myxoma – Location prevalence
concepts.content: 75% of atrial myxomas occur in the left atrium.

concepts.title: Atrial myxoma – Common attachment site
concepts.content: Atrial myxomas are most commonly attached to the fossa ovalis region of the interatrial septum.

concepts.title: Atrial myxoma – Gender prevalence
concepts.content: Atrial myxoma is more common in females.

concepts.title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation systemic symptom dyspnoea
concepts.content: Dyspnoea is a systemic symptom of atrial myxoma.

concepts.title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation systemic symptom fatigue
concepts.content: Fatigue is a systemic symptom of atrial myxoma.

concepts.title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation systemic symptom weight loss
concepts.content: Weight loss is a systemic symptom of atrial myxoma.

concepts.title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation systemic symptom pyrexia of unknown origin
concepts.content: Pyrexia of unknown origin is a systemic symptom of atrial myxoma.

concepts.title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation systemic sign clubbing
concepts.content: Clubbing is a systemic sign associated with atrial myxoma.

concepts.title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation embolic events
concepts.content: Atrial myxoma can cause embolic events.

concepts.title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation atrial fibrillation
concepts.content: Atrial fibrillation can occur in patients with atrial myxoma.

concepts.title: Atrial myxoma – Presentation cardiac murmur
concepts.content: A mid-diastolic murmur and a 'tumour plop' sound can be heard in atrial myxoma.

concepts.title: Atrial myxoma – Investigation echocardiography findings
concepts.content: Echocardiography typically shows a pedunculated heterogeneous mass attached to the fossa ovalis region of the interatrial septum in atrial myxoma.

concepts.title: Atrial septal defects – Definition
concepts.content: Atrial septal defects (ASDs) are congenital heart defects characterized by an opening in the atrial septum, allowing communication between the left and right atria.

concepts.title: Atrial septal defects – Epidemiology in adulthood
concepts.content: ASDs are the most likely congenital heart defect to be diagnosed in adulthood.

concepts.title: Atrial septal defects – Mortality
concepts.content: ASDs carry significant mortality, with 50% of patients dying by 50 years of age if untreated.

concepts.title: Atrial septal defects – Types
concepts.content: Two main types of ASDs are recognized: ostium secundum and ostium primum.

concepts.title: Atrial septal defects – Most common type
concepts.content: Ostium secundum ASDs are the most common type, accounting for approximately 70% of cases.

concepts.title: Atrial septal defects – Clinical feature: Ejection systolic murmur
concepts.content: ASDs commonly present with an ejection systolic murmur due to increased flow across the pulmonary valve.

concepts.title: Atrial septal defects – Clinical feature: Fixed splitting of S2
concepts.content: Fixed splitting of the second heart sound (S2) is a characteristic clinical sign in ASDs.

concepts.title: Atrial septal defects – Complication: Paradoxical embolism
concepts.content: Emboli may pass from the venous system to the left side of the heart through the ASD, causing stroke.

concepts.title: Ostium secundum ASD – Association with Holt-Oram syndrome
concepts.content: Ostium secundum ASDs are associated with Holt-Oram syndrome, characterized by triphalangeal thumbs.

concepts.title: Ostium secundum ASD – ECG findings
concepts.content: Electrocardiogram in ostium secundum ASDs typically shows right bundle branch block (RBBB) with right axis deviation (RAD).

concepts.title: Ostium primum ASD – Presentation timing
concepts.content: Ostium primum ASDs tend to present earlier in life than ostium secundum defects.

concepts.title: Ostium primum ASD – Association with abnormal AV valves
concepts.content: Ostium primum ASDs are associated with abnormalities of the atrioventricular valves.

concepts.title: Ostium primum ASD – ECG findings
concepts.content: Electrocardiogram in ostium primum ASDs typically shows right bundle branch block (RBBB) with left axis deviation (LAD) and a prolonged PR interval.

concepts.title: Atrioventricular block – Definition
concepts.content: Atrioventricular (AV) block, or heart block, is a condition characterized by impaired electrical conduction between the atria and ventricles.

concepts.title: First-degree heart block – Definition
concepts.content: First-degree heart block is a type of AV block characterized by a PR interval greater than 0.2 seconds on ECG.

concepts.title: First-degree heart block – Clinical features
concepts.content: Asymptomatic first-degree heart block is relatively common and does not require treatment.

concepts.title: Second-degree heart block type 1 – Definition
concepts.content: Second-degree heart block type 1 (Mobitz I, Wenckebach) is characterized by progressive prolongation of the PR interval until a dropped beat occurs.

concepts.title: Second-degree heart block type 2 – Definition
concepts.content: Second-degree heart block type 2 (Mobitz II) is characterized by a constant PR interval with P waves often not followed by a QRS complex.

concepts.title: Third-degree heart block – Definition
concepts.content: Third-degree (complete) heart block is characterized by no association between the P waves and QRS complexes on ECG.

concepts.title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Definition
concepts.content: B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is a hormone produced mainly by the left ventricular myocardium in response to strain.

concepts.title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Pathophysiology of elevation
concepts.content: BNP levels rise primarily due to left ventricular strain; causes include heart failure, myocardial ischaemia, and valvular heart disease.

concepts.title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Effect of chronic kidney disease on levels
concepts.content: Reduced excretion of BNP in patients with chronic kidney disease can cause elevated BNP levels independent of cardiac function.

concepts.title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Factors reducing BNP levels
concepts.content: Treatment with ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-2 receptor blockers, and diuretics reduces BNP levels.

concepts.title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Physiological effects
concepts.content: BNP acts as a vasodilator, promotes diuresis and natriuresis, and suppresses sympathetic tone and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

concepts.title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Diagnostic use in acute dyspnoea
concepts.content: A BNP concentration below 100 pg/ml makes heart failure unlikely in patients presenting with acute dyspnoea; elevated levels warrant further investigation.

concepts.title: B-type natriuretic peptide – NICE recommendation for heart failure diagnosis
concepts.content: NICE recommends BNP testing as a helpful tool to rule out a diagnosis of heart failure.

concepts.title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Prognostic value in chronic heart failure
concepts.content: BNP is an extremely useful marker of prognosis in patients with chronic heart failure.

concepts.title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Use in guiding treatment of chronic heart failure
concepts.content: Effective treatment of chronic heart failure lowers BNP levels, which can be used to guide therapy.

concepts.title: B-type natriuretic peptide – Screening for cardiac dysfunction
concepts.content: Screening for cardiac dysfunction using BNP measurement is not currently recommended for the general population.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Definition of Bivalirudin
concepts.content: Bivalirudin is a reversible direct thrombin inhibitor used as an anticoagulant.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Use of Bivalirudin in management
concepts.content: Bivalirudin is used as an anticoagulant in the management of acute coronary syndrome.

concepts.title: Broad complex tachycardia – AV dissociation suggests ventricular tachycardia
concepts.content: The presence of atrioventricular (AV) dissociation during broad complex tachycardia suggests ventricular tachycardia rather than supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

concepts.title: Broad complex tachycardia – Fusion or capture beats indicate ventricular tachycardia
concepts.content: The occurrence of fusion or capture beats during broad complex tachycardia is indicative of ventricular tachycardia rather than supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

concepts.title: Broad complex tachycardia – Positive QRS concordance in chest leads suggests ventricular tachycardia
concepts.content: Positive QRS concordance across the chest leads during broad complex tachycardia supports the diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia over supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

concepts.title: Broad complex tachycardia – Marked left axis deviation suggests ventricular tachycardia
concepts.content: Marked left axis deviation on ECG during broad complex tachycardia is a feature suggestive of ventricular tachycardia rather than supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

concepts.title: Broad complex tachycardia – History of ischaemic heart disease supports ventricular tachycardia diagnosis
concepts.content: A history of ischaemic heart disease in a patient presenting with broad complex tachycardia increases the likelihood that the arrhythmia is ventricular tachycardia rather than supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

concepts.title: Broad complex tachycardia – Lack of response to adenosine suggests ventricular tachycardia
concepts.content: Failure of broad complex tachycardia to respond to adenosine administration suggests the arrhythmia is ventricular tachycardia rather than supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

concepts.title: Broad complex tachycardia – Lack of response to carotid sinus massage suggests ventricular tachycardia
concepts.content: Broad complex tachycardia that does not respond to carotid sinus massage is more likely to be ventricular tachycardia than supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

concepts.title: Broad complex tachycardia – QRS duration greater than 160 ms suggests ventricular tachycardia
concepts.content: A QRS complex duration exceeding 160 milliseconds during broad complex tachycardia is a diagnostic feature favoring ventricular tachycardia over supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

concepts.title: Brugada syndrome – Definition
concepts.content: Brugada syndrome is an inherited cardiovascular disease characterized by a risk of sudden cardiac death.

concepts.title: Brugada syndrome – Inheritance pattern
concepts.content: Brugada syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion.

concepts.title: Brugada syndrome – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Brugada syndrome has an estimated prevalence of 1 in 5,000 to 1 in 10,000 individuals and is more common in Asians.

concepts.title: Brugada syndrome – Pathophysiology genetic variants
concepts.content: A large number of genetic variants exist that cause Brugada syndrome.

concepts.title: Brugada syndrome – SCN5A gene mutation
concepts.content: Approximately 20-40% of Brugada syndrome cases are caused by mutations in the SCN5A gene, which encodes the myocardial sodium ion channel protein.

concepts.title: Brugada syndrome – ECG characteristic ST segment elevation
concepts.content: Brugada syndrome ECG shows convex ST segment elevation greater than 2 mm in one or more of leads V1 to V3, followed by a negative T wave.

concepts.title: Brugada syndrome – ECG partial right bundle branch block
concepts.content: Brugada syndrome ECG may show a partial right bundle branch block pattern.

concepts.title: Brugada syndrome – Flecainide or ajmaline challenge test
concepts.content: Administration of flecainide or ajmaline can unmask or accentuate ECG changes in Brugada syndrome and is the investigation of choice in suspected cases.

concepts.title: Brugada syndrome – Management general measures
concepts.content: General management of Brugada syndrome includes prompt treatment of fever and avoidance of excessive alcohol consumption.

concepts.title: Brugada syndrome – Avoidance of arrhythmia-precipitating drugs
concepts.content: Patients with Brugada syndrome should avoid drugs that may precipitate ventricular arrhythmias, including flecainide, lithium, and tricyclic antidepressants.

concepts.title: Brugada syndrome – Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator
concepts.content: An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is used in the management of Brugada syndrome to prevent sudden cardiac death.

concepts.title: Buerger's disease – Definition
concepts.content: Buerger's disease, also known as thromboangiitis obliterans, is a vasculitis affecting small and medium-sized blood vessels.

concepts.title: Buerger's disease – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Buerger's disease is strongly associated with tobacco smoking, which contributes to inflammation and thrombosis in small and medium-sized vessels.

concepts.title: Buerger's disease – Presentation: extremity ischaemia
concepts.content: Patients with Buerger's disease commonly present with extremity ischaemia due to vessel inflammation and occlusion.

concepts.title: Buerger's disease – Presentation: intermittent claudication
concepts.content: Intermittent claudication is a common symptom in Buerger's disease, caused by reduced blood flow during exercise.

concepts.title: Buerger's disease – Presentation: ischaemic ulcers
concepts.content: Ischaemic ulcers may develop in Buerger's disease due to chronic poor blood supply to the extremities.

concepts.title: Buerger's disease – Presentation: superficial thrombophlebitis
concepts.content: Superficial thrombophlebitis is a clinical feature of Buerger's disease characterized by inflammation and thrombosis of superficial veins.

concepts.title: Buerger's disease – Presentation: Raynaud's phenomenon
concepts.content: Raynaud's phenomenon, characterized by episodic digital ischemia and color changes, can be a feature of Buerger's disease.

concepts.title: Calcium channel blockers – Definition
concepts.content: Calcium channel blockers are medications primarily used in the management of cardiovascular disease by inhibiting voltage-gated calcium channels.

concepts.title: Calcium channel blockers – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Voltage-gated calcium channels are present in myocardial cells, conduction system cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells, mediating calcium influx essential for contraction and conduction.

concepts.title: Calcium channel blockers – Clinical relevance of tissue selectivity
concepts.content: Different types of calcium channel blockers have varying effects on myocardial cells, conduction system cells, and vascular smooth muscle, influencing their clinical uses and side effect profiles.

concepts.title: Verapamil – Indications
concepts.content: Verapamil is indicated for angina, hypertension, and arrhythmias.

concepts.title: Verapamil – Pharmacodynamics
concepts.content: Verapamil is highly negatively inotropic, reducing myocardial contractility significantly.

concepts.title: Verapamil – Drug interactions
concepts.content: Verapamil should not be given with beta-blockers due to the risk of causing heart block.

concepts.title: Verapamil – Side effects and cautions
concepts.content: Side effects of verapamil include heart failure, constipation, hypotension, bradycardia, and flushing.

concepts.title: Diltiazem – Indications
concepts.content: Diltiazem is indicated for angina and hypertension.

concepts.title: Diltiazem – Pharmacodynamics
concepts.content: Diltiazem is less negatively inotropic than verapamil but still requires caution in patients with heart failure or those taking beta-blockers.

concepts.title: Diltiazem – Side effects and cautions
concepts.content: Side effects of diltiazem include hypotension, bradycardia, heart failure, and ankle swelling.

concepts.title: Dihydropyridines (nifedipine, amlodipine, felodipine) – Indications
concepts.content: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are indicated for hypertension, angina, and Raynaud's phenomenon.

concepts.title: Dihydropyridines – Pharmacodynamics
concepts.content: Dihydropyridines primarily affect peripheral vascular smooth muscle more than myocardium, avoiding worsening of heart failure but causing peripheral vasodilation.

concepts.title: Dihydropyridines – Side effects and cautions
concepts.content: Side effects include flushing, headache, and ankle swelling; shorter-acting agents like nifedipine may cause reflex tachycardia due to peripheral vasodilation.

concepts.title: Normal cardiac oxygen saturation levels – Definition
concepts.content: Deoxygenated blood returns to the right side of the heart via the superior vena cava (SVC) and inferior vena cava (IVC) with an oxygen saturation of around 70%. The right atrium (RA), right ventricle (RV), and pulmonary artery (PA) normally have oxygen saturation levels of around 70%. The lungs oxygenate the blood to 98-100%, so the left atrium (LA), left ventricle (LV), and aorta have oxygen saturation levels of 98-100%.

concepts.title: Atrial septal defect (ASD) – Pathophysiology of oxygen saturation changes
concepts.content: In ASD, oxygenated blood from the left atrium (LA) mixes with deoxygenated blood in the right atrium (RA), resulting in intermediate oxygen saturation levels (~85%) in the RA, right ventricle (RV), and pulmonary artery (PA), while the left atrium, left ventricle, and aorta maintain normal saturation (98-100%).

concepts.title: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) – Pathophysiology of oxygen saturation changes
concepts.content: In VSD, oxygenated blood from the left ventricle (LV) mixes with deoxygenated blood in the right ventricle (RV), causing intermediate oxygen saturation (~85%) in the RV and pulmonary artery (PA). The right atrium (RA) remains at normal deoxygenated saturation (~70%). The left atrium, left ventricle, and aorta maintain normal saturation (98-100%).

concepts.title: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) – Pathophysiology of oxygen saturation changes
concepts.content: In PDA, the higher pressure aorta connects to the lower pressure pulmonary artery (PA), causing intermediate oxygen saturation (~85%) only in the pulmonary artery. The right atrium (RA) and right ventricle (RV) maintain normal deoxygenated saturation (~70%), and the left atrium (LA), left ventricle (LV), and aorta have normal oxygen saturation (98-100%).

concepts.title: Ventricular septal defect with Eisenmenger's syndrome – Oxygen saturation changes
concepts.content: In VSD with Eisenmenger's syndrome, the right ventricle (RV), pulmonary artery (PA), and right atrium (RA) have deoxygenated blood saturation (~70%) due to reversed shunting. The left atrium (LA) maintains normal saturation (~100%), but the left ventricle (LV) and aorta show reduced oxygen saturation (~85%).

concepts.title: Patent ductus arteriosus with Eisenmenger's syndrome – Oxygen saturation changes
concepts.content: In PDA with Eisenmenger's syndrome, the right atrium (RA), right ventricle (RV), and pulmonary artery (PA) have deoxygenated saturation (~70%) due to reversed shunting. The left atrium (LA) and left ventricle (LV) maintain normal saturation (~100%), but the aorta shows reduced oxygen saturation (~85%).

concepts.title: Atrial septal defect with Eisenmenger's syndrome – Oxygen saturation changes
concepts.content: In ASD with Eisenmenger's syndrome, the right atrium (RA), right ventricle (RV), and pulmonary artery (PA) have deoxygenated saturation (~70%) due to reversed shunting. The left atrium (LA), left ventricle (LV), and aorta show reduced oxygen saturation (~85%).

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Role of troponin T and I in diagnosis
concepts.content: Troponin T and I have largely replaced other cardiac enzymes for diagnosing acute coronary syndromes due to their high sensitivity and specificity.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Myoglobin as earliest rising cardiac marker
concepts.content: Myoglobin is the first cardiac marker to rise after myocardial injury, increasing within 1-2 hours.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – CK-MB utility in detecting reinfarction
concepts.content: CK-MB is useful for detecting reinfarction because it returns to normal within 2-3 days, unlike troponin T which remains elevated up to 10 days.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Myoglobin timing profile
concepts.content: Myoglobin begins to rise 1-2 hours after myocardial injury, peaks at 6-8 hours, and returns to normal within 1-2 days.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – CK-MB timing profile
concepts.content: CK-MB begins to rise 2-6 hours after myocardial injury, peaks at 16-20 hours, and returns to normal within 2-3 days.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Creatine kinase (CK) timing profile
concepts.content: Creatine kinase (CK) begins to rise 4-8 hours after myocardial injury, peaks at 16-24 hours, and returns to normal within 3-4 days.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Troponin T timing profile
concepts.content: Troponin T begins to rise 4-6 hours after myocardial injury, peaks at 12-24 hours, and remains elevated for 7-10 days.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) timing profile
concepts.content: AST begins to rise 12-24 hours after myocardial injury, peaks at 36-48 hours, and returns to normal within 3-4 days.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) timing profile
concepts.content: LDH begins to rise 24-48 hours after myocardial injury, peaks at 72 hours, and returns to normal within 8-10 days.

concepts.title: Cardiac imaging – Non-invasive techniques overview
concepts.content: Non-invasive cardiac imaging techniques include MRI, CT, and radionuclide imaging, which have rapidly evolved to allow detailed visualization of cardiac structure and function without invasive procedures.

concepts.title: Nuclear imaging – Use of radiotracers in cardiac imaging
concepts.content: Nuclear imaging uses radiotracers that are extracted by normal myocardium to assess myocardial perfusion and viability.

concepts.title: Nuclear imaging – Thallium as a radiotracer
concepts.content: Thallium is a radiotracer used in nuclear cardiac imaging to assess myocardial perfusion by being taken up by normal myocardium.

concepts.title: Nuclear imaging – Technetium-99m sestamibi (MIBI) in SPECT scans
concepts.content: Technetium-99m sestamibi is a radiotracer used in cardiac Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) scans to evaluate myocardial perfusion.

concepts.title: Nuclear imaging – Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) in PET scans
concepts.content: Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) is a radiotracer used in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scans to assess myocardial metabolism and viability.

concepts.title: SPECT imaging – Assessment of myocardial perfusion and viability
concepts.content: Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) assesses myocardial perfusion and viability by acquiring images at rest and during stress to identify reversible or fixed ischaemia.

concepts.title: SPECT imaging – Stress testing methods
concepts.content: Stress images in SPECT are obtained either by exercise or pharmacological agents such as adenosine or dipyridamole to evaluate inducible ischaemia.

concepts.title: Cardiac PET imaging – Current role
concepts.content: Cardiac Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is predominantly used as a research tool currently and is not widely applied in routine clinical practice.

concepts.title: MUGA scan – Definition and purpose
concepts.content: Multi Gated Acquisition (MUGA) scan, also known as radionuclide angiography, is a nuclear imaging technique used to evaluate cardiac function, especially left ventricular ejection fraction.

concepts.title: MUGA scan – Procedure
concepts.content: MUGA scan involves intravenous injection of technetium-99m radionuclide followed by imaging with a gamma camera to assess cardiac function.

concepts.title: MUGA scan – Use as stress test
concepts.content: MUGA scan can be performed as a stress test to evaluate cardiac function under stress conditions.

concepts.title: MUGA scan – Measurement of left ventricular ejection fraction
concepts.content: MUGA scan accurately measures left ventricular ejection fraction and is typically used before and after administration of cardiotoxic drugs to monitor cardiac function.

concepts.title: Cardiac CT – Role in ischaemic heart disease assessment
concepts.content: Cardiac Computed Tomography (CT) is useful in assessing suspected ischaemic heart disease by evaluating coronary artery calcium and lumen anatomy.

concepts.title: Cardiac CT – Calcium scoring
concepts.content: Calcium scoring quantifies the amount of atherosclerotic plaque calcium in coronary arteries, correlating with the risk of future ischaemic events.

concepts.title: Cardiac CT – Contrast-enhanced imaging
concepts.content: Contrast-enhanced cardiac CT allows visualization of the coronary artery lumen to detect stenosis or occlusion.

concepts.title: Cardiac CT – Combined calcium scoring and contrast-enhanced imaging
concepts.content: Combining calcium scoring with contrast-enhanced CT provides a high negative predictive value for excluding ischaemic heart disease.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – Definition
concepts.content: Cardiac tamponade is characterized by the accumulation of pericardial fluid under pressure.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – Beck's triad: Hypotension
concepts.content: Hypotension is a classical feature of cardiac tamponade as part of Beck's triad.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – Beck's triad: Raised jugular venous pressure
concepts.content: Raised jugular venous pressure (JVP) is a classical feature of cardiac tamponade as part of Beck's triad.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – Beck's triad: Muffled heart sounds
concepts.content: Muffled heart sounds are a classical feature of cardiac tamponade as part of Beck's triad.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – Dyspnoea
concepts.content: Dyspnoea is a common presenting symptom in cardiac tamponade.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – Tachycardia
concepts.content: Tachycardia is a common presenting sign in cardiac tamponade.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – Absent Y descent on jugular venous pressure
concepts.content: An absent Y descent on the jugular venous pressure waveform occurs in cardiac tamponade due to limited right ventricular filling.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – Pulsus paradoxus
concepts.content: Pulsus paradoxus is an abnormally large drop in blood pressure during inspiration and is a feature of cardiac tamponade.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – Kussmaul's sign
concepts.content: Kussmaul's sign may be present in cardiac tamponade, but its significance is debated.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – ECG electrical alternans
concepts.content: Electrical alternans on ECG is a characteristic finding in cardiac tamponade.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – Jugular venous pressure comparison with constrictive pericarditis
concepts.content: In cardiac tamponade, the Y descent on jugular venous pressure is absent, whereas in constrictive pericarditis both X and Y descents are present.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – Pulsus paradoxus comparison with constrictive pericarditis
concepts.content: Pulsus paradoxus is present in cardiac tamponade but absent in constrictive pericarditis.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – Kussmaul's sign comparison with constrictive pericarditis
concepts.content: Kussmaul's sign is rare in cardiac tamponade but present in constrictive pericarditis.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis – Characteristic feature: Pericardial calcification on chest X-ray
concepts.content: Pericardial calcification on chest X-ray is a characteristic feature of constrictive pericarditis, not seen in cardiac tamponade.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – Mnemonic for absent Y descent: TAMponade = TAMpaX
concepts.content: The mnemonic 'TAMponade = TAMpaX' is used to remember the absent Y descent in cardiac tamponade jugular venous pressure waveform.

concepts.title: Cardiac tamponade – Management: Urgent pericardiocentesis
concepts.content: Urgent pericardiocentesis is the primary management for cardiac tamponade to relieve pressure from pericardial fluid accumulation.

concepts.title: Cardiomyopathies – Classification update
concepts.content: The old classification of dilated, restrictive, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has been largely abandoned due to high overlap; the latest WHO and American Heart Association classifications reflect this change.

concepts.title: Primary cardiomyopathies – Definition
concepts.content: Primary cardiomyopathies predominantly involve the heart muscle without an identifiable secondary cause.

concepts.title: Genetic cardiomyopathies – Inheritance pattern
concepts.content: Genetic primary cardiomyopathies are typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

concepts.title: Genetic cardiomyopathies – ICD implantation
concepts.content: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators are often inserted in genetic cardiomyopathies to reduce the incidence of sudden cardiac death.

concepts.title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes
concepts.content: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.

concepts.title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Genetic mutation
concepts.content: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is usually caused by a mutation in the gene encoding the β-myosin heavy chain protein.

concepts.title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Echocardiographic findings
concepts.content: Echocardiography in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy shows mitral regurgitation, systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the anterior mitral valve, and asymmetric septal hypertrophy.

concepts.title: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: In arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia, the right ventricular myocardium is replaced by fatty and fibrofatty tissue.

concepts.title: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia – Genetic mutations
concepts.content: Approximately 50% of patients with arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia have mutations in genes encoding desmosomal proteins.

concepts.title: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia – ECG findings
concepts.content: ECG abnormalities in arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia include T wave inversion in leads V1-V3 and an epsilon wave in about 50% of cases, characterized as a terminal notch in the QRS complex.

concepts.title: Mixed cardiomyopathies – Definition
concepts.content: Mixed cardiomyopathies describe patients with a genetic predisposition to cardiomyopathy triggered by secondary processes, reflecting overlap between primary and secondary causes.

concepts.title: Dilated cardiomyopathy – Classic causes
concepts.content: Classic causes of dilated cardiomyopathy include alcohol abuse, Coxsackie B virus infection, wet beri beri (thiamine deficiency), and doxorubicin toxicity.

concepts.title: Restrictive cardiomyopathy – Classic causes
concepts.content: Classic causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy include amyloidosis, post-radiotherapy fibrosis, and Loeffler's endocarditis.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Immediate management with glyceryl trinitrate
concepts.content: Glyceryl trinitrate is used in the immediate management of suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS) to relieve chest pain.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Immediate management with aspirin 300mg
concepts.content: Aspirin 300mg should be administered immediately in suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients; other antiplatelet agents like clopidogrel are not recommended outside hospital.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Oxygen therapy recommendations
concepts.content: Oxygen should not be routinely given in suspected ACS; supplemental oxygen is only indicated if oxygen saturation is below 94%, with specific targets for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Oxygen saturation targets in COPD patients
concepts.content: In patients with COPD at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, oxygen therapy aims for SpO2 of 88-92% until blood gas analysis is available.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – ECG use in suspected ACS
concepts.content: An ECG should be performed as soon as possible in suspected ACS but should not delay transfer to hospital; a normal ECG does not exclude ACS.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Referral criteria for chest pain within 12 hours and abnormal ECG
concepts.content: Patients with current chest pain or chest pain within the last 12 hours and an abnormal ECG require emergency hospital admission.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Referral criteria for chest pain 12-72 hours ago
concepts.content: Patients with chest pain occurring 12 to 72 hours prior should be referred to hospital the same day for assessment.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Assessment for chest pain >72 hours ago
concepts.content: For chest pain occurring more than 72 hours ago, a full assessment including ECG and troponin measurement should be performed before deciding further management.

concepts.title: Stable angina – Definition of typical anginal pain
concepts.content: Typical anginal pain is defined by constricting discomfort in the front of the chest or neck, shoulders, jaw, or arms; precipitated by physical exertion; and relieved by rest or glyceryl trinitrate within about 5 minutes.

concepts.title: Stable angina – Classification of angina based on symptom features
concepts.content: Patients with all three typical angina features have typical angina; those with two features have atypical angina; those with one or none have non-anginal chest pain.

concepts.title: Choking – Definition
concepts.content: Choking is a life-threatening emergency caused by partial or complete airway obstruction.

concepts.title: Choking – Common trigger
concepts.content: Episodes of choking often occur whilst eating.

concepts.title: Choking – Patient behavior during airway obstruction
concepts.content: Patients often clutch their neck during episodes of airway obstruction.

concepts.title: Choking – Initial assessment question
concepts.content: The first step in suspected choking is to ask the patient 'Are you choking?'.

concepts.title: Choking – Mild airway obstruction response to question
concepts.content: In mild airway obstruction, the victim can speak and answers 'yes' to the question 'Are you choking?'.

concepts.title: Choking – Mild airway obstruction other signs
concepts.content: In mild airway obstruction, the victim is able to speak, cough, and breathe.
