concepts.title: Choking – Severe airway obstruction response to question
concepts.content: In severe airway obstruction, the victim is unable to speak and may respond by nodding.

concepts.title: Choking – Severe airway obstruction other signs
concepts.content: In severe airway obstruction, the victim is unable to breathe, breathing sounds wheezy, attempts at coughing are silent, and the victim may be unconscious.

concepts.title: Choking – Management of mild airway obstruction
concepts.content: If mild airway obstruction is present, encourage the patient to cough.

concepts.title: Choking – Management of severe airway obstruction in conscious patient
concepts.content: If severe airway obstruction occurs in a conscious patient, give up to 5 back blows; if unsuccessful, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts; if still unsuccessful, continue the cycle of back blows and abdominal thrusts.

concepts.title: Choking – Management of unconscious patient with airway obstruction
concepts.content: If the patient with airway obstruction is unconscious, call for an ambulance and start cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – First-line diagnostic test
concepts.content: All patients suspected of chronic heart failure should have an N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) blood test as the first-line investigation, regardless of previous myocardial infarction history.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – Interpretation of NT-proBNP levels for referral timing
concepts.content: If NT-proBNP levels are high (>2000 pg/ml), specialist assessment including transthoracic echocardiography should be arranged within 2 weeks; if levels are raised (400-2000 pg/ml), assessment should be arranged within 6 weeks.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – Role of serum natriuretic peptides
concepts.content: B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is a hormone produced mainly by the left ventricular myocardium in response to myocardial strain; very high BNP levels are associated with poor prognosis in chronic heart failure.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – BNP level thresholds
concepts.content: BNP levels are classified as high if >400 pg/ml, raised if 100-400 pg/ml, and normal if <100 pg/ml; corresponding NT-proBNP thresholds are high >2000 pg/ml, raised 400-2000 pg/ml, and normal <400 pg/ml.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – Factors increasing BNP levels
concepts.content: Conditions and factors that increase BNP levels include left ventricular hypertrophy, ischaemia, tachycardia, right ventricular overload, hypoxaemia (including pulmonary embolism), glomerular filtration rate <60 ml/min, sepsis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, age over 70 years, and liver cirrhosis.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – Factors decreasing BNP levels
concepts.content: Factors that decrease BNP levels include obesity and use of medications such as diuretics, ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, angiotensin II receptor blockers, and aldosterone antagonists.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – Role of loop diuretics
concepts.content: Loop diuretics such as furosemide are important for managing fluid overload in chronic heart failure but have not demonstrated long-term mortality reduction.

concepts.title: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction – First-line drug treatment
concepts.content: The first-line drug treatment for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction includes ACE-inhibitor, beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and SGLT2-inhibitor.

concepts.title: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction – ACE-inhibitor intolerance management
concepts.content: If ACE-inhibitors are not tolerated due to cough, switch to angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI); if angioedema develops, switch to angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB).

concepts.title: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction – Use of clinical judgement in drug initiation
concepts.content: Clinical judgement is recommended when initiating the four first-line medications to avoid starting all simultaneously and to identify adverse drug reactions.

concepts.title: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction – Management of persistent symptoms on first-line drugs
concepts.content: If symptoms persist despite first-line treatment, switch ACE-inhibitor to angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor such as sacubitril-valsartan after consulting a heart failure specialist.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – Assessment for iron deficiency
concepts.content: Assess iron deficiency by measuring transferrin saturation, ferritin, and haemoglobin in patients with chronic heart failure.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – Indications for intravenous iron therapy
concepts.content: Consider intravenous iron therapy if haemoglobin is less than 150 g/L and transferrin saturation is below 20% or serum ferritin is less than 100 ng/mL after excluding other causes of iron deficiency.

concepts.title: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction – First-line drug treatment
concepts.content: The first-line drug treatment for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction includes mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and SGLT2-inhibitor.

concepts.title: ACE inhibitors, ARNIs, ARBs and MRAs – Monitoring urea and electrolytes
concepts.content: Measure urea and electrolytes before starting treatment, 1-2 weeks after initiation, 1-2 weeks after each dose increment, and every 3 to 6 months thereafter.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – NYHA classification overview
concepts.content: The New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification is a system used to classify the severity of chronic heart failure based on symptoms and physical activity limitations.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – NYHA Class I definition
concepts.content: NYHA Class I is defined as no symptoms and no limitation of physical activity; ordinary physical exercise does not cause undue fatigue, dyspnoea, or palpitations.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – NYHA Class II definition
concepts.content: NYHA Class II is characterized by mild symptoms and slight limitation of physical activity; patients are comfortable at rest but ordinary activity results in fatigue, palpitations, or dyspnoea.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – NYHA Class III definition
concepts.content: NYHA Class III involves moderate symptoms and marked limitation of physical activity; patients are comfortable at rest but less than ordinary activity causes symptoms.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – NYHA Class IV definition
concepts.content: NYHA Class IV is defined by severe symptoms; patients are unable to carry out any physical activity without discomfort and have symptoms of heart failure even at rest, with increased discomfort on any physical activity.

concepts.title: Clopidogrel – Definition and Drug Class
concepts.content: Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet agent belonging to the thienopyridine class of drugs.

concepts.title: Clopidogrel – Indications in Cardiovascular Disease
concepts.content: Clopidogrel is used in the management of cardiovascular diseases including acute coronary syndrome, ischaemic stroke, and peripheral arterial disease.

concepts.title: Clopidogrel – Use in Combination with Aspirin
concepts.content: Clopidogrel is used in addition to aspirin in certain conditions such as acute coronary syndrome.

concepts.title: Clopidogrel – First-line Use Post-Ischaemic Stroke and in Peripheral Arterial Disease
concepts.content: Following the 2010 NICE technology appraisal, clopidogrel is first-line treatment in patients after ischaemic stroke and those with peripheral arterial disease.

concepts.title: Clopidogrel – Mechanism of Action
concepts.content: Clopidogrel acts as an antagonist of the P2Y12 adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor, inhibiting platelet activation.

concepts.title: Clopidogrel – Related Drugs in Thienopyridine Class
concepts.content: Other thienopyridine drugs with similar mechanisms include prasugrel, ticagrelor, and ticlopidine.

concepts.title: Clopidogrel – Interaction with Proton Pump Inhibitors
concepts.content: Concurrent use of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) may reduce clopidogrel effectiveness; omeprazole and esomeprazole are of particular concern, while lansoprazole is considered safer.

concepts.title: Coarctation of the aorta – Definition
concepts.content: Coarctation of the aorta is a congenital narrowing of the descending aorta.

concepts.title: Coarctation of the aorta – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Coarctation of the aorta is more common in males.

concepts.title: Coarctation of the aorta – Association with Turner's syndrome
concepts.content: Coarctation of the aorta is associated with Turner's syndrome.

concepts.title: Coarctation of the aorta – Association with bicuspid aortic valve
concepts.content: Coarctation of the aorta is associated with bicuspid aortic valve.

concepts.title: Coarctation of the aorta – Association with berry aneurysms
concepts.content: Coarctation of the aorta is associated with berry aneurysms.

concepts.title: Coarctation of the aorta – Association with neurofibromatosis
concepts.content: Coarctation of the aorta is associated with neurofibromatosis.

concepts.title: Coarctation of the aorta – Presentation in infancy
concepts.content: In infancy, coarctation of the aorta presents with heart failure.

concepts.title: Coarctation of the aorta – Presentation in adults
concepts.content: In adults, coarctation of the aorta commonly presents with hypertension.

concepts.title: Coarctation of the aorta – Radio-femoral delay
concepts.content: Coarctation of the aorta causes radio-femoral delay due to obstruction of blood flow.

concepts.title: Coarctation of the aorta – Murmur characteristics
concepts.content: Coarctation of the aorta produces a mid systolic murmur maximal over the back.

concepts.title: Coarctation of the aorta – Apical click
concepts.content: An apical click from the aortic valve may be heard in coarctation of the aorta due to associated bicuspid aortic valve.

concepts.title: Coarctation of the aorta – Rib notching
concepts.content: Notching of the inferior border of the ribs occurs due to collateral vessels in coarctation of the aorta but is not seen in young children.

concepts.title: Combination antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy – Indications for combined use
concepts.content: Patients with comorbid conditions such as established cardiovascular disease (indication for antiplatelet therapy) and atrial fibrillation, venous thromboembolism, or valvular heart disease (indications for anticoagulant therapy) may require both antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapies.

concepts.title: Combination antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy – Bleeding risk
concepts.content: Combination therapy with antiplatelets and anticoagulants increases the risk of bleeding and may not be necessary in all clinical scenarios.

concepts.title: Secondary prevention of stable cardiovascular disease – Antiplatelet therapy recommendation
concepts.content: In stable cardiovascular disease, antiplatelet therapy is normally recommended for all patients as secondary prevention.

concepts.title: Secondary prevention of stable cardiovascular disease with anticoagulant indication – Anticoagulant monotherapy
concepts.content: If a patient with stable cardiovascular disease has an indication for anticoagulation (e.g., atrial fibrillation), anticoagulant monotherapy is indicated without adding antiplatelet therapy.

concepts.title: Post-acute coronary syndrome/percutaneous coronary intervention – Indication for antiplatelet therapy
concepts.content: Patients post-acute coronary syndrome or percutaneous coronary intervention have a strong indication for antiplatelet therapy.

concepts.title: Post-acute coronary syndrome/percutaneous coronary intervention – Triple therapy duration
concepts.content: After acute coronary syndrome or percutaneous coronary intervention, triple therapy (two antiplatelets plus one anticoagulant) is generally prescribed for 4 weeks to 6 months.

concepts.title: Post-acute coronary syndrome/percutaneous coronary intervention – Dual therapy duration
concepts.content: Following triple therapy, dual therapy (one antiplatelet plus one anticoagulant) is used to complete 12 months of treatment.

concepts.title: Post-acute coronary syndrome/percutaneous coronary intervention – Individualized therapy duration
concepts.content: Duration of combination antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy varies between patients depending on individual stroke risk factors, especially in atrial fibrillation.

concepts.title: Venous thromboembolism – Anticoagulant therapy duration in patients on antiplatelets
concepts.content: Patients on antiplatelet therapy who develop venous thromboembolism are typically prescribed anticoagulants for 3 to 6 months.

concepts.title: Venous thromboembolism – Use of ORBIT score for bleeding risk assessment
concepts.content: The ORBIT bleeding risk score should be calculated in patients on antiplatelets who develop venous thromboembolism to guide management decisions.

concepts.title: Venous thromboembolism – Management based on bleeding risk
concepts.content: Patients with low bleeding risk (per ORBIT score) may continue antiplatelet therapy alongside anticoagulants, whereas those with intermediate or high bleeding risk should consider stopping antiplatelets.

concepts.title: Complete heart block – Definition
concepts.content: Third degree heart block is a condition where there is no association between the P waves and QRS complexes on ECG.

concepts.title: Complete heart block – Syncope presentation
concepts.content: Syncope is a clinical feature that can present in patients with complete heart block.

concepts.title: Complete heart block – Heart failure presentation
concepts.content: Heart failure is a clinical feature that can present in patients with complete heart block.

concepts.title: Complete heart block – Regular bradycardia presentation
concepts.content: Complete heart block typically presents with a regular bradycardia of 30-50 beats per minute.

concepts.title: Complete heart block – Wide pulse pressure presentation
concepts.content: Wide pulse pressure is a clinical feature observed in patients with complete heart block.

concepts.title: Complete heart block – Cannon waves in jugular venous pressure
concepts.content: Cannon waves in the neck jugular venous pressure are a clinical sign seen in complete heart block.

concepts.title: Complete heart block – Variable intensity of first heart sound
concepts.content: Variable intensity of the first heart sound (S1) is a clinical feature in complete heart block.

concepts.title: First degree heart block – Definition
concepts.content: First degree heart block is characterized by a PR interval greater than 0.2 seconds on ECG.

concepts.title: Second degree heart block type 1 – Definition
concepts.content: Second degree heart block type 1 (Mobitz I, Wenckebach) is characterized by progressive prolongation of the PR interval until a dropped beat occurs.

concepts.title: Second degree heart block type 2 – Definition
concepts.content: Second degree heart block type 2 (Mobitz II) is characterized by a constant PR interval with P waves often not followed by a QRS complex.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis – Definition
concepts.content: Constrictive pericarditis is a condition characterized by a thickened, fibrotic, and often calcified pericardium that restricts diastolic filling of the heart.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis – Causes
concepts.content: Constrictive pericarditis can be caused by any cause of pericarditis, with tuberculosis being a particularly common cause.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis – Symptom dyspnoea
concepts.content: Dyspnoea is a common presenting symptom of constrictive pericarditis due to impaired cardiac filling.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis – Sign right heart failure
concepts.content: Right heart failure in constrictive pericarditis manifests as ascites, peripheral oedema, and hepatomegaly.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis – Sign raised jugular venous pressure
concepts.content: Raised jugular venous pressure in constrictive pericarditis reflects impaired diastolic filling and elevated right atrial pressure.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis – Sign prominent y descent in jugular venous pulse
concepts.content: Prominent y descent in jugular venous pulse indicates rapid early diastolic emptying of the right atrium followed by abrupt cessation of filling due to the stiff pericardium.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis – Sign normal or prominent x descent in jugular venous pulse
concepts.content: The x descent in jugular venous pulse is normal or prominent in constrictive pericarditis.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis – Sign positive Kussmaul's sign
concepts.content: Kussmaul's sign is positive in constrictive pericarditis, characterized by a paradoxical rise or failure to fall in jugular venous pressure during inspiration.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis – Sign pericardial knock
concepts.content: Pericardial knock is a loud third heart sound (S3) heard in constrictive pericarditis.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis – Investigation chest X-ray pericardial calcification
concepts.content: Chest X-ray in constrictive pericarditis may show pericardial calcification.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis vs Cardiac tamponade – Jugular venous pulse y descent
concepts.content: In cardiac tamponade, the y descent in jugular venous pulse is absent, whereas in constrictive pericarditis both x and y descents are present.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis vs Cardiac tamponade – Pulsus paradoxus
concepts.content: Pulsus paradoxus is present in cardiac tamponade but absent in constrictive pericarditis.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis vs Cardiac tamponade – Kussmaul's sign prevalence
concepts.content: Kussmaul's sign is rare in cardiac tamponade but commonly present in constrictive pericarditis.

concepts.title: Constrictive pericarditis vs Cardiac tamponade – Pericardial calcification on chest X-ray
concepts.content: Pericardial calcification on chest X-ray is characteristic of constrictive pericarditis and not seen in cardiac tamponade.

concepts.title: Dabigatran – Definition and Mechanism of Action
concepts.content: Dabigatran is an oral anticoagulant that acts as a direct thrombin inhibitor.

concepts.title: Dabigatran – Clinical Advantage Over Warfarin
concepts.content: Dabigatran does not require regular monitoring, unlike warfarin.

concepts.title: Venous Thromboembolism – Dabigatran Use in Prophylaxis Post Orthopedic Surgery
concepts.content: Dabigatran is used for prophylaxis of venous thromboembolism following hip or knee replacement surgery.

concepts.title: Non-valvular Atrial Fibrillation – Dabigatran Use for Stroke Prevention
concepts.content: Dabigatran is licensed in the UK for prevention of stroke in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation who have one or more specified risk factors.

concepts.title: Non-valvular Atrial Fibrillation – Stroke Prevention Risk Factors for Dabigatran Use
concepts.content: Risk factors for dabigatran use in non-valvular atrial fibrillation include previous stroke, transient ischaemic attack or systemic embolism; left ventricular ejection fraction below 40%; symptomatic heart failure NYHA class 2 or above; age 75 years or older; or age 65 years or older with diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, or hypertension.

concepts.title: Dabigatran – Major Adverse Effect
concepts.content: Haemorrhage is the major adverse effect associated with dabigatran use.

concepts.title: Dabigatran – Dose Adjustment in Chronic Kidney Disease
concepts.content: Doses of dabigatran should be reduced in patients with chronic kidney disease.

concepts.title: Dabigatran – Contraindication in Severe Renal Impairment
concepts.content: Dabigatran should not be prescribed if creatinine clearance is less than 30 ml/min.

concepts.title: Dabigatran – Reversal Agent
concepts.content: Idarucizumab can be used for rapid reversal of the anticoagulant effects of dabigatran.

concepts.title: Dabigatran – Contraindication in Mechanical Heart Valve Patients
concepts.content: Dabigatran is contraindicated in patients with recent mechanical heart valve replacement due to higher bleeding and thrombotic events compared with warfarin, as shown in the RE-ALIGN study.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Blood pressure control targets
concepts.content: Patients with diabetes mellitus have traditionally been managed with more aggressive blood pressure control to reduce cardiovascular risk; however, evidence suggests that tight control (<130/85 mmHg) reduces stroke slightly but does not significantly improve other outcomes compared to relaxed control (<140-160/90-100 mmHg).

concepts.title: Type 2 diabetes mellitus – Blood pressure target recommendation
concepts.content: NICE recommends a blood pressure target of less than 140/90 mmHg for patients with type 2 diabetes, aligning with targets for patients without diabetes.

concepts.title: Type 1 diabetes mellitus – Blood pressure intervention thresholds
concepts.content: For adults with type 1 diabetes, blood pressure management intervention is recommended at 135/85 mmHg unless albuminuria or two or more metabolic syndrome features are present, in which case the threshold is 130/80 mmHg.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – First-line antihypertensive agents
concepts.content: ACE inhibitors or angiotensin-II receptor blockers (A2RBs) are the first-line antihypertensive agents in diabetes due to their renoprotective effects, regardless of patient age.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus in black African or African-Caribbean patients – Preferred antihypertensive agents
concepts.content: Angiotensin-II receptor blockers (A2RBs) are preferred antihypertensive agents for black African or African-Caribbean diabetic patients.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Subsequent hypertension management
concepts.content: After initial antihypertensive therapy with ACE inhibitors or A2RBs, further hypertension management in diabetic patients follows the same protocols as for non-diabetic patients.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Autonomic neuropathy and antihypertensive therapy
concepts.content: Autonomic neuropathy in diabetic patients may increase the risk of postural hypotension symptoms when taking antihypertensive medications.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Beta-blockers in uncomplicated hypertension
concepts.content: Routine use of beta-blockers in uncomplicated hypertension in diabetic patients should be avoided, especially when combined with thiazides, due to risks of insulin resistance, impaired insulin secretion, and altered autonomic response to hypoglycaemia.

concepts.title: Digoxin – Definition and Indications
concepts.content: Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside mainly used for rate control in atrial fibrillation and sometimes to improve symptoms in heart failure without affecting mortality.

concepts.title: Digoxin – Mechanism of Action on AV Node
concepts.content: Digoxin decreases conduction through the atrioventricular node, slowing the ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation and flutter.

concepts.title: Digoxin – Positive Inotropic Effect Mechanism
concepts.content: Digoxin increases cardiac muscle contraction force by inhibiting the Na+/K+ ATPase pump and stimulating the vagus nerve.

concepts.title: Digoxin – Therapeutic Index
concepts.content: Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index requiring careful dosing and monitoring.

concepts.title: Digoxin – Monitoring Guidelines
concepts.content: Digoxin levels are not routinely monitored except when toxicity is suspected; levels should be measured 8 to 12 hours after the last dose in suspected toxicity.

concepts.title: Digoxin Toxicity – Definition and Plasma Concentration
concepts.content: Digoxin toxicity can occur even within therapeutic plasma concentrations; risk increases progressively from 1.5 to 3 mcg/L.

concepts.title: Digoxin Toxicity – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Symptoms of digoxin toxicity include general malaise, lethargy, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, confusion, yellow-green vision, arrhythmias such as AV block and bradycardia, and gynaecomastia.

concepts.title: Digoxin Toxicity – Hypokalaemia as a Precipitating Factor
concepts.content: Hypokalaemia increases digoxin toxicity risk by enhancing digoxin binding to the Na+/K+ ATPase pump, increasing its inhibitory effects.

concepts.title: Digoxin Toxicity – Other Precipitating Factors
concepts.content: Additional factors increasing digoxin toxicity risk include increasing age, renal failure, dehydration, myocardial ischaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypernatraemia, acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia, hypothermia, hypothyroidism, and interacting drugs.

concepts.title: Digoxin Toxicity – Drug Interactions Increasing Risk
concepts.content: Drugs that increase digoxin toxicity risk include amiodarone, quinidine, verapamil, diltiazem, spironolactone (which reduces digoxin excretion), ciclosporin, and drugs causing hypokalaemia such as thiazide and loop diuretics.

concepts.title: Digoxin Toxicity – Management with Digibind
concepts.content: Digoxin toxicity can be treated with Digibind (digoxin-specific antibody fragments) to neutralize digoxin effects.

concepts.title: Digoxin Toxicity – Arrhythmia Management
concepts.content: Arrhythmias caused by digoxin toxicity should be corrected as part of management.

concepts.title: Digoxin Toxicity – Potassium Monitoring
concepts.content: Potassium levels should be monitored and corrected during digoxin toxicity management.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Driving eligibility general rule
concepts.content: Patients with hypertension can drive unless their treatment causes unacceptable side effects. There is no need to notify the DVLA in such cases.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Group 2 driving disqualification criteria
concepts.content: For drivers with Group 2 entitlement, hypertension disqualifies from driving if resting blood pressure is consistently 180 mmHg systolic or more and/or 100 mmHg diastolic or more.

concepts.title: Elective angioplasty – Driving restriction duration
concepts.content: Patients undergoing elective angioplasty must refrain from driving for 1 week post-procedure.

concepts.title: Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) – Driving restriction duration
concepts.content: Patients who have undergone CABG must not drive for 4 weeks following surgery.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndrome – Driving restriction duration
concepts.content: Patients with acute coronary syndrome must refrain from driving for 4 weeks after the event.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndrome treated by angioplasty – Driving restriction duration
concepts.content: If acute coronary syndrome is successfully treated by angioplasty, patients must refrain from driving for 1 week.

concepts.title: Angina – Driving cessation criteria
concepts.content: Driving must cease if angina symptoms occur at rest or while driving.

concepts.title: Pacemaker insertion – Driving restriction duration
concepts.content: Patients must not drive for 1 week following pacemaker insertion.

concepts.title: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) – Driving restriction for sustained ventricular arrhythmia
concepts.content: If an ICD is implanted for sustained ventricular arrhythmia, the patient must cease driving for 6 months.

concepts.title: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) – Driving restriction for prophylactic implantation
concepts.content: If an ICD is implanted prophylactically, the patient must cease driving for 1 month.

concepts.title: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) – Group 2 driving permanent bar
concepts.content: Having an ICD results in a permanent driving ban for Group 2 drivers.

concepts.title: Catheter ablation for arrhythmia – Driving restriction duration
concepts.content: Successful catheter ablation for an arrhythmia requires 2 days off driving.

concepts.title: Aortic aneurysm – Notification requirement for diameter ≥6 cm
concepts.content: Patients with an aortic aneurysm measuring 6 cm or more must notify the DVLA. Licensing will be permitted subject to annual review.

concepts.title: Aortic aneurysm – Driving disqualification for diameter ≥6.5 cm
concepts.content: An aortic aneurysm with a diameter of 6.5 cm or more disqualifies patients from driving.

concepts.title: Heart transplant – Driving restriction duration and notification
concepts.content: Patients must not drive for 6 weeks after heart transplant surgery. There is no need to notify the DVLA.

concepts.title: Left ventricular hypertrophy – ECG diagnostic criterion
concepts.content: Left ventricular hypertrophy is diagnosed on ECG when the sum of the S wave amplitude in lead V1 and the R wave amplitude in lead V5 or V6 exceeds 40 mm.

concepts.title: Right ventricular hypertrophy – ECG diagnostic criterion
concepts.content: Right ventricular hypertrophy can be identified on ECG by specific changes, though exact voltage criteria are not provided in this content.

concepts.title: Left atrial enlargement – ECG P wave morphology in lead II
concepts.content: Left atrial enlargement is indicated on ECG by a bifid P wave in lead II with a duration greater than 120 milliseconds.

concepts.title: Left atrial enlargement – ECG P wave morphology in lead V1
concepts.content: Left atrial enlargement is also suggested on ECG by a negative terminal portion of the P wave in lead V1.

concepts.title: Right atrial enlargement – ECG P wave amplitude
concepts.content: Right atrial enlargement is characterized on ECG by tall P waves in leads II and V1 that exceed 0.25 mV in amplitude.

concepts.title: Bifascicular block – Definition
concepts.content: Bifascicular block is the combination of right bundle branch block (RBBB) with either left anterior or left posterior hemiblock.

concepts.title: Bifascicular block – ECG feature example
concepts.content: An example of bifascicular block is right bundle branch block (RBBB) combined with left axis deviation indicating left anterior hemiblock.

concepts.title: Trifascicular block – Definition
concepts.content: Trifascicular block is characterized by features of bifascicular block plus the presence of first-degree atrioventricular (AV) block.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – ECG changes in anteroseptal territory
concepts.content: ECG changes in the anteroseptal territory are seen in leads V1 to V4 and correspond to ischemia or infarction in the left anterior descending coronary artery.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – ECG changes in inferior territory
concepts.content: ECG changes in the inferior territory are seen in leads II, III, and aVF and correspond to ischemia or infarction in the right coronary artery.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – ECG changes in anterolateral territory
concepts.content: ECG changes in the anterolateral territory are seen in leads V1 to V6, I, and aVL and correspond to ischemia or infarction in the proximal left anterior descending coronary artery.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – ECG changes in lateral territory
concepts.content: ECG changes in the lateral territory are seen in leads I, aVL, and sometimes V5 to V6 and correspond to ischemia or infarction in the left circumflex coronary artery.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – ECG changes in posterior territory
concepts.content: Posterior territory ECG changes are seen as reciprocal changes in leads V1 to V3 and may indicate infarction usually involving the left circumflex artery or sometimes the right coronary artery.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – reciprocal ECG changes in STEMI
concepts.content: Reciprocal changes in ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) typically include horizontal ST depression, tall broad R waves, upright T waves, and a dominant R wave in lead V2.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – confirmation of posterior infarction by posterior leads
concepts.content: Posterior infarction is confirmed by ST elevation and Q waves in posterior leads V7 to V9, usually indicating involvement of the left circumflex artery or sometimes the right coronary artery.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – new left bundle branch block as diagnostic clue
concepts.content: A new left bundle branch block (LBBB) on ECG may indicate the presence of an acute coronary syndrome and should raise suspicion for this diagnosis.

concepts.title: Digoxin effect – ECG feature: down-sloping ST depression
concepts.content: Digoxin causes a characteristic down-sloping ST depression on ECG, also described as a 'reverse tick' or 'scooped out' appearance.

concepts.title: Digoxin effect – ECG feature: flattened or inverted T waves
concepts.content: Digoxin toxicity or effect can cause flattened or inverted T waves on the ECG.

concepts.title: Digoxin effect – ECG feature: short QT interval
concepts.content: Digoxin use is associated with a shortened QT interval on the ECG.

concepts.title: Digoxin toxicity – arrhythmias: atrioventricular block
concepts.content: Digoxin toxicity can cause arrhythmias including atrioventricular (AV) block.

concepts.title: Digoxin toxicity – arrhythmias: bradycardia
concepts.content: Digoxin toxicity can cause bradycardia as a cardiac arrhythmia.

concepts.title: Hypokalaemia – ECG feature: U waves
concepts.content: Hypokalaemia is characterized on ECG by the presence of U waves.

concepts.title: Hypokalaemia – ECG feature: T wave changes
concepts.content: Hypokalaemia causes small or absent T waves on ECG, and occasionally T wave inversion.

concepts.title: Hypokalaemia – ECG feature: PR interval prolongation
concepts.content: Hypokalaemia is associated with a prolonged PR interval on ECG.

concepts.title: Hypokalaemia – ECG feature: ST segment depression
concepts.content: Hypokalaemia causes ST segment depression on ECG.

concepts.title: Hypokalaemia – ECG feature: QT interval prolongation
concepts.content: Hypokalaemia is associated with a prolonged QT interval on ECG.

concepts.title: Hypothermia – Bradycardia
concepts.content: Bradycardia is a common ECG finding in hypothermia, characterized by a slower than normal heart rate due to decreased metabolic activity and conduction velocity.

concepts.title: Hypothermia – 'J' Wave (Osborne Wave)
concepts.content: 'J' waves, also known as Osborne waves, are small humps seen at the end of the QRS complex on ECG in hypothermia, reflecting abnormal ventricular repolarization.

concepts.title: Hypothermia – First Degree Heart Block
concepts.content: First degree heart block may be observed on ECG in hypothermia, characterized by prolonged PR interval due to slowed atrioventricular conduction.

concepts.title: Hypothermia – Long QT Interval
concepts.content: Hypothermia can cause prolongation of the QT interval on ECG, increasing the risk of ventricular arrhythmias due to delayed ventricular repolarization.

concepts.title: Hypothermia – Atrial and Ventricular Arrhythmias
concepts.content: Atrial and ventricular arrhythmias may occur in hypothermia due to myocardial irritability and conduction abnormalities reflected on ECG.

concepts.title: Left bundle branch block – Definition
concepts.content: Left bundle branch block (LBBB) is a cardiac conduction abnormality characterized by delayed activation of the left ventricle due to blockage in the left bundle branch of the His-Purkinje system.

concepts.title: Left bundle branch block – ECG features
concepts.content: Typical ECG features of LBBB include a 'W' shaped QRS complex in lead V1 and an 'M' shaped QRS complex in lead V6.

concepts.title: Left bundle branch block – Differentiation from right bundle branch block
concepts.content: The mnemonic WiLLiaM MaRRoW helps differentiate LBBB from RBBB: LBBB shows a 'W' pattern in lead V1 and an 'M' pattern in lead V6, whereas RBBB shows an 'M' in V1 and a 'W' in V6.

concepts.title: Left bundle branch block – Clinical significance of new onset
concepts.content: New onset left bundle branch block is always considered pathological and warrants further clinical evaluation.

concepts.title: Left bundle branch block – Causes: myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Myocardial infarction is a common cause of left bundle branch block.

concepts.title: Left bundle branch block – Diagnostic challenge in myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Diagnosing myocardial infarction in patients with pre-existing left bundle branch block is difficult due to altered ECG patterns.

concepts.title: Left bundle branch block – Use of Sgarbossa criteria
concepts.content: The Sgarbossa criteria can assist in diagnosing myocardial infarction in patients with existing left bundle branch block.

concepts.title: Left bundle branch block – Causes: hypertension
concepts.content: Hypertension is a recognized cause of left bundle branch block.

concepts.title: Left bundle branch block – Causes: aortic stenosis
concepts.content: Aortic stenosis is a cause of left bundle branch block due to pressure overload and conduction system involvement.

concepts.title: Left bundle branch block – Causes: cardiomyopathy
concepts.content: Cardiomyopathy can cause left bundle branch block by affecting the myocardial conduction pathways.

concepts.title: Left bundle branch block – Rare causes
concepts.content: Rare causes of left bundle branch block include idiopathic fibrosis, digoxin toxicity, and hyperkalaemia.

concepts.title: ECG – Use in myocardial ischaemia detection
concepts.content: The ECG is primarily used to determine if a patient with chest pain is experiencing a cardiac event related to myocardial ischaemia.

concepts.title: Acute myocardial infarction – Hyperacute T waves
concepts.content: Hyperacute T waves are often the first ECG sign of acute myocardial infarction but typically persist for only a few minutes.

concepts.title: Acute myocardial infarction – ST elevation development
concepts.content: ST elevation may develop on the ECG following the initial hyperacute T waves during an acute myocardial infarction.

concepts.title: Acute myocardial infarction – T wave inversion timing and duration
concepts.content: T waves typically become inverted within the first 24 hours of acute myocardial infarction and this inversion can last from days to months.

concepts.title: Acute myocardial infarction – Pathological Q waves development and persistence
concepts.content: Pathological Q waves develop several hours to days after acute myocardial infarction and usually persist indefinitely on the ECG.

concepts.title: ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) – Clinical definition
concepts.content: STEMI is defined by clinical symptoms consistent with acute coronary syndrome, generally lasting 20 minutes or more, accompanied by persistent ECG changes for over 20 minutes in at least two contiguous leads.

concepts.title: STEMI – ST elevation thresholds in leads V2-3 by age and sex
concepts.content: ST elevation thresholds for STEMI diagnosis in leads V2-3 are: ≥ 2.5 mm in men under 40 years, ≥ 2.0 mm in men over 40 years, and ≥ 1.5 mm in women.

concepts.title: STEMI – ST elevation threshold in other leads
concepts.content: ST elevation of 1 mm or more in leads other than V2-3 is diagnostic for STEMI when accompanied by clinical symptoms.

concepts.title: STEMI – New left bundle branch block (LBBB) as diagnostic criterion
concepts.content: A new left bundle branch block on ECG should be considered diagnostic of STEMI unless there is evidence that it is old.

concepts.title: Posterior myocardial infarction – ECG changes
concepts.content: A posterior myocardial infarction causes ST depression rather than ST elevation on a standard 12-lead ECG.

concepts.title: Sinus bradycardia – Definition and normal variant in athletes
concepts.content: Sinus bradycardia is a slower than normal heart rate originating from the sinoatrial node, typically defined as a heart rate below 60 beats per minute. In athletes, sinus bradycardia is considered a normal variant due to increased vagal tone and enhanced cardiac efficiency.

concepts.title: Junctional rhythm – Definition and normal variant in athletes
concepts.content: Junctional rhythm is an ECG rhythm originating from the atrioventricular junction rather than the sinoatrial node. In athletes, it may be observed as a normal variant due to increased vagal tone and altered autonomic regulation.

concepts.title: First degree heart block – Definition and normal variant in athletes
concepts.content: First degree heart block is characterized by a prolonged PR interval (>200 ms) on ECG without dropped beats. It is considered a normal variant in athletes due to increased vagal tone affecting atrioventricular conduction.

concepts.title: Mobitz type 1 (Wenckebach phenomenon) – Definition and normal variant in athletes
concepts.content: Mobitz type 1 heart block, also known as Wenckebach phenomenon, is characterized by progressive prolongation of the PR interval until a beat is dropped. In athletes, it can be a normal variant due to enhanced vagal tone affecting atrioventricular node conduction.

concepts.title: Cor pulmonale – Increased P wave amplitude
concepts.content: In cor pulmonale, the P wave amplitude on ECG is increased due to right atrial enlargement secondary to pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Left atrial enlargement – Broad, notched (bifid) P waves
concepts.content: Left atrial enlargement is characterized on ECG by broad, notched (bifid) P waves, often most pronounced in lead II, commonly caused by mitral stenosis.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – Absence of P waves
concepts.content: Atrial fibrillation is an arrhythmia characterized on ECG by the absence of P waves due to disorganized atrial electrical activity.

concepts.title: Prolonged PR interval – Definition
concepts.content: A prolonged PR interval is an ECG finding where the PR interval exceeds 200 milliseconds, indicating delayed atrioventricular conduction.

concepts.title: Idiopathic cause – Prolonged PR interval
concepts.content: Idiopathic causes can lead to a prolonged PR interval without identifiable underlying pathology.

concepts.title: Ischaemic heart disease – Cause of prolonged PR interval
concepts.content: Ischaemic heart disease can cause a prolonged PR interval due to impaired conduction from ischemic damage to the atrioventricular node or conduction pathways.

concepts.title: Digoxin toxicity – Cause of prolonged PR interval
concepts.content: Digoxin toxicity can cause a prolonged PR interval by increasing vagal tone and slowing atrioventricular conduction.

concepts.title: Hypokalaemia – Cause of prolonged PR interval
concepts.content: Hypokalaemia can cause a prolonged PR interval by affecting cardiac myocyte membrane potentials and slowing conduction.

concepts.title: Hyperkalaemia – Rare cause of prolonged PR interval
concepts.content: Hyperkalaemia can rarely cause a prolonged PR interval, but this association is much less common than with hypokalaemia.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Cause of prolonged PR interval
concepts.content: Rheumatic fever can cause a prolonged PR interval due to inflammation and scarring of the conduction system.

concepts.title: Aortic root pathology – Cause of prolonged PR interval
concepts.content: Aortic root pathology, such as an abscess secondary to endocarditis, can cause a prolonged PR interval by disrupting the atrioventricular conduction system.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Cause of prolonged PR interval
concepts.content: Lyme disease can cause a prolonged PR interval due to Lyme carditis affecting the atrioventricular node.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Cause of prolonged PR interval
concepts.content: Sarcoidosis can cause a prolonged PR interval by granulomatous infiltration of the cardiac conduction system.

concepts.title: Myotonic dystrophy – Cause of prolonged PR interval
concepts.content: Myotonic dystrophy can cause a prolonged PR interval due to progressive conduction system fibrosis.

concepts.title: Athlete heart – Association with prolonged PR interval
concepts.content: A prolonged PR interval may be seen in athletes due to increased vagal tone causing slower atrioventricular conduction.

concepts.title: Short PR interval – Definition and cause
concepts.content: A short PR interval is an ECG finding characterized by a PR interval less than 120 milliseconds, commonly seen in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome due to accessory pathway conduction.

concepts.title: Right bundle branch block – Definition
concepts.content: Right bundle branch block (RBBB) is a common conduction abnormality seen on electrocardiograms (ECGs) characterized by delayed right ventricular depolarization.

concepts.title: Right bundle branch block – ECG differentiation from left bundle branch block
concepts.content: RBBB can be differentiated from LBBB on ECG using the WiLLiaM MaRRoW mnemonic: RBBB shows an 'M' pattern in lead V1 and a 'W' pattern in lead V6, whereas LBBB shows a 'W' in V1 and an 'M' in V6.

concepts.title: Right bundle branch block – Cause: Normal variant with aging
concepts.content: RBBB can be a normal variant and is more commonly observed with increasing age without underlying pathology.

concepts.title: Right bundle branch block – Cause: Right ventricular hypertrophy
concepts.content: Right ventricular hypertrophy can cause RBBB by altering the conduction pathway in the right ventricle.

concepts.title: Right bundle branch block – Cause: Chronically increased right ventricular pressure (e.g., cor pulmonale)
concepts.content: Chronically increased right ventricular pressure, such as in cor pulmonale, can lead to RBBB due to conduction delay in the right bundle branch.

concepts.title: Right bundle branch block – Cause: Pulmonary embolism
concepts.content: Pulmonary embolism can cause RBBB by increasing right ventricular strain and affecting conduction.

concepts.title: Right bundle branch block – Cause: Myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Myocardial infarction can cause RBBB by damaging the right bundle branch conduction system.

concepts.title: Right bundle branch block – Cause: Atrial septal defect (ostium secundum)
concepts.content: Atrial septal defect of the ostium secundum type can cause RBBB due to right heart volume overload and conduction delay.

concepts.title: Right bundle branch block – Cause: Cardiomyopathy or myocarditis
concepts.content: Cardiomyopathy or myocarditis can cause RBBB by affecting the myocardial conduction system including the right bundle branch.

concepts.title: ST depression – Definition
concepts.content: ST depression on ECG refers to a downward displacement of the ST segment below the isoelectric line, indicating potential myocardial ischemia or other cardiac abnormalities.

concepts.title: ST depression – Cause: Abnormal QRS complexes
concepts.content: ST depression can occur secondary to abnormal QRS complexes such as those seen in left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), left bundle branch block (LBBB), and right bundle branch block (RBBB).

concepts.title: ST depression – Cause: Myocardial ischaemia
concepts.content: Myocardial ischaemia causes ST depression on ECG due to subendocardial injury and reduced oxygen supply to the heart muscle.

concepts.title: ST depression – Cause: Digoxin effect
concepts.content: Digoxin therapy can cause characteristic ST depression on ECG, often described as a 'scooped' or 'reverse tick' appearance, due to its effect on cardiac repolarization.

concepts.title: ST depression – Cause: Hypokalaemia
concepts.content: Hypokalaemia can cause ST depression on ECG due to alterations in myocardial cell membrane potentials affecting repolarization.

concepts.title: ST depression – Cause: Syndrome X
concepts.content: Syndrome X, or microvascular angina, can cause ST depression on ECG due to ischemia from microvascular dysfunction despite normal epicardial coronary arteries.

concepts.title: Myocardial infarction – Cause of ST elevation
concepts.content: Myocardial infarction is a common cause of ST elevation on ECG due to acute ischemic injury to the myocardium.

concepts.title: Pericarditis/myocarditis – Cause of ST elevation
concepts.content: Pericarditis and myocarditis cause ST elevation on ECG due to inflammation of the pericardium or myocardium respectively.

concepts.title: Normal variant 'high take-off' – Cause of ST elevation
concepts.content: 'High take-off' is a normal ECG variant characterized by early repolarization causing ST elevation without underlying pathology.

concepts.title: Left ventricular aneurysm – Cause of ST elevation
concepts.content: Left ventricular aneurysm can cause persistent ST elevation on ECG due to scarred, non-contractile myocardial tissue.

concepts.title: Prinzmetal's angina (coronary artery spasm) – Cause of ST elevation
concepts.content: Prinzmetal's angina causes transient ST elevation on ECG due to coronary artery spasm leading to temporary myocardial ischemia.

concepts.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Cause of ST elevation
concepts.content: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy causes ST elevation on ECG due to transient left ventricular dysfunction often triggered by stress.

concepts.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Rare cause of ST elevation
concepts.content: Subarachnoid haemorrhage can rarely cause ST elevation on ECG due to neurogenic cardiac injury.

concepts.title: Hyperkalaemia – Peaked T waves
concepts.content: Hyperkalaemia causes characteristic peaked T waves on the ECG due to altered cardiac repolarization.

concepts.title: Myocardial ischaemia – Peaked T waves
concepts.content: Myocardial ischaemia can present with peaked T waves on ECG as an early sign of localized cardiac injury.

concepts.title: Myocardial ischaemia – Inverted T waves
concepts.content: Inverted T waves on ECG are a common finding in myocardial ischaemia, indicating myocardial injury or ischemic changes.

concepts.title: Digoxin toxicity – Inverted T waves
concepts.content: Digoxin toxicity can cause inverted T waves on ECG due to its effects on cardiac conduction and repolarization.

concepts.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Inverted T waves
concepts.content: Subarachnoid haemorrhage may cause inverted T waves on ECG due to neurogenic cardiac effects and autonomic disturbances.

concepts.title: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy – Inverted T waves
concepts.content: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is associated with inverted T waves on ECG, reflecting right ventricular structural and electrical abnormalities.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Inverted T waves
concepts.content: Pulmonary embolism can cause inverted T waves on ECG, often seen in the right precordial leads, sometimes as part of the 'S1Q3T3' pattern.

concepts.title: Brugada syndrome – Inverted T waves
concepts.content: Brugada syndrome is characterized by inverted T waves in the right precordial leads on ECG, reflecting sodium channel dysfunction and risk of sudden cardiac death.

concepts.title: Wellen's syndrome – Definition
concepts.content: Wellen's syndrome is an ECG pattern typically caused by high-grade stenosis in the left anterior descending coronary artery.

concepts.title: Wellen's syndrome – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Wellen's syndrome is caused by high-grade stenosis in the left anterior descending coronary artery leading to characteristic ECG changes.

concepts.title: Wellen's syndrome – Clinical presentation
concepts.content: Patients with Wellen's syndrome may have resolved chest pain at the time of presentation.

concepts.title: Wellen's syndrome – Cardiac enzyme levels
concepts.content: Cardiac enzymes in Wellen's syndrome may be normal or minimally elevated.

concepts.title: Wellen's syndrome – ECG feature: T wave changes
concepts.content: Wellen's syndrome is characterized by biphasic or deep T wave inversion in leads V2 and V3 on ECG.

concepts.title: Wellen's syndrome – ECG feature: ST segment
concepts.content: Wellen's syndrome shows minimal ST segment elevation on ECG.

concepts.title: Wellen's syndrome – ECG feature: Q waves
concepts.content: Wellen's syndrome does not show Q waves on ECG.

concepts.title: Eisenmenger's syndrome – Definition
concepts.content: Eisenmenger's syndrome is the reversal of a left-to-right shunt in a congenital heart defect due to pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Eisenmenger's syndrome – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Uncorrected left-to-right shunts cause remodeling of the pulmonary microvasculature, leading to obstruction of pulmonary blood flow and pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Eisenmenger's syndrome – Associated congenital heart defects
concepts.content: Eisenmenger's syndrome is associated with ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, and patent ductus arteriosus.

concepts.title: Eisenmenger's syndrome – Disappearance of original murmur
concepts.content: The original murmur caused by the left-to-right shunt may disappear as Eisenmenger's syndrome develops.

concepts.title: Eisenmenger's syndrome – Cyanosis
concepts.content: Cyanosis is a clinical feature of Eisenmenger's syndrome due to right-to-left shunting and hypoxemia.

concepts.title: Eisenmenger's syndrome – Clubbing
concepts.content: Clubbing of the fingers is a clinical sign seen in Eisenmenger's syndrome.

concepts.title: Eisenmenger's syndrome – Right ventricular failure
concepts.content: Right ventricular failure is a clinical feature resulting from increased pulmonary vascular resistance in Eisenmenger's syndrome.

concepts.title: Eisenmenger's syndrome – Haemoptysis and embolism
concepts.content: Haemoptysis and embolism can occur as complications of Eisenmenger's syndrome.

concepts.title: Eisenmenger's syndrome – Management
concepts.content: Heart-lung transplantation is required for definitive management of Eisenmenger's syndrome.

concepts.title: Flecainide – Drug classification
concepts.content: Flecainide is a Vaughan Williams class 1c antiarrhythmic agent.

concepts.title: Flecainide – Mechanism of action
concepts.content: Flecainide acts as a potent sodium channel blocker, specifically targeting Nav1.5 sodium channels, slowing conduction of the cardiac action potential.

concepts.title: Flecainide – ECG effects
concepts.content: Flecainide use may cause widening of the QRS complex and prolongation of the PR interval on ECG.

concepts.title: Flecainide – Contraindication post-myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Flecainide is contraindicated after myocardial infarction due to increased mortality demonstrated in the Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial (CAST, 1989).

concepts.title: Flecainide – Indications: atrial fibrillation
concepts.content: Flecainide is indicated for the treatment of atrial fibrillation.

concepts.title: Flecainide – Indications: supraventricular tachycardia with accessory pathway
concepts.content: Flecainide is indicated for supraventricular tachycardia associated with accessory pathways, such as Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

concepts.title: Flecainide – Contraindications: structural heart disease
concepts.content: Flecainide is contraindicated in patients with structural heart disease, including heart failure.

concepts.title: Flecainide – Contraindications: sinus node dysfunction and AV block
concepts.content: Flecainide is contraindicated in sinus node dysfunction and in patients with second-degree or greater atrioventricular (AV) block.

concepts.title: Flecainide – Contraindication: atrial flutter
concepts.content: Flecainide is contraindicated in patients with atrial flutter.

concepts.title: Flecainide – Adverse effect: negative inotropy
concepts.content: Flecainide has a negative inotropic effect, reducing myocardial contractility.

concepts.title: Flecainide – Adverse effect: bradycardia
concepts.content: Flecainide can cause bradycardia as an adverse effect.

concepts.title: Flecainide – Adverse effect: proarrhythmia
concepts.content: Flecainide has a proarrhythmic potential, which may worsen or induce arrhythmias.

concepts.title: Flecainide – Adverse effect: oral paraesthesia
concepts.content: Oral paraesthesia is a possible adverse effect of flecainide.

concepts.title: Flecainide – Adverse effect: visual disturbances
concepts.content: Visual disturbances can occur as an adverse effect of flecainide therapy.

concepts.title: Heart failure (chronic) – symptom: dyspnoea
concepts.content: Dyspnoea is a common symptom in chronic heart failure, reflecting impaired cardiac function and pulmonary congestion.

concepts.title: Heart failure (chronic) – symptom: cough
concepts.content: Cough in chronic heart failure may worsen at night and can be associated with pink or frothy sputum due to pulmonary oedema.

concepts.title: Heart failure (chronic) – symptom: orthopnoea
concepts.content: Orthopnoea is difficulty breathing when lying flat, commonly seen in chronic heart failure due to redistribution of fluid into the lungs.

concepts.title: Heart failure (chronic) – symptom: paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea
concepts.content: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea is sudden nighttime breathlessness caused by pulmonary congestion in chronic heart failure.

concepts.title: Heart failure (chronic) – sign: cardiac wheeze
concepts.content: A cardiac wheeze is a wheezing sound heard on auscultation caused by bronchial oedema in chronic heart failure.

concepts.title: Heart failure (chronic) – feature: cardiac cachexia
concepts.content: Cardiac cachexia is weight loss occurring in up to 15% of chronic heart failure patients, which may be masked by oedema-related weight gain.

concepts.title: Heart failure (chronic) – sign: bibasal crackles
concepts.content: Bibasal crackles are abnormal lung sounds heard at the bases of the lungs on examination, indicating pulmonary oedema in chronic heart failure.

concepts.title: Heart failure (chronic) – sign: raised jugular venous pressure
concepts.content: Raised jugular venous pressure is a clinical sign of right-sided heart failure due to elevated central venous pressure.

concepts.title: Heart failure (chronic) – sign: ankle oedema
concepts.content: Ankle oedema is swelling of the ankles caused by fluid accumulation, commonly seen in right-sided heart failure.

concepts.title: Heart failure (chronic) – sign: hepatomegaly
concepts.content: Hepatomegaly is enlargement of the liver due to congestion from right-sided heart failure.

concepts.title: Acute heart failure – Recommended IV loop diuretics
concepts.content: Intravenous loop diuretics such as furosemide or bumetanide are recommended for all patients with acute heart failure. NICE guidelines recommend using a higher dose than the patient's admission dose.

concepts.title: Acute heart failure – Oxygen therapy recommendations
concepts.content: Oxygen should be administered according to British Thoracic Society guidelines, targeting oxygen saturations between 94% and 98% in patients with acute heart failure.

concepts.title: Acute heart failure – Use of vasodilators
concepts.content: Intravenous vasodilators such as glyceryl trinitrate (GTN), isosorbide dinitrate, or sodium nitroprusside may be used to reduce preload and afterload in acute heart failure but are not routinely given to all patients.

concepts.title: Acute heart failure – Vasodilator blood pressure considerations
concepts.content: Nitrates should be considered only if systolic blood pressure is greater than 100 mmHg and may be used in cases of myocardial ischaemia, severe hypertension, or regurgitant aortic or mitral valve disease; hypotension is a major contraindication.

concepts.title: Acute heart failure with respiratory failure – Use of CPAP
concepts.content: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is recommended for patients with acute heart failure who develop respiratory failure.

concepts.title: Acute heart failure with hypotension or cardiogenic shock – Management challenges
concepts.content: Management of acute heart failure with hypotension (e.g., systolic BP < 85 mmHg) or cardiogenic shock is challenging because treatments like loop diuretics and nitrates may worsen hypotension.

concepts.title: Acute heart failure with cardiogenic shock – Use of inotropic agents
concepts.content: Inotropic agents such as dobutamine should be considered in patients with severe left ventricular dysfunction and potentially reversible cardiogenic shock.

concepts.title: Acute heart failure with cardiogenic shock – Use of vasopressor agents
concepts.content: Vasopressor agents such as norepinephrine are normally used only if there is an insufficient response to inotropes and evidence of end-organ hypoperfusion in cardiogenic shock.

concepts.title: Acute heart failure with cardiogenic shock – Mechanical circulatory assistance
concepts.content: Mechanical circulatory assistance devices such as intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation or ventricular assist devices may be used in cardiogenic shock.

concepts.title: Acute heart failure – Use of opiates
concepts.content: Opiates are not routinely recommended for acute heart failure by NICE due to evidence suggesting increased morbidity, despite their previous use to reduce dyspnoea and distress.

concepts.title: Acute heart failure – Continuation of regular heart failure medications
concepts.content: Regular heart failure medications such as beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors should be continued during acute management unless contraindications arise.

concepts.title: Acute heart failure – Indications to stop beta-blockers
concepts.content: Beta-blockers should be stopped in acute heart failure if the patient has a heart rate less than 50 beats per minute, second or third degree atrioventricular block, or shock.

concepts.title: Heart failure – Definition
concepts.content: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome where the heart is unable to pump enough blood to meet the metabolic needs of the body.

concepts.title: Heart failure – Etiology
concepts.content: Heart failure is usually a result of structural or functional heart disease but can also include high-output heart failure.

concepts.title: Heart failure – Classification by ejection fraction
concepts.content: Heart failure can be classified by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) into reduced ejection fraction (HF-rEF) and preserved ejection fraction (HF-pEF).

concepts.title: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HF-rEF) – Definition
concepts.content: HF-rEF is defined as heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction less than 35 to 40%, measured by echocardiography.

concepts.title: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HF-rEF) – Epidemiology
concepts.content: HF-rEF affects approximately 50% of patients diagnosed with heart failure.

concepts.title: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HF-pEF) – Definition
concepts.content: HF-pEF is defined as heart failure with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction on echocardiography.

concepts.title: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HF-pEF) – Epidemiology
concepts.content: HF-pEF affects approximately 50% of patients diagnosed with heart failure.

concepts.title: Heart failure – Systolic dysfunction pathophysiology
concepts.content: Systolic dysfunction in heart failure is characterized by impaired myocardial contraction during systole, typically seen in HF-rEF patients.

concepts.title: Heart failure – Diastolic dysfunction pathophysiology
concepts.content: Diastolic dysfunction in heart failure is characterized by impaired ventricular filling during diastole, typically seen in HF-pEF patients.

concepts.title: Systolic dysfunction – Common causes
concepts.content: Common causes of systolic dysfunction include ischaemic heart disease, dilated cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, and arrhythmias.

concepts.title: Diastolic dysfunction – Common causes
concepts.content: Common causes of diastolic dysfunction include hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, restrictive cardiomyopathy, cardiac tamponade, and constrictive pericarditis.

concepts.title: Heart failure – Classification by time
concepts.content: Heart failure can be classified as acute or chronic, with acute heart failure often representing an acute exacerbation of chronic heart failure.

concepts.title: Acute heart failure – Clinical features
concepts.content: Acute heart failure often presents with urgent symptoms due to left ventricular failure, commonly resulting in pulmonary oedema.

concepts.title: Acute heart failure – Emergency presentation
concepts.content: Pulmonary oedema due to acute heart failure is one of the most common reasons for attendance to the Emergency Department.

concepts.title: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HF-rEF) – Guideline recommendations
concepts.content: Most heart failure management guidelines, such as NICE, provide recommendations primarily for HF-rEF patients and do not extensively cover HF-pEF management.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – S1 Definition
concepts.content: The first heart sound (S1) is caused by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – S1 Softness Causes
concepts.content: S1 is soft if there is a long PR interval or mitral regurgitation.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – S1 Loudness in Mitral Stenosis
concepts.content: S1 is loud in mitral stenosis.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – S2 Definition
concepts.content: The second heart sound (S2) is caused by closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – S2 Softness in Aortic Stenosis
concepts.content: S2 is soft in aortic stenosis.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – S2 Splitting During Inspiration
concepts.content: Splitting of the second heart sound (S2) during inspiration is a normal physiological finding.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – S3 Definition
concepts.content: The third heart sound (S3) is caused by diastolic filling of the ventricle.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – S3 Normal Age Range
concepts.content: S3 is considered normal in individuals younger than 30 years old and may persist in women up to 50 years old.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – S3 Pathological Associations
concepts.content: S3 can be heard in left ventricular failure (e.g., dilated cardiomyopathy), constrictive pericarditis (called a pericardial knock), and mitral regurgitation.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – S4 Definition
concepts.content: The fourth heart sound (S4) is caused by atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – S4 Clinical Associations
concepts.content: S4 may be heard in aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM), and hypertension.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – S4 Timing on ECG
concepts.content: S4 coincides with the P wave on ECG because it is caused by atrial contraction.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – S4 and Double Apical Impulse in HOCM
concepts.content: In hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM), a double apical impulse may be felt due to a palpable S4.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – Pulmonary Valve Auscultation Site
concepts.content: The pulmonary valve is best auscultated at the left second intercostal space, at the upper sternal border.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – Aortic Valve Auscultation Site
concepts.content: The aortic valve is best auscultated at the right second intercostal space, at the upper sternal border.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – Mitral Valve Auscultation Site
concepts.content: The mitral valve is best auscultated at the left fifth intercostal space, just medial to the mid-clavicular line.

concepts.title: Heart Sounds – Tricuspid Valve Auscultation Site
concepts.content: The tricuspid valve is best auscultated at the left fourth intercostal space, at the lower left sternal border.

concepts.title: Heart sounds: S1 – Definition
concepts.content: S1 heart sound is caused by the closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the beginning of ventricular systole.

concepts.title: Mitral stenosis – Cause of loud S1
concepts.content: Mitral stenosis causes a loud first heart sound (S1) due to delayed closure of the mitral valve resulting in increased valve leaflet mobility at closure.

concepts.title: Left-to-right shunts – Cause of loud S1
concepts.content: Left-to-right cardiac shunts cause a loud S1 heart sound due to increased flow across the mitral valve leading to accentuated valve closure.

concepts.title: Short PR interval and atrial premature beats – Cause of loud S1
concepts.content: A short PR interval and atrial premature beats cause a loud S1 by increasing the force of atrial contraction, leading to earlier and more forceful mitral valve closure.

concepts.title: Hyperdynamic states – Cause of loud S1
concepts.content: Hyperdynamic circulatory states cause a loud S1 due to increased cardiac output and forceful closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves.

concepts.title: Mitral regurgitation – Cause of quiet S1
concepts.content: Mitral regurgitation causes a quiet first heart sound (S1) due to incomplete closure of the mitral valve leaflets, reducing the intensity of valve closure sounds.

concepts.title: S2 Heart Sound – Definition and Pathophysiology
concepts.content: S2 heart sound is caused by the closure of the aortic valve (A2) followed closely by the closure of the pulmonary valve (P2).

concepts.title: Loud S2 – Cause: Systemic Hypertension
concepts.content: Systemic hypertension causes a loud A2 component of the S2 heart sound.

concepts.title: Loud S2 – Cause: Pulmonary Hypertension
concepts.content: Pulmonary hypertension causes a loud P2 component of the S2 heart sound.

concepts.title: Loud S2 – Cause: Hyperdynamic States
concepts.content: Hyperdynamic circulatory states can cause a loud S2 heart sound.

concepts.title: Loud S2 – Cause: Atrial Septal Defect without Pulmonary Hypertension
concepts.content: Atrial septal defect without pulmonary hypertension can cause a loud S2 heart sound.

concepts.title: Soft S2 – Cause: Aortic Stenosis
concepts.content: Aortic stenosis causes a soft S2 heart sound due to impaired aortic valve closure.

concepts.title: Fixed Split S2 – Cause: Atrial Septal Defect
concepts.content: Atrial septal defect causes a fixed split of the S2 heart sound due to delayed closure of the pulmonary valve.

concepts.title: Widely Split S2 – Cause: Deep Inspiration
concepts.content: Deep inspiration causes a widely split S2 heart sound by delaying pulmonary valve closure.

concepts.title: Widely Split S2 – Cause: Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB)
concepts.content: Right bundle branch block causes a widely split S2 heart sound due to delayed right ventricular activation and pulmonary valve closure.

concepts.title: Widely Split S2 – Cause: Pulmonary Stenosis
concepts.content: Pulmonary stenosis causes a widely split S2 heart sound by delaying pulmonary valve closure.

concepts.title: Widely Split S2 – Cause: Severe Mitral Regurgitation
concepts.content: Severe mitral regurgitation causes a widely split S2 heart sound by increasing right ventricular volume and delaying pulmonary valve closure.

concepts.title: Reversed (Paradoxical) Split S2 – Definition
concepts.content: A reversed or paradoxical split S2 occurs when the pulmonary valve (P2) closes before the aortic valve (A2).

concepts.title: Reversed Split S2 – Cause: Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB)
concepts.content: Left bundle branch block causes a reversed split S2 by delaying aortic valve closure.

concepts.title: Reversed Split S2 – Cause: Severe Aortic Stenosis
concepts.content: Severe aortic stenosis causes a reversed split S2 by delaying aortic valve closure.

concepts.title: Reversed Split S2 – Cause: Right Ventricular Pacing
concepts.content: Right ventricular pacing causes a reversed split S2 by altering the sequence of ventricular activation and delaying aortic valve closure.

concepts.title: Reversed Split S2 – Cause: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) Syndrome Type B
concepts.content: WPW type B causes a reversed split S2 by causing early pulmonary valve closure (early P2).

concepts.title: Reversed Split S2 – Cause: Patent Ductus Arteriosus
concepts.content: Patent ductus arteriosus causes a reversed split S2 by altering pulmonary and aortic valve closure timing.

concepts.title: Heparin – Definition and Types
concepts.content: Heparin is an anticoagulant with two main types: unfractionated (standard) heparin and low molecular weight heparin (LMWH).

concepts.title: Heparin – Mechanism of Action of Unfractionated Heparin
concepts.content: Unfractionated heparin activates antithrombin III and forms a complex that inhibits thrombin and coagulation factors Xa, IXa, XIa, and XIIa.

concepts.title: Heparin – Mechanism of Action of Low Molecular Weight Heparin
concepts.content: Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) activates antithrombin III, enhancing its inhibition of factor Xa only.

concepts.title: Heparin – Adverse Effect: Bleeding
concepts.content: Heparin therapy can cause bleeding as a common adverse effect.

concepts.title: Heparin – Adverse Effect: Thrombocytopenia
concepts.content: Heparin can cause thrombocytopenia, including heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).

concepts.title: Heparin – Adverse Effect: Osteoporosis and Fracture Risk
concepts.content: Long-term heparin use can cause osteoporosis and increase the risk of fractures.

concepts.title: Heparin – Adverse Effect: Hyperkalaemia
concepts.content: Heparin may cause hyperkalaemia by inhibiting aldosterone secretion.

concepts.title: Heparin – Administration Route of Unfractionated Heparin
concepts.content: Unfractionated heparin is administered intravenously.

concepts.title: Heparin – Administration Route of Low Molecular Weight Heparin
concepts.content: Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is administered subcutaneously.

concepts.title: Heparin – Duration of Action: Unfractionated Heparin
concepts.content: Unfractionated heparin has a short duration of action.

concepts.title: Heparin – Duration of Action: Low Molecular Weight Heparin
concepts.content: Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) has a longer duration of action than unfractionated heparin.

concepts.title: Heparin – Monitoring of Unfractionated Heparin
concepts.content: Unfractionated heparin therapy is monitored using activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT).

concepts.title: Heparin – Monitoring of Low Molecular Weight Heparin
concepts.content: Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is monitored by anti-factor Xa levels, although routine monitoring is generally not required.

concepts.title: Heparin – Clinical Use of Unfractionated Heparin
concepts.content: Unfractionated heparin is useful in situations with high bleeding risk because its anticoagulation effect can be rapidly terminated and is also preferred in renal failure.

concepts.title: Heparin – Clinical Use of Low Molecular Weight Heparin
concepts.content: Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is standard treatment for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and treatment, and acute coronary syndromes.

concepts.title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) – Definition
concepts.content: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is an immune-mediated adverse reaction to heparin characterized by thrombocytopenia and paradoxical thrombosis.

concepts.title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) – Pathophysiology: Antibody Formation
concepts.content: IgG antibodies form against platelet factor 4 (PF4)–heparin complexes in HIT.

concepts.title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) – Pathophysiology: Platelet Activation
concepts.content: In HIT, antibody binding activates platelets by cross-linking FcγIIA receptors, causing thrombosis and platelet consumption.

concepts.title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) – Types: Type I
concepts.content: Type I HIT is a mild, non-immune, early-onset (within 1–2 days) thrombocytopenia that is transient and not clinically significant.

concepts.title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) – Types: Type II
concepts.content: Type II HIT is an immune-mediated thrombocytopenia occurring typically 5–14 days after heparin exposure and is associated with thrombosis.

concepts.title: Hypercalcaemia – Clinical feature: bone pain
concepts.content: Bone pain is a clinical feature of hypercalcaemia, often described as part of the 'bones' symptom cluster.

concepts.title: Hypercalcaemia – Clinical feature: renal stones
concepts.content: Renal stones ('stones') are a clinical feature of hypercalcaemia due to increased calcium excretion.

concepts.title: Hypercalcaemia – Clinical feature: abdominal pain and constipation
concepts.content: Abdominal pain and constipation ('groans') are gastrointestinal clinical features of hypercalcaemia.

concepts.title: Hypercalcaemia – Clinical feature: neuropsychiatric symptoms
concepts.content: Neuropsychiatric symptoms ('psychic moans') such as confusion and depression are clinical features of hypercalcaemia.

concepts.title: Hypercalcaemia – Clinical feature: corneal calcification
concepts.content: Corneal calcification is a clinical feature observed in hypercalcaemia.

concepts.title: Hypercalcaemia – Investigation finding: shortened QT interval on ECG
concepts.content: A shortened QT interval on ECG is an investigation finding associated with hypercalcaemia.

concepts.title: Hypercalcaemia – Clinical feature: hypertension
concepts.content: Hypertension is a clinical feature that can be associated with hypercalcaemia.

concepts.title: Hyperlipidaemia – Palmar xanthoma
concepts.content: Palmar xanthoma is a characteristic xanthoma seen in remnant hyperlipidaemia and may less commonly be observed in familial hypercholesterolaemia.

concepts.title: Hyperlipidaemia – Eruptive xanthoma clinical presentation
concepts.content: Eruptive xanthoma present as multiple red or yellow vesicles on extensor surfaces such as elbows and knees, caused by high triglyceride levels.

concepts.title: Hyperlipidaemia – Causes of eruptive xanthoma
concepts.content: Eruptive xanthoma is caused by familial hypertriglyceridaemia and lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

concepts.title: Hyperlipidaemia – Tendon, tuberous xanthoma and xanthelasma associations
concepts.content: Tendon xanthoma, tuberous xanthoma, and xanthelasma are associated with familial hypercholesterolaemia and remnant hyperlipidaemia.

concepts.title: Xanthelasma – Definition and clinical features
concepts.content: Xanthelasma are yellowish papules and plaques caused by localized lipid deposits commonly seen on the eyelid; they may also occur in patients without lipid abnormalities.

concepts.title: Xanthelasma – Management options
concepts.content: Management options for xanthelasma include surgical excision, topical trichloroacetic acid application, laser therapy, and electrodesiccation.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Definition
concepts.content: Hypertension is a chronic medical condition characterized by persistently elevated blood pressure above normal levels.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Clinical significance
concepts.content: Hypertension is an important risk factor for the development of cardiovascular diseases such as ischaemic heart disease and stroke.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Symptomatology
concepts.content: Patients with hypertension usually do not experience symptoms unless the blood pressure is very high.

concepts.title: Blood pressure – Normal range
concepts.content: Normal blood pressure varies by age, gender, and individual physiology, typically ranging between 90/60 mmHg and 140/90 mmHg in healthy individuals.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Diagnostic criteria
