concepts.content: NICE defines hypertension as a clinic blood pressure reading persistently ≥140/90 mmHg or a 24-hour average blood pressure reading ≥135/85 mmHg.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Classification
concepts.content: Hypertension is classified into primary (essential) hypertension, accounting for 90-95% of cases, and secondary hypertension caused by identifiable underlying conditions.

concepts.title: Primary hypertension – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Primary hypertension results from complex physiological changes associated with aging without a single identifiable cause.

concepts.title: Secondary hypertension – Causes overview
concepts.content: Secondary hypertension is caused by identifiable conditions including renal diseases, endocrine disorders, and other causes such as medications and pregnancy.

concepts.title: Secondary hypertension – Renal causes
concepts.content: Renal causes of secondary hypertension include glomerulonephritis, chronic pyelonephritis, adult polycystic kidney disease, and renal artery stenosis.

concepts.title: Secondary hypertension – Endocrine causes
concepts.content: Endocrine causes of secondary hypertension include primary hyperaldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's syndrome, Liddle's syndrome, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (11-beta hydroxylase deficiency), and acromegaly.

concepts.title: Secondary hypertension – Other causes
concepts.content: Other causes of secondary hypertension include glucocorticoid use, NSAIDs, pregnancy, coarctation of the aorta, and combined oral contraceptive pill use.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Guidelines for diagnosis
concepts.content: NICE published updated guidelines for the management of hypertension in 2019, building on the 2011 guidelines that recommended classifying hypertension into stages and using ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) and home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) for diagnosis.

concepts.title: Hypertension – White coat hypertension phenomenon
concepts.content: White coat hypertension is a condition where patients experience a blood pressure increase of approximately 20 mmHg in clinical settings, leading to potential overdiagnosis if relying solely on clinic readings.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Use of ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM)
concepts.content: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) is used to confirm hypertension diagnosis by providing a more accurate assessment of overall blood pressure and is preferred over home blood pressure monitoring due to higher accuracy.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Use of home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM)
concepts.content: Home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) is recommended to confirm hypertension diagnosis if ABPM is unsuitable or not tolerated by the patient.

concepts.title: Hypertension – ABPM as predictor of cardiovascular events
concepts.content: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) has been shown to be a more accurate predictor of cardiovascular events than clinic blood pressure readings.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Blood pressure classification criteria
concepts.content: Hypertension is classified into stages based on clinic and ABPM or HBPM readings: Stage 1 hypertension is clinic BP ≥140/90 mmHg and ABPM/HBPM average ≥135/85 mmHg; Stage 2 hypertension is clinic BP ≥160/100 mmHg and ABPM/HBPM average ≥150/95 mmHg; Severe hypertension is clinic systolic BP ≥180 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥120 mmHg.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Definition of Stage 1 Hypertension
concepts.content: Stage 1 hypertension is defined as clinic blood pressure (BP) of 140/90 mmHg or higher, with a subsequent ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) daytime average or home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) average of 135/85 mmHg or higher.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Definition of Stage 2 Hypertension
concepts.content: Stage 2 hypertension is defined as clinic BP of 160/100 mmHg or higher, with a subsequent ABPM daytime average or HBPM average of 150/95 mmHg or higher.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Definition of Severe Hypertension
concepts.content: Severe hypertension is defined as clinic systolic BP of 180 mmHg or higher, or clinic diastolic BP of 120 mmHg or higher.

concepts.title: Hypertension – NICE 2019 Treatment Threshold Change for Stage 1 Hypertension
concepts.content: In 2019, NICE lowered the threshold for treating stage 1 hypertension in patients under 80 years of age from a 20% to a 10% 10-year cardiovascular risk.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Use of Angiotensin Receptor Blockers as Alternative to ACE-Inhibitors
concepts.content: Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) can be used instead of ACE-inhibitors for hypertension management where indicated.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Addition of Calcium Channel Blocker or Thiazide-Like Diuretic to ACE-Inhibitor or ARB Therapy
concepts.content: If a patient is already taking an ACE-inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker, then either a calcium channel blocker or a thiazide-like diuretic can be added for hypertension management.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Lifestyle Advice: Salt Intake Reduction
concepts.content: A low salt diet is recommended for hypertension management, aiming for less than 6 grams per day, ideally 3 grams per day. Reducing salt intake by 6 grams per day can lower systolic blood pressure by approximately 10 mmHg.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Lifestyle Advice: Caffeine Intake Reduction
concepts.content: Reducing caffeine intake is recommended as part of lifestyle modifications for hypertension management.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Lifestyle Advice: Smoking Cessation
concepts.content: Stopping smoking is recommended as part of lifestyle advice for managing hypertension.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Lifestyle Advice: Alcohol Reduction
concepts.content: Reducing alcohol consumption is advised as part of lifestyle modifications to manage hypertension.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Lifestyle Advice: Balanced Diet and Exercise
concepts.content: Eating a balanced diet rich in fruit and vegetables, increasing physical activity, and losing weight are recommended lifestyle measures for hypertension management.

concepts.title: Hypertension – Indications for Treatment in Stage 1 Hypertension Patients Under 80 Years
concepts.content: Treatment is recommended for patients under 80 years with stage 1 hypertension (ABPM/HBPM >= 135/85 mmHg) if any of the following apply: target organ damage, established cardiovascular disease, renal disease, diabetes, or a 10-year cardiovascular risk of 10% or greater.

concepts.title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Definition
concepts.content: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) is an autosomal dominant disorder of muscle tissue caused by defects in the genes encoding contractile proteins.

concepts.title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Epidemiology
concepts.content: The estimated prevalence of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is 1 in 500.

concepts.title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Management with amiodarone
concepts.content: Amiodarone is used in the management of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

concepts.title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Management with beta-blockers or verapamil for symptoms
concepts.content: Beta-blockers or verapamil are used to manage symptoms in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

concepts.title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Management with cardioverter defibrillator
concepts.content: A cardioverter defibrillator can be used in the management of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

concepts.title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Management with dual chamber pacemaker
concepts.content: A dual chamber pacemaker can be used in the management of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

concepts.title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Endocarditis prophylaxis
concepts.content: Endocarditis prophylaxis is recommended in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, although see the 2008 NICE guidelines on infective endocarditis prophylaxis.

concepts.title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Drugs to avoid: nitrates
concepts.content: Nitrates should be avoided in the management of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

concepts.title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Drugs to avoid: ACE-inhibitors
concepts.content: ACE-inhibitors should be avoided in the management of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

concepts.title: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy – Drugs to avoid: inotropes
concepts.content: Inotropes should be avoided in the management of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Diagnostic criteria overview
concepts.content: Infective endocarditis is diagnosed if pathological criteria are positive, or if there are 2 major criteria, or 1 major and 3 minor criteria, or 5 minor criteria.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Pathological criteria
concepts.content: Pathological criteria are positive histology or microbiology of pathological material obtained at autopsy or cardiac surgery, including valve tissue, vegetations, embolic fragments, or intracardiac abscess content.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Major criterion: Positive blood cultures with typical organisms
concepts.content: Two positive blood cultures showing typical organisms consistent with infective endocarditis, such as Streptococcus viridans and the HACEK group, fulfill a major criterion.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Major criterion: Persistent bacteremia
concepts.content: Persistent bacteremia is defined as two positive blood cultures taken more than 12 hours apart or three or more positive blood cultures where the pathogen is less specific, such as Staphylococcus aureus or Staphylococcus epidermidis.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Major criterion: Positive serology for specific pathogens
concepts.content: Positive serology for Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella species, or Chlamydia psittaci is considered a major criterion for infective endocarditis diagnosis.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Major criterion: Positive molecular assays
concepts.content: Positive molecular assays detecting specific gene targets related to infective endocarditis pathogens fulfill a major diagnostic criterion.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Major criterion: Echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement
concepts.content: Positive echocardiogram findings such as oscillating intracardiac masses, abscess formation, new valvular regurgitation, or dehiscence of prosthetic valves indicate endocardial involvement and fulfill a major criterion.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Major criterion: New valvular regurgitation
concepts.content: Development of new valvular regurgitation on clinical or echocardiographic assessment is a major diagnostic criterion for infective endocarditis.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Minor criterion: Predisposing heart condition or intravenous drug use
concepts.content: A predisposing heart condition or history of intravenous drug use constitutes a minor diagnostic criterion for infective endocarditis.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Minor criterion: Microbiological evidence not meeting major criteria
concepts.content: Microbiological evidence that does not fulfill major criteria, such as positive blood cultures not typical for infective endocarditis organisms, is a minor diagnostic criterion.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Minor criterion: Fever greater than 38ºC
concepts.content: Fever exceeding 38ºC is a minor clinical criterion supporting the diagnosis of infective endocarditis.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Minor criterion: Vascular phenomena
concepts.content: Vascular phenomena including major arterial emboli, splenomegaly, clubbing, splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions, petechiae, or purpura are minor diagnostic criteria.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Minor criterion: Immunological phenomena
concepts.content: Immunological phenomena such as glomerulonephritis, Osler's nodes, and Roth spots are minor diagnostic criteria for infective endocarditis.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – antibiotic prophylaxis guidelines update
concepts.content: The 2008 NICE guidelines have significantly reduced the list of procedures for which antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis is recommended.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – dental procedures and prophylaxis
concepts.content: NICE guidelines recommend that dental procedures do not require antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent infective endocarditis.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – gastrointestinal tract procedures and prophylaxis
concepts.content: NICE guidelines recommend that upper and lower gastrointestinal tract procedures do not require antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis prevention.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – genitourinary tract procedures and prophylaxis
concepts.content: NICE guidelines recommend that genitourinary tract procedures, including urological, gynaecological, obstetric procedures and childbirth, do not require antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis prevention.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – upper and lower respiratory tract procedures and prophylaxis
concepts.content: NICE guidelines recommend that upper and lower respiratory tract procedures, including ear, nose and throat procedures and bronchoscopy, do not require antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis prevention.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – management of infections in at-risk patients
concepts.content: Any episodes of infection in people at risk of infective endocarditis should be promptly investigated and treated to reduce the risk of developing endocarditis.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – antibiotic therapy during gastrointestinal or genitourinary procedures with suspected infection
concepts.content: If a person at risk of infective endocarditis is undergoing gastrointestinal or genitourinary procedures at a site with suspected infection and receiving antimicrobial therapy, they should be given antibiotics covering organisms that cause infective endocarditis.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – guideline differences between NICE and AHA/ESC
concepts.content: NICE guidelines do not recommend antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures, whereas American Heart Association and European Society of Cardiology guidelines still advocate prophylaxis for high-risk patients undergoing dental procedures.

concepts.title: Inhaled foreign body – Definition
concepts.content: Inhaled foreign body refers to the entry of an external object into the respiratory tract, commonly occurring in younger children.

concepts.title: Inhaled foreign body – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Inhaled foreign body typically occurs in younger children.

concepts.title: Inhaled foreign body – Presentation timing
concepts.content: Presentation of inhaled foreign body is often acute but can sometimes go unnoticed, with up to a third of cases diagnosed after a few days.

concepts.title: Inhaled foreign body – Clinical feature: cough
concepts.content: Cough is a common clinical feature of inhaled foreign body.

concepts.title: Inhaled foreign body – Clinical feature: stridor
concepts.content: Stridor is a common clinical feature of inhaled foreign body.

concepts.title: Inhaled foreign body – Clinical feature: dyspnoea
concepts.content: Dyspnoea is a common clinical feature of inhaled foreign body.

concepts.title: Inhaled foreign body – Pathophysiology: location of foreign body
concepts.content: Aspirated foreign bodies are most likely to be found in the right main bronchus because it is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left main bronchus.

concepts.title: Palpitations – Definition
concepts.content: Palpitations are a common presenting symptom characterized by the sensation of an abnormal or irregular heartbeat.

concepts.title: Palpitations – Causes: Arrhythmias
concepts.content: Arrhythmias are a possible cause of palpitations, involving abnormal heart rhythms that can be episodic or sustained.

concepts.title: Palpitations – Causes: Stress
concepts.content: Stress can cause palpitations by increasing sympathetic nervous system activity, leading to heightened awareness of heartbeats.

concepts.title: Palpitations – Causes: Increased awareness of normal heartbeat and extrasystoles
concepts.content: Increased awareness of normal heartbeat or benign extrasystoles can cause palpitations without underlying pathological arrhythmia.

concepts.title: Palpitations – Investigation: 12-lead ECG
concepts.content: A 12-lead ECG is a first-line investigation for palpitations that records heart rhythm for a few seconds and may detect underlying abnormalities such as prolonged QT or PR intervals or signs of recent myocardial ischaemia.

concepts.title: Palpitations – Investigation: Thyroid function tests
concepts.content: Thyroid function tests are performed to detect thyrotoxicosis, which may precipitate atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias causing palpitations.

concepts.title: Palpitations – Investigation: Urea and electrolytes
concepts.content: Urea and electrolyte tests are used to identify disturbances such as hypokalemia that may contribute to arrhythmias causing palpitations.

concepts.title: Palpitations – Investigation: Full blood count
concepts.content: A full blood count is performed to identify hematological abnormalities that may contribute to palpitations.

concepts.title: Palpitations – Capturing episodic arrhythmias
concepts.content: First-line investigations may be normal in palpitations; capturing episodic arrhythmias requires prolonged monitoring to correlate symptoms with heart rhythm abnormalities.

concepts.title: Palpitations – Investigation: Holter monitoring
concepts.content: Holter monitoring is a portable, battery-operated device that continuously records ECG from 2-3 leads, usually for 24 hours, to detect episodic arrhythmias in patients with palpitations.

concepts.title: Palpitations – Holter monitoring: Patient diary
concepts.content: During Holter monitoring, patients keep a diary to record symptomatic palpitations, which is later compared to ECG recordings to correlate symptoms with arrhythmias.

concepts.title: Palpitations – Holter monitoring: Report parameters
concepts.content: The Holter monitor report summarizes parameters including heart rate, arrhythmias, and ECG waveform changes detected during the monitoring period.

concepts.title: Palpitations – Investigation: External loop recorder
concepts.content: If Holter monitoring is normal and symptoms persist, an external loop recorder may be used to capture infrequent arrhythmias by recording ECG over extended periods.

concepts.title: Palpitations – Investigation: Implantable loop recorder
concepts.content: An implantable loop recorder may be used for long-term ECG monitoring to detect rare arrhythmias in patients with ongoing palpitations and normal initial investigations.

concepts.title: Isolated systolic hypertension – Definition
concepts.content: Isolated systolic hypertension (ISH) is a condition characterized by elevated systolic blood pressure with normal diastolic blood pressure, commonly seen in elderly patients.

concepts.title: Isolated systolic hypertension – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Isolated systolic hypertension affects approximately 50% of people older than 70 years old.

concepts.title: Isolated systolic hypertension – Clinical significance of treatment
concepts.content: The Systolic Hypertension in the Elderly Program (SHEP) in 1991 demonstrated that treating isolated systolic hypertension reduces the risk of strokes and ischaemic heart disease.

concepts.title: Isolated systolic hypertension – First-line drug treatment according to SHEP
concepts.content: Thiazide diuretics were recommended as first-line agents for treating isolated systolic hypertension according to the SHEP trial.

concepts.title: Isolated systolic hypertension – NICE 2011 guideline treatment recommendation
concepts.content: The 2011 NICE guidelines recommend treating isolated systolic hypertension using the same stepwise approach as standard hypertension.

concepts.title: Stable angina – Definition
concepts.content: Stable angina is a clinical condition characterized by chest pain due to myocardial ischemia, typically triggered by exertion or stress and relieved by rest or nitrates.

concepts.title: Ivabradine – Mechanism of action
concepts.content: Ivabradine reduces heart rate by selectively inhibiting the If ('funny') ion current in the sinoatrial node, thereby decreasing cardiac pacemaker activity.

concepts.title: Ivabradine – Therapeutic use in stable angina
concepts.content: Ivabradine is used as an anti-anginal drug to reduce heart rate in patients with stable angina.

concepts.title: Ivabradine – Adverse effect: Visual disturbances
concepts.content: Ivabradine commonly causes visual adverse effects, particularly luminous phenomena such as enhanced brightness or phosphenes.

concepts.title: Ivabradine – Adverse effect: Headache
concepts.content: Headache is a known adverse effect associated with ivabradine therapy.

concepts.title: Ivabradine – Adverse effect: Bradycardia and heart block
concepts.content: Ivabradine can cause bradycardia and heart block as adverse cardiac effects due to excessive heart rate reduction.

concepts.title: Ivabradine – Comparative efficacy in stable angina
concepts.content: There is currently no evidence that ivabradine is superior to existing treatments for stable angina.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Definition
concepts.content: Loop diuretics are medications that inhibit the Na-K-Cl cotransporter (NKCC) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, reducing NaCl absorption and promoting diuresis.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Mechanism of action
concepts.content: Loop diuretics inhibit the NKCC2 cotransporter located on the apical membrane of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, decreasing NaCl reabsorption and increasing diuresis.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – NKCC isoforms targeted
concepts.content: Loop diuretics specifically target the NKCC2 isoform of the Na-K-Cl cotransporter, which is predominantly expressed in the kidneys.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Requirement for glomerular filtration
concepts.content: Loop diuretics must be filtered by the glomerulus into the renal tubules to reach their site of action on the apical membrane of the thick ascending limb.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Dose adjustment in renal impairment
concepts.content: Patients with poor renal function may require escalating doses of loop diuretics to achieve effective tubular concentrations due to reduced glomerular filtration.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Indications in heart failure
concepts.content: Loop diuretics are indicated for managing both acute heart failure (usually administered intravenously) and chronic heart failure (usually administered orally).

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Indications in resistant hypertension
concepts.content: Loop diuretics are used to treat resistant hypertension, particularly in patients with renal impairment.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Hypotension
concepts.content: Loop diuretics can cause hypotension due to volume depletion and vasodilation.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Hyponatraemia
concepts.content: Loop diuretics may cause hyponatraemia due to increased sodium excretion.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia
concepts.content: Loop diuretics can cause hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia by increasing renal excretion of potassium and magnesium.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Hypochloraemic alkalosis
concepts.content: Loop diuretics may cause hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis due to loss of chloride and volume contraction.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Ototoxicity
concepts.content: Loop diuretics can cause ototoxicity, potentially leading to hearing loss or tinnitus.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Hypocalcaemia
concepts.content: Loop diuretics may cause hypocalcaemia by increasing calcium excretion in the urine.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Renal impairment
concepts.content: Loop diuretics can cause renal impairment due to dehydration and direct nephrotoxic effects.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Hyperglycaemia
concepts.content: Loop diuretics may cause hyperglycaemia, although this is less common compared to thiazide diuretics.

concepts.title: Loop diuretics – Adverse effect: Gout
concepts.content: Loop diuretics can precipitate gout by reducing uric acid excretion, leading to hyperuricaemia.

concepts.title: Mitral regurgitation – Definition
concepts.content: Mitral regurgitation (MR), also known as mitral insufficiency, is a condition where blood leaks back through the mitral valve during systole.

concepts.title: Mitral regurgitation – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Mitral regurgitation is the second most common valve disease after aortic stenosis.

concepts.title: Mitral regurgitation – Anatomy
concepts.content: The mitral valve is located between the left atrium and left ventricle of the heart.

concepts.title: Mitral regurgitation – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Mitral regurgitation causes blood to flow backward into the left atrium during systole, reducing the efficiency of the heart and decreasing forward blood flow to the body.

concepts.title: Mitral regurgitation – Clinical significance of trivial regurgitation
concepts.content: Trivial mitral regurgitation is common in otherwise healthy patients and typically does not require treatment.

concepts.title: Mitral regurgitation – Progression and myocardial response
concepts.content: Severe mitral regurgitation can cause the myocardium to thicken over time due to increased oxygen demand exceeding supply, which may lead to decreased efficiency and irreversible heart failure.

concepts.title: Mitral regurgitation – Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for mitral regurgitation include female sex, lower body mass, increasing age, renal dysfunction, prior myocardial infarction, prior mitral stenosis or valve prolapse, and collagen disorders such as Marfan's syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

concepts.title: Mitral regurgitation – Cause: Coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Damage to papillary muscles or chordae tendineae from coronary artery disease or myocardial infarction can impair mitral valve function, leading to mitral regurgitation.

concepts.title: Mitral regurgitation – Cause: Mitral valve prolapse
concepts.content: Mitral valve prolapse occurs when the mitral valve leaflets are deformed and do not close properly, causing backflow and often resulting in a trivial degree of mitral regurgitation.

concepts.title: Mitral regurgitation – Cause: Infective endocarditis
concepts.content: Infective endocarditis can cause vegetations on the mitral valve, preventing proper closure and leading to mitral regurgitation; patients with abnormal valves are at higher risk.

concepts.title: Mitral regurgitation – Cause: Rheumatic fever
concepts.content: Rheumatic fever can cause inflammation of the mitral valve leading to mitral regurgitation, although this is uncommon in developed countries.

concepts.title: Mitral regurgitation – Cause: Congenital
concepts.content: Mitral regurgitation can be caused by congenital abnormalities affecting the mitral valve.

concepts.title: Mitral regurgitation – Clinical features: Asymptomatic presentation
concepts.content: Most patients with mitral regurgitation are asymptomatic, especially in mild to moderate cases.

concepts.title: Myocardial infarction – Risk of complications
concepts.content: Patients are at risk of immediate, early, and late complications following a myocardial infarction (MI).

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest – Cause after myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Cardiac arrest most commonly occurs due to ventricular fibrillation following a myocardial infarction and is the most common cause of death post-MI.

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest – Management post-myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Patients with cardiac arrest following myocardial infarction are managed according to the Advanced Life Support (ALS) protocol including defibrillation.

concepts.title: Cardiogenic shock – Pathophysiology post-myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Cardiogenic shock occurs when extensive ventricular myocardium damage reduces ejection fraction, impairing cardiac output after myocardial infarction.

concepts.title: Cardiogenic shock – Mechanical causes post-myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Mechanical complications such as left ventricular free wall rupture can cause cardiogenic shock after myocardial infarction.

concepts.title: Cardiogenic shock – Management
concepts.content: Management of cardiogenic shock may require inotropic support and/or intra-aortic balloon pump insertion.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – Pathophysiology post-myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Survivors of the acute phase of myocardial infarction may develop chronic heart failure due to ventricular myocardium dysfunction.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – Management with loop diuretics
concepts.content: Loop diuretics such as furosemide reduce fluid overload in chronic heart failure post-myocardial infarction.

concepts.title: Chronic heart failure – Prognosis improvement with ACE-inhibitors and beta-blockers
concepts.content: ACE-inhibitors and beta-blockers improve long-term prognosis in patients with chronic heart failure after myocardial infarction.

concepts.title: Tachyarrhythmias – Common types post-myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia are common tachyarrhythmias following myocardial infarction.

concepts.title: Bradyarrhythmias – Atrioventricular block after inferior myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Atrioventricular block is more common following inferior myocardial infarctions.

concepts.title: Pericarditis – Incidence and timing post-transmural myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Pericarditis occurs in approximately 10% of patients within the first 48 hours following a transmural myocardial infarction.

concepts.title: Pericarditis – Clinical features post-myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Pericarditis pain is typically worse when lying flat; a pericardial rub may be heard and pericardial effusion can be detected by echocardiogram.

concepts.title: Dressler's syndrome – Timing post-myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Dressler's syndrome typically occurs 2 to 6 weeks after myocardial infarction.

concepts.title: Dressler's syndrome – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Dressler's syndrome is thought to be an autoimmune reaction against antigenic myocardial proteins formed during recovery after myocardial infarction.

concepts.title: Dressler's syndrome – Clinical features
concepts.content: Dressler's syndrome is characterized by fever, pleuritic chest pain, and pericarditis following myocardial infarction.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Secondary prevention drug therapy
concepts.content: All patients following a myocardial infarction should be offered dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus a second antiplatelet agent), an ACE inhibitor, a beta-blocker, and a statin as part of secondary prevention.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Dual antiplatelet therapy options
concepts.content: Dual antiplatelet therapy after acute coronary syndrome includes aspirin plus a second antiplatelet agent such as ticagrelor or prasugrel, which have largely replaced clopidogrel as the preferred second agents.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Duration of dual antiplatelet therapy post medically managed ACS
concepts.content: For medically managed acute coronary syndrome, ticagrelor is added to aspirin and ticagrelor is stopped after 12 months.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Duration of dual antiplatelet therapy post PCI
concepts.content: After percutaneous coronary intervention, prasugrel or ticagrelor is added to aspirin and the second antiplatelet agent is stopped after 12 months.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Adjustment of dual antiplatelet therapy duration
concepts.content: The 12-month duration of dual antiplatelet therapy may be altered for patients at high risk of bleeding or those at high risk of further ischaemic events.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Aldosterone antagonist therapy indication post MI
concepts.content: Patients who have had an acute myocardial infarction with symptoms and/or signs of heart failure and left ventricular systolic dysfunction should be started on an aldosterone antagonist licensed for post-MI treatment, such as eplerenone.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Timing of aldosterone antagonist initiation post MI
concepts.content: Aldosterone antagonist therapy should be initiated within 3 to 14 days after myocardial infarction, preferably after starting ACE inhibitor therapy.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Lifestyle advice: diet
concepts.content: Patients post myocardial infarction should be advised to follow a Mediterranean style diet, replacing butter and cheese with plant oil-based products; omega-3 supplements and eating oily fish are not recommended.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Lifestyle advice: exercise
concepts.content: Patients post myocardial infarction should be advised to exercise for 20-30 minutes daily until they become slightly breathless.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Sexual activity recommendations post MI
concepts.content: Sexual activity may be resumed 4 weeks after an uncomplicated myocardial infarction; patients should be reassured that sexual activity does not increase the likelihood of further myocardial infarction.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – PDE5 inhibitor use post MI
concepts.content: Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil) may be used 6 months after myocardial infarction but should be avoided in patients prescribed nitrates or nicorandil.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Definition of STEMI
concepts.content: ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is a type of acute coronary syndrome characterized by persistent ST-segment elevation on ECG, indicating transmural myocardial ischemia and infarction.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Aspirin use in STEMI management
concepts.content: In the absence of contraindications, all patients with STEMI should be given aspirin as part of initial management to inhibit platelet aggregation and reduce mortality.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – P2Y12-receptor antagonists in STEMI
concepts.content: P2Y12-receptor antagonists such as clopidogrel, ticagrelor, and prasugrel are used in STEMI management to inhibit platelet aggregation; ticagrelor is often preferred due to improved outcomes despite a slightly higher bleeding risk.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Prasugrel use in PCI for STEMI
concepts.content: Prasugrel, a P2Y12-receptor antagonist, may be considered in STEMI patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) as recommended by SIGN 2016 guidelines.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Anticoagulation in STEMI with PCI
concepts.content: Unfractionated heparin is usually administered to STEMI patients undergoing PCI; low-molecular-weight heparin is an alternative anticoagulant option.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Oxygen therapy recommendations in STEMI
concepts.content: Routine oxygen administration is not recommended in STEMI; oxygen saturation should be monitored by pulse oximetry, and supplemental oxygen given only if SpO2 is below 94% (88-92% in COPD patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure).

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Primary PCI as gold-standard STEMI treatment
concepts.content: Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the gold-standard treatment for STEMI but may not be available in all centers.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Thrombolysis indication in STEMI
concepts.content: Thrombolysis should be performed in STEMI patients who do not have access to primary PCI.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – tPA mortality benefit over streptokinase in STEMI thrombolysis
concepts.content: Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) provides clear mortality benefits compared to streptokinase when used for thrombolysis in STEMI patients.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – Tenecteplase efficacy and administration in STEMI thrombolysis
concepts.content: Tenecteplase is easier to administer and has non-inferior efficacy compared to alteplase with a similar adverse effect profile in STEMI thrombolysis.

concepts.title: Acute coronary syndromes – ECG assessment 90 minutes after thrombolysis
concepts.content: An ECG should be performed 90 minutes after thrombolysis in STEMI patients to assess the degree of ST-segment resolution and reperfusion success.

concepts.title: Angina – Definition
concepts.content: Angina is chest pain or discomfort caused by myocardial ischaemia due to reduced blood flow to the heart muscle.

concepts.title: Nicorandil – Mechanism of action
concepts.content: Nicorandil is a potassium-channel activator that causes vasodilation through activation of guanylyl cyclase, resulting in increased cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) levels.

concepts.title: Nicorandil – Indications
concepts.content: Nicorandil is used as a vasodilatory drug to treat angina.

concepts.title: Nicorandil – Adverse effect: Headache
concepts.content: Headache is a common adverse effect of nicorandil therapy.

concepts.title: Nicorandil – Adverse effect: Flushing
concepts.content: Flushing is a common adverse effect of nicorandil therapy.

concepts.title: Nicorandil – Adverse effect: Skin, mucosal and eye ulceration
concepts.content: Nicorandil can cause ulceration of the skin, mucous membranes, and eyes as an adverse effect.

concepts.title: Nicorandil – Adverse effect: Gastrointestinal ulcers including anal ulceration
concepts.content: Nicorandil may cause gastrointestinal ulcers, including anal ulceration, as an adverse effect.

concepts.title: Nicorandil – Contraindication: Left ventricular failure
concepts.content: Nicorandil is contraindicated in patients with left ventricular failure.

concepts.title: Hyperlipidaemia – Definition and Treatment with Nicotinic Acid
concepts.content: Nicotinic acid (niacin) is used in the treatment of patients with hyperlipidaemia to modify lipid profiles.

concepts.title: Nicotinic Acid – Lipid Profile Effects
concepts.content: Nicotinic acid lowers cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations and raises HDL cholesterol levels.

concepts.title: Nicotinic Acid – Flushing as an Adverse Effect
concepts.content: Flushing is a common adverse effect of nicotinic acid and is mediated by prostaglandins.

concepts.title: Nicotinic Acid – Impaired Glucose Tolerance as an Adverse Effect
concepts.content: Nicotinic acid can cause impaired glucose tolerance as an adverse effect.

concepts.title: Nicotinic Acid – Myositis as an Adverse Effect
concepts.content: Myositis is a potential adverse effect of nicotinic acid therapy.

concepts.title: Nitrates – Definition
concepts.content: Nitrates are a group of drugs that have vasodilating effects.

concepts.title: Nitrates – Indications
concepts.content: Nitrates are mainly indicated for the management of angina and the acute treatment of heart failure.

concepts.title: Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate – Use in ischaemic heart disease
concepts.content: Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate is the most common drug used in patients with ischaemic heart disease to relieve angina attacks.

concepts.title: Nitrates – Mechanism of action
concepts.content: Nitrates cause the release of nitric oxide in smooth muscle, which activates guanylate cyclase to convert GTP to cGMP, leading to a fall in intracellular calcium levels.

concepts.title: Nitrates – Effects in angina
concepts.content: In angina, nitrates dilate coronary arteries and reduce venous return, which decreases left ventricular work and myocardial oxygen demand.

concepts.title: Nitrates – Side effects
concepts.content: Common side effects of nitrates include hypotension, tachycardia, headaches, and flushing.

concepts.title: Nitrate tolerance – Definition
concepts.content: Nitrate tolerance is a condition where patients develop reduced efficacy of nitrates after repeated use.

concepts.title: Nitrate tolerance – Management with isosorbide mononitrate dosing
concepts.content: To reduce nitrate tolerance, the BNF advises taking the second dose of isosorbide mononitrate after 8 hours instead of 12 hours, allowing blood-nitrate levels to fall for 4 hours and maintaining effectiveness.

concepts.title: Nitrate tolerance – Effect on modified release isosorbide mononitrate
concepts.content: Nitrate tolerance is not seen in patients who take modified release isosorbide mononitrate.

concepts.title: Orthostatic hypotension – Definition
concepts.content: Orthostatic hypotension is a condition characterized by a drop in blood pressure, usually greater than 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic, within three minutes of standing.

concepts.title: Orthostatic hypotension – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Orthostatic hypotension is more common in older adults and patients with neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease, diabetes, or hypertension.

concepts.title: Orthostatic hypotension – Iatrogenic causes
concepts.content: Iatrogenic causes of orthostatic hypotension include the use of alpha-blockers, for example those prescribed for benign prostatic hyperplasia.

concepts.title: Orthostatic hypotension – Clinical feature: Blood pressure drop
concepts.content: A key clinical feature of orthostatic hypotension is a drop in blood pressure greater than 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within three minutes of standing.

concepts.title: Orthostatic hypotension – Presentation: Presyncope
concepts.content: Presyncope, a sensation of impending faintness without loss of consciousness, is a common symptom in orthostatic hypotension.

concepts.title: Orthostatic hypotension – Presentation: Syncope
concepts.content: Syncope, or transient loss of consciousness, can occur as a presentation of orthostatic hypotension.

concepts.title: Orthostatic hypotension – Management: Midodrine
concepts.content: Midodrine is a treatment option used to manage orthostatic hypotension by increasing vascular tone and blood pressure.

concepts.title: Orthostatic hypotension – Management: Fludrocortisone
concepts.content: Fludrocortisone is a treatment option for orthostatic hypotension that works by promoting sodium retention and increasing blood volume.

concepts.title: Permanent Pacemaker – Definition
concepts.content: A permanent pacemaker (PPM) is an electronic device that maintains a consistent and physiologically adequate heart rate when the natural cardiac pacemaker system fails.

concepts.title: Cardiac Conduction System – Physiology
concepts.content: Electrical impulses originate from the sinoatrial (SA) node in the right atrium, causing atrial contraction, then travel to the atrioventricular (AV) node and along Purkinje fibres, culminating in ventricular contraction and effective cardiac output.

concepts.title: Cardiac Conduction System Dysfunction – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Dysfunction at any level of the cardiac conduction system can result in arrhythmias due to impaired electrical impulse generation or conduction.

concepts.title: Permanent Pacemaker – Mechanism of Action
concepts.content: A permanent pacemaker delivers timed electrical stimuli to the myocardium to promote effective contractions and maintain circulation when intrinsic conduction is abnormal.

concepts.title: Permanent Pacemaker – Indications
concepts.content: Indications for permanent pacemaker insertion include persistent symptomatic bradycardia such as sick sinus syndrome, complete heart block, Mobitz type II AV block, and persistent AV block after myocardial infarction.

concepts.title: Permanent Pacemaker – Nomenclature Code First Position
concepts.content: The first position in the pacemaker code denotes the chamber paced: V for ventricle, A for atrium, D for dual (both atrium and ventricle), and O for none (no pacing).

concepts.title: Permanent Pacemaker – Nomenclature Code Second Position
concepts.content: The second position in the pacemaker code denotes the chamber sensed: V for ventricle, A for atrium, D for dual (both atrium and ventricle), and O for none (no sensing).

concepts.title: Permanent Pacemaker – Nomenclature Code Third Position
concepts.content: The third position in the pacemaker code denotes the response to sensing: I for inhibited pacing, T for triggered pacing, D for dual (both inhibited and triggered), and O for none (no response to sensing).

concepts.title: Temporary pacemaker – Indication: symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to atropine
concepts.content: A temporary pacemaker is indicated in patients with symptomatic or haemodynamically unstable bradycardia that does not respond to atropine administration.

concepts.title: Temporary pacemaker – Indication: type 2 or complete heart block post-anterior myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Temporary pacing is indicated for patients who develop type 2 or complete heart block following an anterior myocardial infarction.

concepts.title: Complete heart block post-inferior myocardial infarction – Conservative management if asymptomatic and haemodynamically stable
concepts.content: Complete heart block occurring after an inferior myocardial infarction is common and can be managed conservatively if the patient is asymptomatic and haemodynamically stable, without the need for temporary pacing.

concepts.title: Temporary pacemaker – Indication: trifascicular block prior to surgery
concepts.content: A temporary pacemaker is indicated in patients with trifascicular block who are undergoing surgery to prevent perioperative conduction disturbances.

concepts.title: Parenteral anticoagulation – Indications
concepts.content: Parenteral anticoagulants are used for the prevention of venous thromboembolism and in the management of acute coronary syndrome.

concepts.title: Fondaparinux – Mechanism of action
concepts.content: Fondaparinux activates antithrombin III, which potentiates the inhibition of coagulation factor Xa.

concepts.title: Fondaparinux – Route of administration
concepts.content: Fondaparinux is administered via subcutaneous injection.

concepts.title: Direct thrombin inhibitors – Examples
concepts.content: Examples of direct thrombin inhibitors include bivalirudin and dabigatran.

concepts.title: Direct thrombin inhibitors – Route of administration
concepts.content: Direct thrombin inhibitors such as bivalirudin are generally administered intravenously.

concepts.title: Dabigatran – Classification and route
concepts.content: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor taken orally and is often grouped with direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs).

concepts.title: Bradycardia – Definition
concepts.content: Bradycardia is a peri-arrest rhythm characterized by a slower than normal heart rate that may lead to haemodynamic compromise.

concepts.title: Bradycardia – Haemodynamic compromise indicators
concepts.content: Haemodynamic compromise in bradycardia is indicated by adverse signs such as shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, and heart failure.

concepts.title: Shock – Presentation in bradycardia
concepts.content: Shock as an adverse sign in bradycardia includes hypotension (systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg), pallor, sweating, cold clammy extremities, confusion, or impaired consciousness.

concepts.title: Bradycardia – First line treatment for haemodynamic compromise
concepts.content: Atropine 500 mcg IV is the first line treatment for bradycardia with haemodynamic compromise.

concepts.title: Bradycardia – Second line treatments for unsatisfactory atropine response
concepts.content: If atropine response is unsatisfactory, treatments include atropine up to 3 mg total, transcutaneous pacing, and isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion titrated to response.

concepts.title: Bradycardia – Specialist intervention for refractory cases
concepts.content: Specialist help should be sought for consideration of transvenous pacing if there is no response to atropine, transcutaneous pacing, or inotropic infusions.

concepts.title: Bradycardia – Risk factors for asystole
concepts.content: Risk factors for asystole in bradycardia include complete heart block with broad complex QRS, recent asystole, Mobitz type II AV block, and ventricular pause longer than 3 seconds.

concepts.title: Bradycardia – Specialist referral despite satisfactory atropine response if risk factors present
concepts.content: Even with a satisfactory atropine response, specialist help is indicated to consider transvenous pacing if risk factors for asystole are present.

concepts.title: Peri-arrest tachycardia – unified treatment algorithm
concepts.content: The 2015 Resuscitation Council (UK) guidelines replaced separate algorithms for broad-complex tachycardia, narrow-complex tachycardia, and atrial fibrillation with one unified treatment algorithm for peri-arrest tachycardias.

concepts.title: Peri-arrest tachycardia – initial patient assessment
concepts.content: Initial management of peri-arrest tachycardia includes a basic ABC (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) assessment followed by classification of patients as stable or unstable based on the presence of adverse signs.

concepts.title: Peri-arrest tachycardia – adverse signs indicating instability
concepts.content: Adverse signs indicating instability in peri-arrest tachycardia include shock (hypotension with systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg, pallor, sweating, cold clammy extremities, confusion or impaired consciousness), syncope, myocardial ischaemia, and heart failure.

concepts.title: Peri-arrest tachycardia – management of unstable patients
concepts.content: Unstable patients with peri-arrest tachycardia should receive synchronised DC shocks; up to three shocks can be administered before seeking expert help.

concepts.title: Peri-arrest tachycardia – QRS complex classification for treatment
concepts.content: Treatment after initial stabilisation is guided by QRS complex width (narrow or broad) and rhythm regularity (regular or irregular).

concepts.title: Broad-complex tachycardia – regular rhythm assumption
concepts.content: Regular broad-complex tachycardia is assumed to be ventricular tachycardia unless previously confirmed as supraventricular tachycardia with bundle branch block.

concepts.title: Broad-complex tachycardia – regular rhythm management
concepts.content: Management of regular broad-complex tachycardia includes a loading dose of amiodarone followed by a 24-hour infusion.

concepts.title: Broad-complex tachycardia – irregular rhythm management
concepts.content: Irregular broad-complex tachycardia requires expert help; possible causes include atrial fibrillation with bundle branch block, atrial fibrillation with ventricular pre-excitation, and torsade de pointes.

concepts.title: Narrow-complex tachycardia – regular rhythm initial management
concepts.content: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia is initially managed with vagal manoeuvres followed by intravenous adenosine.

concepts.title: Narrow-complex tachycardia – regular rhythm secondary management
concepts.content: If vagal manoeuvres and IV adenosine are unsuccessful in regular narrow-complex tachycardia, consider atrial flutter and control the rate using beta-blockers.

concepts.title: Narrow-complex tachycardia – irregular rhythm probable diagnosis
concepts.content: Irregular narrow-complex tachycardia is probably atrial fibrillation.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – cardioversion indication in peri-arrest tachycardia
concepts.content: In atrial fibrillation with onset less than 48 hours, consider electrical or chemical cardioversion.

concepts.title: Atrial fibrillation – rate control in peri-arrest tachycardia
concepts.content: Rate control in atrial fibrillation is usually achieved with beta-blockers unless contraindicated.

concepts.title: Postural hypotension – Definition
concepts.content: Postural hypotension is defined as a fall of systolic blood pressure greater than 20 mmHg on standing.

concepts.title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Hypovolaemia
concepts.content: Hypovolaemia is a cause of postural hypotension.

concepts.title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Autonomic dysfunction
concepts.content: Autonomic dysfunction is a cause of postural hypotension.

concepts.title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Autonomic dysfunction in diabetes
concepts.content: Diabetes can cause autonomic dysfunction leading to postural hypotension.

concepts.title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Autonomic dysfunction in Parkinson's disease
concepts.content: Parkinson's disease can cause autonomic dysfunction leading to postural hypotension.

concepts.title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Drugs
concepts.content: Certain drugs can cause postural hypotension.

concepts.title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Drugs – Diuretics
concepts.content: Diuretics are drugs that can cause postural hypotension.

concepts.title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Drugs – Antihypertensives
concepts.content: Antihypertensive drugs can cause postural hypotension.

concepts.title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Drugs – L-dopa
concepts.content: L-dopa is a drug that can cause postural hypotension.

concepts.title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Drugs – Phenothiazines
concepts.content: Phenothiazines are drugs that can cause postural hypotension.

concepts.title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Drugs – Antidepressants
concepts.content: Antidepressants are drugs that can cause postural hypotension.

concepts.title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Drugs – Sedatives
concepts.content: Sedatives are drugs that can cause postural hypotension.

concepts.title: Postural hypotension – Cause: Alcohol
concepts.content: Alcohol consumption can cause postural hypotension.

concepts.title: Potassium-sparing diuretics – Classification
concepts.content: Potassium-sparing diuretics are divided into epithelial sodium channel blockers (amiloride and triamterene) and aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone and eplerenone).

concepts.title: Potassium-sparing diuretics – Hyperkalaemia risk with ACE inhibitors
concepts.content: Potassium-sparing diuretics should be used with caution in patients taking ACE inhibitors because they can precipitate hyperkalaemia.

concepts.title: Amiloride – Mechanism of action
concepts.content: Amiloride blocks the epithelial sodium channel in the distal convoluted tubule of the kidney.

concepts.title: Amiloride – Clinical use
concepts.content: Amiloride is a weak diuretic usually given with thiazide or loop diuretics as an alternative to potassium supplementation to prevent hypokalaemia.

concepts.title: Aldosterone antagonists – Site of action
concepts.content: Aldosterone antagonists such as spironolactone act in the cortical collecting duct of the kidney.

concepts.title: Aldosterone antagonists – Indications in ascites
concepts.content: Spironolactone is used in ascites due to cirrhosis where secondary hyperaldosteronism occurs; relatively large doses such as 100-200 mg are often used.

concepts.title: Aldosterone antagonists – Indications in heart failure
concepts.content: Spironolactone is indicated in the management of heart failure.

concepts.title: Aldosterone antagonists – Indications in nephrotic syndrome
concepts.content: Spironolactone is used in the management of nephrotic syndrome.

concepts.title: Aldosterone antagonists – Indications in Conn's syndrome
concepts.content: Spironolactone is indicated in Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism).

concepts.title: Premature ventricular complexes – Definition
concepts.content: Premature ventricular complexes (PVCs) are beats originating in the ventricular myocardium and are also known as premature ventricular beats or ventricular extrasystoles.

concepts.title: Premature ventricular complexes – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Premature ventricular complexes are common and occur in a wide population group, including individuals with and without underlying cardiac disease.

concepts.title: Premature ventricular complexes – Aetiology idiopathic
concepts.content: The vast majority of premature ventricular complexes are idiopathic, occurring without identifiable underlying cardiac disease.

concepts.title: Premature ventricular complexes – Aetiology hypertension
concepts.content: Hypertension is a recognized cause of premature ventricular complexes.

concepts.title: Premature ventricular complexes – Aetiology myocardial infarction
concepts.content: Myocardial infarction is a recognized cause of premature ventricular complexes.

concepts.title: Premature ventricular complexes – Clinical features asymptomatic
concepts.content: The vast majority of patients with premature ventricular complexes are asymptomatic.

concepts.title: Premature ventricular complexes – Clinical features palpitations
concepts.content: Some patients with premature ventricular complexes experience palpitations, typically described as the sensation of a 'skipped beat'.

concepts.title: Premature ventricular complexes – Clinical features pulse irregularity
concepts.content: During regular premature ventricular complexes, the pulse will feel irregular.

concepts.title: Premature ventricular complexes – ECG features
concepts.content: Premature ventricular complexes originate in the ventricles and produce a wide QRS complex on ECG.

concepts.title: Premature ventricular complexes – Management asymptomatic without cardiac disease
concepts.content: Asymptomatic patients with premature ventricular complexes and no evidence of underlying cardiac disease do not require any further management.

concepts.title: Aortic valve disease – Common valves requiring replacement
concepts.content: The aortic valve is one of the most common valves that require replacement.

concepts.title: Mitral valve disease – Common valves requiring replacement
concepts.content: The mitral valve is one of the most common valves that require replacement.

concepts.title: Prosthetic heart valves – Types of replacement valves
concepts.content: There are two main types of prosthetic heart valves used for replacement: biological (bioprosthetic) and mechanical valves.

concepts.title: Bioprosthetic valves – Origin
concepts.content: Biological (bioprosthetic) valves are usually derived from bovine or porcine tissue.

concepts.title: Bioprosthetic valves – Major disadvantage
concepts.content: Bioprosthetic valves have a major disadvantage of structural deterioration and calcification over time.

concepts.title: Bioprosthetic valves – Age considerations for implantation
concepts.content: Most older patients receive bioprosthetic valves: those over 65 years for aortic valve replacement and over 70 years for mitral valve replacement.

concepts.title: Bioprosthetic valves – Anticoagulation requirements
concepts.content: Long-term anticoagulation is usually not needed with bioprosthetic valves; warfarin may be given for the first 3 months depending on patient factors, and low-dose aspirin is given long-term.

concepts.title: Mechanical valves – Common types implanted
concepts.content: The most common mechanical valve now implanted is the bileaflet valve; ball-and-cage valves are rarely used nowadays.

concepts.title: Mechanical valves – Failure rate
concepts.content: Mechanical valves have a low failure rate.

concepts.title: Mechanical valves – Major disadvantage
concepts.content: Mechanical valves have an increased risk of thrombosis, necessitating long-term anticoagulation.

concepts.title: Mechanical valves – Preferred anticoagulant
concepts.content: Warfarin is preferred over direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) for patients with mechanical heart valves.

concepts.title: Mechanical valves – Aspirin use according to 2017 ESC guidelines
concepts.content: Following the 2017 European Society of Cardiology guidelines, aspirin is only given in addition to warfarin if there is an additional indication such as ischaemic heart disease.

concepts.title: Mechanical valves – Target INR values
concepts.content: The target international normalized ratio (INR) for patients with mechanical valves is 3.0 for aortic valve replacements and 3.5 for mitral valve replacements.

concepts.title: Prosthetic heart valves – Endocarditis prophylaxis guidelines
concepts.content: According to the 2008 NICE guidelines, antibiotic prophylaxis for endocarditis is no longer recommended for common procedures such as dental work in patients with prosthetic heart valves.

concepts.title: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure monitoring – Definition
concepts.content: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure (PAOP) is an indirect measure of left atrial pressure and thus reflects the filling pressure of the left heart.

concepts.title: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure monitoring – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Low resistance in the pulmonary venous system allows PAOP to be measured indirectly by occluding a pulmonary artery branch with a balloon-tipped catheter.

concepts.title: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure monitoring – Measurement technique
concepts.content: The most accurate PAOP measurement is obtained by inflating the balloon at the catheter tip and floating it to occlude a pulmonary artery branch; if occlusion is not possible, the measurement reflects pulmonary artery end diastolic pressure.

concepts.title: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure – Normal values
concepts.content: Normal pulmonary artery occlusion pressure ranges from 8 to 12 mmHg.

concepts.title: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure – Low values and causes
concepts.content: A PAOP less than 5 mmHg indicates hypovolaemia; if low PAOP is accompanied by pulmonary oedema, it suggests acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

concepts.title: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure – High values and cause
concepts.content: A PAOP greater than 18 mmHg indicates fluid overload.

concepts.title: Systemic vascular resistance – Definition and calculation
concepts.content: Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) is derived from mean aortic pressure, mean right atrial pressure, and cardiac output, calculated as SVR = 80 × (mean aortic pressure − mean right atrial pressure) / cardiac output.

concepts.title: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure monitoring – Clinical utility
concepts.content: Combining PAOP measurements with systemic vascular resistance and cardiac output allows accurate classification of patients' hemodynamic status.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Definition
concepts.content: Pulmonary embolism is a condition where one or more emboli obstruct the pulmonary arteries, leading to impaired blood flow in the lungs.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Chest pain characteristic
concepts.content: Chest pain in pulmonary embolism is typically pleuritic, meaning it worsens with breathing or coughing.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Dyspnoea
concepts.content: Dyspnoea, or shortness of breath, is a common presenting symptom of pulmonary embolism.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Haemoptysis
concepts.content: Haemoptysis, or coughing up blood, can be a presenting symptom in pulmonary embolism.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Tachycardia
concepts.content: Tachycardia, defined as a heart rate greater than 100 beats per minute, is a common sign in pulmonary embolism.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Tachypnoea
concepts.content: Tachypnoea, defined as a respiratory rate greater than 16 breaths per minute, is present in most patients with pulmonary embolism.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Respiratory examination findings
concepts.content: The chest examination in pulmonary embolism is classically clear, but real-world clinical practice often reveals abnormal findings such as crackles.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Frequency of classic triad presentation
concepts.content: Only about 10% of patients with pulmonary embolism present with the classic triad of pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, and haemoptysis.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Diagnostic challenge
concepts.content: Pulmonary embolism can present with virtually any cardiorespiratory symptom or sign depending on the embolus location and size, making diagnosis difficult.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Tachypnoea frequency (PIOPED study)
concepts.content: The PIOPED study found tachypnoea (respiratory rate >16/min) in 96% of patients diagnosed with pulmonary embolism.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Crackles frequency (PIOPED study)
concepts.content: Crackles were present in 58% of patients with pulmonary embolism according to the PIOPED study.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Tachycardia frequency (PIOPED study)
concepts.content: Tachycardia (heart rate >100/min) was observed in 44% of pulmonary embolism patients in the PIOPED study.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Fever frequency (PIOPED study)
concepts.content: Fever, defined as temperature >37.8°C, was present in 43% of patients with pulmonary embolism in the PIOPED study.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Well's criteria use tachycardia
concepts.content: The Well's criteria for diagnosing pulmonary embolism include tachycardia but do not include tachypnoea as a criterion.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Clinical presentation frequency
concepts.content: Approximately 10% of patients with pulmonary embolism present with the classic triad of pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, and haemoptysis.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Variability of clinical presentation
concepts.content: Pulmonary embolism can present with virtually any cardiorespiratory symptom or sign depending on the embolus location and size, making diagnosis challenging.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Tachypnea frequency
concepts.content: Tachypnea, defined as respiratory rate greater than 20 breaths per minute, occurs in 96% of patients diagnosed with pulmonary embolism according to the PIOPED study.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Crackles frequency
concepts.content: Crackles are present in 58% of patients with pulmonary embolism as reported by the PIOPED study.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Tachycardia frequency
concepts.content: Tachycardia, defined as heart rate greater than 100 beats per minute, occurs in 44% of pulmonary embolism patients according to the PIOPED study.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Fever frequency
concepts.content: Fever, defined as temperature above 37.8°C, is observed in 43% of patients with pulmonary embolism as per the PIOPED study.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Wells criteria use tachycardia
concepts.content: The Wells criteria for diagnosing pulmonary embolism include tachycardia but do not include tachypnea as a diagnostic parameter.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Initial assessment components
concepts.content: All patients with symptoms or signs suggestive of pulmonary embolism should undergo a detailed history, physical examination, and chest X-ray to exclude alternative diagnoses.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria (PERC) purpose
concepts.content: The PERC rule is used to rule out pulmonary embolism in patients with low pre-test probability, providing reassurance that PE is unlikely if all criteria are absent.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – PERC rule application criteria
concepts.content: The PERC rule should be applied when clinical suspicion of pulmonary embolism is low (pre-test probability <15%) and other diagnoses are feasible.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – NICE 2020 guideline update on PERC
concepts.content: NICE 2020 guidelines recommend the use of the PERC rule to safely exclude pulmonary embolism in low-risk patients based on clinical impression and initial investigations.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – First-line anticoagulant treatment
concepts.content: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are recommended as first-line treatment for most people with venous thromboembolism (VTE), including pulmonary embolism (PE), according to NICE 2020 guidelines.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Anticoagulant choice in active cancer
concepts.content: DOACs are now recommended over low-molecular weight heparin (LMWH) for anticoagulation in patients with active cancer and venous thromboembolism, replacing previous guidelines.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Outpatient treatment in low-risk patients
concepts.content: Outpatient management is recommended for patients with low-risk pulmonary embolism, supported by NICE 2020 guidelines, reflecting a shift from routine hospital admission.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Risk stratification for outpatient treatment
concepts.content: NICE recommends using a validated risk stratification tool to determine suitability for outpatient treatment in pulmonary embolism, though no specific tool is mandated.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Use of Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI) score
concepts.content: The 2018 British Society guidelines support using the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI) score as a risk stratification tool to identify low-risk PE patients suitable for outpatient management.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Criteria for outpatient treatment eligibility
concepts.content: Key criteria for outpatient treatment of pulmonary embolism include haemodynamic stability, absence of significant comorbidities, and adequate home support.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Anticoagulant therapy as cornerstone of management
concepts.content: Anticoagulant therapy is the cornerstone of venous thromboembolism management, historically using warfarin with heparin bridging, now increasingly replaced by DOACs.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Use of DOACs at diagnosis suspicion
concepts.content: NICE 2020 guidelines recommend starting direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) once pulmonary embolism is suspected, continuing if diagnosis is confirmed, replacing previous LMWH bridging.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – First-line DOAC options
concepts.content: Apixaban and rivaroxaban, both direct oral anticoagulants, should be offered as first-line anticoagulant treatment following pulmonary embolism diagnosis.

concepts.title: Pulmonary embolism – Routine cancer screening after VTE diagnosis
concepts.content: Routine cancer screening is no longer recommended following a diagnosis of venous thromboembolism, according to NICE 2020 guidelines.

concepts.title: Pulsus paradoxus – Definition
concepts.content: Pulsus paradoxus is defined as a greater than normal (more than 10 mmHg) fall in systolic blood pressure during inspiration, resulting in a faint or absent pulse during inspiration.

concepts.title: Pulsus paradoxus – Associated conditions
concepts.content: Pulsus paradoxus is commonly observed in severe asthma and cardiac tamponade.

concepts.title: Slow-rising pulse – Definition
concepts.content: A slow-rising or plateau pulse is characterized by a delayed and prolonged upstroke of the arterial pulse wave.

concepts.title: Slow-rising pulse – Associated condition
concepts.content: A slow-rising pulse is typically associated with aortic stenosis.

concepts.title: Collapsing pulse – Definition
concepts.content: A collapsing pulse is characterized by a rapid upstroke and downstroke with a sudden collapse of the arterial pulse.

concepts.title: Collapsing pulse – Associated conditions
concepts.content: Collapsing pulse is associated with aortic regurgitation, patent ductus arteriosus, and hyperkinetic states such as anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, fever, exercise, and pregnancy.

concepts.title: Pulsus alternans – Definition
concepts.content: Pulsus alternans is the regular alternation of the force of the arterial pulse with each heartbeat.

concepts.title: Pulsus alternans – Associated condition
concepts.content: Pulsus alternans is a sign of severe left ventricular failure (LVF).

concepts.title: Bisferiens pulse – Definition
concepts.content: Bisferiens pulse is characterized by a 'double pulse' with two systolic peaks in the arterial waveform.

concepts.title: Bisferiens pulse – Associated condition
concepts.content: Bisferiens pulse is typically seen in mixed aortic valve disease.

concepts.title: Jerky pulse – Definition
concepts.content: A 'jerky' pulse is characterized by a forceful and brisk arterial pulse with a rapid upstroke and a sudden collapse.

concepts.title: Jerky pulse – Associated condition
concepts.content: A jerky pulse is associated with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM).

concepts.title: Bisferiens pulse – Occasional association with HOCM
concepts.content: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) may occasionally be associated with a bisferiens pulse.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Definition
concepts.content: Rheumatic fever is an immunological reaction that develops 2-4 weeks after a Streptococcus pyogenes infection.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Pathophysiology: Immune activation
concepts.content: Streptococcus pyogenes infection activates the innate immune system leading to antigen presentation to T cells.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Pathophysiology: Adaptive immune response
concepts.content: B and T cells produce IgG and IgM antibodies and activate CD4+ T cells in response to Streptococcus pyogenes antigens.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Pathophysiology: Molecular mimicry and cross-reactivity
concepts.content: Antibodies against Streptococcus pyogenes M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin and arterial smooth muscle, causing a type II hypersensitivity reaction.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Pathophysiology: Aschoff bodies
concepts.content: Aschoff bodies are granulomatous nodules found in the myocardium of patients with rheumatic fever.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Diagnostic criteria: Evidence of recent streptococcal infection
concepts.content: Diagnosis requires evidence of recent streptococcal infection demonstrated by raised or rising streptococcal antibodies, positive throat swab, or positive rapid group A streptococcal antigen test.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Diagnostic criteria: Major criteria overview
concepts.content: Diagnosis requires either two major criteria or one major plus two minor criteria in the presence of recent streptococcal infection.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Major criteria: Erythema marginatum
concepts.content: Erythema marginatum is a major diagnostic criterion characterized by a distinctive rash seen in rheumatic fever.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Major criteria: Sydenham's chorea
concepts.content: Sydenham's chorea is a late neurological manifestation of rheumatic fever characterized by involuntary, rapid movements.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Major criteria: Polyarthritis
concepts.content: Polyarthritis involving large joints is a major diagnostic criterion of rheumatic fever.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Major criteria: Carditis and valvulitis
concepts.content: Carditis and valvulitis, including pancarditis, are major criteria; diagnosis requires evidence of endocarditis manifesting as valvulitis with a regurgitant murmur.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Major criteria: Subcutaneous nodules
concepts.content: Subcutaneous nodules are painless lumps over bony prominences and are a major diagnostic criterion in rheumatic fever.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Minor criteria: Raised ESR or CRP
concepts.content: Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP) levels are minor diagnostic criteria in rheumatic fever.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Minor criteria: Pyrexia
concepts.content: Fever (pyrexia) is a minor diagnostic criterion in rheumatic fever.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Minor criteria: Arthralgia
concepts.content: Arthralgia, or joint pain without arthritis, is a minor diagnostic criterion in rheumatic fever.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Minor criteria: Prolonged PR interval
concepts.content: A prolonged PR interval on electrocardiogram is a minor diagnostic criterion in rheumatic fever.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Management: Antibiotic therapy
concepts.content: Oral penicillin V is the first-line antibiotic treatment to eradicate Streptococcus pyogenes in rheumatic fever.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Management: Anti-inflammatory treatment
concepts.content: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are first-line agents for controlling inflammation in rheumatic fever.

concepts.title: Rheumatic fever – Management: Treatment of complications
concepts.content: Management includes treatment of complications such as heart failure that may develop secondary to rheumatic fever.

concepts.title: Saphenous vein – Definition
concepts.content: The saphenous veins are superficial veins of the lower limb consisting of the long (great) saphenous vein and the short (small) saphenous vein.

concepts.title: Long saphenous vein – Clinical use in bypass surgery
concepts.content: The long saphenous vein may be harvested for use as a conduit in bypass surgery.

concepts.title: Long saphenous vein – Treatment of varicose veins
concepts.content: The long saphenous vein can be removed as treatment for varicose veins associated with saphenofemoral junction incompetence.

concepts.title: Long saphenous vein – Origin
concepts.content: The long saphenous vein originates at the first digit of the foot where the dorsal vein merges with the dorsal venous arch.

concepts.title: Long saphenous vein – Course at the medial malleolus and leg
concepts.content: The long saphenous vein passes anterior to the medial malleolus and runs up the medial side of the leg.

concepts.title: Long saphenous vein – Course at the knee
concepts.content: At the knee, the long saphenous vein runs over the posterior border of the medial epicondyle of the femur bone.

concepts.title: Long saphenous vein – Course on the thigh and saphenous opening
concepts.content: The long saphenous vein passes laterally to lie on the anterior surface of the thigh before entering the saphenous opening in the fascia lata.

concepts.title: Long saphenous vein – Termination at saphenofemoral junction
concepts.content: The long saphenous vein joins the femoral vein in the femoral triangle region at the saphenofemoral junction.

concepts.title: Long saphenous vein – Tributaries
concepts.content: The tributaries of the long saphenous vein include the medial marginal vein, superficial epigastric vein, superficial iliac circumflex vein, and superficial external pudendal veins.

concepts.title: Short saphenous vein – Origin
concepts.content: The short saphenous vein originates at the fifth digit of the foot where the dorsal vein merges with the dorsal venous arch, which connects to the great saphenous vein.

concepts.title: Short saphenous vein – Course around the foot and leg
