concepts.content: The short saphenous vein passes around the lateral aspect of the foot, inferior and posterior to the lateral malleolus, and runs along the posterior aspect of the leg alongside the sural nerve.

concepts.title: Short saphenous vein – Course at the knee and drainage
concepts.content: The short saphenous vein passes between the heads of the gastrocnemius muscle and drains into the popliteal vein approximately at or above the level of the knee joint.

concepts.title: Atrial Fibrillation – Anticoagulation Risk Assessment
concepts.content: The CHA2DS2-VASc score is used to determine the need for anticoagulation therapy in patients with atrial fibrillation to prevent stroke.

concepts.title: Heart Failure – Severity Classification
concepts.content: The NYHA (New York Heart Association) classification is a heart failure severity scale that categorizes patients based on symptoms and physical activity limitations.

concepts.title: Deep Vein Thrombosis – Risk Estimation
concepts.content: The Wells score helps estimate the probability of a patient having deep vein thrombosis based on clinical features and risk factors.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Prognosis Assessment
concepts.content: The CURB-65 score is used to assess the prognosis of patients with pneumonia and guide management decisions.

concepts.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea – Symptom Assessment
concepts.content: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale is used to assess daytime sleepiness in patients suspected of having obstructive sleep apnoea.

concepts.title: Prostate Cancer – Prognosis Indicator
concepts.content: The Gleason score indicates the prognosis of prostate cancer based on histological grading of tumor tissue.

concepts.title: Newborn – Immediate Health Assessment
concepts.content: The APGAR score assesses the health of a newborn immediately after birth by evaluating Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, and Respiration.

concepts.title: Labour – Induction Readiness Assessment
concepts.content: The Bishop score is used to assess the likelihood that induction of labour will be required based on cervical status and fetal position.

concepts.title: Pressure Ulcer – Risk Assessment
concepts.content: The Waterlow score assesses the risk of a patient developing pressure sores based on multiple risk factors including mobility and skin condition.

concepts.title: Osteoporosis – Fracture Risk Assessment
concepts.content: The FRAX tool, developed by WHO, calculates a patient's 10-year risk of developing an osteoporosis-related fracture.

concepts.title: Statins – Mechanism of action
concepts.content: Statins inhibit the action of HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis.

concepts.title: Statins – Myopathy adverse effects
concepts.content: Statin-induced myopathy includes myalgia, myositis, rhabdomyolysis, and asymptomatic raised creatine kinase.

concepts.title: Statins – Risk factors for myopathy
concepts.content: Risk factors for statin-induced myopathy include advanced age, female sex, low body mass index, and multisystem diseases such as diabetes mellitus.

concepts.title: Statins – Myopathy risk by statin lipophilicity
concepts.content: Myopathy is more common with lipophilic statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin) than with relatively hydrophilic statins (rosuvastatin, pravastatin, fluvastatin).

concepts.title: Statins – Liver impairment monitoring
concepts.content: NICE 2014 guidelines recommend checking liver function tests at baseline, 3 months, and 12 months during statin therapy; treatment should be discontinued if serum transaminases rise to and persist at three times the upper limit of normal.

concepts.title: Statins – Intracerebral haemorrhage risk in secondary stroke prevention
concepts.content: Statins may increase the risk of intracerebral haemorrhage in patients with a history of stroke; this risk is not observed in primary prevention.

concepts.title: Statins – Recommendation to avoid in patients with prior intracerebral haemorrhage
concepts.content: The Royal College of Physicians recommends avoiding statins in patients with a history of intracerebral haemorrhage.

concepts.title: Statins – Drug interactions with macrolides
concepts.content: Macrolide antibiotics such as erythromycin and clarithromycin interact with statins; statin therapy should be stopped until completion of the macrolide course.

concepts.title: Statins – Contraindication in pregnancy
concepts.content: Statins are contraindicated during pregnancy.

concepts.title: Statins – Indications in established cardiovascular disease
concepts.content: All patients with established cardiovascular disease including stroke, transient ischemic attack, ischemic heart disease, and peripheral arterial disease should receive statins.

concepts.title: Statins – Indications based on 10-year cardiovascular risk
concepts.content: NICE 2014 recommends statin therapy for anyone with a 10-year cardiovascular risk of 10% or greater.

concepts.title: Statins – Use in type 2 diabetes mellitus
concepts.content: Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus should be assessed using QRISK2 to determine the need for statin therapy.

concepts.title: Statins – Use in type 1 diabetes mellitus
concepts.content: Patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus diagnosed more than 10 years ago, or aged over 40 years, or with established nephropathy should receive statins.

concepts.title: Statins – Timing of administration
concepts.content: Statins should be taken at night because the majority of cholesterol synthesis occurs during this time; this is especially important for simvastatin due to its shorter half-life.

concepts.title: Subclavian artery – Definition and function
concepts.content: The subclavian arteries are major vessels of the upper thorax that supply blood to the upper limbs, neck, brain, and thoracic wall.

concepts.title: Subclavian artery – Origin of left subclavian artery
concepts.content: The left subclavian artery arises directly from the arch of the aorta.

concepts.title: Subclavian artery – Origin of right subclavian artery
concepts.content: The right subclavian artery originates from the brachiocephalic trunk, which bifurcates into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries.

concepts.title: Subclavian artery – Course and anatomical relations
concepts.content: The subclavian artery travels laterally, arching upward and laterally behind the clavicle, passing between the anterior and middle scalene muscles within the scalene triangle; it lies posterior to scalenus anterior and anterior to scalenus medius.

concepts.title: Subclavian artery – Transition to axillary artery
concepts.content: As the subclavian artery crosses the lateral border of the first rib, it becomes the axillary artery, which continues to supply the upper limb.

concepts.title: Subclavian artery – Accessibility in subclavian triangle
concepts.content: In the subclavian triangle, the subclavian artery is relatively superficial and accessible for clinical procedures.

concepts.title: Subclavian artery – Vertebral artery branch anatomy and function
concepts.content: The vertebral artery ascends through the transverse foramina of C6 to C1 vertebrae to enter the foramen magnum and contributes to the circle of Willis.

concepts.title: Subclavian artery – Internal thoracic artery branch anatomy and function
concepts.content: The internal thoracic artery (internal mammary artery) descends into the thorax to supply the anterior chest wall and breasts.

concepts.title: Subclavian artery – Thyrocervical trunk branch anatomy and function
concepts.content: The thyrocervical trunk gives off branches to the thyroid gland, neck muscles, and scapular region.

concepts.title: Subclavian artery – Costocervical trunk branch anatomy and function
concepts.content: The costocervical trunk divides into deep cervical and superior intercostal arteries, supplying the upper intercostal spaces and deep neck muscles.

concepts.title: Subclavian artery – Dorsal scapular artery anatomy and function
concepts.content: The dorsal scapular artery supplies the levator scapulae and rhomboid muscles and sometimes arises from the transverse cervical artery.

concepts.title: Subclavian steal syndrome – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Subclavian steal syndrome occurs due to proximal subclavian artery stenosis or occlusion causing reversal of blood flow in the vertebral artery, leading to vertebrobasilar insufficiency.

concepts.title: Subclavian steal syndrome – Clinical features
concepts.content: Symptoms of subclavian steal syndrome include dizziness, syncope, and arm claudication due to vertebrobasilar insufficiency.

concepts.title: Thoracic outlet syndrome – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Thoracic outlet syndrome involves compression of the subclavian artery, vein, and/or brachial plexus as they pass through the scalene triangle.

concepts.title: Thoracic outlet syndrome – Clinical features
concepts.content: Thoracic outlet syndrome presents with upper limb ischaemia, numbness, and weakness due to vascular and/or neural compression.

concepts.title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Definition
concepts.content: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) refers to any tachycardia that is not ventricular in origin, commonly used to describe paroxysmal SVT.

concepts.title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Pathophysiology: AVNRT
concepts.content: Atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia (AVNRT) is the typical mechanism causing sudden onset narrow complex tachycardia in SVT.

concepts.title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Pathophysiology: AVRT and junctional tachycardias
concepts.content: Other causes of SVT include atrioventricular re-entry tachycardias (AVRT) and junctional tachycardias.

concepts.title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Clinical feature: sudden onset narrow complex tachycardia
concepts.content: Episodes of SVT are characterised by sudden onset of narrow complex tachycardia.

concepts.title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Acute management: vagal manoeuvres
concepts.content: Vagal manoeuvres such as the Valsalva manoeuvre and carotid sinus massage are first-line acute treatments for SVT.

concepts.title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Acute management: Valsalva manoeuvre technique
concepts.content: The Valsalva manoeuvre involves trying to blow into an empty plastic syringe to increase vagal tone and terminate SVT.

concepts.title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Acute management: intravenous adenosine dosing
concepts.content: Intravenous adenosine is given as a rapid IV bolus starting with 6 mg, followed by 12 mg if unsuccessful, and then 18 mg if further doses are needed.

concepts.title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Acute management: adenosine contraindications
concepts.content: Adenosine is contraindicated in asthmatic patients; verapamil is preferred in these cases.

concepts.title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Acute management: treatment if vagal manoeuvres and adenosine fail
concepts.content: If vagal manoeuvres and adenosine are ineffective, intravenous verapamil or beta-blockers should be administered.

concepts.title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Acute management: electrical cardioversion
concepts.content: Electrical cardioversion is indicated if pharmacological and vagal manoeuvres fail to terminate SVT.

concepts.title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Prevention: beta-blockers
concepts.content: Beta-blockers can be used to prevent recurrent episodes of SVT.

concepts.title: Supraventricular tachycardia – Prevention: radio-frequency ablation
concepts.content: Radio-frequency ablation is an effective preventive treatment for recurrent SVT episodes.

concepts.title: Takayasu's arteritis – Definition
concepts.content: Takayasu's arteritis is a large vessel vasculitis primarily affecting the aorta and its major branches.

concepts.title: Takayasu's arteritis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Takayasu's arteritis is more common in younger females aged 10-40 years and in Asian populations.

concepts.title: Takayasu's arteritis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Takayasu's arteritis causes occlusion of the aorta and its major branches leading to ischemia and absent limb pulses.

concepts.title: Takayasu's arteritis – Systemic features
concepts.content: Systemic features include malaise and headache due to underlying vasculitis.

concepts.title: Takayasu's arteritis – Unequal blood pressure in upper limbs
concepts.content: Patients may present with unequal blood pressure measurements between the upper limbs.

concepts.title: Takayasu's arteritis – Carotid bruit and tenderness
concepts.content: Carotid artery bruit and tenderness may be present on clinical examination.

concepts.title: Takayasu's arteritis – Absent or weak peripheral pulses
concepts.content: Peripheral pulses may be absent or weak due to arterial occlusion.

concepts.title: Takayasu's arteritis – Limb claudication on exertion
concepts.content: Patients experience claudication in upper and lower limbs during exertion due to ischemia.

concepts.title: Takayasu's arteritis – Aortic regurgitation
concepts.content: Aortic regurgitation occurs in approximately 20% of patients due to aortic root involvement.

concepts.title: Takayasu's arteritis – Association with renal artery stenosis
concepts.content: Takayasu's arteritis is associated with renal artery stenosis due to involvement of renal arteries.

concepts.title: Takayasu's arteritis – Diagnostic investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis requires vascular imaging of the arterial tree using magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) or computed tomography angiography (CTA).

concepts.title: Takayasu's arteritis – Management
concepts.content: First-line treatment for Takayasu's arteritis is corticosteroids to reduce vascular inflammation.

concepts.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Definition
concepts.content: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is a type of non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy characterized by transient apical ballooning of the myocardium.

concepts.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Trigger
concepts.content: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy may be triggered by physical or emotional stress.

concepts.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Pathophysiology description
concepts.content: The term 'Takotsubo' refers to a Japanese octopus trap, reflecting the heart's apical ballooning appearance in this condition.

concepts.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Pathophysiology mechanism
concepts.content: Apical ballooning occurs due to severe hypokinesis of the mid and apical myocardial segments with preserved contraction of the basal segments.

concepts.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Clinical presentation chest pain
concepts.content: Patients with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy commonly present with chest pain.

concepts.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Clinical presentation heart failure features
concepts.content: Patients may exhibit features of heart failure during Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.

concepts.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – ECG findings
concepts.content: Electrocardiogram typically shows ST-segment elevation in Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.

concepts.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Coronary angiogram findings
concepts.content: Coronary angiogram is typically normal in Takotsubo cardiomyopathy despite ECG changes.

concepts.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Treatment
concepts.content: Management of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is primarily supportive.

concepts.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy – Prognosis
concepts.content: The majority of patients with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy improve with supportive treatment.

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Definition
concepts.content: Thrombolysis involves the use of thrombolytic drugs that act as tissue plasminogen activators, converting plasminogen into plasmin, an enzyme that breaks down fibrin and dissolves blood clots.

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Primary Indication
concepts.content: Thrombolytic drugs are primarily used in patients presenting with ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Other Indications
concepts.content: Other indications for thrombolysis include acute ischaemic stroke and pulmonary embolism, although strict inclusion criteria apply.

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Examples of Drugs
concepts.content: Examples of thrombolytic drugs include alteplase, tenecteplase, and streptokinase.

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Active Internal Bleeding
concepts.content: Active internal bleeding is a contraindication to thrombolysis due to increased risk of hemorrhage.

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Recent Haemorrhage, Trauma or Surgery
concepts.content: Recent haemorrhage, trauma, or surgery, including dental extraction, contraindicates thrombolysis due to bleeding risk.

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Coagulation and Bleeding Disorders
concepts.content: Coagulation and bleeding disorders are contraindications to thrombolysis due to elevated hemorrhage risk.

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Intracranial Neoplasm
concepts.content: Presence of an intracranial neoplasm contraindicates thrombolysis because of increased bleeding risk.

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Stroke Within 3 Months
concepts.content: A history of stroke within the previous 3 months is a contraindication to thrombolysis due to hemorrhagic risk.

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Aortic Dissection
concepts.content: Aortic dissection is a contraindication to thrombolysis because it may worsen bleeding and dissection.

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Recent Head Injury
concepts.content: Recent head injury contraindicates thrombolysis due to increased risk of intracranial hemorrhage.

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Contraindication: Severe Hypertension
concepts.content: Severe hypertension is a contraindication to thrombolysis due to increased risk of hemorrhagic complications.

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Side Effect: Haemorrhage
concepts.content: Haemorrhage is a common side effect of thrombolytic therapy due to fibrin breakdown and impaired clotting.

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Side Effect: Hypotension
concepts.content: Hypotension is a side effect of thrombolysis and is more commonly observed with streptokinase.

concepts.title: Thrombolysis – Side Effect: Allergic Reactions with Streptokinase
concepts.content: Allergic reactions may occur with streptokinase administration during thrombolytic therapy.

concepts.title: Torsades de pointes – Definition
concepts.content: Torsades de pointes is a form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with a long QT interval.

concepts.title: Torsades de pointes – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Torsades de pointes may deteriorate into ventricular fibrillation, which can lead to sudden death.

concepts.title: Long QT interval – Congenital causes
concepts.content: Congenital causes of long QT interval include Jervell-Lange-Nielsen syndrome and Romano-Ward syndrome.

concepts.title: Long QT interval – Drug-induced causes
concepts.content: Drugs that can cause long QT interval include antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone, sotalol, class 1a antiarrhythmic drugs, tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics, chloroquine, terfenadine, and erythromycin.

concepts.title: Long QT interval – Electrolyte causes
concepts.content: Electrolyte abnormalities causing long QT interval include hypocalcaemia, hypokalaemia, and hypomagnesaemia.

concepts.title: Long QT interval – Other medical causes
concepts.content: Other medical causes of long QT interval include myocarditis, hypothermia, and subarachnoid haemorrhage.

concepts.title: Torsades de pointes – Management
concepts.content: Intravenous magnesium sulphate is the treatment of choice for torsades de pointes.

concepts.title: Travel-related thrombosis – Definition
concepts.content: Travel-related thrombosis refers to venous thromboembolism (VTE) occurring in association with prolonged travel, especially long-haul flights.

concepts.title: Travel-related thrombosis – Pathophysiology of risk in long-haul flights
concepts.content: Long-haul air travel is associated with increased risk of venous thromboembolism due to prolonged immobility leading to venous stasis and hypercoagulability.

concepts.title: Travel-related thrombosis – Risk of pulmonary embolism by travel distance
concepts.content: Pulmonary embolism risk increases with travel distance: 0.01 cases per million for travel under 5,000 km, 1.5 cases per million for 5,000-10,000 km, and 4.8 cases per million for travel over 10,000 km.

concepts.title: Travel-related thrombosis – Guidelines on prevention from British Committee for Standards in Haematology and SIGN
concepts.content: British Committee for Standards in Haematology (2005) and SIGN (2010) published guidelines on prevention of travel-related thrombosis, but no universal consensus exists.

concepts.title: Travel-related thrombosis – Role of Civil Aviation Authority guidance
concepts.content: The Civil Aviation Authority does not provide specific guidance regarding venous thromboembolism prevention in air travel.

concepts.title: Travel-related thrombosis – Use of anti-embolism stockings in major risk patients
concepts.content: Patients with major risk factors for travel-related thrombosis should consider wearing anti-embolism stockings, which can be purchased or prescribed (class I recommendation).

concepts.title: Travel-related thrombosis – Management of very high risk patients
concepts.content: For very high risk patients (e.g., long-haul flight after recent major surgery), delaying the flight or seeking specialist advice regarding low-molecular weight heparin use should be considered.

concepts.title: Travel-related thrombosis – Role of aspirin in prevention
concepts.content: All guidelines agree that aspirin has no role in preventing travel-related thrombosis in low, medium, or high risk patients.

concepts.title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Definition
concepts.content: Tricuspid regurgitation is a condition characterized by the backflow of blood from the right ventricle into the right atrium during systole due to incompetence of the tricuspid valve.

concepts.title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Sign: Pan-systolic murmur
concepts.content: A pan-systolic murmur is a continuous heart murmur heard throughout systole, commonly associated with tricuspid regurgitation.

concepts.title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Sign: Prominent/giant V waves in jugular venous pressure
concepts.content: Prominent or giant V waves in the jugular venous pressure waveform indicate increased right atrial pressure during ventricular systole, commonly seen in tricuspid regurgitation.

concepts.title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Sign: Pulsatile hepatomegaly
concepts.content: Pulsatile hepatomegaly is an enlarged liver with a palpable pulsation due to transmitted venous pulsations from tricuspid regurgitation.

concepts.title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Sign: Left parasternal heave
concepts.content: A left parasternal heave is a palpable precordial impulse due to right ventricular hypertrophy, which can be present in tricuspid regurgitation.

concepts.title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Cause: Right ventricular infarction
concepts.content: Right ventricular infarction can cause tricuspid regurgitation by impairing right ventricular function and tricuspid valve competence.

concepts.title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Cause: Pulmonary hypertension
concepts.content: Pulmonary hypertension, such as that caused by chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), can lead to tricuspid regurgitation by causing right ventricular pressure overload and valve incompetence.

concepts.title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Cause: Rheumatic heart disease
concepts.content: Rheumatic heart disease can cause tricuspid regurgitation through valvular damage and scarring affecting the tricuspid valve.

concepts.title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Cause: Infective endocarditis
concepts.content: Infective endocarditis, especially in intravenous drug users, can cause tricuspid regurgitation by damaging the tricuspid valve leaflets.

concepts.title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Cause: Ebstein's anomaly
concepts.content: Ebstein's anomaly is a congenital malformation of the tricuspid valve that can cause tricuspid regurgitation due to leaflet displacement and malformation.

concepts.title: Tricuspid regurgitation – Cause: Carcinoid syndrome
concepts.content: Carcinoid syndrome can cause tricuspid regurgitation by inducing fibrous plaque formation on the tricuspid valve leaflets leading to valve dysfunction.

concepts.title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Definition
concepts.content: The Valsalva manoeuvre is a forced exhalation against a closed airway, producing four characteristic phases of blood pressure and heart rate change.

concepts.title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Baroreflex activation
concepts.content: The Valsalva manoeuvre triggers the baroreflex, a key mechanism for assessing autonomic nervous system function.

concepts.title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Clinical use in cardiology
concepts.content: Used as a bedside intervention to terminate some episodes of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) by increasing vagal tone and as part of heart murmur assessment, including accentuation of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and reduction of aortic stenosis murmurs.

concepts.title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Clinical use in autonomic testing
concepts.content: Used to assess baroreflex integrity and diagnose disorders of autonomic function.

concepts.title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Clinical use in ENT and aviation medicine
concepts.content: Used to equalise middle ear pressure during changes in altitude or pressure.

concepts.title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Phase I pathophysiology
concepts.content: Onset of strain with forced exhalation against closed airway increases intrathoracic and intra-abdominal pressure, compressing the aorta and large chest vessels, causing a brief spike in blood pressure and slight heart rate decrease.

concepts.title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Phase II pathophysiology
concepts.content: Continued strain maintains raised intrathoracic pressure, compressing great veins and reducing venous return, leading to decreased ventricular filling, stroke volume, and blood pressure; baroreflex triggers sympathetic activation increasing heart rate and vasoconstriction, causing partial blood pressure recovery.

concepts.title: Valsalva manoeuvre – Phase III pathophysiology
concepts.content: Release of strain causes sudden fall in intrathoracic pressure as normal breathing resumes, leading to transient changes in blood pressure and heart rate (content truncated).

concepts.title: Ventricular tachycardia – Peri-arrest broad complex tachycardia assumption
concepts.content: In a peri-arrest situation, a broad complex tachycardia should be assumed to be ventricular in origin according to the European Resuscitation Council, even though it may result from a supraventricular rhythm with aberrant conduction.

concepts.title: Ventricular tachycardia – Adverse signs indicating immediate cardioversion
concepts.content: Adverse signs in ventricular tachycardia that indicate immediate cardioversion include systolic blood pressure less than 90 mmHg, chest pain, heart failure, and syncope.

concepts.title: Ventricular tachycardia – Immediate cardioversion indication
concepts.content: Immediate cardioversion is indicated in ventricular tachycardia patients presenting with adverse signs such as hypotension, chest pain, heart failure, or syncope.

concepts.title: Ventricular tachycardia – Use of antiarrhythmics in absence of adverse signs
concepts.content: In ventricular tachycardia patients without adverse signs, antiarrhythmic drugs may be used as initial management.

concepts.title: Ventricular tachycardia – Electrical cardioversion after failed antiarrhythmics
concepts.content: If antiarrhythmic drug therapy fails to control ventricular tachycardia, electrical cardioversion with synchronized direct current shocks may be required.

concepts.title: Ventricular tachycardia – Amiodarone administration route
concepts.content: Amiodarone is ideally administered through a central line when used for ventricular tachycardia management.

concepts.title: Ventricular tachycardia – Lidocaine caution in severe left ventricular impairment
concepts.content: Lidocaine should be used with caution in ventricular tachycardia patients who have severe left ventricular impairment.

concepts.title: Ventricular tachycardia – Procainamide use
concepts.content: Procainamide is an antiarrhythmic drug option for the management of ventricular tachycardia.

concepts.title: Ventricular tachycardia – Verapamil contraindication
concepts.content: Verapamil should NOT be used in the management of ventricular tachycardia.

concepts.title: Ventricular tachycardia – Electrophysiological study after failed drug therapy
concepts.content: If drug therapy fails to control ventricular tachycardia, an electrophysiological study (EPS) may be performed for further evaluation and management.

concepts.title: Ventricular tachycardia – Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator indication
concepts.content: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) placement is particularly indicated in ventricular tachycardia patients with significantly impaired left ventricular function.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Definition
concepts.content: Warfarin is an oral anticoagulant historically used as first-line therapy for venous thromboembolism management and stroke risk reduction in atrial fibrillation patients.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Current clinical use
concepts.content: Warfarin use has been largely superseded by direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) due to DOACs requiring less intensive monitoring.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Mechanism of action
concepts.content: Warfarin inhibits epoxide reductase, preventing the reduction of vitamin K to its active hydroquinone form, which is necessary as a cofactor for carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X and protein C.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Indications mechanical heart valves
concepts.content: Warfarin is indicated for anticoagulation in patients with mechanical heart valves, with target INR depending on valve type and location; mitral valves generally require a higher INR than aortic valves.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Indications venous thromboembolism second-line
concepts.content: Warfarin is used as a second-line anticoagulant after DOACs for venous thromboembolism, with a target INR of 2.5, increased to 3.5 if recurrent events occur.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Indications atrial fibrillation second-line
concepts.content: Warfarin is used as a second-line anticoagulant after DOACs for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation, with a target INR of 2.5.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Monitoring with INR
concepts.content: Warfarin therapy is monitored using the international normalized ratio (INR), which is the ratio of the patient's prothrombin time to normal prothrombin time.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Pharmacokinetics and dose adjustment
concepts.content: Warfarin has a long half-life and achieving a stable INR may take several days; various loading regimens exist and computer software is often used to adjust dosing.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Factors potentiating effect
concepts.content: Warfarin effect is potentiated by liver disease, cytochrome P450 enzyme inhibitors such as amiodarone and ciprofloxacin, cranberry juice, drugs that displace warfarin from plasma albumin like NSAIDs, and drugs that inhibit platelet function such as NSAIDs.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Side effect haemorrhage
concepts.content: A major side effect of warfarin therapy is hemorrhage due to its anticoagulant effect.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Teratogenicity and breastfeeding
concepts.content: Warfarin is teratogenic and generally contraindicated in pregnancy but can be used safely in breastfeeding mothers.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Skin necrosis pathophysiology
concepts.content: Warfarin-induced skin necrosis occurs due to an initial reduction in protein C biosynthesis when starting warfarin, causing a temporary procoagulant state that may lead to venular thrombosis and skin necrosis.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Prevention of initial procoagulant state
concepts.content: The initial procoagulant state caused by warfarin-induced protein C reduction is normally avoided by concurrent administration of heparin when starting warfarin therapy.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Purple toes syndrome
concepts.content: Purple toes syndrome is a rare complication of warfarin therapy characterized by painful purple discoloration of the toes.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Interaction with Liver Disease
concepts.content: Liver disease potentiates the effect of warfarin by impairing metabolism, increasing bleeding risk.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Interaction with P450 Enzyme Inhibitors
concepts.content: P450 enzyme inhibitors increase warfarin plasma levels, leading to elevated INR and bleeding risk.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Interaction with Cranberry Juice
concepts.content: Cranberry juice potentiates warfarin effect, increasing INR and bleeding risk.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Interaction with Drugs Displacing Warfarin from Plasma Albumin
concepts.content: Drugs such as NSAIDs displace warfarin from plasma albumin, increasing free warfarin levels and bleeding risk.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Interaction with NSAIDs Inhibiting Platelet Function
concepts.content: NSAIDs inhibit platelet function, increasing bleeding risk when combined with warfarin.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Effect of P450 Enzyme Inducers on INR
concepts.content: P450 enzyme inducers decrease warfarin plasma levels, reducing INR and anticoagulant effect.

concepts.title: Warfarin – P450 Enzyme Inducers Examples
concepts.content: Examples of P450 enzyme inducers that decrease INR include phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone, rifampicin, St John's Wort, chronic alcohol intake, griseofulvin, and smoking.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Effect of P450 Enzyme Inhibitors on INR
concepts.content: P450 enzyme inhibitors increase warfarin plasma levels, increasing INR and bleeding risk.

concepts.title: Warfarin – P450 Enzyme Inhibitors Examples
concepts.content: Examples of P450 enzyme inhibitors that increase INR include ciprofloxacin, clarithromycin, erythromycin, isoniazid, cimetidine, omeprazole, amiodarone, allopurinol, ketoconazole, fluconazole, fluoxetine, sertraline, ritonavir, sodium valproate, acute alcohol intake, and quinupristin.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Management of major bleeding with high INR
concepts.content: In cases of major bleeding such as variceal haemorrhage or intracranial haemorrhage in patients on warfarin, warfarin should be stopped immediately. Administer intravenous vitamin K 5 mg. Use prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) for rapid reversal; if PCC is unavailable, fresh frozen plasma (FFP) may be used, though it takes longer to prepare.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Management of INR >8.0 with minor bleeding
concepts.content: For patients on warfarin with INR greater than 8.0 and minor bleeding, stop warfarin and give intravenous vitamin K 1-3 mg. Repeat vitamin K dose if INR remains elevated after 24 hours. Restart warfarin when INR is less than 5.0.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Management of INR >8.0 without bleeding
concepts.content: In patients on warfarin with INR greater than 8.0 but no bleeding, stop warfarin and give oral vitamin K 1-5 mg using the intravenous preparation administered orally. Repeat vitamin K dose if INR remains elevated after 24 hours. Restart warfarin when INR is less than 5.0.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Management of INR 5.0-8.0 with minor bleeding
concepts.content: For patients on warfarin with INR between 5.0 and 8.0 and minor bleeding, stop warfarin and give intravenous vitamin K 1-3 mg. Restart warfarin when INR is less than 5.0.

concepts.title: Warfarin – Management of INR 5.0-8.0 without bleeding
concepts.content: In patients on warfarin with INR between 5.0 and 8.0 and no bleeding, withhold one or two doses of warfarin and reduce the subsequent maintenance dose.

concepts.title: Prothrombin complex concentrate – Use in intracranial haemorrhage with warfarin
concepts.content: Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) should be considered for rapid reversal of warfarin anticoagulation in cases of intracranial haemorrhage because fresh frozen plasma (FFP) requires time to defrost and prepare.

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Definition
concepts.content: Wolff-Parkinson White (WPW) syndrome is caused by a congenital accessory conducting pathway between the atria and ventricles leading to atrioventricular re-entry tachycardia (AVRT).

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Pathophysiology of Accessory Pathway
concepts.content: The accessory pathway in WPW syndrome does not slow conduction, allowing atrial fibrillation (AF) to rapidly degenerate into ventricular fibrillation (VF).

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Typical Age of Presentation
concepts.content: WPW syndrome typically presents in teenagers and young adults but can occur at any age.

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Palpitations Presentation
concepts.content: Patients with WPW syndrome commonly present with palpitations characterized by sudden onset and offset, often rapid and regular.

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Light-headedness and Pre-syncope Presentation
concepts.content: Light-headedness and pre-syncope are possible presenting symptoms in WPW syndrome.

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – ECG Feature: Short PR Interval
concepts.content: A short PR interval is a possible electrocardiogram (ECG) feature in WPW syndrome.

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – ECG Feature: Wide QRS Complexes with Delta Wave
concepts.content: WPW syndrome ECG may show wide QRS complexes with a slurred upstroke known as a 'delta wave'.

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – ECG Feature: Left Axis Deviation with Right-sided Accessory Pathway
concepts.content: Left axis deviation on ECG is seen in the majority of WPW cases and is associated with a right-sided accessory pathway.

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – ECG Feature: Right Axis Deviation with Left-sided Accessory Pathway
concepts.content: Right axis deviation on ECG is associated with a left-sided accessory pathway in WPW syndrome.

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Differentiation of Type A and Type B
concepts.content: Type A WPW (left-sided pathway) shows a dominant R wave in lead V1, whereas type B WPW (right-sided pathway) does not have a dominant R wave in V1.

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Associations: Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy
concepts.content: WPW syndrome is associated with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM).

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Associations: Mitral Valve Prolapse
concepts.content: WPW syndrome is associated with mitral valve prolapse.

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Associations: Ebstein's Anomaly
concepts.content: WPW syndrome is associated with Ebstein's anomaly.

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Associations: Thyrotoxicosis
concepts.content: WPW syndrome is associated with thyrotoxicosis.

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Associations: Secundum Atrial Septal Defect
concepts.content: WPW syndrome is associated with secundum atrial septal defect (ASD).

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Definitive Treatment
concepts.content: The definitive treatment for WPW syndrome is radiofrequency ablation of the accessory pathway.

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Medical Therapy Options
concepts.content: Medical therapy options for WPW syndrome include sotalol, amiodarone, and flecainide.

concepts.title: Wolff-Parkinson White – Sotalol Contraindication in Atrial Fibrillation
concepts.content: Sotalol should be avoided in WPW patients with coexistent atrial fibrillation because prolonging the AV node refractory period may increase conduction through the accessory pathway, raising ventricular rate and risking ventricular fibrillation.

concepts.title: Acromegaly – Features
concepts.content:
coarse facial appearance, spade-like hands, increase in shoe size
large tongue, prognathism, interdental spaces
excessive sweating and oily skin: caused by sweat gland hypertrophy
features of pituitary tumour: hypopituitarism, headaches, bitemporal hemianopia
raised prolactin in 1/3 of cases → galactorrhoea
6% of patients have MEN-1

concepts.title: Acromegaly – Complications
concepts.content:
hypertension
diabetes (>10%)
cardiomyopathy
colorectal cancer

concepts.title: Acromegaly – Content 1
concepts.content: Growth hormone (GH) levels vary during the day and are therefore not diagnostic.

concepts.title: Acromegaly – Content 2
concepts.content: Serum IGF-1 levels have now overtaken the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) with serial GH measurements as the first-line test. The OGTT test is recommended to confirm the diagnosis if IGF-1 levels are raised.

concepts.title: Acromegaly – Content 3
concepts.content: The Endocrine Society guidelines suggest the following:

concepts.title: Acromegaly – Content 4
concepts.content:
1.1 We recommend measurement of IGF-1 levels in patients with typical clinical manifestations of acromegaly, especially those with acral and facial features.
...
1.5 In patients with elevated or equivocal serum IGF-1 levels, we recommend confirmation of the diagnosis by finding lack of suppression of GH to < 1 µg/L following documented hyperglycemia during an oral glucose load.

concepts.title: Acromegaly – Content 5
concepts.content: Serum IGF-1 may also be used to monitor disease

concepts.title: Acromegaly – Content 7
concepts.content:
in normal patients GH is suppressed to < 2 mu/L with hyperglycaemia
in acromegaly there is no suppression of GH
may also demonstrate impaired glucose tolerance which is associated with acromegaly

concepts.title: Acromegaly – Content 8
concepts.content: A pituitary MRI may demonstrate a pituitary tumour.

concepts.title: Acromegaly – Content 1 (part 2)
concepts.content: Trans-sphenoidal surgery is the first-line treatment for acromegaly in the majority of patients.

concepts.title: Acromegaly – Content 2 (part 2)
concepts.content: If a pituitary tumour is inoperable or surgery unsuccessful then medication may be indicated:

concepts.title: Acromegaly – Content 3 (part 2)
concepts.content:
somatostatin analogue
directly inhibits the release of growth hormone
for example octreotide
effective in 50-70% of patients
pegvisomant
GH receptor antagonist - prevents dimerization of the GH receptor
once daily s/c administration
very effective - decreases IGF-1 levels in 90% of patients to normal
doesn't reduce tumour volume therefore surgery still needed if mass effect
dopamine agonists
for example bromocriptine
the first effective medical treatment for acromegaly, however now superseded by somatostatin analogues
effective only in a minority of patients

concepts.title: Acromegaly – Content 4 (part 2)
concepts.content: External irradiation is sometimes used for older patients or following failed surgical/medical treatment

concepts.title: Addison's disease – Features (1)
concepts.content:
lethargy, weakness, anorexia, nausea & vomiting, weight loss, 'salt-craving'
hyperpigmentation (especially palmar creases)
ACTH is derived from a larger precursor molecule called proopiomelanocortin (POMC). When POMC is cleaved to produce ACTH, other melanocyte-stimulating hormones (MSH) are also produced.

concepts.title: Addison's disease – Features (2)
concepts.content:
These MSHs have the effect of stimulating melanocytes in the skin to produce more melanin, the pigment responsible for skin colour
primary Addison's is associated with hyperpigmentation whereas secondary adrenal insufficiency is not
vitiligo
loss of pubic hair in women
hypotension
hypoglycaemia
hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia may be seen
crisis: collapse, shock, pyrexia

concepts.title: Addison's disease – Primary causes
concepts.content:
tuberculosis
metastases (e.g. bronchial carcinoma)
meningococcal septicaemia (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome)
HIV
antiphospholipid syndrome

concepts.title: Addison's disease – Secondary causes
concepts.content: pituitary disorders (e.g. tumours, irradiation, infiltration)

concepts.title: Addison's disease – Content 1
concepts.content: In a patient with suspected Addison's disease the definite investigation is an ACTH stimulation test (short Synacthen test). Plasma cortisol is measured before and 30 minutes after giving Synacthen 250ug IM. Adrenal autoantibodies such as anti-21-hydroxylase may also be demonstrated.

concepts.title: Addison's disease – Content 2
concepts.content: If an ACTH stimulation test is not readily available (e.g. in primary care) then sending a 9 am serum cortisol can be useful:

concepts.title: Addison's disease – Content 3
concepts.content:
> 500 nmol/l makes Addison's very unlikely
< 100 nmol/l is definitely abnormal
100-500 nmol/l should prompt a ACTH stimulation test to be performed

concepts.title: Addison's disease – Content 4
concepts.content: Associated electrolyte abnormalities are seen in around one-third of undiagnosed patients:

concepts.title: Addison's disease – Content 5
concepts.content:
hyperkalaemia
hyponatraemia
hypoglycaemia
metabolic acidosis

concepts.title: Addison's disease – Patient education is important:
concepts.content:
emphasise the importance of not missing glucocorticoid doses
consider MedicAlert bracelets and steroid cards
patients should be provided with hydrocortisone for injection with needles and syringes to treat an adrenal crisis
discuss how to adjust the glucocorticoid dose during an intercurrent illness (see below)
Management of intercurrent illness
in simple terms the glucocorticoid dose should be doubled, with the fludrocortisone dose staying the same
the Addison's Clinical Advisory Panel have produced guidelines detailing particular scenarios - please see the CKS link for more details

concepts.title: Addisonian crisis – Causes
concepts.content:
sepsis or surgery causing an acute exacerbation of chronic insufficiency (e.g. Addison's, hypopituitarism)
adrenal haemorrhage e.g. Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (fulminant meningococcaemia)
steroid withdrawal (most common precipitant)
inadequate 'sick day rule' management or intercurrent illness (commonly gastroenteritis) in patients with underlying Addison's disease
Signs and symptoms
confusion, syncope, lethargy, convulsions
hypotension, tachycardia, hypothermia
hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia
abdominal pain or cramps

concepts.title: Addisonian crisis – Management (1)
concepts.content:
hydrocortisone 100 mg IM or IV followed by 200 mg per 24 hours as a continuous infusion or 50 mg IV or IM every 6 hours (taper according to response as the patient becomes stable)
1 litre of normal saline infused over 30–60 minutes, then a further 4–6 litres over the first 24 hours if required; include dextrose if hypoglycaemic
no fludrocortisone is required acutely as high-dose cortisol exerts a weak mineralocorticoid effect
once stable, convert to oral replacement after approximately 24 hours, reducing to maintenance dosing over 3–4 days
identify and treat the precipitating cause (e.g.

concepts.content:

educate patients (and carers) about 'sick day rules' and encourage use of steroid alert cards or bracelets to prevent future crises

concepts.title: Adrenal insufficiency – Content 1
concepts.content: Adrenal insufficiency is failure of the adrenal cortex to produce adequate glucocorticoids (± mineralocorticoids and androgens), leading to impaired stress response and metabolic disturbance. It may be primary (Addison’s disease) or secondary/tertiary due to pituitary or hypothalamic disease.

concepts.title: Adrenal insufficiency – Content 3 (1)
concepts.content:
Primary
Addison's disease: (autoimmune adrenalitis - most common non-corticosteroid cause of adrenal insufficiency in the UK)
Other causes: tuberculosis, adrenal haemorrhage (e.g. Waterhouse–Friderichsen), metastatic infiltration, congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Secondary adrenal insufficiency arises from deficient ACTH secretion due to pituitary pathology.

concepts.title: Adrenal insufficiency – Content 3 (2)
concepts.content: Pituitary adenomas, craniopharyngioma, Sheehan’s syndrome, pituitary apoplexy, surgery, radiotherapy, and infiltrative diseases (e.g. sarcoidosis, haemochromatosis). Tertiary adrenal insufficiency results from impaired hypothalamic release of corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), most commonly due to chronic exogenous glucocorticoid therapy.

concepts.title: Adrenal insufficiency – Content 3 (3)
concepts.content: Prolonged corticosteroid use (oral, inhaled, or parenteral) with abrupt withdrawal- the most frequent cause in clinical practice. Hypothalamic damage from tumours (e.g. glioma), radiotherapy, surgery, or infiltrative disease (e.g. sarcoidosis, histiocytosis). Chronic opioid use, which can suppress the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis.

concepts.title: Adrenal insufficiency – Content 5
concepts.content:
General: fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, hypotension, hyponatraemia.
Primary: hyperpigmentation (due to excess ACTH), salt craving, hyperkalaemia.
Secondary/Tertiary: features of pituitary disease; no pigmentation or hyperkalaemia (aldosterone preserved)
Adrenal crisis: hypotension, shock, hypoglycaemia, confusion, vomiting, abdominal pain.

concepts.title: Bartter's syndrome – Features
concepts.content:
usually presents in childhood, e.g. Failure to thrive
polyuria, polydipsia
hypokalaemia
normotension
weakness

concepts.title: Carbimazole – Mechanism of action
concepts.content:
blocks thyroid peroxidase from coupling and iodinating the tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin → reducing thyroid hormone production
in contrast propylthiouracil as well as this central mechanism of action also has a peripheral action by inhibiting 5'-deiodinase which reduces peripheral conversion of T4 to T3

concepts.title: Carbimazole – Adverse effects
concepts.content:
agranulocytosis
crosses the placenta, but may be used in low doses during pregnancy

concepts.title: Combined deficiency of magnesium and calcium – Content 1
concepts.content: Magnesium is required for both PTH secretion and its action on target tissues. Hypomagnesaemia may both cause hypocalcaemia and render patients unresponsive to treatment with calcium and vitamin D supplementation.

concepts.title: Combined deficiency of magnesium and calcium – Content 2
concepts.content: Magnesium is the fourth most abundant cation in the body. The body contains 1000mmol, with half contained in bone and the remainder in muscle, soft tissues and extracellular fluid. There is no one specific hormonal control of magnesium and various hormones including PTH and aldosterone affect the renal handling of magnesium.

concepts.title: Combined deficiency of magnesium and calcium – Content 3
concepts.content: Magnesium and calcium interact at a cellular level also and as a result decreased magnesium will tend to affect the permeability of cellular membranes to calcium, resulting in hyperexcitability.

concepts.title: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia – Clinical features (1)
concepts.content:
the symptoms and signs of CAH vary depending on the specific enzyme deficiency and the severity of the disorder. Common clinical presentations include:
virilization:
female infants may present with ambiguous genitalia due to excessive androgen exposure in utero. male infants appear normal at birth, which can delay diagnosis.

concepts.title: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia – Clinical features (2)
concepts.content:
salt-wasting crisis:
this severe form occurs in about 75% of cases with 21-hydroxylase deficiency
it is characterized by dehydration, hypotension, and electrolyte imbalances, and can be life-threatening if not treated promptly. precocious puberty: Excess androgens can lead to early development of secondary sexual characteristics in both males and females.

concepts.title: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia – Clinical features (3)
concepts.content: infertility: Adults with untreated CAH may experience fertility issues due to hormonal imbalances. height and growth abnormalities: Children with CAH often experience accelerated growth rates initially but may have a shorter adult stature due to early epiphyseal closure.

concepts.title: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia – Diagnosis
concepts.content:
many countries screen newborns for CAH, looking for elevated levels of serum concentration of 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17OHP). This is however not yet done in the UK
ACTH stimulation testing is used to confirm the diagnosis
evaluates the adrenal gland's response to ACTH, with abnormal increases in 17OHP indicating CAH

concepts.title: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia – Management
concepts.content:
primarily involves glucocorticoid replacement to reduce ACTH levels and minimize adrenal androgen production
in cases of mineralocorticoid deficiency fludrocortisone is also prescribed

concepts.content: The side effects of corticosteroids are numerous and represent the single greatest limitation on their usage. Side-effects are more common with systemic and prolonged therapy.

concepts.title: Cushing's syndrome – ACTH dependent causes
concepts.content:
Cushing's disease (80%): pituitary tumour secreting ACTH producing adrenal hyperplasia
ectopic ACTH production (5-10%): e.g. small cell lung cancer is the most common causes

concepts.title: Cushing's syndrome – ACTH independent causes
concepts.content:
iatrogenic: steroids
adrenal adenoma (5-10%)
adrenal carcinoma (rare)
Carney complex: syndrome including cardiac myxoma
micronodular adrenal dysplasia (very rare)

concepts.title: Cushing's syndrome – Pseudo-Cushing's
concepts.content:
mimics Cushing's
often due to alcohol excess or severe depression
causes false positive dexamethasone suppression test or 24 hr urinary free cortisol
insulin stress test may be used to differentiate

concepts.title: Cushing's syndrome – General findings consistent with Cushing's syndrome (1)
concepts.content: A hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis may be seen, along with impaired glucose tolerance. Ectopic ACTH secretion (e.g. secondary to small cell lung cancer) is characteristically associated with very low potassium levels.

concepts.title: Cushing's syndrome – General findings consistent with Cushing's syndrome (2)
concepts.content:
Tests to confirm Cushing's syndrome
The three most commonly used tests are:
overnight (low-dose) dexamethasone suppression test
this is the most sensitive test and is now used first-line to test for Cushing's syndrome
patients with Cushing's syndrome do not have their morning cortisol spike suppressed
24 hr urinary free cortisol
two measurements are required
bedtime salivary cortisol
two measurements are required
Localisation tests
The first-line localisation is 9am and midnight plasma ACTH (and cortisol) levels.

concepts.title: Cushing's syndrome – General findings consistent with Cushing's syndrome (3)
concepts.content:
If ACTH is suppressed then a non-ACTH dependent cause is likely such as an adrenal adenoma
High-dose dexamethasone suppression test
The high-dose dexamethasone suppression test may be used to localise the pathology resulting in Cushing's syndrome. This test may be interpreted as follows:
Cortisol	ACTH	Interpretation
Not suppressed	Suppressed	Cushing's syndrome due to other causes (e.g.

concepts.content:
adrenal adenomas)
Suppressed	ACTH reduced	Cushing's disease (i.e. pituitary adenoma → ACTH secretion)
Not suppressed	Not suppressed	Ectopic ACTH syndrome
Other tests
CRH stimulation
ACTH (and cortisol) rise in pituitary disease
if ectopic/adrenal then no change in ACTH (and cortisol)
Petrosal sinus sampling of ACTH may be needed to differentiate between pituitary and ectopic ACTH secretion.

concepts.title: Cushing's syndrome – General findings consistent with Cushing's syndrome (5)
concepts.content: An insulin stress test is used to differentiate between true Cushing's and pseudo-Cushing's.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus (type 1) – Investigations (1)
concepts.content:
urine should be dipped for glucose and ketones
fasting glucose and random glucose (see below for diagnostic thresholds)
HbA1c is not as useful for patients with a possible or suspected diagnosis of T1DM as it may not accurately reflect a recent rapid rise in serum glucose
C-peptide levels are typically low in patients with T1DM
diabetes-specific autoantibodies are useful to distinguish between type 1 and type 2 diabetes (see below)
Antibody	Notes
Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD)	Present in around 80% of patients with T1DM
Islet cell antibodies (ICA, against cytoplasmic proteins in the beta cell)	Present in around 70-80% of patients with T1DM
Insulin autoantibodies (IAA)	Presence in T1DM correlates strongly with age, found in over 90% of young children with T1DM but only 60% of older patients
Insulinoma-associated-2 autoantibodies (IA-2A)
Diagnostic criteria for type 1 diabetes mellitus
If the patient is symptomatic:
fasting glucose greater than or equal to 7.0 mmol/l
random glucose greater than or equal to 11.1 mmol/l (or after 75g oral glucose tolerance test)
If the patient is asymptomatic the above criteria apply but must be demonstrated on two separate occasions.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus (type 1) – Investigations (2)
concepts.content:
Distinguishing between type 1 and type 2 diabetes meliitus
The major differences are shown in the table below:
Type 1 diabetes	Type 2 diabetes
Age of onset	Typically < 20 years
however, 40% > 30 years
Typically > 40 years
however, may occur in younger, obese patients
Speed of onset	More acute, hours-days	Slower, weeks-months
Weight of patient	Recent weight loss typical	Obesity is strong risk factor and recent weight loss is rare
Features	Features of DKA as above	Milder symptoms e.g.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus (type 1) – Investigations (3)
concepts.content:
polyuria, polydipsia
Ketonuria	Common	Rare
NICE state the following:
Diagnose type 1 diabetes on clinical grounds in adults presenting with hyperglycaemia, bearing in mind that people with type 1 diabetes typically (but not always) have one or more of:
ketosis
rapid weight loss
age of onset below 50 years
BMI below 25 kg/m²
personal and/or family history of autoimmune disease
In terms of diagnosing T1DM, NICE recommend the following on who may need further tests:
Consider further investigation in adults that involves measurement of C-peptide and/or diabetes-specific autoantibody titres if:
type 1 diabetes is suspected but the clinical presentation includes some atypical features (for example, age 50 years or above, BMI of 25 kg/m² or above, slow evolution of hyperglycaemia or long prodrome)
Conversely, for patients suspected of type 2 diabetes, if they over the age of 40 years and respond well to oral hypoglycaemic agents do not need to undergo further testing for type 1 diabetes.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus (type 1) – Investigations (4)
concepts.content:
For those in whom there is a doubt, C-peptide levels and diabetes-specific autoantibodies are the investigations of choice. Example scenarios
a 15-year-old presents with weight loss, lethargy. Ketones and glucose found in the urine. A random serum glucose is 14 mmol/L → T1DM, no need for further investigations
a 38-year-old obese man presents with polyuria.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus (type 1) – Investigations (5)
concepts.content:
A random glucose is 12.5 mmol/L → Intermediate age for T1DM/T2DM, a risk factor for T2DM (obesity) but not clear cut - do C-peptide levels and diabetes-specific autoantibodies
a 52-year-old woman (body mass index 23 kg/m²) presents with polyuria and polydipsia.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus (type 1) – Investigations (6)
concepts.content:
Ketones are present in the urine → age atypical for T1DM but other features consistent - do C-peptide levels and diabetes-specific autoantibodies
a 59-year-old obese man presents with polyuria. A random serum glucose is 12.0 mmol/L → T2DM, no need for further investigations

concepts.content: The diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus can be made by either a plasma glucose or a HbA1c sample. Diagnostic criteria vary according to whether the patient is symptomatic (polyuria, polydipsia etc) or not.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Investigations (1)
concepts.content:
There are 4 main ways to check blood glucose:
a finger-prick bedside glucose monitor
a one-off blood glucose. This may either be fasting or non-fasting
a HbA1c. This measures the amount of glycosylated haemoglobin and represents the average blood glucose over the past 2-3 months
a glucose tolerance test. In this test, a fasting blood glucose is taken after which a 75g glucose load is taken.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Investigations (2)

The diagnostic criteria are determined by WHO. If the patient is symptomatic:
fasting glucose greater than or equal to 7.0 mmol/l

If the patient is asymptomatic the above criteria apply but must be demonstrated on two separate occasions.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – NICE provide guidelines on how drug therapy should be used in T2DM:
concepts.content: *common in exams, much less common in clinical practice

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 1
concepts.content: A number of drugs to treat diabetes mellitus have become available in recent years. Much research has focused around the role of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), a hormone released by the small intestine in response to an oral glucose load

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 2
concepts.content: Whilst it is well known that insulin resistance and insufficient B-cell compensation occur other effects are also seen in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). In normal physiology an oral glucose load results in a greater release of insulin than if the same load is given intravenously - this known as the incretin effect. This effect is largely mediated by GLP-1 and is known to be decreased in T2DM.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 3
concepts.content: Increasing GLP-1 levels, either by the administration of an analogue (glucagon-like peptide-1, GLP-1 mimetics, e.g. exenatide) or inhibiting its breakdown (dipeptidyl peptidase-4 ,DPP-4 inhibitors - the gliptins), is therefore the target of two recent classes of drug.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 4
concepts.content: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) mimetics (e.g. exenatide)

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 5
concepts.content: Exenatide is an example of a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) mimetic. These drugs increase insulin secretion and inhibit glucagon secretion. One of the major advances of GLP-1 mimetics is that they typically result in weight loss, in contrast to many medications such as insulin, sulfonylureas and thiazolidinediones. They are sometimes used in combination with insulin in T2DM to minimise weight gain.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 6
concepts.content: Exenatide must be given by subcutaneous injection within 60 minutes before the morning and evening meals. It should not be given after a meal.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 7
concepts.content: Liraglutide is the other GLP-1 mimetic currently available. One the main advantages of liraglutide over exenatide is that it only needs to be given once a day.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 8
concepts.content: Both exenatide and liraglutide may be combined with metformin and a sulfonylurea. Standard release exenatide is also licensed to be used with basal insulin alone or with metformin. Please see the BNF for a more complete list of licensed indications.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 10
concepts.content: Consider adding exenatide to metformin and a sulfonylurea if:

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 11
concepts.content:
BMI >= 35 kg/m² in people of European descent and there are problems associated with high weight, or
BMI < 35 kg/m² and insulin is unacceptable because of occupational implications or weight loss would benefit other comorbidities.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 12
concepts.content: NICE like patients to have achieved a > 11 mmol/mol (1%) reduction in HbA1c and 3% weight loss after 6 months to justify the ongoing prescription of GLP-1 mimetics.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 13
concepts.content: The major adverse effect of GLP-1 mimetics is nausea and vomiting. The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency has issued specific warnings on the use of exenatide, reporting that is has been linked to severe pancreatitis in some patients.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 14
concepts.content: Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors (e.g. Vildagliptin, sitagliptin)

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 16
concepts.content:
dipeptidyl peptidase-4, DPP-4 inhibitors increase levels of incretins (GLP-1 and GIP) by decreasing their peripheral breakdown
oral preparation
trials to date show that the drugs are relatively well tolerated with no increased incidence of hypoglycaemia
do not cause weight gain

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 17
concepts.content: NICE guidelines on DPP-4 inhibitors

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 18
concepts.content: NICE suggest that a DPP-4 inhibitor might be preferable to a thiazolidinedione if further weight gain would cause significant problems, a thiazolidinedione is contraindicated or the person has had a poor response to a thiazolidinedione

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 1 (part 2)
concepts.content: The long-term management of type 1 diabetics is an important and complex process requiring the input of many different clinical specialties and members of the healthcare team. A diagnosis of type 1 diabetes can still reduce the life expectancy of patients by 13 years and the micro and macrovascular complications are well documented.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 2 (part 2)
concepts.content: NICE released guidelines on the diagnosis and management of type 1 diabetes in 2015. We've only highlighted a very select amount of the guidance here which will be useful for any clinician looking after a patient with type 1 diabetes.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 4 (part 2)
concepts.content:
should be monitored every 3-6 months
adults should have a target of HbA1c level of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or lower. NICE do however recommend taking into account factors such as the person's daily activities, aspirations, likelihood of complications, comorbidities, occupation and history of hypoglycaemia

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 5 (part 2)
concepts.content: Self-monitoring of blood glucose

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 6 (part 2)
concepts.content:
recommend testing at least 4 times a day, including before each meal and before bed
more frequent monitoring is recommended if frequency of hypoglycaemic episodes increases; during periods of illness; before, during and after sport; when planning pregnancy, during pregnancy and while breastfeeding

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 8 (part 2)
concepts.content:
5-7 mmol/l on waking and
4-7 mmol/l before meals at other times of the day

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 10 (part 2)
concepts.content:
offer multiple daily injection basal-bolus insulin regimens, rather than twice-daily mixed insulin regimens, as the insulin injection regimen of choice for all adults
twice-daily insulin detemir is the regime of choice. Once-daily insulin glargine or insulin detemir is an alternative
offer rapid-acting insulin analogues injected before meals, rather than rapid-acting soluble human or animal insulins, for mealtime insulin replacement for adults with type 1 diabetes

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 12 (part 2)
concepts.content: NICE recommend considering adding metformin if the BMI >= 25 kg/m²

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Practical examples (1)
concepts.content:
a patient is newly diagnosed with HbA1c and wants to try lifestyle treatment first. You agree on a target of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%)
you review a patient 6 months after starting metformin. His HbA1c is 51 mmol/mol (6.8%).

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Practical examples (2)
concepts.content:
You increase his metformin from 500mg bd to 500mg tds and reinforce lifestyle factors
Patient already on treatment
Management of T2DM	HbA1c target

Initial drug therapy
Simplified initial management of type 2 diabetes mellitus
Metformin remains the first-line drug of choice in type 2 diabetes mellitus.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Practical examples (3)
concepts.content:
metformin should be titrated up slowly to minimise the possibility of gastrointestinal upset
if standard-release metformin is not tolerated then modified-release metformin should be trialled
SGLT-2 inhibitors
should also be given in addition to metformin if any of the following apply:
the patient has a high risk of developing cardiovascular disease (CVD, e.g.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Practical examples (4)
concepts.content:
QRISK ≥ 10%)
the patient has established CVD
the patient has chronic heart failure
metformin should be established and titrated up before introducing the SGLT-2 inhibitor
SGLT-2 inhibitors should also be started at any point if a patient develops CVD (e.g.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Practical examples (5)
concepts.content:
is diagnosed with ischaemic heart disease), a QRISK ≥ 10% or chronic heart failure
If metformin is contraindicated
if the patient has a risk of CVD, established CVD or chronic heart failure:
SGLT-2 monotherapy
if the patient doesn't have a risk of CVD, established CVD or chronic heart failure:
DPP-4 inhibitor or pioglitazone or a sulfonylurea
SGLT-2 may be used if certain NICE criteria are met
Further drug therapy if HbA1c targets are not met
Simplified further management of type 2 diabetes mellitus if HbA1c targets are not met
If the HbA1c has risen to 58 mmol/mol (7.5%) then further treatment is indicated.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Practical examples (6)
concepts.content: Given the large number of drug therapy options, medication choices depend on individual clinical circumstances (comorbidities, contraindications, weight) and patient preference.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Practical examples (7)
concepts.content:
Second-line therapy
Dual therapy - add one of the following:
metformin + DPP-4 inhibitor
metformin + pioglitazone
metformin + sulfonylurea
metformin + SGLT-2 inhibitor (if NICE criteria met)
Third-line therapy
If a patient does not achieve control on dual therapy then the following options are possible:
metformin + DPP-4 inhibitor + sulfonylurea
metformin + pioglitazone + sulfonylurea
metformin + (pioglitazone or sulfonylurea or DPP-4 inhibitor) + SGLT-2 if certain NICE criteria are met
insulin-based treatment
Further therapy
If triple therapy is not effective or tolerated consider switching one of the drugs for a GLP-1 mimetic:
BMI ≥ 35 kg/m² and specific psychological or other medical problems associated with obesity or
BMI < 35 kg/m² and for whom insulin therapy would have significant occupational implications or weight loss would benefit other significant obesity-related comorbidities
only continue if there is a reduction of at least 11 mmol/mol [1.0%] in HbA1c and a weight loss of at least 3% of initial body weight in 6 months
GLP-1 mimetics should only be added to insulin under specialist care

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Starting insulin
concepts.content:
metformin should be continued. In terms of other drugs NICE advice: 'Review the continued need for other blood glucose-lowering therapies'
NICE recommend starting with human NPH insulin (isophane, intermediate-acting) taken at bed-time or twice daily according to need

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Practical examples
concepts.content:
you review an established type 2 diabetic on maximum dose metformin. Her HbA1c is 55 mmol/mol (7.2%). You do not add another drug as she has not reached the threshold of 58 mmol/mol (7.5%)
a type 2 diabetic is found to have an HbA1c of 62 mmol/mol (7.8%) at annual review. They are currently on maximum dose metformin. You elect to add a sulfonylurea

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Risk factor modification (1)
concepts.content:
Hypertension
blood pressure targets are the same as for patients without type 2 diabetes (see table below)
ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARB) are first-line
an ARB is preferred if the patient has a black African or African-Caribbean family origin
Clinic BP	ABPM / HBPM

concepts.content:
