concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 1 (part 3)
concepts.content: We know that type 2 diabetes mellitus is more common in people of Asian ethnicity and a significant proportion of those patients in the UK will be Muslim. The BMJ published an excellent and comprehensive review of this issue in 20101.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 2 (part 3)
concepts.content: It is important that we can give appropriate advice to Muslim patients to allow them safely observe their fast. This is particularly important from 2014 as Ramadan is due to fall in the long days of the summer months for several years henceforth.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 3 (1)
concepts.content: Clearly it is a personal decision whether a patient decides to fast. It may however be worthwhile exploring the fact that people with chronic conditions are exempt from fasting or may be able to delay fasting to the shorter days of the winter months.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 3 (2)
concepts.content: It is however known that many Muslim patients with diabetes do not class themselves as having a chronic/serious condition which should exempt them from fasting. Around 79% of Muslim patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus fast Ramadan2.There is an excellent patient information leaflet from Diabetes UK and the Muslim Council of Britain which explores these options in more detail.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 4 (part 3)
concepts.content: If a patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus does decide to fast:

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 5 (1)
concepts.content:
they should try and and eat a meal containing long-acting carbohydrates prior to sunrise (Suhoor)
patients should be given a blood glucose monitor to allow them to check their glucose levels, particularly if they feel unwell
for patients taking metformin the expert consensus is that the dose should be split one-third before sunrise (Suhoor) and two-thirds after sunset (Iftar)
expert consensus also recommends switching once-daily sulfonylureas to after sunset.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 5 (2)
concepts.content:
For patients taking twice-daily preparations such as gliclazide it is recommended that a larger proportion of the dose is taken after after sunset
no adjustment is needed for patients taking pioglitazone

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 6 (part 3)
concepts.content:
1. Management of people with diabetes wanting to fast during Ramadan BMJ 2010;340:c3053
2. Salti I et al. Results of the Epidemiology of Diabetes and Ramadan (EPIDIAR) study. Diabetes Care 2004;27:2306-11.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 2 (part 4)
concepts.content:
if a patient is on insulin, they must not stop it due to the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis
check blood glucose more frequently, for example, every 1-2 hours including through the night
consider checking blood or urine ketone levels regularly
maintain normal meal pattern if possible
if appetite is reduced meals could be replaced with carbohydrate-containing drinks (such as milk, milkshakes, fruit juices, and sugary drinks)
aim to drink at least 3 L of fluid (5 pints) a day to prevent dehydration

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 4 (1)
concepts.content:
advise the patient to temporarily stop some oral hypoglycaemics during an acute illness
medication may be restarted once the person is feeling better and eating and drinking for 24-48 hours
metformin: stop treatment if there is a risk of dehydration, to reduce the risk of lactic acidosis.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus – Content 4 (2)
concepts.content:
sulfonylureas: may increase the risk of hypoglycaemia
SGLT-2 inhibitors: check for ketones and stop treatment if acutely unwell and/or at risk of dehydration, due to the risk of euglycaemic DKA
GLP-1 receptor agonists: stop treatment if there is a risk of dehydration, to reduce the risk of AKI
if on insulin therapy, do not stop treatment, as above
monitor blood glucose more frequently as necessary

concepts.title: Diabetic foot disease – Content 1
concepts.content: Diabetic foot disease is an important complication of diabetes mellitus which should be screen for on a regular basis. NICE produced guidelines relating to diabetic foot disease in 2015.

concepts.title: Diabetic foot disease – Content 2
concepts.content: It occurs secondary to two main factors:

concepts.title: Diabetic foot disease – Content 3
concepts.content:
neuropathy: resulting in loss of protective sensation (e.g. not noticing a stone in the shoe), Charcot's arthropathy, dry skin
peripheral arterial disease: diabetes is a risk factor for both macro and microvascular ischaemia

concepts.title: Diabetic foot disease – Content 5
concepts.content:
neuropathy: loss of sensation
ischaemia: absent foot pulses, reduced ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI), intermittent claudication
complications: calluses, ulceration, Charcot's arthropathy, cellulitis, osteomyelitis, gangrene

concepts.title: Diabetic foot disease – Content 6
concepts.content: All patients with diabetes should be screened for diabetic foot disease on at least an annual basis

concepts.title: Diabetic foot disease – Content 7
concepts.content:
screening for ischaemia: done by palpating for both the dorsalis pedis pulse and posterial tibial artery pulse
screening for neuropathy: a 10 g monofilament is used on various parts of the sole of the foot

concepts.title: Diabetic foot disease – Content 8
concepts.content: NICE recommend that we risk stratify patients:

concepts.title: Diabetic foot disease – Low risk	Moderate risk	High risk
concepts.content:
• no risk factors except callus alone	• deformity or
• neuropathy or
• non-critical limb ischaemia.	• previous ulceration or
• previous amputation or
• on renal replacement therapy or

concepts.title: Diabetic foot disease – Low risk	Moderate risk	High risk (part 2)
concepts.content:
• neuropathy and non-critical limb ischaemia together or
• neuropathy in combination with callus and/or deformity or
• non-critical limb ischaemia in combination with callus and/or deformity.

concepts.title: Diabetic foot disease – Content 10
concepts.content: All patients who are moderate or high risk (I.e. any problems other than simple calluses) should be followed up regularly by the local diabetic foot centre.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content:
DKA is caused by uncontrolled lipolysis (not proteolysis) which results in an excess of free fatty acids that are ultimately converted to ketone bodies
The most common precipitating factors of DKA are infection, missed insulin doses and myocardial infarction.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Features
concepts.content:
abdominal pain
polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration
Kussmaul respiration (deep hyperventilation)
Acetone-smelling breath ('pear drops' smell)

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Diagnostic criteria
concepts.content:
American Diabetes Association (2009)	Joint British Diabetes Societies (2013)
Key points
glucose > 13.8 mmol/l
pH < 7.30
serum bicarbonate <18 mmol/l
anion gap > 10
ketonaemia
Key points
glucose > 11 mmol/l or known diabetes mellitus
pH < 7.3
bicarbonate < 15 mmol/l
ketones > 3 mmol/l or urine ketones ++ on dipstick

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Fluid	Volume
concepts.content:
0.9% sodium chloride 1L	1000ml over 1st hour
0.9% sodium chloride 1L with potassium chloride	1000ml over next 2 hours
0.9% sodium chloride 1L with potassium chloride	1000ml over next 2 hours
0.9% sodium chloride 1L with potassium chloride	1000ml over next 4 hours
0.9% sodium chloride 1L with potassium chloride	1000ml over next 4 hours

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Fluid	Volume (part 2)
concepts.content: 0.9% sodium chloride 1L with potassium chloride	1000ml over next 6 hours

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Resolution
concepts.content:
DKA resolution is defined as:
pH >7.3 and
blood ketones < 0.6 mmol/L and
bicarbonate > 15.0mmol/L

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Further points
concepts.content:
both the ketonaemia and acidosis should have been resolved within 24 hours. If this hasn't happened the patient requires senior review from an endocrinologist
if the above criteria are met and the patient is eating and drinking switch to subcutaneous insulin
the patient should be reviewed by the diabetes specialist nurse prior to discharge

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – acute kidney injury
concepts.content: * children/young adults are particularly vulnerable to cerebral oedema following fluid resuscitation in DKA and often need 1:1 nursing to monitor neuro-observations, headache, irritability, visual disturbance, focal neurology etc. It usually occurs 4-12 hours following commencement of treatment but can present at any time. If there is any suspicion a CT head and senior review should be sought

concepts.title: Diabetic neuropathy – Content 2
concepts.content: Diabetes typically leads to sensory loss and not motor loss. Sensory loss typically results in a 'glove and stocking' distribution, with the lower legs affected first due to the length of the sensory neurons supplying this area. Painful diabetic neuropathy is also a common problem in clinical practice.

concepts.title: Diabetic neuropathy – Content 3
concepts.content: NICE updated it's guidance on the management of neuropathic pain in 2013. Diabetic neuropathy is now managed in the same way as other forms of neuropathic pain:

concepts.title: Diabetic neuropathy – Content 4
concepts.content:
first-line treatment: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin
if the first-line drug treatment does not work try one of the other 3 drugs
tramadol may be used as 'rescue therapy' for exacerbations of neuropathic pain
topical capsaicin may be used for localised neuropathic pain (e.g. post-herpetic neuralgia)
pain management clinics may be useful in patients with resistant problems

concepts.title: Diabetic neuropathy – Content 5
concepts.content: Gastrointestinal autonomic neuropathy

concepts.title: Diabetic neuropathy – Content 7
concepts.content:
occurs secondary to autonomic neuropathy
symptoms include erratic blood glucose control, bloating and vomiting
management options include metoclopramide, domperidone or erythromycin (prokinetic agents)

concepts.title: Diabetic neuropathy – Content 10
concepts.content: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease

concepts.title: Diabetic neuropathy – Content 11
concepts.content: caused by decreased lower esophageal sphincter (LES) pressure

concepts.title: Disorders of sex development – Content 1
concepts.content: The table below lists the most common disorders of sex development:

concepts.title: Disorders of sex development – Content 2 (1)
concepts.content:
Name	Karyotype	Notes
Androgen insensitivity syndrome	46 XY	X-linked recessive condition. Defect in androgen receptor results in end-organ resistance to testosterone causing genotypically male children (46XY) to have a female phenotype. Rudimentary vagina and testes present but no uterus. Testosterone, oestrogen and LH levels are elevated
5-α reductase deficiency	46 XY	Autosomal recessive condition.

concepts.title: Disorders of sex development – Content 2 (2)
concepts.content: Results in the inability of males to convert testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). Individuals have ambiguous genitalia in the newborn period. Hypospadias is common. Virilization at puberty. Male pseudohermaphroditism	46 XY	Individual has testes but external genitalia are female or ambiguous.

concepts.title: Disorders of sex development – Content 2 (3)
concepts.content:
may be secondary to androgen insensitivity syndrome
Female pseudohermaphroditism	46 XX	Individual has ovaries but external genitalia are male (virilized) or ambiguous. May be secondary to congenital adrenal hyperplasia
True hermaphroditism	46 XX or 47 XXY	Very rare, both ovarian and testicular tissue are present

concepts.title: DVLA – Content 1
concepts.content: Until recently people with diabetes who used insulin could not hold a HGV licence. The DVLA changed the rules in October 2011. The following standards need to be met (and also apply to patients using other hypoglycaemic inducing drugs such as sulfonylureas):

concepts.title: DVLA – Content 2
concepts.content:
there has not been any severe hypoglycaemic event in the previous 12 months
the driver has full hypoglycaemic awareness
the driver must show adequate control of the condition by regular blood glucose monitoring*, at least twice daily and at times relevant to driving
the driver must demonstrate an understanding of the risks of hypoglycaemia
here are no other debarring complications of diabetes

concepts.title: DVLA – Content 3
concepts.content: From a practical point of view patients on insulin who want to apply for a Group 2 (HGV) licence need to complete a VDIAB1I form.

concepts.title: DVLA – Content 4
concepts.content: Other specific points for group 1 drivers:

concepts.title: DVLA – Content 5
concepts.content:
if on insulin then patient can drive a car as long as they have hypoglycaemic awareness, not more than one episode of hypoglycaemia requiring the assistance of another person within the preceding 12 months and no relevant visual impairment. Drivers are normally contacted by DVLA
if on tablets or exenatide no need to notify DVLA. If tablets may induce hypoglycaemia (e.g. sulfonylureas) then there must not have been more than one episode of hypoglycaemia requiring the assistance of another person within the preceding 12 months
if diet controlled alone then no requirement to inform DVLA

concepts.title: DVLA – Content 6
concepts.content: *to demonstrate adequate control, the Secretary of State's Honorary Medical Advisory Panel on Diabetes Mellitus has recommended that applicants will need to have used blood glucose meters with a memory function to measure and record blood glucose levels for at least 3 months prior to submitting their application

concepts.title: Glycosylated haemoglobin – Content 1
concepts.content: Glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA1c) is the most widely used measure of long-term glycaemic control in diabetes mellitus. HbA1c is produced by the glycosylation of haemoglobin at a rate proportional to the glucose concentration. The level of HbA1c therefore is dependent on:

concepts.title: Glycosylated haemoglobin – Content 2
concepts.content:
red blood cell lifespan
average blood glucose concentration

concepts.title: Glycosylated haemoglobin – Content 3
concepts.content: A number of conditions can interfere with accurate HbA1c interpretation:

concepts.title: Glycosylated haemoglobin – Content 4
concepts.content:
Lower-than-expected levels of HbA1c (due to reduced red blood cell lifespan)	Higher-than-expected levels of HbA1c (due to increased red blood cell lifespan)
Sickle-cell anaemia
GP6D deficiency
Hereditary spherocytosis
Haemodialysis	Vitamin B12/folic acid deficiency
Iron-deficiency anaemia
Splenectomy

concepts.title: Glycosylated haemoglobin – Content 5
concepts.content: HbA1c is generally thought to reflect the blood glucose over the previous '3 months' although there is some evidence it is weighed more strongly to glucose levels of the past 2-4 weeks. NICE recommend 'HbA1c should be checked every 3-6 months until stable, then 6 monthly'.

concepts.title: Glycosylated haemoglobin – Content 6
concepts.content: The relationship between HbA1c and average blood glucose is complex but has been studied by the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT). A new internationally standardised method for reporting HbA1c has been developed by the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry (IFCC). This will report HbA1c in mmol per mol of haemoglobin without glucose attached.

concepts.title: Graves' disease – Features
concepts.content: typical features of thyrotoxicosis

concepts.title: Graves' disease – specific signs limited to Grave's (see below)
concepts.content:
Features seen in Graves' but not in other causes of thyrotoxicosis
eye signs
lid retraction (most common sign, seen in 90%) - sympathetic overactivity leading to overaction of the levator palpebrae superioris and Müller’s muscle → 'staring' appearance
exophthalmos (most specific sign)
ophthalmoplegia
pretibial myxoedema
thyroid acropachy, a triad of:
digital clubbing
soft tissue swelling of the hands and feet
periosteal new bone formation
Autoantibodies
TSH receptor stimulating antibodies (90%)
anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies (75%)
Thyroid scintigraphy
diffuse, homogenous, increased uptake of radioactive iodine

concepts.title: Graves' disease – Content 1
concepts.content: Despite many trials, there is no clear guidance on the optimal management of Graves' disease. Treatment options include anti-thyroid drugs (ATDs, for example carbimazole), radioiodine treatment and surgery.

concepts.title: Graves' disease – Content 2
concepts.content: Anti-thyroid drugs have emerged as the most popular first-line therapy for Graves' disease in recent years. Factors that particularly support their use include anti-thyroid drugs significant symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, or patients with a significant risk of hyperthyroid complications (e.g. elderly patients, cardiovascular disease).

concepts.title: Graves' disease – Content 3
concepts.content: Initial treatment to control symptoms

concepts.title: Graves' disease – Content 4
concepts.content: propranolol is used to help block the adrenergic effects

concepts.title: Graves' disease – Content 5
concepts.content: NICE recommends that patients with Graves' disease are referred to secondary care for ongoing treatment.

concepts.title: Graves' disease – Content 6
concepts.content: NICE suggest carbimazole should be considered in primary care if patients symptoms are not controlled with propanolol

concepts.title: Graves' disease – Content 8
concepts.content:
carbimazole is started at 40mg and reduced gradually to maintain euthyroidism
typically continued for 12-18 months
the major complication of carbimazole therapy is agranulocytosis
an alternative regime is termed 'block-and-replace'
carbimazole is started at 40mg
thyroxine is added when the patient is euthyroid
treatment typically lasts for 6-9 months
patients following an ATD titration regime have been shown to suffer fewer side-effects than those on a block-and-replace regime

concepts.title: Graves' disease – Content 10
concepts.content:
often used in patients who relapse following ATD therapy or are resistant to primary ATD treatment
contraindications include pregnancy (should be avoided for 4-6 months following treatment) and age < 16 years. Thyroid eye disease is a relative contraindication, as it may worsen the condition
the proportion of patients who become hypothyroid depends on the dose given, but as a rule the majority of patient will require thyroxine supplementation after 5 years

concepts.title: Growth hormone therapy – Adverse effects
concepts.content:
headache
benign intracranial hypertension
fluid retention

concepts.title: Gynaecomastia – Content 1
concepts.content: Gynaecomastia describes an abnormal amount of breast tissue in males and is usually caused by an increased oestrogen:androgen ratio. It is important to differentiate the causes of galactorrhoea (due to the actions of prolactin on breast tissue) from those of gynaecomastia

concepts.title: Gynaecomastia – Content 3
concepts.content:
physiological: normal in puberty
syndromes with androgen deficiency: Kallman's, Klinefelter's
testicular failure: e.g. mumps
liver disease
testicular cancer e.g. seminoma secreting hCG
ectopic tumour secretion
hyperthyroidism
haemodialysis
drugs: see below

concepts.title: Gynaecomastia – Content 5
concepts.content:
spironolactone (most common drug cause)
cimetidine
digoxin
cannabis
finasteride
GnRH agonists e.g. goserelin, buserelin
oestrogens, anabolic steroids

concepts.title: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state – Pathophysiology
concepts.content:
hyperglycaemia → ↑ serum osmolality → osmotic diuresis → severe volume depletion
Precipitating factors
intercurrent illness
dementia

concepts.title: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state – Clinical features
concepts.content:
whilst DKA presents within hours of onset, HHS comes on over many days, and consequently, the dehydration and metabolic disturbances may be more extreme
consequences of volume loss
clinical signs of dehydration
polyuria
polydipsia
systemic
lethargy
nausea and vomiting
neurological
altered level of consciousness
focal neurological deficits
haematological
hyperviscosity (may result in myocardial infarctions, stroke and peripheral arterial thrombosis)
There are no precise diagnostic criteria but the following are typically seen
hypovolaemia
marked hyperglycaemia (>30 mmol/L)
significantly raised serum osmolarity (> 320 mosmol/kg)
can be calculated by: 2 * Na+ + glucose + urea
no significant hyperketonaemia (<3 mmol/L)
no significant acidosis (bicarbonate > 15 mmol/l or pH > 7.3 - acidosis can occur due to lactic acidosis or renal impairment)

concepts.title: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state – Management
concepts.content:
fluid replacement
fluid losses in HHS are estimated to be between 100 - 220 ml/kg
IV 0.9% sodium chloride solution
typically given at 0.5 - 1 L/hour depending on clinical assessment
potassium levels should be monitored and added to fluids depending on the level
insulin
should not be given unless blood glucose stops falling while giving IV fluids
venous thromboembolism prophylaxis
patients are at risk of thrombosis due to hyperviscosity

concepts.title: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state – Complications
concepts.content:
vascular complications may occur due to hyperviscosity:
such as myocardial infarction
stroke

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Causes (1)
concepts.content:

alcohol
causes exaggerated insulin secretion
mechanism is thought to be due to the effect of alcohol on the pancreatic microcirculation → redistribution of pancreatic blood flow from the exocrine into the endocrine parts → increased insulin secretion
nesidioblastosis - beta cell hyperplasia
Physiological response to hypoglycaemia
hormonal response: the first response of the body is decreased insulin secretion.

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Causes (2)
concepts.content:
This is followed by increased glucagon secretion. Growth hormone and cortisol are also released but later
sympathoadrenal response: increased catecholamine-mediated (adrenergic) and acetylcholine-mediated (cholinergic) neurotransmission in the peripheral autonomic nervous system and in the central nervous system

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Features (1)
concepts.content: blood glucose levels and the severity of symptoms are not always correlated, especially in patients with diabetes.

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Features (2)
concepts.content:
blood glucose concentrations <3.3 mmol/L cause autonomic symptoms due to the release of glucagon and adrenaline (average frequency in brackets):
Sweating
Shaking
Hunger
Anxiety
Nausea
blood glucose concentrations below <2.8 mmol/L cause neuroglycopenic symptoms due to inadequate glucose supply to the brain:
Weakness
Vision changes
Confusion
Dizziness
Severe and uncommon features of hypoglycaemia include:
Convulsion
Coma
Investigation of hypoglycaemia
if the cause of hypoglycaemia is not clear then a combination of serum insulin and c-peptide levels can be measured
remember that insulin and C-peptide are released in equimolar amounts from the pancreas, making C-peptide a marker of endogenous insulin production.

concepts.title: Insulin – Content 1
concepts.content: Insulin is a peptide hormone, produced by beta cells of the pancreas, and is central to regulating carbohydrate and fat metabolism in the body. Insulin causes cells in the liver, skeletal muscles, and fat tissue to absorb glucose from the blood. In the liver and skeletal muscles, glucose is stored as glycogen, and in fat cells (adipocytes) it is stored as triglycerides.

concepts.title: Insulin – Content 3
concepts.content: The human insulin protein is composed of 51 amino acids, and has a molecular weight of 5808 Da. It is a dimer of an A-chain and a B-chain, which are linked together by disulfide bonds.

concepts.title: Insulin – Content 5
concepts.content: Pro-insulin is formed by the rough endoplasmic reticulum in pancreatic beta cells. Then pro-insulin is cleaved to form insulin and C-peptide. Insulin is stored in secretory granules and released in response to Ca2+.

concepts.title: Insulin – Content 8
concepts.content:
Secreted in response to hyperglycaemia
Glucose utilisation and glycogen synthesis
Inhibits lipolysis
Reduces muscle protein loss
Increases cellular uptake of potassium (via stimulation of Na+/K+ ATPase pump)

concepts.title: Insulin therapy – Content 1
concepts.content: Insulin therapy revolutionised the management of diabetes mellitus when it was developed in the 1920's. It is still the only available treatment for type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) and is widely used in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) where oral hypoglycaemic agents fail to gain adequate control.

concepts.title: MODY – Clinical Features (1)
concepts.content: Patients with MODY often present with mild non-ketotic hyperglycemia that is often detected incidentally or during routine screening. It may also be discovered during pregnancy.

concepts.title: MODY – Clinical Features (2)
concepts.content: Unlike Type 1 diabetes, patients with MODY usually do not present with diabetic ketoacidosis except under severe stress conditions, and unlike Type 2 diabetes, they are often of normal weight and do not exhibit signs of insulin resistance. The specific clinical manifestations and complications can vary depending on the subtype of MODY.

concepts.title: MODY – Clinical Features (3)
concepts.content: For example, individuals with MODY2 generally have mild, stable fasting hyperglycemia and rarely develop severe complications, whereas those with MODY3 or MODY1 may have progressive hyperglycemia and are at higher risk for complications typically associated with diabetes, such as retinopathy, nephropathy, and cardiovascular disease.

concepts.title: MODY – Diagnosis
concepts.content:
MODY should be suspected in individuals with persistent, asymptomatic hyperglycemia detected before the age of 25, without the typical features of Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes.
The diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing, which is crucial for identifying the specific type of MODY, as this has direct implications for management. It's important to remember, however, that genetic testing can be expensive and may not be available in all settings.

concepts.title: MODY – Treatment
concepts.content: The treatment for MODY depends on the specific genetic subtype. For example, MODY2 often does not require specific treatment, as the hyperglycemia is mild and usually does not lead to complications. In contrast, MODY associated with HNF1A often respond well to treatment with low-dose sulfonylureas. Insulin therapy may be necessary in some cases, especially during pregnancy or if sulfonylureas are contraindicated or ineffective.

concepts.content:

concepts.title: Pituitary adenoma – Content 1
concepts.content: A pituitary adenoma is a benign tumour of the pituitary gland. They are common (10% of all people) but in most cases will never be found (asymptomatic) or are found as an incidental findings. They account for around 10% of adult brain tumours.

concepts.title: Pituitary adenoma – Content 2
concepts.content: Pituitary adenomas can be classified according to:

concepts.title: Pituitary adenoma – Content 3
concepts.content:
size (a microadenoma is <1cm and a macroadenoma is ≥1cm)
hormonal status (a secretory/functioning adenoma produces an excess of a particular hormone and a non-secretory/functioning adenoma does not produce a hormone to excess)

concepts.title: Pituitary adenoma – Content 4
concepts.content: Prolactinomas are the most common type and they produce an excess of prolactin. After prolactinomas, non-secreting adenomas are the next most common, then GH-secreting and then ACTH-secreting adenomas.

concepts.title: Pituitary adenoma – Content 5
concepts.content: Pituitary adenomas typically cause symptoms by:

concepts.title: Pituitary adenoma – Content 6
concepts.content:

non-functioning tumours, therefore, present with generalised hypopituitarism
stretching of the dura within/around the pituitary fossa (causing headaches)
compression of the optic chiasm (causing a bitemporal hemianopia due to crossing nasal fibers)

vascular malformation (e.g. aneurysm)

concepts.title: Pituitary adenoma – Content 12
concepts.content: Treatment may include a combination of

concepts.title: Pituitary adenoma – Content 13 (1)
concepts.content:
medical therapy:
prolactinomas are generally treated first-line with dopamine agonists (e.g., cabergoline or bromocriptine).

concepts.title: Pituitary adenoma – Content 13 (2)
concepts.content:
somatostatin analogues (e.g., octreotide, lanreotide) and GH receptor antagonists (e.g., pegvisomant) are used for GH-secreting adenomas
for ACTH-secreting adenomas, medical therapy may include cortisol synthesis inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, metyrapone) and neuromodulators like pasireotide
transsphenoidal surgery
the primary treatment for most pituitary adenomas is transsphenoidal surgery, especially for non-functioning and ACTH- or GH-secreting adenomas
surgical intervention aims to remove the tumour mass, normalise hormone levels, and
non-functioning adenomas are generally diagnosed due to their compressive symptoms (e.g.

concepts.title: Pituitary adenoma – Content 13 (3)
concepts.content:
visual problems) or hormone deficiencies - surgery is therefore the first-line treatment
radiotherapy
indicated for residual or recurrent tumours post-surgery

concepts.title: Prediabetes and impaired glucose regulation – Management (1)
concepts.content:
lifestyle modification: weight loss, increased exercise, change in diet
at least yearly follow-up with blood tests is recommended
NICE recommend metformin for adults at high risk 'whose blood glucose measure (fasting plasma glucose or HbA1c) shows they are still progressing towards type 2 diabetes, despite their participation in an intensive lifestyle-change programme'
Impaired fasting glucose and impaired glucose tolerance
There are two main types of IGR:
impaired fasting glucose (IFG) - due to hepatic insulin resistance
impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) - due to muscle insulin resistance
patients with IGT are more likely to develop T2DM and cardiovascular disease than patients with IFG
Definitions
a fasting glucose greater than or equal to 6.1 but less than 7.0 mmol/l implies impaired fasting glucose (IFG)
impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) is defined as fasting plasma glucose less than 7.0 mmol/l and OGTT 2-hour value greater than or equal to 7.8 mmol/l but less than 11.1 mmol/l
people with IFG should then be offered an oral glucose tolerance test to rule out a diagnosis of diabetes.

concepts.title: Prediabetes and impaired glucose regulation – Management (2)
concepts.content: A result below 11.1 mmol/l but above 7.8 mmol/l indicates that the person doesn't have diabetes but does have IGT

concepts.title: Pregnancy – Management
concepts.content:
propylthiouracil has traditionally been the antithyroid drug of choice
however, propylthiouracil is associated with an increased risk of severe hepatic injury
propylthiouracil is generally used in the first trimester of pregnancy in place of carbimazole, as carbimazole may be associated with an increased risk of congenital abnormalities
maternal free thyroxine levels should be kept in the upper third of the normal reference range to avoid fetal hypothyroidism
thyrotrophin receptor stimulating antibodies should be checked at 30-36 weeks gestation - helps to determine the risk of neonatal thyroid problems
block-and-replace regimes should not be used in pregnancy
radioiodine therapy is contraindicated
Hypothyroidism
Key points
thyroxine is safe during pregnancy
serum thyroid-stimulating hormone measured in each trimester and 6-8 weeks post-partum
women require an increased dose of thyroxine during pregnancy
by up to 50% as early as 4-6 weeks of pregnancy
breastfeeding is safe whilst on thyroxine

concepts.title: Primary hyperaldosteronism – Causes
concepts.content:
bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia: the cause of around 60-70% of cases
adrenal adenoma: 20-30% of cases
unilateral hyperplasia
familial hyperaldosteronism
adrenal carcinoma

concepts.title: Primary hyperaldosteronism – Pathophysiology
concepts.content:
aldosterone is high
renin is low (suppressed by volume expansion)
consequences:
aldosterone → ↑ renal tubular sodium resorption (via ENaC channels in the collecting duct)
↑ K⁺ excretion → hypokalaemia
↑ H⁺ excretion → metabolic alkalosis
hypertension from sodium/water retention

concepts.title: Primary hyperaldosteronism – Features
concepts.content:
hypertension
increasingly recognised but still underdiagnosed cause of hypertension
hypokalaemia
e.g. muscle weakness
this is a classical feature in exams but studies suggest this is seen in only 10-40% of patients, and is more common with adrenal adenomas
metabolic alkalosis

concepts.title: Primary hyperaldosteronism – Investigations (1)
concepts.content: guidelines vary but certain patients should be screened for primary hyperaldosteronism, e.g.

concepts.title: Primary hyperaldosteronism – Investigations (2)
concepts.content:
hypertension with hypokalemia
treatment-resistant hypertension
the 2016 Endocrine Society recommend that a plasma aldosterone/renin ratio is the first-line investigation in suspected primary hyperaldosteronism
should show high aldosterone levels alongside low renin levels (negative feedback due to sodium retention from aldosterone)
following this a high-resolution CT abdomen and adrenal vein sampling is used to differentiate between unilateral and bilateral sources of aldosterone excess
if the CT is normal adrenal venous sampling (AVS) can be used to distinguish between unilateral adenoma and bilateral hyperplasia

concepts.title: Primary hyperaldosteronism – Management
concepts.content:
adrenal adenoma: surgery (laparoscopic adrenalectomy)
bilateral adrenocortical hyperplasia: aldosterone antagonist e.g. spironolactone

concepts.title: Primary hyperparathyroidism – Investigations
concepts.content:
bloods
raised calcium, low phosphate
PTH may be raised or (inappropriately, given the raised calcium) normal
technetium-MIBI subtraction scan
x-ray findings
pepperpot skull
osteitis fibrosa cystica

concepts.title: Primary hyperparathyroidism – Treatment
concepts.content:
the definitive management is total parathyroidectomy
conservative management may be offered if the calcium level is less than 0.25 mmol/L above the upper limit of normal AND the patient is > 50 years AND there is no evidence of end-organ damage
patients not suitable for surgery may be treated with cinacalcet, a calcimimetic
a calcimimetic 'mimics' the action of calcium on tissues by allosteric activation of the calcium-sensing receptor

concepts.title: Prolactin – Content 1
concepts.content:
Notes	Further detail
Source	Anterior pituitary
Function	Stimulates breast development (both initially and further hyperplasia during pregnancy)
Stimulates milk production

concepts.title: Prolactin – Content 2
concepts.content:
It decreases GnRH pulsatility at the hypothalamic level and to a lesser extent, blocks the action of LH on the ovary or testis.
Regulation	Prolactin secretion is under constant inhibition by dopamine

concepts.title: Prolactin – Content 4
concepts.content:
thyrotropin releasing hormone
pregnancy
oestrogen
breastfeeding
sleep
stress
drugs e.g. metoclopramide, antipsychotics

concepts.title: Prolactin – Content 6
concepts.content:
dopamine
dopaminergic agonists

concepts.title: Prolactin and galactorrhoea – Content 1
concepts.content: Prolactin is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland with release being controlled by a wide variety of physiological factors. Dopamine acts as the primary prolactin releasing inhibitory factor and hence dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine may be used to control galactorrhoea. It is important to differentiate the causes of galactorrhoea (due to the actions of prolactin on breast tissue) from those of gynaecomastia

concepts.title: Prolactin and galactorrhoea – Content 3
concepts.content:
men: impotence, loss of libido, galactorrhoea
women: amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea

concepts.title: Prolactin and galactorrhoea – Content 5
concepts.content:
prolactinoma
pregnancy
oestrogens
physiological: stress, exercise, sleep
acromegaly: 1/3 of patients
polycystic ovarian syndrome
primary hypothyroidism (due to thyrotrophin releasing hormone (TRH) stimulating prolactin release)

concepts.title: Prolactin and galactorrhoea – Content 6
concepts.content: Drug causes of raised prolactin

concepts.title: Prolactin and galactorrhoea – Content 7
concepts.content:
metoclopramide, domperidone
phenothiazines
haloperidol
very rare: SSRIs, opioids

concepts.title: Prolactinoma – Features
concepts.content:
excess prolactin in women
amenorrhoea
infertility
galactorrhoea
osteoporosis
excess prolactin in men
impotence
loss of libido
galactorrhoea
other symptoms may be seen with macroadenomas
headache.
visual disturbances (classically, a bitemporal hemianopia (lateral visual fields) or upper temporal quadrantanopia)
symptoms and signs of hypopituitarism

concepts.title: Prolactinoma – Management
concepts.content:
in the majority of cases, symptomatic patients are treated medically with dopamine agonists (e.g. cabergoline, bromocriptine) which inhibit the release of prolactin from the pituitary gland
surgery is performed for patients who cannot tolerate or fail to respond to medical therapy. A trans-sphenoidal approach is generally preferred unless there is a significant extra-pituitary extension

concepts.title: PTH – Content 1
concepts.content: A hormone is a chemical messenger which is secreted by an endocrine gland and designed to generate a specific response by binding to a cellular receptor. This receptor may be intracellular (commonly steroid hormone receptors) or on the cell surface membrane.

concepts.title: PTH – Content 2
concepts.content: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is a polypeptide hormone secreted from the parathyroid gland. It has an important role in calcium homeostasis. It acts on cell-surface receptors to generate a coordinated response throughout the body and maintain blood calcium within a narrow range.

concepts.title: PTH – Content 3
concepts.content: It is vital that calcium does not rise too high or fall too low, as hyper- and hypo- calcaemia can have serious consequences. Calcium enters the body through the intestines and leaves through urine and faeces. The main reservoir of calcium in the body is the bone, containing about 1 kg of complexed calcium and phosphate. In the blood, calcium exists in three main forms:

concepts.title: PTH – Content 4
concepts.content:
free calcium
bound to albumin
complexed with anions

concepts.title: PTH – Content 5
concepts.content: It is free calcium which is physiologically active and can travel into cells to exert a function.

concepts.title: PTH – Content 7
concepts.content: PTH, a single-chain polypeptide containing 84 amino acids, is secreted from the Chief cells of the parathyroid glands, located on the posterior aspect of the thyroid. It is generated in response to low levels of calcium in the blood, where it travels to effector organs to increase levels of the electrolyte back to normal concentrations.

concepts.title: PTH – Content 8
concepts.content: Effector organs associated with PTH include the bone and kidney:

concepts.title: PTH – Content 9
concepts.content:
At the bone PTH acts to increase the activity of osteoclastic cells, which are responsible for bone resorption. In this way, the bone releases some of its calcium, and phosphate, stores into the bloodstream.
At the kidney PTH as two actions. One is to increase the hydroxylation and activation of vitamin D in the proximal convoluted tubules. Another in to increase calcium reabsorption from the distal convoluted tubules and increase phosphate excretion.

concepts.title: PTH – Content 10
concepts.content: Active vitamin D has a similar action to PTH, however, it is a steroid hormone. One of its unique actions is to increase dietary calcium absorption from the intestine by increasing expression of calcium-binding hormone.

concepts.title: PTH – Content 12
concepts.content: While PTH is very important in maintaining adequate levels of calcium in the bloodstream, it is equally as important that its actions don't cause hypercalcaemia. Regulation is therefore vital. This is achieved through a negative feedback loop:

concepts.title: PTH – Content 13
concepts.content:
calcium levels in the blood fall, which is detected by the parathyroid gland
chief cells secrete PTH into the blood
calcium is released from bone and reabsorbed from the renal tubules, causing its level to rise
increased calcium levels are detected by the parathyroid gland, which decreases PTH secretion

concepts.title: PTH – Content 15
concepts.content: Primary hyperparathyroidism is a condition in which the parathyroid gland is overactive. This is often due to hyperplasia, an adenoma or malignancy. Symptoms of hypercalcaemia develop, which includes renal calculi, constipation, polyuria, abdominal pain and low mood. One treatment is surgical removal of the glands.

concepts.title: PTH – Content 16
concepts.content: PTHrp is a polypeptide which has a similar structure to PTH, hence its name 'related peptide'. It can be secreted from cancer cells, notably squamous cell bronchial carcinoma, to cause hypercalcaemia. PTHrp has all the same effects as PTH, however it cannot activate vitamin D.

concepts.title: Riedel's thyroiditis – Content 1
concepts.content: Riedel's thyroiditis is a rare cause of hypothyroidism characterised by dense fibrous tissue replacing the normal thyroid parenchyma. On examination a hard, fixed, painless goitre is noted. It is usually seen in middle-aged women. It is associated with retroperitoneal fibrosis.

concepts.title: Riedel's thyroiditis – Content 2
concepts.content: Venn diagram showing how different causes of thyroid dysfunction may manifest. Note how many causes of hypothyroidism may have an initial thyrotoxic phase.

concepts.title: SGLT-2 inhibitors – Content 1
concepts.content: SGLT-2 inhibitors reversibly inhibit sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT-2) in the renal proximal convoluted tubule to reduce glucose reabsorption and increase urinary glucose excretion.

concepts.title: SGLT-2 inhibitors – Content 2
concepts.content: Examples include canagliflozin, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin.

concepts.title: SGLT-2 inhibitors – Content 3
concepts.content: Important adverse effects include

concepts.title: SGLT-2 inhibitors – Content 4
concepts.content:
urinary and genital infection (secondary to glycosuria). Fournier's gangrene has also been reported
euglycaemic ketoacidosis
SGLT-2 should be immediately stopped
managed in a similar way to standard diabetic ketoacidosis, but 10% glucose infusion is started immediately as glucose is normal by definition (to avoid the insulin infusion causing hypoglycaemia)
increased risk of lower-limb amputation: feet should be closely monitored

concepts.title: SGLT-2 inhibitors – Content 5
concepts.content: Patients taking SGLT-2 drugs often lose weight, which can be beneficial in type 2 diabetes mellitus.

concepts.title: Sick euthyroid syndrome – Content 1
concepts.content: In sick euthyroid syndrome (now referred to as non-thyroidal illness) it is often said that everything (TSH, thyroxine and T3) is low. In the majority of cases however the TSH level is within the >normal range (inappropriately normal given the low thyroxine and T3).

concepts.title: Sick euthyroid syndrome – Content 2
concepts.content: Changes are reversible upon recovery from the systemic illness and hence no treatment is usually needed.

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 1
concepts.content:
Surgery precipitates hormonal and metabolic changes causing the stress response.
Stress response is associated with: substrate mobilization, muscle protein loss, sodium and water retention, suppression of anabolic hormone secretion, activation of the sympathetic nervous system, immunological and haematological changes.
The hypothalamic-pituitary axis and the sympathetic nervous systems are activated and there is a failure of the normal feedback mechanisms of control of hormone secretion.

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 2
concepts.content: A summary of the hormonal changes associated with the stress response:

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 3
concepts.content:
Increased	Decreased	No Change
Growth hormone	Insulin	Thyroid stimulating hormone
Cortisol	Testosterone	Luteinizing hormone
Renin	Oestrogen	Follicle stimulating hormone
Adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH)
Aldosterone
Prolactin
Antidiuretic hormone
Glucagon

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 5
concepts.content:
Stimulates catecholamine release
Causes tachycardia and hypertension

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 7
concepts.content:
ACTH and growth hormone (GH) is stimulated by hypothalamic releasing factors, corticotrophin releasing factor (CRF) and somatotrophin (or growth hormone releasing factor)
Perioperative increased prolactin secretion occurs by release of inhibitory control
Secretion of thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) does not change significantly
ACTH stimulates cortisol production within a few minutes of the start of surgery. More ACTH is produced than needed to produce a maximum adrenocortical response.

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 9
concepts.content:
Significant increases within 4-6 hours of surgery (>1000 nmol litre-1).
The usual negative feedback mechanism fails and concentrations of ACTH and cortisol remain persistently increased.
The magnitude and duration of the increase correlate with the severity of stress and the response is not abolished by the administration of corticosteroids.
The metabolic effects of cortisol are enhanced:

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 10
concepts.content:
Skeletal muscle protein breakdown to provide gluconeogenic precursors and amino acids for protein synthesis in the liver
Stimulation of lipolysis
'Anti-insulin effect'
Mineralocorticoid effects
Anti-inflammatory effects

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 12
concepts.content:
Increased secretion after surgery has a minor role
Most important for preventing muscle protein breakdown and promote tissue repair by insulin growth factors

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 16
concepts.content:
An important vasopressor and enhances haemostasis
Renin is released causing the conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I
Angiotensin II formed by ACE on angiotensin 1, which causes the secretion of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex. This increases sodium reabsorption at the distal convoluted tubule

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 18
concepts.content:
Release inhibited by stress
Occurs via the inhibition of the beta cells in the pancreas by the α2-adrenergic inhibitory effects of catecholamines
Insulin resistance by target cells occurs later
The perioperative period is characterized by a state of functional insulin deficiency

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 19
concepts.content: Thyroxine (T4) and tri-iodothyronine (T3)

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 20
concepts.content: Circulating concentrations are inversely correlated with sympathetic activity and after surgery there is a reduction in thyroid hormone production, which normalises over a few days.

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 21
concepts.content: Metabolic effect of endocrine response

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 23
concepts.content:
Hyperglycaemia is a main feature of the metabolic response to surgery
Due to increase in glucose production and a reduction in glucose utilization
Catecholamines and cortisol promote glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
Initial failure of insulin secretion followed by insulin resistance affects the normal responses
The proportion of the hyperglycaemic response reflects the severity of surgery
Hyperglycaemia impairs wound healing and increase infection rates

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 25
concepts.content:
Initially there is inhibition of protein anabolism, followed later, if the stress response is severe, by enhanced catabolism
The amount of protein degradation is influenced by the type of surgery and also by the nutritional status of the patient
Mainly skeletal muscle protein is affected
The amino acids released form acute phase proteins (fibrinogen, C reactive protein, complement proteins, a2-macroglobulin, amyloid A and ceruloplasmin) and are used for gluconeogenesis
Nutritional support has little effect on preventing catabolism

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 26
concepts.content:
Lipid metabolism
Increased catecholamine, cortisol and glucagon secretion, and insulin deficiency, promotes lipolysis and ketone body production.

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 28
concepts.content:
ADH causes water retention, concentrated urine, and potassium loss and may continue for 3 to 5 days after surgery
Renin causes sodium and water retention

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 30
concepts.content:
Glycoproteins
Interleukins (IL) 1 to 17, interferons, and tumour necrosis factor
Synthesized by activated macrophages, fibroblasts, endothelial and glial cells in response to tissue injury from surgery or trauma
IL-6 main cytokine associated with surgery. Peak 12 to 24 h after surgery and increase by the degree of tissue damage Other effects of cytokines include fever, granulocytosis, haemostasis, tissue damage limitation and promotion of healing.

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 32 (1)
concepts.content:
Opioids suppress hypothalamic and pituitary hormone secretion
At high doses the hormonal response to pelvic and abdominal surgery is abolished.

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 32 (2)
concepts.content:
However, such doses prolong recovery and increase the need for postoperative ventilatory support
Spinal anaesthesia can reduce the glucose, ACTH, cortisol, GH and epinephrine changes, although cytokine responses are unaltered
Cytokine release is reduced in less invasive surgery
Nutrition prevents the adverse effects of the stress response.

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 32 (3)
concepts.content:
Enteral feeding improves recovery
Growth hormone and anabolic steroids may improve outcome
Normothermia decreases the metabolic response

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 33
concepts.content:
References
Deborah Burton, Grainne Nicholson, and George Hall
Endocrine and metabolic response to surgery .

concepts.title: Stress response – Content 34
concepts.content: Contin Educ Anaesth Crit Care Pain (2004) 4(5): 144-147 doi:10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkh040

concepts.title: Subacute (De Quervain's) thyroiditis – Investigations
concepts.content: thyroid scintigraphy: globally reduced uptake of iodine-131

concepts.title: Subacute (De Quervain's) thyroiditis – Management
concepts.content:
usually self-limiting - most patients do not require treatment
thyroid pain may respond to aspirin or other NSAIDs
in more severe cases steroids are used, particularly if hypothyroidism develops
Venn diagram showing how different causes of thyroid dysfunction may manifest. Note how many causes of hypothyroidism may have an initial thyrotoxic phase.

concepts.title: Subclinical hyperthyroidism – Causes
concepts.content:
multinodular goitre, particularly in elderly females
excessive thyroxine may give a similar biochemical picture
The importance in recognising subclinical hyperthyroidism lies in the potential effect on the cardiovascular system (atrial fibrillation) and bone metabolism (osteoporosis). It may also impact on quality of life and increase the likelihood of dementia

concepts.title: Subclinical hyperthyroidism – Management
concepts.content:
TSH levels often revert to normal - therefore levels must be persistently low to warrant intervention
a reasonable treatment option is a therapeutic trial of low-dose antithyroid agents for approximately 6 months in an effort to induce a remission

concepts.title: Subclinical hypothyroidism – Management (1)
concepts.content: Not all patients require treatment. NICE have produced guidelines. Note that not all patients will fall within the age boundaries given and hence these are guidelines in the broader sense.

concepts.title: Subclinical hypothyroidism – Management (2)
concepts.content:
TSH is > 10mU/L and the free thyroxine level is within the normal range
consider offering levothyroxine if the TSH level is > 10 mU/L on 2 separate occasions 3 months apart
TSH is between 5.5 - 10mU/L and the free thyroxine level is within the normal range
if < 65 years consider offering a 6-month trial of levothyroxine if:
the TSH level is 5.5 - 10mU/L on 2 separate occasions 3 months apart,and
there are symptoms of hypothyroidism
in older people (especially those aged over 80 years) follow a 'watch and wait' strategy is often used
if asymptomatic people, observe and repeat thyroid function in 6 months

concepts.title: Sulfonylureas – Content 1
concepts.content: Sulfonylureas are oral hypoglycaemic drugs used in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus. They work by increasing pancreatic insulin secretion and hence are only effective if functional B-cells are present. On a molecular level they bind to an ATP-dependent K+(KATP) channel on the cell membrane of pancreatic beta cells.

concepts.title: Sulfonylureas – Content 3
concepts.content:
hypoglycaemic episodes (more common with long-acting preparations such as chlorpropamide)
weight gain

concepts.title: Sulfonylureas – Content 5
concepts.content:
hyponatraemia secondary to syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion
bone marrow suppression
hepatotoxicity (typically cholestatic)
peripheral neuropathy

concepts.title: Sulfonylureas – Content 6
concepts.content: Sulfonylureas should be avoided in breastfeeding and pregnancy.

concepts.title: Sulfonylureas – Content 2
concepts.content:
hypoglycaemic episodes (more common with long acting preparations such as chlorpropamide)
weight gain

concepts.title: Sulfonylureas – Content 4
concepts.content:
syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion
bone marrow suppression
liver damage (cholestatic)
peripheral neuropathy

concepts.title: Thiazolidinediones – Adverse effects
concepts.content:
weight gain
liver impairment: monitor LFTs
fluid retention - therefore contraindicated in heart failure. The risk of fluid retention is increased if the patient also takes insulin
recent studies have indicated an increased risk of fractures
bladder cancer: recent studies have shown an increased risk of bladder cancer in patients taking pioglitazone (hazard ratio 2.64)

concepts.title: Thyroid cancer – Content 1
concepts.content: Features of hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism are not commonly seen in patients with thyroid malignancies as they rarely secrete thyroid hormones

concepts.title: Thyroid cancer – Content 3
concepts.content:
Type	Percentage
Papillary	70%	Often young females - excellent prognosis
Follicular	20%
Medullary	5%	Cancer of parafollicular (C) cells, secrete calcitonin, part of MEN-2
Anaplastic	1%	Not responsive to treatment, can cause pressure symptoms
Lymphoma	Rare	Associated with Hashimoto's thyroiditis

concepts.title: Thyroid cancer – Content 4
concepts.content: Management of papillary and follicular cancer

concepts.title: Thyroid cancer – Content 5
concepts.content:
total thyroidectomy
followed by radioiodine (I-131) to kill residual cells
monitoring:
neck ultrasound
papillary/follicular carcinoma: yearly thyroglobulin levels to detect early recurrent disease
medullary carcinoma: calcitonin + carcinoembryonic antigen

concepts.title: Thyroid cancer – Content 7
concepts.content:
Type	Notes
Papillary carcinoma
Usually contain a mixture of papillary and colloidal filled follicles
Histologically tumour has papillary projections and pale empty nuclei
Seldom encapsulated
Lymph node metastasis predominate
Haematogenous metastasis rare

concepts.title: Thyroid cancer – Content 8
concepts.content:
Follicular adenoma
Usually present as a solitary thyroid nodule
Malignancy can only be excluded on formal histological assessment

concepts.title: Thyroid cancer – Content 9
concepts.content:
Follicular carcinoma
May appear macroscopically encapsulated, microscopically capsular invasion is seen. Without this finding the lesion is a follicular adenoma.
Vascular invasion predominates
Multifocal disease raree

concepts.title: Thyroid cancer – Content 10
concepts.content:
Medullary carcinoma
C cells derived from neural crest and not thyroid tissue
Serum calcitonin levels often raised
Familial genetic disease accounts for up to 20% cases
Both lymphatic and haematogenous metastasis are recognised, nodal disease is associated with a very poor prognosis.

concepts.title: Thyroid cancer – Content 11
concepts.content:
Anaplastic carcinoma
Most common in elderly females
Local invasion is a common feature
Treatment is by resection where possible, palliation may be achieved through isthmusectomy and radiotherapy. Chemotherapy is ineffective.

concepts.title: Thyroid disorders – Treatment
concepts.content:
This clearly depends on the cause. For patients with hypothyrodism thyroxine is given in the form of levothyroxine to replace the underlying deficiency.
Patients with thyrotoxicosis may be treated with:
propranolol: this is often used at the time of diagnosis to control thyrotoxic symptoms such as tremor
carbimazole: blocks thyroid peroxidase from coupling and iodinating the tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin → reducing thyroid hormone production. Agranulocytosis is an important adverse effect to be aware of
radioiodine treatment

concepts.title: Thyroid eye disease – Pathophysiology
concepts.content:
it is thought to be caused by an autoimmune response against an autoantigen, possibly the TSH receptor → retro-orbital inflammation
the inflammation results in glycosaminoglycan and collagen deposition in the muscles
Prevention
smoking is the most important modifiable risk factor for the development of thyroid eye disease
radioiodine treatment may increase the inflammatory symptoms seen in thyroid eye disease. In a recent study of patients with Graves' disease around 15% developed, or had worsening of, eye disease. Prednisolone may help reduce the risk

concepts.title: Thyroid eye disease – Features
concepts.content:
the patient may be eu-, hypo- or hyperthyroid at the time of presentation
lid retraction (most common sign, seen in 90%)
sympathetic overactivity leading to overaction of the levator palpebrae superioris and Müller’s muscle
→ 'staring' appearance
exophthalmos (most specific sign)
forward protrusion of the eyeball due to inflammation and oedema of the extraocular muscles and orbital fat
conjunctival oedema
optic disc swelling
ophthalmoplegia
inability to close the eyelids may lead to sore, dry eyes. If severe and untreated patients can be at risk of exposure keratopathy

concepts.title: Thyroid eye disease – Management
concepts.content:
smoking cessation
topical lubricants may be needed to help prevent corneal inflammation caused by exposure
steroids
radiotherapy
surgery

concepts.title: Thyroid eye disease – Complications (1)
concepts.content:
Exposure keratopathy
this is the most common complication of thyroid eye disease
due to eyelid retraction and proptosis (exophthalmos) → cornea becomes excessively exposed, disrupting the normal tear film → dryness, irritation, and corneal ulceration
symptoms include foreign body sensation, pain, and photophobia
in severe cases, it can lead to corneal scarring and vision impairment.

concepts.title: Thyroid eye disease – Complications (2)
concepts.content:
Optic neuropathy
one of the most serious complications of thyroid eye disease
occurs when enlarged extraocular muscles compress the optic nerve at the apex of the orbit → a reduction in visual acuity, colour vision deficits, and visual field defect
it requires urgent medical intervention to prevent permanent vision loss.

filters: Gradual change in or loss of vision

concepts.title: Thyroid eye disease – Complications (3)
concepts.content:
Strabismus and diplopia
fibrosis and enlargement of the extraocular muscles can result in restrictive strabismus → misalignment of the eyes → double vision (diplopia)
this not only affects visual function but can also significantly impair the quality of life.

concepts.title: Thyroid eye disease – Complications (4)
concepts.content:
Monitoring patients with established thyroid eye disease
For patients with established thyroid eye disease the following symptoms/signs should indicate the need for urgent review by an ophthalmologist (see EUGOGO guidelines):
unexplained deterioration in vision
awareness of change in intensity or quality of colour vision in one or both eyes
history of eye suddenly 'popping out' (globe subluxation)
obvious corneal opacity
cornea still visible when the eyelids are closed
disc swelling

concepts.title: Thyroid storm – Content 1
concepts.content: Thyroid storm is a rare but life-threatening complication of thyrotoxicosis. It is typically seen in patients with established thyrotoxicosis and is rarely seen as the presenting feature. Iatrogenic thyroxine excess does not usually result in thyroid storm.

concepts.title: Thyroid storm – Content 3
concepts.content:
thyroid or non-thyroidal surgery
trauma
infection
acute iodine load e.g. CT contrast media

concepts.title: Thyroid storm – Content 5

fever > 38.5ºC
tachycardia

nausea and vomiting
hypertension
heart failure

concepts.content:
Graves' disease

amiodarone therapy
contrast
rare, more commonly occurs in elderly patients with pre-existing thyroid disease (e.g. multinodular goitre, Graves')
patients with existing thyrotoxicosis should not receive iodinated contrast medium
administration of iodinated contrast results in a large iodine load to the thyroid → hyperthyroidism developing over 2-12 weeks

concepts.content: Toxic multinodular goitre describes a thyroid gland that contains a number of autonomously functioning thyroid nodules resulting in hyperthyroidism.

concepts.title: Toxic multinodular goitre – Content 2

concepts.title: Toxic multinodular goitre – Content 3

concepts.title: Acute sinusitis – Definition and causative organisms
concepts.content: Acute sinusitis is an inflammation of the mucous membranes of the paranasal sinuses. The sinuses are usually sterile; the most common infectious agents are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and rhinoviruses.

concepts.title: Acute sinusitis – Predisposing factors
concepts.content: Predisposing factors for acute sinusitis include nasal obstruction (e.g. septal deviation or nasal polyps), recent local infection (e.g. rhinitis or dental extraction), swimming/diving, and smoking.

concepts.title: Acute sinusitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Clinical features of acute sinusitis include facial pain (typically frontal pressure pain worse on bending forward), nasal discharge (usually thick and purulent), and nasal obstruction. 'Double-sickening' may occur where an initial viral sinusitis worsens due to secondary bacterial infection.

concepts.title: Acute sinusitis – Management
concepts.content: Management of acute sinusitis: analgesia; intranasal decongestants or nasal saline (limited evidence); intranasal corticosteroids if symptoms present >10 days (NICE). Oral antibiotics not normally required but may be given for severe presentations — phenoxymethylpenicillin first-line, co-amoxiclav if systemically very unwell or high-risk of complications.

concepts.title: Acute sinusitis – Complications and red flags
concepts.content: Red flag features requiring urgent referral include orbital or intracranial complications. Patients should be referred urgently if they develop signs of orbital or intracranial spread.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Definition and classification
concepts.content: Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction of the nasal mucosa to allergens. Classified by duration: seasonal (hay fever — tree pollen March–May, grass pollen May–July, weed pollen June–September); perennial (year-round — house dust mite, pet dander, mould). Classified by severity: mild (normal sleep, no impairment of daily activities); moderate-severe (abnormal sleep, impairment of daily activities). Prevalence: ~20% of UK population. Associated conditions: asthma, eczema, conjunctivitis.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of allergic rhinitis: nasal symptoms — sneezing (often paroxysmal), rhinorrhoea (watery anterior discharge), nasal obstruction/congestion, nasal pruritus; ocular symptoms — itchy, watery, red eyes (allergic conjunctivitis); post-nasal drip; reduced sense of smell; fatigue; 'allergic salute' (rubbing nose upward with palm); 'allergic shiners' (dark circles under eyes from venous congestion); Dennie-Morgan lines (extra fold of skin under lower eyelid).

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Management
concepts.content: Management of allergic rhinitis (stepwise): allergen avoidance; antihistamines (oral — cetirizine, loratadine; intranasal — azelastine); intranasal corticosteroids (most effective for nasal symptoms — beclometasone, fluticasone, mometasone); intranasal decongestants (short-term only); sodium cromoglicate (eye drops for ocular symptoms); leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast — useful if concomitant asthma); allergen immunotherapy (subcutaneous or sublingual — for moderate-severe disease not controlled by pharmacotherapy). Refer to allergy specialist if: uncertain diagnosis, severe disease, immunotherapy considered.

concepts.title: Audiograms – Interpretation principles
concepts.content: Audiogram interpretation: values above the 20 dB line are essentially normal. In sensorineural hearing loss, both air and bone conduction are impaired. In conductive hearing loss, only air conduction is impaired. In mixed hearing loss, both are impaired with air conduction often worse than bone conduction.

concepts.title: Auricular haematoma – Management
concepts.content: Auricular haematomas are common in rugby players and wrestlers. Prompt treatment is important to avoid 'cauliflower ear'. Management: same-day assessment by ENT; incision and drainage is superior to needle aspiration.

concepts.title: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo – Definition and epidemiology
concepts.content: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is one of the most common causes of vertigo. It is characterised by sudden onset dizziness and vertigo triggered by changes in head position. The average age of onset is 55 years; it is less common in younger patients.

concepts.title: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of BPPV: vertigo triggered by change in head position (e.g. rolling over in bed or gazing upwards); may be associated with nausea; each episode typically lasts 10–20 seconds; positive Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre (rapidly lowering patient to supine with extended neck recreates symptoms); rotatory nystagmus.

concepts.title: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo – Management and prognosis
concepts.content: BPPV has a good prognosis and usually resolves spontaneously after a few weeks to months. Symptomatic relief: Epley manoeuvre (successful in ~80% of cases); vestibular rehabilitation (e.g. Brandt-Daroff exercises). Medication (e.g. betahistine) tends to be of limited value. Around half of patients will have recurrence 3–5 years after diagnosis.

concepts.title: Bell's palsy – Definition and epidemiology
concepts.content: Bell's palsy is an acute neurological condition presenting with rapid onset unilateral facial paralysis. The exact cause is unknown but linked to herpes simplex virus. Incidence: 23 per 100,000 person-years. Typically presents in 15–45-year-olds, though peak incidence is 70+. Sex ratio 1:1. It is a clinical diagnosis — no specific diagnostic tests exist.

concepts.title: Bell's palsy – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for Bell's palsy include pregnancy, severe pre-eclampsia, hypertension, obesity, diabetes mellitus, and upper respiratory tract infections. The general consensus is that herpes simplex virus is implicated. Inflammation and oedema of the facial nerve causes compression in the facial canal (passage through the temporal bone), resulting in facial paralysis.

concepts.title: Bell's palsy – Clinical features
concepts.content: Bell's palsy presents with unilateral facial paralysis of acute onset (within 72 hours) involving the forehead and lower face. Upper facial signs: inability to wrinkle forehead and close eye fully. Lower facial signs: loss of nasolabial fold and drooping of mouth (pronounced on smiling). Additional features: ear pain, loss of taste in anterior tongue (35%), hyperacusis (rarer). Severity graded by House-Brackmann scale (1=normal to 6=complete paralysis).

concepts.title: Bell's palsy – Investigations and diagnosis
concepts.content: Bell's palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion. NICE 2019 guidelines state diagnostic investigations (blood tests, imaging) are not required in primary care. Forehead sparing suggests upper motor neurone cause (not Bell's palsy, which is LMN). MRI head is modality of choice if diagnosis uncertain; CT head with contrast if MRI contraindicated. Electrodiagnostic testing used for complete unilateral paralysis.

concepts.title: Bell's palsy – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Differentials for Bell's palsy: stroke/TIA (forehead sparing, arm/leg weakness, slurred speech, visual disturbances); brain tumour (forehead sparing, headache, confusion, weight loss); Ramsay Hunt syndrome (VZV reactivation — facial palsy plus painful vesicular rash around ear); Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi — facial palsy, history of tick bite, erythema migrans).

concepts.title: Bell's palsy – Management
concepts.content: NICE 2019 management: good eye care on affected side (artificial tears/lubricants, tape to close eye overnight, sunglasses); soft diet and straws; prednisolone for patients presenting within 72 hours of onset; antivirals can be considered with prednisolone (not as monotherapy — greatest benefit in severe neurology). If no recovery signs after 3 weeks, refer to ENT or neurology. Other referral indications: worsening/new neurology, UMN signs, abnormal reinnervation.

concepts.title: Bell's palsy – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of Bell's palsy: synkinesis (involuntary movements with voluntary movements — aberrant nerve regeneration; includes crocodile tears syndrome, gustatory sweating, hemifacial spasm); persistent facial weakness; corneal keratitis (impaired eyelid closure); lagophthalmos; abrasive keratopathy. Rare association with Guillain-Barré syndrome or multiple sclerosis. Significant psychosocial distress including depression and anxiety.

concepts.title: Bell's palsy – Prognosis
concepts.content: Recovery from Bell's palsy is generally good. Most patients see signs of recovery within 3 weeks and complete recovery within 4 months. >90% of patients with partial paralysis make a full recovery. ~70% of patients with complete paralysis at presentation make a full recovery. Better prognosis with: improvement within first 2 weeks, younger age, corticosteroids initiated within 72 hours.

concepts.title: Black hairy tongue – Definition and predisposing factors
concepts.content: Black hairy tongue results from defective desquamation of the filiform papillae. Despite the name, the tongue may be brown, green, pink or another colour. Predisposing factors: poor oral hygiene, antibiotics, head and neck radiation, HIV, intravenous drug use.

concepts.title: Black hairy tongue – Management
concepts.content: The tongue should be swabbed to exclude Candida. Management: tongue scraping; topical antifungals if Candida is identified.

concepts.title: Branchial cyst – Definition and clinical features
concepts.content: Branchial cyst: congenital cyst arising from remnant of second branchial cleft. Typically presents in early adulthood (20–30 years). Features: oval, mobile, fluctuant swelling in anterior triangle of neck (between anterior border of SCM and pharynx, at junction of upper and middle thirds of SCM); may become tender if infected; transilluminates. Investigations: ultrasound (first-line); FNAC (cholesterol crystals in aspirate); CT/MRI. Management: surgical excision (risk of malignant transformation if left untreated; also risk of infection). Note: branchial cyst presenting in patient >40 years should raise suspicion of cystic metastasis from head and neck SCC.

concepts.title: Branchial cyst – Investigations and management
concepts.content: Investigations for branchial cyst: exclude other malignancy; ultrasound; referral to ENT; fine-needle aspiration. Management: conservative or surgical excision by ENT surgeons. Antibiotics required for acute infections.

concepts.title: Cholesteatoma – Definition and epidemiology
concepts.content: Cholesteatoma is a non-cancerous growth of squamous epithelium trapped within the skull base causing local destruction. Most common in patients aged 10–20 years (incidence 10 per 100,000 person-years). Sex ratio 1:1. Cleft palate increases risk approximately 100-fold. Often presents as a cystic structure filled with keratin debris.

concepts.title: Cholesteatoma – Aetiology
concepts.content: Cholesteatoma aetiology: congenital (aberrant epithelial remnants from embryological development; rare) or acquired. Primary acquired cholesteatoma (PAC): chronic Eustachian tube dysfunction → negative middle ear pressure → retraction pockets → squamous epithelium invagination. Risk factors: chronic otitis media with effusion, Eustachian tube dysfunction (cleft palate, Down syndrome), immunodeficiency. Secondary acquired cholesteatoma (SAC): squamous epithelium introduced via tympanic membrane perforation (otologic surgery or trauma).

concepts.title: Cholesteatoma – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Cholesteatoma pathophysiology: Eustachian tube dysfunction → negative middle ear pressure → tympanic membrane retraction → keratin accumulation. Keratinocyte migration via perforation or retraction pocket. Cholesteatomas are self-perpetuating through constant keratin shedding. Bone erosion occurs via pressure necrosis, inflammatory mediators (cytokines, MMPs), and osteoclast activation. The incus is most frequently eroded.

concepts.title: Cholesteatoma – Clinical features
concepts.content: Main features of cholesteatoma: foul-smelling non-resolving discharge; hearing loss. Features from local invasion: vertigo; facial nerve palsy; cerebellopontine angle syndrome. Otoscopy: 'attic crust' seen in the uppermost part of the eardrum.

concepts.title: Cholesteatoma – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations for cholesteatoma: otoscopy (retraction pockets, perforations, white keratin debris); pure tone audiometry (conductive hearing loss); CT scan (bony erosion, complications including facial nerve involvement or intracranial extension); MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) distinguishes inflammatory tissue from keratin-filled cysts. Surgical exploration may be required if imaging inconclusive.

concepts.title: Cholesteatoma – Management
concepts.content: Management of cholesteatoma: surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Mastoidectomy (combined approach tympanoplasty or canal wall down mastoidectomy). Regular follow-up required as recurrence rate is significant. Hearing reconstruction may be performed at same time or as second-stage procedure.

concepts.title: Cholesteatoma – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of cholesteatoma: ossicular chain erosion (conductive hearing loss; incus most frequently affected); labyrinthine fistula (sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo); intracranial extension — meningitis, brain abscess, lateral sinus thrombosis (if erosion through tegmen tympani or posterior temporal bone wall).

concepts.title: Chronic rhinosinusitis – Definition and predisposing factors
concepts.content: Chronic rhinosinusitis affects up to 1 in 10 people. Defined as inflammatory disorder of the paranasal sinuses and nasal passages lasting ≥12 weeks. Predisposing factors: atopy (hay fever, asthma), nasal obstruction (septal deviation, nasal polyps), recent local infection (rhinitis, dental extraction), swimming/diving, smoking.

concepts.title: Chronic rhinosinusitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of chronic rhinosinusitis: facial pain (frontal pressure worse on bending forward); nasal discharge (clear if allergic/vasomotor; thicker purulent if secondary infection); nasal obstruction (e.g. mouth breathing); post-nasal drip (may produce chronic cough).

concepts.title: Chronic rhinosinusitis – Management and red flags
concepts.content: Management of recurrent/chronic sinusitis: allergen avoidance; intranasal corticosteroids; nasal irrigation with saline. Red flag symptoms requiring further investigation: unilateral symptoms, persistent symptoms despite 3 months of compliant treatment, epistaxis.

concepts.title: Cochlear implant – Indications and suitability
concepts.content: A cochlear implant is an electronic device offered to patients with severe-to-profound hearing loss. Suitability: in children — audiological assessment and/or difficulty developing basic auditory skills; in adults — completed ≥3-month trial of appropriate hearing aids with objectively demonstrated limited or no benefit. Patients must have exhausted all medical therapies and conventional amplification strategies.

concepts.title: Cochlear implant – Causes of severe-to-profound hearing loss
concepts.content: Causes of severe-to-profound hearing loss requiring cochlear implant: In children — genetic (up to 50%), congenital (maternal CMV, rubella, varicella), idiopathic (up to 30%), infectious (e.g. post-meningitis). In adults — viral-induced sudden hearing loss, ototoxicity (aminoglycoside antibiotics, loop diuretics), otosclerosis, Menière's disease, trauma.

concepts.title: Cochlear implant – Contraindications
concepts.content: Absolute contraindications to cochlear implant: lesions of cranial nerve VIII or brainstem causing deafness; chronic infective otitis media, mastoid cavity or tympanic membrane perforation; cochlear aplasia. Relative contraindications: chronic infective otitis media or mastoid cavity infections; tympanic membrane perforation; patients demonstrating lack of interest in developing enhanced oral communication skills.

concepts.title: Cochlear implant – Surgical complications
concepts.content: Surgical implantation complications: infection, facial paralysis (nerve injury intra-operatively), CSF leakage, meningitis. To reduce meningitis risk, all patients should have up-to-date vaccinations against Streptococcus and Haemophilus. Patients return to outpatient clinic 3–5 weeks post-op for device stimulation. Failure rate requiring reimplantation is ~0.5%; <0.2% of recipients reject or do not use the device.

concepts.title: Cystic hygroma – Definition and clinical features
concepts.content: A cystic hygroma (cystic lymphangioma) is a rare, congenital, benign tumour of the lymphatic system.
