Most common in the posterior triangle of the neck, typically on the left side. 90% diagnosed before age 2 years. Associations: Turner syndrome, maternal alcohol abuse, viral illness during pregnancy. Examination: soft, compressible, non-painful, no movement on swallowing, transillumination detected; may compromise the airway.

concepts.title: Cystic hygroma – Management
concepts.content: Management of cystic hygroma: exclude malignancy; imaging (ultrasound, CT or MRI); observation (some tumours are small, static or slowly regress); surgical excision.

concepts.title: Deafness – Common causes and characteristic features
concepts.content: Most common causes of hearing loss: ear wax, otitis media, otitis externa. Other causes: presbycusis (bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, difficulty following conversations); otosclerosis (autosomal dominant, conductive deafness, tinnitus, flamingo tinge in 10%, positive family history, onset 20–40 years); glue ear (peaks at 2 years, commonest cause of conductive hearing loss in childhood); Menière's disease (recurrent vertigo, tinnitus, sensorineural hearing loss, aural fullness); drug ototoxicity (aminoglycosides, furosemide, aspirin, cytotoxics); noise damage (bilateral, worse at 3000–6000 Hz).

concepts.title: Ear wax – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Impacted ear wax is extremely common. Symptoms: pain, conductive hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo. Main treatment options in primary care: ear drops (olive oil, sodium bicarbonate 5%, almond oil) or irrigation ('ear syringing'). Treatment should not be given if perforation is suspected or patient has grommets.

concepts.title: Epistaxis – Definition and classification
concepts.content: Epistaxis (nosebleeds) is classified as anterior (visible source, usually from Kiesselbach's plexus capillaries) or posterior (more profuse, deeper structures, more common in older patients, higher risk of aspiration and airway compromise).

concepts.title: Epistaxis – Causes
concepts.content: Causes of epistaxis: most are benign and self-limiting. Exacerbating factors: nose picking, nose blowing, trauma, foreign bodies, bleeding disorders, immune thrombocytopenia, Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia, juvenile angiofibroma (highly vascularised benign tumour in adolescent males), cocaine use (vasoconstriction, septal obliteration), hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

concepts.title: Epistaxis – First aid management
concepts.content: First aid for haemodynamically stable epistaxis: sit with torso forward and mouth open (reduces nasopharyngeal blood flow, allows spitting of blood, reduces aspiration risk); pinch the cartilaginous (soft) area of the nose firmly for at least 20 minutes; breathe through the mouth.

concepts.title: Epistaxis – Management after successful first aid
concepts.content: After successful first aid for epistaxis: topical antiseptic (Naseptin — chlorhexidine and neomycin, or mupirocin) to reduce crusting and vestibulitis risk. Consider admission/follow-up if comorbidity (e.g. coronary artery disease, severe hypertension), underlying cause suspected, or age <2 years (haemophilia/leukaemia more likely). Self-care: avoid nose blowing/picking, heavy lifting, exercise, lying flat, alcohol, hot drinks.

concepts.title: Epistaxis – Cautery and packing
concepts.content: If bleeding does not stop after 10–15 minutes of continuous pressure: cautery if bleeding source visible and tolerated (ask patient to blow nose, apply topical local anaesthetic e.g. Co-phenylcaine, apply silver nitrate stick 3–10 seconds until grey-white, cauterise one side of septum only to avoid perforation); packing if cautery not viable or source not visualised (anaesthetise with Co-phenylcaine, pack with head forward, admit for observation). Epistaxis failing all emergency management may require sphenopalatine ligation in theatre.

concepts.title: Facial pain – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Differential diagnosis of facial pain: sinusitis (dull, pressure-like, worse on bending forward, associated nasal symptoms); dental pain (localised, worse with hot/cold, dental history); trigeminal neuralgia (severe, lancinating, unilateral, triggered by light touch); temporomandibular joint dysfunction (jaw pain, clicking, trismus, worse with chewing); cluster headache (periorbital, unilateral, autonomic features — lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, ptosis); atypical facial pain (chronic, poorly localised, no clear organic cause); herpes zoster (dermatomal distribution, vesicular rash); parotid pathology (pre-auricular pain, swelling); nasopharyngeal carcinoma (referred otalgia, nasal obstruction, neck lump).

concepts.title: Gingival hyperplasia – Drug causes
concepts.content: Drug causes of gingival hyperplasia: phenytoin, ciclosporin, calcium channel blockers (especially nifedipine). Other causes include acute myeloid leukaemia (myelomonocytic and monocytic types).

concepts.title: Gingivitis – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Gingivitis is usually secondary to poor dental hygiene. Ranges from simple gingivitis (painless red swelling of gum margin, bleeds on contact) to acute necrotising ulcerative gingivitis (ANUG — painful bleeding gums, halitosis, punched-out ulcers). Simple gingivitis: routine dental review, antibiotics not usually necessary. ANUG: CKS recommends specific management (metronidazole and dental referral).

concepts.title: Hoarseness and voice change – Causes and referral criteria
concepts.content: Causes of hoarseness: laryngitis (most common), voice overuse, GORD, laryngeal cancer, lung cancer. A chest X-ray should be considered to exclude apical lung lesions. Suspected laryngeal cancer referral: 2-week wait to ENT specialist for patients aged ≥45 years with persistent unexplained hoarseness or unexplained lump in the neck.

concepts.title: Laryngopharyngeal reflux – Definition and epidemiology
concepts.content: Laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR) is a condition caused by gastro-oesophageal reflux resulting in inflammatory changes to the larynx/hypopharynx mucosa. Incidence: 500 per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 40–50 years. Sex ratio 1:1. Accounts for approximately 10% of ENT referrals.

concepts.title: Laryngopharyngeal reflux – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for LPR: obesity (increased intra-abdominal pressure), dietary habits (fatty foods, caffeine, alcohol, chocolate, spicy foods), smoking (weakens LES), medications (calcium channel blockers, anticholinergics, nitrates), pregnancy. Underlying causes: LES dysfunction, hiatal hernia, gastroparesis/delayed gastric emptying, prolonged nasogastric tube placement, supine positioning during sleep.

concepts.title: Laryngopharyngeal reflux – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of LPR: globus pharyngeus (sensation of lump in throat) in ~50–70% of patients — typically felt in the midline, worse when swallowing saliva rather than eating/drinking; hoarseness (70%); chronic cough (50%); dysphagia (35%); heartburn (30%); sore throat. Examination: normal neck externally (no masses); posterior pharynx may appear erythematous.

concepts.title: Laryngopharyngeal reflux – Investigations and red flags
concepts.content: In the absence of red flags, LPR can be diagnosed clinically without further investigations. NICE cancer referral red flags: persistent unilateral throat discomfort; dysphagia/odynophagia with food (not just saliva); persistent hoarseness. These warrant urgent investigation.

concepts.title: Laryngopharyngeal reflux – Management
concepts.content: LPR management: lifestyle modification first-line (weight reduction, avoid dietary triggers — caffeine, alcohol, chocolate, spicy foods, citrus, high-fat meals; smoking cessation; avoid late evening meals; elevate head of bed for nocturnal symptoms). If insufficient: PPI trial for 2–3 months (NICE CKS); H2 receptor antagonists if PPI contraindicated. Sodium alginate liquids (e.g. Gaviscon). Refer to ENT/gastroenterology if symptoms persist or red flags. Fundoplication reserved for refractory cases.

concepts.title: Leukoplakia – Definition and clinical features
concepts.content: Leukoplakia is a premalignant condition presenting as white, hard spots on oral mucous membranes. More common in smokers. It is a diagnosis of exclusion — candidiasis and lichen planus should be considered, especially if lesions can be 'rubbed off'. Types: homogeneous (uniformly flat, lower malignant risk); non-homogeneous/speckled (irregular with erythematous areas, higher malignant risk); proliferative verrucous (multiple slow-growing verrucous plaques, high malignant risk). Most commonly on buccal mucosa, gingiva, lateral tongue borders, floor of mouth. Usually asymptomatic.

concepts.title: Leukoplakia – Management
concepts.content: Leukoplakia management: risk factor modification (smoking cessation, alcohol reduction). Biopsies performed to exclude squamous cell carcinoma. Regular follow-up required as malignant transformation to SCC occurs in ~1% of patients. Surgical excision using traditional surgery, laser ablation, or cryotherapy. No clear guidelines exist for management.

concepts.title: Ludwig's angina – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Ludwig's angina is a type of progressive cellulitis invading the floor of the mouth and soft tissues of the neck. Over 70% of cases result from dental infections (particularly second or third mandibular molars). Less common causes: peritonsillar abscesses, mandibular fractures, oral lacerations/piercings, sialadenitis, oral malignancy. Predisposing factors: dental cavities, previous dental procedures, diabetes mellitus, malnutrition, alcoholism, AIDS, other immunosuppressive conditions.

concepts.title: Ludwig's angina – Pathophysiology and causative organisms
concepts.content: Ludwig's angina occurs when infection spreads contiguously from a nearby source into the sublingual and submandibular space, then progresses to parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal spaces, encircling the airway. Infections are typically polymicrobial from oral flora. Most commonly isolated pathogens: Streptococcus viridans, Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Peptostreptococcus spp., Bacteroides spp., Fusobacterium spp. In immunocompromised patients: Pseudomonas aeruginosa may also be involved.

concepts.title: Ludwig's angina – Clinical features
concepts.content: Ludwig's angina features: neck swelling (most common), often with dental pain or following recent dental procedure; dysphagia (35%); pharyngodynia (25%); fever (25%); trismus (15%); dysphonia (15%). Signs: bilateral submandibular swelling, elevated or protruding tongue, signs of respiratory distress if airway compromise present (dyspnoea 15%, tachypnoea, stridor). Life-threatening emergency — airway obstruction can occur rapidly.

concepts.title: Ludwig's angina – Management
concepts.content: Ludwig's angina management: airway management (priority — urgent assessment); intravenous antibiotics covering polymicrobial oral flora. Clinical diagnosis — investigations (FBC, CRP) should not delay initial management. CT scan may be performed to assess extent.

concepts.title: Malignant otitis externa – Definition and epidemiology
concepts.content: Malignant (necrotising) otitis externa is an uncommon, severe infection of the external auditory canal and surrounding structures. Found in immunocompromised individuals — 90% of cases in diabetics. Most commonly caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Infection commences in the soft tissues of the external auditory meatus, progresses to involve soft tissues and bony ear canal, then progresses to temporal bone osteomyelitis.

concepts.title: Malignant otitis externa – Clinical features
concepts.content: Key features of malignant otitis externa: diabetes (90%) or immunosuppression; severe, unrelenting, deep-seated otalgia; temporal headaches; purulent otorrhoea; possibly dysphagia, hoarseness, and/or facial nerve dysfunction. Granulation tissue at the osseo-cartilaginous junction on examination.

concepts.title: Malignant otitis externa – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations for malignant otitis externa: microbiological swab (Pseudomonas aeruginosa most commonly implicated); blood tests (FBC, CRP, ESR, blood cultures); audiometry (conductive hearing loss may indicate middle ear/skull base involvement); CT temporal bones (soft tissue inflammation, bone erosion); MRI (superior for early changes and intracranial/vascular complications); gallium or technetium bone scan (high sensitivity for osteomyelitis); biopsy of granulation tissue if diagnosis uncertain.

concepts.title: Malignant otitis externa – Management
concepts.content: Management of malignant otitis externa: antipseudomonal antibiotics — NICE recommends initial treatment with ciprofloxacin (oral or IV depending on severity); treatment duration typically 6–8 weeks minimum (some cases 3–6 months); IV-to-oral transition when clinical improvement evident. Fungal MOE: voriconazole or amphotericin B. Adjunctive: aural toilet, strict glycaemic control in diabetics, pain management. Surgical intervention if needed: debridement, mastoidectomy, abscess drainage. Non-resolving otitis externa with worsening pain should be referred urgently to ENT.

concepts.title: Malignant otitis externa – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of malignant otitis externa: cranial nerve involvement (most common — facial nerve VII first, then IX, X, XI, XII); osteomyelitis of temporal bone and skull base; meningitis; intracranial abscess (epidural or brain); dural sinus thrombosis (sigmoid or cavernous sinus — headache, fever); death if untreated.

concepts.title: Mastoiditis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Mastoiditis typically develops when infection spreads from the middle ear to the mastoid air spaces of the temporal bone. Features: severe otalgia (classically behind the ear), history of recurrent otitis media, fever, patient typically very unwell, swelling/erythema/tenderness over the mastoid process, external ear may protrude forwards, ear discharge if eardrum has perforated. Diagnosis is typically clinical; CT may be ordered if complications suspected.

concepts.title: Mastoiditis – Management and complications
concepts.content: Management of mastoiditis: IV antibiotics. Complications: facial nerve palsy, hearing loss, meningitis.

concepts.title: Ménière's disease – Definition and pathophysiology
concepts.content: Ménière's disease is a disorder of the inner ear of unknown cause, characterised by excessive pressure and progressive dilation of the endolymphatic system. More common in middle-aged adults but may occur at any age. Equal prevalence in men and women.

concepts.title: Ménière's disease – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of Ménière's disease: recurrent episodes of vertigo (usually the prominent symptom), tinnitus, and sensorineural hearing loss; sensation of aural fullness or pressure; nystagmus and positive Romberg test; episodes last minutes to hours; typically unilateral but bilateral symptoms may develop after several years.

concepts.title: Ménière's disease – Natural history
concepts.content: Natural history of Ménière's disease: symptoms resolve in the majority of patients after 5–10 years; the majority of patients will be left with a degree of hearing loss; psychological distress is common.

concepts.title: Ménière's disease – Management
concepts.content: Management of Ménière's disease: ENT assessment required to confirm diagnosis; patients should inform the DVLA and cease driving until satisfactory symptom control. Acute attacks: buccal or intramuscular prochlorperazine; admission sometimes required. Prevention: betahistine and vestibular rehabilitation exercises may be of benefit.

concepts.title: Mouth lesions – 2-week wait referral criteria
concepts.content: 2-week wait referrals to oral surgery required for: unexplained oral ulceration or mass persisting >3 weeks; unexplained red or red-and-white patches that are painful, swollen or bleeding; unexplained one-sided head/neck pain >4 weeks with earache but normal otoscopy; unexplained recent neck lump or previously undiagnosed lump changed over 3–6 weeks; unexplained persistent sore or painful throat; oral cavity signs/symptoms persisting >6 weeks not definitively diagnosed as benign. Higher suspicion in patients >40 years, smokers, heavy drinkers, or those who chew tobacco or betel nut.

concepts.title: Nasal polyps – Associations and clinical features
concepts.content: Nasal polyps occur in ~1% of UK adults; 2–4 times more common in men; uncommon in children and elderly. Associations: asthma (particularly late-onset), aspirin sensitivity, infective sinusitis, cystic fibrosis (nasal polyps in a child should raise suspicion for CF), Kartagener's syndrome, Churg-Strauss syndrome. Samter's triad: asthma + aspirin sensitivity + nasal polyposis. Features: nasal obstruction, rhinorrhoea, sneezing, poor taste and smell. Unilateral symptoms or bleeding always require further investigation.

concepts.title: Nasal polyps – Management
concepts.content: Management of nasal polyps: all patients with suspected nasal polyps should be referred to ENT for full examination; topical corticosteroids shrink polyp size in ~80% of patients.

concepts.title: Nasal septal haematoma – Clinical features
concepts.content: Nasal septal haematoma is an important complication of nasal trauma — haematoma between septal cartilage and overlying perichondrium. May be precipitated by relatively minor trauma. Features: nasal obstruction (most common symptom), pain, rhinorrhoea. Examination: bilateral red swelling arising from nasal septum (boggy on probing, distinguishing it from firm deviated septum).

concepts.title: Nasal septal haematoma – Management and complications
concepts.content: Management of nasal septal haematoma: surgical drainage; intravenous antibiotics. If untreated, irreversible septal necrosis may develop within 3–4 days due to pressure-related ischaemia of cartilage, resulting in 'saddle-nose' deformity.

concepts.title: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a squamous cell carcinoma of the nasopharynx. Rare in most parts of the world, but common in individuals from Southern China. Associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection.

concepts.title: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Presenting features of nasopharyngeal carcinoma: systemic — cervical lymphadenopathy; local — otalgia, unilateral serous otitis media, nasal obstruction/discharge/epistaxis, cranial nerve palsies (III–VI). Imaging: combined CT and MRI. Treatment: radiotherapy is first-line therapy.

concepts.title: Neck lumps – Differential diagnosis by condition
concepts.content: Characteristic features of neck lump conditions: reactive lymphadenopathy (most common, history of local/viral infection); lymphoma (rubbery, painless, night sweats, splenomegaly, pain with alcohol); thyroid swelling (moves upwards on swallowing); thyroglossal cyst (<20 years, midline, moves upwards with tongue protrusion, may be painful if infected); pharyngeal pouch (older men, midline, gurgles on palpation, dysphagia, regurgitation, aspiration); cystic hygroma (congenital, left neck, transilluminates, 90% before age 2); branchial cyst (oval, mobile, between SCM and pharynx, early adulthood); cervical rib (adult females, 10% develop thoracic outlet syndrome); carotid aneurysm (pulsatile lateral mass, no movement on swallowing).

concepts.title: Otitis externa – Causes and clinical features
concepts.content: Otitis externa is a common reason for primary care attendance. Causes: bacterial infection (Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa), fungal infection, seborrhoeic dermatitis, contact dermatitis (allergic and irritant); recent swimming is a common trigger. Features: ear pain, itch, discharge; otoscopy shows red, swollen or eczematous canal. Key distinguishing feature from otitis media: tenderness on manipulation of pinna or tragus.

concepts.title: Otitis externa – Variations in presentation
concepts.content: Variations in otitis externa: acute (rapid onset within 48 hours, intense pain, often unilateral); chronic (persistent/recurrent >3 months, less severe pain, more pruritus, thickening and lichenification of canal skin, may be bilateral); fungal (more pruritus than pain, characteristic fungal elements, often follows prolonged antibiotic treatment); necrotising/malignant (severe persistent otalgia, granulation tissue at osseo-cartilaginous junction, cranial nerve palsies, elderly diabetic or immunocompromised).

concepts.title: Otitis externa – Management
concepts.content: Initial management of otitis externa: topical antibiotic or combined topical antibiotic with steroid; if tympanic membrane perforated, aminoglycosides are traditionally not used (concerns about ototoxicity); if canal debris present, consider removal; if canal extensively swollen, ear wick may be inserted. Second-line: consider contact dermatitis secondary to neomycin; oral antibiotics (flucloxacillin) if infection spreading; swab inside ear canal; empirical antifungal. If fails to respond to topical antibiotics, refer to ENT.

concepts.title: Otosclerosis – Definition and epidemiology
concepts.content: Otosclerosis is the replacement of normal bone by vascular spongy bone, causing progressive conductive deafness due to fixation of the stapes at the oval window. Autosomal dominant inheritance. Incidence: 30 per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 30–40 years. More common in females (2:1). Typically affects young adults with onset at 20–40 years.

concepts.title: Otosclerosis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Otosclerosis pathophysiology: localised increase in bone remodelling in the otic capsule (particularly around the fissula ante fenestram anterior to the oval window) → increased osteoclastic activity → otospongiotic lesions → maturation into dense sclerotic bone → stapes footplate fixation → impaired sound transmission → conductive hearing loss. Cochlear involvement may cause sensorineural hearing loss via disruption of endolymphatic fluid dynamics or damage to cochlear hair cells.

concepts.title: Otosclerosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of otosclerosis: progressive bilateral conductive hearing loss (first symptom, gradual onset, initially one ear then bilateral in ~80%); tinnitus (ringing or buzzing); dizziness or balance problems (less common, vestibular involvement); Schwartz's sign (reddish-blue hue behind tympanic membrane — 'flamingo flush' in 10% of patients); audiometry shows conductive hearing loss with characteristic dip at 2 kHz (Carhart notch).

concepts.title: Otosclerosis – Management
concepts.content: Management of otosclerosis: hearing aid; stapedectomy (surgical procedure). Stapedectomy complications: sensorineural hearing loss (small risk of further inner ear damage), dizziness and balance issues (usually resolve within days/weeks), tympanic membrane perforation, taste disturbances or facial nerve injury (rare).

concepts.title: Parotid gland – Benign tumour types and features
concepts.content: Benign parotid tumours: up to 80% of all salivary gland tumours occur in the parotid; up to 80% are benign. Pleomorphic adenoma (80% of benign parotid tumours): most common, slow growing, lobular, not well encapsulated, recurrence 1–5%, malignant degeneration 2–10% if observed long periods. Warthin's tumour (5%): second most common, strongly associated with smoking, most common bilateral benign neoplasm, marked male predominance, sixth–seventh decades, malignant transformation almost unheard of. Monomorphic adenoma (<5%): slow growing, single cell type. Haemangioma: 90% of parotid tumours in children <1 year, hypervascular, spontaneous regression may occur.

concepts.title: Parotid gland – Malignant tumour types and features
concepts.content: Malignant parotid tumours: mucoepidermoid carcinoma (30% of parotid malignancies, usually low potential for invasiveness/metastasis depending on grade); adenoid cystic carcinoma (unpredictable growth, perineural spread with skip lesions, distant visceral metastasis more common, 5-year survival 35%); acinic cell carcinoma (intermediate grade, perineural invasion, low distant metastasis potential, 5-year survival 80%); adenocarcinoma (from secretory portion, regional nodal and distant metastasis risk, 5-year survival up to 75% with small lesions/no nodal involvement); lymphoma (large rubbery lesion, diagnose via regional nodal biopsy, treat with chemotherapy ± radiotherapy).

concepts.title: Parotid gland – Diagnostic evaluation
concepts.content: Diagnostic evaluation of parotid lesions: plain X-rays to exclude calculi; sialography to delineate ductal anatomy; FNAC used in most cases; superficial parotidectomy may be diagnostic or therapeutic; CT/MRI for staging malignant disease. Where malignancy is suspected, primary approach should be definitive resection rather than excisional biopsy.

concepts.title: Parotid gland – Surgical treatment
concepts.content: Parotid gland surgery: for benign disease — superficial parotidectomy; for malignant disease — radical or extended radical parotidectomy (facial nerve included in resection if involved); neck dissection determined by potential for nodal involvement.

concepts.title: Parotid gland – Other disorders (HIV, Sjögren's, sarcoidosis)
concepts.content: Other parotid disorders: HIV — lymphoepithelial cysts (bilateral, multicystic, symmetrical swelling; low malignant transformation risk; usually conservative management). Sjögren's syndrome — autoimmune, parotid enlargement, xerostomia, keratoconjunctivitis sicca; 90% female; bilateral non-tender enlargement; increased risk of subsequent lymphoma; treatment supportive. Sarcoidosis — parotid involvement in 6%; bilateral in most cases; non-tender; xerostomia may occur; usually conservative management.

concepts.title: Perforated tympanic membrane – Causes and management
concepts.content: Most common cause of perforated tympanic membrane is infection. Other causes: barotrauma, direct trauma. May cause hearing loss (depending on size) and increased risk of otitis media. Management: no treatment needed in majority — tympanic membrane usually heals after 6–8 weeks (avoid water in ear/swimming during this time); antibiotics commonly prescribed for perforations following acute otitis media (NICE 2008 supports this); myringoplasty if tympanic membrane does not heal spontaneously.

concepts.title: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is a collection of pus in the tissue surrounding the tonsils, typically developing as a complication of bacterial tonsillitis. Incidence: 30 per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 30–40 years. Most common causative organism: Streptococcus pyogenes (GABHS). Other organisms: Staphylococcus aureus, Fusobacterium necrophorum, Haemophilus influenzae, anaerobes, EBV, CMV, adenovirus.

concepts.title: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of peritonsillar abscess: severe throat pain lateralising to one side; difficulty swallowing and speaking; deviation of uvula to the unaffected side; trismus (difficulty opening mouth); reduced neck mobility; systemic features — fever and chills, malaise. Patients need urgent review by ENT specialist.

concepts.title: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) – Management
concepts.content: Management of peritonsillar abscess: needle aspiration (first-line surgical intervention, especially with significant trismus; may need repeating); intraoral incision and drainage (if needle aspiration fails or large abscess); quinsy tonsillectomy (recurrent cases or failed other interventions). Antibiotic therapy: penicillin combined with beta-lactamase inhibitor first-line; macrolide or clindamycin if penicillin allergic. Analgesia (NSAIDs or paracetamol). Steroids may be considered. Tonsillectomy should be considered to prevent recurrence.

concepts.title: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of peritonsillar abscess: airway obstruction (most serious — expanding abscess pushes uvula/tonsil towards midline); spread of infection (cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis, deep neck space infections, parapharyngeal/retropharyngeal abscesses; systemic spread — sepsis or Lemierre's syndrome from Fusobacterium necrophorum); bleeding (erosion into carotid artery sheath). Long-term: recurrence requiring tonsillectomy; voice changes and swallowing difficulties; rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis (uncommon).

concepts.title: Pharyngeal pouch – Definition and epidemiology
concepts.content: A pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum) is an outpouching of the pharyngeal mucosa through an area of muscular weakness at the posterior pharyngeal wall called Killian's dehiscence (between cricopharyngeus and thyropharyngeus muscles). It is a pseudodiverticulum (does not involve all layers). Incidence: 2 per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 70+ years. More common in males (5:1). Typically affects older males.

concepts.title: Pharyngeal pouch – Aetiology
concepts.content: Proposed mechanisms for pharyngeal pouch: uncoordinated swallowing; impaired relaxation of cricopharyngeus muscle → increased pressure in distal pharynx; anatomical predisposition to larger Killian's dehiscence. Risk factors: older age (uncommon under 40, most common in seventh decade or later); male sex (5x more common); positive family history (related to anatomically larger Killian's dehiscence).

concepts.title: Pharyngeal pouch – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of pharyngeal pouch: dysphagia (85%); regurgitation of food (40%); cough and aspiration (35%); halitosis; neck swelling; gurgling sound when swallowing; weight loss from eating difficulties. Examination: Boyce's sign (neck swelling that gurgles on palpation); signs of weight loss/malnutrition. Sudden worsening of dysphagia or haemoptysis may suggest malignancy — 2-week wait referral.

concepts.title: Pharyngeal pouch – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations for pharyngeal pouch: oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) as initial investigation for dysphagia; barium swallow (gold standard — barium pools in pouch and does not move between films, confirming diagnosis; also called oesophagram; usually performed after OGD if pouch suspected).

concepts.title: Pharyngeal pouch – Management
concepts.content: Management of pharyngeal pouch: all patients with symptoms should be referred to ENT. Mild symptoms or unable to have surgery: watch-and-wait approach. Surgery: endoscopic techniques (rigid endoscopes) now preferred over open surgery — quicker, less invasive, more cost-effective, shorter recovery; diathermy laser or stapling technique used endoscopically. Open surgery (diverticulectomy) only after 2 failed endoscopic surgeries or contraindications (e.g. poor cervical spine mobility due to osteoarthritis). NICE 2015 guidelines.

concepts.title: Pharyngeal pouch – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of pharyngeal pouch: malnutrition (up to 31% of patients); aspiration pneumonia (up to 12%); small increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma within the pouch (reported incidence up to 1.1%, due to chronic mucosal inflammation).

concepts.title: Pleomorphic adenoma – Definition and epidemiology
concepts.content: Pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumour) is the most common salivary gland tumour and the most common benign parotid tumour. Incidence: 3 per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 40–50 years. More common in females (2:1). Within the parotid, 80% of neoplasms are benign; of these, 80% are pleomorphic adenomas. Over 80% arise in the parotid gland.

concepts.title: Pleomorphic adenoma – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Pleomorphic adenoma pathophysiology: proliferation of epithelial (polygonal) and myoepithelial (spindle-shaped) cells of the ducts with increase in stromal components (mucoid, myxoid or cartilaginous extracellular matrix). Slow-growing, lobular, not well encapsulated — contained within a nodular pseudo-capsule. The tumour can grow beyond the capsule, creating risk of recurrence if any nodule remains at surgery. Malignant transformation potential lies within the different cell types.

concepts.title: Pleomorphic adenoma – Clinical features
concepts.content: Clinical features of pleomorphic adenoma: slow-growing, painless, firm mass in the pre-auricular region (parotid); gradual onset unilateral swelling; typically movable (non-adherent to overlying skin or deep structures); no overlying skin changes; facial nerve function intact (facial palsy suggests malignant change or alternative diagnosis); size typically 2–6 cm; generally painless (pain may occur with rapid expansion due to cystic degeneration or haemorrhage). When in submandibular gland: upper neck mass. When in minor salivary glands (palate): submucosal swelling.

concepts.title: Pleomorphic adenoma – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations for pleomorphic adenoma: ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration (FNA) or core needle biopsy (tissue diagnosis prior to definitive treatment); ultrasound scan (high-resolution imaging, cost-effective); CT scan and MRI for surgical planning and assessment of local invasion. NICE: urgent 2-week referral for persistent unexplained lumps in parotid or submandibular glands.

concepts.title: Pleomorphic adenoma – Management
concepts.content: Management of pleomorphic adenoma: surgical excision. Options: superficial parotidectomy (superficial lobe of parotid removed); extracapsular dissection (less tissue removed, lower complication risk). At least 5 mm resection margins required during extracapsular dissection to reduce recurrence. Radiotherapy discussed at MDT if invasive malignancy suspected (generally not indicated for benign disease).

concepts.title: Pleomorphic adenoma – Complications and prognosis
concepts.content: Main complication of pleomorphic adenoma: malignant transformation (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma, most frequently as adenocarcinoma) — risk 1.5% in first 5 years, increases to 9.5% after 15 years. Rapid enlargement should prompt consideration of malignant transformation. Recurrence rate 1–5% with appropriate excision. Surgical complications: facial nerve injury (most important — CN VII intimately related to parotid; may cause dribbling, corneal drying); Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating); salivary fistula; lingual/hypoglossal nerve injury in submandibular surgery.

concepts.title: Post-operative tonsillectomy complications – Haemorrhage
concepts.content: Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage: all post-tonsillectomy haemorrhages should be assessed by ENT. Primary (reactionary) haemorrhage: most commonly in first 6–8 hours post-surgery; managed by immediate return to theatre. Secondary haemorrhage: occurs 5–10 days after surgery; often associated with wound infection; treatment usually admission and antibiotics; severe bleeding may require surgery; occurs in ~1–2% of all tonsillectomies.

concepts.title: Presbycusis – Definition and epidemiology
concepts.content: Presbycusis is age-related sensorineural hearing loss. Incidence: 1000 per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 70+ years. Sex ratio 1:1 (males at slightly higher risk — 55%:45%). In the USA, 25–30% of 65–74 year-olds have impaired hearing; for those >75 years, incidence is 40–50%. Characterised by gradual decline in hearing ability, particularly in the high-frequency range.

concepts.title: Presbycusis – Aetiology
concepts.content: Aetiology of presbycusis (multifactorial): arteriosclerosis (diminished cochlear perfusion and oxygenation); diabetes (accelerates arteriosclerosis); accumulated noise exposure; drug exposure (salicylates, chemotherapy agents, aminoglycosides, loop diuretics); stress; genetic factors (early ageing of auditory system); oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (apoptosis of cochlear hair cells); smoking and alcohol (vascular changes reducing inner ear blood flow); systemic conditions (hypertension, hyperlipidaemia — microvascular changes).

concepts.title: Presbycusis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Clinical features of presbycusis: chronic, slowly progressive history; speech becoming difficult to understand; need for increased volume on television/radio; difficulty using telephone; loss of directionality of sound; worsening in noisy environments; hyperacusis (heightened sensitivity to certain frequencies — less common); tinnitus (uncommon). Audiometry: bilateral sensorineural hearing loss pattern.

concepts.title: Presbycusis – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations for presbycusis: otoscopy (normal — to rule out otosclerosis, cholesteatoma, conductive causes); tympanometry (normal middle ear function with hearing loss — Type A); audiometry (bilateral sensorineural pattern hearing loss); blood tests including inflammatory markers and specific antibodies (normal).

concepts.title: Ramsay Hunt syndrome – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) is caused by reactivation of the varicella zoster virus in the geniculate ganglion of the seventh cranial nerve. Features: auricular pain (often first feature), facial nerve palsy, vesicular rash around the ear, vertigo, tinnitus. Management: oral aciclovir and corticosteroids.

concepts.title: Rinne's and Weber's test – Interpretation
concepts.content: Rinne's test: tuning fork on mastoid process until no longer heard, then repositioned over external acoustic meatus. Positive test (normal): AC > BC. Negative test: BC > AC = conductive deafness. Weber's test: tuning fork in middle of forehead. Normal: midline. Unilateral sensorineural deafness: sound localises to unaffected side. Unilateral conductive deafness: sound localises to affected side.

concepts.title: Salivary glands – Anatomy and pathology overview
concepts.content: Three pairs of salivary glands: parotid (serous — most tumours), submandibular (mixed — most stones), sublingual (mucous). Tumour rule of 80s: 80% parotid, 80% of these are pleomorphic adenomas, 80% in superficial lobe. Malignant features: short history, painful, hot skin, hard, fixation, CN VII involvement. Salivary stones: 80% are submandibular; recurrent unilateral pain and swelling on eating; may become infected → Ludwig's angina; plain X-rays and sialography; surgical removal.

concepts.title: Sore throat – Management and antibiotic indications
concepts.content: Sore throat management: paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain relief; antibiotics not routinely indicated; single dose oral corticosteroid may reduce severity and duration (not yet in UK guidelines). NICE indications for antibiotics: marked systemic upset; unilateral peritonsillitis; history of rheumatic fever; increased risk from acute infection (e.g. child with diabetes or immunodeficiency); ≥3 Centor criteria. If antibiotics indicated: phenoxymethylpenicillin or clarithromycin (if penicillin-allergic).

concepts.title: Sore throat – Centor and FeverPAIN scoring systems
concepts.content: Centor criteria (1 point each, max 4): tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy/lymphadenitis, history of fever, absence of cough. Score 0–2: 3–17% likelihood of streptococcal isolation. Score 3–4: 32–56%. FeverPAIN criteria (1 point each, max 5): Fever >38°C, Purulence, Attend rapidly (≤3 days), Severely Inflamed tonsils, No cough or coryza. Score 0–1: 13–18%; Score 2–3: 34–40%; Score 4–5: 62–65% likelihood of streptococcal isolation.

concepts.title: Submandibular gland – Sialolithiasis
concepts.content: Sialolithiasis (salivary gland stones): 80% of all salivary gland calculi occur in the submandibular gland; 70% of these are radio-opaque; composed of calcium phosphate or calcium carbonate. Patients develop colicky pain and post-prandial swelling of the gland. Investigation: sialography to demonstrate obstruction site and other stones. Management: stones in distal Wharton's duct may be removed orally; other stones and chronic inflammation usually require gland excision.

concepts.title: Submandibular gland – Sialadenitis and tumours
concepts.content: Sialadenitis: usually Staphylococcus aureus infection; pus may be seen leaking from duct; erythema noted; submandibular abscess is a serious complication (may spread through deep fascial spaces and occlude airway). Submandibular tumours: only 8% of salivary gland tumours; of these, 50% are malignant (usually adenoid cystic carcinoma); diagnosis by FNAC; imaging with CT and MRI; all masses of submandibular glands should generally be excised due to high malignancy prevalence.

concepts.title: Sudden-onset sensorineural hearing loss – Definition and management
concepts.content: Sudden-onset sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) requires urgent referral to ENT. The majority of SSNHL cases are idiopathic. An MRI scan is usually performed to exclude a vestibular schwannoma. High-dose oral corticosteroids are used by ENT for all cases of SSNHL.

concepts.title: Thyroglossal cyst – Definition and clinical features
concepts.content: A thyroglossal cyst arises from persistence of the thyroglossal duct (which normally atrophies after the thyroid descends from the floor of the pharynx during development). The foramen caecum is the point of attachment of the thyroglossal duct to the tongue. More common in patients <20 years. Features: usually midline, between the isthmus of the thyroid and the hyoid bone; moves upwards with protrusion of the tongue; may be painful if infected.

concepts.title: Thyroid surgery – Complications
concepts.content: Complications following thyroid surgery: recurrent laryngeal nerve damage (anatomical complication); bleeding (haematoma in confined space may rapidly lead to respiratory compromise due to laryngeal oedema); damage to parathyroid glands resulting in hypocalcaemia.

concepts.title: Tinnitus – Causes
concepts.content: Causes of tinnitus: idiopathic (no underlying cause found in majority); Ménière's disease (hearing loss, vertigo, tinnitus, aural fullness); otosclerosis (onset 20–40 years, conductive deafness, flamingo tinge in 10%); sudden-onset sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL — mostly idiopathic); acoustic neuroma (hearing loss, vertigo, absent corneal reflex, associated with NF2); hearing loss (noise exposure, presbycusis); drugs (aspirin/NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, quinine); impacted ear wax.

concepts.title: Tinnitus – Assessment and management
concepts.content: Tinnitus assessment: audiological assessment to detect underlying hearing loss; imaging — non-pulsatile tinnitus does not require imaging unless unilateral or other neurological/otological signs (MRI of internal auditory meatuses first-line); pulsatile tinnitus generally requires imaging for vascular cause (MRA often used). Management: investigate and treat underlying cause; amplification devices (more beneficial if associated hearing loss); psychological therapy (e.g. CBT) for limited group; tinnitus support groups.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Aetiology
concepts.content: Acute tonsillitis is predominantly caused by viral (70% of cases) and bacterial infections. Most common bacterial cause: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus). Other bacteria: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Bordetella pertussis, Fusobacterium spp., Treponema pallidum. Most common viral cause: adenoviruses, followed by rhinoviruses, influenza, parainfluenza, Epstein-Barr virus. Viral tonsillitis is more common but bacterial tends to be more severe.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Acute tonsillitis features: sore throat (99%), fever >38°C (82%), dysphagia (66%), nasal congestion/headache/earache/cough (47% — suggests viral aetiology; absence of cough more likely bacterial). Examination: severely inflamed tonsils (87%), painfully enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes (49%), purulent tonsils (41% — suggestive of bacterial cause). Do not examine if epiglottitis suspected (young child, muffled voice, excessive drooling — call anaesthetist and ENT surgeon).

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Management
concepts.content: Tonsillitis management: reassurance (symptoms last ~1 week, most resolve without treatment); paracetamol or ibuprofen; adequate fluid intake. Antibiotics not routinely indicated. If antibiotics indicated: phenoxymethylpenicillin or erythromycin (penicillin-allergic) for 7 or 10 days. Single dose oral corticosteroid may reduce pain severity/duration (not yet in UK guidelines). Special groups: if on DMARDs or carbimazole, check FBC urgently; if immunosuppressed, seek urgent specialist advice.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of tonsillitis: acute otitis media (common, benign, self-limiting; antibiotics reduce risk); peritonsillar abscess/quinsy or neck abscess (usually within first 2 months; spiking fever, neck pain, dysphagia; antibiotics reduce risk; drainage required); acute sinusitis (0.4% of untreated patients). Rare complications if bacterial infection untreated: scarlet fever (blanching erythematous papular rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor); acute rheumatic fever (<1:100,000; arthritis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, chorea, carditis); acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (haematuria, oedema, vomiting, anorexia); streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (multiple organ failure, shock).

concepts.title: Tonsillectomy – Indications
concepts.content: NICE indications for tonsillectomy (all criteria must be met): sore throats due to tonsillitis (not recurrent URTIs); 7 episodes per year for 1 year, 5 per year for 2 years, or 3 per year for 3 years; episodes are disabling and prevent normal functioning. Other established indications: recurrent febrile convulsions secondary to tonsillitis; obstructive sleep apnoea, stridor or dysphagia secondary to enlarged tonsils; peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) unresponsive to standard treatment.

concepts.title: Tonsillectomy – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of tonsillectomy: primary (<24 hours) — haemorrhage in 2–3% (most commonly due to inadequate haemostasis), pain (may increase for up to 6 days); secondary (24 hours to 10 days) — haemorrhage (most commonly due to infection), pain.

concepts.title: Vertigo – Differential diagnosis by cause
concepts.content: Differential diagnosis of vertigo: viral labyrinthitis (recent viral infection, sudden onset, nausea/vomiting, hearing may be affected); vestibular neuronitis (recent viral infection, recurrent attacks lasting hours/days, no hearing loss); BPPV (gradual onset, triggered by head position change, episodes 10–20 seconds); Ménière's disease (hearing loss, tinnitus, aural fullness); vertebrobasilar ischaemia (elderly, dizziness on neck extension); acoustic neuroma (hearing loss, vertigo, tinnitus, absent corneal reflex, NF2). Other causes: posterior circulation stroke, trauma, multiple sclerosis, ototoxicity (e.g. gentamicin).

concepts.title: Vestibular neuronitis – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Vestibular neuronitis develops following viral infection. Features: recurrent vertigo attacks lasting hours or days; nausea and vomiting may be present; horizontal nystagmus usually present; no hearing loss or tinnitus (distinguishes from labyrinthitis). Differential: viral labyrinthitis; posterior circulation stroke (HiNTs exam used to distinguish). Management: buccal or IM prochlorperazine for severe cases; short oral course of prochlorperazine or antihistamine (cinnarizine, cyclizine, or promethazine) for less severe cases; vestibular rehabilitation exercises preferred for chronic symptoms.

concepts.title: Viral labyrinthitis – Definition and clinical features
concepts.content: Labyrinthitis is an inflammatory disorder of the membranous labyrinth affecting both vestibular and cochlear end organs. Viral labyrinthitis is the most common form. Average age of presentation: 40–70 years. Distinguished from vestibular neuronitis: vestibular neuronitis involves only the vestibular nerve (no hearing impairment); labyrinthitis involves both vestibular nerve and labyrinth (both vertigo and hearing impairment). Features: vertigo (not triggered by movement but exacerbated by it); nausea and vomiting; hearing loss (unilateral or bilateral, varying severity); tinnitus; preceding/concurrent URTI symptoms.

concepts.title: Viral labyrinthitis – Signs and management
concepts.content: Signs of labyrinthitis: spontaneous unidirectional horizontal nystagmus towards the unaffected side; sensorineural hearing loss (shown by Rinne's and Weber's tests); abnormal head impulse test (impaired vestibulo-ocular reflex); gait disturbance (patient may fall towards affected side). Management: episodes usually self-limiting; prochlorperazine or antihistamines may help reduce dizziness.

concepts.title: Zinc deficiency – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of zinc deficiency: acrodermatitis (red, crusted lesions with acral distribution — peri-orificial and perianal); alopecia; short stature; hypogonadism; hepatosplenomegaly; geophagia (ingesting clay/soil); cognitive impairment. Acrodermatitis enteropathica is a recessively inherited partial defect in intestinal zinc absorption.

concepts.title: Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) – Clinical features
concepts.content: Acoustic neuromas (vestibular schwannomas) are benign intracranial tumours. Features predicted by affected cranial nerves: CN VIII — hearing loss, vertigo, tinnitus; CN V — absent corneal reflex; CN VII — facial palsy. Audiometry reveals high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Bilateral acoustic neuromas are seen in neurofibromatosis type 2. Contrast-enhanced MRI is the gold standard for diagnosis.

concepts.title: Epiglottitis – Clinical features and emergency management
concepts.content: Epiglottitis features suggesting the diagnosis: young child, muffled voice, excessive drooling and pooling of saliva. Do not examine the pharynx if epiglottitis is suspected. Call for an anaesthetist and ENT surgeon immediately. Acute epiglottitis is a life-threatening emergency.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – ENT context and management
concepts.content: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) may be caused by or associated with enlarged tonsils. Tonsillectomy is indicated for OSA secondary to enlarged tonsils. OSA is associated with snoring and is a recognised indication for tonsillectomy in the ENT context.

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – ENT presentation and clinical features
concepts.content: Infectious mononucleosis (IM), caused by Epstein-Barr virus, commonly presents with fatigue, fever, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy mimicking acute tonsillitis. Physical examination reveals posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and a rash (especially after amoxicillin or ampicillin for presumed bacterial infection). Monospot test positive. Important differential for peritonsillar abscess and acute tonsillitis.

concepts.title: Laryngomalacia – Definition and epidemiology
concepts.content: Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital anomaly of the larynx and the most common cause of stridor in neonates, characterised by inward collapse of supraglottic structures during inspiration. Incidence: 10 per 100,000 person-years. More common in males (1.6:1). Typically presents within the first two weeks of life. Usually self-limiting, resolving by 18–24 months as laryngeal cartilage matures.

concepts.title: Laryngomalacia – Aetiology
concepts.content: Laryngomalacia aetiology: neuromuscular immaturity (inadequate tone/coordination of arytenoid muscles, associated with prematurity and neurological conditions); GORD (may exacerbate laryngeal collapse via inflammation and oedema); anatomical abnormalities (shortening/malpositioning of aryepiglottic folds). Risk factors: male sex, premature birth, firstborn status.

concepts.title: Laryngomalacia – Classification
concepts.content: Laryngomalacia classification: Type I (Curling — inward curling of mucosa overlying arytenoid cartilages during inspiration, omega-shaped laryngeal inlet, most common ~75%); Type II (Prolapsing — prolapse of mucosa overlying cuneiform and corniculate cartilages into glottis during inspiration, ~15%); Type III (Posterior Displacement — posterior displacement/malpositioning of epiglottis and aryepiglottic folds, ~10%, often more severe, may require early surgical intervention).

concepts.title: Laryngomalacia – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of laryngomalacia: inspiratory stridor (high-pitched and crowing; intermittent, occurring in supine position, when feeding or when agitated); symptoms increase in severity during first 8 months but tend to resolve by 18–24 months; respiratory distress, failure to thrive and cyanosis are rare.

concepts.title: Laryngomalacia – Management
concepts.content: Management of laryngomalacia: 99% of cases resolve spontaneously by 18–24 months; symptomatic relief by hyperextending the neck during episodes of stridor; oxygen saturation should be monitored; laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy only indicated for severe features or diagnostic difficulty. Surgical intervention only required for severe respiratory distress: tracheostomy, laryngoplasty, excision of redundant mucosa, laser epiglottopexy, or laser division of aryepiglottic folds.

concepts.title: Laryngomalacia – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of laryngomalacia: failure to thrive (most frequent — increased work of breathing and feeding difficulties → inadequate weight gain); respiratory distress (apnoea, cyanosis, or life-threatening respiratory failure in severe cases); GORD (significant association — reflux exacerbates airway obstruction); obstructive sleep apnoea (dynamic airway collapse → disrupted sleep); recurrent pneumonia (aspiration due to feeding difficulties); pulmonary hypertension (rare but potentially fatal — from chronic hypoxaemia in severe untreated cases).

concepts.title: Inhaled foreign body – Clinical features
concepts.content: Inhaled foreign body (IFB) is most common in children aged 1–5 years. Commonly aspirated objects: food particles (nuts, seeds), small toys (beads), organic materials (teeth). Right bronchial system more frequently involved due to more vertical orientation. Classic triad: coughing paroxysms, wheezing, decreased breath sounds. Features: sudden onset choking or gagging, coughing paroxysms, stridor (if above vocal cords), wheezing or asymmetric breath sounds, decreased air entry, cyanosis or respiratory distress, tachypnoea and tachycardia.

concepts.title: Otosclerosis – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Differential diagnosis of otosclerosis: Ménière's disease (episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, aural fullness; low-frequency SNHL on audiometry; endolymphatic hydrops on MRI); CSOM (persistent/recurrent otorrhoea, conductive hearing loss from tympanic membrane perforation and ossicular disruption; flat tympanogram vs Carhart's notch at 2000 Hz); acoustic neuroma (progressive SNHL, tinnitus, disequilibrium; high-frequency SNHL on audiometry; delayed ABR wave I-V interpeak latency; intracanalicular or CPA mass on contrast MRI).

concepts.title: Otitis media – ENT context and management overview
concepts.content: Otitis media is one of the most common causes of hearing loss. Acute otitis media (AOM): infection of the middle ear space, rapid onset ear pain, fever, general malaise; bulging red tympanic membrane on otoscopy. Otitis media with effusion (glue ear): peaks at age 2 years; commonest cause of conductive hearing loss and elective surgery in childhood; hearing loss is usually the presenting feature; secondary problems include speech/language delay, behavioural or balance problems.

concepts.title: Rhinosinusitis – Definition and classification
concepts.content: Rhinosinusitis is inflammation of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses. Classified by duration: acute (<12 weeks, complete resolution); chronic (≥12 weeks, no complete resolution). Classified by cause: infectious (viral — most common; bacterial; fungal); non-infectious (allergic; non-allergic; mixed). Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS) is defined as bacterial infection of the sinuses lasting <12 weeks. Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is defined as inflammation of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses for ≥12 weeks with or without nasal polyps.

concepts.title: Rhinosinusitis – Epidemiology and aetiology
concepts.content: Rhinosinusitis epidemiology: affects approximately 15% of the UK population; one of the most common reasons for antibiotic prescriptions. Aetiology: viral (rhinovirus, influenza, parainfluenza — most common); bacterial (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis); fungal (Aspergillus — usually immunocompromised). Risk factors: allergic rhinitis, nasal polyps, deviated nasal septum, dental infections, anatomical variations, immunosuppression, smoking, swimming/diving.

concepts.title: Rhinosinusitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Clinical features of rhinosinusitis: nasal blockage/obstruction/congestion; nasal discharge (anterior or posterior — may be purulent in bacterial); facial pain/pressure/fullness (worse on bending forward); reduction or loss of smell (hyposmia/anosmia); headache; fever; cough (post-nasal drip). Bacterial sinusitis more likely if: symptoms >10 days without improvement, severe symptoms (high fever >39°C, purulent nasal discharge, facial pain), symptoms that worsen after initial improvement ('double sickening').

concepts.title: Rhinosinusitis – Management
concepts.content: Management of acute rhinosinusitis: most cases are viral and self-limiting (7–10 days); saline nasal irrigation; intranasal corticosteroids (reduce inflammation and oedema); analgesia; decongestants (short-term use only — risk of rhinitis medicamentosa). Antibiotics: not routinely recommended; consider if: severe symptoms, immunocompromised, at risk of complications, symptoms >10 days without improvement. If antibiotics indicated: amoxicillin first-line (co-amoxiclav if penicillin-allergic or no response to amoxicillin). Refer to ENT if: recurrent acute episodes, chronic rhinosinusitis not responding to treatment, complications suspected.

concepts.title: Rhinosinusitis – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of rhinosinusitis (rare but serious): orbital cellulitis/abscess (most common complication — periorbital oedema, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, reduced visual acuity); intracranial extension (meningitis, subdural empyema, brain abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis); osteomyelitis of frontal bone (Pott's puffy tumour — frontal swelling with fluctuance). Cavernous sinus thrombosis: headache, high fever, periorbital oedema, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, papilloedema.

concepts.title: Epistaxis – Causes and classification
concepts.content: Epistaxis (nosebleed) is classified by site: anterior (90% — Little's area/Kiesselbach's plexus on anterior nasal septum; more common in children and young adults; usually less severe); posterior (10% — sphenopalatine artery; more common in elderly; more severe, may require hospital admission). Causes: local (trauma — nose picking most common, nasal fracture; rhinitis; nasal polyps; foreign body; tumours); systemic (hypertension, anticoagulants, NSAIDs, bleeding disorders, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, cocaine use, alcohol).

concepts.title: Epistaxis – Management
concepts.content: Management of epistaxis: first aid — patient leans forward, pinches soft part of nose for 10–15 minutes; avoid leaning back (blood swallowed may cause nausea/vomiting). If bleeding continues: cauterisation with silver nitrate (anterior bleeds); nasal packing (anterior or posterior); examination under anaesthesia and surgical ligation of sphenopalatine artery (posterior bleeds). Investigations: FBC, clotting screen, group and save if significant blood loss. Refer to ENT if: posterior bleed, recurrent bleeds, suspected tumour, significant blood loss, failed first-line management.

concepts.title: Hearing loss – Classification and causes
concepts.content: Hearing loss is classified as: conductive (sound transmission problem in outer/middle ear — wax impaction, otitis media, otosclerosis, perforated TM, cholesteatoma); sensorineural (cochlear or auditory nerve problem — presbycusis, noise-induced, Ménière's disease, acoustic neuroma, ototoxic drugs, sudden SNHL); mixed (both components). Causes by age: children — otitis media with effusion (glue ear) most common; adults — presbycusis most common. Ototoxic drugs: aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, cisplatin, quinine, aspirin (high doses).

concepts.title: Hearing loss – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations for hearing loss: otoscopy (visualise ear canal and tympanic membrane); tuning fork tests (Rinne's and Weber's — distinguish conductive from sensorineural); audiometry (pure tone audiogram — gold standard for quantifying and characterising hearing loss); tympanometry (middle ear function — Type A normal, Type B flat = effusion, Type C negative pressure = Eustachian tube dysfunction); speech audiometry; auditory brainstem response (ABR); MRI (acoustic neuroma, intracranial pathology); blood tests (inflammatory markers, autoimmune screen if bilateral SNHL).

concepts.title: Glue ear (otitis media with effusion) – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Glue ear (otitis media with effusion, OME): peak age 2 years; most common cause of conductive hearing loss in children. Features: hearing loss (main presenting feature), speech/language delay, behavioural problems, balance difficulties, recurrent ear infections. Otoscopy: dull, retracted tympanic membrane; amber or blue discolouration; no light reflex. Tympanometry: Type B (flat) curve. Management: watchful waiting for 3 months (most resolve spontaneously); hearing aids; grommets (ventilation tubes) — NICE recommends if persistent bilateral OME with hearing loss >25 dB for >3 months; adenoidectomy may be performed concurrently.

concepts.title: Acute otitis media – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Acute otitis media (AOM): most common in children aged 6 months–2 years. Causative organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis (bacterial); RSV, rhinovirus, influenza (viral). Features: otalgia (ear pain), fever, irritability, pulling at ear (infants), hearing loss, otorrhoea if perforation occurs. Otoscopy: bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane; loss of light reflex; may see perforation with discharge. Management: analgesia first-line; antibiotics if: <2 years with bilateral AOM, otorrhoea, systemically unwell, immunocompromised, or symptoms >72 hours. Amoxicillin first-line; co-amoxiclav if no improvement after 48 hours.

concepts.title: Acute otitis media – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of acute otitis media: tympanic membrane perforation (usually heals spontaneously); mastoiditis (most common intratemporal complication — post-auricular pain, swelling, erythema, forward displacement of pinna); hearing loss (usually transient); facial nerve palsy; labyrinthitis; meningitis; intracranial abscess; lateral sinus thrombosis; cholesteatoma (from chronic disease).

concepts.title: Cholesteatoma – Definition and clinical features
concepts.content: Cholesteatoma is an abnormal collection of keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear or mastoid. Types: congenital (behind intact TM, usually anterior superior quadrant); acquired (secondary to retraction pocket or TM perforation). Features: painless, foul-smelling otorrhoea (most common presenting feature); conductive hearing loss; recurrent ear infections unresponsive to treatment; tinnitus. Otoscopy: pearly white mass visible through TM, or keratin debris in attic region. Complications: facial nerve palsy, labyrinthitis, meningitis, intracranial abscess, erosion of ossicles.

concepts.title: BPPV – Definition and pathophysiology
concepts.content: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is the most common cause of vertigo. Caused by displacement of otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) from the utricle into the semicircular canals (most commonly posterior canal — 90%). This causes abnormal endolymph movement with head position changes, triggering vertigo. Incidence increases with age. More common in females (2:1). Associated with: head trauma, vestibular neuronitis, Ménière's disease, prolonged bed rest, osteoporosis.

concepts.title: BPPV – Clinical features and diagnosis
concepts.content: BPPV features: brief episodes of vertigo (typically 10–60 seconds) triggered by specific head movements (rolling over in bed, looking up, bending forward); nausea (common); no hearing loss or tinnitus. Dix-Hallpike test: gold standard diagnostic test — patient moved from sitting to lying with head turned 45° to affected side; positive if nystagmus and vertigo reproduced after brief latency (2–20 seconds); nystagmus is upbeat and torsional (top pole of eye beats towards affected ear); fatigues with repeated testing.

concepts.title: BPPV – Management
concepts.content: Management of BPPV: Epley manoeuvre (particle repositioning manoeuvre) — first-line treatment; highly effective (80–90% success rate); repositions displaced otoconia back to utricle; patient should avoid lying flat for 24–48 hours after procedure. Brandt-Daroff exercises — home exercise programme if Epley not available or for residual symptoms. Vestibular suppressants (prochlorperazine, antihistamines) — not recommended for BPPV specifically as they do not treat the underlying cause. Surgical canal plugging — reserved for refractory cases. Most cases resolve spontaneously within weeks to months.

concepts.title: Nasal fracture – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Nasal fracture is the most common facial fracture. Mechanism: direct trauma. Features: nasal pain and tenderness, epistaxis, nasal deformity (deviation, depression), periorbital bruising, nasal obstruction. Examination: assess for nasal septal haematoma (boggy bilateral swelling of nasal septum — requires urgent drainage). Management: analgesia; ice pack; nasal fracture reduction — ideally performed at 5–10 days (after swelling subsides but before bony union). Refer to ENT if: septal haematoma, significant deformity, suspected CSF rhinorrhoea.

concepts.title: Deviated nasal septum – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Deviated nasal septum (DNS): deviation of the nasal septum from the midline. May be congenital or acquired (trauma). Features: unilateral or bilateral nasal obstruction; recurrent sinusitis; snoring; epistaxis (from turbulent airflow). Management: medical (intranasal corticosteroids, decongestants); surgical — septoplasty (surgical straightening of nasal septum); may be combined with turbinate reduction (septorhinoplasty if cosmetic correction also required).

concepts.title: Snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea – Pathophysiology and assessment
concepts.content: Snoring results from vibration of soft tissues of the upper airway during sleep. Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is characterised by repeated episodes of partial or complete upper airway obstruction during sleep causing apnoeas (≥10 seconds cessation of airflow) or hypopnoeas (≥50% reduction in airflow). Risk factors: obesity (most important), male sex, age, alcohol, sedatives, smoking, enlarged tonsils/adenoids, retrognathia, macroglossia. Assessment: Epworth Sleepiness Scale; polysomnography (gold standard) or overnight oximetry (screening). AHI (apnoea-hypopnoea index): mild 5–14, moderate 15–29, severe ≥30 events/hour.

concepts.title: Snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: OSA clinical features: loud snoring (reported by partner), witnessed apnoeas, excessive daytime sleepiness (Epworth score >10), morning headaches, poor concentration, nocturia, reduced libido, irritability. Complications: hypertension, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, road traffic accidents. Management: lifestyle modification (weight loss, alcohol avoidance, positional therapy); CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure — gold standard for moderate-severe OSA); mandibular advancement device (mild-moderate); surgical options (uvulopalatopharyngoplasty, tonsillectomy if enlarged tonsils, nasal surgery). DVLA notification required if excessive daytime sleepiness.

concepts.title: Facial palsy (Bell's palsy) – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Bell's palsy is an acute, idiopathic, unilateral lower motor neurone facial nerve (CN VII) palsy. Incidence: 20–30 per 100,000 per year. Peak incidence: 15–45 years. Aetiology: idiopathic (most common); associated with HSV-1 reactivation (most evidence); other causes of facial palsy: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (VZV reactivation — vesicular rash in ear), Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, parotid tumour, cholesteatoma, acoustic neuroma, stroke (UMN — forehead sparing), Guillain-Barré syndrome.

concepts.title: Facial palsy (Bell's palsy) – Clinical features
concepts.content: Bell's palsy features: unilateral LMN facial weakness (all branches affected — forehead involved, distinguishing from UMN/stroke); drooping of mouth; inability to close eye (lagophthalmos — risk of corneal exposure); loss of forehead wrinkling; altered taste (anterior 2/3 tongue — chorda tympani); hyperacusis (stapedius branch); reduced lacrimation; post-auricular pain (often precedes palsy). House-Brackmann grading scale used to assess severity (I = normal, VI = complete paralysis).

concepts.title: Facial palsy (Bell's palsy) – Management and prognosis
concepts.content: Management of Bell's palsy: oral prednisolone (started within 72 hours of onset — improves recovery rate; NICE recommends 50 mg/day for 10 days); antivirals (aciclovir or valaciclovir — added to steroids if severe palsy, though evidence less strong); eye care (artificial tears, lubricating eye ointment at night, eye patch or tape if unable to close eye — prevents corneal exposure). Prognosis: 85% recover completely within 3 weeks to 3 months; 15% have incomplete recovery; poor prognostic factors: complete paralysis, age >60, hypertension, diabetes, severe pain.

concepts.title: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) – Definition and clinical features
concepts.content: Croup is a viral infection of the upper respiratory tract causing subglottic oedema and airway obstruction. Most common cause: parainfluenza virus. Predominantly affects children aged 6 months–3 years. Features: prodromal URTI; characteristic barking cough ('seal-like'); inspiratory stridor; hoarse voice; low-grade fever; symptoms typically worse at night. Westley croup score used to assess severity. Croup score: mild (0–2), moderate (3–7), severe (≥8).

concepts.title: Croup – Management
concepts.content: Management of croup: mild — reassurance, oral dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg single dose); moderate — oral/IM dexamethasone (0.15–0.6 mg/kg), nebulised adrenaline (1:1000, 0.5 mL/kg up to 5 mL) for immediate relief; severe — as above plus hospital admission, oxygen, consider intubation. Nebulised budesonide alternative to dexamethasone. Avoid distressing child (crying worsens obstruction). Humidified air — no evidence of benefit.

concepts.title: Epiglottitis – Definition, aetiology and clinical features
concepts.content: Epiglottitis is a life-threatening infection causing acute inflammation and oedema of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures. Most common causative organism: Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) — now rare due to vaccination; Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae in adults. Peak incidence: 2–7 years (children); adults increasingly affected. Features: rapid onset (hours); high fever; severe sore throat; dysphagia; drooling (inability to swallow saliva); muffled 'hot potato' voice; stridor (late sign); tripod position (leaning forward, neck extended); toxic appearance. Do NOT examine throat — may precipitate complete obstruction.

concepts.title: Epiglottitis – Investigations and management
concepts.content: Epiglottitis investigations: lateral neck X-ray (thumb sign — enlarged epiglottis; only if diagnosis uncertain and patient stable); direct laryngoscopy under GA (gold standard — shows cherry-red swollen epiglottis). Management: EMERGENCY — call anaesthetist and ENT surgeon immediately; secure airway (intubation or tracheostomy); IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone or co-amoxiclav); IV dexamethasone (reduce oedema); oxygen; IV fluids. Admit to ICU. Do NOT attempt throat examination, IV access, or distress patient before airway secured.

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Aetiology and epidemiology
concepts.content: Infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever) is caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV, human herpesvirus 4). Incidence: 45 per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 15–24 years. Sex ratio 1:1. Transmission: saliva ('kissing disease'). EBV infects B lymphocytes via CD21 receptor → polyclonal B cell activation → atypical lymphocytes (Downey cells) → heterophile antibody production.

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Infectious mononucleosis features: prodrome (1–2 weeks — fatigue, malaise, anorexia); fever; sore throat (exudative tonsillitis — may be severe); lymphadenopathy (posterior cervical most characteristic; also anterior cervical, axillary, inguinal); splenomegaly (50% — risk of splenic rupture); hepatomegaly (10–15%); rash (maculopapular — 10–15%; almost universal if given amoxicillin/ampicillin); palatal petechiae; periorbital oedema. Complications: splenic rupture (0.1–0.5%), airway obstruction from tonsillar hypertrophy, haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopaenia, hepatitis, meningitis, encephalitis, Guillain-Barré.

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Investigations and management
concepts.content: Investigations for infectious mononucleosis: monospot test (Paul-Bunnell test — detects heterophile antibodies; sensitivity 85%, specificity 100%; may be negative in first week); FBC (lymphocytosis with >10% atypical lymphocytes); LFTs (elevated in 80%); EBV-specific antibodies (VCA IgM — confirms acute infection; EBNA IgG — past infection). Management: supportive (rest, analgesia, adequate hydration); avoid contact sports for 4 weeks (splenic rupture risk); avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin (causes rash); corticosteroids if severe tonsillar hypertrophy causing airway compromise. Return to sport: 4 weeks minimum, longer if splenomegaly persists.

concepts.title: Ear wax (cerumen impaction) – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Ear wax (cerumen) impaction: common cause of conductive hearing loss. Features: hearing loss, tinnitus, otalgia, sensation of fullness, dizziness. Otoscopy: brown/yellow waxy material occluding canal. Management: softening agents (olive oil, sodium bicarbonate drops — 3–5 days before irrigation); ear irrigation (syringing — contraindicated if perforation, previous ear surgery, or recurrent otitis externa); manual removal (microsuction — preferred in ENT; Jobson-Horne probe). Prevention: avoid cotton buds (push wax deeper); regular softening drops if prone to impaction.

concepts.title: Noise-induced hearing loss – Pathophysiology and management
concepts.content: Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL): caused by damage to cochlear hair cells from prolonged or acute loud noise exposure. Characteristic audiometric pattern: notch at 4 kHz (then 3 and 6 kHz). Temporary threshold shift (TTS): reversible hearing loss after acute noise exposure. Permanent threshold shift (PTS): irreversible loss after repeated exposure. Tinnitus often accompanies NIHL. Management: hearing protection (primary prevention); hearing aids; tinnitus management; occupational health referral if work-related. Employers have legal duty to protect workers from noise >85 dB(A) (Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005).

concepts.title: Audiogram interpretation – Key patterns
concepts.content: Audiogram interpretation: normal hearing threshold <25 dB HL. Conductive hearing loss: air conduction (AC) thresholds elevated; bone conduction (BC) normal; air-bone gap present. Sensorineural hearing loss: both AC and BC thresholds elevated; no air-bone gap; BC = AC. Mixed hearing loss: both AC and BC elevated; air-bone gap present. Key patterns: presbycusis — bilateral high-frequency SNHL (sloping); noise-induced — bilateral notch at 4 kHz; otosclerosis — conductive HL with Carhart notch at 2 kHz; Ménière's disease — low-frequency SNHL (fluctuating); acoustic neuroma — unilateral high-frequency SNHL.

concepts.title: Stridor – Differential diagnosis by age
concepts.content: Differential diagnosis of stridor: neonates/infants — laryngomalacia (most common; inspiratory; worse supine/feeding; resolves by 18–24 months), subglottic stenosis (congenital or post-intubation), vocal cord paralysis, vascular ring; children — croup (viral; barking cough; worse at night; 6 months–3 years), epiglottitis (bacterial; rapid onset; drooling; toxic; do NOT examine), inhaled foreign body (sudden onset; unilateral wheeze; asymmetric breath sounds), bacterial tracheitis (Staphylococcus aureus; toxic; purulent secretions); adults — laryngeal carcinoma, thyroid goitre, anaphylaxis, angioedema.

concepts.title: Neck lump – Diagnostic approach
concepts.content: Diagnostic approach to neck lump: history — duration, rate of growth, associated symptoms (fever, weight loss, dysphagia, hoarseness, otalgia), risk factors (smoking, alcohol, age >40). Examination — site (anterior/posterior triangle, midline/lateral), consistency (soft, firm, hard), mobility, tenderness, transillumination, pulsatility, skin changes. Investigations: FBC, CRP, ESR, LFTs, TFTs, monospot; ultrasound (first-line imaging); FNAC or core biopsy; CT/MRI neck; PET-CT for unknown primary; panendoscopy (direct laryngoscopy, oesophagoscopy, bronchoscopy). 2-week wait referral: any unexplained neck lump in adult; lump in parotid/submandibular gland.

concepts.title: Thyroglossal cyst – Management
concepts.content: Management of thyroglossal cyst: Sistrunk procedure (surgical excision of cyst, tract, and central portion of hyoid bone — reduces recurrence rate from 50% to <5%). Complications if untreated: infection (thyroglossal abscess), malignant transformation (rare — papillary thyroid carcinoma most common). Pre-operative thyroid imaging recommended to confirm normal thyroid tissue present (as thyroglossal cyst may represent only functional thyroid tissue in some patients).

concepts.title: Laryngeal carcinoma – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Laryngeal carcinoma: most common type is squamous cell carcinoma. Risk factors: smoking (most important), alcohol, HPV infection, asbestos exposure. Types: glottic (most common — vocal cord; presents early with hoarseness; good prognosis); supraglottic (presents late — dysphagia, neck lump, referred otalgia; worse prognosis); subglottic (rare; presents with airway obstruction). Features: persistent hoarseness (>3 weeks — urgent 2WW referral for age ≥45 years), dysphagia, stridor, neck lump, weight loss. Investigations: laryngoscopy + biopsy; CT/MRI neck and chest. Management: early disease — radiotherapy or endoscopic laser surgery; advanced disease — total laryngectomy ± radiotherapy/chemotherapy.

concepts.title: Vocal cord nodules and polyps – Clinical features and management
