concepts.content: Vocal cord nodules (singer's nodules): bilateral, symmetrical benign lesions at junction of anterior and middle thirds of vocal cords. Caused by vocal overuse/misuse. Features: hoarseness, voice fatigue, reduced vocal range. Management: voice rest, speech therapy (first-line); surgical excision if conservative treatment fails. Vocal cord polyps: usually unilateral; associated with smoking, vocal overuse, hypothyroidism, GORD. Features: hoarseness. Management: treat underlying cause; surgical excision (microlaryngoscopy).

concepts.title: Dysphagia – Differential diagnosis and red flags
concepts.content: Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) differential diagnosis: oropharyngeal (neuromuscular — stroke, motor neurone disease, myasthenia gravis, Parkinson's; structural — tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess, epiglottitis, pharyngeal pouch, head and neck cancer); oesophageal (mechanical — oesophageal carcinoma, benign stricture, Schatzki ring, extrinsic compression; motility — achalasia, diffuse oesophageal spasm, systemic sclerosis). Red flags requiring urgent investigation: progressive dysphagia, weight loss, haematemesis, anaemia, age >55 years with new dysphagia. 2-week wait referral for suspected upper GI cancer.

concepts.title: Anosmia – Causes and management
concepts.content: Anosmia (loss of smell) causes: nasal/sinonasal (most common — rhinitis, rhinosinusitis, nasal polyps, nasal obstruction); post-viral (COVID-19 most common cause of sudden anosmia; also post-influenza, post-URTI); head trauma (cribriform plate fracture — shearing of olfactory nerve fibres); neurological (Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis); congenital (Kallmann syndrome — anosmia + hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism); toxic (smoking, cocaine, medications). Management: treat underlying cause; olfactory training (smell training with 4 distinct odours twice daily for 3+ months — evidence for post-viral anosmia); intranasal corticosteroids (if inflammatory cause); refer to ENT or neurology if persistent.

concepts.title: Auricular haematoma – Definition and management
concepts.content: Auricular haematoma (cauliflower ear): haematoma between auricular cartilage and perichondrium following blunt trauma to the ear. Common in contact sports (boxing, rugby, wrestling). Features: painful, fluctuant swelling of the auricle; loss of normal auricular contours. Management: urgent drainage (needle aspiration or incision and drainage); compression dressing to prevent reaccumulation; antibiotics to prevent perichondritis. If untreated: fibrosis and calcification → permanent deformity ('cauliflower ear'). Perichondritis: infection of auricular cartilage — most commonly Pseudomonas aeruginosa; treat with ciprofloxacin.

concepts.title: Acute sinusitis – Definition and clinical features
concepts.content: Acute sinusitis is inflammation of the paranasal sinuses lasting <12 weeks. Most commonly viral (rhinovirus, influenza). Features: facial pain/pressure (worse on bending forward); nasal congestion/obstruction; purulent nasal discharge; reduced sense of smell; headache; post-nasal drip; fever. Maxillary sinus most commonly affected (cheek pain, dental pain). Frontal sinus (forehead pain). Ethmoid sinus (pain between eyes). Sphenoid sinus (vertex/occipital headache). Bacterial sinusitis suggested by: symptoms >10 days, severe symptoms, double-sickening pattern.

concepts.title: Cough – ENT causes
concepts.content: ENT causes of chronic cough: post-nasal drip (most common ENT cause — rhinitis, rhinosinusitis, nasal polyps; tickling sensation in throat; worse at night; mucus visible in posterior pharynx); laryngopharyngeal reflux (acid irritation of larynx/pharynx; associated hoarseness, globus); vocal cord dysfunction (paradoxical vocal cord motion — inspiratory stridor, throat tightness); laryngeal hypersensitivity; chronic laryngitis; upper airway cough syndrome. Management: treat underlying cause; intranasal corticosteroids and antihistamines for post-nasal drip; PPI trial for LPR.

concepts.title: Dizziness – Approach and classification
concepts.content: Dizziness is a broad term encompassing: vertigo (illusion of movement — rotatory, most commonly peripheral vestibular cause); presyncope (feeling of impending faint — cardiovascular cause); disequilibrium (unsteadiness without head sensation — cerebellar, proprioceptive, or multisensory); non-specific dizziness (anxiety, hyperventilation, medication side effects). Peripheral vs central vertigo: peripheral (BPPV, vestibular neuronitis, labyrinthitis, Ménière's — sudden onset, severe, fatigable nystagmus, no neurological signs); central (posterior circulation stroke, cerebellar pathology — gradual onset, less severe, non-fatigable nystagmus, neurological signs present).

concepts.title: HiNTs examination – Distinguishing peripheral from central vertigo
concepts.content: HiNTs (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) examination: used to distinguish peripheral from central cause of acute vestibular syndrome. Head Impulse test: positive (catch-up saccade) = peripheral; negative (normal VOR) = central (concerning for posterior circulation stroke). Nystagmus: unidirectional horizontal = peripheral; direction-changing or vertical = central. Test of Skew: absent = peripheral; present (vertical misalignment) = central. HiNTs more sensitive than MRI in first 24–48 hours for posterior circulation stroke.

concepts.title: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia – ENT features
concepts.content: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT, Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome): autosomal dominant condition causing abnormal blood vessel formation. ENT features: recurrent epistaxis (most common presenting feature — 90% of patients; begins in childhood; often severe and recurrent); telangiectasias on lips, tongue, nasal mucosa, face, fingers. Systemic features: pulmonary AVMs (haemoptysis, dyspnoea, paradoxical emboli), hepatic AVMs, cerebral AVMs. Management of epistaxis in HHT: humidification, lubricants, cauterisation, laser treatment, bevacizumab (anti-VEGF), septodermoplasty.

concepts.title: Paediatric ENT – Common presentations and referral criteria
concepts.content: Common paediatric ENT presentations: glue ear (OME) — most common cause of conductive hearing loss in children; croup — viral, barking cough, inspiratory stridor, 6 months–3 years; epiglottitis — bacterial, rapid onset, drooling, toxic; laryngomalacia — most common cause of stridor in neonates; tonsillitis — recurrent, NICE criteria for tonsillectomy; adenoid hypertrophy — nasal obstruction, snoring, OME, recurrent otitis media; inhaled foreign body — sudden onset choking. Referral criteria: hearing loss in child — urgent audiology; stridor in neonate — urgent ENT; suspected epiglottitis — emergency ENT and anaesthetics.

concepts.title: Tracheostomy – Indications and complications
concepts.content: Tracheostomy indications: upper airway obstruction (tumour, trauma, bilateral vocal cord paralysis, angioedema); prolonged mechanical ventilation (ICU); airway protection (impaired swallowing/cough reflex); pulmonary toilet (secretion management). Types: surgical (standard) vs percutaneous dilatational (bedside, ICU). Complications: immediate — haemorrhage, false passage, pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema; early — tube displacement, obstruction, infection, surgical emphysema; late — tracheal stenosis (most common late complication), tracheomalacia, tracheo-oesophageal fistula, tracheo-innominate fistula (life-threatening haemorrhage), decannulation failure.

concepts.title: Cochlear implants – Indications and overview
concepts.content: Cochlear implants: electronic devices that bypass damaged hair cells and directly stimulate the auditory nerve. Indications (NICE TA166): bilateral severe-profound SNHL (>90 dB HL) in adults who do not benefit adequately from hearing aids; children with bilateral severe-profound SNHL. Components: external (microphone, speech processor, transmitter coil) and internal (receiver-stimulator, electrode array in cochlea). Outcomes: significant improvement in speech understanding; best outcomes with early implantation in children (before age 2 if possible) and short duration of deafness in adults. Contraindications: cochlear ossification, absent auditory nerve.

concepts.title: Acoustic neuroma – Epidemiology and investigations
concepts.content: Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) epidemiology: incidence 1–2 per 100,000 per year; accounts for 8% of all intracranial tumours; peak incidence 40–60 years; equal sex distribution. Unilateral in 95% (bilateral = neurofibromatosis type 2). Investigations: pure tone audiogram (asymmetric high-frequency SNHL); auditory brainstem response (ABR — prolonged wave I-V interpeak latency); MRI with gadolinium (gold standard — shows intracanalicular or CPA mass). Management options: observation (small tumours, elderly); stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife); surgical excision (translabyrinthine, retrosigmoid, or middle fossa approach).

concepts.title: ENT emergencies – Summary
concepts.content: ENT emergencies requiring immediate action: epiglottitis (do NOT examine throat; call anaesthetist and ENT; secure airway); Ludwig's angina (airway management priority; IV antibiotics); post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage (return to theatre if primary; admission and antibiotics if secondary); epistaxis with haemodynamic compromise (resuscitation; posterior packing; surgical ligation); malignant otitis externa with intracranial complications (IV antipseudomonal antibiotics; neurosurgical input); nasal septal haematoma (urgent drainage within 24 hours to prevent cartilage necrosis); auricular haematoma (urgent drainage to prevent cauliflower ear); sudden SNHL (urgent ENT; high-dose steroids within 2 weeks of onset).

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Definition
concepts.content: Acute bronchitis is a type of chest infection.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Definition
concepts.content: Acute bronchitis is usually self-limiting in nature.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Acute bronchitis is a result of inflammation of the trachea.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Acute bronchitis is a result of inflammation of the major bronchi.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Acute bronchitis is associated with oedematous large airways.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Acute bronchitis is associated with the production of sputum.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Prognosis
concepts.content: The disease course of acute bronchitis usually resolves before 3 weeks.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Prognosis
concepts.content: 25% of patients with acute bronchitis will still have a cough beyond 3 weeks.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Viral infection is the leading cause of acute bronchitis.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Around 80% of acute bronchitis episodes occur in autumn or winter.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients with acute bronchitis typically present with acute onset cough.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: The cough in acute bronchitis may or may not be productive.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients with acute bronchitis typically present with acute onset sore throat.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients with acute bronchitis typically present with acute onset rhinorrhoea.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients with acute bronchitis typically present with acute onset wheeze.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: The majority of patients with acute bronchitis have a normal chest examination.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Some patients with acute bronchitis may present with low-grade fever.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Some patients with acute bronchitis may present with wheeze on examination.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Sputum, wheeze, breathlessness may be absent in acute bronchitis, whereas at least one tends to be present in pneumonia.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: No other focal chest signs (dullness to percussion, crepitations, bronchial breathing) are present in acute bronchitis other than wheeze.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Systemic features (malaise, myalgia, and fever) may be absent in acute bronchitis, whereas they tend to be present in pneumonia.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Investigations
concepts.content: Acute bronchitis is typically a clinical diagnosis.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Investigations
concepts.content: If CRP testing is available, it may be used to guide whether antibiotic therapy is indicated for acute bronchitis.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Management of acute bronchitis includes analgesia.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Management of acute bronchitis includes good fluid intake.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Consider antibiotic therapy for acute bronchitis if patients are systemically very unwell.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Consider antibiotic therapy for acute bronchitis if patients have pre-existing co-morbidities.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Consider antibiotic therapy for acute bronchitis if patients have a CRP of 20-100mg/L (offer delayed prescription).

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Consider antibiotic therapy for acute bronchitis if patients have a CRP >100mg/L (offer antibiotics immediately).

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: The BNF currently recommends doxycycline first-line for acute bronchitis.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Doxycycline cannot be used in children or pregnant women for acute bronchitis.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Alternatives to doxycycline for acute bronchitis include amoxicillin.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Definition
concepts.content: Allergic rhinitis is an inflammatory disorder of the nose where the nose become sensitized to allergens such as house dust mites and grass, tree and weed pollens.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Classification
concepts.content: Allergic rhinitis may be classified as seasonal.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Seasonal Rhinitis
concepts.content: Seasonal rhinitis occurs around the same time every year.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Hay Fever
concepts.content: Seasonal rhinitis which occurs secondary to pollens is known as hay fever.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Perennial Rhinitis
concepts.content: Perennial rhinitis symptoms occur throughout the year.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Occupational Rhinitis
concepts.content: Occupational rhinitis symptoms follow exposure to particular allergens within the work place.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of allergic rhinitis include sneezing.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of allergic rhinitis include bilateral nasal obstruction.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of allergic rhinitis include clear nasal discharge.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of allergic rhinitis include post-nasal drip.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of allergic rhinitis include nasal pruritus.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Management
concepts.content: Management of allergic rhinitis includes allergen avoidance.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Management
concepts.content: For mild-to-moderate intermittent, or mild persistent symptoms of allergic rhinitis, oral or intranasal antihistamines are used.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Management
concepts.content: For moderate-to-severe persistent symptoms of allergic rhinitis, or if initial drug treatment is ineffective, intranasal corticosteroids are used.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Management
concepts.content: A short course of oral corticosteroids are occasionally needed to cover important life events for allergic rhinitis.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Management
concepts.content: There may be a role for short courses of topical nasal decongestants (e.g. oxymetazoline) in allergic rhinitis.

concepts.title: Allergic rhinitis – Management
concepts.content: Topical nasal decongestants should not be used for prolonged periods as increasing doses are required to achieve the same effect (tachyphylaxis) and rebound hypertrophy of the nasal mucosa (rhinitis medicamentosa) may occur upon withdrawal.

concepts.title: Allergy tests – Skin prick test
concepts.content: The skin prick test is the most commonly used allergy test as it is easy to perform and inexpensive.

concepts.title: Allergy tests – Skin prick test procedure
concepts.content: In a skin prick test, drops of diluted allergen are placed on the skin after which the skin is pierced using a needle.

concepts.title: Allergy tests – Skin prick test capacity
concepts.content: A large number of allergens can be tested in one skin prick test session.

concepts.title: Allergy tests – Skin prick test controls
concepts.content: A skin prick test normally includes a histamine (positive) and sterile water (negative) control.

concepts.title: Allergy tests – Skin prick test results
concepts.content: A wheal will typically develop if a patient has an allergy in a skin prick test.

concepts.title: Allergy tests – Skin prick test interpretation time
concepts.content: Skin prick test results can be interpreted after 15 minutes.

concepts.title: Allergy tests – Skin prick test utility
concepts.content: Skin prick tests are useful for food allergies and also pollen allergies.

concepts.title: Allergy tests – Radioallergosorbent test (RAST)
concepts.content: The Radioallergosorbent test (RAST) determines the amount of IgE that reacts specifically with suspected or known allergens, for example IgE to egg protein.

concepts.title: Allergy tests – RAST results
concepts.content: RAST results are given in grades from 0 (negative) to 6 (strongly positive).

concepts.title: Allergy tests – RAST utility
concepts.content: RAST is useful for food allergies, inhaled allergens (e.g. Pollen) and wasp/bee venom.

concepts.title: Allergy tests – Blood tests
concepts.content: Blood tests may be used when skin prick tests are not suitable, for example if there is extensive eczema or if the patient is taking antihistamines.

concepts.title: Allergy tests – Skin patch testing
concepts.content: Skin patch testing is useful for contact dermatitis.

concepts.title: Allergy tests – Skin patch testing procedure
concepts.content: Around 30-40 allergens are placed on the back for skin patch testing.

concepts.title: Allergy tests – Skin patch testing irritants
concepts.content: Irritants may also be tested for in skin patch testing.

concepts.title: Allergy tests – Skin patch testing results
concepts.content: The patches are removed 48 hours later with the results being read by a dermatologist after a further 48 hours.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy (CMPI/CMPA) occurs in around 3-6% of all children.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Presentation time
concepts.content: CMPI/CMPA typically presents in the first 3 months of life in formula-fed infants.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Presentation in breastfed infants
concepts.content: CMPI/CMPA is rarely seen in exclusively breastfed infants.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Types of reactions
concepts.content: Both immediate (IgE mediated) and delayed (non-IgE mediated) reactions are seen in CMPI/CMPA.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Terminology
concepts.content: The term CMPA is usually used for immediate reactions and CMPI for mild-moderate delayed reactions.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of CMPI/CMPA include regurgitation and vomiting.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of CMPI/CMPA include diarrhoea.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of CMPI/CMPA include urticaria.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of CMPI/CMPA include atopic eczema.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of CMPI/CMPA include 'colic' symptoms: irritability, crying.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of CMPI/CMPA include wheeze.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of CMPI/CMPA include chronic cough.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Complications
concepts.content: Rarely angioedema and anaphylaxis may occur in CMPI/CMPA.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Diagnosis
concepts.content: Diagnosis of CMPI/CMPA is often clinical (e.g. improvement with cow's milk protein elimination).

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations for CMPI/CMPA include skin prick/patch testing.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations for CMPI/CMPA include total IgE and specific IgE (RAST) for cow's milk protein.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Management (severe symptoms)
concepts.content: If CMPI/CMPA symptoms are severe (e.g. failure to thrive) refer to a paediatrician.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Management (formula-fed, mild-moderate)
concepts.content: For formula-fed infants with mild-moderate CMPI/CMPA symptoms, extensive hydrolysed formula (eHF) milk is the first-line replacement formula.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Management (formula-fed, severe or no response)
concepts.content: For infants with severe CMPA or if no response to eHF, amino acid-based formula (AAF) is used.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Soya intolerance
concepts.content: Around 10% of infants with CMPI/CMPA are also intolerant to soya milk.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Management (breastfed)
concepts.content: If breastfed, continue breastfeeding for CMPI/CMPA.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Management (breastfed maternal diet)
concepts.content: For breastfed infants with CMPI/CMPA, eliminate cow's milk protein from maternal diet.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Management (breastfed maternal supplements)
concepts.content: Consider prescribing calcium supplements for breastfeeding mothers whose babies have, or are suspected to have, CMPI, to prevent deficiency whilst they exclude dairy from their diet.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Management (breastfed, after stopping)
concepts.content: Use eHF milk when breastfeeding stops, until 12 months of age and at least for 6 months.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Prognosis
concepts.content: CMPI usually resolves in most children.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Prognosis (IgE mediated)
concepts.content: In children with IgE mediated intolerance, around 55% will be milk tolerant by the age of 5 years.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Prognosis (non-IgE mediated)
concepts.content: In children with non-IgE mediated intolerance, most children will be milk tolerant by the age of 3 years.

concepts.title: Cow's milk protein intolerance/allergy – Challenge
concepts.content: A challenge is often performed in the hospital setting as anaphylaxis can occur.

concepts.title: Food allergy in children and young people – NICE guidelines
concepts.content: The 2011 NICE guidelines differentiate between IgE mediated and non-IgE mediated allergies.

concepts.title: Food allergy in children and young people – Food intolerance
concepts.content: The NICE guidance does not govern food intolerance, which is not caused by immune system dysfunction.

concepts.title: Food allergy in children and young people – First step
concepts.content: The first step is to identify possible food allergy and differentiate the possible causes: IgE-mediated and Non-IgE-mediated.

concepts.title: Food allergy in children and young people – IgE-mediated skin symptoms
concepts.content: IgE-mediated food allergy skin symptoms include pruritus, erythema, urticaria, and angioedema.

concepts.title: Food allergy in children and young people – Non-IgE-mediated skin symptoms
concepts.content: Non-IgE-mediated food allergy skin symptoms include pruritus and atopic eczema.

concepts.title: Food allergy in children and young people – IgE-mediated gastrointestinal symptoms
concepts.content: IgE-mediated food allergy gastrointestinal symptoms include nausea, gastro-oesophageal reflux, colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhoea.

concepts.title: Food allergy in children and young people – Non-IgE-mediated gastrointestinal symptoms
concepts.content: Non-IgE-mediated food allergy gastrointestinal symptoms include loose or frequent stools, blood and/or mucus in stools, abdominal pain, infantile colic, food refusal or aversion, constipation, and perianal redness.

concepts.title: Food allergy in children and young people – IgE-mediated respiratory symptoms
concepts.content: IgE-mediated food allergy respiratory symptoms include upper respiratory tract symptoms (nasal itching, sneezing, rhinorrhoea or congestion with or without conjunctivitis) and lower respiratory tract symptoms (cough, chest tightness, wheezing or shortness of breath).

concepts.title: Food allergy in children and young people – Non-IgE-mediated other symptoms
concepts.content: Non-IgE-mediated food allergy other symptoms include pallor, tiredness, and faltering growth plus one or more gastrointestinal symptoms above (with or without significant atopic eczema).

concepts.title: Food allergy in children and young people – Symptoms of anaphylaxis
concepts.content: Symptoms of anaphylaxis are mentioned in the context of food allergy.

concepts.title: Food allergy in children and young people – Investigations (IgE-mediated)
concepts.content: If the history is suggestive of an IgE-mediated allergy, offer a skin prick test or blood tests for specific IgE antibodies to the suspected foods and likely co-allergens.

concepts.title: Food allergy in children and young people – Management (non-IgE-mediated)
concepts.content: If the history is suggestive of a non-IgE-mediated allergy, eliminate the suspected allergen for 2-6 weeks, then reintroduce.

concepts.title: Food allergy in children and young people – Dietitian consultation
concepts.content: NICE advise to 'consult a dietitian with appropriate competencies about nutritional adequacies, timings and follow-up' for non-IgE-mediated food allergies.

concepts.title: Latex allergy – Type I hypersensitivity
concepts.content: Sensitivity to latex may cause type I hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis).

concepts.title: Latex allergy – Type IV hypersensitivity
concepts.content: Sensitivity to latex may cause type IV hypersensitivity (allergic contact dermatitis).

concepts.title: Latex allergy – Irritant contact dermatitis
concepts.content: Sensitivity to latex may cause irritant contact dermatitis.

concepts.title: Latex allergy – Risk factors
concepts.content: Latex allergy is more common in children with myelomeningocele spina bifida.

concepts.title: Latex-fruit syndrome – Association
concepts.content: Many people who are allergic to latex are also allergic to fruits, particularly banana, pineapple, avocado, chestnut, kiwi fruit, mango, passion fruit and strawberry.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Definition
concepts.content: Oral allergy syndrome, also known as pollen-food allergy, is an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to specific raw, plant-based foods including fruits, vegetables, nuts and certain spices.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Clinical features
concepts.content: Oral allergy syndrome typically presents with mild tingling or pruritus of the lips, tongue and mouth.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: This hypersensitivity reaction is initiated by cross-reaction with a non-food allergen, most commonly birch pollen whereby the protein in the food is similar but not identical in structure to the original allergen.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Association with pollen allergies
concepts.content: OAS is strongly linked with pollen allergies and presents with seasonal variation.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Effect of cooking
concepts.content: Cooking culprit food, and thereby denaturing the proteins, prevents symptoms occurring in OAS.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome vs food allergies – Cause
concepts.content: A food allergy is caused by direct sensitivity to a protein present in food. OAS is caused by cross-sensitisation to a structurally similar allergen present in pollen.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome vs food allergies – Non-plant foods
concepts.content: Non-plant foods do not cause OAS because there are no cross-reactive allergens in pollen which would be structurally similar to meat.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome vs food allergies – Stability of allergens
concepts.content: Food allergies may be caused by plant or non-plant foods and allergens occur in response to substances that are more stable and able to survive stomach enzymes and acid processing and cooking.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome vs food allergies – Systemic symptoms and anaphylaxis
concepts.content: Food allergies are more likely to cause systemic symptoms (vomiting and diarrhoea) and are more likely to lead to anaphylaxis because the allergens are not readily broken down.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome vs food allergies – OAS symptom limitation
concepts.content: The symptoms of OAS are normally limited to the oropharynx because the proteins that cause the symptoms are denatured by stomach enzymes.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Epidemiology
concepts.content: About 2% of the UK population has OAS but this is probably under-diagnosed.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Prevalence in pollen allergy
concepts.content: About 1/2 of patients with a general pollen allergy and 3/4 of patients with an allergy to birch pollen (the most common allergen in the UK) report symptoms of OAS.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Associations
concepts.content: OAS is associated with Birch pollen allergy (most common) and Rye grass pollen allergy.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Association with Latex allergy
concepts.content: OAS is associated with Rubber latex allergy.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Presentation suspicion
concepts.content: OAS should be suspected in a patient with a history of seasonal allergy symptoms (rhinitis, conjunctivitis and asthma) who present with symptoms minutes after eating a specific raw food.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Most common symptoms
concepts.content: Itching and tingling of the lips, tongue and mouth are the most common symptoms of OAS.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Mild swelling and redness
concepts.content: Mild swelling and redness of the lips, tongue and throat may occur in OAS.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Severe cases
concepts.content: In severe cases of OAS, patients develop nausea and vomiting.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Symptom resolution
concepts.content: OAS symptoms fully resolve within one hour of contact.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Complications
concepts.content: Anaphylaxis is a very rare complication of OAS.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Signs (between episodes)
concepts.content: Most patients will have no visible signs during or between episodes of OAS.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Signs (visible)
concepts.content: Some patients may have visible swelling and redness of the lips, tongue and oral mucosa in OAS.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Signs of anaphylaxis
concepts.content: Patients with anaphylaxis present with wheeze, hives, hypotension and collapse.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Investigations (diagnosis)
concepts.content: OAS is a clinical diagnosis.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Investigations (rule out/confirm)
concepts.content: Further tests can be used to rule out diagnoses such as food allergies and to confirm the diagnosis when the history is unclear.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Investigations (standard tests)
concepts.content: Standard IgE RAST and skin prick testing may be performed to identify common allergens such as pollens which co-exist with OAS.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Investigations (pollen allergies and associated foods)
concepts.content: Common pollen allergies have specific associated foods which cause OAS. For example, birch allergy is associated with sensitivity to, amongst others, carrot, parsley and spinach.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Investigations (food-specific IgE testing)
concepts.content: Food-specific IgE testing for OAS is unreliable and rarely performed clinically because the food does not survive processing.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Investigations (skin prick testing with culprit foods)
concepts.content: Skin prick testing with culprit foods is more commonly used for OAS.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Investigations (positive skin prick test)
concepts.content: A positive skin prick test for OAS would cause a small, itchy lump to develop on the skin.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Management (avoidance)
concepts.content: Avoidance of culprit foods is the only required modification for the vast majority of patients with OAS.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Management (symptomatic)
concepts.content: If culprit food is eaten and symptoms develop, an oral antihistamine can be taken for OAS.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Management (anaphylaxis)
concepts.content: If symptoms of anaphylaxis develop in OAS, an ambulance should be called.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Management (anaphylaxis treatment)
concepts.content: Intramuscular adrenaline may be required for anaphylaxis in OAS.

concepts.title: Oral allergy syndrome – Management (cooked foods)
concepts.content: Patients should be informed that once cooked, culprit foods should not cause symptoms in OAS.

concepts.title: Penicillin allergy – Prevalence
concepts.content: Allergy to penicillin based antibiotics is common.

concepts.title: Penicillin allergy – Misdiagnosis
concepts.content: Many patients who report a penicillin allergy may be describing an intolerance/side-effects (e.g. diarrhoea) or a coincidental rash (e.g. amoxicillin in patients with infectious mononucleosis).

concepts.title: Penicillin allergy – Cross-reactivity with cephalosporins
concepts.content: Around 0.5-6.5% of patients who are allergic to penicillin are also allergic to cephalosporins.

concepts.title: Penicillin allergy – BNF guidance on cephalosporins
concepts.content: The principal side-effect of the cephalosporins is hypersensitivity and about 0.5-6.5% of penicillin-sensitive patients will also be allergic to the cephalosporins.

concepts.title: Penicillin allergy – BNF guidance (immediate hypersensitivity)
concepts.content: Patients with a history of immediate hypersensitivity to penicillin should not receive a cephalosporin.

concepts.title: Penicillin allergy – BNF guidance (essential cephalosporin)
concepts.content: If a cephalosporin is essential in penicillin-allergic patients because a suitable alternative antibacterial is not available, then cefixime, cefotaxime, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, or cefuroxime can be used with caution.

concepts.title: Penicillin allergy – BNF guidance (cephalosporins to avoid)
concepts.content: Cefaclor, cefadroxil, cefalexin, cefradine, and ceftaroline fosamil should be avoided in penicillin-allergic patients if a cephalosporin is essential.

concepts.title: Penicillin allergy – Types of penicillin
concepts.content: It is important to be aware of other types of penicillin and their trade names to avoid accidental prescription.

concepts.title: Penicillin allergy – Examples of penicillin types
concepts.content: Types of penicillin include phenoxymethylpenicillin, benzylpenicillin, flucloxacillin, amoxicillin, ampicillin, co-amoxiclav (Augmentin), co-fluampicil (Magnapen), piperacillin with tazobactam (Tazocin), and ticarcillin with clavulanic acid (Timentin).

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Classification of reactions
concepts.content: Allergic reactions to venom may be broadly considered as either local or systemic.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Local reactions definition
concepts.content: Redness, swelling and pain limited to the skin and soft tissues directly related to the site of venom exposure, but spreading >10 cm from the site may be defined as 'local' reactions.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Systemic reactions definition
concepts.content: Systemic reactions may refer to cutaneous reactions that are relatively distant from the exposure site e.g. widespread redness, itching, urticaria and/or angioedema (not affecting the mouth or throat).

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Anaphylaxis management
concepts.content: Anaphylaxis may occur with or without evidence of systemic cutaneous reaction and any reaction in which there is any airway compromise or signs and symptoms of haemodynamic compromise should be managed as anaphylactic in nature.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Acute phase management
concepts.content: Broadly speaking, the management of venom allergy in the acute phase is supportive.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Anaphylaxis treatment
concepts.content: Anaphylaxis should be managed with intramuscular adrenaline, intravenous steroids and intravenous anti-histamines as required.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Anaphylaxis additional treatment
concepts.content: Oxygen and nebulised bronchodilators may also be required for anaphylaxis.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Referral to allergy specialist
concepts.content: People who've had a systemic reaction to an insect bite should be referred to an allergy specialist.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Testing recommendation (systemic reaction)
concepts.content: Testing for venom allergy is recommended in any patient with a history of a systemic reaction causing airway compromise or haemodynamic instability.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Testing recommendation (systemic cutaneous reaction)
concepts.content: Testing for venom allergy may also be beneficial in patients with a history of a systemic cutaneous reaction where the allergen is felt to be difficult to avoid e.g. an allergy to bee stings in a beekeeper.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Self-management plan
concepts.content: Patients with a history of a systemic reaction should be provided with a self-management plan, including guidance on the use of anti-histamines and adrenaline auto-injectors.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Medical alert device
concepts.content: Patients should also be advised to wear a medical alert device for venom allergy.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Venom immunotherapy (VIT)
concepts.content: Venom immunotherapy (VIT) is considered to be one of the most effective immunotherapies in use.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – VIT recommendation criteria
concepts.content: VIT may be recommended for patients with a history of a previous reaction which presented with airway and/or haemodynamic compromise and raised levels of venom-specific immunoglobulin E on either skin prick or in vitro testing.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – BSACI guidance on VIT contraindications
concepts.content: The British Society for Allergy and Clinical Immunology guidance advises that VIT should not be performed in patients without demonstrable venom-specific IgE or in those with a recent history of anaphylaxis or systemic reaction.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Repeat allergy testing
concepts.content: Repeat allergy testing should be considered in those with a clear reaction history but no evidence of a venom-specific IgE.

concepts.title: Venom allergy – Baseline tryptase level
concepts.content: A baseline tryptase level should also be performed to exclude indolent mastocytosis (relevant because this may predict subsequent systemic reactions during the course of immunotherapy).

concepts.title: Asbestos-related lung disease – Overview
concepts.content: Asbestos can cause a variety of lung diseases from benign pleural plaques to mesothelioma.

concepts.title: Pleural plaques – Definition
concepts.content: Pleural plaques are benign and do not undergo malignant change.

concepts.title: Pleural plaques – Management
concepts.content: They, therefore don't require any follow-up.

concepts.title: Pleural plaques – Epidemiology
concepts.content: They are the most common form of asbestos-related lung disease and generally occur after a latent period of 20-40 years.

concepts.title: Diffuse pleural thickening – Aetiology
concepts.content: Asbestos exposure may cause diffuse pleural thickening in a similar pattern to that seen following an empyema or haemothorax.

concepts.title: Diffuse pleural thickening – Clinical features
concepts.content: This may be associated with a restrictive deficit on spirometry.

concepts.title: Asbestosis – Definition
concepts.content: Asbestosis is the name given to the lung fibrosis caused by asbestos.

concepts.title: Asbestosis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: It is a lower lobe fibrosis.

concepts.title: Asbestosis – Complications
concepts.content: Patients are at increased risk of developing lung cancer (the risk is synergistic with smoking).

concepts.title: Mesothelioma – Definition
concepts.content: Mesothelioma is a malignant disease of the pleura.

concepts.title: Mesothelioma – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: There is a strong link with asbestos exposure (especially crocidolite, 'blue' asbestos).

concepts.title: Mesothelioma – Epidemiology
concepts.content: The latent period between exposure and disease is typically 30-40 years.

concepts.title: Mesothelioma – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Workers who smoke and are exposed to asbestos have a much greater risk of lung cancer but not of mesothelioma.

concepts.title: Mesothelioma – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features progressive shortness-of-breath chest pain pleural effusion

concepts.title: Mesothelioma – Investigations
concepts.content: CXR: pleural effusion, pleural thickening

concepts.title: Mesothelioma – Investigations
concepts.content: pleural fluid is often blood-stained

concepts.title: Mesothelioma – Investigations
concepts.content: pleural biopsy is required for diagnosis

concepts.title: Mesothelioma – Management
concepts.content: chemotherapy radiotherapy supportive care

concepts.title: Mesothelioma – Prognosis
concepts.content: very poor, median survival is 8-14 months

concepts.title: Asthma – Definition
concepts.content: Asthma is a common chronic inflammatory disease of the airways characterised by variable and recurring symptoms, reversible airflow obstruction, and bronchospasm.

concepts.title: Asthma – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Asthma is thought to be caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors.

concepts.title: Asthma – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of asthma include worsening dyspnoea, wheeze and cough that is not responding to salbutamol.

concepts.title: Asthma – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Asthma symptoms may be triggered by a respiratory tract infection.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management
concepts.content: NICE updated their asthma guidelines in 2017.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management
concepts.content: The key change in NICE 2017 guidelines is a move away from recommending a salbutamol inhaler as the first step for adults with asthma.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management
concepts.content: NICE 2017 guidelines recommend a short-acting beta2-agonist (SABA) as a reliever therapy for all patients with asthma.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management
concepts.content: NICE 2017 guidelines recommend an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) as the first-line preventer therapy for asthma.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management: Step 1
concepts.content: Step 1 of asthma management involves using a short-acting beta2-agonist (SABA) as required.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management: Step 2
concepts.content: Step 2 of asthma management involves adding an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) at a low dose.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management: Step 3
concepts.content: Step 3 of asthma management involves adding a long-acting beta2-agonist (LABA).

concepts.title: Asthma – Management: Step 3 (LABA response)
concepts.content: If there is no response to LABA in Step 3, stop it and increase the ICS dose.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management: Step 3 (Inadequate control with LABA)
concepts.content: If there is benefit from LABA but control is still inadequate in Step 3, continue LABA and increase the ICS dose.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management: Step 4
concepts.content: Step 4 of asthma management involves considering increasing ICS to a high dose, or adding a fourth drug e.g. leukotriene receptor antagonist, theophylline.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management: Step 5
concepts.content: Step 5 of asthma management involves continuous use of oral steroids.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Definition
concepts.content: Bronchiolitis is a common lung infection in young children and infants.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Bronchiolitis causes inflammation and congestion in the small airways (bronchioles) of the lung.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Bronchiolitis is almost always caused by a virus.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: The most common cause of Bronchiolitis is respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Bronchiolitis features coryzal symptoms.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Bronchiolitis features a dry cough.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Bronchiolitis features increasing breathlessness.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Bronchiolitis features wheezing.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Bronchiolitis features low-grade fever.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Bronchiolitis features poor feeding.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Management
concepts.content: Management of Bronchiolitis includes supportive care.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Management
concepts.content: Supportive care for Bronchiolitis includes ensuring adequate intake.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Management
concepts.content: Supportive care for Bronchiolitis includes nasal saline drops.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Management
concepts.content: Supplemental oxygen may be used in Bronchiolitis if saturations are persistently < 92%.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Management
concepts.content: Nebulised hypertonic saline may be used in selected cases of Bronchiolitis.

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Definition
concepts.content: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder that affects mostly the lungs, but also the pancreas, liver, kidneys, and intestine.

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Long-term issues include difficulty breathing and coughing up mucus as a result of frequent lung infections.

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Genetics
concepts.content: Genetics autosomal recessive gene is on chromosome 7 encodes for the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Genetics
concepts.content: most common mutation is delta-F508

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Respiratory Features
concepts.content: Respiratory recurrent chest infections

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Respiratory Features
concepts.content: bronchiectasis

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Respiratory Features
concepts.content: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Gastrointestinal Features
concepts.content: Gastrointestinal pancreatic insufficiency: malabsorption, diabetes mellitus

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Gastrointestinal Features
concepts.content: distal intestinal obstruction syndrome (DIOS)

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Gastrointestinal Features
concepts.content: cirrhosis and portal hypertension

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Other Features
concepts.content: Other male infertility

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Other Features
concepts.content: osteoporosis

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Other Features
concepts.content: arthropathy

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Management
concepts.content: Management physiotherapy

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Management
concepts.content: antibiotics

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Management
concepts.content: bronchodilators

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Management
concepts.content: dornase alfa (DNase)

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Management
concepts.content: lung transplantation

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Management
concepts.content: pancreatic enzyme replacement

concepts.title: Influenza – Definition
concepts.content: Influenza, commonly known as 'the flu', is an infectious disease caused by an influenza virus.

concepts.title: Influenza – Clinical features
concepts.content: Symptoms can be mild to severe.

concepts.title: Influenza – Clinical features
concepts.content: The most common symptoms include: a high fever

concepts.title: Influenza – Clinical features
concepts.content: runny nose

concepts.title: Influenza – Clinical features
concepts.content: sore throat

concepts.title: Influenza – Clinical features
concepts.content: muscle pains

concepts.title: Influenza – Clinical features
concepts.content: headache

concepts.title: Influenza – Clinical features
concepts.content: coughing

concepts.title: Influenza – Clinical features
concepts.content: feeling tired

concepts.title: Influenza – Management
concepts.content: Management supportive care

concepts.title: Influenza – Management
concepts.content: antiviral medications such as oseltamivir or zanamivir may be used in selected cases

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Definition
concepts.content: Lung cancer is a malignant lung tumor characterized by uncontrolled cell growth in tissues of the lung.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Lung cancer growth can spread beyond the lung by the process of metastasis into nearby tissue or other parts of the body.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Types
concepts.content: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for 85% of lung cancer cases.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Types (NSCLC)
concepts.content: Squamous cell carcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Types (NSCLC)
concepts.content: Adenocarcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Types (NSCLC)
concepts.content: Large cell carcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Types
concepts.content: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) accounts for 15% of lung cancer cases.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Clinical features
concepts.content: A clinical feature of lung cancer is cough.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Clinical features
concepts.content: A clinical feature of lung cancer is haemoptysis.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Clinical features
concepts.content: A clinical feature of lung cancer is dyspnoea.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Clinical features
concepts.content: A clinical feature of lung cancer is chest pain.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Clinical features
concepts.content: A clinical feature of lung cancer is weight loss.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Clinical features
concepts.content: A clinical feature of lung cancer is clubbing.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Clinical features
concepts.content: A clinical feature of lung cancer is recurrent pneumonia.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Management (NSCLC)
concepts.content: Management for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) includes surgery.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Management (NSCLC)
concepts.content: Management for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) includes radiotherapy.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Management (NSCLC)
concepts.content: Management for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) includes chemotherapy.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Management (SCLC)
concepts.content: Management for small cell lung cancer (SCLC) includes chemotherapy.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Management (SCLC)
concepts.content: Management for small cell lung cancer (SCLC) includes radiotherapy.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Prognosis
concepts.content: The prognosis for lung cancer is poor, with an overall 5-year survival rate of around 15%.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Definition
concepts.content: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is a sleep disorder that involves a decrease or complete halt in airflow despite an ongoing effort to breathe.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Obstructive sleep apnoea occurs when the muscles that support the soft tissues in your throat, such as your tongue and soft palate, temporarily relax.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: When these muscles relax, your airway is narrowed or closed, and breathing is momentarily cut off.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of Obstructive sleep apnoea include snoring.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of Obstructive sleep apnoea include witnessed apnoeas.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of Obstructive sleep apnoea include daytime sleepiness.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of Obstructive sleep apnoea include morning headaches.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Management
concepts.content: Management of Obstructive sleep apnoea includes weight loss.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Management
concepts.content: Management of Obstructive sleep apnoea includes CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure).

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Management
concepts.content: Management of Obstructive sleep apnoea includes mandibular advancement devices.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Management
concepts.content: Management of Obstructive sleep apnoea includes surgery.

concepts.title: Silicosis – Definition
concepts.content: Silicosis is a form of occupational lung disease.

concepts.title: Silicosis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Silicosis is caused by inhalation of crystalline silica dust.

concepts.title: Silicosis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Silicosis is marked by inflammation.

concepts.title: Silicosis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Silicosis is marked by scarring.

concepts.title: Silicosis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: The scarring in silicosis is in the form of nodular lesions.

concepts.title: Silicosis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: The nodular lesions in silicosis are found in the upper lobes of the lungs.

concepts.title: Silicosis – Definition
concepts.content: Silicosis is a type of pneumoconiosis.

concepts.title: Silicosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: A feature of silicosis is dyspnoea.

concepts.title: Silicosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: A feature of silicosis is cough.

concepts.title: Silicosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: A feature of silicosis is fatigue.

concepts.title: Silicosis – Investigations
concepts.content: CXR investigation for silicosis shows multiple small nodules in the upper zones.

concepts.title: Silicosis – Investigations
concepts.content: CXR investigation for silicosis shows eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes.

concepts.title: Silicosis – Management
concepts.content: Management for silicosis includes supportive care.

concepts.title: Silicosis – Management
concepts.content: Management for silicosis includes oxygen therapy.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Definition
concepts.content: Pneumonia is an inflammatory condition of the lung affecting primarily the small air sacs known as alveoli.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Clinical features
concepts.content: Symptoms of pneumonia typically include some combination of productive or dry cough, chest pain, fever, and trouble breathing.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Clinical features
concepts.content: The severity of pneumonia is variable.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Pneumonia is usually caused by infection with viruses or bacteria and less commonly by other microorganisms.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Causes of Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) include Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common), Haemophilus influenzae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Legionella pneumophila.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP).

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Causes of Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) include Gram-negative bacilli (e.g., Pseudomonas, Klebsiella) and Staphylococcus aureus.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Management
concepts.content: The CURB-65 score is used to assess the severity of pneumonia.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Management
concepts.content: Components of the CURB-65 score include Confusion, Urea > 7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate > 30/min, Blood pressure < 90 mmHg systolic or < 60 mmHg diastolic, and Age > 65 years.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Management
concepts.content: A CURB-65 score of 0-1 indicates suitability for home treatment.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Management
concepts.content: A CURB-65 score of 2 indicates the need for hospital admission.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Management
concepts.content: A CURB-65 score of 3-5 indicates the need for intensive care assessment.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Management
concepts.content: Recommended antibiotics for Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) include amoxicillin, clarithromycin, and doxycycline.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Management
concepts.content: Recommended antibiotics for Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) include co-amoxiclav, piperacillin/tazobactam, and cephalosporins.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Definition
concepts.content: A pneumothorax is a collection of air in the pleural space.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: This air pushes on the outside of your lung and makes it collapse.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Primary spontaneous pneumothorax
concepts.content: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) occurs in people without underlying lung disease.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Primary spontaneous pneumothorax Epidemiology
concepts.content: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) is more common in tall, thin young men.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax
concepts.content: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP) occurs in people with underlying lung disease.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax Aetiology
concepts.content: Underlying lung diseases associated with Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP) include COPD, asthma, and cystic fibrosis.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Traumatic pneumothorax
concepts.content: Traumatic pneumothorax results from injury to the chest.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Clinical features
concepts.content: A feature of pneumothorax is sudden onset of pleuritic chest pain.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Clinical features
concepts.content: A feature of pneumothorax is shortness of breath.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Clinical features
concepts.content: A feature of pneumothorax is reduced breath sounds on the affected side.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Clinical features
concepts.content: A feature of pneumothorax is hyper-resonant to percussion.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Management (Small PSP)
concepts.content: Management for small Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) (< 2cm) is discharge with follow-up.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Management (Large PSP or symptomatic)
concepts.content: Management for large Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) (> 2cm) or symptomatic PSP is aspiration.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Management (PSP Aspiration Failure)
concepts.content: If aspiration fails for Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP), a chest drain is required.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Management (SSP)
concepts.content: Management for Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP) is a chest drain.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Tension pneumothorax (Emergency)
concepts.content: Tension pneumothorax is a medical emergency.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Tension pneumothorax Pathophysiology
concepts.content: In tension pneumothorax, air enters the pleural space on inspiration but cannot escape on expiration.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Tension pneumothorax Pathophysiology (Consequences)
concepts.content: Tension pneumothorax results in increasing pressure in the chest, mediastinal shift, and cardiovascular collapse.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Tension pneumothorax Clinical features
concepts.content: A feature of tension pneumothorax is tracheal deviation away from the affected side.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Tension pneumothorax Clinical features
concepts.content: A feature of tension pneumothorax is hypotension.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Tension pneumothorax Clinical features
concepts.content: A feature of tension pneumothorax is tachycardia.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Tension pneumothorax Clinical features
concepts.content: A feature of tension pneumothorax is distended neck veins.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Tension pneumothorax Management
concepts.content: Immediate management for tension pneumothorax is needle decompression.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Tension pneumothorax Management
concepts.content: After immediate needle decompression for tension pneumothorax, a chest drain is required.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Definition
concepts.content: Pulmonary hypertension is a type of high blood pressure that affects the arteries in your lungs and the right side of your heart.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Primary pulmonary hypertension is a cause of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: COPD is a cause of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Pulmonary embolism is a cause of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Connective tissue diseases are a cause of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Left heart disease is a cause of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Clinical features
concepts.content: Dyspnoea is a clinical feature of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Clinical features
concepts.content: Fatigue is a clinical feature of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Clinical features
concepts.content: Chest pain is a clinical feature of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Clinical features
concepts.content: Syncope is a clinical feature of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Clinical features
concepts.content: Peripheral oedema is a clinical feature of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Clinical features
concepts.content: Raised JVP is a clinical feature of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Management
concepts.content: Management of pulmonary hypertension includes treating the underlying cause.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Management
concepts.content: Oxygen therapy is a management option for pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Management
concepts.content: Diuretics are a management option for pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Management
concepts.content: Anticoagulation is a management option for pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Management
concepts.content: Vasodilators are a management option for pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Management
concepts.content: Calcium channel blockers are a type of vasodilator used in the management of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Management
concepts.content: Prostanoids are a type of vasodilator used in the management of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Management
concepts.content: Endothelin receptor antagonists are a type of vasodilator used in the management of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Management
concepts.content: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors are a type of vasodilator used in the management of pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Pulmonary hypertension – Management
concepts.content: Lung transplantation is a management option for pulmonary hypertension.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Definition
concepts.content: Respiratory failure is a condition in which the respiratory system fails in one or both of its gas exchange functions: oxygenation and carbon dioxide elimination.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Type 1 Definition
concepts.content: Type 1 respiratory failure is defined as hypoxaemia (PaO2 < 8 kPa) with a normal or low PaCO2.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Type 2 Definition
concepts.content: Type 2 respiratory failure is defined as hypoxaemia (PaO2 < 8 kPa) with hypercapnia (PaCO2 > 6.0 kPa).

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Causes of Type 1
concepts.content: Causes of Type 1 respiratory failure include pulmonary oedema.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Causes of Type 1
concepts.content: Causes of Type 1 respiratory failure include pneumonia.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Causes of Type 1
concepts.content: Causes of Type 1 respiratory failure include ARDS.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Causes of Type 1
concepts.content: Causes of Type 1 respiratory failure include pulmonary embolism.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Causes of Type 1
concepts.content: Causes of Type 1 respiratory failure include pneumothorax.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Causes of Type 2
concepts.content: Causes of Type 2 respiratory failure include COPD.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Causes of Type 2
concepts.content: Causes of Type 2 respiratory failure include severe asthma.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Causes of Type 2
concepts.content: Causes of Type 2 respiratory failure include neuromuscular disease.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Causes of Type 2
concepts.content: Causes of Type 2 respiratory failure include chest wall deformities.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Causes of Type 2
concepts.content: Causes of Type 2 respiratory failure include obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Management
concepts.content: Management of respiratory failure includes oxygen therapy.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Management
concepts.content: Management of respiratory failure includes treating the underlying cause.

concepts.title: Respiratory failure – Management
concepts.content: Management of respiratory failure includes mechanical ventilation (invasive or non-invasive).

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Definition
concepts.content: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem inflammatory disease.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: The cause of Sarcoidosis is unknown.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Sarcoidosis manifests as non-caseating granulomas.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Non-caseating granulomas appear in various organs in Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Lungs are the most commonly affected organ in Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Dry cough is a respiratory feature of Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Dyspnoea is a respiratory feature of Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Chest pain is a respiratory feature of Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Erythema nodosum is an other feature of Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Lupus pernio is an other feature of Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Lymphadenopathy is an other feature of Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Hepatosplenomegaly is an other feature of Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Uveitis is an other feature of Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Hypercalcaemia is an other feature of Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Investigations
concepts.content: CXR shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy in Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Investigations
concepts.content: CXR shows pulmonary infiltrates in Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Investigations
concepts.content: Spirometry shows a restrictive defect in Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Investigations
concepts.content: Serum ACE may be elevated in Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Investigations
concepts.content: Biopsy of affected organ shows non-caseating granulomas in Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Management
concepts.content: Corticosteroids are used in the management of Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Sarcoidosis – Management
concepts.content: Methotrexate is used in the management of Sarcoidosis.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Definition
concepts.content: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease usually caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) bacteria.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Affected Body Parts
concepts.content: Tuberculosis generally affects the lungs, but can also affect other parts of the body.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Latent Tuberculosis
concepts.content: Most Tuberculosis infections do not have symptoms, in which case it is known as latent tuberculosis.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Progression of Latent Infection
concepts.content: About 10% of latent Tuberculosis infections progress to active disease.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Mortality of Untreated Active Disease
concepts.content: If left untreated, active Tuberculosis disease kills about half of those affected.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Primary TB Clinical Features
concepts.content: Primary TB is usually asymptomatic.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Primary TB Clinical Features
concepts.content: Primary TB may cause a fever.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Primary TB Clinical Features
concepts.content: Primary TB may cause pleural effusion.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Post-primary TB Clinical Features
concepts.content: Post-primary TB (reactivation) can present with cough.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Post-primary TB Clinical Features
concepts.content: Post-primary TB (reactivation) can present with haemoptysis.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Post-primary TB Clinical Features
concepts.content: Post-primary TB (reactivation) can present with dyspnoea.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Post-primary TB Clinical Features
concepts.content: Post-primary TB (reactivation) can present with fever.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Post-primary TB Clinical Features
concepts.content: Post-primary TB (reactivation) can present with night sweats.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Post-primary TB Clinical Features
concepts.content: Post-primary TB (reactivation) can present with weight loss.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – CXR Findings
concepts.content: CXR investigation for Tuberculosis may show upper lobe consolidation.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – CXR Findings
concepts.content: CXR investigation for Tuberculosis may show cavitation.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – CXR Findings
concepts.content: CXR investigation for Tuberculosis may show pleural effusion.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Sputum Investigations
concepts.content: Sputum for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) and culture is an investigation for Tuberculosis.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Tuberculin Skin Test
concepts.content: Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) is an investigation for Tuberculosis.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Interferon-gamma Release Assay
concepts.content: Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is an investigation for Tuberculosis.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Management Duration
concepts.content: Management of Tuberculosis involves a combination of antibiotics for at least 6 months.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Management Antibiotics
concepts.content: Antibiotics used in the management of Tuberculosis include isoniazid.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Management Antibiotics
concepts.content: Antibiotics used in the management of Tuberculosis include rifampicin.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Management Antibiotics
concepts.content: Antibiotics used in the management of Tuberculosis include pyrazinamide.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Management Antibiotics
concepts.content: Antibiotics used in the management of Tuberculosis include ethambutol.

concepts.title: Upper respiratory tract infection – Definition
concepts.content: An upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) is an illness caused by an acute infection, which involves the upper respiratory tract including the nose, sinuses, pharynx, or larynx.

concepts.title: Upper respiratory tract infection – Clinical features
concepts.content: This commonly includes tonsillitis, pharyngitis, laryngitis, sinusitis, otitis media, and the common cold.

concepts.title: Upper respiratory tract infection – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Causes mostly viral (rhinovirus, coronavirus, adenovirus, influenza, parainfluenza)

concepts.title: Upper respiratory tract infection – Management
concepts.content: Management supportive care: analgesia, hydration

concepts.title: Upper respiratory tract infection – Management
concepts.content: antibiotics are not usually required

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Definition
concepts.content: Acute bronchitis is a type of chest infection which is usually self-limiting in nature.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Acute bronchitis is a result of inflammation of the trachea and major bronchi and is therefore associated with oedematous large airways and the production of sputum.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Prognosis
concepts.content: The disease course of acute bronchitis usually resolves before 3 weeks.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Prognosis
concepts.content: 25% of patients with acute bronchitis will still have a cough beyond 3 weeks.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Viral infection is the leading cause of acute bronchitis.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Around 80% of acute bronchitis episodes occur in autumn or winter.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients with acute bronchitis typically present with an acute onset of cough.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: The cough in acute bronchitis may or may not be productive.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients with acute bronchitis typically present with an acute onset of sore throat.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients with acute bronchitis typically present with an acute onset of rhinorrhoea.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients with acute bronchitis typically present with an acute onset of wheeze.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: The majority of patients with acute bronchitis will have a normal chest examination.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Some patients with acute bronchitis may present with low-grade fever.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Some patients with acute bronchitis may present with wheeze on examination.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis vs. Pneumonia – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Sputum, wheeze, and breathlessness may be absent in acute bronchitis, whereas at least one tends to be present in pneumonia.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis vs. Pneumonia – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: In acute bronchitis, there are no other focal chest signs (dullness to percussion, crepitations, bronchial breathing) other than wheeze, unlike pneumonia.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis vs. Pneumonia – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Systemic features (malaise, myalgia, and fever) may be absent in acute bronchitis, whereas they tend to be present in pneumonia.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Investigations
concepts.content: Acute bronchitis is typically a clinical diagnosis.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Investigations
concepts.content: CRP testing may be used to guide whether antibiotic therapy is indicated for acute bronchitis if available.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Management for acute bronchitis includes analgesia.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Management for acute bronchitis includes good fluid intake.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
