concepts.content: Consider antibiotic therapy for acute bronchitis if patients are systemically very unwell.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Consider antibiotic therapy for acute bronchitis if patients have pre-existing co-morbidities.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Consider antibiotic therapy for acute bronchitis if patients have a CRP of 20-100mg/L (offer delayed prescription).

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Consider antibiotic therapy for acute bronchitis if patients have a CRP >100mg/L (offer antibiotics immediately).

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: The BNF currently recommends doxycycline first-line for acute bronchitis.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Doxycycline cannot be used in children or pregnant women for acute bronchitis.

concepts.title: Acute bronchitis – Management
concepts.content: Alternatives to doxycycline for acute bronchitis include amoxicillin.

concepts.title: Asthma – Definition
concepts.content: Asthma is a common chronic inflammatory disease of the airways characterised by variable and recurring symptoms, reversible airflow obstruction, and bronchospasm.

concepts.title: Asthma – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Asthma is thought to be caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors.

concepts.title: Asthma – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features worsening dyspnoea, wheeze and cough that is not responding to salbutamol maybe triggered by a respiratory tract infection.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management
concepts.content: NICE updated their asthma guidelines in 2017.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management
concepts.content: The key change in NICE 2017 guidelines is a move away from recommending a salbutamol inhaler as the first step for adults with asthma.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management
concepts.content: NICE 2017 guidelines recommend a short-acting beta2-agonist (SABA) as a reliever therapy for all patients with asthma.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management
concepts.content: NICE 2017 guidelines recommend an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) as the first-line preventer therapy for asthma.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management Step 1
concepts.content: Step 1 of asthma management involves a short-acting beta2-agonist (SABA) as required.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management Step 2
concepts.content: Step 2 of asthma management involves adding an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) at a low dose.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management Step 3
concepts.content: Step 3 of asthma management involves adding a long-acting beta2-agonist (LABA).

concepts.title: Asthma – Management Step 3 (LABA response)
concepts.content: If there is no response to LABA in asthma management, stop it and increase the ICS dose.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management Step 3 (LABA benefit)
concepts.content: If there is benefit from LABA but control is still inadequate, continue LABA and increase the ICS dose.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management Step 4
concepts.content: Step 4 of asthma management involves considering increasing ICS to a high dose, or adding a fourth drug e.g. leukotriene receptor antagonist, theophylline.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management Step 5
concepts.content: Step 5 of asthma management involves continuous use of oral steroids.

concepts.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – Definition
concepts.content: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic and ultimately fatal disease characterized by a progressive decline in lung function.

concepts.title: Pulmonary fibrosis – Definition
concepts.content: The term pulmonary fibrosis means scarring of lung tissue.

concepts.title: Pulmonary fibrosis – Presentation
concepts.content: Pulmonary fibrosis is the cause of worsening dyspnoea (shortness of breath).

concepts.title: Fibrosis – Prognosis
concepts.content: Fibrosis is usually associated with a poor prognosis.

concepts.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – Aetiology
concepts.content: The term idiopathic is used because the cause of pulmonary fibrosis is still unknown.

concepts.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features progressive dyspnoea.

concepts.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features dry cough.

concepts.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features clubbing.

concepts.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features bibasal fine end-inspiratory crackles.

concepts.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – Investigations
concepts.content: CXR: bilateral lower zone reticulo-nodular shadowing.

concepts.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – Investigations
concepts.content: High-resolution CT: peripheral, subpleural reticulation with honeycombing.

concepts.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – Investigations
concepts.content: Spirometry: restrictive defect (FEV1/FVC > 70%, reduced FVC).

concepts.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – Management
concepts.content: Management pirfenidone.

concepts.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – Management
concepts.content: Management nintedanib.

concepts.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – Management
concepts.content: Management pulmonary rehabilitation.

concepts.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – Management
concepts.content: Management oxygen therapy.

concepts.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – Management
concepts.content: Management lung transplantation.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Pathogenesis
concepts.content: Lymphoid hyperplasia or a faecolith leads to obstruction of the appendiceal lumen, followed by gut organisms invading the appendix wall, resulting in oedema, ischaemia and potentially perforation.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Most common acute abdominal condition requiring surgery. Can occur at any age but is most common in young people aged 10-20 years.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Pain migration pattern
concepts.content: Peri-umbilical abdominal pain (visceral stretching of appendix lumen, as appendix is a midgut structure) radiating to the right iliac fossa due to localised parietal peritoneal inflammation. The migration of pain from centre to right iliac fossa has been shown to be one of the strongest indicators of appendicitis.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Pain characteristics on movement
concepts.content: Patients often report the pain being worse on coughing or going over speed bumps. Children typically cannot hop on the right leg due to the pain.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Vomiting pattern
concepts.content: Vomit once or twice but marked and persistent vomiting is unusual.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Diarrhoea presentation
concepts.content: Diarrhoea is rare. However, pelvic appendicitis may cause localised rectal irritation resulting in some loose stools. A pelvic abscess may also cause diarrhoea.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Temperature characteristics
concepts.content: Mild pyrexia is common with temperature usually 37.5-38°C. Higher temperatures are more typical of conditions like mesenteric adenitis.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Anorexia
concepts.content: Anorexia is very common. It is very unusual for patients with appendicitis to be hungry.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Typical symptom triad
concepts.content: Around 50% of patients have the typical symptoms of anorexia, peri-umbilical pain and nausea followed by more localised right lower quadrant pain.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Examination findings in perforation
concepts.content: Generalised peritonitis if perforation has occurred or localised peritonism with rebound and percussion tenderness, guarding and rigidity.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Retrocaecal presentation
concepts.content: Retrocaecal appendicitis may have relatively few signs.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Digital rectal examination findings
concepts.content: Digital rectal examination may reveal boggy sensation if pelvic abscess is present, or even right-sided tenderness with a pelvic appendix.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Rovsing's sign
concepts.content: Palpation in the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right iliac fossa. Now thought to be of limited value.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Psoas sign
concepts.content: Pain on extending hip if retrocaecal appendix is present.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Diagnostic criteria
concepts.content: Typically raised inflammatory markers coupled with compatible history and examination findings should be enough to justify appendicectomy.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Leucocytosis
concepts.content: A neutrophil-predominant leucocytosis is seen in 80-90% of cases.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Urine analysis findings
concepts.content: Useful to exclude pregnancy in women, renal colic and urinary tract infection. In patients with appendicitis, urinalysis may show mild leucocytosis but no nitrites.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Imaging indications
concepts.content: There are no definite rules on the use of imaging and its use is often determined by the patient's gender, age, body habitus and the likelihood of appendicitis.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Ultrasound indications
concepts.content: Ultrasound is useful in females where pelvic organ pathology is suspected. Although it is not always possible to visualise the appendix on ultrasound, the presence of free fluid (always pathological in males) should raise suspicion. It is also useful in children as it avoids radiation exposure and has good diagnostic accuracy in paediatrics.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – CT imaging role
concepts.content: Contrast-enhanced CT imaging is widely used in adult patients with suspected appendicitis, particularly when the diagnosis is unclear. Ultrasound may still be useful first-line for female patients to exclude gynaecological pathology.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Surgical approach
concepts.content: Appendicectomy can be performed via either an open or laparoscopic approach. Laparoscopic appendicectomy is now the treatment of choice.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Prophylactic antibiotics
concepts.content: Administration of prophylactic intravenous antibiotics reduces wound infection rates.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Management of perforation
concepts.content: Patients with perforated appendicitis (typical around 15-20%) require copious abdominal lavage.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Management of appendix mass
concepts.content: Patients without peritonitis who have an appendix mass should receive broad-spectrum antibiotics and consideration given to performing an interval appendicectomy.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Differential diagnosis in older patients
concepts.content: Be wary in the older patients who may have either an underlying caecal malignancy or perforated sigmoid diverticular disease.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Conservative management with antibiotics
concepts.content: Trials have looked at the use of intravenous antibiotics alone in the treatment of appendicitis. The evidence currently suggests that whilst this is successful in the majority of patients, it is associated with a longer hospital stay and up to 20% of patients go on to have an appendicectomy within 12 months.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – Definition
concepts.content: Inflammation of the gallbladder.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – Calculous pathophysiology
concepts.content: Develops secondary to gallstones in 90% of patients (acute calculous cholecystitis).

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – Acalculous cholecystitis
concepts.content: The remaining 10% of cases are referred to as acalculous cholecystitis, typically seen in hospitalised and severely ill patients. Multifactorial pathophysiology includes gallbladder stasis, hypoperfusion and infection. Associated with high morbidity and mortality rates.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – Acalculous in immunosuppressed patients
concepts.content: In immunosuppressed patients it may develop secondary to Cryptosporidium or cytomegalovirus.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – Right upper quadrant pain
concepts.content: Right upper quadrant pain which may radiate to the right shoulder.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – Fever and systemic upset
concepts.content: Fever and signs of systemic upset.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – Murphy's sign
concepts.content: Murphy's sign on examination: inspiratory arrest upon palpation of the right upper quadrant.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – Liver function tests
concepts.content: Liver function tests are typically normal.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – Mirizzi syndrome
concepts.content: Deranged LFTs may indicate Mirizzi syndrome - a gallstone impacted in the distal cystic duct causing extrinsic compression of the common bile duct.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – First-line investigation
concepts.content: Ultrasound is the first-line investigation of choice.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – HIDA scan indication
concepts.content: If the diagnosis remains unclear then cholescintigraphy (HIDA scan) may be used.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – HIDA scan mechanism
concepts.content: Technetium-labelled HIDA (hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid) is injected IV and taken up selectively by hepatocytes and excreted into bile. In acute cholecystitis there is cystic duct obstruction (secondary to oedema associated with inflammation or an obstructing stone) and hence the gallbladder will not be visualised.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – Antibiotic treatment
concepts.content: Intravenous antibiotics.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – Timing of cholecystectomy
concepts.content: NICE now recommend early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, within 1 week of diagnosis. Previously, surgery was delayed for several weeks until the inflammation has subsided.

concepts.title: Cholecystitis – Management in pregnancy
concepts.content: Pregnant women should also proceed to early laparoscopic cholecystectomy - this reduces the chances of maternal-fetal complications.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Common causes
concepts.content: Usually due to alcohol or gallstones.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Autodigestion of pancreatic tissue by the pancreatic enzymes, leading to necrosis.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Epigastric pain characteristics
concepts.content: Severe epigastric pain that may radiate through to the back.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Vomiting
concepts.content: Vomiting is common.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Examination findings
concepts.content: Examination may reveal epigastric tenderness, ileus and low-grade fever.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Cullen's and Grey-Turner's signs
concepts.content: Periumbilical discolouration (Cullen's sign) and flank discolouration (Grey-Turner's sign) is described but rare.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Purtscher retinopathy
concepts.content: Ischaemic (Purtscher) retinopathy may cause temporary or permanent blindness.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Serum amylase findings
concepts.content: Raised in 75% of patients, typically greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal. Levels do not correlate with disease severity. Specificity for pancreatitis is around 90%.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Other causes of raised amylase
concepts.content: Other causes of raised amylase include pancreatic pseudocyst, mesenteric infarct, perforated viscus, acute cholecystitis, and diabetic ketoacidosis.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Serum lipase
concepts.content: More sensitive and specific than serum amylase. It also has a longer half-life than amylase and may be useful for late presentations greater than 24 hours.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Diagnosis without imaging
concepts.content: A diagnosis of acute pancreatitis can be made without imaging if characteristic pain plus amylase/lipase greater than 3 times normal level.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Role of ultrasound
concepts.content: Early ultrasound imaging is important to assess the aetiology as this may affect management, for example patients with gallstones or biliary obstruction.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – CT imaging
concepts.content: Other imaging options include contrast-enhanced CT.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Severity scoring systems
concepts.content: Several scoring systems are used to identify cases of severe pancreatitis which may require intensive care management, including the Ranson score, Glasgow score and APACHE II.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Factors indicating severe disease
concepts.content: Common factors indicating severe pancreatitis include hypoxia (strongly correlated as it reflects early systemic involvement and risk of respiratory failure), age greater than 55 years, hypocalcaemia, hyperglycaemia, neutrophilia, and elevated LDH and AST. Note that the actual amylase level is not of prognostic value.

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – GET SMASHED mnemonic for causes
concepts.content: Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps (other viruses include Coxsackie B), Autoimmune (e.g. polyarteritis nodosa) and Ascaris infection, Scorpion venom, Hypertriglyceridaemia/Hyperchylomicronaemia/Hypercalcaemia/Hypothermia, ERCP, Drugs (azathioprine, mesalazine, didanosine, bendroflumethiazide, furosemide, pentamidine, steroids, sodium valproate).

concepts.title: Acute pancreatitis – Mesalazine vs sulfasalazine risk
concepts.content: Pancreatitis is 7 times more common in patients taking mesalazine than sulfasalazine.

concepts.title: Acute liver failure – Definition
concepts.content: Rapid onset of hepatocellular dysfunction leading to a variety of systemic complications.

concepts.title: Acute liver failure – Paracetamol overdose
concepts.content: Paracetamol overdose is a common cause of acute liver failure.

concepts.title: Acute liver failure – Alcohol as cause
concepts.content: Alcohol is a cause of acute liver failure.

concepts.title: Acute liver failure – Viral hepatitis
concepts.content: Viral hepatitis (usually A or B) can cause acute liver failure.

concepts.title: Acute liver failure – Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
concepts.content: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a cause of acute liver failure.

concepts.title: Acute liver failure – Jaundice
concepts.content: Jaundice is a feature of acute liver failure.

concepts.title: Acute liver failure – Coagulopathy
concepts.content: Coagulopathy with raised prothrombin time occurs in acute liver failure.

concepts.title: Acute liver failure – Hypoalbuminaemia
concepts.content: Hypoalbuminaemia is a feature of acute liver failure.

concepts.title: Acute liver failure – Hepatic encephalopathy
concepts.content: Hepatic encephalopathy occurs in acute liver failure.

concepts.title: Acute liver failure – Hepatorenal syndrome
concepts.content: Renal failure is common in acute liver failure, termed hepatorenal syndrome.

concepts.title: Acute liver failure – Assessment of synthetic function
concepts.content: Liver function tests do not always accurately reflect the synthetic function of the liver. This is best assessed by looking at the prothrombin time and albumin level.

concepts.title: Upper GI bleeding – Common causes
concepts.content: Most commonly due to either oesophageal varices or peptic ulcer disease.

concepts.title: Upper GI bleeding – Haematemesis characteristics
concepts.content: The most common presenting feature. Often bright red but may sometimes be described as coffee ground.

concepts.title: Upper GI bleeding – Melaena definition
concepts.content: The passage of altered blood per rectum, typically black and tarry.

concepts.title: Upper GI bleeding – Raised urea mechanism
concepts.content: A raised urea may be seen due to the protein meal of the blood.

concepts.title: Upper GI bleeding – Glasgow-Blatchford score
concepts.content: The Glasgow-Blatchford score at first assessment helps clinicians decide whether patients can be managed as outpatients or not.

concepts.title: Upper GI bleeding – Rockall score
concepts.content: The Rockall score is used after endoscopy and provides a percentage risk of rebleeding and mortality. Includes age, features of shock, co-morbidities, aetiology of bleeding and endoscopic stigmata of recent haemorrhage.

concepts.title: Upper GI bleeding – Blatchford score zero
concepts.content: Patients with a Blatchford score of 0 may be considered for early discharge.

concepts.title: Oesophageal varices – Volume and features
concepts.content: Usually a large volume of fresh blood. Swallowed blood may cause melaena. Often associated with haemodynamic compromise. May stop spontaneously but re-bleeds are common until appropriately managed.

concepts.title: Oesophagitis – Bleeding characteristics
concepts.content: Small volume of fresh blood, often streaking vomit. Melaena rare. Often ceases spontaneously. Usually history of antecedent GORD-type symptoms.

concepts.title: Mallory-Weiss tear – Definition
concepts.content: A mucosal laceration at the gastro-oesophageal junction, usually caused by forceful retching or vomiting.

concepts.title: Mallory-Weiss tear – Typical presentation
concepts.content: Typically brisk small to moderate volume of bright red blood following a bout of repeated vomiting. Melaena is rare. Usually ceases spontaneously.

concepts.title: Mallory-Weiss tear – Preceding triggers
concepts.content: Preceding triggers may include alcohol excess, gastritis or pregnancy-related vomiting.

concepts.title: Mallory-Weiss tear – Investigation
concepts.content: An upper endoscopy is recommended to confirm the diagnosis, exclude alternative causes of upper gastrointestinal bleeding and provide endoscopic therapy if active bleeding is seen.

concepts.title: Mallory-Weiss tear – Conservative management
concepts.content: Most tears stop bleeding spontaneously and can be managed conservatively with antiemetics and proton pump inhibitors.

concepts.title: Mallory-Weiss tear – Endoscopic intervention
concepts.content: Endoscopic intervention (e.g. clipping, injection therapy or thermal coagulation) is used if ongoing or recurrent bleeding occurs.

concepts.title: Ascites – Definition
concepts.content: Accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity.

concepts.title: Ascites – Prophylactic antibiotics indication
concepts.content: NICE recommend offering prophylactic oral ciprofloxacin or norfloxacin for people with cirrhosis and ascites with an ascitic protein of 15 g/litre or less, until the ascites has resolved.

concepts.title: Ascites – TIPS consideration
concepts.content: A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) may be considered in some patients.

concepts.title: IBS – Diagnostic duration
concepts.content: The diagnosis of IBS should be considered if the patient has had abdominal pain, bloating, or change in bowel habit for at least 6 months.

concepts.title: IBS – Positive diagnostic criteria
concepts.content: A positive diagnosis of IBS should be made if the patient has abdominal pain relieved by defecation or associated with altered bowel frequency or stool form, in addition to 2 of the following 4 symptoms: altered stool passage (straining, urgency, incomplete evacuation), abdominal bloating, symptoms made worse by eating, passage of mucus.

concepts.title: IBS – Associated features
concepts.content: Features such as lethargy, nausea, backache and bladder symptoms may also support the diagnosis.

concepts.title: IBS – Red flag features
concepts.content: Red flag features include rectal bleeding, unexplained/unintentional weight loss, family history of bowel or ovarian cancer, and onset after 60 years of age.

concepts.title: IBS – Primary care investigations
concepts.content: Suggested primary care investigations are full blood count, ESR/CRP, and coeliac disease screen (tissue transglutaminase antibodies).

concepts.title: IBS – First-line for pain
concepts.content: For pain, cramping and bloating: antispasmodic agents (e.g. mebeverine).

concepts.title: IBS – First-line for constipation
concepts.content: For constipation: laxatives but avoid lactulose.

concepts.title: IBS – First-line for diarrhoea
concepts.content: For diarrhoea: loperamide is first-line.

concepts.title: IBS – Linaclotide indication
concepts.content: For patients with constipation who are not responding to conventional laxatives, linaclotide may be considered if optimal or maximum tolerated doses of previous laxatives from different classes have not helped and they have had constipation for at least 12 months.

concepts.title: IBS – Second-line pharmacological treatment
concepts.content: Low-dose tricyclic antidepressants (e.g. amitriptyline 5-10 mg) are used in preference to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

concepts.title: IBS – Psychological interventions
concepts.content: If symptoms do not respond to pharmacological treatments after 12 months and who develop a continuing symptom profile (refractory IBS), consider referring for cognitive behavioural therapy, hypnotherapy or psychological therapy.

concepts.title: Cirrhosis – Common causes in UK
concepts.content: Alcohol, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and viral hepatitis (B and C).

concepts.title: Cirrhosis – Traditional diagnosis method
concepts.content: Traditionally a liver biopsy was used. This procedure is however associated with adverse effects such as bleeding and pain.

concepts.title: Cirrhosis – Transient elastography
concepts.content: Transient elastography (brand name Fibroscan) uses a 50-MHz wave passed into the liver from a small transducer on the end of an ultrasound probe. Measures the stiffness of the liver which is a proxy for fibrosis.

concepts.title: Cirrhosis – NICE screening recommendations
concepts.content: NICE recommend offering transient elastography to people with hepatitis C virus infection, men who drink over 50 units of alcohol per week and women who drink over 35 units of alcohol per week and have done so for several months, and people diagnosed with alcohol-related liver disease.

concepts.title: Cirrhosis – Upper endoscopy for varices
concepts.content: NICE recommend doing an upper endoscopy to check for varices in patients with a new diagnosis of cirrhosis.

concepts.title: Cirrhosis – Hepatocellular cancer surveillance
concepts.content: Liver ultrasound every 6 months (+/- alpha-fetoprotein) to check for hepatocellular cancer.

concepts.title: Malnutrition – NICE definition criteria 1
concepts.content: A Body Mass Index (BMI) of less than 18.5.

concepts.title: Malnutrition – NICE definition criteria 2
concepts.content: Unintentional weight loss greater than 10% within the last 3-6 months.

concepts.title: Malnutrition – NICE definition criteria 3
concepts.content: A BMI of less than 20 and unintentional weight loss greater than 5% within the last 3-6 months.

concepts.title: Malnutrition – Prevalence in elderly
concepts.content: Around 10% of patients aged over 65 years are malnourished, the vast majority of those living independently.

concepts.title: Malnutrition – MUST screening tool
concepts.content: Screening for malnutrition is mostly done using MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screen Tool). It should be done on admission to care/nursing homes and hospital, or if there is a concern. It takes into account BMI, recent weight change and the presence of acute disease.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Definition
concepts.content: An autoimmune condition caused by sensitivity to the protein gluten.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Prevalence
concepts.content: Thought to affect around 1% of the UK population.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Repeated exposure to gluten leads to villous atrophy which in turn causes malabsorption.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – HLA associations
concepts.content: Strongly associated with HLA-DQ2 (95% of patients) and HLA-DQ8 (80%).

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Associated conditions
concepts.content: Conditions associated with coeliac disease include dermatitis herpetiformis (a vesicular, pruritic skin eruption) and autoimmune disorders (type 1 diabetes mellitus and autoimmune hepatitis).

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Screening indications symptoms
concepts.content: NICE suggest screening patients with chronic or intermittent diarrhoea, failure to thrive or faltering growth (in children), persistent or unexplained gastrointestinal symptoms including nausea and vomiting, prolonged fatigue, recurrent abdominal pain cramping or distension, sudden or unexpected weight loss, and unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia or other unspecified anaemia.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Screening indications conditions
concepts.content: NICE suggest screening patients with autoimmune thyroid disease, dermatitis herpetiformis, irritable bowel syndrome, type 1 diabetes, and first-degree relatives with coeliac disease.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Anaemia complications
concepts.content: Anaemia due to iron, folate and vitamin B12 deficiency. Folate deficiency is more common than vitamin B12 deficiency in coeliac disease.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Hyposplenism
concepts.content: Hyposplenism is a complication of coeliac disease.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Bone complications
concepts.content: Osteoporosis and osteomalacia are complications.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Lactose intolerance
concepts.content: Lactose intolerance is a complication.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – T-cell lymphoma
concepts.content: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma of small intestine is a complication.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Reproductive complications
concepts.content: Subfertility and unfavourable pregnancy outcomes are complications.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Malignancy risk
concepts.content: Rare complications include oesophageal cancer and other malignancies.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – First-choice serology
concepts.content: Tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibodies (IgA) are first-choice according to NICE.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Endomyseal antibody
concepts.content: Endomyseal antibody (IgA) is used in diagnosis.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – IgA deficiency testing
concepts.content: Need to look for selective IgA deficiency, which would give a false negative coeliac result. If IgA deficiency, test for IgG endomyseal antibodies, IgG deamidated gliadin peptide (DGP) or IgG transglutaminase antibodies.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Anti-gliadin antibody
concepts.content: Anti-gliadin antibody (IgA or IgG) tests are not recommended by NICE.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Gluten reintroduction before testing
concepts.content: If patients are already taking a gluten-free diet they should be asked, if possible, to reintroduce gluten for at least 6 weeks prior to testing.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Endoscopic biopsy gold standard
concepts.content: Endoscopic intestinal biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis and should be performed in all patients with suspected coeliac disease to confirm or exclude the diagnosis. Traditionally done in the duodenum but jejunal biopsies are also sometimes performed.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Biopsy findings
concepts.content: Findings supportive of coeliac disease include villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes, and lamina propria infiltration with lymphocytes.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Gluten-containing cereals
concepts.content: Gluten-containing cereals include wheat (bread, pasta, pastry), barley (beer), rye, and oats (though some patients with coeliac disease appear able to tolerate oats).

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Whisky safety
concepts.content: Whisky is made using malted barley. Proteins such as gluten are however removed during the distillation process making it safe to drink for patients with coeliac disease.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Gluten-free foods
concepts.content: Notable foods which are gluten-free include rice, potatoes, and corn (maize).

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Monitoring compliance
concepts.content: Tissue transglutaminase antibodies may be checked to check compliance with a gluten-free diet.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Pneumococcal vaccination
concepts.content: Patients with coeliac disease often have a degree of functional hyposplenism. For this reason, all patients with coeliac disease are offered the pneumococcal vaccine. Coeliac UK recommends that everyone with coeliac disease is vaccinated against pneumococcal infection and has a booster every 5 years.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Influenza vaccination
concepts.content: Current guidelines suggest giving the influenza vaccine on an individual basis.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Definition
concepts.content: A Gram positive rod that produces an exotoxin which causes intestinal damage leading to pseudomembranous colitis.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Pathophysiology mechanism
concepts.content: Develops when the normal gut flora are suppressed by broad-spectrum antibiotics. Anaerobic gram-positive, spore-forming, toxin-producing bacillus. Transmission via the faecal-oral route by ingestion of spores. Releases two exotoxins (toxin A and toxin B) that act on intestinal epithelial cells and inflammatory cells resulting in colitis.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Leading antibiotic cause
concepts.content: Second and third-generation cephalosporins are now the leading cause of C. difficile. Clindamycin is historically associated.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Proton pump inhibitors as risk factor
concepts.content: Proton pump inhibitors are a risk factor.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Clinical features
concepts.content: Diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and a raised white blood cell count (WCC) is characteristic. If severe, toxic megacolon may develop.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Severity scale mild
concepts.content: Mild: Normal WCC.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Severity scale moderate
concepts.content: Moderate: Increased WCC (less than 15 x 10^9/L), typically 3-5 loose stools per day.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Severity scale severe
concepts.content: Severe: Increased WCC (greater than 15 x 10^9/L) or an acutely increased creatinine (greater than 50% above baseline) or a temperature greater than 38.5°C or evidence of severe colitis (abdominal or radiological signs).

concepts.title: C. difficile – Severity scale life-threatening
concepts.content: Life-threatening: Hypotension, partial or complete ileus, toxic megacolon, or CT evidence of severe disease.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Diagnosis method
concepts.content: Diagnosis is made by detecting C. difficile toxin (CDT) in the stool. C. difficile antigen positivity only shows exposure to the bacteria, rather than current infection.

concepts.title: C. difficile – First episode first-line treatment
concepts.content: Oral vancomycin for 10 days.

concepts.title: C. difficile – First episode second-line treatment
concepts.content: Oral fidaxomicin.

concepts.title: C. difficile – First episode third-line treatment
concepts.content: Oral vancomycin +/- IV metronidazole.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Recurrence rate
concepts.content: Recurrent infection occurs in around 20% of patients, increasing to 50% after their second episode.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Recurrence within 12 weeks
concepts.content: Within 12 weeks of symptom resolution: oral fidaxomicin.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Recurrence after 12 weeks
concepts.content: After 12 weeks of symptom resolution: oral vancomycin OR fidaxomicin.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Life-threatening treatment
concepts.content: Oral vancomycin AND IV metronidazole.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Bezlotoxumab
concepts.content: A monoclonal antibody which targets C. difficile toxin B. NICE do not currently support its use to prevent recurrences as it is not cost-effective.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Faecal microbiota transplant
concepts.content: May be considered for patients who have had 2 or more previous episodes.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Isolation requirements
concepts.content: Isolation in side room: the patient should remain isolated until there has been no diarrhoea (types 5-7 on the Bristol Stool Chart) for at least 48 hours.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Hand hygiene
concepts.content: Hand washing is essential - alcohol gel does not kill the spores of C. difficile.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Definition
concepts.content: A form of inflammatory bowel disease that commonly affects the terminal ileum and colon but may be seen anywhere from the mouth to anus.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Genetic susceptibility
concepts.content: The cause is unknown but there is a strong genetic susceptibility.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Transmural inflammation
concepts.content: Inflammation occurs in all layers, down to the serosa. This is why patients with Crohn's are prone to strictures, fistulas and adhesions.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Distribution pattern
concepts.content: 80% of patients have small bowel involvement, usually in the ileum, with around 30% of patients having ileitis exclusively. 50% of patients have ileocolitis. 20% of patients have colitis exclusively. 30% of patients have perianal disease.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Age of presentation
concepts.content: Typically presents in late adolescence or early adulthood.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Non-specific symptoms
concepts.content: Presentation may be non-specific symptoms such as weight loss and lethargy.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Diarrhoea in adults
concepts.content: Diarrhoea is the most prominent symptom in adults. Crohn's colitis may cause bloody diarrhoea.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Abdominal pain in children
concepts.content: Abdominal pain is the most prominent symptom in children.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Perianal disease
concepts.content: Perianal disease includes skin tags or ulcers.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Extra-intestinal features prevalence
concepts.content: Extra-intestinal features are more common in patients with colitis or perianal disease.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Laboratory findings
concepts.content: Raised inflammatory markers, increased faecal calprotectin, anaemia, low vitamin B12 and vitamin D.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – CRP correlation
concepts.content: C-reactive protein correlates well with disease activity.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Investigation of choice
concepts.content: Colonoscopy is the investigation of choice. Features suggestive of Crohn's include deep ulcers and skip lesions.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Histological features
concepts.content: Inflammation in all layers from mucosa to serosa, goblet cells, and granulomas.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Small bowel enema findings
concepts.content: High sensitivity and specificity for examination of the terminal ileum. Findings include strictures (Kantor's string sign), proximal bowel dilation, rose thorn ulcers, and fistulae.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Smoking cessation importance
concepts.content: Patients should be strongly advised to stop smoking. Smoking makes Crohn's worse.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – NSAIDs and COCP
concepts.content: Some studies suggest an increased risk of relapse secondary to NSAIDs and the combined oral contraceptive pill but the evidence is patchy.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Inducing remission with glucocorticoids
concepts.content: Glucocorticoids (oral, topical or intravenous) are generally used to induce remission. Budesonide is an alternative in a subgroup of patients.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Enteral feeding
concepts.content: Enteral feeding with an elemental diet may be used in addition to or instead of other measures to induce remission, particularly if there is concern regarding the side-effects of steroids (for example in young children).

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – 5-ASA drugs
concepts.content: 5-ASA drugs (e.g. mesalazine) are used second-line to glucocorticoids but are not as effective.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Azathioprine as add-on
concepts.content: Azathioprine or mercaptopurine may be used as an add-on medication to induce remission but is not used as monotherapy. Methotrexate is an alternative to azathioprine.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Infliximab indication
concepts.content: Infliximab is useful in refractory disease and fistulating Crohn's. Patients typically continue on azathioprine or methotrexate.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Metronidazole for perianal disease
concepts.content: Metronidazole is often used for isolated peri-anal disease.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Maintaining remission first-line
concepts.content: Azathioprine or mercaptopurine is used first-line to maintain remission. TPMT activity should be assessed before starting.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Maintaining remission second-line
concepts.content: Methotrexate is used second-line.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Surgical rate
concepts.content: Around 80% of patients with Crohn's disease will eventually have surgery.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Ileocaecal resection
concepts.content: Stricturing terminal ileal disease is treated with ileocaecal resection.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Perianal fistulae investigation
concepts.content: MRI is the investigation of choice for suspected perianal fistulae - can be used to determine if there is an abscess and if the fistula is simple (low fistula) or complex (high fistula that passes through or above muscle layers).

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Perianal fistulae medical management
concepts.content: Patients with symptomatic perianal fistulae are usually given oral metronidazole. Anti-TNF agents such as infliximab may also be effective in closing and maintaining closure of perianal fistulas.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Draining seton
concepts.content: A draining seton is used for complex fistulae. A seton is a piece of surgical thread that's left in the fistula for several weeks to keep it open.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Perianal abscess management
concepts.content: Requires incision and drainage combined with antibiotic therapy. A draining seton may also be placed if a tract is identified.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Small bowel cancer risk
concepts.content: Small bowel cancer (standard incidence ratio = 40).

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Colorectal cancer risk
concepts.content: Colorectal cancer (standard incidence ratio = 2, i.e. less than the risk associated with ulcerative colitis).

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Osteoporosis complication
concepts.content: Osteoporosis is a complication.

concepts.title: IBD – Arthritis related to activity
concepts.content: Pauciarticular, asymmetric arthritis related to disease activity. Arthritis is the most common extra-intestinal feature in both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

concepts.title: IBD – Erythema nodosum
concepts.content: Erythema nodosum related to disease activity.

concepts.title: IBD – Episcleritis
concepts.content: Episcleritis related to disease activity. More common in Crohn's disease.

concepts.title: IBD – Osteoporosis
concepts.content: Osteoporosis is common to both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

concepts.title: IBD – Arthritis unrelated to activity
concepts.content: Polyarticular, symmetric arthritis unrelated to disease activity.

concepts.title: IBD – Uveitis
concepts.content: Uveitis unrelated to disease activity. More common in ulcerative colitis.

concepts.title: IBD – Pyoderma gangrenosum
concepts.content: Pyoderma gangrenosum unrelated to disease activity.

concepts.title: IBD – Clubbing
concepts.content: Clubbing unrelated to disease activity.

concepts.title: IBD – Primary sclerosing cholangitis
concepts.content: Primary sclerosing cholangitis unrelated to disease activity. Much more common in ulcerative colitis.

concepts.title: Constipation – Definition
concepts.content: Infrequent bowel movements or difficulty passing stools.

concepts.title: Diarrhoea – WHO definition
concepts.content: Greater than 3 loose or watery stools per day.

concepts.title: Diarrhoea – Acute definition
concepts.content: Acute diarrhoea is less than 14 days.

concepts.title: Diarrhoea – Chronic definition
concepts.content: Chronic diarrhoea is greater than 14 days.

concepts.title: Ulcerative colitis – Definition
concepts.content: Inflammatory bowel disease affecting the colon and rectum with continuous inflammation.

concepts.title: Ulcerative colitis – Distribution
concepts.content: Inflammation always starts at the rectum and never spreads beyond the ileocaecal valve.

concepts.title: Ulcerative colitis – Bloody diarrhoea
concepts.content: Bloody diarrhoea is the primary symptom.

concepts.title: Ulcerative colitis – Severity mild
concepts.content: Mild: less than 4 stools per day, only a small amount of blood.

concepts.title: Ulcerative colitis – Severity moderate
concepts.content: Moderate: 4-6 stools per day, varying amounts of blood, no systemic upset.

concepts.title: Ulcerative colitis – Severity severe
concepts.content: Severe: greater than 6 bloody stools per day plus features of systemic upset (pyrexia, tachycardia, anaemia, raised inflammatory markers).

concepts.title: Ulcerative colitis – Proctitis treatment
concepts.content: Topical (rectal) aminosalicylate. For distal colitis rectal mesalazine has been shown to be superior to rectal steroids and oral aminosalicylates.

concepts.title: Ulcerative colitis – Severe colitis treatment
concepts.content: Should be treated in hospital. IV steroids are usually given first-line. IV ciclosporin may be used if steroids are contraindicated.

concepts.title: Ulcerative colitis – 72-hour rule
concepts.content: If after 72 hours there has been no improvement, consider adding IV ciclosporin to IV corticosteroids or consider surgery.

concepts.title: Ulcerative colitis – Maintaining remission
concepts.content: Following a severe relapse or 2 or more exacerbations in the past year: oral azathioprine or oral mercaptopurine.

concepts.title: Ulcerative colitis – Methotrexate not recommended
concepts.content: Methotrexate is not recommended for the management of UC (in contrast to Crohn's disease).

concepts.title: Ulcerative colitis – Surgical indications
concepts.content: Surgery is considered when UC is unresponsive to optimal medical therapy or in the presence of serious complications such as toxic megacolon or perforation.

concepts.title: Ulcerative colitis – Restorative proctocolectomy
concepts.content: The preferred surgical approach involves total colectomy with the formation of an ileal pouch joined to the anal canal (IPAA). A temporary loop ileostomy is created and later reversed.

concepts.title: GORD – Definition
concepts.content: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease characterized by reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus.

concepts.title: GORD – Heartburn
concepts.content: Burning retrosternal sensation.

concepts.title: GORD – Acid regurgitation
concepts.content: Acid regurgitation into the mouth.

concepts.title: GORD – Dysphagia
concepts.content: Dysphagia may occur.

concepts.title: GORD – PPI first-line
concepts.content: Proton pump inhibitors are first-line treatment.

concepts.title: GORD – Barrett's oesophagus
concepts.content: Barrett's oesophagus is a complication where squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium, increasing cancer risk.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease – Definition
concepts.content: Ulceration of the stomach or duodenum.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease – H. pylori association
concepts.content: Helicobacter pylori is the most common cause.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease – NSAIDs as cause
concepts.content: NSAIDs are a major cause of peptic ulcers.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease – Epigastric pain
concepts.content: Epigastric pain is the main symptom.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease – Duodenal ulcer pain timing
concepts.content: Duodenal ulcer pain is typically relieved by eating.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease – Gastric ulcer pain timing
concepts.content: Gastric ulcer pain is typically worsened by eating.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease – Endoscopy diagnosis
concepts.content: Upper GI endoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease – H. pylori eradication
concepts.content: Triple therapy: PPI plus two antibiotics (amoxicillin and clarithromycin or metronidazole) for 7 days.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease – Perforation complication
concepts.content: Perforation is a serious complication.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease – Bleeding complication
concepts.content: Upper GI bleeding is a complication.

concepts.title: Diverticular disease – Definition
concepts.content: Outpouchings of the colonic mucosa through the muscular wall.

concepts.title: Diverticular disease – Common location
concepts.content: Most commonly affects the sigmoid colon.

concepts.title: Diverticular disease – Asymptomatic diverticulosis
concepts.content: Most patients with diverticulosis are asymptomatic.

concepts.title: Diverticulitis – Definition
concepts.content: Inflammation of diverticula.

concepts.title: Diverticulitis – Left lower quadrant pain
concepts.content: Classically causes left lower quadrant pain.

concepts.title: Diverticulitis – Fever
concepts.content: Fever is common in diverticulitis.

concepts.title: Diverticulitis – Change in bowel habit
concepts.content: May cause diarrhoea or constipation.

concepts.title: Diverticulitis – CT diagnosis
concepts.content: CT abdomen is the investigation of choice.

concepts.title: Diverticulitis – Antibiotic treatment
concepts.content: Antibiotics are first-line for uncomplicated diverticulitis.

concepts.title: Diverticulitis – Perforation complication
concepts.content: Perforation may occur requiring surgery.

concepts.title: Diverticulitis – Fistula formation
concepts.content: Fistulae may form, commonly colovesical.

concepts.title: Gallstones – Definition
concepts.content: Stones formed in the gallbladder.

concepts.title: Gallstones – Risk factors 4Fs
concepts.content: Female, Fat, Fertile, Forty.

concepts.title: Gallstones – Asymptomatic
concepts.content: Most gallstones are asymptomatic.

concepts.title: Biliary colic – Definition
concepts.content: Pain caused by gallstone temporarily obstructing the cystic duct.

concepts.title: Biliary colic – Pain characteristics
concepts.content: Severe right upper quadrant pain, often after fatty meals, lasting 30 minutes to several hours.

concepts.title: Biliary colic – Normal LFTs
concepts.content: Liver function tests are typically normal in uncomplicated biliary colic.

concepts.title: Biliary colic – Ultrasound diagnosis
concepts.content: Ultrasound is the first-line investigation.

concepts.title: Biliary colic – Elective cholecystectomy
concepts.content: Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the definitive treatment.

concepts.title: Acute cholangitis – Definition
concepts.content: Infection of the bile duct, usually due to obstruction.

concepts.title: Acute cholangitis – Charcot's triad
concepts.content: Fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice.

concepts.title: Acute cholangitis – Reynolds' pentad
concepts.content: Charcot's triad plus hypotension and confusion.

concepts.title: Acute cholangitis – Raised ALP
concepts.content: Obstructive pattern of LFTs with raised alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin.

concepts.title: Acute cholangitis – ERCP treatment
concepts.content: ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction is the treatment of choice.

concepts.title: Acute cholangitis – Antibiotics
concepts.content: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are essential.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Definition
concepts.content: Inherited disorder of iron metabolism leading to iron overload.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – HFE gene mutation
concepts.content: Caused by mutations in the HFE gene, most commonly C282Y.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Bronze diabetes
concepts.content: Classical triad: bronze skin pigmentation, diabetes mellitus, and cirrhosis.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Arthropathy
concepts.content: Arthropathy affecting small joints of the hands.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Cardiomyopathy
concepts.content: Dilated cardiomyopathy may occur.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Raised ferritin
concepts.content: Raised serum ferritin and transferrin saturation.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Genetic testing
concepts.content: HFE gene testing confirms diagnosis.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Venesection treatment
concepts.content: Regular venesection is the mainstay of treatment.

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Definition
concepts.content: Inflammation of the liver.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Transmission
concepts.content: Faecal-oral transmission.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Self-limiting
concepts.content: Usually self-limiting acute infection.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Transmission
concepts.content: Blood-borne and sexual transmission.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Chronic infection
concepts.content: Can lead to chronic infection, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Surface antigen
concepts.content: HBsAg positive indicates active infection.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Vaccination
concepts.content: Effective vaccination available.

concepts.title: Hepatitis C – Transmission
concepts.content: Primarily blood-borne transmission.

concepts.title: Hepatitis C – Chronic infection rate
concepts.content: Around 80% develop chronic infection.

concepts.title: Hepatitis C – Direct-acting antivirals
concepts.content: Treated with direct-acting antivirals with high cure rates.

concepts.title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Definition
concepts.content: Chronic hepatitis of unknown cause with autoimmune features.

concepts.title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Female predominance
concepts.content: More common in young and middle-aged women.

concepts.title: Autoimmune hepatitis – ANA and SMA
concepts.content: Associated with positive ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibodies.

concepts.title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Steroid treatment
concepts.content: Treated with corticosteroids and azathioprine.

concepts.title: Gastric cancer – Definition
concepts.content: Malignant tumor of the stomach.

concepts.title: Gastric cancer – H. pylori risk
concepts.content: Helicobacter pylori infection is a major risk factor.

concepts.title: Gastric cancer – Weight loss
concepts.content: Weight loss and anorexia are common.

concepts.title: Gastric cancer – Dyspepsia
concepts.content: Persistent dyspepsia in older patients.

concepts.title: Gastric cancer – Vomiting
concepts.content: Vomiting may occur, especially with gastric outlet obstruction.

concepts.title: Gastric cancer – Upper GI bleeding
concepts.content: May present with upper GI bleeding.

concepts.title: Gastric cancer – Endoscopy diagnosis
concepts.content: Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy is diagnostic.

concepts.title: Gastric cancer – Surgical resection
concepts.content: Surgical resection offers the only chance of cure.

concepts.title: Oesophageal cancer – Types
concepts.content: Squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma.

concepts.title: Oesophageal cancer – Adenocarcinoma association
concepts.content: Adenocarcinoma associated with Barrett's oesophagus and GORD.

concepts.title: Oesophageal cancer – Squamous risk factors
concepts.content: Squamous cell carcinoma associated with smoking and alcohol.

concepts.title: Oesophageal cancer – Progressive dysphagia
concepts.content: Progressive dysphagia is the main symptom.

concepts.title: Oesophageal cancer – Weight loss
concepts.content: Weight loss is common.

concepts.title: Oesophageal cancer – Endoscopy and biopsy
concepts.content: Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy is diagnostic.

concepts.title: Oesophageal cancer – Staging CT
concepts.content: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging.

concepts.title: Oesophageal cancer – Oesophagectomy
concepts.content: Oesophagectomy with chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy.

concepts.title: Pancreatic cancer – Definition
concepts.content: Malignant tumor of the pancreas, usually adenocarcinoma.

concepts.title: Pancreatic cancer – Poor prognosis
concepts.content: Very poor prognosis with low 5-year survival.

concepts.title: Pancreatic cancer – Painless jaundice
concepts.content: Painless jaundice if tumor in head of pancreas.

concepts.title: Pancreatic cancer – Epigastric pain
concepts.content: Epigastric pain radiating to back.

concepts.title: Pancreatic cancer – Weight loss
concepts.content: Significant weight loss.

concepts.title: Pancreatic cancer – CA 19-9
concepts.content: CA 19-9 tumor marker may be raised.

concepts.title: Pancreatic cancer – CT diagnosis
concepts.content: CT pancreas is the main diagnostic investigation.

concepts.title: Pancreatic cancer – Whipple procedure
concepts.content: Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) for resectable tumors.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – Definition
concepts.content: Malignant tumor of the colon or rectum.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – Change in bowel habit
concepts.content: Change in bowel habit is a key symptom.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – Rectal bleeding
concepts.content: Rectal bleeding, especially in older patients.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – Iron deficiency anaemia
concepts.content: May present with iron deficiency anaemia.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – Colonoscopy diagnosis
concepts.content: Colonoscopy with biopsy is diagnostic.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – CEA marker
concepts.content: CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) may be raised.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – Surgical resection
concepts.content: Surgical resection is the main treatment.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – Adjuvant chemotherapy
concepts.content: Adjuvant chemotherapy for advanced disease.

concepts.title: Haemorrhoids – Definition
concepts.content: Swollen vascular cushions in the anal canal.

concepts.title: Haemorrhoids – Internal vs external
concepts.content: Internal haemorrhoids above the dentate line, external below.

concepts.title: Haemorrhoids – Painless bleeding
concepts.content: Bright red painless rectal bleeding.

concepts.title: Haemorrhoids – Prolapse
concepts.content: May prolapse through the anus.

concepts.title: Haemorrhoids – Conservative management
concepts.content: Increase dietary fiber and fluid intake.

concepts.title: Haemorrhoids – Rubber band ligation
concepts.content: Rubber band ligation for internal haemorrhoids.

concepts.title: Haemorrhoids – Haemorrhoidectomy
concepts.content: Surgical haemorrhoidectomy for severe cases.

concepts.title: Anal fissure – Definition
concepts.content: Tear in the lining of the anal canal.

concepts.title: Anal fissure – Painful defecation
concepts.content: Severe pain during and after defecation.

concepts.title: Anal fissure – Bright red bleeding
concepts.content: Small amount of bright red blood on toilet paper.

concepts.title: Anal fissure – Posterior midline
concepts.content: Most commonly occurs in the posterior midline.

concepts.title: Anal fissure – GTN ointment
concepts.content: Topical glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) ointment first-line.

concepts.title: Anal fissure – Botulinum toxin
concepts.content: Botulinum toxin injection for chronic fissures.

concepts.title: Anal fissure – Lateral sphincterotomy
concepts.content: Lateral internal sphincterotomy for refractory cases.

concepts.title: Hernias – Definition
concepts.content: Protrusion of an organ or tissue through an abnormal opening.

concepts.title: Inguinal hernia – Most common
concepts.content: Most common type of hernia.

concepts.title: Inguinal hernia – Direct vs indirect
concepts.content: Direct hernias protrude through Hesselbach's triangle. Indirect hernias pass through the internal inguinal ring.

concepts.title: Inguinal hernia – Reducible
concepts.content: Reducible hernias can be pushed back.

concepts.title: Inguinal hernia – Incarceration
concepts.content: Incarcerated hernias cannot be reduced.

concepts.title: Inguinal hernia – Strangulation
concepts.content: Strangulated hernias have compromised blood supply, causing severe pain and requiring emergency surgery.

concepts.title: Inguinal hernia – Surgical repair
concepts.content: Surgical repair with mesh is the definitive treatment.

concepts.title: Femoral hernia – Female predominance
concepts.content: More common in women.

concepts.title: Femoral hernia – High strangulation risk
concepts.content: Higher risk of strangulation than inguinal hernias.

concepts.title: Umbilical hernia – Congenital
concepts.content: Common in infants, often resolve spontaneously.

concepts.title: Incisional hernia – Post-surgical
concepts.content: Occurs at the site of previous surgical incision.

concepts.title: Hiatus hernia – Definition
concepts.content: Herniation of the stomach through the diaphragmatic hiatus.

concepts.title: Hiatus hernia – Sliding type
concepts.content: Sliding hiatus hernia: gastro-oesophageal junction moves above the diaphragm. Most common type.

concepts.title: Hiatus hernia – Rolling type
concepts.content: Rolling (para-oesophageal) hiatus hernia: gastro-oesophageal junction remains below diaphragm but part of stomach herniates.

concepts.title: Hiatus hernia – GORD symptoms
concepts.content: Often asymptomatic or associated with GORD symptoms.

concepts.title: Hiatus hernia – Barium swallow
concepts.content: Diagnosed on barium swallow or endoscopy.

concepts.title: Hiatus hernia – PPI treatment
concepts.content: Managed with PPIs for reflux symptoms.

concepts.title: Hiatus hernia – Surgical repair
concepts.content: Fundoplication surgery for severe cases.

concepts.title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Definition
concepts.content: Acute inflammation of the liver due to alcohol consumption.

concepts.title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Spectrum of disease
concepts.content: Part of the spectrum of alcoholic liver disease, which includes fatty liver, alcoholic hepatitis, and cirrhosis.

concepts.title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Jaundice
concepts.content: Jaundice is a key feature.

concepts.title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Hepatomegaly
concepts.content: Tender hepatomegaly may be present.

concepts.title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Fever
concepts.content: Fever is common.

concepts.title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Raised AST and ALT
concepts.content: AST is typically higher than ALT (AST:ALT ratio greater than 2:1).

concepts.title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Maddrey discriminant function
concepts.content: Maddrey discriminant function is used to assess severity and guide treatment.

concepts.title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Corticosteroids
concepts.content: Corticosteroids (prednisolone) for severe cases with Maddrey score greater than or equal to 32.

concepts.title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Abstinence
concepts.content: Alcohol abstinence is essential.

concepts.title: Alcoholic hepatitis – Nutritional support
concepts.content: Nutritional support is important as patients are often malnourished.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Definition
concepts.content: Reduced haemoglobin concentration below normal range.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Iron deficiency in GI disease
concepts.content: Iron deficiency anaemia is common in GI bleeding, coeliac disease, and inflammatory bowel disease.

concepts.title: Anaemia – B12 deficiency causes
concepts.content: Vitamin B12 deficiency may occur in pernicious anaemia, terminal ileal disease (Crohn's), or post-gastrectomy.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Folate deficiency causes
concepts.content: Folate deficiency may occur in coeliac disease, alcohol excess, or dietary insufficiency.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Chronic disease anaemia
concepts.content: Anaemia of chronic disease is normochromic normocytic and occurs in chronic inflammatory conditions like IBD.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Definition
concepts.content: Psychological disorders characterized by abnormal eating habits.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa
concepts.content: Anorexia nervosa involves restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Bulimia nervosa
concepts.content: Bulimia nervosa involves recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – GI complications
concepts.content: GI complications include delayed gastric emptying, constipation, and refeeding syndrome.

concepts.title: GI perforation – Definition
concepts.content: Full-thickness breach of the gastrointestinal tract wall.

concepts.title: GI perforation – Causes
concepts.content: Causes include peptic ulcer disease, diverticulitis, appendicitis, trauma, and iatrogenic (endoscopy).

concepts.title: GI perforation – Sudden severe pain
concepts.content: Sudden onset severe abdominal pain.

concepts.title: GI perforation – Peritonitis signs
concepts.content: Signs of peritonitis: rigid abdomen, guarding, rebound tenderness.

concepts.title: GI perforation – Free air on imaging
concepts.content: Free air under the diaphragm on erect chest X-ray or CT.

concepts.title: GI perforation – Emergency surgery
concepts.content: Emergency laparotomy or laparoscopy is required.

concepts.title: GI perforation – Broad-spectrum antibiotics
concepts.content: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are essential.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism – Definition
concepts.content: Reduced splenic function.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism – Causes
concepts.content: Causes include coeliac disease, sickle cell disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and splenectomy.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism – Infection risk
concepts.content: Increased risk of infection with encapsulated organisms (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis).

concepts.title: Hyposplenism – Howell-Jolly bodies
concepts.content: Blood film shows Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells, and acanthocytes.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism – Vaccination
concepts.content: Vaccination against pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and meningococcus is essential.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism – Prophylactic antibiotics
concepts.content: Lifelong prophylactic penicillin V (or erythromycin if penicillin allergic) is recommended.

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Definition
concepts.content: Acute viral infection caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Triad
concepts.content: Classic triad: fever, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Splenomegaly
concepts.content: Splenomegaly occurs in about 50% of cases.

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Hepatomegaly
concepts.content: Hepatomegaly and deranged LFTs may occur.

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Atypical lymphocytes
concepts.content: Blood film shows atypical lymphocytes.

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Monospot test
concepts.content: Monospot test (heterophile antibody test) is positive.

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Self-limiting
concepts.content: Usually self-limiting, supportive management.

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Avoid contact sports
concepts.content: Avoid contact sports for 4-6 weeks due to risk of splenic rupture.

concepts.title: Malabsorption – Definition
concepts.content: Impaired absorption of nutrients from the gastrointestinal tract.

concepts.title: Malabsorption – Causes
concepts.content: Causes include coeliac disease, Crohn's disease, chronic pancreatitis, bacterial overgrowth, and lactose intolerance.

concepts.title: Malabsorption – Chronic diarrhoea
concepts.content: Chronic diarrhoea, often steatorrhoea (fatty, pale, bulky stools).

concepts.title: Malabsorption – Weight loss
concepts.content: Weight loss despite adequate dietary intake.

concepts.title: Malabsorption – Nutritional deficiencies
concepts.content: Nutritional deficiencies: iron, B12, folate, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).

concepts.title: Malabsorption – Faecal elastase
concepts.content: Faecal elastase is low in pancreatic insufficiency.

concepts.title: Malabsorption – Treat underlying cause
concepts.content: Treatment involves addressing the underlying cause and nutritional supplementation.

concepts.title: Mesenteric adenitis – Definition
concepts.content: Inflammation of mesenteric lymph nodes, usually viral.

concepts.title: Mesenteric adenitis – Mimics appendicitis
concepts.content: Often mimics appendicitis with right lower quadrant pain.

concepts.title: Mesenteric adenitis – Preceding URTI
concepts.content: Often follows an upper respiratory tract infection.

concepts.title: Mesenteric adenitis – More common in children
concepts.content: More common in children and adolescents.

concepts.title: Mesenteric adenitis – Self-limiting
concepts.content: Usually self-limiting, supportive management.

concepts.title: Necrotising enterocolitis – Definition
concepts.content: Life-threatening condition affecting premature neonates, characterized by intestinal necrosis.

concepts.title: Necrotising enterocolitis – Premature infants
concepts.content: Primarily affects premature infants, especially those with very low birth weight.

concepts.title: Necrotising enterocolitis – Feeding intolerance
concepts.content: Feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, and bloody stools.

concepts.title: Necrotising enterocolitis – Pneumatosis intestinalis
concepts.content: Abdominal X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in bowel wall).

concepts.title: Necrotising enterocolitis – NBM and antibiotics
concepts.content: Nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids, and broad-spectrum antibiotics.

concepts.title: Necrotising enterocolitis – Surgery for perforation
concepts.content: Surgery if perforation or clinical deterioration.

concepts.title: Perianal abscess – Definition
concepts.content: Collection of pus in the perianal region.

concepts.title: Perianal abscess – Severe pain
concepts.content: Severe perianal pain, swelling, and fever.

concepts.title: Perianal abscess – Incision and drainage
concepts.content: Treatment is incision and drainage.

concepts.title: Perianal fistula – Definition
concepts.content: Abnormal tract between the anal canal and perianal skin.

concepts.title: Perianal fistula – Discharge
concepts.content: Persistent discharge from perianal opening.

concepts.title: Perianal fistula – Associated with Crohn's
concepts.content: Commonly associated with Crohn's disease.

concepts.title: Perianal fistula – MRI investigation
concepts.content: MRI is the investigation of choice.

concepts.title: Perianal fistula – Seton placement
concepts.content: Treatment may involve seton placement or fistulotomy.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Definition
concepts.content: Inflammation of the peritoneum.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Primary vs secondary
concepts.content: Primary (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) occurs without obvious source. Secondary peritonitis follows perforation or surgery.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – SBP in cirrhosis
concepts.content: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis occurs in patients with cirrhosis and ascites.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Abdominal pain and rigidity
concepts.content: Severe abdominal pain with guarding and rigidity.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Ascitic tap
concepts.content: Ascitic tap shows neutrophil count greater than 250 cells/mm³ in SBP.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Antibiotics for SBP
concepts.content: IV cefotaxime for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Surgery for secondary
concepts.content: Secondary peritonitis requires emergency surgery to address the source.

concepts.title: B12/folate deficiency – Definition
concepts.content: Deficiency of vitamin B12 and/or folate leading to macrocytic anaemia.

concepts.title: B12 deficiency – Causes
concepts.content: Causes include pernicious anaemia, terminal ileal disease or resection, dietary insufficiency (vegans), and gastrectomy.

concepts.title: Folate deficiency – Causes
concepts.content: Causes include dietary insufficiency, coeliac disease, alcohol excess, and certain medications (methotrexate).

concepts.title: B12 deficiency – Neurological features
concepts.content: B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord: peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, and cognitive impairment.

concepts.title: B12/folate deficiency – Macrocytic anaemia
concepts.content: Macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils on blood film.

concepts.title: B12 deficiency – Intrinsic factor antibodies
concepts.content: Intrinsic factor antibodies are specific for pernicious anaemia.

concepts.title: B12 deficiency – IM replacement
concepts.content: Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin replacement.

concepts.title: Folate deficiency – Oral supplementation
concepts.content: Oral folic acid supplementation.

concepts.title: B12/folate – Replace B12 first
concepts.content: Always replace B12 before folate to avoid precipitating subacute combined degeneration.

concepts.title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Type I antibodies
concepts.content: Type I: Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) and/or anti-smooth muscle antibodies (SMA). Affects both adults and children.

concepts.title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Type II antibodies
concepts.content: Type II: Anti-liver/kidney microsomal type 1 antibodies (LKM1). Affects children only.

concepts.title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Type III antibodies
concepts.content: Type III: Soluble liver-kidney antigen. Affects adults in middle-age.

concepts.title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Amenorrhoea
concepts.content: Amenorrhoea is a common feature.

concepts.title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Raised IgG
concepts.content: Raised IgG levels are characteristic.

concepts.title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Piecemeal necrosis
concepts.content: Liver biopsy shows inflammation extending beyond limiting plate (piecemeal necrosis) and bridging necrosis.

concepts.title: Autoimmune hepatitis – Liver transplant
concepts.content: Liver transplantation may be required in advanced disease.

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – Metaplasia definition
concepts.content: Metaplasia of the lower oesophageal mucosa, with squamous epithelium replaced by columnar epithelium.

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – Cancer risk
concepts.content: 50-100 fold increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – Short vs long
concepts.content: Short Barrett's is less than 3cm, long Barrett's is greater than 3cm. Length correlates with chances of identifying metaplasia.

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – Prevalence
concepts.content: Overall prevalence may be around 1 in 20, identified in up to 12% of those undergoing endoscopy for reflux.

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – Histology
concepts.content: Columnar epithelium may resemble cardiac region of stomach or small intestine (with goblet cells, brush border).

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – GORD strongest risk
concepts.content: GORD is the single strongest risk factor.

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – Male predominance
concepts.content: Male gender (7:1 ratio).

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – Smoking risk
concepts.content: Smoking is a risk factor.

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – Central obesity risk
concepts.content: Central obesity is a risk factor.

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – Alcohol not independent
concepts.content: Alcohol does not seem to be an independent risk factor.

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – Asymptomatic
concepts.content: Barrett's oesophagus itself is asymptomatic but patients often have coexistent GORD symptoms.

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – High-dose PPI
concepts.content: High-dose proton pump inhibitor is commonly used.

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – PPI evidence limited
concepts.content: Evidence that PPIs reduce progression to dysplasia or induce regression is limited.

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – Surveillance interval
concepts.content: For patients with metaplasia (but not dysplasia), endoscopy is recommended every 3-5 years.

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – Radiofrequency ablation
concepts.content: Radiofrequency ablation is preferred first-line treatment for dysplasia, particularly low-grade.

concepts.title: Barrett's oesophagus – Endoscopic mucosal resection
concepts.content: Endoscopic mucosal resection is an option for dysplasia.

concepts.title: Bile-acid malabsorption – Definition
concepts.content: Cause of chronic diarrhoea due to excessive bile acid production (primary) or reduced absorption (secondary).

concepts.title: Bile-acid malabsorption – Steatorrhoea
concepts.content: Can lead to steatorrhoea and fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) malabsorption.

concepts.title: Bile-acid malabsorption – Ileal disease
concepts.content: Secondary causes often seen in patients with ileal disease such as Crohn's.

concepts.title: Bile-acid malabsorption – Cholecystectomy
concepts.content: Cholecystectomy is a secondary cause.

concepts.title: Bile-acid malabsorption – SIBO
concepts.content: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth is a secondary cause.

concepts.title: Bile-acid malabsorption – SeHCAT test
concepts.content: SeHCAT is the test of choice. Nuclear medicine test using selenium homocholic acid taurine with scans 7 days apart.

concepts.title: Bile-acid malabsorption – Cholestyramine treatment
concepts.content: Bile acid sequestrants (e.g., cholestyramine) are used for management.

concepts.title: Bilirubin – Heme breakdown
concepts.content: Bilirubin is a by-product of heme breakdown from red blood cells and hepatic heme-containing proteins.

concepts.title: Bilirubin – Unconjugated form
concepts.content: Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin in blood and taken up by hepatocytes for conjugation.

concepts.title: Bilirubin – Conjugation
concepts.content: Conjugation in hepatocytes renders bilirubin water-soluble for excretion into bile.

concepts.title: Bilirubin – Intestinal processing
concepts.content: Bacterial proteases produce urobilinogen from bilirubin; majority forms urobilin and stercobilin excreted in faeces.

concepts.title: Bilirubin – Enterohepatic circulation
concepts.content: Around 10% of bilirubin re-enters portal circulation and is excreted via kidneys in urine.

concepts.title: Bilirubin – Haemolysis cause
concepts.content: Raised unconjugated bilirubin occurs with haemolysis (pre-hepatic source).

concepts.title: Gilbert's syndrome – Mild deficiency
concepts.content: Mild glucuronyl transferase deficiency results in Gilbert's syndrome.

concepts.title: Crigler-Najjar – Moderate to severe
concepts.content: Moderate to severe glucuronyl transferase deficiency seen in Crigler-Najjar syndrome types I and II.

concepts.title: Neonatal jaundice – Transient deficiency
concepts.content: Transient glucuronyl transferase deficiency contributes to physiological neonatal jaundice.

concepts.title: Conjugated bilirubin – Dubin-Johnson
concepts.content: Raised conjugated bilirubin from defective excretion in Dubin-Johnson syndrome.

concepts.title: Jaundice – Threshold
concepts.content: Jaundice appears when bilirubin exceeds 35 μmol/L.

concepts.title: Cholestasis – Physical causes
concepts.content: Physical causes of cholestasis include gallstones, pancreatic and cholangiocarcinoma.

concepts.title: Cholestasis – Functional causes
