concepts.content: Functional causes include drug-induced, pregnancy-related, and post-operative cholestasis.

concepts.title: Budd-Chiari – Definition
concepts.content: Hepatic vein thrombosis, usually in context of haematological disease or procoagulant condition.

concepts.title: Budd-Chiari – Polycythaemia cause
concepts.content: Polycythaemia rubra vera is a cause.

concepts.title: Budd-Chiari – Thrombophilia causes
concepts.content: Thrombophilia: activated protein C resistance, antithrombin III deficiency, protein C and S deficiencies.

concepts.title: Budd-Chiari – Pregnancy cause
concepts.content: Pregnancy is a cause.

concepts.title: Budd-Chiari – OCP cause
concepts.content: Combined oral contraceptive pill accounts for around 20% of cases.

concepts.title: Budd-Chiari – Classic triad
concepts.content: Classic triad: sudden onset severe abdominal pain, ascites with abdominal distension, and tender hepatomegaly.

concepts.title: Budd-Chiari – Doppler ultrasound
concepts.content: Ultrasound with Doppler flow studies is very sensitive and should be the initial radiological investigation.

concepts.title: Carcinoid syndrome – Liver metastases
concepts.content: Usually occurs when metastases are present in liver and release serotonin into systemic circulation.

concepts.title: Carcinoid syndrome – Lung carcinoid
concepts.content: May occur with lung carcinoid as mediators are not cleared by the liver.

concepts.title: Carcinoid syndrome – Flushing
concepts.content: Flushing is often the earliest symptom.

concepts.title: Carcinoid syndrome – Diarrhoea feature
concepts.content: Diarrhoea is a key feature.

concepts.title: Carcinoid syndrome – Bronchospasm
concepts.content: Bronchospasm may occur.

concepts.title: Carcinoid syndrome – Hypotension
concepts.content: Hypotension is a feature.

concepts.title: Carcinoid syndrome – Heart valve disease
concepts.content: Right heart valvular stenosis (left heart can be affected in bronchial carcinoid).

concepts.title: Carcinoid syndrome – ACTH secretion
concepts.content: Other molecules such as ACTH and GHRH may be secreted, causing Cushing's syndrome.

concepts.title: Carcinoid syndrome – Pellagra
concepts.content: Pellagra (niacin deficiency) can develop as dietary tryptophan is diverted to serotonin.

concepts.title: Carcinoid syndrome – 5-HIAA test
concepts.content: Urinary 5-HIAA is used for investigation.

concepts.title: Carcinoid syndrome – Chromogranin A
concepts.content: Plasma chromogranin A is used for investigation.

concepts.title: Carcinoid syndrome – Octreotide
concepts.content: Somatostatin analogues (e.g., octreotide) are used for management.

concepts.title: Carcinoid syndrome – Cyproheptadine
concepts.content: Cyproheptadine may help with diarrhoea.

concepts.title: Cholestyramine – Mechanism
concepts.content: Bile acid sequestrant that decreases bile acid reabsorption in small intestine, upregulating cholesterol conversion to bile acid.

concepts.title: Cholestyramine – LDL reduction
concepts.content: Main effect is to reduce LDL cholesterol.

concepts.title: Cholestyramine – Crohn's use
concepts.content: Occasionally used in Crohn's disease for diarrhoea following bowel resection.

concepts.title: Cholestyramine – Abdominal cramps
concepts.content: Adverse effects include abdominal cramps and constipation.

concepts.title: Cholestyramine – Fat-soluble vitamins
concepts.content: Decreases absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

concepts.title: Cholestyramine – Gallstones
concepts.content: May cause cholesterol gallstones.

concepts.title: Cholestyramine – Triglycerides
concepts.content: May raise level of triglycerides.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Gram positive rod
concepts.content: Gram positive rod producing exotoxin causing intestinal damage and pseudomembranous colitis.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Broad-spectrum antibiotics
concepts.content: Develops when normal gut flora suppressed by broad-spectrum antibiotics.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Cephalosporins leading cause
concepts.content: Second and third-generation cephalosporins are now the leading cause.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Clindamycin historical
concepts.content: Clindamycin is historically associated but aetiology has evolved.

concepts.title: C. difficile – PPI risk factor
concepts.content: Proton pump inhibitors are a risk factor.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Spore-forming
concepts.content: Anaerobic gram-positive, spore-forming, toxin-producing bacillus.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Faecal-oral transmission
concepts.content: Transmission via faecal-oral route by ingestion of spores.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Toxins A and B
concepts.content: Releases two exotoxins (toxin A and toxin B) that act on intestinal epithelial cells and inflammatory cells.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Raised WCC
concepts.content: A raised white blood cell count is characteristic.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Toxic megacolon
concepts.content: If severe, toxic megacolon may develop.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Severity mild
concepts.content: Mild: Normal WCC, typically 3-5 loose stools per day.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Severity moderate
concepts.content: Moderate: Raised WCC (less than 15 × 10⁹/L).

concepts.title: C. difficile – Severity severe
concepts.content: Severe: WCC greater than 15 × 10⁹/L, or acutely raised creatinine (greater than 50% above baseline), or temperature greater than 38.5°C, or evidence of severe colitis.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Life-threatening features
concepts.content: Life-threatening: Hypotension, partial or complete ileus, toxic megacolon, or CT evidence of severe disease.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Toxin detection
concepts.content: Diagnosis made by detecting C. difficile toxin (CDT) in stool.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Antigen vs toxin
concepts.content: C. difficile antigen positivity shows exposure to bacteria, not current infection.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Review antibiotics
concepts.content: Current antibiotic therapy should be reviewed and stopped if possible.

concepts.title: C. difficile – First-line vancomycin
concepts.content: First-line therapy is oral vancomycin for 10 days.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Second-line fidaxomicin
concepts.content: Second-line therapy is oral fidaxomicin.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Third-line combination
concepts.content: Third-line therapy is oral vancomycin +/- IV metronidazole.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Recurrence rate
concepts.content: Recurrent infection occurs in around 20% of patients, increasing to 50% after second episode.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Recurrence within 12 weeks
concepts.content: Within 12 weeks of symptom resolution: oral fidaxomicin.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Recurrence after 12 weeks
concepts.content: After 12 weeks of symptom resolution: oral vancomycin OR fidaxomicin.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Life-threatening treatment
concepts.content: Life-threatening infection: oral vancomycin AND IV metronidazole. Surgery may be considered.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Bezlotoxumab
concepts.content: Bezlotoxumab is a monoclonal antibody targeting C. difficile toxin B. NICE do not support its use as not cost-effective.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Faecal transplant
concepts.content: Faecal microbiota transplant may be considered for patients with 2 or more previous episodes.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Isolation requirement
concepts.content: Isolation in side room until no diarrhoea (Bristol Stool Chart types 5-7) for at least 48 hours.

concepts.title: C. difficile – PPE requirements
concepts.content: All staff should wear disposable gloves and apron during contact with patients.

concepts.title: C. difficile – Hand washing essential
concepts.content: Hand washing is essential - alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Prevalence
concepts.content: Affects around 1% of the UK population.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – HLA-DQ2
concepts.content: Strongly associated with HLA-DQ2 (95% of patients).

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – HLA-DQ8
concepts.content: Associated with HLA-DQ8 (80% of patients).

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Dermatitis herpetiformis
concepts.content: Associated with dermatitis herpetiformis (vesicular, pruritic skin eruption).

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Chronic diarrhoea screening
concepts.content: Chronic or intermittent diarrhoea is an indication for screening.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Failure to thrive
concepts.content: Failure to thrive or faltering growth in children is an indication for screening.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Persistent GI symptoms
concepts.content: Persistent or unexplained gastrointestinal symptoms including nausea and vomiting are indications for screening.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Prolonged fatigue
concepts.content: Prolonged fatigue ('tired all the time') is an indication for screening.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Recurrent abdominal pain
concepts.content: Recurrent abdominal pain, cramping or distension are indications for screening.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Unexpected weight loss
concepts.content: Sudden or unexpected weight loss is an indication for screening.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Iron deficiency
concepts.content: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia is an indication for screening.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Folate more common
concepts.content: Folate deficiency is more common than vitamin B12 deficiency in coeliac disease.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Hyposplenism complication
concepts.content: Hyposplenism is a complication.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Osteoporosis
concepts.content: Osteoporosis and osteomalacia are complications.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Lactose intolerance
concepts.content: Lactose intolerance is a complication.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – T-cell lymphoma
concepts.content: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma of small intestine is a complication.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Subfertility
concepts.content: Subfertility and unfavourable pregnancy outcomes are complications.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Oesophageal cancer risk
concepts.content: Rare: oesophageal cancer and other malignancies.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – TTG first-choice
concepts.content: Tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibodies (IgA) are first-choice according to NICE.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Endomyseal antibody
concepts.content: Endomyseal antibody (IgA) is used for diagnosis.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – IgA deficiency test
concepts.content: Need to test for selective IgA deficiency, which would give false negative coeliac result.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – IgG if IgA deficient
concepts.content: If IgA deficiency, test for IgG endomyseal antibodies, IgG deamidated gliadin peptide (DGP), or IgG transglutaminase antibodies.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Anti-gliadin not recommended
concepts.content: Anti-gliadin antibody (IgA or IgG) tests are not recommended by NICE.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Reintroduce gluten
concepts.content: If patients taking gluten-free diet, reintroduce gluten for at least 6 weeks prior to testing.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Biopsy gold standard
concepts.content: Endoscopic intestinal biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Duodenal biopsy
concepts.content: Traditionally done in duodenum but jejunal biopsies also sometimes performed.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Villous atrophy finding
concepts.content: Villous atrophy is a finding supportive of coeliac disease.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Crypt hyperplasia finding
concepts.content: Crypt hyperplasia is a finding supportive of coeliac disease.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Intraepithelial lymphocytes
concepts.content: Increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes is a finding supportive of coeliac disease.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Lamina propria infiltration
concepts.content: Lamina propria infiltration with lymphocytes is a finding supportive of coeliac disease.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Gluten-free diet
concepts.content: Management involves a gluten-free diet.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Wheat contains gluten
concepts.content: Wheat (bread, pasta, pastry) contains gluten.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Barley contains gluten
concepts.content: Barley (beer) contains gluten.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Whisky safe
concepts.content: Whisky is made using malted barley but proteins removed during distillation, making it safe.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Rye contains gluten
concepts.content: Rye contains gluten.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Oats tolerance
concepts.content: Some patients appear able to tolerate oats.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Rice gluten-free
concepts.content: Rice is gluten-free.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Potatoes gluten-free
concepts.content: Potatoes are gluten-free.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Corn gluten-free
concepts.content: Corn (maize) is gluten-free.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – TTG compliance check
concepts.content: Tissue transglutaminase antibodies may be checked to monitor compliance with gluten-free diet.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Pneumococcal vaccine
concepts.content: All patients offered pneumococcal vaccine due to functional hyposplenism.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Vaccine booster 5 years
concepts.content: Coeliac UK recommends pneumococcal booster every 5 years.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Influenza individual basis
concepts.content: Influenza vaccine given on individual basis.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – Sporadic 95%
concepts.content: Sporadic colon cancer accounts for 95% of cases.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – HNPCC 5%
concepts.content: Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal carcinoma (HNPCC) accounts for 5% of cases.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – FAP less than 1%
concepts.content: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) accounts for less than 1% of cases.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – APC gene loss
concepts.content: More than half of sporadic colon cancers show allelic loss of the APC gene.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – K-ras activation
concepts.content: Activation of K-ras oncogene contributes to invasive carcinoma.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – p53 deletion
concepts.content: Deletion of p53 and DCC tumour suppressor genes leads to invasive carcinoma.

concepts.title: HNPCC – Lynch syndrome
concepts.content: HNPCC (Lynch syndrome) is an autosomal dominant condition and most common form of inherited colon cancer.

concepts.title: HNPCC – Cancer development rate
concepts.content: Around 70-80% of HNPCC patients develop cancers.

concepts.title: HNPCC – Proximal colon
concepts.content: Cancers often affect proximal colon and are poorly differentiated and highly aggressive.

concepts.title: HNPCC – MSH2 mutation
concepts.content: MSH2 mutation accounts for 60% of HNPCC cases.

concepts.title: HNPCC – MLH1 mutation
concepts.content: MLH1 mutation accounts for 30% of HNPCC cases.

concepts.title: HNPCC – DNA mismatch repair
concepts.content: Mutations affect genes involved in DNA mismatch repair leading to microsatellite instability.

concepts.title: HNPCC – Endometrial cancer risk
concepts.content: Patients at higher risk of endometrial cancer, next most common association after colon cancer.

concepts.title: HNPCC – Amsterdam criteria
concepts.content: Amsterdam criteria: at least 3 family members with colon cancer, spanning at least 2 generations, at least one case before age 50.

concepts.title: FAP – Autosomal dominant
concepts.content: FAP is a rare autosomal dominant condition.

concepts.title: FAP – Hundreds of polyps
concepts.content: Leads to formation of hundreds of polyps by age 30-40 years.

concepts.title: FAP – Inevitable carcinoma
concepts.content: Patients inevitably develop carcinoma.

concepts.title: FAP – APC gene chromosome 5
concepts.content: Due to mutation in adenomatous polyposis coli gene (APC) on chromosome 5.

concepts.title: FAP – Genetic testing
concepts.content: Genetic testing done by analysing DNA from white blood cells.

concepts.title: FAP – Proctocolectomy in twenties
concepts.content: Patients generally have total proctocolectomy with IPAA formation in their twenties.

concepts.title: FAP – Duodenal tumour risk
concepts.content: Patients at risk from duodenal tumours.

concepts.title: Gardner's syndrome – FAP variant
concepts.content: Gardner's syndrome is a variant of FAP with osteomas of skull and mandible, retinal pigmentation, thyroid carcinoma, and epidermoid cysts.

concepts.title: Constipation – Definition detailed
concepts.content: Defecation that is unsatisfactory because of infrequent stools (less than 3 times weekly), difficult stool passage (with straining or discomfort), or seemingly incomplete defecation.

concepts.title: Constipation – Infrequent hard stools
concepts.content: The passage of infrequent hard stools is the main feature.

concepts.title: Constipation – Exclude secondary causes
concepts.content: Investigate and exclude any secondary causes, consider red flag symptoms.

concepts.title: Constipation – Exclude impaction
concepts.content: Exclude any faecal impaction.

concepts.title: Constipation – Increase fibre
concepts.content: Advice on increasing dietary fibre.

concepts.title: Constipation – Adequate fluids
concepts.content: Ensure adequate fluid intake.

concepts.title: Constipation – Activity levels
concepts.content: Ensure adequate activity levels.

concepts.title: Constipation – Bulk-forming first-line
concepts.content: First-line laxative is bulk-forming laxative such as ispaghula.

concepts.title: Constipation – Osmotic second-line
concepts.content: Second-line is osmotic laxative such as macrogol.

concepts.title: Constipation – Overflow diarrhoea
concepts.content: Overflow diarrhoea is a complication.

concepts.title: Constipation – Urinary retention
concepts.content: Acute urinary retention is a complication.

concepts.title: Constipation – Haemorrhoids complication
concepts.content: Haemorrhoids are a complication.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Genetic susceptibility
concepts.content: Strong genetic susceptibility but cause unknown.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Transmural inflammation
concepts.content: Inflammation occurs in all layers down to serosa.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Strictures fistulas adhesions
concepts.content: Transmural inflammation causes patients to be prone to strictures, fistulas, and adhesions.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – 80% small bowel
concepts.content: 80% of patients have small bowel involvement, usually ileum, with 30% having ileitis exclusively.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – 50% ileocolitis
concepts.content: 50% of patients have ileocolitis.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – 20% colitis only
concepts.content: 20% of patients have colitis exclusively.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – 30% perianal
concepts.content: 30% of patients have perianal disease.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Late adolescence onset
concepts.content: Typically presents in late adolescence or early adulthood.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Non-specific symptoms
concepts.content: May present with non-specific symptoms such as weight loss and lethargy.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Diarrhoea prominent adult
concepts.content: Diarrhoea is the most prominent symptom in adults.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Bloody diarrhoea colitis
concepts.content: Crohn's colitis may cause bloody diarrhoea.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Pain prominent child
concepts.content: Abdominal pain is the most prominent symptom in children.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Skin tags ulcers
concepts.content: Perianal disease includes skin tags or ulcers.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Extra-intestinal colitis
concepts.content: Extra-intestinal features more common in patients with colitis or perianal disease.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Raised inflammatory markers
concepts.content: Raised inflammatory markers are found.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Faecal calprotectin
concepts.content: Increased faecal calprotectin is found.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Low B12 and D
concepts.content: Low vitamin B12 and vitamin D are found.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – CRP correlates
concepts.content: C-reactive protein correlates well with disease activity.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Colonoscopy choice
concepts.content: Colonoscopy is the investigation of choice.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Deep ulcers skip lesions
concepts.content: Features suggestive of Crohn's include deep ulcers and skip lesions.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Transmural histology
concepts.content: Histology shows inflammation in all layers from mucosa to serosa.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Goblet cells
concepts.content: Goblet cells are seen on histology.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Granulomas
concepts.content: Granulomas are seen on histology.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Kantor's string sign
concepts.content: Small bowel enema shows strictures with 'Kantor's string sign'.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Proximal bowel dilation
concepts.content: Proximal bowel dilation is seen on small bowel enema.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Rose thorn ulcers
concepts.content: 'Rose thorn' ulcers are seen on small bowel enema.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Fistulae on imaging
concepts.content: Fistulae may be seen on small bowel enema.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Stop smoking priority
concepts.content: Patients should be strongly advised to stop smoking.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – NSAIDs may relapse
concepts.content: Some studies suggest increased risk of relapse secondary to NSAIDs but evidence is patchy.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – OCP may relapse
concepts.content: Some studies suggest increased risk of relapse secondary to combined oral contraceptive pill but evidence is patchy.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Glucocorticoids induce remission
concepts.content: Glucocorticoids (oral, topical, or intravenous) are generally used to induce remission.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Budesonide alternative
concepts.content: Budesonide is an alternative in a subgroup of patients.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Enteral feeding
concepts.content: Enteral feeding with elemental diet may be used to induce remission, particularly if concern about steroid side-effects.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – 5-ASA second-line
concepts.content: 5-ASA drugs (e.g., mesalazine) are used second-line to glucocorticoids but not as effective.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Azathioprine add-on
concepts.content: Azathioprine or mercaptopurine may be used as add-on to induce remission but not as monotherapy.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Methotrexate alternative
concepts.content: Methotrexate is an alternative to azathioprine.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Infliximab refractory
concepts.content: Infliximab is useful in refractory disease and fistulating Crohn's.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Metronidazole perianal
concepts.content: Metronidazole is often used for isolated perianal disease.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Azathioprine maintain remission
concepts.content: Azathioprine or mercaptopurine is used first-line to maintain remission.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – TPMT before azathioprine
concepts.content: TPMT activity should be assessed before starting azathioprine or mercaptopurine.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Methotrexate second-line maintain
concepts.content: Methotrexate is used second-line to maintain remission.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – 80% surgery
concepts.content: Around 80% of patients will eventually have surgery.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Ileocaecal resection
concepts.content: Stricturing terminal ileal disease treated with ileocaecal resection.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Segmental resections
concepts.content: Segmental small bowel resections may be performed.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Stricturoplasty
concepts.content: Stricturoplasty is a surgical option.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – MRI for fistulae
concepts.content: MRI is investigation of choice for suspected perianal fistulae.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Simple vs complex fistula
concepts.content: MRI determines if fistula is simple (low) or complex (high, passing through or above muscle layers).

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Metronidazole symptomatic fistula
concepts.content: Patients with symptomatic perianal fistulae usually given oral metronidazole.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Anti-TNF for fistulae
concepts.content: Anti-TNF agents such as infliximab may be effective in closing and maintaining closure of perianal fistulas.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Draining seton
concepts.content: A draining seton is used for complex fistulae.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Seton definition
concepts.content: A seton is surgical thread left in fistula for several weeks to keep it open and prevent abscess formation.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Perianal abscess drainage
concepts.content: Perianal abscess requires incision and drainage combined with antibiotic therapy.

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Small bowel cancer risk
concepts.content: Small bowel cancer risk (standard incidence ratio = 40).

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Colorectal cancer risk lower
concepts.content: Colorectal cancer risk (standard incidence ratio = 2, less than ulcerative colitis).

concepts.title: Crohn's disease – Osteoporosis risk
concepts.content: Patients at risk of osteoporosis.

concepts.title: Gastroenteritis – Diarrhoea cause
concepts.content: May be accompanied by abdominal pain or nausea/vomiting.

concepts.title: Antibiotic therapy – Diarrhoea
concepts.content: More common with broad-spectrum antibiotics.

concepts.title: Constipation – Overflow diarrhoea
concepts.content: History of alternating diarrhoea and constipation. May lead to faecal incontinence in elderly.

concepts.title: IBS – Diarrhoea predominant
concepts.content: Most consistent features are abdominal pain, bloating, and change in bowel habit. May have diarrhoea-predominant or constipation-predominant IBS.

concepts.title: IBS – Associated symptoms
concepts.content: Features such as lethargy, nausea, backache, and bladder symptoms may be present.

concepts.title: UC – Bloody diarrhoea
concepts.content: Bloody diarrhoea may be seen. Crampy abdominal pain and weight loss common. Faecal urgency and tenesmus.

concepts.title: Crohn's – Bloody less common
concepts.content: Crampy abdominal pains and diarrhoea. Bloody diarrhoea less common than in UC. Malabsorption, mouth ulcers, perianal disease, intestinal obstruction.

concepts.title: Colorectal cancer – Site-dependent symptoms
concepts.content: Symptoms depend on site: diarrhoea, rectal bleeding, anaemia, constitutional symptoms (weight loss, anorexia).

concepts.title: Coeliac – Children presentation
concepts.content: In children may present with failure to thrive, diarrhoea, and abdominal distension.

concepts.title: Coeliac – Adults presentation
concepts.content: In adults lethargy, anaemia, diarrhoea, and weight loss. Other autoimmune conditions may coexist.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Diarrhoea
concepts.content: Thyrotoxicosis is associated with diarrhoea.

concepts.title: Laxative abuse – Diarrhoea
concepts.content: Laxative abuse causes diarrhoea.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Diarrhoea
concepts.content: Appendicitis may be associated with diarrhoea.

concepts.title: Radiation enteritis – Diarrhoea
concepts.content: Radiation enteritis causes diarrhoea.

concepts.title: Diarrhoea – Stool culture indications
concepts.content: NICE recommend stool sample if: systemically unwell, blood/pus in stool, immunocompromised, recent antibiotics/PPI/hospital, recent foreign travel, or public health indication.

concepts.title: Diarrhoea – Bloods not routine
concepts.content: Bloods not routinely indicated.

concepts.title: Diarrhoea – Severe complications
concepts.content: If severe, may show acute kidney injury, hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia.

concepts.title: Diverticulosis – Extremely common
concepts.content: Extremely common disorder with multiple outpouchings of bowel wall, most commonly sigmoid colon.

concepts.title: Diverticulosis – Terminology
concepts.content: Diverticular disease is for symptomatic patients; diverticulosis is more accurate for diverticula being present.

concepts.title: Diverticulosis – Increasing age
concepts.content: Increasing age is a risk factor.

concepts.title: Diverticulosis – Low-fibre diet
concepts.content: Low-fibre diet is a risk factor.

concepts.title: Painful diverticular disease – Features
concepts.content: Altered bowel habit, colicky left sided abdominal pain. High fibre diet recommended.

concepts.title: Diverticulitis – Classical presentation
concepts.content: Left iliac fossa pain and tenderness, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, features of infection.

concepts.title: Diverticulitis – Mild oral antibiotics
concepts.content: Mild attacks treated with oral antibiotics.

concepts.title: Diverticulitis – Severe hospital management
concepts.content: Significant episodes: nil by mouth, IV fluids, IV antibiotics (cephalosporin + metronidazole).

concepts.title: Diverticulitis – Abscess complication
concepts.content: Abscess formation is a complication.

concepts.title: Diverticulitis – Peritonitis complication
concepts.content: Peritonitis is a complication.

concepts.title: Diverticulitis – Obstruction complication
concepts.content: Obstruction is a complication.

concepts.title: Drug-induced liver – Hepatocellular pattern
concepts.content: Paracetamol, sodium valproate, phenytoin, MAOIs, halothane, anti-TB drugs, statins, alcohol, amiodarone, methyldopa, nitrofurantoin cause hepatocellular pattern.

concepts.title: Drug-induced liver – Cholestatic pattern
concepts.content: OCP, flucloxacillin, co-amoxiclav, erythromycin, anabolic steroids, phenothiazines, sulphonylureas, fibrates cause cholestasis.

concepts.title: Drug-induced liver – Cirrhosis causes
concepts.content: Methotrexate, methyldopa, amiodarone cause liver cirrhosis.

concepts.title: Dyspepsia – Urgent dysphagia
concepts.content: All patients with dysphagia need urgent referral.

concepts.title: Dyspepsia – Urgent upper abdominal mass
concepts.content: All patients with upper abdominal mass consistent with stomach cancer need urgent referral.

concepts.title: Dyspepsia – Urgent age 55 weight loss
concepts.content: Patients aged ≥55 with weight loss AND upper abdominal pain/reflux/dyspepsia need urgent referral.

concepts.title: Dyspepsia – Non-urgent haematemesis
concepts.content: Patients with haematemesis need non-urgent referral.

concepts.title: Dyspepsia – Non-urgent age 55 resistant
concepts.content: Patients aged ≥55 with treatment-resistant dyspepsia need non-urgent referral.

concepts.title: Dyspepsia – Review medications
concepts.content: Review medications for possible causes of dyspepsia.

concepts.title: Dyspepsia – Lifestyle advice
concepts.content: Provide lifestyle advice.

concepts.title: Dyspepsia – PPI trial or test and treat
concepts.content: Trial of full-dose PPI for one month OR test and treat approach for H. pylori.

concepts.title: H. pylori – C13 urea breath test
concepts.content: Initial diagnosis: carbon-13 urea breath test or stool antigen test.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Test of cure not needed
concepts.content: No need to check eradication if symptoms resolved following test and treat.

concepts.title: H. pylori – C13 for repeat testing
concepts.content: If repeat testing required, carbon-13 urea breath test should be used.

concepts.title: Oesophageal cancer – Dysphagia features
concepts.content: Dysphagia with weight loss, anorexia, or vomiting during eating. Past history of Barrett's, GORD, smoking, alcohol.

concepts.title: Oesophagitis – Dysphagia
concepts.content: History of heartburn. Odynophagia but no weight loss and systemically well.

concepts.title: Oesophageal candidiasis – Dysphagia
concepts.content: History of HIV or risk factors such as steroid inhaler use.

concepts.title: Achalasia – Dysphagia both liquids solids
concepts.content: Dysphagia of both liquids and solids from the start. Heartburn. Regurgitation of food leading to cough, aspiration pneumonia.

concepts.title: Pharyngeal pouch – Dysphagia
concepts.content: More common in older men. Posteromedial herniation between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus. Dysphagia, regurgitation, aspiration, chronic cough. Halitosis.

concepts.title: Systemic sclerosis – Dysphagia
concepts.content: CREST syndrome features. Oesophageal dysmotility with decreased LES pressure (contrast to achalasia with increased LES pressure).

concepts.title: Myasthenia gravis – Dysphagia
concepts.content: Extraocular muscle weakness or ptosis. Dysphagia with liquids as well as solids.

concepts.title: Globus hystericus – Dysphagia
concepts.content: History of anxiety. Symptoms intermittent and relieved by swallowing.

concepts.title: GORD – Endoscopy age over 55
concepts.content: Age greater than 55 years is an indication for upper GI endoscopy.

concepts.title: GORD – Endoscopy symptoms over 4 weeks
concepts.content: Symptoms greater than 4 weeks or persistent despite treatment is an indication.

concepts.title: GORD – Endoscopy dysphagia
concepts.content: Dysphagia is an indication for upper GI endoscopy.

concepts.title: GORD – Endoscopy relapsing symptoms
concepts.content: Relapsing symptoms is an indication.

concepts.title: GORD – Endoscopy weight loss
concepts.content: Weight loss is an indication.

concepts.title: GORD – 24-hr pH monitoring
concepts.content: If endoscopy negative, consider 24-hour oesophageal pH monitoring (gold standard test for diagnosis).

concepts.title: GORD – Endoscopy-proven full-dose PPI
concepts.content: Endoscopically proven oesophagitis: full dose PPI for 1-2 months.

concepts.title: GORD – Response low-dose PPI
concepts.content: If response to full-dose PPI, then low dose treatment as required.

concepts.title: GORD – No response double-dose
concepts.content: If no response, then double-dose PPI for 1 month.

concepts.title: GORD – Endoscopy-negative full-dose
concepts.content: Endoscopically negative reflux disease: full dose PPI for 1 month.

concepts.title: GORD – Negative response low-dose
concepts.content: If response, offer low dose treatment, possibly as-required with limited repeat prescriptions.

concepts.title: GORD – No response H2RA prokinetic
concepts.content: If no response, then H2RA or prokinetic for one month.

concepts.title: GORD – Oesophagitis complication
concepts.content: Oesophagitis is a complication.

concepts.title: GORD – Ulcers complication
concepts.content: Ulcers are a complication.

concepts.title: GORD – Anaemia complication
concepts.content: Anaemia is a complication.

concepts.title: GORD – Benign strictures
concepts.content: Benign strictures are a complication.

concepts.title: GORD – Oesophageal carcinoma complication
concepts.content: Oesophageal carcinoma is a complication.

concepts.title: Gilbert's syndrome – Autosomal recessive
concepts.content: Autosomal recessive condition of defective bilirubin conjugation due to deficiency of UDP glucuronosyltransferase.

concepts.title: Gilbert's syndrome – Prevalence
concepts.content: Prevalence approximately 1-2% in general population.

concepts.title: Gilbert's syndrome – Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
concepts.content: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (not in urine).

concepts.title: Gilbert's syndrome – Jaundice triggers
concepts.content: Jaundice may only be seen during intercurrent illness, exercise, or fasting.

concepts.title: Gilbert's syndrome – Genetic testing
concepts.content: Genetic testing for UGT1A1 promoter region polymorphism provides definitive diagnosis.

concepts.title: Gilbert's syndrome – No treatment
concepts.content: No treatment required.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Chromosome 6
concepts.content: Caused by inheritance of mutations in HFE gene on both copies of chromosome 6.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – 1 in 10 carriers
concepts.content: 1 in 10 people of European descent carry a mutation in genes affecting iron metabolism, mainly HFE.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – 1 in 200 prevalence
concepts.content: Prevalence in people of European descent is 1 in 200, more common than cystic fibrosis.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Early symptoms
concepts.content: Early symptoms include fatigue, erectile dysfunction, and arthralgia (often of hands).

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Hepatomegaly
concepts.content: Liver: stigmata of chronic liver disease, hepatomegaly, cirrhosis, hepatocellular deposition.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Cardiac failure
concepts.content: Cardiac failure secondary to dilated cardiomyopathy.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Hypogonadism
concepts.content: Hypogonadism secondary to cirrhosis and pituitary dysfunction (hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism).

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Hand arthritis
concepts.content: Arthritis especially of the hands.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Reversible cardiomyopathy
concepts.content: Cardiomyopathy and skin pigmentation are reversible with treatment.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Irreversible cirrhosis
concepts.content: Liver cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, and arthropathy are irreversible.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Transferrin saturation screening
concepts.content: Transferrin saturation is considered the most useful marker for screening general population.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Ferritin not early
concepts.content: Ferritin should be measured but not usually abnormal in early stages of iron accumulation.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Family genetic testing
concepts.content: Testing family members: genetic testing for HFE mutation.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Transferrin over 55% men
concepts.content: Transferrin saturation greater than 55% in men or greater than 50% in women.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Raised ferritin iron
concepts.content: Raised ferritin (e.g., greater than 500 μg/L) and iron.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Low TIBC
concepts.content: Low TIBC.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – C282Y H63D mutations
concepts.content: Molecular genetic testing for C282Y and H63D mutations.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – MRI quantify iron
concepts.content: MRI is generally used to quantify liver and/or cardiac iron.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Biopsy if cirrhosis
concepts.content: Liver biopsy now generally only used if suspected hepatic cirrhosis.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Venesection first-line
concepts.content: Venesection is first-line treatment.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Monitor transferrin ferritin
concepts.content: Monitoring: transferrin saturation below 50% and serum ferritin below 50 μg/L.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Desferrioxamine second-line
concepts.content: Desferrioxamine may be used second-line.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Desferrioxamine mechanism
concepts.content: Parenteral iron-chelating agent that binds free iron (Fe³⁺) to form ferrioxamine, excreted by kidneys.

concepts.title: Haemochromatosis – Desferrioxamine indications
concepts.content: Reserved for patients who cannot tolerate venesection (anaemia, poor venous access) or secondary haemochromatosis.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Gram-negative
concepts.content: Gram-negative bacteria associated with gastrointestinal problems, principally peptic ulcer disease.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Chemotaxis flagella
concepts.content: Chemotaxis away from low pH areas, using flagella to burrow into mucous lining.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Urease alkalinization
concepts.content: Secretes urease converting urea to NH3, alkalinizing acidic environment for increased survival.

concepts.title: H. pylori – CagA toxin
concepts.content: Releases bacterial cytotoxins (e.g., CagA toxin) disrupting gastric mucosa.

concepts.title: H. pylori – 95% duodenal ulcers
concepts.content: 95% of duodenal ulcers associated with H. pylori.

concepts.title: H. pylori – 75% gastric ulcers
concepts.content: 75% of gastric ulcers associated with H. pylori.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Gastric cancer association
concepts.content: Associated with gastric cancer.

concepts.title: H. pylori – MALT lymphoma
concepts.content: B cell lymphoma of MALT tissue (eradication causes regression in 80% of patients).

concepts.title: H. pylori – Atrophic gastritis
concepts.content: Associated with atrophic gastritis.

concepts.title: H. pylori – No role in GORD
concepts.content: No role in GORD for eradication of H. pylori.

concepts.title: H. pylori – First-line eradication
concepts.content: First-line: PPI + amoxicillin + (clarithromycin OR metronidazole) for 7 days.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Ongoing symptoms treatment
concepts.content: If ongoing symptoms: PPI + amoxicillin + (clarithromycin OR metronidazole, whichever not used first line).

concepts.title: H. pylori – Penicillin-allergic
concepts.content: If penicillin-allergic: PPI + metronidazole + clarithromycin.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Urea breath test procedure
concepts.content: Patients consume drink with carbon-13 enriched urea. Urea broken down by H. pylori urease. After 30 mins exhale into glass tube. Mass spectrometry calculates 13C CO2.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Urea breath timing
concepts.content: Should not be performed within 4 weeks of antibacterial or 2 weeks of antisecretory drug.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Urea breath sensitivity
concepts.content: Sensitivity 95-98%, specificity 97-98%.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Urea breath eradication check
concepts.content: May be used to check for H. pylori eradication.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Rapid urease test
concepts.content: Biopsy sample mixed with urea and pH indicator. Colour change if H. pylori urease activity. Sensitivity 90-95%, specificity 95-98%.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Serum antibody limitation
concepts.content: Remains positive after eradication. Sensitivity 85%, specificity 80%.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Culture sensitivity
concepts.content: Culture provides antibiotic sensitivity information. Sensitivity 70%, specificity 100%.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Gastric biopsy histology
concepts.content: Histological evaluation alone, no culture. Sensitivity 95-99%, specificity 95-99%.

concepts.title: H. pylori – Stool antigen test
concepts.content: Sensitivity 90%, specificity 95%.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Ammonia glutamine
concepts.content: Aetiology thought to include excess absorption of ammonia and glutamine from bacterial breakdown of proteins in gut.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Acute and chronic
concepts.content: May be seen with acute liver failure or chronic disease.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Minimal covert
concepts.content: Many patients with cirrhosis develop subtle symptoms like mild cognitive impairment before features become recognisable ('minimal' or 'covert' hepatic encephalopathy).

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – TIPSS precipitates
concepts.content: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting (TIPSS) may precipitate encephalopathy.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Confusion altered GCS
concepts.content: Confusion, altered GCS.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Asterixis
concepts.content: Asterixis: 'liver flap', arrhythmic negative myoclonus with frequency of 3-5 Hz.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Constructional apraxia
concepts.content: Constructional apraxia: inability to draw 5-pointed star.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Triphasic waves
concepts.content: Triphasic slow waves on EEG.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Raised ammonia
concepts.content: Raised ammonia level (supportive but not diagnostic - levels do not correlate well with severity).

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Grade I
concepts.content: Grade I: Irritability.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Grade II
concepts.content: Grade II: Confusion, inappropriate behaviour.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Grade III
concepts.content: Grade III: Incoherent, restless.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Grade IV
concepts.content: Grade IV: Coma.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – SBP precipitant
concepts.content: Infection (e.g., spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) is a precipitating factor.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – GI bleed precipitant
concepts.content: GI bleed is a precipitating factor.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Post-TIPSS
concepts.content: Post transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt is a precipitating factor.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Constipation precipitant
concepts.content: Constipation is a precipitating factor.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Drugs precipitant
concepts.content: Drugs (sedatives, diuretics) are precipitating factors.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Hypokalaemia precipitant
concepts.content: Hypokalaemia is a precipitating factor.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Renal failure precipitant
concepts.content: Renal failure is a precipitating factor.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Lactulose first-line
concepts.content: NICE recommend lactulose first-line, with addition of rifaximin for secondary prophylaxis.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Lactulose mechanism
concepts.content: Lactulose promotes excretion of ammonia and increases metabolism of ammonia by gut bacteria.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Rifaximin mechanism
concepts.content: Antibiotics such as rifaximin modulate gut flora resulting in decreased ammonia production.

concepts.title: Hepatic encephalopathy – Embolisation transplant
concepts.content: Other options include embolisation of portosystemic shunts and liver transplantation in selected patients.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – HBsAg first marker
concepts.content: Surface antigen (HBsAg) is first marker to appear and causes production of anti-HBs.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – HBsAg acute 1-6 months
concepts.content: HBsAg normally implies acute disease (present for 1-6 months).

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – HBsAg chronic over 6 months
concepts.content: If HBsAg present for greater than 6 months, implies chronic disease (infective).

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Anti-HBs immunity
concepts.content: Anti-HBs implies immunity (either exposure or immunisation). Negative in chronic disease.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Anti-HBc previous infection
concepts.content: Anti-HBc implies previous (or current) infection. IgM anti-HBc appears during acute or recent infection for about 6 months. IgG anti-HBc persists.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – HBeAg viral replication
concepts.content: HBeAg is protein from breakdown of hepatitis B core antigen. Presence indicates active viral replication and high infectivity.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Immunisation serology
concepts.content: Previous immunisation: anti-HBs positive, all others negative.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Previous not carrier
concepts.content: Previous hepatitis B (greater than 6 months ago), not carrier: anti-HBc positive, HBsAg negative.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Carrier serology
concepts.content: Previous hepatitis B, now carrier: anti-HBc positive, HBsAg positive.

concepts.title: Viral hepatitis – Nausea vomiting anorexia
concepts.content: Common symptoms include nausea and vomiting, anorexia.

concepts.title: Viral hepatitis – Myalgia
concepts.content: Myalgia is a common symptom.

concepts.title: Viral hepatitis – Lethargy
concepts.content: Lethargy is a common symptom.

concepts.title: Viral hepatitis – RUQ pain
concepts.content: Right upper quadrant pain is a common symptom.

concepts.title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Definition
concepts.content: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is a rare autosomal dominant condition caused by a defect in porphobilinogen deaminase, an enzyme involved in the biosynthesis of haem.

concepts.title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: In Acute intermittent porphyria, the defect in porphobilinogen deaminase results in the toxic accumulation of delta aminolaevulinic acid and porphobilinogen.

concepts.title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Clinical presentation overview
concepts.content: Acute intermittent porphyria characteristically presents with abdominal and neuropsychiatric symptoms in 20-40 year olds and is more common in females (5:1).

concepts.title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Incidence
concepts.content: The incidence of Acute intermittent porphyria is 0.01 cases per 100,000 person-years.

concepts.title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Peak incidence age
concepts.content: The peak incidence of Acute intermittent porphyria is between 30-40 years of age.

concepts.title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Sex ratio
concepts.content: Acute intermittent porphyria is more common in females with a sex ratio of 5:1.

concepts.title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Abdominal clinical features
concepts.content: Abdominal clinical features of Acute intermittent porphyria include abdominal pain and vomiting.

concepts.title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Neurological clinical features
concepts.content: Neurological clinical features of Acute intermittent porphyria include motor neuropathy.

concepts.title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Psychiatric clinical features
concepts.content: Psychiatric clinical features of Acute intermittent porphyria include depression.

concepts.title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Autonomic clinical features
concepts.content: Common autonomic clinical features of Acute intermittent porphyria include hypertension and tachycardia.

concepts.title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Urine investigation finding
concepts.content: Classically, in Acute intermittent porphyria, urine turns deep red on standing.

concepts.title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Urinary porphobilinogen levels
concepts.content: Investigations for Acute intermittent porphyria show raised urinary porphobilinogen, which is elevated between attacks and to a greater extent during acute attacks.

concepts.title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Porphobilinogen deaminase assay
concepts.content: Diagnosis of Acute intermittent porphyria involves an assay of red cells for porphobilinogen deaminase.

concepts.title: Acute intermittent porphyria – Serum aminolaevulinic acid and porphobilinogen levels
concepts.content: Investigations for Acute intermittent porphyria show raised serum levels of delta aminolaevulinic acid and porphobilinogen.

concepts.content: Barbiturates are drugs which may precipitate an acute attack of Acute intermittent porphyria.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Definition
concepts.content: Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is a malignant disease of the bone marrow arising from myeloid cell lines. Immature cells are released into the blood, impairing normal haematopoiesis and causing anaemia, bleeding, and infections. It is the most common acute leukaemia in adults, with a median age of diagnosis of 65 years. AML is associated with environmental factors, pre-existing haematological disorders, and genetic abnormalities. Diagnosis requires bone marrow biopsy, and treatment involves chemotherapy or haematopoietic cell transplantation. Remission is common, but relapse frequently occurs.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Epidemiology
concepts.content: The incidence of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is 5.00 cases per 100,000 person-years. The peak incidence occurs in individuals aged 70 years and older. AML is more common in males, with a sex ratio of 1.3:1.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Aetiology – Genetic Factors
concepts.content: Genetic factors contributing to Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) include chromosomal abnormalities such as translocations t(8;21), t(15;17), and t(9;11). Gene mutations impacting cell proliferation and apoptosis, including FLT3, NPM1, and CEBPA, are also significant.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Aetiology – Environmental Exposures
concepts.content: Environmental exposures linked to Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) include previous chemotherapy or radiation therapy, leading to therapy-related AML. Exposure to benzene and other petrochemicals, as well as ionising radiation, also increases risk.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Aetiology – Haematological Disorders
concepts.content: Antecedent haematological disorders such as myelodysplastic syndromes and myeloproliferative neoplasms predispose individuals to secondary Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML).

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Aetiology – Genetic Syndromes
concepts.content: Genetic syndromes associated with an increased risk of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) include Down syndrome, Fanconi anaemia, and Li-Fraumeni syndrome.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Pathophysiology – Genetic Mutations
concepts.content: Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) arises from genetic mutations in haematopoietic progenitor cells, which disrupt normal cell proliferation and differentiation.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Pathophysiology – Blast Accumulation and Bone Marrow Failure
concepts.content: The disruption in cell proliferation and differentiation in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) results in the accumulation of immature cells, known as blasts, in the bone marrow and peripheral blood, ultimately leading to bone marrow failure.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Pathophysiology – First Hit Mutation
concepts.content: The pathogenesis of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) often begins with a 'first hit' mutation, such as in FLT3, NPM1, or DNMT3A genes, which confers a proliferative advantage to a haematopoietic stem cell, leading to its clonal expansion.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Pathophysiology – Second Hit Mutation
concepts.content: A 'second hit' mutation subsequently occurs in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), affecting a gene involved in haematopoietic differentiation, such as RUNX1 or CEBPA. This mutation further promotes proliferation and blocks differentiation, leading to the accumulation of immature blasts.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Pathophysiology – Blast Accumulation and Cytopenias
concepts.content: The accumulation of immature blasts in the bone marrow in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) suppresses normal haematopoiesis, leading to clinical manifestations such as anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Pathophysiology – Organ Invasion
concepts.content: As Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) progresses, leukaemic blasts can invade other organs, including the spleen, liver, and central nervous system, resulting in organomegaly and other clinical manifestations.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Classification – WHO Groups
concepts.content: The World Health Organization (WHO) classification system for Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) includes six main groups: AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities, AML with myelodysplasia-related features, Therapy-related AML and MDS, AML not otherwise specified, Myeloid sarcoma, and Myeloid proliferations related to Down syndrome.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Classification – FAB Subtypes
concepts.content: The French-American-British (FAB) classification system for Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) includes eight subtypes: M0 (acute myeloblastic leukaemia without maturation), M1 (acute myeloblastic leukaemia with minimal granulocyte maturation), M2 (acute myeloblastic leukaemia with granulocyte maturation), M3 (acute promyelocytic leukaemia), M4 (acute myelomonocytic leukaemia), M5 (acute monocytic leukaemia), M6 (acute erythroid leukaemia), and M7 (acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia).

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – General Presentation
concepts.content: Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) typically presents with sudden onset and rapid progression of symptoms. Some patients may be asymptomatic, but common features include pancytopenia, leading to anaemia, bleeding, and infections.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Fever
concepts.content: Fever in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is mostly due to infections, but can also occur solely due to the leukaemia itself. Immature leucocytes predispose patients to frequent infections.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Anaemia Symptoms
concepts.content: Anaemia in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) can manifest as shortness of breath, palpitations, weakness, fatigue, dizziness, and pallor.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Thrombocytopenia Symptoms
concepts.content: Thrombocytopenia in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) can lead to ecchymoses, petechiae, gingival bleeding, epistaxis, and menorrhagia.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Coagulopathy in APL
concepts.content: Coagulopathy is a unique clinical feature of acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL), a subtype of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). It presents as bleeding secondary to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and is considered a medical emergency.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Bone Pain
concepts.content: Bone pain in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) can present as sternal discomfort or aching in the extremities, resulting from the expansion of the medullary cavity by the leukaemic process.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Leukaemia Cutis
concepts.content: Leukaemia cutis, characterized by nodular, violaceous skin lesions, is observed in up to 13% of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) patients. It is mostly associated with acute monocytic leukaemia or acute myelomonocytic leukaemia subtypes.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Gingival Hypertrophy
concepts.content: Gingival hypertrophy in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is primarily associated with the monocytic subtype and is caused by infiltration of leukaemic cells.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – CNS Involvement
concepts.content: Central nervous system (CNS) involvement in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) can manifest as headache, visual changes, and nerve palsies. It is mostly associated with acute monocytic leukaemia or acute myelomonocytic leukaemia subtypes.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Clinical Features – Organomegaly
concepts.content: Organomegaly, including adenopathy, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly, is an uncommon clinical feature in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), occurring in approximately 10% of patients for each. It is caused by the infiltration of leukaemic cells.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – FBC with Differential
concepts.content: Full blood count (FBC) with differential in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) typically shows normocytic, normochromic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and a leucocyte count that may be low, normal, or raised.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – Peripheral Blood Smear Findings
concepts.content: Peripheral blood smear in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) reveals raised myeloblasts, which are immature cells with large nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and pale blue cytoplasm. Auer rods, pink/red, rod-shaped cytoplasmic granular inclusions that are myeloperoxidase positive and pathognomonic of myeloblasts, are mostly seen with acute promyelocytic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – Coagulation Panel for DIC
concepts.content: A coagulation panel for disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) typically shows raised prothrombin time (PT), raised activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), low platelet count, elevated D-dimer concentration, and decreased fibrinogen concentration.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – Serum Electrolytes
concepts.content: Serum electrolyte abnormalities in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), due to increased cell lysis, include hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, and hyperuricemia.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – Bone Marrow Aspiration and Biopsy
concepts.content: Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy is the confirmatory test for Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), with a diagnosis established by the presence of ≥ 20% myeloblasts in the bone marrow.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – Immunophenotyping Markers
concepts.content: Immunophenotyping in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) typically shows expression of markers such as CD13, CD33, CD34, CD117, and HLA-DR for the majority of subtypes.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – Cytogenetic Abnormalities
concepts.content: Cytogenetic abnormalities in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) can be identified by conventional karyotypic analysis, reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), or fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH). Specific abnormalities like t(8;21), inv(16), t(16;16), and t(15;17) define AML irrespective of the blast count.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Investigations – Molecular Studies
concepts.content: Molecular studies in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) identify abnormalities in specific genes such as FLT3, NPM1, KIT, CEBPA, IDH1, IDH2, p53, or RUNX1.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Differential Diagnosis – Acute Lymphocytic Leukaemia
concepts.content: Acute lymphocytic leukaemia (ALL) shares similar clinical features with Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). However, ALL is distinguished by the absence of Auer rods, presence of lymphoblasts, myeloperoxidase negativity, and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) positivity.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Differential Diagnosis – Myelodysplastic Syndrome
concepts.content: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) presents with anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and infections, similar to Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). Key differentiating features include blast counts less than 20% and the presence of pseudo-Pelger-Huet abnormality (neutrophils with bilobed nuclei).

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Differential Diagnosis – Myeloproliferative Neoplasms
concepts.content: Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) can present with infections and abnormalities in different cell lines, similar to Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). However, MPN is characterized by the presence of JAK2 mutation and thrombocytosis.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Differential Diagnosis – Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia in Blast Crisis
concepts.content: Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) in blast crisis can mimic Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) with anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and infections. Differentiation relies on the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome or t(9:22) and raised matured cells in CML.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – General Principles
concepts.content: The general management of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) involves intensive chemotherapy, with treatment decisions depending on the AML type, prognostic factors, patient comorbidities, age, and preferences. The primary goal for most patients is to achieve complete remission, defined as less than 5% blast cells in the bone marrow or peripheral blood.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – Acute Promyelocytic Leukaemia (APL)
concepts.content: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL), a distinct form of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), is a medical emergency. Its treatment differs significantly, utilizing all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and arsenic to induce the maturation of immature malignant cells.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – Chemotherapy Agents
concepts.content: Chemotherapy for Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) often involves cytarabine and anthracyclines, such as daunorubicin. Targeted agents like midostaurin, ivosidenib, or enasidenib may be added for specific genetic mutations.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – Induction Chemotherapy
concepts.content: Induction chemotherapy in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is an intensive combination chemotherapy regimen aimed at achieving complete remission. Failure or relapse may necessitate re-induction therapy.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – Consolidation Chemotherapy
concepts.content: Consolidation chemotherapy for Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is an intensive treatment administered after complete remission to destroy any remaining tumour cells.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – Maintenance Chemotherapy
concepts.content: Maintenance chemotherapy in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is a non-myelosuppressive treatment designed to maintain remission.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – Haematopoietic Cell Transplantation (HCT)
concepts.content: Haematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) is indicated for Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) patients with unfavourable prognostic factors or those who fail to achieve remission through chemotherapy. Allogeneic HCT is the preferred approach.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Management – Supportive Treatment
concepts.content: Supportive treatment in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) includes preventing and treating infections (e.g., antibiotic prophylaxis for febrile neutropenia, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis), immunisations, maintaining hygiene, nutritional support, antiemetics like ondansetron, and transfusions for severe anaemia or thrombocytopenia.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Complications – Tumour Lysis Syndrome
concepts.content: Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is an oncologic emergency in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), typically occurring after initiating cytotoxic therapy. Rapid destruction of tumour cells leads to a massive release of intracellular components, causing hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and hyperuricemia, which can result in acute kidney injury. Clinical features include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, lethargy, hematuria, seizures, arrhythmias, tetany, muscle cramps, and paresthesia.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Complications – Leukostasis
concepts.content: Leukostasis in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is caused by an excessive number of leukaemic cells (hyperleukocytosis, white blood cell count greater than 50 x 10^9/µL), leading to increased blood viscosity. It typically presents with respiratory or neurological distress, with clinical features such as chest pain, headache, altered mental status, and priapism.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Complications – Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
concepts.content: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a complication of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), especially associated with acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL).

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Complications – Severe Neutropenia
concepts.content: Severe neutropenia, defined as an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) less than 500 cells/µL, is a complication of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) and carries a high risk of infections.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Complications – Severe Thrombocytopenia
concepts.content: Severe thrombocytopenia, with platelet counts less than 10,000/µL or active bleeding, is a complication of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML).

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Complications – Severe Anaemia
concepts.content: Severe anaemia in Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is typically normocytic and normochromic. A haemoglobin level of ≤8 g/dL necessitates a transfusion.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Complications – Venous Thromboembolism
concepts.content: Venous thromboembolism is a complication of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), mostly occurring during the first three months of treatment.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Prognosis – Overview
concepts.content: The prognosis of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is affected by clinical characteristics and cytogenetic features. The 5-year survival rate is 24%, with improvements in survival time due to advancements in treatment.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Prognosis – Favourable Clinical Factors
concepts.content: Favourable clinical factors for the prognosis of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) include age less than 50 years, an ECOG performance status score less than 3 or a Karnofsky score greater than 60%, absence of medical comorbidities, no antecedent haematologic disorder, and no prior exposure to cytotoxic agents or radiation.

concepts.title: Acute myeloid leukaemia – Prognosis – Favourable Cytogenetic Factors
concepts.content: Favourable cytogenetic factors for the prognosis of Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) include an MDR 1-negative phenotype, specific translocations such as t(8;21), inv(16), t(16;16), and t(15;17), as well as NPM1 and CEBPA mutations.

concepts.title: Amyloidosis - Definition
concepts.content: Amyloidosis is a rare disease characterized by the deposition of abnormal protein called amyloid in various organs and tissues. The amyloid protein can accumulate in any part of the body, including the heart, kidneys, liver, spleen, and nervous system, leading to organ dysfunction and failure. The diagnosis of amyloidosis requires a high index of suspicion and a combination of clinical, laboratory, and imaging tests, as well as tissue biopsy for confirmation.

concepts.title: Amyloidosis - Epidemiology
concepts.content: The incidence of amyloidosis is 0.80 cases per 100,000 person-years, with a peak incidence between 60-70 years and a 1:1 sex ratio.

concepts.title: Amyloidosis - Aetiology
concepts.content: The tendency for proteins to fold irregularly and form amyloid fibrils can be increased by a sustained increase in the concentration of the protein due to a pathology, or the presence of an unstable protein with a tendency to fold incorrectly. A combination of environmental and genetic factors is thought to lead to amyloidogenesis.

concepts.title: Amyloidosis - AA Subtype Aetiology
concepts.content: AA amyloidosis typically results as a complication of severe long-term inflammatory disorders, such as Crohn's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, malignancies, and conditions predisposing to recurrent infections.

concepts.title: Amyloidosis - AL Subtype Aetiology
concepts.content: AL amyloidosis usually complicates the excessive proliferation of a single clone of plasma cells and can be associated with multiple myeloma, Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, or non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

concepts.title: Amyloidosis - ATTR Subtype Aetiology
concepts.content: ATTR amyloidosis is an autosomal-dominant disease associated with at least 100 different TTR mutations, the most common being the substitution of methionine for valine at position 30.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Definition
concepts.content: Aplastic anaemia is a rare, potentially life-threatening haematological condition characterised by pancytopenia and hypocellular bone marrow. It results in insufficiency of all three blood cell lines: erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes. The pathophysiology typically involves damage to the pluripotent stem cells leading to bone marrow failure.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Aetiology – Idiopathic
concepts.content: Aplastic anaemia can be idiopathic, meaning there is no identifiable cause.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Aetiology – Congenital causes
concepts.content: Congenital causes of aplastic anaemia include Fanconi anaemia and dyskeratosis congenita.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Aetiology – Drug-induced causes
concepts.content: Drugs such as cytotoxics, chloramphenicol, sulphonamides, phenytoin, and gold can cause aplastic anaemia.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Aetiology – Toxin exposure
concepts.content: Exposure to toxins like benzene can lead to aplastic anaemia.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Aetiology – Infectious causes
concepts.content: Infections with parvovirus or hepatitis viruses can cause aplastic anaemia.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Aetiology – Radiation exposure
concepts.content: Radiation exposure can be an aetiological factor for aplastic anaemia.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Pathophysiology – Core mechanism
concepts.content: Aplastic anaemia is characterised by pancytopenia and hypocellular bone marrow, arising from the failure of haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) within the bone marrow, leading to insufficient production of blood cells.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Pathophysiology – Initial insult to HSCs
concepts.content: The initial insult to haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) or their microenvironment can be mediated by immune mechanisms (cytotoxic T-lymphocytes targeting HSCs) or direct toxic effects from drugs or radiation. Damaged HSCs undergo apoptosis or become senescent.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Pathophysiology – Consequences of HSC failure
concepts.content: Diminished HSCs lead to inadequate replenishment of erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes. This results in anaemia (fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea), leukocyte depletion (frequent infections), and thrombocytopenia (petechiae, ecchymoses, increased bleeding risk).

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Pathophysiology – Bone marrow biopsy findings
concepts.content: Bone marrow biopsy in aplastic anaemia typically reveals a hypocellular marrow with fatty infiltration and residual islands of haematopoietic tissue, confirming the diagnosis when correlated with peripheral blood pancytopenia.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Pathophysiology – Molecular mechanisms
concepts.content: At a molecular level, mutations in genes like TERT, TERC, and GATA2 may compromise telomere maintenance and genomic stability in HSCs. Autoimmune destruction is facilitated by aberrant expression of antigens on HSCs targeted by autoreactive T-cells.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Pathophysiology – Cytokine dysregulation
concepts.content: Cytokine dysregulation, specifically elevated levels of interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), contributes to suppression of haematopoiesis through induction of apoptosis in progenitor cells.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Acquired Aplastic Anaemia overview
concepts.content: Acquired aplastic anaemia includes idiopathic, drug-induced, chemical exposure, infectious, and radiation-induced causes.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Acquired Aplastic Anaemia: Idiopathic
concepts.content: Idiopathic acquired aplastic anaemia has no identifiable cause and accounts for the majority of cases.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Acquired Aplastic Anaemia: Drug-induced
concepts.content: Drug-induced acquired aplastic anaemia is commonly associated with medications such as chloramphenicol, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and chemotherapeutic agents.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Acquired Aplastic Anaemia: Chemical exposure
concepts.content: Chemical exposure to substances like benzene and other organic solvents can cause acquired aplastic anaemia.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Acquired Aplastic Anaemia: Infectious causes
concepts.content: Infectious causes of acquired aplastic anaemia include viral infections such as Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), hepatitis viruses, and HIV.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Acquired Aplastic Anaemia: Radiation-induced
concepts.content: Radiation-induced acquired aplastic anaemia results from ionising radiation exposure.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Inherited Aplastic Anaemia overview
concepts.content: Inherited aplastic anaemia includes Fanconi anaemia, dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, and Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Inherited Aplastic Anaemia: Fanconi anaemia
concepts.content: Fanconi anaemia is an autosomal recessive disorder characterised by congenital abnormalities, progressive pancytopenia, and increased cancer risk, diagnosed via chromosomal breakage tests.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Inherited Aplastic Anaemia: Dyskeratosis congenita
concepts.content: Dyskeratosis congenita is an X-linked recessive or autosomal dominant disorder involving mutations in telomerase complex genes, presenting with mucocutaneous abnormalities and bone marrow failure.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Inherited Aplastic Anaemia: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome
concepts.content: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder featuring exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, skeletal abnormalities, and bone marrow dysfunction, associated with SBDS gene mutations.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Inherited Aplastic Anaemia: Diamond-Blackfan anaemia
concepts.content: Diamond-Blackfan anaemia is a congenital pure red cell aplasia presenting in infancy or early childhood, involving mutations in ribosomal protein genes.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Severity: Mild
concepts.content: Mild aplastic anaemia is defined by bone marrow cellularity 20-30%, absolute neutrophil count (ANC) >1.5 x 10^9/L, platelet count >50 x 10^9/L, and reticulocyte count >60 x 10^9/L.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Severity: Moderate
concepts.content: Moderate aplastic anaemia is defined by bone marrow cellularity 10-20%, ANC 0.5-1.5 x 10^9/L, platelet count 20-50 x 10^9/L, and reticulocyte count 20-60 x 10^9/L.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Classification – Severity: Severe
concepts.content: Severe aplastic anaemia is defined by bone marrow cellularity less than 25%, ANC less than 0.5 x 10^9/L, platelet count less than 20 x 10^9/L, and reticulocyte count less than 20 x 10^9/L.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Clinical Features – Haematological findings
concepts.content: Clinical features of aplastic anaemia include normochromic, normocytic anaemia, leukopenia (with lymphocytes relatively spared), and thrombocytopenia.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Clinical Features – General presentation
concepts.content: The clinical presentation of aplastic anaemia is variable but often includes fatigue (secondary to anaemia), recurrent infections (due to neutropenia) and bleeding tendencies (owing to thrombocytopenia).

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Clinical Features – Later developments
concepts.content: A minority of patients with aplastic anaemia may later develop paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria or myelodysplasia.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Diagnosis – Confirmation method
concepts.content: Diagnosis of aplastic anaemia is confirmed by bone marrow biopsy showing hypocellularity without infiltration by abnormal cells or fibrosis.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Differential Diagnosis – Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS)
