concepts.content: Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS) is differentiated from aplastic anaemia by the presence of dysplasia in one or more cell lines and often a hypercellular or normocellular marrow, whereas aplastic anaemia has a hypocellular marrow without dysplasia.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Differential Diagnosis – Paroxysmal Nocturnal Haemoglobinuria (PNH)
concepts.content: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Haemoglobinuria (PNH) is differentiated from aplastic anaemia by the presence of episodic haemolysis and confirmed by flow cytometry showing CD55/CD59 deficient red cells.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Differential Diagnosis – Hypoplastic Myelodysplastic Syndrome
concepts.content: Hypoplastic Myelodysplastic Syndrome is differentiated from aplastic anaemia by the presence of dysplasia in one or more cell lines, despite a hypocellular marrow.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Management – Supportive Care: Blood products
concepts.content: Supportive care for aplastic anaemia includes administration of blood products.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Management – Supportive Care: Infection prevention and treatment
concepts.content: Supportive care for aplastic anaemia involves the prevention and treatment of infection.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Management – Immunosuppression: Anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) and anti-lymphocyte globulin (ALG)
concepts.content: Immunosuppression for aplastic anaemia includes Anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) and anti-lymphocyte globulin (ALG), which are prepared in animals and can cause serum sickness, often requiring steroid cover.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Management – Immunosuppression: Ciclosporin
concepts.content: Ciclosporin may also be given as part of immunosuppressive therapy for aplastic anaemia.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Management – Stem Cell Transplantation: Allogeneic transplants
concepts.content: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation is a treatment option for aplastic anaemia, with a success rate of up to 80%.

concepts.title: Aplastic anaemia – Prognosis – Influencing factors
concepts.content: Prognosis for aplastic anaemia depends on several factors including patient age, severity of pancytopenia, response to treatment, and availability of suitable donors for transplantation.

concepts.title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Definition
concepts.content: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) is a condition characterised by the destruction of red blood cells by autoantibodies directed against red blood cell surface antigens.

concepts.title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia may present with symptoms of anaemia such as fatigue and pallor, as well as jaundice due to the breakdown of red blood cells.

concepts.title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Investigations
concepts.content: The direct Coombs test is a key investigation for autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and will be positive. This test helps to differentiate it from other causes of haemolysis like hereditary spherocytosis.

concepts.title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Warm AIHA
concepts.content: Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is a type of AIHA mediated by IgG antibodies. It is associated with extravascular haemolysis.

concepts.title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Cold AIHA
concepts.content: Cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is a type of AIHA mediated by IgM antibodies. It involves complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Beta-thalassaemia major is a severe genetic disorder caused by homozygous mutations in the HBB gene on chromosome 11, leading to a complete absence of beta-globin chain synthesis.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia – Clinical Presentation
concepts.content: Patients with beta-thalassaemia major are highly symptomatic and require medical intervention, contrasting with the milder beta-thalassaemia trait.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia – Prognosis
concepts.content: Beta-thalassaemia major is associated with a shortened life expectancy compared to the general population.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Definition
concepts.content: Beta-thalassemia trait, also known as beta-thalassemia minor, indicates a patient is a carrier of beta-thalassemia without manifesting the disease itself. It is an inherited blood disorder, present from birth, affecting haemoglobin formation. Symptoms are much milder and complications significantly fewer compared to beta-thalassemia major.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Epidemiology
concepts.content: The incidence of beta-thalassemia trait is 1.00 cases per 100,000 person-years, with a peak incidence between 20-30 years. The sex ratio is 1:1.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Aetiology and Risk Factors
concepts.content: Beta-thalassemia trait is genetically inherited, requiring at least one parent to have beta-thalassemia or the trait. Inheritance is equal for men and women. It is the most common recessive disease globally, with 1-5% of the world's population being carriers. High-risk ethnic backgrounds include Mediterranean (Italy, Greece, Cyprus, Turkey), South Asian (India, Bangladesh, Pakistan), Middle Eastern, and Chinese/Southeast Asian populations.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Patients with beta-thalassemia trait are typically asymptomatic and show no signs on examination. However, they may develop microcytic and hypochromic anaemia, which can cause fatigue and dyspnoea, particularly during pregnancy due to dilutional anaemia. Beta-thalassemia trait does not progress to beta-thalassemia major and has no other associated health complications.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Pregnancy Complications
concepts.content: During pregnancy and labour, patients with beta-thalassemia trait experience a 25% increased rate of anaemia and a 250% increased rate of requiring blood transfusions.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Investigations: NHS Screening Programme
concepts.content: The NHS Sickle Cell and Thalassemia (SCT) Screening Programme routinely offers testing for beta-thalassemia trait to pregnant women (antenatal screening) and expectant fathers (if the mother tests positive). In 'high risk' trusts (>=2% positive antenatal screens), all women are tested. In 'low risk' trusts (<1% positive screens), screening is based on FBC, and a Family Origin Questionnaire (FOQ) determines the need for partner testing.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Investigations: General Testing
concepts.content: Testing for beta-thalassemia trait can be requested outside antenatal screening via a GP or by self-referral to SCT centres. This is available for both male and female patients and is useful for those with a family history of thalassemia or whose partner has thalassemia.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Investigations: Full Blood Count (FBC) Findings
concepts.content: A Full Blood Count (FBC) in beta-thalassemia trait typically shows microcytic anaemia, with normal to moderately low haemoglobin (Hb), low Mean Corpuscular Haemoglobin (MCH) usually 19-23 pg, and low Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) usually 60-70 fL.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Investigations: Diagnosis Confirmation
concepts.content: Diagnosis of beta-thalassemia trait is confirmed using haemoglobin electrophoresis with quantitation of haemoglobin F (HbF) and A2 (HbA2). Levels of HbA2 are elevated in carriers, ranging from 3.6-7%, compared to 2.2-3.2% in unaffected individuals.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Differential Diagnosis: Iron Deficiency Anaemia
concepts.content: Iron deficiency anaemia shares similarities with beta-thalassemia trait, both presenting as microcytic anaemia (low Hb, low Hct). However, iron deficiency anaemia is an acquired condition due to lack of iron, lacks structural abnormality, and has normal HbA2 levels, unlike beta-thalassemia trait.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Differential Diagnosis: Beta-thalassaemia Major
concepts.content: Beta-thalassaemia major shares the same genetic mutation on the HBB gene on chromosome 11 with beta-thalassemia trait. However, beta-thalassaemia major is characterized by homozygosity for the mutation, leading to more severe symptoms requiring medical intervention and a shortened life expectancy, unlike the trait.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Differential Diagnosis: Sickle Cell Disease
concepts.content: Sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathy that presents as anaemia and is tested for during pregnancy, similar to beta-thalassemia trait. However, sickle cell disease is caused by abnormal haemoglobin S formation, leading to significant complications like painful sickle cell crises and thromboembolism, and more severe anaemia. Its aetiology is also more common in patients from African and Caribbean backgrounds. If a carrier of beta-thalassemia or sickle cell has a child with another haemoglobinopathy carrier, hereditary complications can arise.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia trait – Management
concepts.content: The majority of patients with beta-thalassemia trait do not require any treatment, and there are no specific treatment guidelines for beta-thalassemia trait.

concepts.title: Blood Products: Red Blood Cells - Transfusion in ALL
concepts.content: In Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia (ALL), red blood cell or platelet transfusions can be used to correct pancytopenia. Prophylactic antibiotics are also considered in cases of severe neutropenia.

concepts.title: Blood Products: Red Blood Cells - Transfusion in AML
concepts.content: Transfusions are indicated for severe anaemia and thrombocytopenia in the management of Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML).

concepts.title: Blood Products: Red Blood Cells - Transfusion Threshold in AML
concepts.content: In Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML), a transfusion is needed for severe normocytic, normochromic anaemia when the haemoglobin level is â‰¤8 g/dL.

concepts.title: Blood Products: Red Blood Cells - Transfusion in Hereditary Spherocytosis
concepts.content: Red cell transfusions are indicated in severely affected individuals with Hereditary Spherocytosis or during clinical scenarios when they develop anaemia (e.g., during pregnancy or aplastic anaemia). They are not indicated on an ongoing basis due to the risk of iron overload.

concepts.title: Burkitt's lymphoma – Clinical features: Abdominal mass and bowel obstruction
concepts.content: Burkitt's lymphoma can present with a large abdominal mass and symptoms of bowel obstruction.

concepts.title: Burkitt's lymphoma – Investigations: MYC rearrangement by FISH
concepts.content: Fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) is used to identify a MYC rearrangement in all individuals newly presenting with histologically high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which includes Burkitt's lymphoma.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Asymptomatic presentation
concepts.content: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is often detected incidentally during routine blood tests, with patients having no apparent symptoms.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Persistent lymphocytosis
concepts.content: The most common finding in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is persistent lymphocytosis, often detected during routine blood tests.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – B symptoms
concepts.content: General systemic symptoms, known as B symptoms, including fever, night sweats and weight loss, can occur in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). These are less common than in other lymphomas and may indicate a more aggressive disease course.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Fatigue
concepts.content: Fatigue is a common symptom in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), potentially due to anaemia or general malaise associated with the disease.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: Lymphadenopathy, characterized by painless, firm, rubbery lymph nodes, is a complication of direct tumour infiltration in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), most commonly observed in the cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Splenomegaly
concepts.content: Splenomegaly, presenting with abdominal discomfort and early satiety, is a complication of direct tumour infiltration in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Hepatomegaly
concepts.content: Hepatomegaly, though less common than splenomegaly, can occur in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) due to direct tumour infiltration.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Bone marrow infiltration complications
concepts.content: Bone marrow infiltration in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) can lead to complications such as anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA)
concepts.content: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA), characterized by a positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT), is an autoimmune complication that can occur in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)
concepts.content: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), characterized by a low platelet count, is an autoimmune complication that can occur in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA)
concepts.content: Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA), a rare cause of severe anaemia, is an autoimmune complication that can occur in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Acquired von Willebrand disease
concepts.content: Acquired von Willebrand disease, a rare bleeding tendency, is an autoimmune complication that can occur in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Full Blood Count (FBC) findings
concepts.content: A Full Blood Count (FBC) in suspected Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) typically reveals lymphocytosis (>5 x 10^9/L), which may be accompanied by anaemia or thrombocytopenia in advanced stages. A differential count will show an absolute increase in lymphocytes.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Blood Film findings
concepts.content: Morphological examination of a peripheral blood smear in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) can reveal smudge cells, a characteristic feature. However, this finding is not specific and cannot be used alone for diagnosis.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Immunophenotyping by Flow Cytometry
concepts.content: Immunophenotyping by flow cytometry is the gold standard for diagnosing Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). Peripheral blood lymphocytes are analysed for expression of various cell surface markers. A typical CLL phenotype shows co-expression of CD19, CD5 and CD23 along with weak expression of surface immunoglobulin and absence or low expression of FMC7 and CD79b.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Bone Marrow Aspiration/Biopsy
concepts.content: Bone marrow aspiration/biopsy is not necessary for the diagnosis of Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) if flow cytometry is conclusive, but it can provide information about bone marrow infiltration which aids in staging.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Cytogenetic Analysis (FISH)
concepts.content: Cytogenetic analysis using Fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) can detect chromosomal abnormalities associated with prognosis in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). Deletion 17p or TP53 mutation indicates poor prognosis, while deletion 13q as a sole abnormality indicates favourable prognosis.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Serum Immunoglobulins
concepts.content: Serum immunoglobulin levels should be assessed at diagnosis and monitored during follow-up in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), as hypogammaglobulinaemia is common and can contribute to increased susceptibility to infections.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Other investigations (not routinely required)
concepts.content: Other investigations such as lymph node biopsy, computed tomography (CT) scan, or positron emission tomography (PET) scan may be performed based on individual patient symptoms or disease stage in Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). However, these are not routinely required for the diagnosis.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia is characterised by the destruction of red blood cells by autoantibodies. Patients may present with symptoms of anaemia such as fatigue, pallor, and jaundice.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Immune thrombocytopenia
concepts.content: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia involves autoantibodies destroying platelets, leading to thrombocytopenia. This can result in easy bruising, petechiae, or more serious bleeding complications.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Recurrent infections due to hypogammaglobulinaemia and neutropenia
concepts.content: Patients with Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia may experience recurrent infections due to hypogammaglobulinaemia and neutropenia. Infections commonly involve the respiratory tract but can also include herpes zoster reactivation.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Richter's transformation
concepts.content: Richter's transformation is a rare but serious complication of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia where CLL transforms into an aggressive lymphoma. Patients may present with rapidly enlarging lymph nodes, splenomegaly, and B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss).

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Definition
concepts.content: Cryoglobulinaemia is a family of rare conditions characterized by the presence of cryoglobulins in the blood. It is a type of vasculitis, causing irritation and inflammation of blood vessels.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Cryoglobulins
concepts.content: Cryoglobulins are atypical proteins in the blood that may clump together at body temperatures below 98.6 F (37 C). These clumps can block blood flow, damaging the skin, joints, nerves, kidneys, and liver.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Type 1
concepts.content: Type 1 cryoglobulinaemia involves one kind of monoclonal atypical protein and is most often linked to blood cancers.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Type 2
concepts.content: Type 2 cryoglobulinaemia involves both monoclonal and polyclonal atypical proteins and is most often linked to hepatitis C virus.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Type 3
concepts.content: Type 3 cryoglobulinaemia involves a mix of polyclonal proteins and is most often linked to autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – General Symptoms
concepts.content: Some individuals with cryoglobulinaemia may experience no symptoms, while for others, symptoms might come and go.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Cutaneous Manifestations
concepts.content: Cutaneous manifestations of cryoglobulinaemia include purple skin spots (lesions), which may appear black or brown on darker skin, open leg sores (ulcers), purpura, and Raynaud's phenomenon.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Joint Pain
concepts.content: Joint pain, similar to that experienced in rheumatoid arthritis, is a common symptom of cryoglobulinaemia.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Peripheral Neuropathy
concepts.content: Cryoglobulinaemia can cause peripheral neuropathy, damaging nerves in the fingers and toes, leading to numbness and other neurological problems.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Causes: Infections
concepts.content: Cryoglobulinaemia has been linked to various infections, most commonly Hepatitis C, but also Hepatitis B, HIV, Epstein-Barr, toxoplasmosis, and malaria.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Causes: Cancers
concepts.content: Certain blood cancers, such as multiple myeloma, Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, and chronic lymphocytic leukemia, can cause cryoglobulinaemia.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Causes: Autoimmune Diseases
concepts.content: Autoimmune diseases, where the immune system mistakenly attacks healthy tissues, increase the risk of cryoglobulinaemia. Examples include lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, and Sjogren syndrome.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Risk Factors: Sex and Age
concepts.content: Cryoglobulinaemia occurs more frequently in women than in men, and symptoms most often begin in middle age.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Risk Factors: Associated Diseases
concepts.content: Cryoglobulinaemia is linked with diseases such as hepatitis C, HIV, multiple myeloma, Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, lupus, and Sjogren syndrome.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Renal Complications
concepts.content: Cryoglobulinaemia can affect the kidneys, leading to symptoms such as protein or blood in the urine, high blood pressure, glomerulonephritis, and potentially kidney failure.

concepts.title: Cryoglobulinaemia – Extremity Complications
concepts.content: Complications affecting the extremities due to cryoglobulinaemia include ulcers or gangrene.

concepts.title: Cryoprecipitate - Composition
concepts.content: Cryoprecipitate is a plasma-derived blood product rich in clotting factors, containing Factor VIII, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor (vWF), and Factor XIII.

concepts.title: Cryoprecipitate - Indications
concepts.content: Cryoprecipitate is primarily indicated for the replacement of fibrinogen in cases of acquired or congenital deficiency, such as in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) or massive haemorrhage, particularly when fibrinogen levels are critically low.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a pathological process characterized by the widespread activation of the coagulation cascade, leading to the formation of microthrombi in small and medium-sized vessels throughout the body. This process consumes coagulation factors and platelets, which can lead to a paradoxical state of both thrombosis and hemorrhage. The activation of the coagulation cascade is often triggered by the release of tissue factor into the circulation.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) include sepsis (particularly with gram-negative bacteria), severe trauma (such as major crush injuries or burns), obstetric complications (like amniotic fluid embolism or abruptio placentae), and malignancies (especially adenocarcinomas and acute promyelocytic leukaemia).

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Investigations
concepts.content: The diagnosis of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is based on a combination of clinical findings and laboratory tests. Key laboratory findings include thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), low levels of fibrinogen, and elevated levels of fibrin degradation products (FDPs) and D-dimer. The peripheral blood smear may show schistocytes (fragmented red blood cells).

concepts.title: Factor V Leiden – Definition
concepts.content: Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia, affecting 5% of the UK population.

concepts.title: Factor V Leiden – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Factor V Leiden is characterized by activated protein C resistance.

concepts.title: Factor V Leiden – Risk (heterozygous)
concepts.content: Individuals heterozygous for Factor V Leiden have a 4-5 times increased risk of thrombosis.

concepts.title: Factor V Leiden – Risk (homozygous)
concepts.content: Individuals homozygous for Factor V Leiden have a 10 times increased risk of thrombosis.

concepts.title: Factor V Leiden – Screening recommendations
concepts.content: Screening recommendations exist for Factor V Leiden.

concepts.title: Two-level DVT Wells score
concepts.content: The two-level DVT Wells score is a clinical decision rule used to estimate the pre-test probability of deep vein thrombosis. A score of 2 or more is considered 'DVT likely', while a score of 1 or less is considered 'DVT unlikely'.

concepts.title: Investigation of suspected DVT
concepts.content: If DVT is likely (Wells score >= 2), a proximal leg vein ultrasound scan should be performed within 4 hours. If the scan is negative, a D-dimer test is performed. If DVT is unlikely (Wells score <= 1), a D-dimer test is performed first. If the D-dimer is positive, a proximal leg vein ultrasound is performed.

concepts.title: Anticoagulation
concepts.content: Initial treatment for DVT is with a direct-acting oral anticoagulant (DOAC) such as apixaban or rivaroxaban. Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is an alternative. The duration of anticoagulation is typically 3 months for a provoked DVT and 6 months for an unprovoked DVT.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Target cells
concepts.content: Target cells are a pathological red cell form seen in sickle-cell anaemia.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia – Target cells
concepts.content: Target cells are a pathological red cell form seen in beta-thalassaemia.

concepts.title: Iron deficiency anaemia – Target cells
concepts.content: Target cells are a pathological red cell form seen in iron deficiency anaemia.

concepts.title: Myelofibrosis – 'Tear-drop' poikilocytes
concepts.content: 'Tear-drop' poikilocytes are a pathological red cell form seen in myelofibrosis.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Spherocytes
concepts.content: Spherocytes are a pathological red cell form seen in hereditary spherocytosis.

concepts.title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Spherocytes
concepts.content: Spherocytes are a pathological red cell form seen in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Basophilic stippling
concepts.content: Basophilic stippling is a pathological red cell form seen in lead poisoning.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia – Basophilic stippling
concepts.content: Basophilic stippling is a pathological red cell form seen in beta-thalassaemia.

concepts.title: Sideroblastic anaemia – Basophilic stippling
concepts.content: Basophilic stippling is a pathological red cell form seen in sideroblastic anaemia.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Basophilic stippling
concepts.content: Basophilic stippling is a pathological red cell form seen in myelodysplastic syndrome.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Heinz bodies
concepts.content: Heinz bodies are a pathological red cell form seen in G6PD deficiency.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Schistocytes ('helmet cells')
concepts.content: Schistocytes ('helmet cells') are a pathological red cell form seen in disseminated intravascular coagulation.

concepts.title: Iron deficiency anaemia – 'Pencil' poikilocytes
concepts.content: 'Pencil' poikilocytes are a pathological red cell form seen in iron deficiency anaemia.

concepts.title: Macrocytic anaemia – Hypersegmented neutrophils
concepts.content: Hypersegmented neutrophils are an abnormality seen in megaloblastic anaemia, which is a type of macrocytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Classification
concepts.content: Blood product transfusion complications may be broadly classified into immunological (acute haemolytic, non-haemolytic febrile, allergic/anaphylaxis), infective, transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO), and other (hyperkalaemia, iron overload, clotting) reactions.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Non-haemolytic febrile reaction Aetiology
concepts.content: Non-haemolytic febrile reactions are thought to be caused by antibodies reacting with white cell fragments in the blood product and cytokines that have leaked from the blood cell during storage. They are also due to white blood cell HLA antibodies, often the result of sensitization by previous pregnancies or transfusions.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Non-haemolytic febrile reaction Clinical features
concepts.content: Clinical features of a non-haemolytic febrile reaction include fever and chills.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Non-haemolytic febrile reaction Epidemiology
concepts.content: Non-haemolytic febrile reactions occur in 1-2% of red cell transfusions and 10-30% of platelet transfusions.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Non-haemolytic febrile reaction Management
concepts.content: Management of a non-haemolytic febrile reaction involves slowing or stopping the transfusion, administering paracetamol, and monitoring the patient.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Minor allergic reaction Aetiology
concepts.content: Minor allergic reactions are thought to be caused by foreign plasma proteins.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Minor allergic reaction Clinical features
concepts.content: Clinical features of a minor allergic reaction include pruritus and urticaria.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Minor allergic reaction Management
concepts.content: Management of a minor allergic reaction involves temporarily stopping the transfusion, administering an antihistamine, and monitoring the patient. If symptoms resolve, the transfusion may be continued.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Anaphylaxis Aetiology
concepts.content: Anaphylaxis can be caused by patients with IgA deficiency who have anti-IgA antibodies.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Anaphylaxis Clinical features
concepts.content: Clinical features of anaphylaxis include hypotension, dyspnoea, wheezing, and angioedema. Symptoms typically arise within minutes of starting the transfusion.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Anaphylaxis Management
concepts.content: Management of anaphylaxis involves immediately and permanently stopping the transfusion, administering intramuscular adrenaline, providing ABC support, oxygen, and fluids. Antihistamines, corticosteroids, and bronchodilators should also be considered.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Acute haemolytic reaction Aetiology
concepts.content: Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction results from an ABO blood group mismatch, usually due to human error, causing massive intravascular haemolysis by IgM-type antibodies.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Acute haemolytic reaction Clinical features
concepts.content: Symptoms of an acute haemolytic reaction begin minutes after transfusion starts and include fever, abdominal pain, chest pain, agitation, and hypotension.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Acute haemolytic reaction Management
concepts.content: Treatment for an acute haemolytic reaction includes immediate transfusion termination, generous fluid resuscitation with saline solution, and informing the lab. Complications include disseminated intravascular coagulation and renal failure.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Acute haemolytic reaction Investigations
concepts.content: To confirm diagnosis of an acute haemolytic reaction, check the identity of the patient/name on the blood product, and send blood for a direct Coombs test, repeat typing, and cross-matching.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) Aetiology
concepts.content: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) is caused by an excessive rate of transfusion or pre-existing heart failure.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) Clinical features
concepts.content: Clinical features of transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) include pulmonary oedema and hypertension. This is a key difference from TRALI.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) Management
concepts.content: Management of transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) involves slowing or stopping the transfusion, and considering intravenous loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) and oxygen.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is a non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema thought to be secondary to increased vascular permeability caused by host neutrophils that become activated by substances in donated blood.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) Clinical features
concepts.content: Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is characterized by the development of hypoxaemia/acute respiratory distress syndrome within 6 hours of transfusion. Features include hypoxia, pulmonary infiltrates on chest x-ray, fever, and hypotension.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) Management
concepts.content: Management of transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) involves stopping the transfusion, providing oxygen, and supportive care.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Infective complications
concepts.content: Infective complications of blood transfusions include bacterial and viral transmissions. The risk varies with blood product type, storage conditions, components, and duration of storage.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Red Blood Cell (RBC) Infective complications
concepts.content: Red Blood Cells (RBCs) are primarily at risk for transmitting viral agents such as HIV, HBV, and HCV. Bacterial contamination is less common but possible, particularly from skin flora during collection. Viral infections can lead to chronic disease states such as chronic hepatitis or AIDS, while bacterial infections may manifest as sepsis.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Platelet Infective complications
concepts.content: Platelets are stored at room temperature, increasing the risk of bacterial proliferation. Common contaminants include Staphylococcus epidermidis and Bacillus cereus. Bacterial contamination of platelets is more likely to lead to rapid onset of sepsis and septic shock.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Prion transmission (vCJD)
concepts.content: Although the absolute risk is very small, variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD) may be transmitted via blood transfusion. Steps taken to minimize this risk include leucodepletion of all donations since late 1999, fractionation of plasma derivatives from imported plasma since 1999, and exclusion of blood component recipients from donating blood since 2004.

concepts.title: Blood products – CMV transmission
concepts.content: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is transmitted in leucocytes.

concepts.title: Blood products – Leucocyte depletion
concepts.content: Most blood products (except granulocyte transfusions) are now leucocyte depleted.

concepts.title: Blood products – Requirement for CMV negative blood
concepts.content: CMV negative products are rarely required due to leucocyte depletion.

concepts.title: Blood products – Irradiated blood composition
concepts.content: Irradiated blood products are depleted of T-lymphocytes.

concepts.title: Blood products – Purpose of irradiated blood
concepts.content: Irradiated blood products are used to avoid transfusion-associated graft versus host disease (TA-GVHD).

concepts.title: Graft versus host disease – Cause of TA-GVHD
concepts.content: Transfusion-associated graft versus host disease (TA-GVHD) is caused by engraftment of viable donor T lymphocytes.

concepts.title: Blood products – Indications for CMV negative blood: Granulocyte transfusions
concepts.content: CMV negative blood is indicated for granulocyte transfusions.

concepts.title: Blood products – Indications for CMV negative blood: Intra-uterine transfusions
concepts.content: CMV negative blood is indicated for intra-uterine transfusions.

concepts.title: Blood products – Indications for CMV negative blood: Neonates
concepts.content: CMV negative blood is indicated for neonates up to 28 days post expected date of delivery.

concepts.title: Blood products – Indications for CMV negative blood: Pregnancy
concepts.content: CMV negative blood is indicated for elective transfusions during pregnancy (not during labour or delivery).

concepts.title: Blood products – Indications for Irradiated blood: Granulocyte transfusions
concepts.content: Irradiated blood is indicated for granulocyte transfusions.

concepts.title: Blood products – Indications for Irradiated blood: Intra-uterine transfusions
concepts.content: Irradiated blood is indicated for intra-uterine transfusions.

concepts.title: Blood products – Indications for Irradiated blood: Neonates
concepts.content: Irradiated blood is indicated for neonates up to 28 days post expected date of delivery.

concepts.title: Blood products – Indications for Irradiated blood: Bone marrow/stem cell transplants
concepts.content: Irradiated blood is indicated for bone marrow / stem cell transplants.

concepts.title: Blood products – Indications for Irradiated blood: Immunocompromised patients
concepts.content: Irradiated blood is indicated for immunocompromised patients (e.g., chemotherapy or congenital).

concepts.title: Blood products – Indications for Irradiated blood: Hodgkin lymphoma
concepts.content: Irradiated blood is indicated for patients with or previous Hodgkin lymphoma.

concepts.title: Fresh Frozen Plasma – Indications
concepts.content: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is most suited for 'clinically significant' but without 'major haemorrhage' in patients with a prothrombin time (PT) ratio or activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) ratio > 1.5.

concepts.title: Fresh Frozen Plasma – Volume
concepts.content: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is typically administered in volumes of 150-220 mL.

concepts.title: Fresh Frozen Plasma – Prophylactic Use
concepts.content: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) can be used prophylactically in patients undergoing invasive surgery where there is a risk of significant bleeding.

concepts.title: Fresh Frozen Plasma – Universal Donor
concepts.content: The universal donor of Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) is AB blood because it lacks any anti-A or anti-B antibodies.

concepts.title: Cryoprecipitate – Composition and Primary Use
concepts.content: Cryoprecipitate contains concentrated Factor VIII:C, von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, Factor XIII and fibronectin, and is most commonly used to replace fibrinogen.

concepts.title: Cryoprecipitate – Volume
concepts.content: Cryoprecipitate is administered in a much smaller volume than FFP, typically 15-20mL.

concepts.title: Cryoprecipitate – Indications (Fibrinogen Concentration)
concepts.content: Cryoprecipitate is most suited for patients with 'clinically significant' bleeding but without 'major haemorrhage' who have a fibrinogen concentration < 1.5 g/L.

concepts.title: Cryoprecipitate – Example Use Cases
concepts.content: Example use cases for cryoprecipitate include disseminated intravascular coagulation, liver failure, hypofibrinogenaemia secondary to massive transfusion, emergency situations for haemophiliacs (when specific factors are not available), and von Willebrand disease.

concepts.title: Cryoprecipitate – Prophylactic Use (Surgery)
concepts.content: Cryoprecipitate can be used prophylactically in patients undergoing invasive surgery where there is a risk of significant bleeding and the fibrinogen concentration is < 1.0 g/L.

concepts.title: Prothrombin Complex Concentrate – Emergency Reversal
concepts.content: Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) is used for the emergency reversal of anticoagulation in patients with either severe bleeding or a head injury with suspected intracerebral haemorrhage.

concepts.title: Prothrombin Complex Concentrate – Prophylactic Use (Surgery)
concepts.content: Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) can be used prophylactically in patients undergoing emergency surgery depending on the particular circumstance.

concepts.title: Haematology – DOAC Indications: Stroke prevention in non-valvular AF
concepts.content: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are used for the prevention of stroke in non-valvular AF. NICE stipulate that certain other risk factors should be present, including prior stroke or transient ischaemic attack, age 75 years or older, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or heart failure.

concepts.title: Venous thromboembolism – DOAC Indications: Post-surgical VTE prevention
concepts.content: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are used for the prevention of venous thromboembolism (VTE) following hip/knee surgery.

concepts.title: Deep vein thrombosis – DOAC Indications: Treatment of DVT and PE
concepts.content: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are used for the treatment of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE).

concepts.title: Haematology – Dabigatran: Mechanism and Excretion
concepts.content: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor and is majority renal excreted.

concepts.title: Haematology – Rivaroxaban: Mechanism and Excretion
concepts.content: Rivaroxaban is a direct factor Xa inhibitor and is majority liver excreted.

concepts.title: Haematology – Apixaban: Mechanism and Excretion
concepts.content: Apixaban is a direct factor Xa inhibitor and is majority faecal excreted.

concepts.title: Haematology – Edoxaban: Mechanism and Excretion
concepts.content: Edoxaban is a direct factor Xa inhibitor and is majority faecal excreted.

concepts.title: Haematology – Dabigatran: Reversal Agent
concepts.content: The reversal agent for Dabigatran is Idarucizumab.

concepts.title: Haematology – Rivaroxaban: Reversal Agent
concepts.content: The reversal agent for Rivaroxaban is Andexanet alfa.

concepts.title: Haematology – Apixaban: Reversal Agent
concepts.content: The reversal agent for Apixaban is Andexanet alfa.

concepts.title: Haematology – Edoxaban: Reversal Agent
concepts.content: There is no authorised reversal agent for Edoxaban, although andexanet alfa has been studied. Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) is often used in clinical practice.

concepts.title: Graft versus host disease – Definition
concepts.content: Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) is a serious complication of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). It occurs when donor T cells attack recipient tissues due to immunogenetic differences.

concepts.title: Graft versus host disease – Distinction from Transplant Rejection
concepts.content: Graft-versus-host disease is distinct from transplant rejection, where the recipient’s immune system attacks the donor tissue.

concepts.title: Graft versus host disease – Other Occurrences
concepts.content: GVHD may also occur after solid organ transplantation or blood transfusion in immunocompromised patients.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) is associated with Hodgkin's lymphoma.

concepts.title: Burkitt's lymphoma – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) is associated with Burkitt's lymphoma.

concepts.title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Human Immunodeficiency Virus type 1 (HIV-1) is associated with high-grade B-cell lymphoma, a type of Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

concepts.title: Haemolytic anaemias – Hereditary causes
concepts.content: Hereditary haemolytic anaemias can be subdivided into membrane, metabolism or haemoglobin defects.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Cause of haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: Hereditary spherocytosis is a membrane defect that causes hereditary haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Cause of haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: G6PD deficiency is a metabolism defect that causes hereditary haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Cause of haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: Sickle cell anaemia is a haemoglobinopathy that causes hereditary haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Beta-thalassaemia – Cause of haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: Thalassaemia is a haemoglobinopathy that causes hereditary haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Haemolytic anaemias – Acquired causes
concepts.content: Acquired haemolytic anaemias can be subdivided into immune (Coombs-positive) and non-immune (Coombs-negative) causes.

concepts.title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Immune cause
concepts.content: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (warm/cold antibody type) is an immune (Coombs-positive) cause of acquired haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Transfusion reactions – Immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: Transfusion reaction (alloimmune) is an immune (Coombs-positive) cause of acquired haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Drug-induced haemolytic anaemia – Immune cause
concepts.content: Drugs like methyldopa and penicillin can cause immune (Coombs-positive) acquired haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura – Non-immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA), including TTP/HUS, is a non-immune (Coombs-negative) cause of acquired haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Non-immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA), including DIC, is a non-immune (Coombs-negative) cause of acquired haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Malignancy – Non-immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: Malignancy can cause microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA), a non-immune (Coombs-negative) acquired haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Pre-eclampsia – Non-immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: Pre-eclampsia can cause microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA), a non-immune (Coombs-negative) acquired haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Prosthetic heart valves – Non-immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: Prosthetic heart valves are a non-immune (Coombs-negative) cause of acquired haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Non-immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is a non-immune (Coombs-negative) cause of acquired haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Malaria – Non-immune cause of haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: Infections like malaria are a non-immune (Coombs-negative) cause of acquired haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Drug-induced haemolytic anaemia – Non-immune cause
concepts.content: Drugs like dapsone can cause non-immune (Coombs-negative) acquired haemolytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Zieve syndrome – Definition
concepts.content: Zieve syndrome is a rare clinical syndrome of Coombs-negative haemolysis, cholestatic jaundice, and transient hyperlipidaemia associated with heavy alcohol use, typically following a binge.

concepts.title: Zieve syndrome – Management
concepts.content: Zieve syndrome typically resolves with abstinence from alcohol.

concepts.title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) is most commonly idiopathic but may be secondary to a lymphoproliferative disorder, infection or drugs.

concepts.title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Investigations (General features)
concepts.content: General features of haemolytic anaemia: anaemia, reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin, raised lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and indirect bilirubin.

concepts.title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Investigations (Blood film)
concepts.content: Blood film: spherocytes and reticulocytes.

concepts.title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – Investigations (Specific feature)
concepts.content: Specific features of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia: positive direct antiglobulin test (Coombs' test).

concepts.title: Warm AIHA – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: In warm AIHA the antibody (usually IgG) causes haemolysis best at body temperature and haemolysis tends to occur in extravascular sites, for example the spleen.

concepts.title: Warm AIHA – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Causes of warm AIHA: idiopathic, autoimmune disease (e.g. systemic lupus erythematosus), neoplasia, lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, drugs (e.g. methyldopa).

concepts.title: Warm AIHA – Management
concepts.content: Management of warm AIHA: treatment of any underlying disorder, steroids (+/- rituximab) are generally used first-line.

concepts.title: Cold AIHA – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: The antibody in cold AIHA is usually IgM and causes haemolysis best at 4 deg C. Haemolysis is mediated by complement and is more commonly intravascular.

concepts.title: Cold AIHA – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of cold AIHA may include symptoms of Raynaud's and acrocynaosis.

concepts.title: Cold AIHA – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Causes of cold AIHA: neoplasia (e.g. lymphoma), infections (e.g. mycoplasma, EBV).

concepts.title: Cold AIHA – Management
concepts.content: Patients with cold AIHA respond less well to steroids.

concepts.title: Hereditary angioedema – Definition
concepts.content: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is an autosomal dominant condition associated with low plasma levels of the C1 inhibitor (C1-INH, C1 esterase inhibitor) protein.

concepts.title: Hereditary angioedema – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) is a multifunctional serine protease inhibitor; the probable mechanism behind attacks in Hereditary angioedema is uncontrolled release of bradykinin resulting in oedema of tissues.

concepts.title: Hereditary angioedema – Investigations
concepts.content: During an attack of Hereditary angioedema, the C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) level is low.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Definition
concepts.content: Hereditary spherocytosis is the most common hereditary haemolytic anaemia in people of northern European descent.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Pathophysiology - Genetic basis
concepts.content: Hereditary spherocytosis is caused by autosomal dominant mutations affecting proteins that anchor the cytoskeleton to the plasma membrane, such as spectrin.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Pathophysiology - Red blood cell morphology
concepts.content: In hereditary spherocytosis, the normal biconcave disc shape of red blood cells is replaced by a sphere-shaped red blood cell.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Pathophysiology - Red blood cell destruction
concepts.content: Red blood cell survival is reduced in hereditary spherocytosis as they are destroyed by the spleen.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Pathophysiology - Splenic trapping
concepts.content: Spherocytes in hereditary spherocytosis cannot deform adequately to traverse the splenic cords, leading to them becoming trapped and destroyed by splenic macrophages (extravascular haemolysis).

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Clinical features - Failure to thrive
concepts.content: Patients with hereditary spherocytosis may present with failure to thrive.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Clinical features - Jaundice
concepts.content: Jaundice can be a clinical feature of hereditary spherocytosis.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Clinical features - Gallstones
concepts.content: Gallstones can be a clinical feature of hereditary spherocytosis.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Clinical features - Splenomegaly
concepts.content: Splenomegaly is a common clinical feature in hereditary spherocytosis.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Clinical features - Aplastic crisis
concepts.content: An aplastic crisis precipitated by parvovirus infection can occur in hereditary spherocytosis.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Clinical features - Haemolysis variability
concepts.content: The degree of haemolysis in hereditary spherocytosis is variable.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Clinical features - MCHC
concepts.content: In hereditary spherocytosis, the Mean Corpuscular Haemoglobin Concentration (MCHC) is elevated.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Diagnosis - Osmotic fragility test
concepts.content: The osmotic fragility test was previously recommended for diagnosing hereditary spherocytosis but is now deemed unreliable and no longer recommended.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Diagnosis - BJH guidelines for typical cases
concepts.content: The British Journal of Haematology (BJH) guidelines state that patients with a family history of Hereditary Spherocytosis (HS), typical clinical features (spherocytes, raised MCHC, increased reticulocytes) do not require any additional tests for diagnosis.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Diagnosis - BJH guidelines for equivocal cases
concepts.content: If the diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis is equivocal, the British Journal of Haematology (BJH) recommends the EMA binding test and the cryohaemolysis test.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Diagnosis - Atypical presentations
concepts.content: For atypical presentations of hereditary spherocytosis, electrophoresis analysis of erythrocyte membranes is the method of choice.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Management - Acute haemolytic crisis
concepts.content: During an acute haemolytic crisis in hereditary spherocytosis, treatment is generally supportive, and transfusion may be necessary.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Management - Folate replacement
concepts.content: Longer-term management for hereditary spherocytosis includes folate replacement.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – Management - Splenectomy
concepts.content: Splenectomy is a longer-term treatment option for hereditary spherocytosis.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Definition
concepts.content: Hodgkin's lymphoma is a malignant proliferation of lymphocytes characterised by the presence of the Reed-Sternberg cell. It has a bimodal age distribution, being most common in the third and seventh decades.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Histological Classification: Nodular Sclerosing
concepts.content: Nodular sclerosing is the most common histological type of Hodgkin's lymphoma, accounting for around 70% of cases. It is associated with a good prognosis, is more common in women, and is characterised by lacunar cells.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Histological Classification: Mixed Cellularity
concepts.content: Mixed cellularity accounts for around 20% of Hodgkin's lymphoma cases. It is associated with a good prognosis and a large number of Reed-Sternberg cells.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Histological Classification: Lymphocyte Predominant
concepts.content: Lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma accounts for around 5% of cases and is associated with the best prognosis.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Histological Classification: Lymphocyte Depleted
concepts.content: Lymphocyte depleted Hodgkin's lymphoma is rare and is associated with the worst prognosis.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: 'B' Symptoms
concepts.content: The presence of 'B' symptoms implies a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma. These symptoms include weight loss > 10% in the last 6 months, fever > 38ºC, and night sweats.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: Age
concepts.content: Age > 45 years is a factor associated with a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma, as identified in a 1998 NEJM paper.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: Disease Stage
concepts.content: Stage IV disease is a factor associated with a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma, as identified in a 1998 NEJM paper.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: Haemoglobin Level
concepts.content: A haemoglobin level < 10.5 g/dl is a factor associated with a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma, as identified in a 1998 NEJM paper.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: Lymphocyte Count
concepts.content: A lymphocyte count < 600/µl or < 8% is a factor associated with a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma, as identified in a 1998 NEJM paper.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: Gender
concepts.content: Being male is a factor associated with a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma, as identified in a 1998 NEJM paper.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: Albumin Level
concepts.content: An albumin level < 40 g/l is a factor associated with a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma, as identified in a 1998 NEJM paper.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Prognosis: White Blood Cell Count
concepts.content: A white blood count > 15,000/µl is a factor associated with a poor prognosis in Hodgkin's lymphoma, as identified in a 1998 NEJM paper.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Staging Imaging
concepts.content: Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) is the mainstay of imaging for staging Hodgkin's lymphoma.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Ann-Arbor Staging System Overview
concepts.content: The Ann-Arbor staging system was historically the main way patients with Hodgkin's lymphoma were staged.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Ann-Arbor Stage I
concepts.content: Ann-Arbor Stage I involves a single lymph node.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Ann-Arbor Stage II
concepts.content: Ann-Arbor Stage II involves 2 or more lymph nodes/regions on the same side of the diaphragm.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Ann-Arbor Stage III
concepts.content: Ann-Arbor Stage III involves nodes on both sides of the diaphragm.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Ann-Arbor Stage IV
concepts.content: Ann-Arbor Stage IV involves spread beyond lymph nodes.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Ann-Arbor Subdivision A
concepts.content: Ann-Arbor staging subdivision 'A' indicates no systemic symptoms other than pruritus.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Ann-Arbor Subdivision B
concepts.content: Ann-Arbor staging subdivision 'B' indicates weight loss > 10% in the last 6 months, fever > 38°C, or night sweats, which signifies a poor prognosis.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano Classification Overview
concepts.content: The Lugano classification is a system used to stage Hodgkin's lymphoma and other lymphomas, updating the Ann Arbor system by incorporating modern imaging techniques, particularly PET scans.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano Stage I
concepts.content: Lugano Stage I involves a single lymph node region (I) or a single extralymphatic organ or site (IE).

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano Stage II
concepts.content: Lugano Stage II involves two or more lymph node regions on the same side of the diaphragm (II) or localized involvement of an extralymphatic organ or site and one or more lymph node regions on the same side of the diaphragm (IIE).

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano Stage III
concepts.content: Lugano Stage III involves lymph node regions on both sides of the diaphragm (III), which may also be accompanied by localized involvement of an extralymphatic organ or site (IIIE), involvement of the spleen (IIIS), or both (IIIE+S).

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano Stage IV
concepts.content: Lugano Stage IV involves diffuse or disseminated involvement of one or more extralymphatic organs, with or without associated lymph node involvement.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano A/B Symptom Designation
concepts.content: In the Lugano classification, 'A' designates the absence of significant symptoms, while 'B' designates the presence of fever, night sweats, or weight loss.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano E Designation
concepts.content: In the Lugano classification, the letter 'E' denotes the presence of extranodal disease.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano S Designation
concepts.content: In the Lugano classification, the letter 'S' denotes involvement of the spleen.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano X Designation
concepts.content: In the Lugano classification, the letter 'X' denotes bulky disease (large tumor mass).

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Lugano Classification and PET Scans
concepts.content: The Lugano classification emphasizes the role of PET scans in determining the stage of Hodgkin's lymphoma, particularly in assessing metabolic activity.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Management Mainstay
concepts.content: Chemotherapy is the mainstay of treatment for Hodgkin's lymphoma.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – ABVD Chemotherapy Regimen
concepts.content: ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine) is considered the standard chemotherapy regimen for Hodgkin's lymphoma.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – BEACOPP Chemotherapy Regimen
concepts.content: BEACOPP (bleomycin, etoposide, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, procarbazine, and prednisone) is an alternative chemotherapy regimen for Hodgkin's lymphoma with better remission rates but higher toxicity.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Radiotherapy
concepts.content: Radiotherapy is a treatment option for Hodgkin's lymphoma.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Combined Modality Therapy (CMT)
concepts.content: Combined modality therapy (CMT), involving chemotherapy followed by radiotherapy, is used in the management of Hodgkin's lymphoma.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation
concepts.content: Hematopoietic cell transplantation may be used for relapsed or refractory classic Hodgkin lymphoma.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Complications of Treatment (Long-term Survival)
concepts.content: Most patients with Hodgkin's lymphoma now achieve long-term survival free of the disease with modern therapy, making complications of treatment a significant concern.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Complications of Treatment (Secondary Malignancies)
concepts.content: Secondary malignancies, particularly solid tumors such as breast and lung cancer, are a risk associated with Hodgkin's lymphoma treatment.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism – Definition
concepts.content: Hyposplenism refers to reduced splenic function.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Causes of hyposplenism include splenectomy, sickle-cell anaemia, coeliac disease, dermatitis herpetiformis, Graves' disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and amyloidosis.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism – Clinical features
concepts.content: Blood film features of hyposplenism include Howell-Jolly bodies and siderocytes.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Definition
concepts.content: Immune (or idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is an immune-mediated reduction in the platelet count. Antibodies are directed against the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa or Ib-V-IX complex.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Epidemiology - Adult vs. Childhood
concepts.content: Children with ITP usually have an acute thrombocytopenia that may follow infection or vaccination. In contrast, adults tend to have a more chronic condition.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is more common in older females.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Clinical features - Incidental finding
concepts.content: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) may be detected incidentally following routine blood tests.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Clinical features - Petechiae/Purpura
concepts.content: Symptomatic patients with Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) may present with petechiae and purpura.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Clinical features - Bleeding
concepts.content: Symptomatic patients with Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) may present with bleeding, such as epistaxis.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Clinical features - Catastrophic bleeding
concepts.content: Catastrophic bleeding, such as intracranial bleeding, is not a common presentation of Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Investigations - Full Blood Count
concepts.content: A full blood count in Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) typically shows isolated thrombocytopenia.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Investigations - Bone Marrow Examination
concepts.content: A bone marrow examination is no longer routinely used in the investigation of Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Investigations - Antiplatelet Antibody Testing
concepts.content: Antiplatelet antibody testing for Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) has poor sensitivity and does not affect clinical management, so it is not commonly performed.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Management - First-line treatment
concepts.content: The first-line treatment for Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is oral prednisolone.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Management - IVIG
concepts.content: Pooled normal human immunoglobulin (IVIG) may be used in Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) if active bleeding or an urgent invasive procedure is required, as it raises the platelet count quicker than steroids.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Management - Splenectomy
concepts.content: Splenectomy is now less commonly used in the management of Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Evan's Syndrome
concepts.content: Evan's syndrome is characterized by Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) in association with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA).

concepts.title: Iron deficiency anaemia – Definition
concepts.content: Iron deficiency anaemia is the most common anaemia worldwide. Iron is needed to make the haemoglobin in red blood cells, therefore a deficiency of iron leads to a reduction in red blood cells/haemoglobin i.e. anaemia.

concepts.title: Iron deficiency anaemia – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Globally, iron deficiency is the most common cause of anaemia. Preschool-age children have the highest prevalence of iron deficiency anaemia.

concepts.title: Iron deficiency anaemia – Serum iron
concepts.content: In Iron deficiency anaemia, serum iron is low, typically less than 8.

concepts.title: Anaemia of chronic disease – Serum iron
concepts.content: In Anaemia of chronic disease, serum iron is low, typically less than 15.

concepts.title: Iron deficiency anaemia – TIBC
concepts.content: In Iron deficiency anaemia, Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) is high.

concepts.title: Anaemia of chronic disease – TIBC
concepts.content: In Anaemia of chronic disease, Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) is low.

concepts.title: Iron deficiency anaemia – Transferrin saturation
concepts.content: In Iron deficiency anaemia, transferrin saturation is low.

concepts.title: Anaemia of chronic disease – Transferrin saturation
concepts.content: In Anaemia of chronic disease, transferrin saturation is low.

concepts.title: Iron deficiency anaemia – Ferritin
concepts.content: In Iron deficiency anaemia, ferritin is low.

concepts.title: Anaemia of chronic disease – Ferritin
concepts.content: In Anaemia of chronic disease, ferritin is high.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Investigations: Antiplatelet autoantibodies
concepts.content: Antiplatelet autoantibodies (usually IgG) are investigated in Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Investigations: Bone marrow aspiration
concepts.content: Bone marrow aspiration shows megakaryocytes in the marrow in Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). This should be carried out prior to the commencement of steroids in order to rule out leukaemia.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Management: Oral prednisolone
concepts.content: Oral prednisolone is a first-line treatment for Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), with 80% of patients responding.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Management: Splenectomy
concepts.content: Splenectomy is considered for Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) if platelets are < 30 after 3 months of steroid therapy.

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Management: IV immunoglobulins
concepts.content: IV immunoglobulins can be used in the management of Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

concepts.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura – Management: Immunosuppressive drugs
concepts.content: Immunosuppressive drugs, such as cyclophosphamide, are used in the management of Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

concepts.title: Intravascular haemolysis – Haptoglobin decrease
concepts.content: Haptoglobin binds to free haemoglobin. A decrease in haptoglobin is an interpretation of intravascular haemolysis.

concepts.title: Hereditary spherocytosis – MCHC increased
concepts.content: Increased MCHC is a laboratory finding in hereditary spherocytosis.

concepts.title: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – MCHC increased
concepts.content: Increased MCHC is a laboratory finding in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, associated with spherocytosis.

concepts.title: Microcytic anaemia – MCHC decreased
concepts.content: Decreased MCHC is a laboratory finding in microcytic anaemia (e.g., iron deficiency).

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Definition
concepts.content: Lead poisoning is the result of lead, a heavy metal, building up in the body, often over months or years. Even small amounts of lead can cause serious health problems.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Vulnerable populations
concepts.content: Children younger than age 6 are especially vulnerable to lead poisoning, which can severely affect how a child's body grows and brain develops.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Common sources in children
concepts.content: Lead-based paint and lead-contaminated dust in older buildings are common sources of lead poisoning in children. Other sources include contaminated air, water and soil.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Occupational exposure
concepts.content: Adults who work with batteries, do home renovations or work in auto repair shops might be exposed to lead.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Lead in paint
concepts.content: Lead-based paints for homes, children's toys and household furniture have been banned in the United States since 1978. Most lead poisoning in children results from eating chips of deteriorating lead-based paint.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Water pipes and canned goods
concepts.content: Lead pipes, brass plumbing fixtures and copper pipes soldered with lead can release lead particles into tap water. Lead solder in food cans, banned in the United States, is still used in some countries.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Soil contamination
concepts.content: Lead particles from leaded gasoline or paint settle on soil and can last years. Lead-contaminated soil is still a major problem around highways and in some urban settings.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Household dust
concepts.content: Household dust can contain lead from lead paint chips or from contaminated soil brought in from outside.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Pottery
concepts.content: Glazes found on some ceramics, china and porcelain can contain lead that can leach into food served or stored in the pottery.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Toys
concepts.content: Lead is sometimes found in toys and other products produced abroad.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Cosmetics
concepts.content: Tiro, an eye cosmetic from Nigeria, has been linked to lead poisoning. Kohl is another eye makeup that may contain lead.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Herbal or folk remedies
concepts.content: Lead poisoning has been linked to greta and azarcon, traditional Hispanic medicines, as well as some from India, China and other countries.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Tamarind candy
concepts.content: Some candies made with the tropical fruit tamarind have been found to contain lead, possibly due to how the candy was processed or stored.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Lead bullets
concepts.content: Time spent at firing ranges can lead to exposure to lead.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Cause: Occupations
concepts.content: People are exposed to lead and can bring it home on their clothes when they work in auto repair, mining, pipe fitting, battery manufacturing, painting, construction and certain other fields.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Risk factor: Age
concepts.content: Infants and young children are more likely to be exposed to lead than are older children. They might chew paint that flakes off walls and woodwork, and their hands can be contaminated with lead dust. Young children also absorb lead more easily, and it's more harmful for them than it is for adults and older children.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Risk factor: Living in an older home
concepts.content: Although the use of lead-based paints has been banned since the 1970s, older homes and buildings often retain remnants of this paint. People renovating an older home are at even higher risk.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Risk factor: Certain hobbies
concepts.content: Making stained glass and some jewelry requires the use of lead solder. Refinishing old furniture might put you in contact with layers of lead paint.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Risk factor: Living in developing countries
concepts.content: Developing countries often have less strict rules regarding exposure to lead than do developed countries. American families who adopt a child from another country might want to have the child's blood tested for lead poisoning.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Risk factor: Pregnancy
concepts.content: Lead can harm an unborn child. If you're pregnant or planning a pregnancy, be especially careful to avoid exposure to lead.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Developmental delay
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include developmental delay.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Learning difficulties
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include learning difficulties.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Irritability
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include irritability.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Loss of appetite
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include loss of appetite.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Weight loss
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include weight loss.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Sluggishness and fatigue
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include sluggishness and fatigue.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Abdominal pain
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include abdominal pain.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Vomiting
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include vomiting.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Constipation
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include constipation.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Hearing loss
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include hearing loss.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in children: Seizures
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in children include seizures.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in newborns: Premature birth
concepts.content: Babies exposed to lead before birth might be born early.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in newborns: Low birth weight
concepts.content: Babies exposed to lead before birth might have lower birth weight.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in newborns: Slowed growth
concepts.content: Babies exposed to lead before birth might have slowed growth.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: High blood pressure
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include high blood pressure.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: Joint and muscle pain
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include joint and muscle pain.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: Difficulties with memory or concentration
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include difficulties with memory or concentration.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: Headache
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include headache.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: Abdominal pain
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include abdominal pain.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: Mood disorders
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include mood disorders.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: Reduced sperm count and abnormal sperm
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include reduced sperm count and abnormal sperm.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Clinical features in adults: Miscarriage, stillbirth or premature birth
concepts.content: Signs and symptoms of lead poisoning in adults might include miscarriage, stillbirth or premature birth.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Investigation: Blood test
concepts.content: A blood test can be used to check the blood lead level.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Investigation: Basophilic stippling
concepts.content: Basophilic stippling on a blood film is associated with lead poisoning.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Complication: Brain development damage in children
concepts.content: The greatest risk of lead poisoning in children is to brain development, where damage that can't be reversed can happen.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Complication: Kidney and nervous system damage
concepts.content: High lead levels can damage the kidneys and nervous system in both children and adults.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Complication: Seizures, unconsciousness and death
concepts.content: Very high lead levels may cause seizures, unconsciousness and death.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Prevention: Wash hands and toys
concepts.content: To help reduce hand-to-mouth transfer of contaminated dust or soil, wash children's hands after outdoor play, before eating and at bedtime. Wash their toys regularly.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Prevention: Clean dusty surfaces
concepts.content: Clean floors with a wet mop and wipe furniture, windowsills and other dusty surfaces with a damp cloth.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Prevention: Remove shoes before entering the house
concepts.content: Remove shoes before entering the house to help keep lead-based soil outside.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Prevention: Run cold water
