concepts.content: If you have older plumbing containing lead pipes or fittings, run your cold water for at least a minute before using. Don't use hot tap water to make baby formula or for cooking.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Prevention: Keep children from playing on soil
concepts.content: Provide children with a sandbox that's covered when not in use. Plant grass or cover bare soil with mulch.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Prevention: Choose healthy foods
concepts.content: Regular meals and good nutrition might help lower lead absorption. Children especially need enough calcium, vitamin C and iron in their diets to help keep lead from being absorbed.

concepts.title: Lead poisoning – Prevention: Maintain painted surfaces in your home
concepts.content: If your home has lead-based paint, check regularly for peeling paint and fix problems promptly. Try not to sand, which generates dust particles that contain lead.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Definition
concepts.content: Lymphadenopathy refers to the condition of enlarged lymph nodes, typically indicating an immune response to an infection or malignancy. Understanding its underlying causes and appropriate management is crucial in patient care.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Background: Lymphatic System Function
concepts.content: The lymphatic system, comprising lymph vessels, nodes, and other tissues, plays a critical role in body's immunity. Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures that produce and store cells that fight infection and disease. They filter the lymph fluid as it flows through them, trapping bacteria, viruses, and other foreign substances to be destroyed by white blood cells.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Background: Mechanism of Enlargement
concepts.content: Lymphadenopathy usually occurs when lymph nodes produce more cells or become filled with debris from a destroyed cell.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: Infectious Mononucleosis
concepts.content: Infectious mononucleosis can cause lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: HIV
concepts.content: HIV, including seroconversion illness, can cause lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: Eczema with Secondary Infection
concepts.content: Eczema with secondary infection can cause lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: Rubella
concepts.content: Rubella can cause lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: Toxoplasmosis
concepts.content: Toxoplasmosis can cause lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: CMV
concepts.content: CMV can cause lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: Tuberculosis
concepts.content: Tuberculosis can cause lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Infective Causes: Roseola Infantum
concepts.content: Roseola infantum can cause lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Neoplastic Causes: Leukaemia
concepts.content: Leukaemia can cause lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Neoplastic Causes: Lymphoma
concepts.content: Lymphoma can cause lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Other Causes: Autoimmune Conditions
concepts.content: Autoimmune conditions such as SLE and rheumatoid arthritis can cause lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Other Causes: Graft Versus Host Disease
concepts.content: Graft versus host disease can cause lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Other Causes: Sarcoidosis
concepts.content: Sarcoidosis can cause lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Lymphadenopathy – Other Causes: Drugs
concepts.content: Drugs such as phenytoin, allopurinol, and isoniazid can cause lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Clinical Features: Lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: Lymphadenopathy is a clinical feature of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, presenting as a persistent or progressive, painless, firm, rubbery lymph node.

concepts.title: Castleman's disease – Clinical Features: Lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: Painless lymph node enlargement can occur in any lymph node group, commonly in the neck, axillae, or inguinal areas, with nodes being firm and non-tender on examination.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Clinical Features: Lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: Lymphadenopathy is a common feature of Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, often presenting as painless enlargement of peripheral lymph nodes which are usually symmetrical and non-tender.

concepts.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia – Rai Staging: Stage I
concepts.content: Rai stage I of Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is characterized by lymphadenopathy and has an overall survival of 7 years.

concepts.title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Clinical Features: Lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: In Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, lymphadenopathy can occur anywhere in the body, including the groin and abdomen.

concepts.title: Hodgkin's lymphoma – Clinical Features: Lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: In Hodgkin's lymphoma, lymphadenopathy is usually limited to the upper body (neck, chest, or axilla) and can experience alcohol-induced pain in the node.

concepts.title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome – Clinical Features: Lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: Lymphadenopathy is a clinical feature of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

concepts.title: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia – Clinical Features: Lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: Painless lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly may be found on physical examination in Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia, due to infiltration of the disease into lymphoid tissues.

concepts.title: Suspected Haematological Malignancy in Young People – Clinical Features: Generalised Lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: Generalised lymphadenopathy in a person aged 0-24 years should prompt a very urgent full blood count (within 48 hours) to investigate for leukaemia.

concepts.title: Macrocytic anaemia – Definition
concepts.content: Macrocytic anaemia can be divided into causes associated with a megaloblastic bone marrow and those with a normoblastic bone marrow.

concepts.title: Macrocytic anaemia – Megaloblastic Aetiology
concepts.content: Megaloblastic causes of macrocytic anaemia include vitamin B12 deficiency and folate deficiency (e.g., secondary to methotrexate).

concepts.title: Macrocytic anaemia – Normoblastic Aetiology
concepts.content: Normoblastic causes of macrocytic anaemia include alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, reticulocytosis, myelodysplasia, and cytotoxic drugs.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Management
concepts.content: Any of the following features in a person aged 0-24 years should prompt a very urgent full blood count (within 48 hours) to investigate for leukaemia: Pallor

concepts.title: Methaemoglobinaemia – Definition and Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Methaemoglobinaemia describes haemoglobin which has been oxidised from Fe2+ to Fe3+. This is normally regulated by NADH methaemoglobin reductase, which transfers electrons from NADH to methaemoglobin resulting in the reduction of methaemoglobin to haemoglobin. There is tissue hypoxia as Fe3+ cannot bind oxygen, and hence the oxidation dissociation curve is moved to the left.

concepts.title: Methaemoglobinaemia – Congenital Aetiology
concepts.content: Congenital causes of methaemoglobinaemia include haemoglobin chain variants (HbM, HbH) and NADH methaemoglobin reductase deficiency.

concepts.title: Methaemoglobinaemia – Association with G6PD Deficiency
concepts.content: Some variants of G6PD deficiency have been associated with methaemoglobinaemia, leading to cyanosis and dyspnoea.

concepts.title: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance – Definition
concepts.content: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), also known as benign paraproteinaemia and monoclonal gammopathy, is a common condition that causes a paraproteinaemia and is often mistaken for myeloma.

concepts.title: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance – Prognosis
concepts.content: Around 10% of patients with MGUS eventually develop myeloma at 10 years, with 50% at 15 years.

concepts.title: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance – Non-IgM MGUS
concepts.content: Non-IgM MGUS is the most common subtype and may progress to multiple myeloma or AL amyloidosis.

concepts.title: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance – IgM MGUS
concepts.content: IgM MGUS may progress to Waldenström macroglobulinaemia or lymphoma.

concepts.title: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance – Light chain MGUS
concepts.content: Light chain MGUS has an increased risk of renal disease or AL amyloidosis.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Definition
concepts.content: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a heterogeneous group of clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorders characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis, peripheral blood cytopenias, and a risk of progression to acute myeloid leukaemia (AML).

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) predominantly affect older adults, with a median age at diagnosis of 70-75 years.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Aetiology
concepts.content: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) arise from genetic mutations in hematopoietic stem cells.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Risk factors
concepts.content: Around 90% of Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) cases are primary, with the remaining 10% secondary to causes such as chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Secondary MDS typically develops around 5 years post-treatment.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: The key pathophysiological feature of Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is ineffective hematopoiesis leading to peripheral cytopenias despite a typically hypercellular bone marrow.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Clinical features: Anaemia
concepts.content: Common presentations of Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) include fatigue, weakness, and pallor due to anaemia.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Clinical features: Neutropenia
concepts.content: Common presentations of Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) include recurrent infections due to neutropenia.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Clinical features: Thrombocytopenia
concepts.content: Common presentations of Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) include easy bruising or bleeding due to thrombocytopenia.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Clinical features: Asymptomatic
concepts.content: Some patients with Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) may be asymptomatic and are diagnosed incidentally on routine blood counts.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Diagnosis: Overview
concepts.content: The diagnosis of Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is based on peripheral blood counts, bone marrow examination, and cytogenetic analysis.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Diagnosis: Bone marrow biopsy
concepts.content: Bone marrow biopsy in Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) typically shows dysplastic changes in hematopoietic cells and a varying degree of blasts.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Diagnosis: Cytogenetic analysis
concepts.content: Cytogenetic analysis in Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) can identify specific chromosomal abnormalities that may have prognostic implications.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Management: Overview
concepts.content: Treatment of Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) depends on the subtype of MDS, the patient's age and overall health, and the severity of symptoms.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Management: Supportive care
concepts.content: Management options for Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) include supportive care, such as blood transfusions and growth factors.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Management: Disease-modifying therapy
concepts.content: Management options for Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) include disease-modifying therapy, such as hypomethylating agents and lenalidomide.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Management: Immunosuppressive therapy
concepts.content: Management options for Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) include immunosuppressive therapy.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic syndrome – Management: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
concepts.content: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only potentially curative option for Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), but it is limited by the patient's age and comorbidities.

concepts.title: Myelofibrosis – Definition
concepts.content: Myelofibrosis is a rare haematologic myeloproliferative disorder characterized by the replacement of bone marrow with collagen and fibrosis. It results in haematological abnormalities, profound fatigue, massive splenomegaly, and extramedullary haematopoiesis. The disease may transform into acute myeloid leukaemia.

concepts.title: Myelofibrosis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Myelofibrosis is thought to be caused by hyperplasia of abnormal megakaryocytes. The resultant release of platelet-derived growth factor is believed to stimulate fibroblasts, leading to bone marrow fibrosis. Haematopoiesis develops in the liver and spleen (extramedullary haematopoiesis).

concepts.title: Myelofibrosis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Myelofibrosis has an incidence of 0.40 cases per 100,000 person-years. It typically affects older adults, with a peak incidence between 60-70 years. The sex ratio is 1:1. The median survival is 6 years.

concepts.title: Myelofibrosis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Myelofibrosis typically manifests in the 50 and older age group, though cases have been reported in children. There is a familial relationship and a preponderance in Ashkenazi Jews. Genes implicated include JAK2, MPL, and CALR.

concepts.title: Myelofibrosis – Clinical features: Anaemia
concepts.content: Myelofibrosis can present with symptoms of anaemia, such as fatigue, which is the most common presenting symptom, and pallor.

concepts.title: Myelofibrosis – Clinical features: Splenomegaly
concepts.content: Patients with Myelofibrosis often present with massive splenomegaly.

concepts.title: Myelofibrosis – Clinical features: Hypermetabolic symptoms
concepts.content: Hypermetabolic symptoms in Myelofibrosis include weight loss and night sweats.

concepts.title: Myelofibrosis – Laboratory findings: Anaemia
concepts.content: Laboratory findings in Myelofibrosis include anaemia.

concepts.title: Myelofibrosis – Laboratory findings: White blood cell and platelet count
concepts.content: Early in the disease, Myelofibrosis may show high white blood cell (WBC) and platelet counts.

concepts.title: Myelofibrosis – Laboratory findings: Blood film
concepts.content: A blood film in Myelofibrosis typically shows 'tear-drop' poikilocytes and multiple forms of immature red cells.

concepts.title: Myelofibrosis – Laboratory findings: Bone marrow biopsy
concepts.content: Bone marrow aspirate in Myelofibrosis is usually a 'dry tap', meaning it is unobtainable. A trephine biopsy is therefore needed to demonstrate marked fibrosis.

concepts.title: Myelofibrosis – Laboratory findings: Urate and LDH
concepts.content: Myelofibrosis is associated with high urate and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels, reflecting increased cell turnover.

concepts.title: Neutropenia – Definition
concepts.content: Neutropenia is characterized by low functional neutrophils, which can occur even if total white cell counts are high, leading to recurrent or severe infections.

concepts.title: Neutropenia – Severe Neutropenia Definition
concepts.content: Severe neutropenia is defined as an absolute neutrophil count of <500 cells/µL, which is associated with a high risk of infections.

concepts.title: Neutropenia – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Neutropenia leads to recurrent or severe infections.

concepts.title: Neutropenia – Management
concepts.content: Patients with neutropenia may require antibiotic prophylaxis.

concepts.title: Acute Myeloid Leukaemia – Clinical Features
concepts.content: In Acute Myeloid Leukaemia, neutropenia can lead to recurrent or severe infections.

concepts.title: Myelodysplastic Syndrome – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Recurrent infections due to neutropenia are common presentations of Myelodysplastic Syndrome.

concepts.title: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: In Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia, abnormal lymphoblasts alter the bone marrow niche, leading to cytopenias such as neutropenia, which causes associated clinical symptoms like infections.

concepts.title: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia – Clinical Features
concepts.content: In Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia, bone marrow infiltration can lead to neutropenia, resulting in susceptibility to infections.

concepts.title: Chemotherapy – Complications
concepts.content: Myelosuppression, a common complication of chemotherapy, leads to neutropenia, increasing susceptibility to infections.

concepts.title: Neutropenic sepsis – Definition
concepts.content: Neutropenic sepsis is a relatively common complication of cancer therapy, usually as a consequence of chemotherapy. It most commonly occurs 7-14 days after chemotherapy. It may be defined as a neutrophil count of < 0.5 * 109 in a patient who is having anticancer treatment and has one of the following: a temperature higher than 38ºC or other signs or symptoms consistent with clinically significant sepsis

concepts.title: Neutropenic sepsis – Aetiology
concepts.content: coagulase-negative, Gram-positive bacteria are the most common cause, particularly Staphylococcus epidermidis. this is probably due to the use of indwelling lines in patients with cancer

concepts.title: Neutropenic sepsis – Prophylaxis
concepts.content: if it is anticipated that patients are likely to have a neutrophil count of < 0.5 * 109 as a consequence of their treatment they should be offered a fluoroquinolone

concepts.title: Neutropenic sepsis – Initial empirical antibiotic therapy
concepts.content: antibiotics must be started immediately, do not wait for the WBC. NICE recommends starting empirical antibiotic therapy with piperacillin with tazobactam (Tazocin) immediately

concepts.title: Neutropenic sepsis – Vancomycin in central venous access
concepts.content: many units add vancomycin if the patient has central venous access but NICE do not support this approach

concepts.title: Neutropenic sepsis – Outpatient assessment and risk stratification
concepts.content: following this initial treatment patients are usually assessed by a specialist and risk-stratified to see if they may be able to have outpatient treatment

concepts.title: Neutropenic sepsis – Alternative antibiotics for non-response
concepts.content: if patients are still febrile and unwell after 48 hours an alternative antibiotic such as meropenem is often prescribed +/- vancomycin

concepts.title: Neutropenic sepsis – Investigations for fungal infections
concepts.content: if patients are not responding after 4-6 days the Christie guidelines suggest ordering investigations for fungal infections (e.g. HRCT), rather than just starting therapy antifungal therapy blindly

concepts.title: Neutropenic sepsis – Role of G-CSF
concepts.content: there may be a role for G-CSF in selected patients

concepts.title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Definition
concepts.content: Lymphoma is the malignant proliferation of lymphocytes which accumulate in lymph nodes or other organs. Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is every type of lymphoma that is not Hodgkin's lymphoma. Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma may affect either B or T-cells and can be further classified as high grade or low grade.

concepts.title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is the 6th most common cause of cancer in the UK.

concepts.title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Risk factors
concepts.content: Elderly age is a risk factor for Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

concepts.title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Clinical features
concepts.content: Painless lymphadenopathy (non-tender, rubbery, asymmetrical) is a symptom of Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

concepts.title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Investigations
concepts.content: Excisional node biopsy is the diagnostic investigation of choice for Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

concepts.title: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma – Staging
concepts.content: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is staged using the Lugano staging system.

concepts.title: Normocytic anaemia – Anaemia of chronic disease
concepts.content: Anaemia of chronic disease is a cause of normocytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Normocytic anaemia – Chronic kidney disease
concepts.content: Chronic kidney disease is a cause of normocytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Normocytic anaemia – Aplastic anaemia
concepts.content: Aplastic anaemia is a cause of normocytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Normocytic anaemia – Haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: Haemolytic anaemia is a cause of normocytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Normocytic anaemia – Acute blood loss
concepts.content: Acute blood loss is a cause of normocytic anaemia.

concepts.title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Definition
concepts.content: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) is an acquired disorder leading to haemolysis (mainly intravascular) of haematological cells. It is thought to be caused by increased sensitivity of cell membranes to complement due to a lack of glycoprotein glycosyl-phosphatidylinositol (GPI).

concepts.title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is thought to be caused by increased sensitivity of cell membranes to complement due to a lack of glycoprotein glycosyl-phosphatidylinositol (GPI).

concepts.title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients are more prone to venous thrombosis.

concepts.title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: GPI can be thought of as an anchor which attaches surface proteins to the cell membrane.

concepts.title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Complications
concepts.content: Aplastic anaemia may develop in some patients with Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

concepts.title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Investigations
concepts.content: Flow cytometry of blood to detect low levels of CD59 and CD55 has now replaced Ham's test as the gold standard investigation in PNH.

concepts.title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria – Management
concepts.content: Blood product replacement is a management strategy for Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

concepts.title: Platelet transfusion – Indication (Active Bleeding)
concepts.content: Platelet transfusion may be used if active bleeding or an urgent invasive procedure is required, as it raises the platelet count quicker than steroids.

concepts.title: Platelet transfusion – Emergency Management (Severe Bleeding)
concepts.content: For emergency situations involving severe bleeding or critically low platelet counts, immediate intervention includes high-dose IVIg and/or platelet transfusions.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia – Definition and Classification
concepts.content: Polycythaemia is a condition that may be classified as relative, primary (polycythaemia rubra vera), or secondary.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia – Relative Causes
concepts.content: Relative causes of polycythaemia include dehydration and stress (Gaisbock syndrome).

concepts.title: Polycythaemia – Primary Cause
concepts.content: The primary cause of polycythaemia is polycythaemia rubra vera.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia – Secondary Causes
concepts.content: Secondary causes of polycythaemia include COPD, altitude, obstructive sleep apnoea, and excessive erythropoietin production due to conditions such as cerebellar haemangioma, hypernephroma, hepatoma, and uterine fibroids.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia – Red Cell Mass Studies
concepts.content: Red cell mass studies are used to differentiate between true (primary or secondary) polycythaemia and relative polycythaemia. In true polycythaemia, the total red cell mass is > 35 ml/kg in males and > 32 ml/kg in women.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Definition
concepts.content: Polycythaemia vera is a myeloproliferative disorder caused by clonal proliferation of a marrow stem cell leading to an increase in red cell volume, often accompanied by overproduction of neutrophils and platelets.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Genetics
concepts.content: A mutation in JAK2 is present in approximately 95% of patients with polycythaemia vera.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Epidemiology
concepts.content: The incidence of polycythaemia vera peaks in the sixth decade.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Clinical features
concepts.content: Pruritus, typically after a hot bath, is a feature of Polycythaemia vera.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Investigations
concepts.content: The British Committee for Standards in Haematology (BCSH) recommends a full blood count/film, which may show raised haematocrit; neutrophils, basophils, and platelets raised in half of patients.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Investigations (JAK2 negative)
concepts.content: If JAK2 mutation is negative and there are no obvious secondary causes, the BCSH suggests red cell mass testing.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Other features
concepts.content: A raised leukocyte alkaline phosphatase may be seen in Polycythaemia vera.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Diagnostic Criteria (JAK2-positive)
concepts.content: For JAK2-positive polycythaemia vera, diagnosis requires high haematocrit (>0.52 in men, >0.48 in women) OR raised red cell mass (>25% above predicted).

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Diagnostic Criteria (JAK2-negative)
concepts.content: For JAK2-negative PRV, diagnosis requires raised red cell mass (>25% above predicted) OR haematocrit >0.60 in men, >0.56 in women.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Management - Aspirin
concepts.content: Aspirin reduces the risk of thrombotic events in Polycythaemia vera.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Management - Venesection
concepts.content: Venesection is the first-line treatment to keep the haemoglobin in the normal range for Polycythaemia vera.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Management - Chemotherapy (Hydroxyurea)
concepts.content: Hydroxyurea is a chemotherapy option for Polycythaemia vera, with a slight increased risk of secondary leukaemia.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Management - Chemotherapy (Phosphorus-32)
concepts.content: Phosphorus-32 therapy is a chemotherapy option for Polycythaemia vera.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Prognosis - Thrombotic events
concepts.content: Thrombotic events are a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in Polycythaemia vera.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Prognosis - Progression to myelofibrosis
concepts.content: 5-15% of patients with Polycythaemia vera progress to myelofibrosis.

concepts.title: Polycythaemia vera – Prognosis - Progression to acute leukaemia
concepts.content: 5-15% of patients with Polycythaemia vera progress to acute leukaemia (risk increased with chemotherapy treatment).

concepts.title: Post-thrombotic syndrome – Definition
concepts.content: Post-thrombotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome that patients may develop following a DVT, resulting from venous outflow obstruction and venous insufficiency leading to chronic venous hypertension.

concepts.title: Post-thrombotic syndrome – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Post-thrombotic syndrome develops following a Deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

concepts.title: Post-thrombotic syndrome – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Venous outflow obstruction and venous insufficiency lead to chronic venous hypertension in post-thrombotic syndrome.

concepts.title: Post-thrombotic syndrome – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients with post-thrombotic syndrome may experience painful, heavy calves.

concepts.title: Post-thrombotic syndrome – Management
concepts.content: Compression stockings are not recommended to reduce the risk of post-thrombotic syndrome following a deep vein thrombosis.

concepts.title: Venous thromboembolism - Pregnancy as a risk factor
concepts.content: Pregnancy is a common predisposing factor for venous thromboembolism (VTE).

concepts.title: Venous thromboembolism - Puerperium as a risk factor
concepts.content: The puerperium period is a common predisposing factor for venous thromboembolism (VTE).

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Classification
concepts.content: Primary immunodeficiency disorders are classified according to which component of the immune system they affect.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Chronic granulomatous disease: Underlying defect
concepts.content: Chronic granulomatous disease is caused by a lack of NADPH oxidase, which reduces the ability of phagocytes to produce reactive oxygen species.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Chronic granulomatous disease: Clinical features
concepts.content: Chronic granulomatous disease causes recurrent pneumonias and abscesses, particularly due to catalase-positive bacteria (e.g. Staphylococcus aureus) and fungi (e.g. Aspergillus).

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Chronic granulomatous disease: Investigations
concepts.content: Chronic granulomatous disease is diagnosed by a negative nitroblue-tetrazolium test and an abnormal dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry test.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Chediak-Higashi syndrome: Underlying defect
concepts.content: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by a defect in lysosomal trafficking regulator protein.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Chediak-Higashi syndrome: Clinical features
concepts.content: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is characterized by giant granules in neutrophils and platelets.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Leukocyte adhesion deficiency: Underlying defect
concepts.content: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency is caused by a defect of LFA-1 integrin (CD18) protein on neutrophils.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Leukocyte adhesion deficiency: Clinical features
concepts.content: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency presents with recurrent bacterial infections, delay in umbilical cord sloughing, and absence of neutrophils/pus at sites of infection.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Common variable immunodeficiency: Underlying defect
concepts.content: Common variable immunodeficiency has many varying causes, leading to low antibody levels, specifically in immunoglobulin (Ig) types IgG, IgM and IgA.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Common variable immunodeficiency: Clinical features
concepts.content: Common variable immunodeficiency presents with recurrent chest infections and may predispose to autoimmune disorders and lymphoma.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Bruton's (x-linked) congenital agammaglobulinaemia: Underlying defect
concepts.content: Bruton's (x-linked) congenital agammaglobulinaemia is an X-linked recessive condition caused by a defect in the Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene, leading to a severe block in B cell development.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Bruton's (x-linked) congenital agammaglobulinaemia: Clinical features
concepts.content: Bruton's (x-linked) congenital agammaglobulinaemia presents with recurrent bacterial infections and absence of B-cells with reduced immunoglobulins of all classes.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Selective immunoglobulin A deficiency: Underlying defect
concepts.content: Selective immunoglobulin A deficiency is caused by a maturation defect in B cells.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Selective immunoglobulin A deficiency: Clinical features
concepts.content: Selective immunoglobulin A deficiency is the most common primary antibody deficiency, presenting with recurrent sinus and respiratory infections. It is associated with coeliac disease and may cause false negative coeliac antibody screens. Severe reactions to blood transfusions may occur (anti-IgA antibodies → anaphylaxis).

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – DiGeorge syndrome: Underlying defect
concepts.content: DiGeorge syndrome is caused by a 22q11.2 deletion, leading to failure to develop the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – DiGeorge syndrome: Clinical features
concepts.content: Common features of DiGeorge syndrome include congenital heart disease (e.g. tetralogy of Fallot), learning difficulties, hypocalcaemia, recurrent viral/fungal diseases, and cleft palate.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Severe combined immunodeficiency: Underlying defect
concepts.content: Severe combined immunodeficiency has many varying causes; the most common (X-linked) is due to a defect in the common gamma chain, a protein used in the receptors for IL-2 and other interleukins. Other causes include adenosine deaminase deficiency.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Severe combined immunodeficiency: Clinical features
concepts.content: Severe combined immunodeficiency presents with recurrent infections due to viruses, bacteria, and fungi, and reduced T-cell receptor excision circles. Stem cell transplantation may be successful.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Ataxic telangiectasia: Underlying defect
concepts.content: Ataxic telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive condition caused by a defect in DNA repair enzymes.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Ataxic telangiectasia: Clinical features
concepts.content: Ataxic telangiectasia features include cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasia (spider angiomas), recurrent chest infections, and a 10% risk of developing malignancy, lymphoma or leukaemia.

concepts.title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome – Underlying defect
concepts.content: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is inherited in an X-linked recessive fashion and is caused by a mutation in the WASP gene.

concepts.title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome – Clinical features
concepts.content: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome causes primary immunodeficiency due to combined B- and T-cell dysfunction. Features include recurrent bacterial infections (e.g. chest), eczema, thrombocytopaenia, and low IgM levels. There is an increased risk of autoimmune disorders and malignancy.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Hyper IgM Syndromes: Underlying defect
concepts.content: Hyper IgM Syndromes are caused by mutations in the CD40 gene.

concepts.title: Primary immunodeficiency – Hyper IgM Syndromes: Clinical features
concepts.content: Hyper IgM Syndromes present with infection/Pneumocystis pneumonia, hepatitis, and diarrhoea.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Definition
concepts.content: Sickle-cell anaemia is an autosomal recessive condition that results from the synthesis of an abnormal haemoglobin chain termed HbS.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Sickle-cell anaemia is more common in people of African descent as the heterozygous condition offers some protection against malaria.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Clinical features
concepts.content: Symptoms in homozygotes don't tend to develop until 4-6 months when the abnormal HbSS molecules take over from fetal haemoglobin.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Normal haemoglobin is designated as HbAA.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Investigations
concepts.content: The definitive diagnosis of sickle cell disease is by haemoglobin electrophoresis.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management
concepts.content: Crisis management for sickle-cell anaemia includes analgesia (e.g., opiates), rehydration, and oxygen.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Crises types
concepts.content: Recognised types of sickle-cell crises include thrombotic (vaso-occlusive/painful crises), acute chest syndrome, anaemic, aplastic, sequestration, and infection.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Thrombotic crises
concepts.content: Thrombotic crises, also known as painful crises or vaso-occlusive crises, are precipitated by infection, dehydration, or deoxygenation (e.g., high altitude).

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Acute chest syndrome
concepts.content: Acute chest syndrome is caused by vaso-occlusion within the pulmonary microvasculature, leading to infarction in the lung parenchyma.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Acute chest syndrome management
concepts.content: Management of acute chest syndrome includes pain relief, respiratory support (e.g., oxygen therapy), antibiotics, transfusion to improve oxygenation, and incentive spirometry to reduce atelectasis and improve alveolar ventilation.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Aplastic crises
concepts.content: Aplastic crises are caused by infection with parvovirus, leading to a sudden fall in haemoglobin and bone marrow suppression with a reduced reticulocyte count.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Sequestration crises
concepts.content: Sequestration crises involve sickling within organs such as the spleen or lungs, causing pooling of blood with worsening of anaemia and an increased reticulocyte count.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Complications
concepts.content: The majority of adult patients with sickle-cell will have an atrophied spleen due to repeated infarction.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Risk factors for VTE
concepts.content: Sickle cell disease is an underlying condition that increases the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE).

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Crisis management: Analgesia
concepts.content: Analgesia, e.g., opiates, is used in the crisis management of sickle-cell anaemia.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Crisis management: Rehydration
concepts.content: Rehydration is used in the crisis management of sickle-cell anaemia.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Crisis management: Oxygen
concepts.content: Oxygen is used in the crisis management of sickle-cell anaemia.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Crisis management: Antibiotics
concepts.content: Antibiotics should be considered in the crisis management of sickle-cell anaemia if there is evidence of infection.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Crisis management: Blood transfusion
concepts.content: Blood transfusion is used in the crisis management of sickle-cell anaemia.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Crisis management: Exchange transfusion
concepts.content: Exchange transfusion is used in the crisis management of sickle-cell anaemia, e.g., if neurological complications are present.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Longer-term management: Hydroxyurea
concepts.content: Hydroxyurea is used in the longer-term management of sickle-cell anaemia.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Longer-term management: Hydroxyurea mechanism
concepts.content: Hydroxyurea increases HbF levels and is used in the prophylactic management of sickle-cell anaemia to prevent painful episodes.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management - Longer-term management: Pneumococcal vaccine
concepts.content: Sickle-cell patients should receive the pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine every 5 years.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Analgesia
concepts.content: Analgesia, such as opiates, is part of the general management for sickle-cell crises.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Rehydration
concepts.content: Rehydration is a general management step for sickle-cell crises.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Oxygen therapy
concepts.content: Oxygen therapy is a general management step for sickle-cell crises.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Antibiotics
concepts.content: Antibiotics should be considered in the management of sickle-cell crises if there is evidence of infection.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Blood transfusion indications (Anaemia)
concepts.content: Blood transfusion is indicated in sickle-cell crises for severe or symptomatic anaemia.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Blood transfusion indications (Pregnancy)
concepts.content: Blood transfusion is indicated in sickle-cell crises during pregnancy.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Blood transfusion indications (Pre-operative)
concepts.content: Blood transfusion is indicated in sickle-cell crises pre-operatively.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Blood transfusion (Hb S percentage)
concepts.content: During blood transfusion for sickle-cell crises, do not rapidly reduce the percentage of Hb S containing cells.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Exchange transfusion indications (Acute vaso-occlusive crisis)
concepts.content: Exchange transfusion is indicated in sickle-cell crises for acute vaso-occlusive crisis (stroke, acute chest syndrome, multiorgan failure, splenic sequestration crisis).

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Management: Exchange transfusion (Hb S percentage)
concepts.content: Exchange transfusion for sickle-cell crises aims to rapidly reduce the percentage of Hb S containing cells.

concepts.title: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura – Pathogenesis
concepts.content: Abnormally large and sticky multimers of von Willebrand's factor cause platelets to clump within vessels in Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).

concepts.title: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura – ADAMTS13 deficiency
concepts.content: In Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), there is a deficiency of ADAMTS13, a metalloprotease enzyme that breaks down large multimers of von Willebrand's factor.

concepts.title: Thymoma – Definition
concepts.content: Thymomas are the most common tumour of the anterior mediastinum and is usually detected between the sixth and seventh decades of life.

concepts.title: Thymoma – Associated Conditions (Myasthenia Gravis)
concepts.content: Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma in 30-40% of patients.

concepts.title: Thymoma – Associated Conditions (Red Cell Aplasia)
concepts.content: Red cell aplasia is associated with thymoma.

concepts.title: Thymoma – Associated Conditions (Dermatomyositis)
concepts.content: Dermatomyositis is associated with thymoma.

concepts.title: Thymoma – Associated Conditions (SLE)
concepts.content: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is associated with thymoma.

concepts.title: Thymoma – Associated Conditions (SIADH)
concepts.content: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is associated with thymoma.

concepts.title: Thymoma – Complications (Airway Compression)
concepts.content: Compression of the airway can be a cause of death in thymoma.

concepts.title: Thymoma – Complications (Cardiac Tamponade)
concepts.content: Cardiac tamponade can be a cause of death in thymoma.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Definition and Epidemiology
concepts.content: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is the commonest red blood cell enzyme defect. It is more common in people from the Mediterranean and Africa and is inherited in an X-linked recessive fashion.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Precipitating factors
concepts.content: Many drugs can precipitate a crisis as well as infections and broad (fava) beans.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – G6PD role in pentose phosphate pathway
concepts.content: G6PD is the first step in the pentose phosphate pathway, which converts glucose-6-phosphate→ 6-phosphogluconolactone. This reaction also results in nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) → NADPH (glucose-6-phosphate + NADP → 6-phosphogluconolactone + NADPH).

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Role of NADPH and glutathione
concepts.content: NADPH is important for converting oxidized glutathione back to its reduced form. Reduced glutathione protects red blood cells from oxidative damage by oxidants such as superoxide anion (O2-) and hydrogen peroxide.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Mechanism of oxidative stress
concepts.content: ↓ G6PD → ↓ reduced NADPH → ↓ reduced glutathione → increased red cell susceptibility to oxidative stress.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Neonatal jaundice
concepts.content: Neonatal jaundice is often seen.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Intravascular haemolysis
concepts.content: Intravascular haemolysis.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Gallstones
concepts.content: Gallstones are common.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Splenomegaly
concepts.content: Splenomegaly may be present.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Blood film findings
concepts.content: Heinz bodies on blood films. Bite and blister cells may also be seen.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Diagnostic test
concepts.content: Diagnosis is made by using a G6PD enzyme assay.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Timing of G6PD enzyme assay
concepts.content: Levels should be checked around 3 months after an acute episode of hemolysis, RBCs with the most severely reduced G6PD activity will have hemolysed → reduced G6PD activity → not be measured in the assay → false negative results.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Drugs causing haemolysis
concepts.content: Anti-malarials: primaquine. Ciprofloxacin. Sulph- group drugs: sulphonamides, sulphasalazine, sulfonylureas.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Drugs thought to be safe
concepts.content: Penicillins. Cephalosporins. Macrolides. Tetracyclines. Trimethoprim.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Gender and inheritance
concepts.content: G6PD deficiency: Male (X-linked recessive).

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Ethnicity
concepts.content: G6PD deficiency: African + Mediterranean descent.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Typical history
concepts.content: G6PD deficiency: Neonatal jaundice, infection/drugs precipitate haemolysis, gallstones.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Blood film findings (comparison)
concepts.content: G6PD deficiency: Heinz bodies.

concepts.title: G6PD deficiency – Diagnostic test (comparison)
concepts.content: G6PD deficiency: Measure enzyme activity of G6PD.

concepts.title: Anatomy – Lymphatic drainage of the ovaries
concepts.content: The ovaries drain to the para-aortic lymphatics via the gonadal vessels.

concepts.title: Anatomy – Lymphatic drainage of the uterine fundus (para-aortic)
concepts.content: The uterine fundus has a lymphatic drainage that runs with the ovarian vessels and may thus drain to the para-aortic nodes.

concepts.title: Anatomy – Lymphatic drainage of the uterine fundus (inguinal)
concepts.content: Some drainage [of the uterine fundus] may also pass along the round ligament to the inguinal nodes.

concepts.title: Anatomy – Lymphatic drainage of the body of the uterus
concepts.content: The body of the uterus drains through lymphatics contained within the broad ligament to the iliac lymph nodes.

concepts.title: Anatomy – Lymphatic drainage of the cervix (external iliac)
concepts.content: The cervix drains into three potential nodal stations; laterally through the broad ligament to the external iliac nodes.

concepts.title: Anatomy – Lymphatic drainage of the cervix (presacral)
concepts.content: The cervix drains into three potential nodal stations; along the lymphatics of the uterosacral fold to the presacral nodes.

concepts.title: Anatomy – Lymphatic drainage of the cervix (internal iliac)
concepts.content: The cervix drains into three potential nodal stations; posterolaterally along lymphatics lying alongside the uterine vessels to the internal iliac nodes.

concepts.title: Thrombophilia – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Factor V Leiden (activated protein C resistance) is the most common inherited cause of thrombophilia.

concepts.title: Factor V Leiden – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Heterozygous Factor V Leiden has a prevalence of 5% and a relative risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) of 4.

concepts.title: Prothrombin gene mutation – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Heterozygous Prothrombin gene mutation has a prevalence of 1.5% and a relative risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) of 3.

concepts.title: Protein C deficiency – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Protein C deficiency has a prevalence of 0.3% and a relative risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) of 10.

concepts.title: Protein S deficiency – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Protein S deficiency has a prevalence of 0.1% and a relative risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) of 5-10.

concepts.title: Antithrombin III deficiency – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Antithrombin III deficiency has a prevalence of 0.02% and a relative risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) of 10-20.

concepts.content: increased risk with advancing age

concepts.title: Sideroblastic anaemia – Definition
concepts.content: Sideroblastic anaemia is a condition where red cells fail to completely form haem, whose biosynthesis takes place partly in the mitochondrion. This leads to deposits of iron in the mitochondria that form a ring around the nucleus called a ring sideroblast.

concepts.title: Sideroblastic anaemia – Classification

concepts.title: Splenomegaly – Massive splenomegaly causes
concepts.content: Myelofibrosis is a cause of massive splenomegaly.

concepts.title: Splenomegaly – Other causes
concepts.content: Portal hypertension, secondary to cirrhosis, is a cause of splenomegaly.

concepts.title: Sickle-cell anaemia – Spleen atrophy
concepts.content: The majority of adult patients with sickle-cell anaemia will have an atrophied spleen due to repeated infarction.

concepts.title: Thrombocytopenia – Causes of severe thrombocytopenia
concepts.content: Causes of severe thrombocytopenia include ITP, DIC, TTP, and haematological malignancy.

concepts.title: Thrombocytopenia – Causes of moderate thrombocytopenia
concepts.content: Causes of moderate thrombocytopenia include heparin induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), drug-induced (e.g. quinine, diuretics, sulphonamides, aspirin, thiazides), alcohol, liver disease, hypersplenism, viral infection (EBV, HIV, hepatitis), pregnancy, SLE/antiphospholipid syndrome, and vitamin B12 deficiency.

concepts.title: Thrombocytopenia – Pseudothrombocytopenia
concepts.content: Pseudothrombocytopenia has been reported in association with the use of EDTA as an anticoagulant.

concepts.title: Thrombocytosis – Definition
concepts.content: Thrombocytosis is an abnormally high platelet count, usually > 400 * 109/l.

concepts.title: Thrombocytosis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Reactive thrombocytosis can occur in response to stress such as a severe infection or surgery.

concepts.title: Essential thrombocytosis – Definition
concepts.content: Essential thrombocytosis is a myeloproliferative disorder where megakaryocyte proliferation leads to an overproduction of platelets.

concepts.title: Essential thrombocytosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: A platelet count > 600 * 109/l is a feature of essential thrombocytosis.

concepts.title: Essential thrombocytosis – Investigations
concepts.content: A JAK2 mutation is found in around 50% of patients with essential thrombocytosis.

concepts.title: Essential thrombocytosis – Management
concepts.content: Hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide) is widely used to reduce the platelet count in essential thrombocytosis.

concepts.title: Tranexamic acid – Definition
concepts.content: Tranexamic acid is a synthetic derivative of lysine.

concepts.title: Tranexamic acid – Mechanism of action
concepts.content: Tranexamic acid's primary mode of action is as an antifibrinolytic that reversibly binds to lysine receptor sites on plasminogen or plasmin. This prevents plasmin from binding to and degrading fibrin.

concepts.title: Tranexamic acid – Clinical use: Menorrhagia
concepts.content: Tranexamic acid is most commonly prescribed to help treat menorrhagia.

concepts.title: Tranexamic acid – Clinical use: Trauma (CRASH 2 trial)
concepts.content: The role of tranexamic acid in trauma was investigated in the CRASH 2 trial and has been shown to be of benefit in bleeding trauma when administered in the first 3 hours.

concepts.title: Tranexamic acid – Administration in major haemorrhage
concepts.content: Tranexamic acid is given as an IV bolus followed by an infusion in cases of major haemorrhage.

concepts.title: Tranexamic acid – Ongoing research: Traumatic brain injury
concepts.content: There is also ongoing research looking at the role of tranexamic acid in traumatic brain injury.

concepts.title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Definition
concepts.content: Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is a potentially deadly condition related to the treatment of high-grade lymphomas and leukaemias.

concepts.title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Tumour lysis syndrome can occur in the absence of chemotherapy but is usually triggered by the introduction of combination chemotherapy. On occasion, it can occur with steroid treatment alone.

concepts.title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Tumour lysis syndrome occurs from the breakdown of the tumour cells and the subsequent release of chemicals from the cell.

concepts.title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Electrolyte abnormalities
concepts.content: Tumour lysis syndrome leads to a high potassium and high phosphate level in the presence of a low calcium.

concepts.title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Clinical suspicion
concepts.content: Tumour lysis syndrome should be suspected in any patient presenting with an acute kidney injury in the presence of a high phosphate and high uric acid level.

concepts.title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Prevention: IV fluids
concepts.content: IV fluids are used in the prevention of Tumour lysis syndrome.

concepts.title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Prevention: High-risk patients
concepts.content: Patients at higher risk of Tumour lysis syndrome should receive either allopurinol or rasburicase for prevention.

concepts.title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Rasburicase mechanism
concepts.content: Rasburicase is a recombinant version of urate oxidase, an enzyme that metabolizes uric acid to allantoin. Allantoin is much more water-soluble than uric acid and is, therefore, more easily excreted by the kidneys.

concepts.title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Rasburicase indication
concepts.content: Rasburicase is generally preferred now for patients at a higher risk of developing Tumour lysis syndrome.

concepts.title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Allopurinol indication
concepts.content: Allopurinol is generally used for patients in lower-risk groups for Tumour lysis syndrome.

concepts.title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Rasburicase and Allopurinol co-administration
concepts.content: Rasburicase and allopurinol should not be given together in the management of tumour lysis syndrome as this reduces the effect of rasburicase.

concepts.title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Cairo-Bishop scoring system
concepts.content: From 2004, Tumour lysis syndrome has been graded using the Cairo-Bishop scoring system.

concepts.title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Laboratory TLS criteria
concepts.content: Laboratory tumor lysis syndrome is defined by abnormality in two or more of the following, occurring within three days before or seven days after chemotherapy: uric acid > 475umol/l or 25% increase, potassium > 6 mmol/l or 25% increase, phosphate > 1.125mmol/l or 25% increase, calcium < 1.75mmol/l or 25% decrease.

concepts.title: Tumour lysis syndrome – Clinical TLS criteria
concepts.content: Clinical tumor lysis syndrome is defined as laboratory tumour lysis syndrome plus one or more of the following: increased serum creatinine (1.5 times upper limit of normal), cardiac arrhythmia or sudden death, seizure.

concepts.title: Von Willebrand's disease – Definition
concepts.content: Von Willebrand's disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder.

concepts.title: Von Willebrand's disease – Inheritance
concepts.content: The majority of cases of Von Willebrand's disease are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion.

concepts.title: Von Willebrand's disease – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Von Willebrand's disease characteristically behaves like a platelet disorder, with epistaxis and menorrhagia being common, whilst haemoarthroses and muscle haematomas are rare.

concepts.title: Von Willebrand's disease – Role of von Willebrand factor
concepts.content: Von Willebrand factor is a large glycoprotein which forms massive multimers up to 1,000,000 Da in size.

concepts.title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 1
concepts.content: Type 1 Von Willebrand's disease involves a partial reduction in von Willebrand factor and accounts for 80% of patients.

concepts.title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 2
concepts.content: Type 2 Von Willebrand's disease is characterized by an abnormal form of von Willebrand factor.

concepts.title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 2A
concepts.content: Type 2A VWD is caused by defective platelet adhesion due to decreased high molecular weight VWF multimers (i.e. the VWF protein is too small).

concepts.title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 2B
concepts.content: Type 2B VWD is characterised by a pathological increase of VWF-platelet interaction.

concepts.title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 2M
concepts.content: Type 2M VWD is caused by a decrease in VWF-platelet interaction (not related to loss of high molecular weight multimers).

concepts.title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 2N
concepts.content: Type 2N VWD is caused by abnormal binding of the VWF to Factor VIII.

concepts.title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 3
concepts.content: Type 3 Von Willebrand's disease is the most severe form and involves a total lack of von Willebrand factor.

concepts.title: Von Willebrand's disease – Type 3 Inheritance
concepts.content: Type 3 von Willebrand's disease is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.

concepts.title: Von Willebrand's disease – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigation for Von Willebrand's disease may show a prolonged bleeding time.

concepts.title: Von Willebrand's disease – Management
concepts.content: Tranexamic acid can be used for mild bleeding in Von Willebrand's disease.

concepts.title: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia – Definition
concepts.content: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia is an uncommon condition seen in older men. It is a lymphoplasmacytoid malignancy characterised by the secretion of a monoclonal IgM paraprotein

concepts.title: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia – Clinical features (Systemic upset)
concepts.content: systemic upset: weight loss, lethargy

concepts.title: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia – Clinical features (Hyperviscosity syndrome)
concepts.content: hyperviscosity syndrome e.g. visual disturbance

concepts.title: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia – Pathophysiology (IgM configuration)
concepts.content: the pentameric configuration of IgM increases serum viscosity

concepts.title: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia – Clinical features (Hepatosplenomegaly)
concepts.content: hepatosplenomegaly

concepts.title: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia – Clinical features (Lymphadenopathy)
concepts.content: lymphadenopathy

concepts.title: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia – Clinical features (Cryoglobulinaemia)
concepts.content: cryoglobulinaemia e.g. Raynaud's

concepts.title: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia – Investigations (Monoclonal IgM paraproteinaemia)
concepts.content: monoclonal IgM paraproteinaemia

concepts.title: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia – Investigations (Bone marrow biopsy)
concepts.content: bone marrow biopsy is diagnostic

concepts.title: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia – Investigations (Bone marrow infiltration)
concepts.content: infiltration of the bone marrow with lymphoplasmacytoid lymphoma cells

concepts.title: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia – Management
concepts.content: typically rituximab-based combination chemotherapy

concepts.title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome – Definition
concepts.content: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome causes primary immunodeficiency due to a combined B- and T-cell dysfunction.

concepts.title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome – Inheritance
concepts.content: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is inherited in a X-linked recessive fashion.

concepts.title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome – Genetic Aetiology
concepts.content: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is thought to be caused by mutation in the WASP gene.

concepts.title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome – Clinical features: Recurrent bacterial infections
concepts.content: recurrent bacterial infections (e.g. Chest)

concepts.title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome – Clinical features: Eczema
concepts.content: eczema

concepts.title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome – Clinical features: Thrombocytopaenia
concepts.content: thrombocytopaenia

concepts.title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome – Investigations: Low IgM levels
concepts.content: low IgM levels

concepts.title: Definition
concepts.content: Antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired disorder characterised by a predisposition to both venous and arterial thromboses, recurrent fetal loss and thrombocytopenia. It may occur as a primary disorder or secondary to other conditions, most commonly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

concepts.title: Complications in Pregnancy
concepts.content: In pregnancy, the following complications may occur: recurrent miscarriage, IUGR, pre-eclampsia, placental abruption, pre-term delivery, and venous thromboembolism.

concepts.title: Management in Pregnancy
concepts.content: Management in pregnancy includes low-dose aspirin commenced once pregnancy is confirmed, and low molecular weight heparin once a fetal heart is seen on ultrasound.

concepts.title: Cause of Thrombophilia
concepts.content: Antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired cause of thrombophilia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Definition
concepts.content: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is a malignancy of precursor cells from the lymphocyte lineage, the most common of which is B-cell ALL.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is the most common childhood malignancy.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Clinical features
concepts.content: Any combination of persistent fever, pallor, unusual bleeding, lymphadenopathy and/or organomegaly should raise suspicions for Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Incidence
concepts.content: The incidence of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is 1.00 cases per 100,000 person-years.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Peak Incidence Age
concepts.content: The peak incidence of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is between 1-5 years of age.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Sex Ratio
concepts.content: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is more common in males with a sex ratio of 1.5:1.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Genetic Aetiology
concepts.content: An increased risk of developing Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is observed among monozygotic twins and individuals with chromosomal abnormalities, including trisomy 21, Klinefelter's syndrome, and other inherited conditions with genetic instability, such as Fanconi anaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Viral Exposure Aetiology
concepts.content: Viral exposure is considered a contributing factor to the development of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Environmental Aetiology
concepts.content: Environmental factors, including smoking or radiation exposure, are considered contributing factors to the development of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Pathophysiology Definition
concepts.content: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is a haematological malignancy characterised by the clonal expansion of immature lymphoid precursors, known as lymphoblasts.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Pathogenesis Overview
concepts.content: The pathogenesis of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia involves a complex series of genetic, epigenetic, and microenvironmental alterations that disrupt normal haematopoiesis and immune function.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Initial Genetic Events
concepts.content: The pathogenesis of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia often begins with a somatic mutation in a progenitor cell within the bone marrow, leading to the formation of an aberrant clone of cells that proliferate uncontrollably.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Fusion Genes in Pathogenesis
concepts.content: Common mutations observed in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia involve rearrangements of BCR-ABL1, E2A-PBX1, and MLL genes, resulting in fusion proteins with increased or novel oncogenic activity.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Transcription Factor Mutations
concepts.content: Mutations in transcription factors such as TAL1 and PAX5, critical for normal B-cell development, contribute to leukemogenesis by disrupting normal differentiation pathways in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Tumour Suppressor Gene Mutations
concepts.content: Mutations in tumour suppressor genes such as TP53 and deletions in chromosomes 9 and 13 facilitate the survival and expansion of abnormal clones by preventing apoptosis in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – DNA Methylation Changes
concepts.content: Changes in DNA methylation patterns can lead to the silencing of tumour suppressor genes in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Histone Modifications
concepts.content: Histone modifications can alter chromatin structure and gene expression, contributing to the malignant phenotype in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Microenvironmental Factors
concepts.content: The bone marrow microenvironment provides crucial support for leukemic cell survival and proliferation, influencing drug resistance and relapse in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – WHO Classification
concepts.content: The World Health Organization (WHO) classification of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is based on immunophenotype, cytogenetics, and molecular genetics.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – B-cell ALL
concepts.content: B-cell Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (B-ALL) accounts for approximately 85% of all ALL cases.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – T-cell ALL
concepts.content: T-cell Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (T-ALL) accounts for approximately 15% of all ALL cases.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Genetic Subtypes
concepts.content: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is further classified into genetic subtypes based on recurrent cytogenetic abnormalities and molecular mutations, such as BCR-ABL1 fusion, ETV6-RUNX1 fusion, and KMT2A rearrangements.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Clinical Presentation Overview
concepts.content: The clinical presentation of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is highly variable and depends on the extent of bone marrow infiltration and extramedullary involvement.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Non-specific Clinical Presentation
concepts.content: Non-specific symptoms such as fatigue, fever, and weight loss are common in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Organomegaly Presentation
concepts.content: Organomegaly, including hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, is frequently observed in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Constitutional Fever
concepts.content: Fever (50%) is a common constitutional symptom in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Fever due to Infection
concepts.content: Fever (50%) in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia can also be due to infection secondary to neutropenia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Lymphadenopathy Presentation
concepts.content: Lymphadenopathy is present in 50% of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Thrombocytopenia Manifestations
concepts.content: Unusual bleeding and bruising are common due to thrombocytopenia in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Anaemia Manifestations
concepts.content: Anaemia in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presents with pallor, fatigue, and shortness of breath.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Musculoskeletal Pain
concepts.content: Musculoskeletal pain, particularly bone and joint pain, is common in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, affecting 25% of children.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – CNS Involvement Headache
concepts.content: Headache and vomiting may indicate central nervous system (CNS) involvement in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Testicular Enlargement
concepts.content: Testicular enlargement is a rare presentation of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Mediastinal Mass Symptoms
concepts.content: A mediastinal mass in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia can cause cough, dyspnoea, and superior vena cava obstruction.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – FBC for Haematological Derangements
concepts.content: A full blood count (FBC) is required in suspected Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases to assess for haematological derangements.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Thrombocytopenia on FBC
concepts.content: Thrombocytopenia is present in 75% of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Anaemia on FBC
concepts.content: Anaemia is present in 75% of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – WBC Count on FBC
concepts.content: White blood cell (WBC) count can be low, normal, or high in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Low WBC Count Interpretation
concepts.content: A low white blood cell (WBC) count is present in 50% of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Infection Screen
concepts.content: An infection screen is required in suspected Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases with fever to check for active infection.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Coagulation Profile
concepts.content: A coagulation profile is required in suspected Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases to assess for any clotting derangements.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Metabolic Panel for Complications
concepts.content: Urea, electrolytes, lactate dehydrogenase, and uric acid are required in suspected Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases to assess for complications such as tumour lysis syndrome.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Diagnostic Requirements
concepts.content: Diagnosis of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia requires examination of cell morphology and immunophenotyping; cytogenetics and molecular analysis are necessary for classification.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Peripheral Blood Smear
concepts.content: A peripheral blood smear is always required to examine circulating lymphoblasts in the presence of an abnormal full blood count.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Bone Marrow Aspiration
concepts.content: Bone marrow aspiration is a key investigation for Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia; a biopsy is only needed if insufficient cells are obtained.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Lymph Node Biopsy
concepts.content: A lymph node biopsy, preferably excisional or needle over fine needle aspiration, is an early investigation in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia if there is significant lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Cerebrospinal Fluid Analysis
concepts.content: All children diagnosed with Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia undergo a lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis to assess for CNS involvement.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Lymphoblast Identification in Morphology
concepts.content: Examination of samples in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia may identify WBCs with characteristic morphological features of lymphoblasts, including large nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and scant cytoplasm.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Normal Peripheral Smear Findings
concepts.content: Findings on a peripheral smear for Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia may be normal if leukaemia is still confined to the bone marrow.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Diagnostic Threshold for Lymphoblasts
concepts.content: The most commonly accepted threshold for diagnosis of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is when lymphoblasts occupy >20% of bone marrow.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Immunophenotyping for Diagnosis Confirmation
concepts.content: Immunophenotyping confirms the diagnosis of Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia by identifying common lymphoid antigens and features, and the absence of myeloid properties in abnormal cells.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Immunophenotyping for Lineage Determination
concepts.content: Immunophenotyping determines whether Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia lymphoblasts are of B or T cell lineage through analysis of surface antigens.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Cytogenetic and Molecular Analysis for Classification
concepts.content: Cytogenetic and molecular analysis is not required for diagnosis but is necessary to categorise Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia according to the WHO classification.

concepts.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – Techniques for Cytogenetic and Molecular Analysis
concepts.content: Identification of cytogenetic features in Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia involves chromosomal banding techniques and fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH), while various molecular techniques are used for characteristic molecular features.

concepts.title: Acute epiglottitis – Definition
concepts.content: Acute epiglottitis is a severe inflammation of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic tissues, posing a significant risk of swift airway blockage. While historically prevalent in children aged 2-7, its incidence has shifted towards adults, largely due to the Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) vaccine.

concepts.title: Acute epiglottitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: The incidence of acute epiglottitis is approximately 2 per 100,000 person-years. Although its demographic has shifted, it is still most frequently observed in infants.

concepts.title: Acute epiglottitis – Aetiology
concepts.content: Historically, Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) was the primary bacterial cause of acute epiglottitis. Current bacterial pathogens include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Group A streptococci, and Staphylococcus aureus. Viral, fungal, and non-infectious factors like thermal injury can also contribute.

concepts.title: Acute epiglottitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients with acute epiglottitis often present with a severe sore throat and painful swallowing (odynophagia), leading to drooling. A muffled 'hot potato' voice is characteristic, along with high-pitched inspiratory stridor and respiratory distress with tachypnea.

concepts.title: Acute epiglottitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: A high-grade fever is a common clinical feature of acute epiglottitis. Patients may adopt a tripod or sniffing position, leaning forward with a chin thrust and open mouth, to facilitate breathing.

concepts.title: Acute epiglottitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Crucially, direct examination of the throat in suspected acute epiglottitis is contraindicated due to the significant risk of precipitating acute airway obstruction, which can be life-threatening.

concepts.title: Acute epiglottitis – Investigations
concepts.content: A lateral neck radiograph is a key investigation for acute epiglottitis, often revealing the characteristic 'thumb sign,' indicative of a swollen epiglottis.

concepts.title: Acute epiglottitis – Investigations
concepts.content: Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy, performed only by experienced personnel, can directly visualize the inflamed epiglottis and supraglottic structures, aiding in diagnosis and assessing airway compromise.

concepts.title: Acute epiglottitis – Investigations
concepts.content: Blood cultures and throat swabs are essential investigations to identify the causative pathogen in acute epiglottitis, guiding targeted antibiotic therapy.

concepts.title: Acute epiglottitis – Management
concepts.content: Airway management is paramount in acute epiglottitis and typically occurs in an Intensive Care Unit (ICU) setting. Endotracheal intubation or tracheostomy may be required to secure the airway and prevent obstruction.

concepts.title: Acute epiglottitis – Management
concepts.content: Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, such as third-generation cephalosporins, are initiated promptly to cover common bacterial pathogens while awaiting culture results.

concepts.title: Acute epiglottitis – Management
concepts.content: Supportive care for acute epiglottitis includes intravenous fluids to maintain hydration, analgesics for pain relief, and antipyretics to manage fever. The use of corticosteroids remains controversial.

concepts.title: Acute epiglottitis – Prevention
concepts.content: Prevention of acute epiglottitis is primarily achieved through Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) vaccination, which has significantly reduced the incidence of the disease, especially in children.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Definition
concepts.content: Genital herpes is a prevalent viral sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by either Herpes Simplex Virus type 1 (HSV-1) or type 2 (HSV-2).

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Definition
concepts.content: Herpes simplex virus establishes a lifelong infection, remaining dormant (latent) within the sensory neurons of the affected individual.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Definition
concepts.content: Transmission of genital herpes is possible even when an infected individual exhibits no visible symptoms, a phenomenon known as asymptomatic shedding.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Epidemiology
concepts.content: The incidence of genital herpes is approximately 300 cases per 100,000 person-years, indicating its common occurrence.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Epidemiology
concepts.content: The peak incidence of genital herpes is observed in individuals between 20 and 30 years of age.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Genital herpes is predominantly caused by HSV-2, but HSV-1 is increasingly responsible for genital infections, often due to orogenital contact.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: A significant risk factor for acquiring genital herpes is having multiple sexual partners.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: The presence of other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) increases the risk of contracting genital herpes.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Female sex is identified as a risk factor for genital herpes infection.
