concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Immunosuppression is a recognized risk factor that can increase susceptibility to genital herpes.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) initiates infection by adhering to heparan sulphate molecules present on the surface of host cells.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Following adhesion, HSV enters the host cell and proceeds to replicate its genetic material within the cell's nucleus.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: After replication, the virus spreads to the sensory nerve endings, marking a critical step in its dissemination.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Retrograde transport of HSV to the dorsal root ganglia leads to the establishment of a latent infection.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Reactivation of latent HSV can be triggered by various factors, including UV light exposure, psychological stress, and immunosuppression.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Upon reactivation, HSV undergoes anterograde transport, moving back along the nerve to the epidermis, where lesions typically appear.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
concepts.content: Primary genital herpes often presents with grouped, painful blisters that typically rupture after 2-3 days.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
concepts.content: After blistering, crusted erosions or ulcers form on the external genitalia, characteristic of primary genital herpes.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
concepts.content: Lesions associated with primary genital herpes can extend to the thigh, buttocks, cervix, and rectum.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
concepts.content: Dysuria, or painful urination, is a common symptom in women experiencing primary genital herpes.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
concepts.content: Urinary retention can occur in severe cases of primary genital herpes, particularly in women.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
concepts.content: Inguinal lymphadenopathy, swelling of lymph nodes in the groin, is observed in approximately 30% of primary genital herpes cases.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
concepts.content: Around 50% of individuals with primary genital herpes experience systemic illness, including headache, fever, myalgia, and general malaise.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (primary)
concepts.content: The symptoms of primary genital herpes can persist for up to 20 days, making it a prolonged initial episode.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (recurrent)
concepts.content: Recurrent genital herpes episodes are often preceded by a prodrome of tingling or burning sensations up to 48 hours before lesion appearance.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (recurrent)
concepts.content: Lesions during recurrent episodes of genital herpes are typically less severe and tend to appear in the same anatomical area as previous outbreaks.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features (recurrent)
concepts.content: Recurrent genital herpes lesions generally heal within 10 days, a shorter duration compared to primary infections.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Investigations
concepts.content: Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) or Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT) is the first-line investigation for genital herpes, as per BASHH 2014 guidelines.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Investigations
concepts.content: Viral culture may be utilized for diagnosing genital herpes if PCR/NAAT testing is not readily available.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Investigations
concepts.content: Serology for HSV type-specific IgG antibodies can be performed to determine past exposure and differentiate between HSV-1 and HSV-2.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Management
concepts.content: Antiviral therapy, including medications like aciclovir, valaciclovir, and famciclovir, is used to manage genital herpes.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Management
concepts.content: Antiviral therapy for genital herpes effectively reduces the severity and duration of outbreaks but does not provide a cure for the infection.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Management
concepts.content: For individuals experiencing frequent recurrences of genital herpes, suppressive antiviral therapy may be prescribed to reduce outbreak frequency.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Definition
concepts.content: Bacterial vaginosis is characterized by an overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria, primarily Gardnerella vaginalis, coupled with a reduction in beneficial lactic acid-producing lactobacilli, leading to an elevated vaginal pH.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Association with sexual activity
concepts.content: Although not classified as a sexually transmitted infection (STI), bacterial vaginosis is observed almost exclusively in women who are sexually active.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Incidence
concepts.content: The incidence of bacterial vaginosis is approximately 5,000 cases per 100,000 person-years, indicating its prevalence within the population.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Peak age
concepts.content: Bacterial vaginosis most commonly affects women between 20 and 30 years of age, representing the peak incidence period for this condition.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Abnormal vaginal discharge
concepts.content: A key clinical feature of bacterial vaginosis is an abnormal vaginal discharge, often described as having a 'fishy' odor.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Odor characteristics
concepts.content: The characteristic 'fishy' odor associated with bacterial vaginosis typically worsens after sexual intercourse, during menstruation, or following washing with soap.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Asymptomatic presentation
concepts.content: Approximately 50% of individuals with bacterial vaginosis may not experience any noticeable symptoms, making it an often asymptomatic condition.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Discharge appearance
concepts.content: The vaginal discharge in bacterial vaginosis is typically thin, homogeneous, and white-grey, often coating the vaginal walls.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Absence of itching
concepts.content: Unlike candidiasis, bacterial vaginosis typically does not present with vulval or vaginal itching.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Absence of other symptoms
concepts.content: Patients with bacterial vaginosis usually do not experience dysuria, dyspareunia, or abdominal pain.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Amsel's criteria
concepts.content: Diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis is typically made using Amsel's criteria, requiring at least three out of four specific clinical findings.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Amsel's criteria components
concepts.content: Amsel's criteria include thin white homogeneous discharge, presence of clue cells on microscopy, vaginal pH >4.5, and a positive whiff test.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Asymptomatic management
concepts.content: Treatment for asymptomatic bacterial vaginosis is generally not required, except in specific situations such as prior to termination of pregnancy.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Symptomatic management
concepts.content: Symptomatic bacterial vaginosis is typically managed with oral metronidazole for 5-7 days, achieving a 70-80% cure rate, though relapse within 3 months is common.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Single dose metronidazole
concepts.content: A single 2g dose of metronidazole can be considered for symptomatic bacterial vaginosis if there are concerns regarding patient adherence to a longer course.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Alternative treatments
concepts.content: Alternative treatment options for bacterial vaginosis include topical metronidazole or topical clindamycin.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Management in pregnancy
concepts.content: In pregnant women, oral metronidazole is recommended throughout pregnancy, including the first trimester, according to recent guidelines.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Increased STI susceptibility
concepts.content: A complication of bacterial vaginosis is an increased susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections, including HIV.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Increased PID risk
concepts.content: Bacterial vaginosis increases the risk of developing pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), a serious infection of the female reproductive organs.

concepts.title: Bacterial vaginosis – Pregnancy complications
concepts.content: In pregnancy, bacterial vaginosis is associated with an increased risk of adverse outcomes such as preterm birth, premature rupture of membranes, and postpartum endometritis.

concepts.title: Infectious diarrhoea – Definition
concepts.content: Campylobacter jejuni is a gram-negative, spiral-shaped bacterium. It is recognized as one of the most frequent bacterial causes of gastroenteritis globally.

concepts.title: Infectious diarrhoea – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Campylobacter jejuni is the causative agent, characterized as a gram-negative, curved or spiral-shaped, non-sporulating bacterium.

concepts.title: Infectious diarrhoea – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Transmission of Campylobacter infection primarily occurs through consumption of undercooked poultry, unpasteurised milk, or contaminated water sources.

concepts.title: Infectious diarrhoea – Clinical features
concepts.content: The incubation period for Campylobacter infection typically ranges from 1 to 3 days, preceding the onset of symptoms.

concepts.title: Infectious diarrhoea – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients may experience a prodrome including fever, headache, and myalgia before the main gastrointestinal symptoms manifest.

concepts.title: Infectious diarrhoea – Clinical features
concepts.content: Key symptoms include diarrhoea, which can be bloody, accompanied by abdominal cramping, nausea, and vomiting.

concepts.title: Infectious diarrhoea – Clinical features
concepts.content: The infection is typically self-limiting, with symptoms usually resolving within 5 to 7 days without specific intervention.

concepts.title: Infectious diarrhoea – Investigations
concepts.content: Stool culture remains the gold standard for diagnosing Campylobacter infection, though PCR testing is increasingly utilized for detection.

concepts.title: Infectious diarrhoea – Management
concepts.content: Management of Campylobacter infection primarily involves fluid replacement, as antibiotics are not routinely advised due to the self-limiting nature.

concepts.title: Infectious diarrhoea – Management
concepts.content: For severe cases or immunocompromised patients, azithromycin is the first-line antibiotic, with ciprofloxacin as an alternative despite increasing resistance.

concepts.title: Notifiable diseases – Management
concepts.content: Campylobacter infection is classified as a notifiable disease, requiring reporting to public health authorities for surveillance and control.

concepts.title: Infectious diarrhoea – Complications
concepts.content: Potential complications of Campylobacter infection include reactive arthritis, Guillain-Barré syndrome (due to molecular mimicry), and rarely, haemolytic uraemic syndrome.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Definition
concepts.content: Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection affecting the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue.

concepts.title: Erysipelas – Definition
concepts.content: Erysipelas is a more superficial form of bacterial infection, specifically affecting the dermis and superficial subcutaneous tissue.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Cellulitis is a common condition. It typically presents unilaterally; bilateral cellulitis is rare and suggests an alternative diagnosis.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Most Common Pathogen
concepts.content: The most common pathogen causing cellulitis is Streptococcus pyogenes, also known as Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Second Most Common Pathogen
concepts.content: Staphylococcus aureus, including Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), is the second most common pathogen in cellulitis.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Risk Factors (Skin/Medical)
concepts.content: Risk factors for cellulitis include tinea pedis, eczema/psoriasis, diabetes, intravenous drug use (IVDU), alcoholism, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Clinical Features (Local)
concepts.content: Clinical features of cellulitis include erythema with reasonably well-defined margins, swelling, warmth, and tenderness, commonly on the shins.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Clinical Features (Severe)
concepts.content: In severe cellulitis, blisters or bullae may be present. Systemic upset can manifest as fever, malaise, and nausea.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Investigations (Blood Tests)
concepts.content: Investigations for cellulitis include a Full Blood Count (FBC) which may show leucocytosis, and Urea & Electrolytes (U&E) where AKI indicates systemic response.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Investigations (Inflammatory Markers)
concepts.content: C-reactive protein (CRP) and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) are inflammatory markers used in the investigation of cellulitis.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Investigations (Cultures)
concepts.content: A wound swab is only indicated if the wound is open or weeping. Blood cultures should be taken if there is a significant systemic response.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Eron Classification Class I
concepts.content: Eron Class I cellulitis presents with no systemic toxicity and no uncontrolled comorbidities.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Eron Classification Class II
concepts.content: Eron Class II cellulitis indicates the patient is systemically unwell OR has comorbidities that are not well-controlled.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Eron Classification Class III
concepts.content: Eron Class III cellulitis involves significant systemic upset, such as confusion, tachycardia, or hypotension, or is limb-threatening.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Eron Classification Class IV
concepts.content: Eron Class IV cellulitis signifies sepsis or a severe, life-threatening condition like necrotising fasciitis.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Management (Class I Oral)
concepts.content: For Eron Class I cellulitis, oral flucloxacillin is the first-line treatment. Alternatives for penicillin allergy include clarithromycin, erythromycin, or doxycycline.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Management (Class III-IV IV)
concepts.content: Patients with Eron Class III-IV cellulitis require admission and intravenous antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav, clindamycin, cefuroxime, or ceftriaxone.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Management (Supportive Care)
concepts.content: Supportive management for cellulitis includes marking the erythema margins to monitor spread and elevating the affected leg.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Admission Criteria (Severity)
concepts.content: Admission criteria for cellulitis include Eron Class III/IV, severe or rapidly deteriorating condition, or very young (<1 year) or frail patients.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Admission Criteria (Specific Cases)
concepts.content: Specific cases requiring admission for cellulitis include immunocompromised patients, those with significant lymphoedema, or facial/periorbital cellulitis.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Definition
concepts.content: Hepatitis A is a viral hepatitis caused by the hepatitis A virus (HAV), an RNA picornavirus. It is primarily transmitted via the faecal-oral route and notably does not lead to chronic infection.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Epidemiology (Incidence)
concepts.content: The incidence of Hepatitis A is approximately 1.2 per 100,000 person-years. This viral infection shows a peak incidence in individuals aged between 30 and 40 years.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Aetiology (Virus)
concepts.content: Hepatitis A is caused by the Hepatitis A Virus (HAV), which is classified as an RNA picornavirus.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Aetiology (Transmission)
concepts.content: Transmission of Hepatitis A occurs via the faecal-oral route, often through contaminated food or water, shellfish, travel to endemic areas, men who have sex with men (MSM), and intravenous drug users (IVDU).

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Clinical Features (Incubation)
concepts.content: The incubation period for Hepatitis A typically ranges from 2 to 6 weeks.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Clinical Features (Prodrome)
concepts.content: The prodromal symptoms of Hepatitis A include fever, general malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Clinical Features (Jaundice)
concepts.content: Jaundice in Hepatitis A presents with dark urine, pale stools, and pruritus. Hepatomegaly is also a common finding.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Clinical Features (Course)
concepts.content: Hepatitis A is typically a self-limiting infection, with most individuals recovering without specific treatment.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Investigations (Serology)
concepts.content: Serological testing for Hepatitis A includes anti-HAV IgM, indicating acute infection, and anti-HAV IgG, which signifies past infection or immunity.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Investigations (Liver Function Tests)
concepts.content: Investigations for Hepatitis A typically reveal elevated Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) and Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST), along with raised bilirubin levels.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Management (Supportive Care)
concepts.content: Management of Hepatitis A is primarily supportive, focusing on symptom relief. Patients should avoid alcohol for 6 months and hepatotoxic drugs.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Management (Public Health & Follow-up)
concepts.content: Hepatitis A is a notifiable disease, requiring public health notification. Follow-up with Liver Function Tests (LFTs) is necessary until they normalize.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Management (Post-exposure Prophylaxis)
concepts.content: Post-exposure prophylaxis for Hepatitis A involves either the HAV vaccine (preferred) or Human Normal Immunoglobulin (HNIG) for those unable to receive the vaccine.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Complications (Common)
concepts.content: The majority of individuals with Hepatitis A recover fully within 6 months. However, a relapsing course can occur in 15% of cases.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Complications (Severe)
concepts.content: Severe complications of Hepatitis A include fulminant liver failure (0.4%). Rare complications include acalculous cholecystitis, pancreatitis, aplastic anaemia, post-viral encephalitis, and reactive arthritis.

concepts.title: Hepatitis A – Prognosis
concepts.content: The overall mortality rate for Hepatitis A is approximately 0.1%, increasing to 1.8% in individuals over 50 years of age. Importantly, Hepatitis A does not lead to chronic infection.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Definition
concepts.content: Hepatitis B is a viral liver inflammation caused by the Hepatitis B virus (HBV), an enveloped, partially double-stranded DNA virus. It can lead to both acute and chronic liver conditions.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Epidemiology
concepts.content: The incidence of Hepatitis B is approximately 0.8 cases per 100,000 person-years, indicating its prevalence within the population.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Hepatitis B shows a peak incidence in individuals aged 30 to 40 years, suggesting a higher risk of new infections within this demographic.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Globally, there are approximately 250 million carriers of Hepatitis B, highlighting its significant worldwide burden.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Aetiology/Transmission
concepts.content: Perinatal transmission is the most common route in endemic areas, with over 90% risk without immunisation.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Aetiology/Transmission
concepts.content: Sexual transmission of Hepatitis B is prevalent among men who have sex with men (MSM), sex workers, and individuals with multiple partners.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Aetiology/Transmission
concepts.content: Percutaneous transmission occurs through intravenous drug use (IVDU) needle sharing, tattoos, and piercings.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Aetiology/Transmission
concepts.content: Blood transfusion as a source of Hepatitis B is now rare due to rigorous screening protocols.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Liver damage in Hepatitis B is primarily immune-mediated, resulting from cytotoxic T-cell lysis of infected hepatocytes.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: CD4+ T-cells activate CD8+ T-cells, which then release IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha, contributing to liver inflammation.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: The immune tolerance phase of HBV infection is characterized by high HBV DNA levels with no significant liver damage.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: The immune clearance/active phase involves HBeAg clearance and active liver damage.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Immune control phase signifies remission with normalized liver function tests (LFTs).

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Immune escape refers to reactivation of the virus, potentially leading to renewed liver damage.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Serology interpretation
concepts.content: HBsAg (surface antigen) indicates active acute or chronic Hepatitis B infection.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Serology interpretation
concepts.content: Anti-HBs (protective antibody) signifies either past infection with recovery or successful vaccination.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Serology interpretation
concepts.content: HBeAg indicates active viral replication and high infectivity.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Serology interpretation
concepts.content: Anti-HBe suggests reduced viral replication and lower infectivity.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Serology interpretation
concepts.content: Anti-HBc IgM is a marker for acute Hepatitis B infection.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Serology interpretation
concepts.content: Anti-HBc IgG indicates either past or chronic Hepatitis B infection.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Clinical features (acute)
concepts.content: The majority of acute Hepatitis B infections are asymptomatic.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Clinical features (acute)
concepts.content: Symptomatic acute Hepatitis B can present with fatigue, anorexia, nausea, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Clinical features (acute)
concepts.content: Fulminant hepatitis is a rare but severe complication of acute Hepatitis B, occurring in less than 1% of cases.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Clinical features (chronic)
concepts.content: Chronic Hepatitis B is defined by the persistence of HBsAg positivity for more than six months.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Clinical features (chronic)
concepts.content: Chronic Hepatitis B increases the risk of developing serious complications such as cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and hepatocellular carcinoma.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Management
concepts.content: Acute Hepatitis B infection is managed with supportive care.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Management
concepts.content: Chronic Hepatitis B is treated with antiviral medications such as tenofovir, entecavir, and pegylated interferon.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Management
concepts.content: Hepatitis B vaccination involves a 3-dose schedule (0, 1, and 6 months), with an accelerated schedule also available.

concepts.title: Hepatitis B – Prevention
concepts.content: Prevention includes vaccination of neonates born to HBsAg-positive mothers with HBIG and vaccine within 24 hours of birth.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Definition
concepts.content: HIV is a lentivirus, an RNA retrovirus that causes progressive immunodeficiency by targeting immune cells.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Variants
concepts.content: There are two main variants of HIV: HIV-1, which is globally prevalent, and HIV-2, primarily found in West Africa, known for lower transmission rates and slower disease progression.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Epidemiology
concepts.content: The peak incidence of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) infection is typically observed in individuals between 30 and 40 years of age.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Sexual Transmission
concepts.content: HIV is primarily transmitted through sexual contact, with unprotected receptive anal intercourse carrying the highest risk of transmission.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Parenteral Transmission
concepts.content: Parenteral transmission of HIV occurs through routes such as sharing needles among intravenous drug users and accidental needlestick injuries.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Vertical Transmission
concepts.content: Vertical transmission of HIV from mother to child can occur during pregnancy, childbirth, or through breastfeeding.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Blood Transfusion Risk
concepts.content: Transmission of HIV via blood transfusion is now rare in settings where blood products are routinely screened for the virus.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Genetic Resistance
concepts.content: Individuals with the CCR5-delta32 genetic mutation exhibit natural resistance to HIV infection, as it prevents the virus from entering cells.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Viral Entry
concepts.content: The HIV gp120 protein binds to CD4 receptors and either CXCR4 (on T cells) or CCR5 (on macrophages) to gain entry into host cells.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Reverse Transcription
concepts.content: HIV's reverse transcriptase enzyme converts its RNA genome into double-stranded DNA, which is then integrated into the host cell's genome.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Immunodeficiency Mechanism
concepts.content: HIV progressively destroys CD4+ T cells, leading to a compromised immune system and the development of immunodeficiency.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Seroconversion Timing
concepts.content: Seroconversion, the period when HIV antibodies become detectable, typically occurs 3 to 12 weeks following initial infection.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Seroconversion Symptoms
concepts.content: Approximately 60-80% of individuals experience symptomatic seroconversion, presenting with a glandular fever-like illness.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Glandular Fever-like Illness
concepts.content: Symptoms of acute HIV seroconversion can include sore throat, lymphadenopathy, malaise, myalgia, arthralgia, diarrhoea, maculopapular rash, and mouth ulcers.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Seroconversion Meningoencephalitis
concepts.content: In rare cases, acute HIV seroconversion may manifest with meningoencephalitis, indicating central nervous system involvement.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - CD4 200-500 Complications
concepts.content: With CD4 counts between 200-500 cells/mm³, HIV patients may develop oral thrush (Candida), shingles (VZV), hairy leukoplakia (EBV), and Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8).

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - CD4 100-200 Complications
concepts.content: When CD4 counts fall to 100-200 cells/mm³, complications such as cryptosporidiosis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, PML (JC virus), PCP (Pneumocystis jirovecii), and HIV dementia can occur.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - CD4 50-100 Complications
concepts.content: At CD4 counts of 50-100 cells/mm³, patients are susceptible to aspergillosis, oesophageal candidiasis, cryptococcal meningitis, and primary CNS lymphoma (EBV).

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - CD4 <50 Complications
concepts.content: With CD4 counts below 50 cells/mm³, severe complications like CMV retinitis and Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection are common.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - HIV Antibody/Antigen Test
concepts.content: Initial diagnosis of HIV involves an antibody/antigen test, which detects both p24 antigen and HIV antibodies.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - HIV RNA Viral Load
concepts.content: HIV RNA viral load testing quantifies the amount of HIV genetic material in the blood, indicating disease activity and treatment effectiveness.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - CD4 T-cell Count
concepts.content: CD4 T-cell count measures the number of CD4+ T lymphocytes, a key indicator of immune system health and HIV disease progression.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Resistance Testing
concepts.content: Resistance testing is performed before initiating Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) to identify viral mutations that may confer resistance to specific drugs.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - HAART Initiation
concepts.content: Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART) should be initiated immediately upon diagnosis of HIV, as per 2015 BHIVA guidelines.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - HAART Regimen
concepts.content: A typical HAART regimen consists of two Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) combined with either a Protease Inhibitor (PI) or a Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor (NNRTI).

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Entry Inhibitors
concepts.content: Entry inhibitors for HIV include maraviroc, which blocks the CCR5 co-receptor, and enfuvirtide, which targets the gp41 fusion protein.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - NRTIs
concepts.content: Common Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) used in HIV treatment include zidovudine, abacavir, tenofovir, and emtricitabine.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - NNRTIs
concepts.content: Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NNRTIs) commonly prescribed for HIV include nevirapine and efavirenz.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - PIs
concepts.content: Protease Inhibitors (PIs) used in HIV therapy include indinavir and ritonavir, with ritonavir also acting as a P450 inhibitor to boost other PIs.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus - Integrase Inhibitors
concepts.content: Integrase inhibitors, such as raltegravir and dolutegravir, prevent HIV DNA from integrating into the host cell's genome.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Definition
concepts.content: Lyme disease is a multisystemic tick-borne illness caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi (B. afzelii, B. garinii in Europe/Asia). It is transmitted by Ixodes ticks and progresses through early localised, early disseminated, and late disseminated stages.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Epidemiology
concepts.content: The incidence of Lyme disease is approximately 12 per 100,000 person-years, with a peak incidence observed in individuals aged 6-15 years.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Aetiology
concepts.content: Lyme disease is caused by the Borrelia burgdorferi spirochete. The primary vectors are Ixodes scapularis in the USA and Ixodes ricinus in Europe. The risk of transmission is highest after 36-48 hours of tick attachment.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Early Clinical Features: Erythema Migrans
concepts.content: Erythema migrans, a 'bulls-eye' rash, is a hallmark early clinical feature of Lyme disease, appearing 1-4 weeks post-tick bite. It is typically >5cm, painless, slowly enlarges, and is present in approximately 80% of early cases.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Early Clinical Features: Systemic Symptoms
concepts.content: Early systemic symptoms of Lyme disease, occurring within 30 days of infection, include headache, lethargy, fever, and arthralgia.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Late Clinical Features: Cardiovascular
concepts.content: Late clinical features of Lyme disease, manifesting after 30 days, can include cardiovascular complications such as heart block and peri/myocarditis.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Late Clinical Features: Neurological
concepts.content: Neurological manifestations in late Lyme disease (after 30 days) include facial nerve palsy, radicular pain, and meningitis.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Investigations: Clinical Diagnosis
concepts.content: Lyme disease is diagnosed clinically if erythema migrans is present, allowing for immediate antibiotic treatment without further testing.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Investigations: Serology
concepts.content: ELISA for Borrelia antibodies is the first-line investigation. If negative but Lyme disease is suspected within 4 weeks, repeat ELISA 4-6 weeks later. A positive or equivocal ELISA result warrants a confirmatory immunoblot test.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Management: Early Disease
concepts.content: Early Lyme disease is managed with Doxycycline. Amoxicillin is an alternative if Doxycycline is contraindicated, such as during pregnancy.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Management: Disseminated Disease
concepts.content: Disseminated Lyme disease requires treatment with Ceftriaxone. Patients should be monitored for a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after the initial antibiotic dose.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Management: Asymptomatic Tick Bites
concepts.content: For asymptomatic tick bites, routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended according to NICE guidelines.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Complications: Neuroborreliosis
concepts.content: Neuroborreliosis, a complication of Lyme disease, can manifest as lymphocytic meningitis, facial nerve palsy, and radiculoneuritis.

concepts.title: Lyme disease – Complications: Lyme Carditis and Chronic Arthritis
concepts.content: Lyme carditis, presenting as AV block or myopericarditis, and chronic arthritis are significant complications of Lyme disease.

concepts.title: Malaria – Definition
concepts.content: Non-falciparum malaria is caused by various Plasmodium species, including P. vivax (the most prevalent), P. ovale, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi.

concepts.title: Malaria – General Clinical Features
concepts.content: Common clinical manifestations of non-falciparum malaria include fever, headache, and an enlarged spleen (splenomegaly).

concepts.title: Malaria – P. vivax/ovale Fever Pattern
concepts.content: Infections with Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale typically present with a cyclical fever occurring approximately every 48 hours.

concepts.title: Malaria – P. malariae Fever Pattern
concepts.content: Plasmodium malariae infections are characterized by a distinct cyclical fever pattern that recurs every 72 hours.

concepts.title: Malaria – P. malariae and Nephrotic Syndrome
concepts.content: Plasmodium malariae infection is notably associated with the development of nephrotic syndrome, a kidney disorder.

concepts.title: Malaria – P. vivax/ovale Hypnozoite Stage
concepts.content: Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale have a hypnozoite liver stage, which can lead to relapses even after initial treatment.

concepts.title: Malaria – Management in Chloroquine-Sensitive Areas
concepts.content: In regions where malaria is sensitive to chloroquine, treatment options include Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) or chloroquine, as recommended by WHO.

concepts.title: Malaria – Management in Chloroquine-Resistant Areas
concepts.content: For non-falciparum malaria in areas with chloroquine resistance, Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) is the recommended management.

concepts.title: Malaria – Management of P. vivax/ovale Relapse Prevention
concepts.content: Following acute treatment for P. vivax or P. ovale malaria, primaquine should be administered to eliminate liver hypnozoites and prevent future relapses. ACTs should be avoided in pregnancy.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Definition
concepts.content: Meningitis is characterized by inflammation of the meninges, the protective membranes enveloping the brain and spinal cord. The underlying causes of this condition can vary significantly depending on the patient's age group.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Aetiology (0-3 months)
concepts.content: In infants aged 0-3 months, common bacterial causes of meningitis include Group B Streptococcus, which is the most prevalent pathogen in neonates. Other significant causative agents are Escherichia coli and Listeria monocytogenes.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Aetiology (Group B Streptococcus)
concepts.content: Group B Streptococcus is a primary bacterial cause of meningitis, particularly noted for its high incidence in neonates (0-3 months). It is considered the most common pathogen responsible for meningitis in this vulnerable age group.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Aetiology (E. coli)
concepts.content: Escherichia coli (E. coli) is a significant bacterial pathogen implicated in meningitis, especially in the youngest patient demographic, specifically infants aged 0-3 months. Its presence necessitates prompt and effective antimicrobial treatment.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Aetiology (Listeria monocytogenes)
concepts.content: Listeria monocytogenes is a bacterial cause of meningitis, notably affecting infants aged 0-3 months and individuals over 60 years. It is also a critical pathogen to consider in immunosuppressed patients due to their heightened susceptibility.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Aetiology (3 months-6 years)
concepts.content: For children between 3 months and 6 years, the primary bacterial causes of meningitis include Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae. These pathogens are responsible for the majority of cases in this age bracket.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Aetiology (Neisseria meningitidis)
concepts.content: Neisseria meningitidis is a significant bacterial cause of meningitis, particularly prevalent in children aged 3 months to 6 years and adults aged 6-60 years. It is known for its potential to cause outbreaks.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Aetiology (Streptococcus pneumoniae)
concepts.content: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading bacterial cause of meningitis across various age groups, including children aged 3 months to 6 years, adults aged 6-60 years, and individuals over 60 years. Vaccination can prevent many cases.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Aetiology (Haemophilus influenzae)
concepts.content: Haemophilus influenzae is a bacterial pathogen responsible for meningitis, primarily observed in children aged 3 months to 6 years. The introduction of the Hib vaccine has significantly reduced the incidence of this type of meningitis.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Aetiology (6-60 years)
concepts.content: In individuals aged 6 to 60 years, the most common bacterial pathogens causing meningitis are Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae. These two organisms account for a substantial proportion of meningitis cases in this broad age group.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Aetiology (>60 years)
concepts.content: For patients over 60 years of age, the predominant bacterial causes of meningitis include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Listeria monocytogenes. The elderly population is particularly susceptible to these infections.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Aetiology (Immunosuppressed)
concepts.content: Immunosuppressed individuals are at an elevated risk for meningitis caused by specific pathogens. Listeria monocytogenes is a particularly important causative agent to consider in this patient population due to their compromised immune defenses.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Aetiology (Group B Streptococcus in Neonates)
concepts.content: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is the most frequent bacterial cause of meningitis in neonates, specifically within the 0-3 month age bracket. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial due to the severity of GBS infections in this population.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Bacterial CSF Appearance
concepts.content: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in bacterial meningitis typically presents with a cloudy or turbid appearance due to the presence of inflammatory cells and bacteria.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Bacterial CSF Glucose
concepts.content: CSF glucose levels in bacterial meningitis are characteristically low, often less than half of the plasma glucose concentration, reflecting bacterial consumption of glucose.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Bacterial CSF Protein
concepts.content: Elevated CSF protein levels, typically exceeding 1 g/L, are a common finding in bacterial meningitis, indicating increased vascular permeability and inflammation.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Bacterial CSF WBC Count
concepts.content: Bacterial meningitis is associated with a high CSF white blood cell (WBC) count, ranging from 10 to 5000 polymorphonuclear leukocytes per cubic millimeter.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Viral CSF Appearance
concepts.content: CSF in viral meningitis can appear clear or slightly cloudy. The appearance is less turbid than in bacterial infections.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Viral CSF Glucose
concepts.content: CSF glucose levels in viral meningitis are typically normal, usually 60-80% of plasma glucose. However, some viral causes like mumps or herpes encephalitis can cause low glucose.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Viral CSF Protein
concepts.content: CSF protein levels in viral meningitis are typically normal or mildly raised, generally less pronounced than in bacterial infections.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Viral CSF WBC Count
concepts.content: Viral meningitis typically shows a CSF white blood cell (WBC) count between 15 and 1000 lymphocytes per cubic millimeter, with a lymphocytic predominance.

concepts.title: Mumps – CSF Glucose in Meningitis
concepts.content: Mumps virus can cause meningitis with unusually low CSF glucose levels in a proportion of cases, deviating from the typical normal glucose seen in most viral meningitis.

concepts.title: Encephalitis – Herpes CSF Glucose
concepts.content: Herpes encephalitis can present with low CSF glucose, a finding that can sometimes overlap with bacterial or tuberculous meningitis, requiring careful differential diagnosis.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Tuberculous CSF Appearance
concepts.content: CSF in tuberculous meningitis often appears slightly cloudy and may form a fibrin web upon standing, a characteristic finding.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Tuberculous CSF Glucose
concepts.content: CSF glucose levels in tuberculous meningitis are typically low, often less than half of the plasma glucose, similar to bacterial meningitis.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Tuberculous CSF Protein
concepts.content: Tuberculous meningitis is characterized by high CSF protein levels, typically exceeding 1 g/L, reflecting significant inflammation and blood-brain barrier disruption.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Tuberculous CSF WBC Count
concepts.content: CSF white blood cell (WBC) count in tuberculous meningitis ranges from 30 to 300 lymphocytes per cubic millimeter, with a lymphocytic predominance.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Ziehl-Neelsen Stain Sensitivity
concepts.content: The Ziehl-Neelsen stain for Mycobacterium tuberculosis in CSF has a low sensitivity of approximately 20%, making it an unreliable sole diagnostic tool for tuberculous meningitis.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – NAAT for MTB DNA
concepts.content: Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) for Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA are the preferred diagnostic method for tuberculous meningitis due to their higher sensitivity compared to traditional staining.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Fungal CSF Appearance
concepts.content: CSF in fungal meningitis typically appears cloudy, similar to bacterial meningitis, reflecting the inflammatory response to fungal pathogens.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Fungal CSF Glucose
concepts.content: CSF glucose levels are low in fungal meningitis, a finding consistent with microbial consumption of glucose, similar to bacterial and tuberculous etiologies.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Fungal CSF Protein
concepts.content: High CSF protein levels are characteristic of fungal meningitis, indicating an inflammatory response and increased permeability of the blood-brain barrier.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Fungal CSF WBC Count
concepts.content: Fungal meningitis typically presents with a CSF white blood cell (WBC) count ranging from 20 to 200 lymphocytes per cubic millimeter, primarily lymphocytic.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Initial Management: Urgent Transfer
concepts.content: Patients with suspected bacterial meningitis require urgent transfer to hospital for immediate medical assessment and intervention.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Pre-hospital Benzylpenicillin
concepts.content: Administer pre-hospital intramuscular benzylpenicillin if meningococcal disease is suspected, provided it does not delay urgent transfer to hospital.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Initial Management: ABC Approach
concepts.content: The initial management of suspected bacterial meningitis should always follow the ABC (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) approach to stabilize the patient.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Senior Review Warning Signs
concepts.content: A senior review is indicated if warning signs are present, such as a rapidly progressive rash, poor perfusion, extreme respiratory or heart rates, abnormal pH/WBC/lactate, GCS <12 or drop of 2, or poor fluid response.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Contraindications for Immediate Lumbar Puncture
concepts.content: Delay lumbar puncture if severe sepsis/rapidly evolving rash, severe respiratory/cardiac compromise, significant bleeding risk, signs of raised ICP, focal neurological signs, papilloedema, continuous seizures, or GCS ≤9.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Lumbar Puncture Procedure
concepts.content: If no contraindications for delayed LP, establish IV access, take bloods and blood cultures, then perform lumbar puncture.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Antibiotic Administration Timing
concepts.content: If lumbar puncture cannot be performed within one hour, administer IV antibiotics immediately after obtaining blood cultures.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Antibiotic Regimen (3 months-60 years)
concepts.content: For patients aged 3 months to 60 years with suspected bacterial meningitis, the recommended antibiotic is intravenous ceftriaxone.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Antibiotic Regimen (≥60 years)
concepts.content: Patients aged 60 years and older with suspected bacterial meningitis should receive intravenous ceftriaxone combined with amoxicillin or ampicillin.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Antibiotic Regimen (<3 months)
concepts.content: For infants younger than 3 months with suspected bacterial meningitis, the antibiotic regimen includes intravenous cefotaxime plus amoxicillin or ampicillin.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Vancomycin Indication
concepts.content: Intravenous vancomycin should be added to the antibiotic regimen if there is a history of recent prolonged/multiple antibiotic use or travel to areas with resistant pneumococci.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Adjunctive Dexamethasone
concepts.content: Consider adjunctive IV dexamethasone, especially if pneumococcal meningitis is suspected in adults, ideally before or with the first antibiotic dose, and no later than 12 hours after.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Dexamethasone Contraindications
concepts.content: Avoid adjunctive dexamethasone in cases of septic shock, meningococcal septicaemia, immunocompromised patients, or post-surgical meningitis.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Contact Prophylaxis
concepts.content: Oral ciprofloxacin (single dose, preferred) or rifampicin should be offered to close contacts within 7 days before onset. Meningococcal vaccination is given if serotype is known.

concepts.title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Definition
concepts.content: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a bacterial strain that played a significant role in highlighting the risks associated with infections acquired within healthcare settings.

concepts.title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Screening (Elective Admissions)
concepts.content: Screening for MRSA is mandatory for all patients scheduled for elective admissions, with exceptions for day patients undergoing termination of pregnancy, ophthalmic surgery, or those admitted to mental health trusts.

concepts.title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Screening (Emergency Admissions)
concepts.content: Since 2011, all patients admitted as emergencies are required to undergo screening for Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) upon admission to healthcare facilities.

concepts.title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Screening Method (Swab Sites)
concepts.content: MRSA screening involves collecting samples from the nasal passages and any existing skin lesions or wounds to detect the presence of the bacteria.

concepts.title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Screening Method (Swab Technique)
concepts.content: For nasal screening, a swab should be carefully rotated around the inner rim of the nose for five seconds. The microbiology form must be clearly marked as 'MRSA screen'.

concepts.title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Screening Documentation
concepts.content: When submitting samples for MRSA screening, it is crucial to ensure that the microbiology request form is explicitly labeled 'MRSA screen' for proper processing and identification.

concepts.title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Carrier Suppression (Nasal)
concepts.content: For nasal carriage of MRSA, treatment involves applying mupirocin 2% in white soft paraffin three times daily (TDS) to the nose for a duration of five days.

concepts.title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Carrier Suppression (Skin)
concepts.content: To suppress MRSA carriage on the skin, chlorhexidine gluconate should be applied once daily (OD) for five days to specific areas including the axilla, groin, and perineum.

concepts.title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Infection Treatment (Primary Antibiotics)
concepts.content: Effective antibiotics for treating MRSA infections include vancomycin, teicoplanin, and linezolid, which are typically used to combat resistant strains.

concepts.title: Hospital acquired infections – MRSA Infection Treatment (Antibiotics to Avoid Monotherapy)
concepts.content: Antibiotics such as rifampicin, macrolides, tetracyclines, and aminoglycosides should not be administered as monotherapy for MRSA infections due to the significant risk of developing resistance.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Active TB Initial Treatment
concepts.content: The initial phase of active tuberculosis treatment, lasting two months, involves a four-drug regimen known as RIPE: Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol. This intensive phase aims to rapidly reduce bacterial load and prevent drug resistance.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Active TB Continuation Treatment
concepts.content: Following the initial phase, the continuation phase for active tuberculosis treatment extends for four months. During this period, the regimen typically consists of two drugs: Rifampicin and Isoniazid, to ensure complete eradication of the infection.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Latent TB 3-Month Regimen
concepts.content: Treatment for latent tuberculosis can involve a three-month regimen combining isoniazid and rifampicin, with pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) supplementation to prevent peripheral neuropathy. This option is often preferred for patients under 35 years with hepatotoxicity concerns.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Latent TB 6-Month Regimen
concepts.content: An alternative treatment for latent tuberculosis is a six-month course of isoniazid, also supplemented with pyridoxine. This regimen is typically chosen for HIV or transplant patients due to potential rifamycin interactions, which can complicate other drug therapies.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Meningeal TB Treatment
concepts.content: Meningeal tuberculosis requires a prolonged treatment course of at least 12 months. This regimen includes the addition of corticosteroids to the standard anti-tuberculosis drugs, which helps to reduce inflammation and improve outcomes in this severe form of the disease.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Directly Observed Therapy (DOT)
concepts.content: Directly Observed Therapy (DOT), administered three times a week, is crucial for specific patient groups with tuberculosis. It ensures medication adherence and treatment completion, particularly for homeless individuals with active TB and all prisoners with active or latent TB.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Rifampicin Adverse Effects
concepts.content: Rifampicin, a key anti-TB drug, can cause several adverse effects including potent liver enzyme induction, hepatitis, and flu-like symptoms. Patients may also notice harmless orange discoloration of secretions, such as urine and tears.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Isoniazid Adverse Effects
concepts.content: Isoniazid can lead to peripheral neuropathy, which is preventable with pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) supplementation. Other notable adverse effects include hepatitis, agranulocytosis, and its action as a liver enzyme inhibitor, requiring careful monitoring.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Pyrazinamide Adverse Effects
concepts.content: Pyrazinamide, an anti-TB medication, is associated with adverse effects such as hyperuricaemia, which can precipitate gout. Patients may also experience arthralgia (joint pain), myalgia (muscle pain), and hepatitis, necessitating liver function monitoring.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Ethambutol Adverse Effects
concepts.content: Ethambutol is known for its potential to cause optic neuritis, an inflammation of the optic nerve. Therefore, it is crucial to check visual acuity both before and regularly during treatment to detect and manage this adverse effect promptly.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS)
concepts.content: Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS) can occur approximately 3-6 weeks after initiating anti-tuberculosis treatment, particularly in immunocompromised patients. It often manifests as paradoxical worsening of existing lesions or the appearance of new ones, such as enlarging lymph nodes.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Mantoux test procedure
concepts.content: The Mantoux test involves injecting 0.1ml of Purified Protein Derivative (PPD) intradermally to assess for tuberculosis infection.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Mantoux test reading time
concepts.content: Results of the Mantoux test should be interpreted between 48 and 72 hours after the intradermal injection.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Mantoux test negative result
concepts.content: An induration of less than 5mm at the injection site typically indicates a negative Mantoux test result.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Mantoux test positive result
concepts.content: An induration of 5mm or greater on a Mantoux test suggests tuberculosis infection, irrespective of prior BCG vaccination.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Mantoux test strongly positive result
concepts.content: An induration exceeding 15mm in a Mantoux test is considered a strongly positive result, indicating a high likelihood of TB infection.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Mantoux test false negatives
concepts.content: False negative Mantoux results can occur in conditions such as miliary tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, HIV, lymphoma, and in infants under 6 months old.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – IGRA indications
concepts.content: Interferon-Gamma Release Assay (IGRA) is utilized when Mantoux test results are positive or inconclusive, or when false negative tuberculin tests are suspected.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – CXR findings in active TB
concepts.content: Chest X-ray (CXR) in active tuberculosis may reveal upper lobe cavitation, characteristic of reactivated TB, or bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, though unilateral is more typical of primary TB.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Sputum smear for diagnosis
concepts.content: Diagnosis of tuberculosis often involves sputum smear microscopy, requiring three specimens. It is a rapid and inexpensive method, using Ziehl-Neelsen stain to detect acid-fast bacilli.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Sputum smear sensitivity
concepts.content: Sputum smear for tuberculosis has a sensitivity ranging from 50-80%, which can drop to 20-30% in individuals with HIV infection.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Sputum culture gold standard
concepts.content: Sputum culture is considered the gold standard for tuberculosis diagnosis, offering higher sensitivity than smear or NAAT, and allowing for drug susceptibility testing. Results typically take 1-3 weeks with liquid media.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – NAAT for diagnosis
concepts.content: Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT) provides rapid tuberculosis diagnosis within 24-48 hours. It is more sensitive than sputum smear but less sensitive than culture.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – All mycobacteria stain positive on Ziehl-Neelsen
concepts.content: It is important to note that all mycobacteria will stain positive with the Ziehl-Neelsen stain, not exclusively Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis Definition
concepts.content: Viral meningitis is characterized by inflammation of the leptomeninges caused by a viral agent. It is generally considered a more benign condition compared to bacterial meningitis, with approximately 3000 confirmed cases reported annually in the UK, though the actual incidence is likely higher.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis Aetiology
concepts.content: The most common causes of viral meningitis are non-polio enteroviruses, including coxsackievirus and echovirus. Other viral agents that can lead to this condition include mumps virus, herpes simplex virus (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), varicella-zoster virus (herpes zoster), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and measles virus.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis Risk Factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for developing viral meningitis include extremes of age, particularly in children under 5 years old and the elderly. Immunocompromised individuals, such as those with renal failure or diabetes, and intravenous drug users (IVDU) are also at increased risk.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis Clinical Features
concepts.content: Common clinical features of viral meningitis include headache, neck stiffness, photophobia (often milder than in bacterial meningitis), confusion, and fever. Less common manifestations, such as focal neurological deficits or seizures, may suggest meningoencephalitis.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis CSF Opening Pressure
concepts.content: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis in viral meningitis typically reveals an opening pressure ranging from 10 to 20 cmH2O, which is within or slightly above the normal range.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis CSF Cell Count
concepts.content: CSF findings in viral meningitis usually show a cell count between 10 and 300 cells/µL, predominantly consisting of lymphocytes. This lymphocytic pleocytosis helps differentiate it from bacterial meningitis.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis CSF Glucose and Protein
concepts.content: CSF analysis for viral meningitis typically shows glucose levels between 2.8-4.2 mmol/L, or approximately two-thirds of the serum glucose level. Protein levels are usually in the range of 0.5-1 g/dL.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis Diagnosis and Supportive Treatment
concepts.content: Diagnosis of viral meningitis is confirmed via lumbar puncture (LP). Management primarily involves supportive treatment. If bacterial meningitis or encephalitis cannot be definitively ruled out, empirical treatment with ceftriaxone and intravenous aciclovir is initiated.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Viral Meningitis Prognosis and Specific Treatment
concepts.content: Viral meningitis is generally a self-limiting condition, with symptoms typically resolving within 7-14 days. Aciclovir treatment is specifically indicated if herpes simplex virus (HSV) is suspected as the causative agent.

concepts.title: Sepsis – Definition
concepts.content: Sepsis is a critical condition characterized by life-threatening organ dysfunction resulting from the body's uncontrolled response to an infection. Early recognition and intervention are crucial for improved patient outcomes.

concepts.title: Sepsis – Septic Shock Definition
concepts.content: Septic shock is a severe form of sepsis, identified by persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥65 mmHg and serum lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. It is associated with significantly higher mortality rates.

concepts.title: Sepsis – qSOFA Criteria
concepts.content: The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score is a rapid screening tool for sepsis. Criteria include respiratory rate ≥22/min, altered mentation (Glasgow Coma Scale <15), and systolic blood pressure ≤100 mmHg. A score of ≥2 indicates a high risk of sepsis.

concepts.title: Sepsis – Sepsis-6 Bundle
concepts.content: The Sepsis-6 bundle outlines key interventions to be initiated within one hour of sepsis recognition. These include obtaining blood cultures, administering intravenous antibiotics, giving an IV fluid bolus (500ml crystalloid), monitoring urine output, measuring serum lactate, and providing high-flow oxygen.

concepts.title: Sepsis – Septic Shock Management
concepts.content: Management of septic shock primarily involves vasopressor support. Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor to achieve a mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥65 mmHg. Hydrocortisone may be considered if the patient remains refractory to vasopressors.

concepts.title: Sepsis – Organ Dysfunction Markers
concepts.content: Key markers indicating organ dysfunction in sepsis include elevated lactate levels (>2 mmol/L), acute kidney injury (AKI), coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, raised bilirubin, and a reduced Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). These reflect the severity of the host response.

concepts.title: Sepsis – Target MAP in Septic Shock
concepts.content: In the management of septic shock, the primary hemodynamic goal is to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of ≥65 mmHg. This target ensures adequate organ perfusion while minimizing the risks associated with excessive vasopressor use.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Definition
concepts.content: Pneumonia is characterized by an infection affecting the lung parenchyma. It is categorized into community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) and hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP), with HAP occurring more than 48 hours post-admission.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Aetiology (CAP) - Streptococcus pneumoniae
concepts.content: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most frequent bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), accounting for approximately 80% of cases.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Aetiology (CAP) - Haemophilus influenzae
concepts.content: Haemophilus influenzae is another common bacterial pathogen implicated in the development of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP).

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Aetiology (CAP) - Staphylococcus aureus
concepts.content: Staphylococcus aureus can cause community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), particularly as a secondary infection following an influenza illness.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Aetiology (CAP) - Atypical pathogens
concepts.content: Atypical pathogens causing community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) include Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, and Chlamydophila pneumoniae.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Aetiology (CAP) - Klebsiella pneumoniae
concepts.content: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a notable cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), frequently observed in individuals with a history of alcoholism.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Aetiology (CAP) - Viruses
concepts.content: Various viruses can also be responsible for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) cases.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Clinical features
concepts.content: Key clinical features of pneumonia include fever, cough (potentially productive with rusty sputum in pneumococcal cases), pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, tachypnoea, and tachycardia.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Clinical features - Consolidation signs
concepts.content: Physical examination may reveal signs of lung consolidation, such as dullness to percussion, bronchial breathing, and increased vocal resonance.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – CURB-65 score
concepts.content: The CURB-65 score assesses pneumonia severity: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory Rate ≥30/min, Blood Pressure <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic, Age ≥65.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – CURB-65 score interpretation
concepts.content: CURB-65 score 0-1 suggests home treatment. A score of 2 indicates hospital admission. Scores 3-5 denote severe pneumonia, warranting consideration for ICU care.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations for pneumonia include a chest X-ray (CXR) showing lobar consolidation, FBC, CRP, U&E, blood cultures, and sputum culture. Urine antigen tests for pneumococcal/Legionella are also used. ABG is performed if severe.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Management (CAP) - CURB-65 0-1
concepts.content: For community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) with a CURB-65 score of 0-1, management typically involves oral amoxicillin.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Management (CAP) - CURB-65 2
concepts.content: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) with a CURB-65 score of 2 is managed with oral amoxicillin combined with clarithromycin.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Management (CAP) - CURB-65 3-5 (Option 1)
concepts.content: Severe community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) with a CURB-65 score of 3-5 is managed with intravenous (IV) co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Management (CAP) - CURB-65 3-5 (Option 2)
concepts.content: Alternatively, severe community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) with a CURB-65 score of 3-5 can be managed with intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone plus clarithromycin.

concepts.title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis A PEP - HNIG Use
concepts.content: Hepatitis A post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) with Human Normal Immunoglobulin (HNIG) is reserved for individuals unable to receive the vaccine or requiring rapid protection, such as immunosuppressed patients.

concepts.title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis A PEP - Vaccine Preference
concepts.content: The Hepatitis A vaccine is the preferred method for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) in most cases, offering effective protection against the virus.

concepts.title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis B PEP - Known Responder
concepts.content: For Hepatitis B post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) in a known responder (anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL) with an HBsAg-positive source, a booster dose of vaccine is indicated.

concepts.title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis B PEP - Non-Responder
concepts.content: If a non-responder (anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL) is exposed to an HBsAg-positive source, Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) and a booster vaccine are given for PEP.

concepts.title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis B PEP - Unknown Source
concepts.content: For Hepatitis B PEP with an unknown source and a non-responder, both HBIG and a booster vaccine are administered to provide protection.

concepts.title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis B PEP - Primary Course
concepts.content: A primary course for Hepatitis B PEP involves an accelerated vaccination schedule, potentially with HBIG if the exposure risk is high.

concepts.title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis C PEP - No Effective Prophylaxis
concepts.content: There is currently no effective post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) available for Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection.

concepts.title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis C PEP - Monitoring
concepts.content: Following potential Hepatitis C exposure, baseline HCV serology and RNA (PCR) are performed, with repeat HCV RNA at 6 and 12 weeks, and antibody testing at 3 and 6 months.

concepts.title: Viral hepatitides – Hepatitis C PEP - Seroconversion Management
concepts.content: If Hepatitis C seroconversion occurs after exposure, early hepatology referral for direct-acting antivirals is crucial for effective treatment.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus – HIV PEP - First-line Regimen
concepts.content: First-line HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) typically involves tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine (Truvada) combined with raltegravir.

concepts.title: Human immunodeficiency virus – HIV PEP - Timing and Duration
concepts.content: HIV PEP should be initiated as soon as possible, ideally within 1-2 hours and no later than 72 hours post-exposure, for a 4-week course.

concepts.title: Varicella zoster – VZV PEP - VZIG Use
concepts.content: Varicella Zoster Immunoglobulin (VZIG) is recommended for IgG-negative pregnant women or immunosuppressed individuals after significant VZV exposure.

concepts.title: Varicella zoster – VZV PEP - Aciclovir Alternative
concepts.content: If VZIG is unavailable or more than 10 days have passed since exposure, oral aciclovir can be used for VZV post-exposure prophylaxis.

concepts.title: Transmission risks – Needlestick Injuries
concepts.content: Needlestick injuries carry varying transmission risks: Hepatitis B 20-30% (if HBeAg positive), Hepatitis C 0.5-2%, and HIV 0.3%.

concepts.title: Sepsis – Risk Factors
concepts.content: Individuals with hyposplenism are at an elevated risk of developing post-splenectomy sepsis. This severe infection is commonly caused by encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Capnocytophaga canimorsus, often transmitted through dog bites.

concepts.title: Sepsis – Vaccination Schedule
concepts.content: For patients undergoing splenectomy, essential vaccinations include pneumococcal, Hib, and meningococcal type C. These should ideally be administered two weeks before or after the procedure. The recommended schedule involves MenC + Hib at two weeks post-splenectomy, followed by MenACWY one month later.

concepts.title: Sepsis – Ongoing Vaccinations
concepts.content: Lifelong vaccination is crucial for individuals post-splenectomy. This includes an annual influenza vaccination to protect against seasonal strains. Additionally, a pneumococcal vaccine booster is required every five years to maintain adequate immunity against Streptococcus pneumoniae.

concepts.title: Sepsis – Antibiotic Prophylaxis
concepts.content: Patients post-splenectomy typically require antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent severe infections. Penicillin V is commonly prescribed for at least two years, and often until the age of 16. Many patients, particularly those with ongoing risk, may continue lifelong prophylaxis.

concepts.title: Sepsis – Diagnosing Hyposplenism
concepts.content: The diagnosis of hyposplenism can be suggested by the presence of Howell-Jolly bodies on a blood film, though this method is not entirely reliable. The most sensitive diagnostic technique for assessing splenic function is a radionucleotide-labelled red cell scan.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Dysuria
concepts.content: Dysuria, characterized by painful or difficult urination, is a common symptom of urinary tract infection (UTI).

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Frequency
concepts.content: Increased urinary frequency, the need to urinate more often than usual, is a typical clinical feature of urinary tract infection (UTI).

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Urgency
concepts.content: Urinary urgency, a sudden and compelling need to pass urine, is a common presentation in patients with urinary tract infection (UTI).

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Urine appearance
concepts.content: Cloudy or offensive-smelling urine can indicate a urinary tract infection (UTI), often due to the presence of bacteria and white blood cells.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Lower abdominal pain
concepts.content: Lower abdominal pain or discomfort is a frequent symptom reported by individuals experiencing a urinary tract infection (UTI).

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Low-grade fever
concepts.content: A low-grade fever may be present in cases of lower urinary tract infection (UTI), indicating a systemic response to the infection.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Acute confusion in elderly
concepts.content: In elderly patients, acute confusion or delirium can be the primary or sole presentation of a urinary tract infection (UTI).

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Investigations: Urine dipstick findings
concepts.content: A urine dipstick showing positive nitrite or the presence of leukocytes and red blood cells strongly suggests a urinary tract infection (UTI).

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Investigations: Urine culture indications
concepts.content: Urine culture is indicated for UTI diagnosis in women over 65, those with recurrent UTIs, pregnant women, men, patients with haematuria, and catheterized individuals.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Management (non-pregnant women): First-line antibiotics
concepts.content: For non-pregnant women with UTI, NICE guidelines recommend trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin for 3 days as first-line antibiotic treatment.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Management (non-pregnant women): Urine culture
concepts.content: In non-pregnant women with UTI, a urine culture should be sent if the patient is over 65 years old or presents with haematuria.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Management (pregnant women): Antibiotic choices
concepts.content: Pregnant women with UTI can be treated with nitrofurantoin (avoid near term), amoxicillin, or cefalexin for 7 days.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Management (pregnant women): Trimethoprim contraindication
concepts.content: Trimethoprim is teratogenic in the first trimester and should be avoided throughout pregnancy due to potential harm to the fetus.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Management (pregnant women): Asymptomatic bacteriuria
concepts.content: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnant women must be treated to prevent complications such as pyelonephritis, which poses risks to both mother and fetus.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Management (pregnant women): Test of cure
concepts.content: A test of cure is essential after treating UTI in pregnant women to confirm eradication of the infection and prevent recurrence.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Management (men): Antibiotic regimen
concepts.content: For men with UTI, a 7-day course of trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin is typically prescribed.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Management (men): Pre-antibiotic urine culture
concepts.content: In men, a urine culture should be obtained before initiating antibiotic treatment for UTI to guide appropriate therapy.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Management (men): Urology referral
concepts.content: Urology referral is not routinely necessary for a single, uncomplicated urinary tract infection in men.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Management (catheterised): Asymptomatic bacteriuria
concepts.content: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterized patients should not be treated with antibiotics, as it is often colonization rather than infection.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Management (catheterised): Symptomatic treatment
concepts.content: Symptomatic urinary tract infection in catheterized patients requires a 7-day course of antibiotics.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Management (catheterised): Catheter removal/change
concepts.content: Consider removing or changing the catheter if it has been in place for more than 7 days in a symptomatic catheterized UTI patient.

concepts.title: Acute pyelonephritis – Management: Hospital admission
concepts.content: Hospital admission should be considered for patients diagnosed with acute pyelonephritis, especially if severe or complicated.

concepts.title: Acute pyelonephritis – Management: Antibiotic regimen
concepts.content: Acute pyelonephritis in non-pregnant individuals is typically managed with a broad-spectrum cephalosporin or quinolone for 10-14 days.

concepts.title: Vaccinations – Live Attenuated Vaccine Types
concepts.content: Live attenuated vaccines utilize weakened forms of the pathogen to induce immunity. They are generally not recommended for immunocompromised individuals.

concepts.title: Vaccinations – Examples of Live Attenuated Vaccines
concepts.content: Examples of live attenuated vaccines include BCG, MMR, intranasal influenza, oral rotavirus, oral polio, yellow fever, and oral typhoid.

concepts.title: Vaccinations – Live Attenuated Vaccine Contraindication
concepts.content: Live attenuated vaccines are generally contraindicated in individuals who are immunocompromised due to the risk of uncontrolled infection.

concepts.title: Vaccinations – Inactivated Vaccine Types
concepts.content: Inactivated vaccines contain killed versions of the pathogen, which cannot replicate but still trigger an immune response.

concepts.title: Vaccinations – Examples of Inactivated Vaccines
concepts.content: Examples of inactivated vaccines include rabies, hepatitis A, and intramuscular influenza vaccines.

concepts.title: Vaccinations – Toxoid Vaccine Types
concepts.content: Toxoid vaccines use inactivated bacterial toxins to stimulate an immune response against the toxin, rather than the bacteria itself.

concepts.title: Vaccinations – Examples of Toxoid Vaccines
concepts.content: Tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccines are examples of toxoid vaccines.

concepts.title: Vaccinations – Subunit/Conjugate Vaccine Types
concepts.content: Subunit vaccines contain only specific parts of the pathogen (e.g., proteins, sugars), while conjugate vaccines link these parts to a carrier protein to enhance immune response.

concepts.title: Vaccinations – Examples of Subunit/Conjugate Vaccines
concepts.content: Examples include pneumococcal (conjugate), Haemophilus (conjugate), meningococcal (conjugate), hepatitis B, and HPV vaccines.

concepts.title: Vaccinations – mRNA Vaccine Types
concepts.content: mRNA vaccines deliver genetic instructions to cells to produce a viral protein, triggering an immune response.

concepts.title: Vaccinations – Examples of mRNA Vaccines
concepts.content: Some COVID-19 vaccines are examples of mRNA vaccine technology.

concepts.title: Vaccinations – Viral Vector Vaccine Types
concepts.content: Viral vector vaccines use a modified virus to deliver genetic material that prompts an immune response against the target pathogen.
