concepts.title: Vaccinations – Examples of Viral Vector Vaccines
concepts.content: Some Ebola and COVID-19 vaccines are examples of viral vector vaccine technology.

concepts.title: Influenza – Vaccine Indications: Age and Chronic Respiratory Disease
concepts.content: Influenza vaccination is indicated for individuals over 65 years old and those with chronic respiratory diseases, including asthmatics on inhaled steroids.

concepts.title: Influenza – Vaccine Indications: Chronic Cardiac and Renal Disease
concepts.content: Indications for influenza vaccine include chronic heart disease and chronic kidney disease stages 3-5.

concepts.title: Influenza – Vaccine Indications: Chronic Liver, Neurological Disease, and Diabetes
concepts.content: Influenza vaccination is recommended for individuals with chronic liver disease, chronic neurological disease, and diabetes mellitus.

concepts.title: Influenza – Vaccine Indications: Immunosuppression and Asplenia
concepts.content: Immunosuppression and asplenia are key indications for influenza vaccination.

concepts.title: Influenza – Vaccine Indications: Pregnancy, Healthcare Workers, and Care Home Residents
concepts.content: Pregnant women, healthcare workers, and care home residents are indicated for influenza vaccination.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Pneumococcal Vaccine Indications: Age and Asplenia
concepts.content: Pneumococcal vaccination is indicated for individuals over 65 years old and those with asplenia.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Pneumococcal Vaccine Indications: Chronic Respiratory Disease
concepts.content: Indications for pneumococcal vaccine include chronic respiratory diseases such as COPD, bronchiectasis, CF, and ILD. Asthma is an indication only if oral steroids are used.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Pneumococcal Vaccine Indications: Chronic Cardiac and Renal Disease
concepts.content: Pneumococcal vaccination is indicated for chronic heart disease and chronic kidney disease stages 4-5.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Pneumococcal Vaccine Indications: Chronic Liver Disease and Diabetes
concepts.content: Indications for pneumococcal vaccine include chronic liver disease and diabetes requiring medication.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Pneumococcal Vaccine Indications: Immunosuppression and Cochlear Implants
concepts.content: Pneumococcal vaccination is indicated for immunosuppression (including any stage HIV) and individuals with cochlear implants.

concepts.title: Pneumonia – Pneumococcal Vaccine Indications: CSF Leaks
concepts.content: Individuals with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leaks are indicated for pneumococcal vaccination.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Definition
concepts.content: PUO is a prolonged febrile illness characterized by temperatures exceeding 38.3°C on multiple occasions over at least three weeks, with no diagnosis established after one week of inpatient investigation.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Classical Classification
concepts.content: Classical Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) encompasses cases arising from infections, malignancies, and non-infectious inflammatory diseases, representing a primary category of the condition.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Hospital-acquired Classification
concepts.content: Hospital-acquired Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) is defined by causes such as nosocomial infections, thromboembolic disease, and drug-induced fevers, occurring in an inpatient setting.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Neutropenic Classification
concepts.content: Neutropenic Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) primarily affects chemotherapy patients, with infections being the predominant underlying cause due to compromised immune function.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – HIV-associated Classification
concepts.content: HIV-associated Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) is linked to opportunistic infections, various malignancies, or the HIV virus itself, often presenting in individuals with compromised immunity.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Infectious Causes
concepts.content: Infections account for approximately 30% of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) cases, with common examples including tuberculosis and various abscesses.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Malignancy Causes
concepts.content: Malignancies contribute to about 20% of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) cases, notably lymphoma, hypernephroma, leukaemia, and atrial myxoma.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Non-infectious Inflammatory Causes
concepts.content: Non-infectious inflammatory conditions, such as Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), temporal arteritis, and rheumatoid arthritis, are significant causes of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO).

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Miscellaneous Causes
concepts.content: Miscellaneous factors account for approximately 50% of Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) cases, including drug fevers and factitious fever, often presenting diagnostic challenges.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Diagnostic Approach: History
concepts.content: A thorough history for PUO diagnosis includes assessing travel, occupational/animal exposures, and current medications to identify potential etiologies.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Diagnostic Approach: Laboratory Tests
concepts.content: Key laboratory investigations for PUO include FBC, ESR/CRP, HIV test, blood cultures, urinalysis, and CXR to screen for infectious and inflammatory causes.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Diagnostic Approach: Imaging
concepts.content: Imaging modalities such as CT, MRI, and PET scans are crucial in the diagnostic workup of PUO to localize potential sources of fever.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Diagnostic Approach: Biopsies
concepts.content: Biopsies or bone marrow examination are indicated in the diagnostic approach to PUO when initial investigations fail to yield a diagnosis.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Management: Outpatient Evaluation
concepts.content: Outpatient evaluation is often suitable for patients with Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO), allowing for comprehensive assessment without immediate hospitalization.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Management: Empirical Antibiotics
concepts.content: Empirical antibiotics are generally not recommended for PUO unless a life-threatening infection is strongly suspected, to avoid masking the underlying cause.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Prognosis: Undiagnosed Cases
concepts.content: Up to 50% of PUO cases remain undiagnosed even after extensive evaluation, highlighting the diagnostic challenge of this condition.

concepts.title: Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) – Prognosis: Good Outcome
concepts.content: The majority of patients with undiagnosed PUO ultimately have a good prognosis, despite the lack of a definitive diagnosis.

concepts.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa – Definition
concepts.content: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an aerobic, Gram-negative rod-shaped bacterium. It is a significant cause of infections, especially in individuals who are immunocompromised or hospitalized, contributing to a range of clinically important conditions.

concepts.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa – Chest infections
concepts.content: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a common cause of chest infections, particularly noted for its prevalence and severity in patients with cystic fibrosis. These infections can lead to significant respiratory morbidity and require targeted antibiotic therapy.

concepts.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa – Skin infections
concepts.content: Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes various skin infections, including severe burns, wound infections, and 'hot tub' folliculitis. These infections often present with characteristic blue-green pus due to pyocyanin production and require prompt treatment.

concepts.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa – Otitis externa
concepts.content: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a primary cause of otitis externa, especially in diabetic patients, where it can progress to malignant otitis externa. This severe form involves osteomyelitis of the skull base and requires aggressive management.

concepts.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa – Urinary tract infections
concepts.content: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a significant pathogen in urinary tract infections (UTIs), particularly in hospital-acquired settings or in patients with indwelling catheters. These infections can be challenging to treat due to antibiotic resistance.

concepts.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa – Gram stain
concepts.content: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is characterized as a Gram-negative rod, a key feature observed during microscopic examination. This morphological classification guides initial antibiotic selection and diagnostic pathways for suspected infections.

concepts.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa – Lactose fermentation
concepts.content: A distinguishing laboratory feature of Pseudomonas aeruginosa is its inability to ferment lactose. This characteristic helps differentiate it from other Gram-negative enteric bacteria in biochemical tests, aiding in accurate identification.

concepts.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa – Oxidase test
concepts.content: Pseudomonas aeruginosa tests positive for oxidase, indicating the presence of cytochrome c oxidase. This enzymatic activity is a crucial biochemical marker used in its identification, distinguishing it from many other Gram-negative bacteria.

concepts.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa – Toxin production
concepts.content: Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces both endotoxin, causing fever and shock, and exotoxin A. Exotoxin A inhibits protein synthesis by ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor EF-2, contributing significantly to the bacterium's virulence and pathogenicity.

concepts.title: Staphylococci – Basics
concepts.content: Staphylococci are Gram-positive cocci that are facultative anaerobes and catalase positive. They are a major cause of hospital-acquired and community-acquired infections.

concepts.title: Staphylococcus aureus – Characteristics
concepts.content: Staphylococcus aureus is a coagulase-positive species of Staphylococcus. It is a leading cause of skin and soft tissue infections, as well as more serious invasive diseases.

concepts.title: Staphylococcus aureus – Associated Infections
concepts.content: S. aureus is responsible for a wide range of infections, including skin and soft tissue infections like abscesses, cellulitis, and impetigo, as well as osteomyelitis and toxic shock syndrome.

concepts.title: Staphylococcus epidermidis – Characteristics
concepts.content: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a coagulase-negative species of Staphylococcus. It is a common commensal of the skin and a frequent cause of nosocomial infections.

concepts.title: Streptococci – Basics
concepts.content: Streptococci are Gram-positive cocci that grow in chains. They are classified based on their hemolytic properties (alpha, beta, or gamma) on blood agar.

concepts.title: Streptococci – Alpha-hemolytic
concepts.content: Alpha-hemolytic streptococci cause partial hemolysis on blood agar, resulting in a greenish discoloration. This group includes Streptococcus pneumoniae and the viridans streptococci.

concepts.title: Streptococcus pneumoniae – Associated Infections
concepts.content: S. pneumoniae is a leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia, bacterial meningitis, and otitis media. It is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide.

concepts.title: Streptococci – Beta-hemolytic
concepts.content: Beta-hemolytic streptococci cause complete hemolysis on blood agar, creating a clear zone around the colony. They are further classified by Lancefield grouping (e.g., Group A, Group B).

concepts.title: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A) – Associated Infections
concepts.content: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Strep) causes a variety of infections, including pharyngitis (strep throat), impetigo, cellulitis, and necrotizing fasciitis type 2.

concepts.title: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A) – Immune Sequelae
concepts.content: Infections with S. pyogenes can lead to immune-mediated complications such as acute rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

concepts.title: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A) – Scarlet Fever
concepts.content: Scarlet fever is a systemic illness caused by erythrogenic toxins produced by some strains of S. pyogenes, characterized by a distinctive rash and fever.

concepts.title: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B) – Associated Infections
concepts.content: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Strep) is a leading cause of serious infections in newborns, including neonatal meningitis and septicemia.

concepts.title: Enterococcus (Group D) – Associated Infections
concepts.content: Enterococci, formerly classified as Group D streptococci, are a common cause of urinary tract infections, bacteremia, and endocarditis, particularly in hospital settings.

concepts.title: Toxic Shock Syndrome – Aetiology
concepts.content: Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome is a severe, acute illness caused by the release of toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1), a superantigen produced by Staphylococcus aureus.

concepts.title: Toxic Shock Syndrome – Clinical Criteria: Fever
concepts.content: A key diagnostic criterion for toxic shock syndrome, as defined by the CDC, is a high fever, typically greater than 38.9°C (102.0°F).

concepts.title: Toxic Shock Syndrome – Clinical Criteria: Hypotension
concepts.content: Hypotension, with a systolic blood pressure of less than 90 mmHg, is a critical diagnostic criterion for toxic shock syndrome, indicating circulatory collapse.

concepts.title: Toxic Shock Syndrome – Clinical Criteria: Rash
concepts.content: A diffuse, erythematous macular rash is a characteristic finding in toxic shock syndrome. This rash can resemble a sunburn and may be widespread.

concepts.title: Toxic Shock Syndrome – Clinical Criteria: Desquamation
concepts.content: Desquamation, or peeling of the skin, particularly on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, is a late-stage sign of toxic shock syndrome, occurring 1-2 weeks after onset.

concepts.title: Toxic Shock Syndrome – Clinical Criteria: Multi-organ Involvement
concepts.content: The diagnosis of toxic shock syndrome requires evidence of involvement of at least three organ systems, reflecting the systemic nature of the illness.

concepts.title: Toxic Shock Syndrome – Management: Source Control
concepts.content: A critical first step in managing toxic shock syndrome is to identify and remove the source of the infection, such as a retained tampon or an abscess.

concepts.title: Toxic Shock Syndrome – Management: Fluid Resuscitation
concepts.content: Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation is essential to manage the profound hypotension and distributive shock characteristic of toxic shock syndrome.

concepts.title: Toxic Shock Syndrome – Management: Antibiotics
concepts.content: Prompt administration of intravenous antibiotics is a cornerstone of treatment for toxic shock syndrome to eradicate the causative bacteria and halt toxin production.

concepts.title: Strongyloides stercoralis – Definition
concepts.content: Strongyloides stercoralis is a human parasitic nematode worm. Its larvae, found in soil, penetrate the skin, leading to the infection known as strongyloidiasis.

concepts.title: Strongyloides stercoralis – Gastrointestinal Clinical Features
concepts.content: Patients infected with Strongyloides stercoralis commonly present with gastrointestinal symptoms including diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and bloating.

concepts.title: Strongyloides stercoralis – Cutaneous Larval Penetration
concepts.content: Papulovesicular lesions can develop at sites where Strongyloides larvae penetrate the skin, typically on the soles of the feet or buttocks.

concepts.title: Strongyloides stercoralis – Larva Currens
concepts.content: Larva currens is a characteristic clinical feature of strongyloidiasis, presenting as a pruritic, linear, and urticarial rash caused by larval migration within the skin.

concepts.title: Strongyloides stercoralis – Pulmonary Manifestations
concepts.content: Migration of Strongyloides larvae to the lungs can induce pneumonitis, a condition that shares similarities with Loeffler's syndrome.

concepts.title: Strongyloides stercoralis – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis of Strongyloides stercoralis involves identifying rhabditiform larvae in stool microscopy (eggs are typically absent) and performing serology, such as ELISA for Strongyloides IgG, which offers high sensitivity. Eosinophilia may be present, but can be absent in hyperinfection.

concepts.title: Strongyloides stercoralis – Treatment
concepts.content: The primary treatment for Strongyloides stercoralis infection involves the administration of antiparasitic medications, specifically ivermectin and albendazole.

concepts.title: Malaria – Definition
concepts.content: Malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum is the most severe form of the disease.

concepts.title: Malaria – Transmission
concepts.content: The female Anopheles mosquito is responsible for transmitting Plasmodium falciparum, causing malaria.

concepts.title: Malaria – Aetiology
concepts.content: Plasmodium falciparum is recognized as the most dangerous species of malaria-causing parasites due to its severe clinical manifestations.

concepts.title: Malaria – Other Plasmodium Species
concepts.content: Other Plasmodium species that cause malaria include P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi, each with distinct clinical profiles.

concepts.title: Malaria – Vector
concepts.content: The female Anopheles mosquito acts as the primary vector for the transmission of all Plasmodium species, including P. falciparum.

concepts.title: Malaria – Clinical Features: Fever
concepts.content: Patients with Plasmodium falciparum malaria often present with fever, which may be irregular and not follow the cyclical pattern seen in other malaria species.

concepts.title: Malaria – Clinical Features: General Symptoms
concepts.content: Common clinical features of malaria include headache, myalgia (muscle pain), and rigors (shivering or trembling).

concepts.title: Malaria – Complications: Cerebral Malaria
concepts.content: Cerebral malaria is a severe complication characterized by neurological symptoms such as seizures and coma, indicating central nervous system involvement.

concepts.title: Malaria – Complications: Severe Anaemia
concepts.content: Severe anaemia is a critical complication of malaria, particularly in children, contributing significantly to morbidity and mortality.

concepts.title: Malaria – Complications: ARDS
concepts.content: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) can develop as a severe complication of malaria, leading to significant respiratory compromise.

concepts.title: Malaria – Complications: Acute Renal Failure
concepts.content: Acute renal failure is a potentially life-threatening complication of severe malaria, requiring prompt medical intervention.

concepts.title: Malaria – Complications: Hypoglycaemia
concepts.content: Hypoglycaemia, or low blood sugar, is a serious and common complication in severe malaria, especially in children and pregnant women.

concepts.title: Malaria – Complications: Blackwater Fever
concepts.content: Blackwater fever, characterized by haemoglobinuria due to massive haemolysis, is a severe and often fatal complication of falciparum malaria.

concepts.title: Malaria – Investigations: Thick Blood Film
concepts.content: A thick blood film is highly sensitive for diagnosing malaria by detecting the presence of parasites, particularly useful for screening.

concepts.title: Malaria – Investigations: Thin Blood Film
concepts.content: A thin blood film is crucial for identifying the specific Plasmodium species causing malaria and quantifying parasite density.

concepts.title: Malaria – Investigations: Giemsa Stain
concepts.content: Giemsa stain is the standard method for staining blood films in malaria diagnosis, allowing clear visualization of parasites.

concepts.title: Malaria – Investigations: Fields Stain
concepts.content: Fields stain is employed for rapid malaria screening in resource-limited settings due to its quick staining properties.

concepts.title: Malaria – Investigations: Repeated Blood Films
concepts.content: Repeated blood films may be necessary to definitively rule out malaria infection, especially if initial tests are negative but suspicion remains high.

concepts.title: Malaria – Investigations: Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDTs)
concepts.content: Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) detect plasmodial histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP-2) for quick malaria diagnosis.

concepts.title: Malaria – Investigations: RDT Sensitivity/Specificity
concepts.content: RDTs for falciparum malaria exhibit sensitivity ranging from 77-99% and specificity from 83-98%, aiding in rapid diagnosis.

concepts.title: Malaria – Investigations: Thrombocytopenia
concepts.content: Thrombocytopenia (low platelet count) is a characteristic finding in blood tests for malaria.

concepts.title: Malaria – Investigations: Anaemia
concepts.content: Normochromic normocytic anaemia is a common haematological finding in malaria patients.

concepts.title: Malaria – Investigations: White Cell Count
concepts.content: A normal white cell count is typically observed in blood tests for malaria, distinguishing it from bacterial infections.

concepts.title: Malaria – Investigations: Reticulocytosis
concepts.content: Reticulocytosis, an increase in immature red blood cells, can be present in malaria due to increased red blood cell destruction.

concepts.title: Malaria – Management: Uncomplicated Falciparum Malaria
concepts.content: Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) is the first-line treatment for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

concepts.title: Malaria – Management: Severe Falciparum Malaria
concepts.content: Intravenous artesunate is the recommended treatment for severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria, offering rapid parasite clearance.

concepts.title: Malaria – Management: ACT in Pregnancy
concepts.content: Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) should generally be avoided in pregnant women, especially during the first trimester.

concepts.title: Malaria – Management: Alternative Treatments
concepts.content: If ACTs are unavailable, an alternative treatment for malaria is quinine combined with doxycycline or clindamycin.

concepts.title: Malaria – Prophylaxis: Atovaquone-Proguanil
concepts.content: Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) is a common chemoprophylaxis option for preventing malaria, suitable for many regions.

concepts.title: Malaria – Prophylaxis: Doxycycline
concepts.content: Doxycycline is an effective and widely used medication for malaria prophylaxis, particularly in areas with drug-resistant strains.

concepts.title: Malaria – Prophylaxis: Mefloquine
concepts.content: Mefloquine is a long-acting antimalarial drug used for prophylaxis, often taken weekly, but with potential neuropsychiatric side effects.

concepts.title: Malaria – Prophylaxis: Chloroquine
concepts.content: Chloroquine can be used for malaria prophylaxis in regions where Plasmodium falciparum remains sensitive to the drug.

concepts.title: Malaria – Prophylaxis: DEET Insect Repellent
concepts.content: DEET insect repellent provides mechanical protection against mosquito bites, a key component of malaria prophylaxis.

concepts.title: Malaria – Prophylaxis: Permethrin-Treated Bed Nets
concepts.content: Permethrin-treated bed nets offer effective mechanical protection by creating a barrier against mosquito bites during sleep.

concepts.title: Malaria – Prophylaxis: Appropriate Clothing
concepts.content: Wearing appropriate clothing, such as long sleeves and trousers, provides a physical barrier against mosquito bites for malaria prevention.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Macrophage infection
concepts.content: Mycobacterium tuberculosis primarily targets and infects alveolar macrophages within the host's lungs, initiating the disease process.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Lymph node migration
concepts.content: Following infection, macrophages containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis migrate from the lungs to regional lymph nodes, contributing to systemic spread.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Ghon complex formation
concepts.content: The combination of a primary lung lesion and infected regional lymph nodes is characteristic of early tuberculosis, forming what is known as a Ghon complex.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Granuloma formation
concepts.content: A hallmark of tuberculosis is the formation of granulomas, which are organized collections of epithelioid histiocytes, often featuring caseous necrosis at their core.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Type IV hypersensitivity
concepts.content: The inflammatory response in tuberculosis, crucial for containing the infection, is primarily mediated by a delayed-type (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Disease containment and dissemination
concepts.content: In immunocompetent individuals, tuberculosis infection is often contained. However, in immunocompromised patients, the disease may disseminate, leading to miliary TB.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Risk factors for active disease
concepts.content: Key risk factors for developing active tuberculosis include silicosis, chronic renal failure, HIV infection, solid organ transplantation with immunosuppression, and intravenous drug use.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Geographical and exposure risk factors
concepts.content: Living in or having lived in regions such as Asia, Latin America, Eastern Europe, or Africa, and exposure to an infectious TB case, are significant risk factors.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Other medical risk factors
concepts.content: Additional medical risk factors for active TB include haematological malignancy, anti-TNF treatment, previous gastrectomy, and apical fibrosis.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Latent TB definition
concepts.content: Latent tuberculosis is characterized by an asymptomatic and non-infectious state, where the individual cannot transmit the disease to others.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Latent TB diagnosis
concepts.content: Diagnosis of latent TB involves a positive Mantoux test or IGRA, combined with a normal chest X-ray to rule out active disease.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Latent TB treatment options
concepts.content: NICE guidelines offer two main treatment options for latent TB: a 3-month regimen of isoniazid (with pyridoxine) and rifampicin, or a 6-month course of isoniazid (with pyridoxine).

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Latent TB treatment choice (hepatotoxicity)
concepts.content: For individuals under 35, the 3-month regimen of isoniazid and rifampicin is preferred if concerns about hepatotoxicity are present.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis – Latent TB treatment choice (drug interactions)
concepts.content: The 6-month isoniazid regimen is recommended when rifamycin interactions are a concern, particularly in patients with HIV or those who have undergone transplantation.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Definition
concepts.content: Infection of the endocardium, most commonly affecting heart valves. Acute IE involves virulent organisms on normal valves; subacute IE involves less virulent organisms on previously abnormal valves.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Causative organisms overview
concepts.content: Streptococcus viridans is the most common cause overall (subacute, dental procedures). Staphylococcus aureus is most common in IVDU and hospital-acquired IE (acute). Staphylococcus epidermidis causes prosthetic valve endocarditis.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – HACEK and other organisms
concepts.content: HACEK organisms (Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) cause culture-negative IE. Streptococcus bovis is associated with colorectal cancer. Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) and Bartonella cause culture-negative IE.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Systemic features
concepts.content: Fever, malaise, night sweats, and weight loss are the classic systemic features. A new or changing heart murmur is a key finding. Splenomegaly may be present in subacute disease.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Peripheral stigmata
concepts.content: Splinter haemorrhages (linear subungual haemorrhages). Osler nodes: painful nodules on finger pulps (immune complex deposition). Janeway lesions: painless erythematous macules on palms and soles (septic emboli). Roth spots: retinal haemorrhages with pale centres.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Duke criteria major
concepts.content: Major criteria: (1) Positive blood cultures with typical organisms (S. viridans, S. bovis, HACEK, S. aureus, Enterococcus) in 2 separate sets, or persistently positive. (2) Evidence of endocardial involvement on echo or new valvular regurgitation.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Duke criteria minor and diagnosis
concepts.content: Minor criteria: predisposing condition or IVDU; fever >38°C; vascular phenomena; immunological phenomena (Osler nodes, Roth spots, GN, RF); microbiological evidence not meeting major. Definite IE: 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Blood cultures
concepts.content: Three sets of blood cultures should be taken from different venepuncture sites before commencing antibiotics. This maximises the chance of identifying the causative organism and guiding targeted antibiotic therapy.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Echocardiography
concepts.content: Transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE) is more sensitive than transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) for detecting vegetations and perivalvular abscesses. ECG may show new conduction defects suggesting aortic root abscess.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Antibiotic management
concepts.content: IV antibiotics for 4–6 weeks. Native valve streptococcal: amoxicillin + gentamicin. Native valve staphylococcal (MSSA): flucloxacillin ± gentamicin. MRSA: vancomycin. Prosthetic valve: vancomycin + rifampicin + gentamicin.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Surgical indications
concepts.content: Surgery is indicated for: heart failure due to valve dysfunction (most common indication), uncontrolled infection (persistent bacteraemia, abscess formation), and prevention of embolism (large vegetations >10 mm).

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Cardiac complications
concepts.content: Heart failure is the most common cause of death in IE (due to valve destruction). Perivalvular abscess formation. Conduction defects (aortic root abscess). Pericarditis.

concepts.title: Infective endocarditis – Embolic and renal complications
concepts.content: Embolic complications: stroke, splenic/renal infarcts, mycotic aneurysms. Right-sided IE (IVDU) causes septic pulmonary emboli. Renal complications: immune complex glomerulonephritis causing haematuria and proteinuria.

concepts.title: Chlamydia – Definition and epidemiology
concepts.content: Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection in the UK. Most prevalent in sexually active individuals under 25 years. Often asymptomatic, facilitating silent transmission.

concepts.title: Chlamydia – Clinical features in women
concepts.content: Often asymptomatic (up to 70%). Symptoms include: vaginal discharge, intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding, dysuria, pelvic pain. Cervicitis on examination. Can ascend to cause pelvic inflammatory disease.

concepts.title: Chlamydia – Clinical features in men
concepts.content: Often asymptomatic. Urethral discharge (clear or white), dysuria. Non-gonococcal urethritis. Can cause epididymo-orchitis. Reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome: urethritis, arthritis, conjunctivitis) is a complication.

concepts.title: Chlamydia – Diagnosis
concepts.content: Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) is the gold standard. First-catch urine sample in men; vulvovaginal swab in women. Endocervical or urethral swabs also acceptable. Chlamydia screening offered to all sexually active under-25s annually.

concepts.title: Chlamydia – Management
concepts.content: First-line: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. Alternative: azithromycin 1 g stat (if adherence concern). In pregnancy: azithromycin or erythromycin (doxycycline contraindicated). Partner notification and testing essential.

concepts.title: Chlamydia – Complications
concepts.content: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) in women: risk of ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, infertility. Epididymo-orchitis in men. Reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome). Neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia if untreated maternal infection.

concepts.title: Gonorrhoea – Definition and microbiology
concepts.content: Gonorrhoea is caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a Gram-negative diplococcus. It is the second most common bacterial STI in the UK. Transmitted through unprotected sexual contact.

concepts.title: Gonorrhoea – Clinical features
concepts.content: Men: urethral discharge (purulent), dysuria. Women: often asymptomatic; vaginal discharge, dysuria, intermenstrual bleeding. Pharyngeal and rectal infection possible. Disseminated gonococcal infection: septic arthritis, skin lesions, fever.

concepts.title: Gonorrhoea – Diagnosis
concepts.content: NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) is the gold standard for diagnosis. Gram stain of urethral discharge showing intracellular Gram-negative diplococci is diagnostic in men. Culture needed for antibiotic sensitivity testing.

concepts.title: Gonorrhoea – Management
concepts.content: First-line: IM ceftriaxone 1 g single dose (BASHH guidelines). Azithromycin previously added but now removed due to resistance concerns. Test of cure recommended. Partner notification essential. Increasing antibiotic resistance is a major concern.

concepts.title: Syphilis – Causative organism and transmission
concepts.content: Caused by Treponema pallidum, a spirochaetal bacterium. Transmitted through direct contact with syphilitic sores (chancres) during sexual contact. Can also be transmitted vertically (congenital syphilis).

concepts.title: Syphilis – Primary syphilis
concepts.content: Presents 9–90 days after exposure. Painless indurated ulcer (chancre) at the site of inoculation (genitals, anus, mouth). Associated with painless regional lymphadenopathy. Chancre heals spontaneously within 3–6 weeks.

concepts.title: Syphilis – Secondary syphilis
concepts.content: Occurs 4–10 weeks after primary infection. Systemic features: fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy. Rash: non-itchy maculopapular rash involving palms and soles (characteristic). Condylomata lata (flat wart-like lesions). Mucous patches.

concepts.title: Syphilis – Tertiary and neurosyphilis
concepts.content: Tertiary syphilis (years later): gummas (granulomatous lesions), cardiovascular syphilis (aortitis, aortic regurgitation, aortic aneurysm). Neurosyphilis: tabes dorsalis (posterior column degeneration), general paresis of the insane, Argyll Robertson pupil.

concepts.title: Syphilis – Diagnosis and management
concepts.content: Serology: non-treponemal tests (VDRL, RPR) for screening; treponemal tests (TPHA, FTA-ABS) for confirmation. Treatment: IM benzylpenicillin (penicillin G) is first-line for all stages. Doxycycline if penicillin-allergic. Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction may occur after first dose.

concepts.title: Influenza – Definition and virology
concepts.content: Influenza is caused by influenza A or B RNA viruses (Orthomyxoviridae). Influenza A is responsible for pandemics due to antigenic shift (reassortment of gene segments). Influenza B causes seasonal epidemics only.

concepts.title: Influenza – Antigenic variation
concepts.content: Antigenic drift: minor mutations in haemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) causing seasonal epidemics. Antigenic shift: major reassortment of gene segments between human and animal strains causing pandemics (only influenza A).

concepts.title: Influenza – Clinical features
concepts.content: Abrupt onset fever, rigors, myalgia, headache, malaise. Dry cough, sore throat, rhinitis. Symptoms typically last 3–7 days. Elderly and immunocompromised may develop severe disease. Secondary bacterial pneumonia (S. aureus, S. pneumoniae) is a key complication.

concepts.title: Influenza – Management and antivirals
concepts.content: Supportive care for most patients. Antivirals (oseltamivir/zanamivir) within 48 hours of symptom onset for high-risk groups (elderly, immunocompromised, chronic disease). Annual vaccination recommended for at-risk groups.

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever) is caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a herpesvirus. Transmitted via saliva ('kissing disease'). EBV infects B lymphocytes via CD21 receptor.

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Classic triad: fever, pharyngitis (exudative tonsillitis), lymphadenopathy (especially posterior cervical). Splenomegaly (50%). Hepatitis (elevated LFTs). Maculopapular rash if given amoxicillin/ampicillin (90% of cases).

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Investigations
concepts.content: Monospot test (heterophile antibody test): positive in ~85% after first week. FBC: atypical lymphocytes (activated CD8+ T cells). Elevated LFTs. EBV-specific serology (VCA IgM/IgG, EBNA) for confirmation. Avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin.

concepts.title: Infectious mononucleosis – Management and complications
concepts.content: Supportive treatment. Avoid contact sports for 4 weeks due to splenic rupture risk. Avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin (causes rash). Complications: splenic rupture, airway obstruction, haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, encephalitis. EBV associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

concepts.title: Measles – Definition and transmission
concepts.content: Measles is caused by a paramyxovirus (RNA virus). Highly contagious, transmitted via respiratory droplets. Incubation period 10–14 days. Notifiable disease. Prevented by MMR vaccine (live attenuated).

concepts.title: Measles – Clinical features
concepts.content: Prodrome (3–4 days): fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis. Koplik spots: white spots on buccal mucosa (pathognomonic, appear before rash). Rash: maculopapular, starts behind ears/face, spreads downward, lasts 5–6 days. Fever throughout.

concepts.title: Measles – Complications
concepts.content: Otitis media (most common complication). Pneumonia (primary viral or secondary bacterial). Encephalitis (1 in 1000 cases). Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE): rare, fatal, years after infection. Increased susceptibility to other infections due to immune suppression.

concepts.title: Mumps – Clinical features and complications
concepts.content: Caused by paramyxovirus. Parotitis (parotid gland swelling) is the hallmark. Orchitis in post-pubertal males (20–30%): can cause subfertility. Meningitis (most common cause of viral meningitis pre-vaccination). Pancreatitis. Oophoritis in females. CSF may show low glucose (unusual for viral meningitis).

concepts.title: Varicella zoster – Chickenpox (primary infection)
concepts.content: Primary VZV infection causes chickenpox. Highly contagious via respiratory droplets and direct contact. Incubation 10–21 days. Prodrome: fever, malaise. Rash: pruritic vesicles in different stages simultaneously ('dew drops on a rose petal'), starts on trunk.

concepts.title: Varicella zoster – Shingles (herpes zoster)
concepts.content: Reactivation of latent VZV in dorsal root ganglia. Dermatomal distribution of painful vesicular rash. Prodrome: burning/tingling pain in affected dermatome. Post-herpetic neuralgia is a common complication (persistent pain after rash resolves). Ophthalmic zoster can threaten vision.

concepts.title: Varicella zoster – Management
concepts.content: Chickenpox: supportive (calamine lotion, antihistamines). Aciclovir for immunocompromised or severe disease. Shingles: oral aciclovir/valaciclovir within 72 hours of rash onset. Analgesia for post-herpetic neuralgia (amitriptyline, gabapentin). VZIG for post-exposure prophylaxis in high-risk individuals.

concepts.title: Croup – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is a viral infection causing subglottic oedema and airway obstruction. Most commonly caused by parainfluenza virus (type 1 most common). Affects children aged 6 months to 3 years. Peak incidence in autumn.

concepts.title: Croup – Clinical features
concepts.content: Barking ('seal-like') cough, hoarse voice, inspiratory stridor. Low-grade fever. Symptoms worse at night. Mild: barking cough, no stridor at rest. Moderate: stridor at rest, mild recession. Severe: stridor at rest, marked recession, agitation, cyanosis.

concepts.title: Croup – Management
concepts.content: Mild: single dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg. Moderate-severe: oral/IM/IV dexamethasone 0.15–0.6 mg/kg. Nebulised adrenaline (epinephrine) for severe/impending obstruction (temporary effect). Humidified air has no proven benefit. Hospital admission if moderate-severe.

concepts.title: Whooping cough – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Whooping cough (pertussis) is caused by Bordetella pertussis, a Gram-negative coccobacillus. Highly contagious via respiratory droplets. Notifiable disease. Prevented by DTaP/IPV/Hib vaccine. Maternal vaccination at 16–32 weeks protects neonates.

concepts.title: Whooping cough – Clinical stages
concepts.content: Catarrhal stage (1–2 weeks): coryzal symptoms, mild cough, most infectious. Paroxysmal stage (2–6 weeks): paroxysmal coughing fits ending in inspiratory 'whoop', post-tussive vomiting, cyanosis during attacks. Convalescent stage: gradual resolution over weeks to months.

concepts.title: Whooping cough – Management
concepts.content: Azithromycin (first-line) or clarithromycin for 7 days. Erythromycin alternative. Antibiotics most effective in catarrhal stage; reduce infectivity but may not shorten illness if started in paroxysmal stage. Notify public health. Exclude from school/work for 48 hours after starting antibiotics.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Acute otitis media (AOM) is a middle ear infection, most common in children under 5. Causative organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common), Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis. Often follows viral upper respiratory tract infection.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Ear pain (otalgia), fever, hearing loss, irritability in children. Bulging erythematous tympanic membrane on otoscopy. Management: analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen). Antibiotics (amoxicillin) if: bilateral in <2 years, otorrhoea, systemically unwell, or no improvement after 2–3 days.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Inflammation of the tonsils, most commonly caused by Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes). Viral causes include EBV, adenovirus. Centor criteria help identify bacterial cause: tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, absence of cough.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Management
concepts.content: Most cases are viral and self-limiting. Bacterial tonsillitis: phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) for 10 days. Amoxicillin should be avoided (rash if EBV). Clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic. Tonsillectomy for recurrent tonsillitis (7 episodes in 1 year, or 5/year for 2 years, or 3/year for 3 years).

concepts.title: Osteomyelitis – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Osteomyelitis is infection of bone. Most common organism: Staphylococcus aureus. In sickle cell disease: Salmonella is the most common cause. Haematogenous spread is most common in children (metaphysis of long bones). Contiguous spread from adjacent infection in adults.

concepts.title: Osteomyelitis – Clinical features and investigations
concepts.content: Localised bone pain, tenderness, swelling, fever. Raised WBC, CRP, ESR. Blood cultures positive in ~50%. X-ray: initially normal; periosteal reaction and bone destruction after 10–14 days. MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality.

concepts.title: Osteomyelitis – Management
concepts.content: IV antibiotics initially (flucloxacillin for S. aureus; adjust based on cultures). Prolonged course: typically 4–6 weeks total (IV then oral). Surgical debridement for chronic osteomyelitis, sequestra, or failure to respond to antibiotics.

concepts.title: Septic arthritis – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Septic arthritis is a joint space infection, constituting an orthopaedic emergency. Most common organism: Staphylococcus aureus. In sexually active young adults: Neisseria gonorrhoeae. In children: S. aureus, Streptococcus, H. influenzae. Haematogenous spread most common.

concepts.title: Septic arthritis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Acute onset hot, swollen, tender joint with severely restricted range of movement. Fever and systemic upset. Most commonly affects knee, hip, shoulder. Monoarthritis. Any prosthetic joint infection must be considered septic until proven otherwise.

concepts.title: Septic arthritis – Investigations and management
concepts.content: Joint aspiration: urgent Gram stain and culture of synovial fluid (WBC >50,000 cells/mm³ suggests infection). Blood cultures. Management: IV antibiotics (flucloxacillin first-line; ceftriaxone if gonococcal suspected). Joint washout/drainage. Orthopaedic emergency.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Oral thrush
concepts.content: Oral candidiasis (thrush) presents as white plaques on the oral mucosa that can be wiped off, leaving a red base. Caused by Candida albicans. Risk factors: antibiotics, inhaled corticosteroids, immunosuppression, dentures. Treatment: nystatin suspension or oral fluconazole.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Vulvovaginal candidiasis
concepts.content: Presents with vulval itching, soreness, and thick white 'cottage cheese' discharge. Vaginal pH normal (<4.5). Microscopy shows budding yeast/pseudohyphae. Treatment: clotrimazole pessary (single dose) or oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose. Recurrent: fluconazole weekly for 6 months.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Invasive candidiasis
concepts.content: Invasive candidiasis (candidaemia) occurs in immunocompromised patients (neutropenia, ICU, TPN, central lines). Presents as persistent fever not responding to antibiotics. Treatment: IV echinocandin (caspofungin) or fluconazole. Remove central lines.

concepts.title: Covid-19 – Definition and transmission
concepts.content: COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2, a betacoronavirus. Transmitted primarily via respiratory droplets and aerosols. Incubation period 2–14 days (median 5 days). Notifiable disease.

concepts.title: Covid-19 – Clinical features
concepts.content: Common: fever, dry cough, fatigue, anosmia/ageusia (loss of smell/taste). Dyspnoea in moderate-severe disease. Severe: pneumonia, ARDS, cytokine storm. Long COVID: persistent symptoms >12 weeks (fatigue, brain fog, breathlessness).

concepts.title: Notifiable diseases – Overview and examples
concepts.content: Certain infectious diseases must be notified to the local authority designated officer (LADO)/Public Health England under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010. Examples: meningococcal disease, TB, measles, mumps, rubella, whooping cough, cholera, typhoid, food poisoning, malaria, rabies, viral haemorrhagic fevers.

concepts.title: Notifiable diseases – Reporting process
concepts.content: Clinicians must notify the local authority designated officer (LADO) on suspicion of a notifiable disease — confirmation is not required before notifying. Notification must be made within 3 days (or 24 hours for urgent cases). Labs also notify PHE directly.

concepts.title: Necrotising fasciitis – Definition and types
concepts.content: Necrotising fasciitis is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection of the deep fascia causing necrosis of fascia and subcutaneous tissue. Type 1: polymicrobial (mixed aerobic/anaerobic). Type 2: Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) — more common in healthy adults.

concepts.title: Necrotising fasciitis – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Severe pain disproportionate to skin findings, rapidly spreading erythema, skin necrosis, crepitus (gas in tissues), systemic toxicity. 'Pain out of proportion' is a key warning sign. Management: urgent surgical debridement (do not delay for imaging), broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, ICU care.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Distinction
concepts.content: Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis: infection anterior to the orbital septum. Orbital (postseptal) cellulitis: infection posterior to the orbital septum — more serious. Orbital cellulitis features: proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, reduced visual acuity, pain on eye movement. Most commonly follows sinusitis.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Management
concepts.content: Periorbital cellulitis: oral co-amoxiclav. Orbital cellulitis: urgent hospital admission, IV antibiotics (co-amoxiclav or cefuroxime + metronidazole), CT orbit to assess extent, ophthalmology and ENT review, surgical drainage if abscess present.

concepts.title: Impetigo – Definition and management
concepts.content: Impetigo is a superficial bacterial skin infection. Non-bullous (most common): honey-coloured crusted lesions, caused by S. aureus or S. pyogenes. Bullous: fluid-filled blisters, caused by S. aureus toxins. Treatment: topical fusidic acid or mupirocin. Oral flucloxacillin or cefalexin for widespread disease. Exclude from school until lesions crusted/healed.

concepts.title: Urethritis – Non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU)
concepts.content: NGU (non-specific urethritis/NSU) presents with urethral discharge and/or dysuria; asymptomatic in up to 30% of men. Common causes: Chlamydia trachomatis, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Mycoplasma genitalium. Diagnosis: urethral swab (Gram stain for leukocytes and Gram-negative diplococci) + NAAT for Chlamydia.

concepts.title: Urethritis – Management of NGU
concepts.content: First-line: oral doxycycline for 7 days or single dose azithromycin. Complications if untreated: epididymitis, subfertility, reactive arthritis. Partner notification and testing essential.

concepts.title: Acute cholangitis – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Acute cholangitis is bacterial infection of the biliary tract, usually caused by biliary obstruction (gallstones most common). Organisms: E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, Bacteroides. Risk factors: choledocholithiasis, biliary strictures, ERCP.

concepts.title: Acute cholangitis – Charcot's triad and Reynold's pentad
concepts.content: Charcot's triad: right upper quadrant pain, fever/rigors, jaundice. Reynold's pentad adds hypotension and altered mental status — indicates severe cholangitis with septic shock.

concepts.title: Acute cholangitis – Management
concepts.content: IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or cephalosporin + metronidazole). Urgent biliary decompression via ERCP (preferred) or percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography. Cholecystectomy after recovery for gallstone aetiology.

concepts.title: Brain abscess – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Brain abscess is a focal collection of pus within the brain parenchyma. Sources: contiguous spread (sinusitis, otitis media, dental infection), haematogenous (endocarditis, lung abscess), direct inoculation (trauma, surgery). Common organisms: Streptococcus (most common), Staphylococcus, anaerobes.

concepts.title: Brain abscess – Clinical features
concepts.content: Classic triad: headache, fever, focal neurological deficit. Raised intracranial pressure: nausea, vomiting, papilloedema. Seizures. Altered consciousness. Meningism if abscess ruptures into ventricle (life-threatening).

concepts.title: Brain abscess – Investigations and management
concepts.content: CT/MRI: ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema. Stereotactic aspiration for diagnosis and drainage. Blood cultures. IV antibiotics: ceftriaxone + metronidazole ± vancomycin (if MRSA suspected). Dexamethasone for oedema. Treat underlying source.

concepts.title: Breast abscess/mastitis – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Mastitis is inflammation of breast tissue, most commonly in breastfeeding women (lactational mastitis). Caused by Staphylococcus aureus entering via nipple fissures. Can progress to breast abscess if untreated.

concepts.title: Breast abscess/mastitis – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Mastitis: breast pain, erythema, swelling, fever, flu-like symptoms. Management: continue breastfeeding/expressing, flucloxacillin for 10–14 days. Breast abscess: fluctuant swollen area; requires ultrasound-guided aspiration or incision and drainage. Flucloxacillin post-drainage.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Types and aetiology
concepts.content: Bacterial: Staphylococcus aureus, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae (purulent discharge, bilateral). Viral: adenovirus most common (watery discharge, follicular reaction, preauricular lymphadenopathy). Allergic: bilateral, itchy, watery discharge, papillary reaction. Neonatal: Chlamydia or Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Management
concepts.content: Bacterial: chloramphenicol eye drops or ointment (self-limiting in most cases). Viral: self-limiting; lubricating drops. Gonococcal (neonatal): IM ceftriaxone. Chlamydial (neonatal): oral erythromycin. Allergic: topical antihistamines (sodium cromoglicate, olopatadine).

concepts.title: Cutaneous fungal infection – Types and aetiology
concepts.content: Dermatophyte infections (tinea): tinea pedis (athlete's foot), tinea corporis (ringworm), tinea cruris (groin), tinea capitis (scalp), tinea unguium (onychomycosis). Caused by Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton. Pityriasis versicolor: Malassezia furfur (hypo/hyperpigmented patches).

concepts.title: Cutaneous fungal infection – Management
concepts.content: Topical antifungals (clotrimazole, terbinafine, miconazole) for most tinea infections. Oral terbinafine or itraconazole for tinea capitis and onychomycosis (poor topical penetration). Pityriasis versicolor: topical ketoconazole or selenium sulphide shampoo.

concepts.title: Cutaneous warts – Definition and management
concepts.content: Cutaneous warts are caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly types 1, 2, 4. Common warts (verruca vulgaris): rough, raised lesions on hands. Plantar warts (verrucae): on soles of feet. Most resolve spontaneously. Treatment: salicylic acid (first-line), cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Epididymitis: inflammation of the epididymis. Orchitis: inflammation of the testis. Often occur together (epididymo-orchitis). In men under 35: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae most common. In men over 35: E. coli and coliforms (associated with UTI/prostatism). Mumps orchitis in post-pubertal males.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Unilateral scrotal pain and swelling, fever. Prehn's sign: pain relieved by elevation (differentiates from testicular torsion). Urethral discharge if STI cause. Investigations: urethral swab/NAAT for STIs, urine culture, scrotal ultrasound. Management: doxycycline + ceftriaxone (STI cause); ciprofloxacin (enteric cause).

concepts.title: Folliculitis – Definition and management
concepts.content: Folliculitis is inflammation of hair follicles, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Presents as pustules or papules centred on hair follicles. Hot tub folliculitis caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Treatment: topical antiseptics (chlorhexidine) or topical antibiotics (fusidic acid). Oral flucloxacillin for widespread/recurrent disease.

concepts.title: Gangrene – Types and management
concepts.content: Dry gangrene: ischaemic necrosis without infection; peripheral vascular disease. Wet gangrene: infected necrosis; polymicrobial. Gas gangrene: Clostridium perfringens produces gas in tissues; life-threatening. Fournier's gangrene: necrotising fasciitis of perineum. Management: surgical debridement, IV antibiotics (penicillin + clindamycin for Clostridium), hyperbaric oxygen adjunct.

concepts.title: Head lice – Definition and management
concepts.content: Head lice (Pediculus humanus capitis) are obligate human ectoparasites. Transmission via direct head-to-head contact. Presents with scalp pruritus. Diagnosis: detection combing with fine-toothed comb on wet hair. Treatment: dimeticone (first-line, physical insecticide), malathion (chemical). Wet combing as alternative. No school exclusion required.

concepts.title: Human papilloma virus infection – Genital warts
concepts.content: Genital warts (condylomata acuminata) are caused by HPV types 6 and 11 (low-risk, non-oncogenic). Soft, fleshy, cauliflower-like lesions on genitalia, perineum, perianal area. Treatment: topical podophyllotoxin (self-applied), imiquimod, or cryotherapy. Highly contagious.

concepts.title: Human papilloma virus infection – Oncogenic types and vaccination
concepts.content: HPV types 16 and 18 (high-risk) cause cervical, anal, oropharyngeal, vulval, vaginal, and penile cancers. HPV vaccination (Gardasil 9): offered to girls and boys aged 12–13 in the UK. Protects against HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58. Cervical screening (smear test) detects high-risk HPV.

concepts.title: Infectious colitis – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Infectious colitis is inflammation of the colon due to infection. Bacterial causes: Campylobacter jejuni (most common), Salmonella, Shigella (dysentery), E. coli O157:H7 (VTEC), Clostridioides difficile (antibiotic-associated). Viral: norovirus, rotavirus. Parasitic: Entamoeba histolytica (amoebic colitis).

concepts.title: Infectious colitis – Clostridioides difficile
concepts.content: C. difficile colitis follows antibiotic use (especially clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, co-amoxiclav). Presents with watery diarrhoea, fever, abdominal pain. Toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin). Diagnosis: stool toxin PCR. Treatment: oral vancomycin (first-line) or fidaxomicin. Metronidazole for mild disease only. Severe: IV metronidazole + oral vancomycin.

concepts.title: Infectious colitis – Shigella (dysentery)
concepts.content: Shigella causes bacillary dysentery: bloody diarrhoea with mucus, fever, abdominal cramps. Very low infectious dose (10–100 organisms). Faecal-oral transmission. Notifiable disease. Treatment: azithromycin or ciprofloxacin for severe cases. Complications: haemolytic uraemic syndrome (S. dysenteriae type 1).

concepts.title: Lower respiratory tract infection – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: LRTI encompasses infections of the lower airways: bronchitis, bronchiolitis, and pneumonia. Acute bronchitis: usually viral (rhinovirus, influenza). Bronchiolitis: RSV in infants under 2 years. Pneumonia: bacterial (S. pneumoniae most common), viral, atypical organisms.

concepts.title: Lower respiratory tract infection – Bronchiolitis
concepts.content: RSV bronchiolitis is the most common cause of hospitalisation in infants under 1 year. Presents with wheeze, tachypnoea, subcostal recession, poor feeding. Management: supportive (oxygen, nasogastric feeding). Palivizumab (anti-RSV monoclonal antibody) for high-risk infants (prematurity, congenital heart disease).

concepts.title: Perianal abscesses and fistulae – Definition and management
concepts.content: Perianal abscess: collection of pus in the perianal/ischiorectal space. Caused by infection of anal glands (cryptoglandular theory). Organisms: E. coli, Bacteroides, Enterococcus. Management: surgical incision and drainage. Fistula-in-ano: abnormal tract between anal canal and perianal skin — often develops after abscess. Management: fistulotomy, seton suture, or advancement flap.

concepts.title: Perianal abscesses and fistulae – Crohn's association
concepts.content: Perianal fistulae are strongly associated with Crohn's disease (present in up to 30% of Crohn's patients). Complex fistulae in Crohn's may require combined medical (infliximab, azathioprine) and surgical management. MRI pelvis is the investigation of choice for fistula assessment.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum. Primary (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, SBP): infection without obvious source, occurs in cirrhosis with ascites. Secondary: perforation of viscus (peptic ulcer, appendix, diverticular disease). Tertiary: persistent/recurrent peritonitis after treatment.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – SBP diagnosis and management
concepts.content: SBP occurs in cirrhotic patients with ascites. Diagnostic paracentesis: neutrophil count >250 cells/mm³ in ascitic fluid. Organisms: E. coli, Klebsiella, Streptococcus. Treatment: IV cefotaxime or ceftriaxone for 5 days. Prophylaxis: norfloxacin or ciprofloxacin for high-risk patients (ascitic protein <15 g/L or previous SBP).

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Secondary peritonitis management
concepts.content: Secondary peritonitis from perforation requires urgent surgical intervention. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone + metronidazole). Resuscitation with IV fluids. Laparotomy/laparoscopy for source control. ICU care for severe sepsis.

concepts.title: Surgical site infection – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Surgical site infection (SSI) is infection occurring within 30 days of surgery (or 1 year if implant). Superficial: skin and subcutaneous tissue. Deep incisional: fascia and muscle layers. Organ/space: any anatomical area opened during surgery. Most common organisms: S. aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, E. coli.

concepts.title: Surgical site infection – Prevention and management
concepts.content: Prevention: pre-operative MRSA screening and decolonisation, antibiotic prophylaxis (single dose before incision), skin preparation (chlorhexidine), normothermia, glycaemic control. Management: wound opening and drainage, wound swab for culture, antibiotics guided by sensitivities. MRSA SSI: vancomycin or teicoplanin.

concepts.title: Trichomonas vaginalis – Definition and clinical features
concepts.content: Trichomonas vaginalis is a flagellated protozoan causing a common STI. Women: offensive, frothy, yellow-green vaginal discharge; vulvovaginal soreness; dysuria; strawberry cervix (colpitis macularis). Men: often asymptomatic; urethral discharge, dysuria. Vaginal pH >4.5.

concepts.title: Trichomonas vaginalis – Diagnosis and management
concepts.content: Diagnosis: wet mount microscopy (motile trichomonads — low sensitivity ~60%); NAAT (most sensitive). Treatment: oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 5–7 days, or 2 g single dose. Partner notification and treatment essential. Avoid alcohol with metronidazole (disulfiram-like reaction).

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Overview and causes
concepts.content: Viral exanthema refers to rashes caused by viral infections. Classic childhood exanthems: first disease (measles), second disease (scarlet fever — bacterial), third disease (rubella), fourth disease (Filatov-Dukes — staphylococcal), fifth disease (parvovirus B19 — slapped cheek), sixth disease (roseola infantum — HHV-6).

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Roseola infantum (sixth disease)
concepts.content: Caused by HHV-6 (human herpesvirus 6). Affects infants 6–24 months. High fever for 3–5 days followed by sudden defervescence and appearance of rose-pink maculopapular rash (trunk then spreads). Febrile convulsions may occur during febrile phase. Self-limiting; no specific treatment.

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Parvovirus B19 (fifth disease)
concepts.content: Erythema infectiosum ('slapped cheek syndrome') caused by parvovirus B19. Bright red facial rash followed by lacy reticular rash on trunk/limbs. Child is infectious before rash appears, not after. Aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease. Hydrops fetalis if maternal infection in first 20 weeks.

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Rubella
concepts.content: Rubella (German measles) caused by Togavirus. Mild maculopapular rash starting on face, spreading downward. Suboccipital and postauricular lymphadenopathy (characteristic). Congenital rubella syndrome if maternal infection in first trimester: cataracts, deafness, congenital heart disease, microcephaly. Prevented by MMR vaccine.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Definition and aetiology
concepts.content: Viral gastroenteritis is the most common cause of acute diarrhoea and vomiting worldwide. Norovirus: most common in adults, winter vomiting disease, outbreaks in hospitals/care homes, 12–48 hour incubation. Rotavirus: most common in children under 5, prevented by oral rotavirus vaccine. Adenovirus, astrovirus also cause gastroenteritis.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Management
concepts.content: Supportive management: oral rehydration therapy (ORS) is the mainstay. IV fluids if unable to tolerate oral intake. Antiemetics (ondansetron) may be used. No antibiotics (viral aetiology). Norovirus: isolate affected patients, strict hand hygiene (alcohol gel ineffective — soap and water required). Exclude from work/school for 48 hours after last episode.

concepts.title: 5-HT3 antagonists – Mechanism of action and primary use
concepts.content: 5-HT3 antagonists are antiemetics used mainly in the management of chemotherapy-related nausea. They act primarily in the chemoreceptor trigger zone area of the medulla oblongata.

concepts.title: 5-HT3 antagonists – Examples and drug-specific notes
concepts.content: Examples include ondansetron and palonosetron. Palonosetron is a second-generation 5-HT3 antagonist whose main advantage is a reduced effect on the QT interval compared to first-generation agents.

concepts.title: 5-HT3 antagonists – Adverse effects
concepts.content: Adverse effects include prolonged QT interval and constipation (common).

concepts.title: Aphasia – Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia
concepts.content: Due to a lesion of the superior temporal gyrus, typically supplied by the inferior division of the left MCA. This area forms speech before sending it to Broca's area. Lesions result in sentences that make no sense, word substitution and neologisms but speech remains fluent ('word salad'). Comprehension is impaired.

concepts.title: Aphasia – Broca's (expressive) aphasia
concepts.content: Due to a lesion of the inferior frontal gyrus, typically supplied by the superior division of the left MCA. Speech is non-fluent, laboured, and halting. Repetition is impaired. Comprehension is normal.

concepts.title: Aphasia – Conduction aphasia
concepts.content: Classically due to a stroke affecting the arcuate fasciculus — the connection between Wernicke's and Broca's area. Speech is fluent but repetition is poor. The patient is aware of the errors they are making. Comprehension is normal.

concepts.title: Aphasia – Global aphasia
concepts.content: A large lesion affecting all three areas (Wernicke's, Broca's, and arcuate fasciculus) results in severe expressive and receptive aphasia. The patient may still be able to communicate using gestures.

concepts.title: Arnold-Chiari malformation – Definition and features
concepts.content: Arnold-Chiari malformation describes the downward displacement (herniation) of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum. Malformations may be congenital or acquired through trauma. Features include non-communicating hydrocephalus (from obstruction of CSF outflow), headache, and syringomyelia.

concepts.title: Ataxia – Cerebellar localisation
concepts.content: Cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause peripheral ataxia ('finger-nose ataxia'). Cerebellar vermis lesions cause gait ataxia.

concepts.title: Ataxia telangiectasia – Definition and genetics
concepts.content: Ataxia telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the ATM gene which encodes for DNA repair enzymes. It is one of the inherited combined immunodeficiency disorders, typically presenting in early childhood with abnormal movements.

concepts.title: Ataxia telangiectasia – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features include cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasia (spider angiomas), IgA deficiency resulting in recurrent chest infections, and a 10% risk of developing malignancy (lymphoma or leukaemia, but also non-lymphoid tumours).

concepts.title: Autonomic dysreflexia – Pathophysiology and triggers
concepts.content: Occurs in patients with spinal cord injury at or above T6. Afferent signals (most commonly from faecal impaction or urinary retention) trigger a sympathetic spinal reflex via thoracolumbar outflow. The usual centrally mediated parasympathetic response is prevented by the cord lesion, resulting in an unbalanced physiological response.

concepts.title: Autonomic dysreflexia – Clinical features
concepts.content: Characterised by extreme hypertension, flushing and sweating above the level of the cord lesion, and agitation. In untreated cases, severe consequences of extreme hypertension have been reported, including haemorrhagic stroke.

concepts.title: Autonomic dysreflexia – Management
concepts.content: Management involves removal or control of the triggering stimulus and treatment of any life-threatening hypertension and/or bradycardia.

concepts.title: Autonomic neuropathy – Definition and pathophysiology
concepts.content: Autonomic neuropathy describes dysfunction of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems, leading to impaired cardiovascular, genitourinary, gastrointestinal and sudomotor regulation. Damage affects small myelinated and unmyelinated autonomic fibres via metabolic, immune-mediated, neurodegenerative, infective or drug-induced mechanisms.

concepts.title: Autonomic neuropathy – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features include postural hypotension (≥30/15 mmHg drop), reduced or absent heart rate variability with deep breathing (an earlier and more sensitive sign than BP changes), erectile dysfunction, impaired sweating or anhidrosis, gastroparesis (early satiety, nausea, bloating), and pupillary denervation hypersensitivity (dilates with adrenaline).

concepts.title: Autonomic neuropathy – Causes
concepts.content: Causes include diabetes (most common), Guillain-Barré syndrome, multiple system atrophy/Shy-Drager syndrome, Parkinson's disease, infections (HIV, Chagas' disease, neurosyphilis), drugs (antihypertensives, tricyclic antidepressants), and structural lesions (craniopharyngioma).

concepts.title: Autonomic neuropathy – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations include cardiovascular autonomic tests (HR variability, lying/standing BP), sweat testing (QSART or thermoregulatory), pupillary pharmacological testing, blood tests (HbA1c, B12, autoimmune screen, HIV, syphilis), MRI brain/spine if central pathology suspected, and nerve conduction studies with small-fibre assessments. In autonomic neuropathy, the classical finding is denervation hypersensitivity of the iris dilator muscle.

concepts.title: Autonomic neuropathy – Management
concepts.content: Treat underlying cause (optimise glycaemic control, stop offending drugs, treat infections). For postural hypotension: conservative measures (fluids, salt, compression stockings, slow positional changes) then fludrocortisone or midodrine. Erectile dysfunction: PDE5 inhibitors. Sweat dysfunction: moisturisers, temperature regulation. MDT input including neurology, physiotherapy and occupational therapy.

concepts.title: Bell's palsy – Definition and epidemiology
concepts.content: Bell's palsy is an acute, unilateral, idiopathic facial nerve paralysis. The aetiology is unknown although the role of herpes simplex virus has been investigated. Peak incidence is 20–40 years and the condition is more common in pregnant women.

concepts.title: Bell's palsy – Clinical features
concepts.content: Presents with lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy (forehead affected). In contrast, an upper motor neuron lesion spares the upper face. Additional features include post-auricular pain (may precede paralysis), altered taste, dry eyes, and hyperacusis.

concepts.title: Bell's palsy – Management
concepts.content: All patients should receive oral prednisolone within 72 hours of onset. There is ongoing debate about adding antiviral medications; antiviral treatment alone is not recommended. UpToDate recommends addition of antivirals for severe facial palsy. Eye care is important to prevent exposure keratopathy: prescribe artificial tears and eye lubricants; if unable to close the eye at bedtime, tape it closed using microporous tape.

concepts.title: Bell's palsy – Follow-up and prognosis
concepts.content: If paralysis shows no sign of improvement after 3 weeks, refer urgently to ENT. A referral to plastic surgery may be appropriate for more long-standing weakness (e.g. several months). Most patients make a full recovery within 3–4 months. If untreated, around 15% of patients have permanent moderate to severe weakness.

concepts.title: Brachial plexus – Anatomy and origin
concepts.content: The brachial plexus arises from anterior rami of C5 to T1. Sections of the plexus (mnemonic: Real Teenagers Drink Cold Beer): Roots (posterior triangle, between scalenus anterior and medius), Trunks (posterior to middle third of clavicle), Divisions (apex of axilla), Cords (related to axillary artery), Branches.

concepts.title: Brachial plexus injuries – Erb-Duchenne paralysis
concepts.content: Erb-Duchenne paralysis results from damage to C5 and C6 roots. Features include winged scapula and may be caused by a breech presentation.

concepts.title: Brachial plexus injuries – Klumpke's paralysis
concepts.content: Klumpke's paralysis results from damage to T1. Features include loss of intrinsic hand muscles and is due to traction.

concepts.title: Brain abscess – Causes and pathogenesis
concepts.content: Brain abscesses may result from extension of sepsis from middle ear or sinuses, trauma or surgery to the scalp, penetrating head injuries, or embolic events from endocarditis.

concepts.title: Brain abscess – Clinical features
concepts.content: Presenting symptoms depend on the site of the abscess. Features include headache (often dull and persistent), fever (may be absent; usually not the swinging pyrexia seen at other sites), focal neurology (e.g. oculomotor or abducens nerve palsy from raised ICP), nausea, papilloedema, and seizures.

concepts.title: Brain abscess – Management
concepts.content: Management includes surgery (craniotomy with debridement of the abscess cavity), IV antibiotics (IV 3rd-generation cephalosporin + metronidazole), and intracranial pressure management with dexamethasone.

concepts.title: Brain lesions – Parietal lobe features
concepts.content: Parietal lobe lesions cause sensory inattention, apraxias, astereognosis (tactile agnosia), inferior homonymous quadrantanopia, and Gerstmann's syndrome (dominant parietal): alexia, acalculia, finger agnosia and right-left disorientation.

concepts.title: Brain lesions – Occipital lobe features
concepts.content: Occipital lobe lesions cause homonymous hemianopia (with macula sparing), cortical blindness, and visual agnosia.

concepts.title: Brain lesions – Temporal lobe features
concepts.content: Temporal lobe lesions cause Wernicke's aphasia (fluent speech with word substitution and neologisms), superior homonymous quadrantanopia, auditory agnosia, and prosopagnosia (difficulty recognising faces).
