Peak incidence is in postmenopausal women aged 60–70 years; 75% of cases occur after the menopause. Incidence is rising, largely due to increasing rates of obesity.

concepts.title: Endometrial cancer – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for Type I endometrial cancer are related to unopposed oestrogen exposure: obesity (peripheral aromatisation of androgens to oestrogen in adipose tissue), nulliparity, late menopause (>52 years), early menarche, polycystic ovarian syndrome, oestrogen-only HRT, tamoxifen use (acts as oestrogen agonist on endometrium), and diabetes mellitus. Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer) carries a 40–60% lifetime risk. Protective factors include combined OCP use and multiparity.

concepts.title: Endometrial cancer – Clinical features
concepts.content: Postmenopausal bleeding is the presenting symptom in approximately 90% of cases and must be investigated urgently. In premenopausal women, presentation includes intermenstrual bleeding, menorrhagia, or irregular periods. Other features include offensive vaginal discharge (if tumour necrosis), pelvic pain (advanced disease), and systemic symptoms (weight loss, fatigue). On examination, the uterus may be enlarged.

concepts.title: Endometrial cancer – NICE referral criteria
concepts.content: NICE 2-week wait referral criteria: postmenopausal bleeding (not on HRT); postmenopausal women on HRT with unexplained bleeding after stopping HRT for 6 weeks; women aged ≥55 years with unexplained vaginal discharge who are thrombocytotic or have haematuria. Consider referral: women aged <55 years with postmenopausal bleeding; women with intermenstrual bleeding and negative examination.

concepts.title: Endometrial cancer – Investigations
concepts.content: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS): endometrial thickness >4–5 mm in postmenopausal women warrants further investigation (sensitivity 80–90% for endometrial cancer). Endometrial biopsy (Pipelle): first-line tissue sampling, performed in outpatients (sensitivity 80–90%). Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy: gold standard for visualisation and sampling. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis: staging. MRI pelvis: assesses depth of myometrial invasion and cervical involvement.

concepts.title: Endometrial cancer – FIGO 2009 staging
concepts.content: FIGO staging: Stage IA – tumour confined to endometrium or invades <50% of myometrium; Stage IB – invades ≥50% of myometrium; Stage II – cervical stromal invasion; Stage IIIA – uterine serosa or adnexa; Stage IIIB – vaginal or parametrial involvement; Stage IIIC1 – pelvic lymph node metastases; Stage IIIC2 – para-aortic lymph node metastases; Stage IVA – bladder or bowel mucosa; Stage IVB – distant metastases including inguinal nodes.

concepts.title: Endometrial cancer – Management: surgery
concepts.content: Standard surgical treatment is total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TH+BSO), performed laparoscopically where possible. Pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenectomy is performed for staging in intermediate and high-risk disease. Omentectomy may be performed for high-grade tumours. Fertility-sparing management (progestin therapy with LNG-IUS or oral medroxyprogesterone acetate) may be considered for Stage IA, Grade 1 endometrioid cancer in young women wishing to preserve fertility.

concepts.title: Endometrial cancer – Management: adjuvant therapy
concepts.content: Adjuvant radiotherapy: vaginal brachytherapy reduces vaginal vault recurrence in intermediate-risk disease; external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) is used for high-risk or node-positive disease. Chemotherapy (paclitaxel + carboplatin) is used for advanced (Stage III–IV) or high-grade (serous, clear cell) disease. Hormonal therapy (progestogens) may be used for metastatic low-grade endometrioid cancer.

concepts.title: Endometrial cancer – Prognosis and complications
concepts.content: Five-year survival: Stage I – 85–90%; Stage II – 75%; Stage III – 45–60%; Stage IV – 15–25%. Overall 5-year survival is approximately 78%. Treatment complications include lymphoedema, bladder instability, vaginal stenosis, bowel dysfunction, vesicovaginal or rectovaginal fistulae, and premature menopause with associated osteoporosis and cardiovascular risk.

concepts.title: Endometriosis – Definition and overview
concepts.content: Endometriosis is a chronic, oestrogen-dependent inflammatory condition defined by the presence of endometrial-like tissue (glands and stroma) outside the uterine cavity. Common sites include the ovaries (endometriomas/'chocolate cysts'), pelvic peritoneum, uterosacral ligaments, rectovaginal septum, bladder, and bowel. It affects approximately 10% of women of reproductive age.

concepts.title: Endometriosis – Aetiology: theories of pathogenesis
concepts.content: Several theories explain endometriosis: (1) Retrograde menstruation (Sampson's theory) – reflux of endometrial cells through the fallopian tubes into the peritoneal cavity; (2) Coelomic metaplasia – transformation of peritoneal mesothelial cells into endometrial-like tissue; (3) Lymphatic/vascular dissemination – explains distant sites (lung, brain); (4) Genetic predisposition – first-degree relatives have a 7-fold increased risk; (5) Environmental factors – dioxin exposure may impair immune clearance of refluxed endometrial cells.

concepts.title: Endometriosis – Pathophysiology: inflammation and hormonal dysregulation
concepts.content: Ectopic endometrial tissue responds to cyclical hormonal changes, causing repeated local inflammation, cytokine release (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6), and prostaglandin production, which drives pain. Endometriotic lesions produce their own oestrogen via aromatase activity and show progesterone resistance, explaining why progestogen therapy is sometimes ineffective. Chronic inflammation leads to adhesion formation, fibrosis, and distortion of pelvic anatomy.

concepts.title: Endometriosis – Pathophysiology: subfertility mechanisms
concepts.content: Endometriosis impairs fertility through multiple mechanisms: distorted pelvic anatomy and adhesions obstructing tubal function; impaired folliculogenesis and oocyte quality; altered peritoneal fluid environment (elevated cytokines, macrophages) impairing sperm function and fertilisation; impaired endometrial receptivity reducing implantation rates; and increased risk of ectopic pregnancy. Subfertility affects approximately 30–50% of women with endometriosis.

concepts.title: Endometriosis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Classic symptoms: cyclical pelvic pain (dysmenorrhoea), chronic pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia (pain during intercourse), subfertility, and cyclical bowel or urinary symptoms (dyschezia, dysuria, haematuria, rectal bleeding) that worsen during menstruation. Symptoms do not correlate with disease stage. On examination: fixed retroverted uterus, uterosacral ligament nodularity, adnexal mass (endometrioma), and tenderness on pelvic examination. Delayed diagnosis of 4–10 years is common.

concepts.title: Endometriosis – Investigations: imaging
concepts.content: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS): first-line imaging; can identify ovarian endometriomas (chocolate cysts with ground-glass echogenicity) and deep infiltrating endometriosis of the rectovaginal septum and bladder. Pelvic MRI: superior to USS for mapping deep infiltrating endometriosis, particularly bowel and bladder involvement, and for surgical planning. A normal ultrasound does not exclude endometriosis.

concepts.title: Endometriosis – Investigations: diagnostic laparoscopy and CA125
concepts.content: Diagnostic laparoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis. It allows direct visualisation and biopsy of lesions, and surgical removal at the same procedure. Findings include: fixed retroverted uterus, endometriomas, chocolate cysts, adhesions, peritoneal deposits, and powder-burn lesions. Serum CA125 is not used to diagnose endometriosis; a raised level (>35 IU/ml) may be consistent with endometriosis but is non-specific.

concepts.title: Endometriosis – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Key differentials: primary dysmenorrhoea (pelvic pain, no pelvic findings); adenomyosis (enlarged boggy uterus, endometrial tissue in myometrium on MRI); PID (fever, abnormal discharge, positive STI swabs); ovarian cyst (simple follicular cyst, not endometrioma); PCOS (irregular periods, multiple simple cysts, no other pelvic deposits); IBS/IBD (GI symptoms, no cyclical pattern, positive GI investigations); interstitial cystitis (urinary symptoms, negative imaging, positive dipstick).

concepts.title: Endometriosis – ASRM staging
concepts.content: The ASRM (American Society for Reproductive Medicine) classification stages endometriosis based on laparoscopic findings: Stage I (minimal) – isolated implants, no adhesions; Stage II (mild) – superficial implants <5 cm, no adhesions; Stage III (moderate) – multiple superficial and deep implants, peritubal/periovarian adhesions; Stage IV (severe) – multiple deep implants, large endometriomas, dense adhesions. Limitations: stage does not correlate with symptom severity; patients with Stage I may have severe pain.

concepts.title: Endometriosis – Management: analgesia (NICE 2017)
concepts.content: A short trial (3 months) of paracetamol or an NSAID alone or in combination is recommended as first-line management for endometriosis-related pain. If pain relief is inadequate, consider hormonal treatments or referral to secondary care. NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated pain and are effective for dysmenorrhoea. Opioids may be required for severe pain but are not recommended for long-term use.

concepts.title: Endometriosis – Management: hormonal treatment
concepts.content: Hormonal treatments suppress ovarian function and oestrogen production, reducing lesion activity and pain. Options include: combined oral contraceptive pill (oestrogen + progesterone); progestogen-only contraceptives (pill, implant, IUS, injection); GnRH agonists (induce temporary menopause, used short-term due to bone density loss; add-back HRT may be used); GnRH antagonists; androgenic agents (danazol – rarely used due to side effects). All hormonal treatments act as contraceptives and should be discussed with the patient.

concepts.title: Endometriosis – Management: surgical treatment
concepts.content: Surgical treatment via laparoscopy is the only potentially curative option. It involves systematic inspection of the pelvis, biopsy of suspected lesions, and removal or ablation of endometriotic deposits. Laparoscopic excision is preferred over ablation for deep infiltrating disease. Endometriomas should be excised (cystectomy) rather than drained. Hysterectomy with BSO may be considered for severe, refractory disease in women who have completed their family. Surgery improves pain and fertility outcomes.

concepts.title: Fibroid degeneration – Definition and overview
concepts.content: Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) are common benign tumours of smooth muscle affecting approximately 20% of women of reproductive age. 'Red' (carneous) degeneration describes ischaemic necrosis of myocytes secondary to outgrowing their blood supply and is the most common form of fibroid degeneration. It most commonly presents during pregnancy when increased circulating oestrogen drives rapid fibroid growth.

concepts.title: Fibroid degeneration – Epidemiology and aetiology
concepts.content: Fibroid degeneration complicates approximately 5% of pregnancies complicated by fibroids. Risk factors for fibroids include: African-Caribbean ethnicity (3–9 times higher incidence), age 30–50 years, nulliparity, obesity, and family history. Fibroids are oestrogen-dependent and regress after the menopause. Red degeneration is most common in the second trimester (12th–22nd week) of pregnancy.

concepts.title: Fibroid degeneration – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: During pregnancy, rising oestrogen and progesterone levels stimulate rapid fibroid growth. When the fibroid outgrows its blood supply, central ischaemia leads to haemorrhagic infarction of myocytes (red/carneous degeneration). The fibroid becomes oedematous and haemorrhagic, with a characteristic red appearance on cut section. This triggers an acute inflammatory response causing localised peritonism.

concepts.title: Fibroid degeneration – Clinical features
concepts.content: Typical presentation is in the second trimester of pregnancy (12th–22nd week) with acute localised abdominal pain over the fibroid, low-grade fever (37.5–38.5°C), and uterine tenderness. The pain may be severe and constant. Nausea and vomiting may occur. Vital signs show mild tachycardia. Fetal heart rate is typically normal. The uterus is tender on palpation, often with localised peritonism over the fibroid.

concepts.title: Fibroid degeneration – Investigations
concepts.content: Blood tests: full blood count (raised white cell count, elevated CRP indicating inflammation), but these are non-specific. Ultrasound: confirms fibroid location and size; may show heterogeneous echogenicity within the fibroid consistent with degeneration. MRI: more sensitive for detecting degeneration (shows characteristic signal changes). CTG: continuous fetal monitoring to assess fetal wellbeing. Urine culture: to exclude urinary tract infection as a differential.

concepts.title: Fibroid degeneration – Management
concepts.content: Management during pregnancy is conservative: reassurance, adequate analgesia (paracetamol first-line; opioids such as codeine or morphine for severe pain), hydration, and rest. NSAIDs should be used with caution in pregnancy due to risk of premature closure of the ductus arteriosus (avoid after 28 weeks). Surgical myomectomy during pregnancy is rarely indicated due to high risk of haemorrhage and preterm labour. Symptoms typically resolve within 1–2 weeks.

concepts.title: Gestational trophoblastic disorders – Definition and classification
concepts.content: Gestational trophoblastic disorders (GTD) are a spectrum of conditions arising from abnormal proliferation of placental trophoblastic tissue. They include: complete hydatidiform mole (benign, all chromosomes paternal); partial hydatidiform mole (benign, triploid); invasive mole; choriocarcinoma (malignant); and placental site trophoblastic tumour. Collectively, gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) refers to the malignant forms requiring chemotherapy.

concepts.title: Gestational trophoblastic disorders – Complete hydatidiform mole: genetics and pathology
concepts.content: A complete hydatidiform mole occurs when an empty (anucleate) egg is fertilised by a single sperm that then duplicates its own DNA, resulting in a diploid karyotype (46XX or 46XY) in which all chromosomes are of paternal origin (androgenetic). No fetal parts are present. The trophoblast proliferates abnormally, producing grape-like vesicles. Approximately 2–3% progress to choriocarcinoma.

concepts.title: Gestational trophoblastic disorders – Complete mole: clinical features
concepts.content: Clinical features of a complete hydatidiform mole: vaginal bleeding in the first or early second trimester; exaggerated symptoms of pregnancy (severe hyperemesis); uterus large for dates; very high serum hCG levels (often >100,000 IU/L); hypertension (pre-eclampsia before 20 weeks); hyperthyroidism (hCG mimics TSH). On ultrasound: 'snowstorm' appearance with no fetal parts.

concepts.title: Gestational trophoblastic disorders – Complete mole: management
concepts.content: Management: urgent referral to a specialist trophoblastic disease centre; suction curettage (evacuation of the uterus) under ultrasound guidance; histological examination of evacuated material. Effective contraception is recommended to avoid pregnancy for the next 12 months (to allow hCG monitoring). Serial serum hCG measurements are performed to detect persistent GTD or malignant transformation. Anti-D immunoglobulin is given to RhD-negative women.

concepts.title: Gestational trophoblastic disorders – Partial hydatidiform mole
concepts.content: A partial hydatidiform mole occurs when a normal haploid egg is fertilised by two sperms, or by one sperm with duplication of paternal chromosomes, resulting in a triploid karyotype (69XXX, 69XXY, or 69XYY). Both maternal and paternal chromosomes are present. Fetal parts may be seen on ultrasound. Clinical features are less dramatic than a complete mole; hCG levels are lower. Risk of malignant transformation is approximately 0.5–1%.

concepts.title: Miscarriage – Definition and epidemiology
concepts.content: Miscarriage is defined as the spontaneous loss of pregnancy before 24 weeks of gestation. It occurs in approximately 30% of all pregnancies (including unrecognised pregnancies) and in 1 in 8 known pregnancies. Most miscarriages occur in the first trimester. Incidence is approximately 350 cases per 100,000 person-years, with peak incidence at age 30–40 years. Recurrent miscarriage (3 or more consecutive losses) affects approximately 1% of couples.

concepts.title: Miscarriage – Aetiology: fetal and maternal causes
concepts.content: Chromosomal abnormalities are the most common cause of first trimester miscarriage (50–60% of cases). Other causes: antiphospholipid syndrome (present in 15% of women with recurrent miscarriage, particularly first trimester); thrombophilia (factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation – associated with second trimester loss); endocrine disorders (PCOS, thyroid disease, diabetes, hyperprolactinaemia); infections (bacterial vaginosis associated with late miscarriage); uterine abnormalities (septate, bicornuate, or arcuate uterus; cervical incompetence; fibroids).

concepts.title: Miscarriage – Aetiology: risk factors for further miscarriage
concepts.content: The two most important risk factors for further miscarriage are increasing maternal age (93% risk of miscarriage in women aged ≥45 years) and previous miscarriages (40% risk of further miscarriage after three consecutive losses). Other risk factors include: smoking, obesity, stress, high-dose radiation, heavy metal exposure, sperm abnormalities, old paternal age, and tight clothing in males.

concepts.title: Miscarriage – Classification of types
concepts.content: Miscarriage types: Complete – all products of conception expelled, bleeding stops, no further treatment needed. Incomplete – fetus expelled but placenta partially retained, bleeding persists, surgical management often needed. Missed (silent) – fetus died in utero, no symptoms, small for dates uterus, diagnosed on ultrasound. Threatened – viable pregnancy with bleeding and closed cervical os; 75% settle. Inevitable – non-viable pregnancy with bleeding and open cervical os. Recurrent – 3 or more consecutive miscarriages (1% of patients).

concepts.title: Miscarriage – Clinical features
concepts.content: Clinical features vary by type. Common features: vaginal bleeding (ranging from brownish spotting to heavy bright-red blood with clots, occurring in 20–30% of pregnant women in the first trimester); lower abdominal cramping pain; vaginal fluid or tissue discharge; loss of pregnancy symptoms (nausea, breast tenderness); lower back pain. A missed miscarriage often presents with no symptoms and is diagnosed incidentally on ultrasound.

concepts.title: Miscarriage – Referral criteria
concepts.content: Immediate hospital admission: any haemodynamic instability. Immediate referral to EPAU or out-of-hours gynaecology: suspicion of ectopic pregnancy. Referral to EPAU: symptoms suggesting early pregnancy problem (excluding abdominal pain, pelvic tenderness, cervical motion tenderness) and >6 weeks pregnant or unknown gestation; any doubt about pregnancy viability. If bleeding but no pain and <6 weeks pregnant: expectant management with repeat pregnancy test after 7–10 days.

concepts.title: Miscarriage – Investigations
concepts.content: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS): confirms location and viability of pregnancy; if status unclear, repeat scan after minimum 7 days. Serum beta-hCG: serial measurements to assess trend (falling levels confirm miscarriage; rising levels suggest viable pregnancy or ectopic). Recurrent miscarriage investigations: karyotyping of both partners; TVUS for structural abnormalities; antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant); thrombophilia screen.

concepts.title: Miscarriage – Management: expectant, medical, and surgical
concepts.content: Expectant management (first-line, NICE 2023): wait 7–14 days for spontaneous completion; suitable for haemodynamically stable women. Medical management: mifepristone 200 mg orally followed 24–48 hours later by misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally (for missed miscarriage); misoprostol alone for incomplete miscarriage. Surgical management: vacuum aspiration (manual or electric) under local or general anaesthesia; surgical management preferred if haemodynamic instability, infection, or failed medical management.

concepts.title: Miscarriage – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include: incomplete miscarriage with retained products of conception requiring surgical evacuation; haemorrhagic shock (especially with incomplete or inevitable miscarriage); infection/sepsis (endometritis, approximately 3% of cases); psychological morbidity (grief, depression, anxiety, PTSD); Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions) following repeated surgical evacuation; and sensitisation in RhD-negative women (anti-D immunoglobulin required for all surgical and some medical management).

concepts.title: Ovarian torsion – Definition and overview
concepts.content: Ovarian torsion is the twisting of the ovary (and often the fallopian tube) on its pedicle, causing obstruction of venous drainage followed by arterial occlusion, leading to ischaemia and potential necrosis. It is an acute gynaecological emergency requiring prompt surgical intervention to preserve ovarian function. It accounts for approximately 3% of gynaecological emergencies.

concepts.title: Ovarian torsion – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Ovarian torsion has an incidence of approximately 6 cases per 100,000 person-years. It predominantly affects women of reproductive age (peak 20–30 years) but can occur at any age including in children and postmenopausal women. It is more common on the right side (due to the sigmoid colon limiting left-sided torsion). It is the fifth most common gynaecological emergency.

concepts.title: Ovarian torsion – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors: ovarian masses >5 cm (most important – benign cysts, dermoid cysts, endometriomas increase risk); reproductive age (hormonal influences increase ovarian size); pregnancy (corpus luteum cysts, increased ovarian mobility); ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (from fertility treatment); previous ovarian surgery; and abnormally long utero-ovarian ligaments (congenital). In children, torsion may occur on a normal ovary.

concepts.title: Ovarian torsion – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Torsion initially obstructs venous and lymphatic drainage, causing ovarian oedema and enlargement. Progressive twisting then occludes arterial supply, leading to ischaemia and infarction. Inflammatory mediators (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6) are released, causing peritoneal irritation and pain. Reperfusion injury (reactive oxygen species) may occur if detorsion is performed after prolonged ischaemia. Necrosis and loss of ovarian function occur if untreated.

concepts.title: Ovarian torsion – Clinical features
concepts.content: Classic presentation: sudden onset, severe, unilateral pelvic pain (often colicky, radiating to the groin, flank, or back), nausea and vomiting (in up to 70%), and low-grade fever if necrosis is present. Pain may be intermittent (intermittent torsion with spontaneous detorsion). On examination: unilateral adnexal tenderness, possible adnexal mass, and peritoneal signs if necrosis. Haemodynamic instability is rare unless rupture occurs.

concepts.title: Ovarian torsion – Investigations
concepts.content: Pregnancy test: mandatory first step to exclude ectopic pregnancy. Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler: first-line imaging; may show enlarged ovary, peripherally displaced follicles, free pelvic fluid, and absent or reduced blood flow. Normal Doppler does not exclude torsion (intermittent torsion). MRI: useful when ultrasound inconclusive; high-resolution imaging differentiates adnexal masses. Laparoscopy: gold standard for diagnosis and immediate treatment; negative imaging should not delay surgery if clinical suspicion is high.

concepts.title: Ovarian torsion – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Key differentials: ectopic pregnancy (unilateral pain, positive hCG, absent intrauterine sac on USS); appendicitis (pain migrating from periumbilical to right iliac fossa, fever, raised WCC, no adnexal mass); pelvic inflammatory disease (bilateral pain, abnormal discharge, cervical excitation, positive STI swabs); ruptured ovarian cyst (sudden pain, free fluid on USS, often less severe); urolithiasis (loin to groin pain, haematuria, no adnexal mass).

concepts.title: Ovarian torsion – Management
concepts.content: Initial management: IV fluids, analgesia, and urgent pelvic ultrasound. Surgical intervention: laparoscopy should be performed irrespective of ultrasound findings if clinical suspicion is high. Conservative management via detorsion (untwisting the ovary) is attempted first, even if the ovary appears ischaemic (black/blue), as recovery is possible. Oophorectomy is only performed if necrosis is confirmed or detorsion fails. Follow-up ultrasound at 6 weeks post-operatively to assess ovarian function.

concepts.title: Placenta praevia – Definition and classification
concepts.content: Placenta praevia occurs when the placenta implants in the lower uterine segment, partially or completely covering the internal cervical os. AIUM/RCOG classification: Grade 1 (low-lying) – lower edge 0.5–2 cm from internal os; Grade 2 (marginal) – reaches but does not cover the os; Grade 3 (partial) – partially covers the os; Grade 4 (complete) – completely covers the os. Prognosis worsens with higher grades.

concepts.title: Placenta praevia – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Placenta praevia has an incidence of approximately 20 cases per 100,000 person-years. Low-lying placenta is found in 4–6% of pregnancies before 20 weeks; however, up to 90% of these resolve spontaneously as the uterus grows (placental migration). Only 10% of complete praevias resolve. Incidence is rising due to increasing caesarean section rates.

concepts.title: Placenta praevia – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors: previous uterine scarring (most important – caesarean section, uterine rupture, endometriosis, D&C); previous placenta praevia (increases risk to 4–8% in subsequent pregnancies); multiparity and multiple pregnancies; advanced maternal age; smoking; and assisted reproductive technology. The mechanism involves abnormal trophoblastic invasion of the lower uterine segment, possibly due to scarring directing implantation inferiorly.

concepts.title: Placenta praevia – Clinical features
concepts.content: The hallmark is painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding, typically after 20 weeks (mean gestational age at first bleed: 30 weeks; one-third present before this). Severity ranges from spotting to life-threatening haemorrhage. The uterus is not tender (unlike placental abruption). Fetal presentation may be abnormal (transverse or oblique lie, unstable lie). Vaginal and rectal examinations are contraindicated. Intercourse should be avoided.

concepts.title: Placenta praevia – Investigations
concepts.content: Transabdominal ultrasound detects placenta praevia in approximately 95% of cases; transvaginal ultrasound in nearly 100%. Typically detected at 20-week anomaly scan. Follow-up transvaginal USS at 32 weeks for persistent low-lying placenta; if still present, repeat at 36 weeks to plan delivery. Additional investigations: FBC (anaemia, platelet disorder), clotting studies (if platelets abnormal), blood type and cross-match, Kleihauer test (RhD-negative mothers), CTG (fetal wellbeing), LFTs and U&E (exclude pre-eclampsia).

concepts.title: Placenta praevia – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Key differentials for antepartum haemorrhage: placental abruption (painful, tender uterus, concealed or revealed bleeding, fetal compromise); miscarriage (cramping pain, products of conception, more common in first/second trimester); placenta accreta (abnormally invasive placenta, associated with uterine scarring, diagnosed on USS/MRI); local causes (cervical ectropion, cervical polyps, cervicitis, genital lacerations, malignancy).

concepts.title: Placenta praevia – Management
concepts.content: Acute haemorrhage: ABCDE approach, IV access, FBC/cross-match, corticosteroids if <34 weeks, tocolytics if contracting, anti-D if RhD-negative, caesarean section if maternal/fetal compromise. Routine management: pelvic rest (no intercourse, no vaginal examination), corticosteroids at 34–36 weeks, follow-up USS. Delivery planning: Grade 1/2 may attempt vaginal delivery if lower edge >2 cm from os; Grade 3/4 (major praevia) require elective caesarean at 37–38 weeks.

concepts.title: Placenta praevia – Complications
concepts.content: Maternal complications: major haemorrhage requiring blood transfusion; emergency caesarean section; hysterectomy (if placenta accreta co-exists or haemorrhage uncontrollable); maternal death. Fetal complications: preterm birth (most common); intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR); fetal death from haemorrhage or hypoxia; malpresentation requiring caesarean. Placenta accreta spectrum (accreta, increta, percreta) is a serious complication associated with previous uterine scarring.

concepts.title: Placental abruption – Definition and overview
concepts.content: Placental abruption is the premature separation of a normally sited placenta from the uterine wall before delivery of the fetus. It is a major cause of antepartum haemorrhage (accounting for approximately 30% of cases) and a significant cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality. Bleeding may be revealed (external), concealed (behind the placenta), or mixed.

concepts.title: Placental abruption – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors: pre-eclampsia and hypertension (most important); smoking; cocaine use; abdominal trauma; chorioamnionitis; alcohol use; advanced maternal age; multiparity; previous placental abruption (recurrence risk approximately 8% in subsequent pregnancy, rising to 25% after two abruptions); thrombophilia; premature rupture of membranes; and polyhydramnios (sudden uterine decompression).

concepts.title: Placental abruption – Clinical features
concepts.content: Vaginal bleeding (variable volume; 20% of abruptions are concealed with no external bleeding); sudden onset severe abdominal pain (constant, not colicky); uterine tenderness and rigidity ('woody' uterus); uterine hypertonicity; fetal compromise (abnormal CTG, fetal bradycardia); and maternal shock (disproportionate to visible blood loss if concealed). Back pain may be present. Fetal parts may be difficult to palpate due to uterine rigidity.

concepts.title: Placental abruption – Investigations
concepts.content: Ultrasound: may show retroplacental haematoma (sensitivity only 25–50%; a normal scan does not exclude abruption). CTG: essential for fetal wellbeing assessment. Blood tests: FBC (anaemia, thrombocytopaenia), coagulation profile (DIC – prolonged PT/APTT, low fibrinogen, elevated D-dimer), Kleihauer-Betke test (quantify feto-maternal haemorrhage in RhD-negative women), LFTs and renal function (exclude pre-eclampsia), cross-match.

concepts.title: Placental abruption – Management
concepts.content: Initial resuscitation: ABCDE, IV access (2 large-bore cannulae), blood transfusion, FFP/cryoprecipitate for DIC. Delivery: immediate delivery if maternal or fetal compromise (emergency caesarean section); conservative management if <37 weeks without compromise (aim for vaginal delivery if possible). Corticosteroids: single dose between 24th and 34th weeks (preterm birth risk). Anti-D immunoglobulin: all non-sensitised RhD-negative women regardless of prior prophylaxis. Active management of third stage of labour to prevent PPH.

concepts.title: Placental abruption – Complications
concepts.content: Maternal complications: severe haemorrhage and hypovolaemic shock; disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC); acute kidney injury; hysterectomy (to control bleeding); maternal death; recurrence in future pregnancies. Fetal complications: premature birth; stillbirth; low birth weight; hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy; cerebral palsy. Couvelaire uterus (extravasation of blood into myometrium) may impair uterine contractility and worsen PPH.

concepts.title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome – Definition and overview
concepts.content: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a complex endocrine disorder affecting 5–20% of women of reproductive age. It is characterised by a combination of ovarian dysfunction, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound. The aetiology involves both hyperinsulinaemia and elevated luteinising hormone, with overlap with the metabolic syndrome.

concepts.title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome – Epidemiology
concepts.content: PCOS has an incidence of approximately 90 cases per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence is in women aged 30–40 years. It is the most common endocrine disorder in women of reproductive age and the most common cause of anovulatory infertility.

concepts.title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome – Clinical features
concepts.content: Clinical features: subfertility and infertility (anovulatory cycles); menstrual disturbances (oligomenorrhoea, amenorrhoea); hirsutism and acne (due to hyperandrogenism); obesity (present in 50–80%); acanthosis nigricans (due to insulin resistance); and psychological symptoms (depression, anxiety). Women with PCOS are at increased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, endometrial cancer, and obstructive sleep apnoea.

concepts.title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome – Investigations
concepts.content: Pelvic ultrasound: polycystic ovaries defined as ≥12 follicles (2–9 mm diameter) in one or both ovaries and/or increased ovarian volume (>10 cm³). Hormonal profile: FSH, LH (raised LH:FSH ratio is classical but no longer required for diagnosis), prolactin (may be mildly elevated), TSH (exclude thyroid disease), testosterone (may be mildly elevated; if markedly raised, consider other causes such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia or androgen-secreting tumour). Glucose tolerance test: screen for impaired glucose tolerance/type 2 diabetes.

concepts.title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome – Diagnosis: Rotterdam criteria
concepts.content: The Rotterdam criteria (most widely used) require 2 of the following 3 features: (1) oligo- and/or anovulation (oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea); (2) clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, or elevated total/free testosterone); (3) polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (≥12 follicles 2–9 mm in one or both ovaries and/or ovarian volume >10 cm³). Other causes of hyperandrogenism must be excluded.

concepts.title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome – Management: general and hirsutism
concepts.content: General: weight reduction (even 5–10% weight loss can restore ovulation and improve metabolic parameters); combined oral contraceptive pill (regulates cycle, induces monthly bleed, reduces androgen levels). Hirsutism and acne: third-generation COCP (fewer androgenic effects) or co-cyprindiol (anti-androgen action; increased VTE risk). If COCP fails: topical eflornithine; spironolactone, flutamide, or finasteride under specialist supervision.

concepts.title: Polycystic ovarian syndrome – Management: infertility
concepts.content: Infertility management in PCOS should be supervised by a specialist. Weight reduction is first-line. Clomifene (anti-oestrogen, blocks hypothalamic oestrogen receptors, stimulates FSH secretion) is the most effective treatment for ovulation induction (2007 NEJM trial). Risk of multiple pregnancy with clomifene. Metformin (alone or combined with clomifene) is used particularly in obese patients; RCOG (2008) concluded metformin is not first-line. Gonadotrophins and laparoscopic ovarian drilling are second-line options.

concepts.title: Premature ovarian failure – Definition, epidemiology, and aetiology
concepts.content: Premature ovarian failure (POF), also called premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), is cessation of normal ovarian function before the age of 40 years. Incidence is approximately 30 cases per 100,000 person-years; affects approximately 1% of women under 40 and 0.1% under 30. Causes include: genetic disorders (Turner syndrome, fragile X premutation); autoimmune disease (most common cause in developed countries); iatrogenic (chemotherapy, pelvic radiotherapy, bilateral oophorectomy); and idiopathic (50% of cases).

concepts.title: Premature ovarian failure – Clinical features and management
concepts.content: Clinical features: secondary amenorrhoea (primary presenting symptom); climacteric symptoms (hot flushes, night sweats, vaginal dryness); infertility; and features of the underlying cause. Investigations: raised FSH (>25 IU/L on two occasions ≥4 weeks apart), low oestradiol, low AMH. Management: hormone replacement therapy (HRT) until the natural age of menopause (51 years) to prevent osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease; fertility treatment (oocyte donation is most effective); psychological support.

concepts.title: Premenstrual syndrome – Definition and overview
concepts.content: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) describes the emotional and physical symptoms experienced during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle that resolve with the onset of menstruation. It only occurs in the presence of ovulatory menstrual cycles and does not occur prior to puberty, during pregnancy, or after the menopause. Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a severe form meeting DSM-5 criteria.

concepts.title: Premenstrual syndrome – Epidemiology
concepts.content: PMS has an incidence of approximately 500 cases per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence is in women aged 30–40 years. Up to 80% of women experience some premenstrual symptoms; approximately 5–8% have severe symptoms meeting criteria for PMDD. PMS is the most common gynaecological complaint in women of reproductive age.

concepts.title: Premenstrual syndrome – Clinical features
concepts.content: Emotional/psychological features: mood swings, irritability, increased anger, anxiety, tension, low mood, tearfulness, difficulty concentrating. Physical features: breast tenderness or swelling, bloating and abdominal discomfort, headache, fatigue, increased appetite (carbohydrate cravings), sleep disturbance. Symptoms occur exclusively in the luteal phase (after ovulation) and remit shortly after menstruation begins. Symptom-free intervals during the follicular phase are essential for diagnosis.

concepts.title: Premenstrual syndrome – Management
concepts.content: Mild PMS: lifestyle advice (regular exercise, dietary modification, stress reduction, sleep hygiene). Moderate PMS: new-generation combined oral contraceptive pill containing drospirenone 3 mg + ethinylestradiol 0.030 mg (e.g., Yasmin) – drospirenone has anti-mineralocorticoid and anti-androgenic properties. Severe PMS/PMDD: SSRIs (e.g., fluoxetine, sertraline) given continuously or in the luteal phase only (days 15–28 of cycle) – effective for emotional symptoms.

concepts.title: Ruptured ovarian cysts – Definition and overview
concepts.content: Ovarian cyst rupture occurs when the wall of an ovarian cyst breaks, releasing its contents into the peritoneal cavity. It is a common cause of acute pelvic pain in women of reproductive age. Most ruptured cysts are benign functional cysts (follicular or corpus luteum cysts). Haemorrhagic cysts may cause significant haemoperitoneum requiring surgical intervention.

concepts.title: Ruptured ovarian cysts – Aetiology and clinical features
concepts.content: Aetiology: spontaneous rupture (most common), physical activity, trauma, sexual intercourse, or increased intra-abdominal pressure. Clinical features: sudden onset, unilateral, sharp pelvic pain (may become diffuse if haemoperitoneum); nausea and vomiting; peritoneal signs (guarding, rebound tenderness) if haemoperitoneum; haemodynamic instability if significant haemorrhage; low-grade fever; and urinary or GI symptoms. On examination: unilateral adnexal tenderness, possible cervical excitation.

concepts.title: Ruptured ovarian cysts – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Key differentials: ectopic pregnancy (positive hCG, absent intrauterine sac on USS, cervical excitation); ovarian torsion (severe colicky pain, enlarged ovary, absent Doppler flow); appendicitis (right iliac fossa pain, fever, raised WCC, no adnexal mass); PID (bilateral pain, discharge, positive STI swabs, fever); urolithiasis (loin to groin pain, haematuria, no adnexal mass); diverticulitis (left iliac fossa pain, fever, altered bowel habit).

concepts.title: Ruptured ovarian cysts – Management
concepts.content: Conservative management for haemodynamically stable patients: analgesia (NSAIDs, paracetamol, opioids), IV fluids, serial observations, and serial haematocrit monitoring. Surgical management (laparoscopic preferred): indicated for haemodynamic instability, significant haemoperitoneum, ongoing haemorrhage, or diagnostic uncertainty. Laparotomy may be required for massive haemorrhage. Ovarian cystectomy (preserving ovary) is preferred over oophorectomy. Histology of excised tissue is recommended.

concepts.title: Urogenital prolapse – Definition and types
concepts.content: Urogenital (pelvic organ) prolapse is the descent of one or more pelvic organs (bladder, uterus, vaginal vault, rectum) into or beyond the vaginal canal due to weakness of the pelvic floor support structures. Types: anterior compartment (cystocele – bladder prolapse; urethrocele – urethral prolapse); posterior compartment (rectocele – rectal prolapse; enterocele – small bowel prolapse); apical compartment (uterine prolapse; vault prolapse post-hysterectomy).

concepts.title: Urogenital prolapse – Epidemiology and aetiology
concepts.content: Pelvic organ prolapse affects approximately 50% of parous women to some degree; symptomatic prolapse affects 10–20%. Peak incidence is in women aged 70+. Risk factors: vaginal childbirth (most important – especially prolonged second stage, instrumental delivery, large baby); multiparity; obesity; chronic increased intra-abdominal pressure (constipation, chronic cough, heavy lifting); oestrogen deficiency (postmenopause); connective tissue disorders; and previous pelvic surgery.

concepts.title: Urogenital prolapse – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Normal pelvic floor support depends on the levator ani muscle complex (pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus, puborectalis) and the endopelvic fascia (pubocervical fascia anteriorly, rectovaginal fascia posteriorly, cardinal and uterosacral ligaments apically). Childbirth causes direct muscle trauma, pudendal nerve injury, and fascial tears. Oestrogen deficiency leads to atrophy of supporting tissues. Chronic increased intra-abdominal pressure progressively weakens these structures.

concepts.title: Urogenital prolapse – Clinical features
concepts.content: Symptoms: sensation of a vaginal bulge or 'something coming down' (most common complaint); urinary symptoms (stress incontinence, urgency, frequency, incomplete bladder emptying, recurrent UTIs); defecatory dysfunction (constipation, incomplete evacuation, need to digitally reduce prolapse to defaecate); sexual dysfunction (dyspareunia, reduced sensation); and low back or pelvic pressure. Symptoms worsen with prolonged standing and improve with lying down.

concepts.title: Urogenital prolapse – Management: conservative
concepts.content: Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) is first-line for Stage I–II prolapse; supervised PFMT for at least 3–6 months before considering surgery. Vaginal pessaries (ring, shelf, or Gellhorn pessaries) provide mechanical support and are suitable for women who decline surgery, are unfit for surgery, or during pregnancy. Topical oestrogen improves vaginal tissue quality and reduces pessary complications. Lifestyle modifications: weight loss, treat constipation, avoid heavy lifting.

concepts.title: Urogenital prolapse – Management: surgical
concepts.content: Surgical options: anterior colporrhaphy (repair of cystocele); posterior colporrhaphy (repair of rectocele); sacrocolpopexy (abdominal/laparoscopic fixation of vaginal vault to sacrum using mesh – gold standard for vault prolapse); sacrospinous fixation (vaginal approach, fixes vault to sacrospinous ligament); Manchester repair (amputation of cervix + anterior repair); hysterectomy (if uterine prolapse). Mesh use in vaginal prolapse surgery is restricted in the UK due to complications (pain, erosion, dyspareunia).

concepts.title: Vaginal candidiasis – Definition, epidemiology, and aetiology
concepts.content: Vaginal candidiasis (vulvovaginal candidiasis) is a fungal infection of the vagina and vulva, caused by Candida species in 80–90% of cases by Candida albicans. It is the second most common cause of vaginal discharge after bacterial vaginosis. Incidence is approximately 200 cases per 100,000 person-years; peak age 25–35 years. Risk factors: diabetes mellitus, antibiotic use (disrupts normal flora), corticosteroids, pregnancy, immunosuppression (HIV), and tight synthetic clothing.

concepts.title: Vaginal candidiasis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Symptoms: intense vulval pruritus (most prominent symptom), vulval soreness and burning, thick white 'cottage cheese' or curd-like vaginal discharge (typically odourless), dyspareunia, and external dysuria (burning on micturition). Signs: vulval and vaginal erythema and oedema, adherent white plaques on vaginal walls, excoriation, and fissuring. The absence of offensive odour and the presence of marked erythema help distinguish candidiasis from BV.

concepts.title: Vaginal candidiasis – Management: acute and recurrent
concepts.content: Acute treatment: local (intravaginal) clotrimazole 500 mg pessary as a single dose (first-line); oral fluconazole 150 mg as a single dose (equally effective, preferred by many women); oral itraconazole 200 mg twice daily for 1 day as alternative. In pregnancy: local treatments only (clotrimazole); oral azoles are contraindicated. Recurrent candidiasis (≥4 episodes per year, BASHH definition): induction with fluconazole 150 mg every 3 days for 3 doses, followed by maintenance fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months.

concepts.title: Combined contraceptive patch – Mechanism and cycle
concepts.content: The Evra patch is the only combined contraceptive patch licensed for use in the UK. The patch cycle lasts 4 weeks: the patch is worn and changed weekly for 3 consecutive weeks, followed by a patch-free week during which a withdrawal bleed occurs.

concepts.title: Combined contraceptive patch – Delayed patch change at end of week 1 or 2
concepts.content: If the patch change is delayed at the end of week 1 or week 2: if the delay is less than 48 hours, change immediately and no further precautions are needed. If the delay is greater than 48 hours, change immediately and use barrier contraception for the next 7 days. If unprotected sex occurred during the extended patch-free interval or in the last 5 days, emergency contraception must be considered.

concepts.title: Combined contraceptive patch – Delayed patch removal at end of week 3
concepts.content: If patch removal is delayed at the end of week 3, remove the patch as soon as possible and apply the new patch on the usual cycle start day for the next cycle, even if withdrawal bleeding is occurring. No additional contraception is needed.

concepts.title: Combined contraceptive patch – Delayed application at start of new cycle
concepts.content: If patch application is delayed at the end of a patch-free week (i.e., delayed start of a new cycle), additional barrier contraception should be used for 7 days following any delay at the start of a new patch cycle.

concepts.title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – Advantages
concepts.content: Advantages of the COCP: highly effective (failure rate <1 per 100 woman-years); does not interfere with sex; reversible on stopping; usually makes periods regular, lighter, and less painful; reduced risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer (effect may last several decades after cessation); reduced risk of colorectal cancer; may protect against pelvic inflammatory disease; may reduce ovarian cysts, benign breast disease, and acne vulgaris.

concepts.title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – Disadvantages
concepts.content: Disadvantages of the COCP: requires daily adherence; offers no protection against sexually transmitted infections; increased risk of venous thromboembolic disease; increased risk of breast and cervical cancer; increased risk of stroke and ischaemic heart disease (especially in smokers); temporary side-effects including headache, nausea, and breast tenderness. A Cochrane review did not support a causal relationship between COCP use and weight gain.

concepts.title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – UKMEC contraindications: UKMEC 3 conditions
concepts.content: UKMEC 3 conditions for the COCP (disadvantages generally outweigh advantages): age >35 years and smoking <15 cigarettes/day; BMI >35 kg/m²; family history of thromboembolic disease in first-degree relatives aged <45 years; controlled hypertension; immobility (e.g. wheelchair use); carrier of known gene mutations associated with breast cancer (e.g. BRCA1/BRCA2); current gallbladder disease. Diabetes mellitus diagnosed >20 years ago may be UKMEC 3 or 4 depending on severity.

concepts.title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – UKMEC contraindications: UKMEC 4 conditions
concepts.content: UKMEC 4 conditions for the COCP (unacceptable health risk): age >35 years and smoking ≥15 cigarettes/day; migraine with aura; history of thromboembolic disease or thrombogenic mutation; history of stroke or ischaemic heart disease; breastfeeding <6 weeks post-partum; uncontrolled hypertension; current breast cancer; major surgery with prolonged immobilisation; positive antiphospholipid antibodies (e.g. in SLE).

concepts.title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – Counselling: starting and taking the pill
concepts.content: If the COCP is started within the first 5 days of the cycle, no additional contraception is needed. If started at any other point, use alternative contraception (e.g. condoms) for the first 7 days. The pill should be taken at the same time every day. The conventional 21-day active pill followed by 7-day break is now supplemented by 'tailored' regimes (2019 guidelines): no pill-free interval, or 'tricycling' (three 21-day packs back-to-back before a 4–7 day break). There is no medical benefit from having a withdrawal bleed.

concepts.title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – Counselling: factors reducing efficacy
concepts.content: Factors that may reduce COCP efficacy: vomiting within 2 hours of taking the pill; medications that induce diarrhoea or vomiting (e.g. orlistat); liver enzyme-inducing drugs. Concurrent non-enzyme-inducing antibiotics no longer require additional precautions (FSRH 2011 guidelines; BNF updated accordingly). Precautions should still be taken with enzyme-inducing antibiotics such as rifampicin.

concepts.title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – Missed pill: 1 pill missed
concepts.content: FSRH guidance for COCP containing 30–35 micrograms ethinylestradiol: if 1 pill is missed at any time in the cycle, take the last pill even if it means taking two pills in one day, then continue taking pills daily. No additional contraceptive protection is needed.

concepts.title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – Missed pill: 2 or more pills missed
concepts.content: If 2 or more COCP pills are missed: take the last pill even if it means taking two in one day, leave any earlier missed pills, and continue taking pills daily. Use condoms or abstain from sex until 7 consecutive days of pill-taking are re-established. If pills are missed in week 1 (Days 1–7): consider emergency contraception if unprotected sex occurred in the pill-free interval or in week 1. If missed in week 2 (Days 8–14): no emergency contraception needed after 7 consecutive days. If missed in week 3 (Days 15–21): finish the current pack and start a new pack the next day, omitting the pill-free interval.

concepts.title: Combined oral contraceptive pill – Special situations: switching pills
concepts.content: When switching between COCP preparations, the BNF and FSRH give apparently contradictory advice. The FSRH Clinical Effectiveness Unit states the pill-free interval does not need to be omitted. The BNF advises missing the pill-free interval if the progestogen component changes. Given the uncertainty, it is best to follow the BNF guidance.

concepts.title: Contraception for women aged over 40 years – General principles
concepts.content: No method of contraception is contraindicated by age alone. All methods are UKMEC 1 for women over 40, except the COCP (UKMEC 2 for women ≥40 years) and Depo-Provera (UKMEC 2 for women >45 years). Women still require effective contraception until the menopause despite significantly declined fertility by age 40.

concepts.title: Contraception for women aged over 40 years – COCP and Depo-Provera considerations
concepts.content: COCP in perimenopausal women: may help maintain bone mineral density; may reduce menopausal symptoms; a pill containing <30 µg ethinylestradiol may be more suitable for women >40 years. Depo-Provera: women should be advised of a potential delay in return of fertility of up to 1 year for women >40 years; associated with a small loss in bone mineral density, usually recovered after discontinuation.

concepts.title: Contraception for women aged over 40 years – When to stop contraception
concepts.content: FSRH guidance on stopping contraception: Non-hormonal methods (IUD, condoms, natural family planning) – stop after 2 years of amenorrhoea if <50 years; after 1 year of amenorrhoea if ≥50 years. COCP – can be continued to age 50, then switch to non-hormonal or progestogen-only method. Implant, POP, IUS – can be continued beyond 50 years; if amenorrhoeic, check FSH and stop after 1 year if FSH ≥30 IU/L, or stop at 55 years.

concepts.title: Contraception for women aged over 40 years – HRT and contraception
concepts.content: HRT cannot be relied upon for contraception; a separate method is needed. The POP may be used with HRT as long as the HRT has a progestogen component (the POP cannot be relied upon to protect the endometrium). The IUS is licensed to provide the progestogen component of HRT.

concepts.title: Emergency contraception – Levonorgestrel: mechanism, dosing, and timing
concepts.content: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception: mode of action not fully understood; acts to stop ovulation and inhibit implantation. Single dose of levonorgestrel 1.5 mg (a progestogen). Must be taken within 72 hours of unprotected sexual intercourse (UPSI); efficacy decreases with time (84% effective if used within 72 hours). May be offered after 72 hours if the client is aware of reduced effectiveness (unlicensed indication). The dose should be doubled for BMI >26 or weight >70 kg, and for those taking enzyme-inducing drugs (although a copper IUD is preferable in the latter).

concepts.title: Emergency contraception – Levonorgestrel: safety and follow-up
concepts.content: Levonorgestrel is safe and well-tolerated. Disturbance of the current menstrual cycle is seen in a significant minority of women. Vomiting occurs in approximately 1%; if vomiting occurs within 3 hours the dose should be repeated. Levonorgestrel can be used more than once in a menstrual cycle if clinically indicated. Hormonal contraception can be started immediately after using levonorgestrel (Levonelle) for emergency contraception. Breastfeeding is not restricted after levonorgestrel use.

concepts.title: Emergency contraception – Ulipristal acetate: mechanism, dosing, and timing
concepts.content: Ulipristal acetate (EllaOne) is a selective progesterone receptor modulator. Primary mode of action is inhibition of ovulation. Dose: 30 mg orally as soon as possible, no later than 120 hours (5 days) after unprotected intercourse. Concomitant use with levonorgestrel is not recommended. Caution should be exercised in patients with severe asthma. Ulipristal can be used more than once in the same cycle.

concepts.title: Emergency contraception – Ulipristal acetate: effect on subsequent contraception and breastfeeding
concepts.content: Ulipristal may reduce the effectiveness of subsequent hormonal contraception. The pill, patch, or ring should be started or restarted 5 days after taking ulipristal; barrier methods should be used during this 5-day period. Breastfeeding should be delayed for one week after taking ulipristal. There are no such breastfeeding restrictions on levonorgestrel.

concepts.title: Emergency contraception – Copper IUD: efficacy and timing
concepts.content: The copper IUD is the most effective method of emergency contraception and should be offered to all women who meet the criteria. It is 99% effective regardless of where it is used in the cycle. Must be inserted within 5 days of UPSI; if a woman presents after more than 5 days, an IUD may be fitted up to 5 days after the likely ovulation date. The IUD may inhibit fertilisation or implantation. Prophylactic antibiotics may be given if the patient is at high risk of sexually transmitted infection.

concepts.title: Emergency contraception – Copper IUD: ongoing use and removal
concepts.content: The copper IUD used for emergency contraception may be left in situ to provide long-term contraception. If the client wishes for the IUD to be removed, it should be kept in place until at least the next period to ensure the emergency contraceptive effect is complete.

concepts.title: Epilepsy and contraception – UKMEC categories
concepts.content: For women taking phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, primidone, topiramate, or oxcarbazepine: COCP and POP are UKMEC 3; implant is UKMEC 2; Depo-Provera, IUD, and IUS are UKMEC 1. For lamotrigine: COCP is UKMEC 3; POP, implant, Depo-Provera, IUD, and IUS are UKMEC 1. If a COCP is chosen for women on lamotrigine, it should contain a minimum of 30 µg ethinylestradiol. The FSRH recommends consistent use of condoms in addition to other contraception for women with epilepsy.

concepts.title: Implantable contraceptives – Nexplanon: pharmacology and insertion
concepts.content: Nexplanon has replaced Implanon as the subdermal contraceptive implant. Both release the progestogen etonogestrel. Nexplanon improvements over Implanon: redesigned applicator to prevent deep insertions; radiopaque for easier localisation if impalpable. Inserted in the proximal non-dominant arm, just overlying the tricep. Primary mechanism: prevents ovulation; also thickens cervical mucus.

concepts.title: Implantable contraceptives – Nexplanon: efficacy, duration, and key advantages
concepts.content: Nexplanon is the most effective form of contraception (failure rate 0.07 per 100 woman-years). It lasts 3 years. It does not contain oestrogen and can therefore be used in women with a past history of thromboembolism or migraine. It can be inserted immediately following a termination of pregnancy. Additional contraceptive methods are needed for the first 7 days if not inserted on days 1–5 of the menstrual cycle.

concepts.title: Implantable contraceptives – Nexplanon: adverse effects and interactions
concepts.content: Main adverse effect: irregular or heavy bleeding (sometimes managed with co-prescription of COCP; speculum examination and STI check if bleeding continues). Progestogen effects: headache, nausea, breast pain. Interactions: enzyme-inducing drugs (certain antiepileptics and rifampicin) may reduce efficacy. FSRH advises switching to a method unaffected by enzyme-inducing drugs, or using additional contraception until 28 days after stopping the enzyme-inducing treatment.

concepts.title: Implantable contraceptives – Nexplanon: contraindications
concepts.content: UKMEC 3 contraindications for Nexplanon (proven risks generally outweigh advantages): ischaemic heart disease or stroke (for continuation; initiation is UKMEC 2); unexplained or suspicious vaginal bleeding; past breast cancer; severe liver cirrhosis; liver cancer. UKMEC 4 contraindication (unacceptable risk): current breast cancer.

concepts.title: Injectable contraceptives – Depo-Provera: pharmacology and dosing
concepts.content: Depo-Provera is the main injectable contraceptive used in the UK, containing medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg given via intramuscular injection every 12 weeks. It can be given up to 14 weeks after the last dose without the need for extra precautions (the BNF advises a pregnancy test if the interval is >12 weeks and 5 days, though this is not commonly adhered to in family planning). Primary mechanism: inhibits ovulation. Secondary effects: cervical mucus thickening and endometrial thinning.

concepts.title: Injectable contraceptives – Depo-Provera: adverse effects and contraindications
concepts.content: Adverse effects: irregular bleeding; weight gain; potential increased risk of osteoporosis (should only be used in adolescents if no other method is suitable); the injection cannot be reversed once given; delayed return to fertility (up to 12 months). Contraindications: current breast cancer is UKMEC 4; past breast cancer is UKMEC 3. Noristerat is the other injectable contraceptive licensed in the UK (given every 8 weeks), but is rarely used in clinical practice.

concepts.title: Intrauterine contraceptive devices – IUD vs IUS: mode of action and effectiveness
concepts.content: Both the IUD (copper) and IUS (levonorgestrel-releasing) are more than 99% effective. IUD mode of action: primary mechanism is prevention of fertilisation by decreasing sperm motility and survival, possibly via copper ions. IUS mode of action: levonorgestrel prevents endometrial proliferation and causes cervical mucus thickening. The IUS (Mirena) is also used in the management of menorrhagia.

concepts.title: Intrauterine contraceptive devices – IUD: duration and reliability
concepts.content: The copper IUD can be relied upon immediately following insertion. IUDs with copper on the stem only are effective for 5 years; IUDs with copper on both the stem and arms of the T may be effective for up to 10 years. IUDs make periods heavier, longer, and more painful.

concepts.title: Intrauterine contraceptive devices – IUS (Mirena): duration and bleeding effects
concepts.content: The Mirena IUS (levonorgestrel 20 mcg/24 hrs) can be relied upon after 7 days. It is effective for 8 years; if used in women ≥45 years, it is effective until age 55 years. If used as endometrial protection for women taking oestrogen-only HRT, it is only licensed for 5 years. Initially causes frequent uterine bleeding and spotting; later, women typically have intermittent light menses with less dysmenorrhoea, and some become amenorrhoeic.

concepts.title: Intrauterine contraceptive devices – Potential problems
concepts.content: Potential problems with IUDs/IUS: uterine perforation (up to 2 per 1,000 insertions; higher in breastfeeding women); ectopic pregnancy risk is increased proportionally but the absolute number of ectopics is reduced compared to no contraception; pelvic inflammatory disease (small increased risk in the first 20 days after insertion, returning to baseline thereafter); expulsion (risk approximately 1 in 20, most likely in the first 3 months).

concepts.title: Intrauterine contraceptive devices – Newer IUS systems: Jaydess and Kyleena
concepts.content: Jaydess IUS: licensed for 3 years; smaller frame and narrower inserter tube than Mirena; contains 13.5 mg levonorgestrel (compared to 52 mg in Mirena), resulting in lower serum LNG levels. Kyleena IUS: contains 19.5 mg LNG; smaller than Mirena; licensed for 5 years; lower serum LNG levels than Mirena; lower rate of amenorrhoea compared to Mirena.

concepts.title: Natural family planning – Clinical indicators of fertility
concepts.content: The major clinical indicators of fertility used in natural family planning are: changes in cervical mucus (becoming clearer, more slippery, and stretchy around ovulation); changes in the cervix (softer, higher, and more open around ovulation); and changes in basal body temperature (rises by approximately 0.2°C after ovulation).

concepts.title: Postpartum contraception – POP and COCP timing
concepts.content: After giving birth, women require contraception after day 21. POP: can be started at any time postpartum (breastfeeding and non-breastfeeding); after day 21, additional contraception should be used for the first 2 days; a small amount of progestogen enters breast milk but is not harmful to the infant. COCP: absolutely contraindicated (UKMEC 4) if breastfeeding <6 weeks post-partum; UKMEC 2 if breastfeeding 6 weeks–6 months; may reduce breast milk production; should not be used in the first 21 days due to increased VTE risk; after day 21, additional contraception for the first 7 days.

concepts.title: Postpartum contraception – IUD/IUS timing and lactational amenorrhoea method
concepts.content: The IUD or IUS can be inserted within 48 hours of childbirth or after 4 weeks (not between 48 hours and 4 weeks due to increased risk of expulsion). Lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM): 98% effective providing the woman is fully breastfeeding (no supplementary feeds), amenorrhoeic, and less than 6 months post-partum. An inter-pregnancy interval of less than 12 months between childbirth and conceiving again is associated with increased risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, and small for gestational age babies.

concepts.title: Progestogen-only pill – UKMEC 3 contraindications
concepts.content: UKMEC 3 conditions for the POP (disadvantages generally outweigh advantages): severe or decompensated liver cirrhosis; history of benign or malignant liver tumours; use of liver enzyme-inducing drugs (e.g. rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin); history of breast cancer more than 5 years ago; undiagnosed vaginal bleeding; ischaemic heart disease or stroke (for continuation); SLE with antiphospholipid antibodies; severe hypertension (systolic ≥160 mmHg or diastolic ≥100 mmHg); multiple cardiovascular risk factors.

concepts.title: Progestogen-only pill – UKMEC 4 contraindications
concepts.content: UKMEC 4 conditions for the POP (unacceptable health risk): current breast cancer (diagnosed within the last 5 years or ongoing disease); pregnancy (although not harmful if taken inadvertently during early pregnancy, the POP should not be initiated in pregnant individuals).

concepts.title: Progestogen-only pill – Counselling: starting and taking the POP
concepts.content: Most common problem: irregular vaginal bleeding. Starting: if commenced up to and including day 5 of the cycle, provides immediate protection; otherwise use additional contraception (e.g. condoms) for the first 2 days. If switching from a COCP, gives immediate protection if continued directly from the end of a pill packet (Day 21). The POP should be taken at the same time every day, without a pill-free break. Antibiotics have no effect on the POP (unless they alter the P450 enzyme system, e.g. rifampicin). Liver enzyme inducers may reduce effectiveness.

concepts.title: Progestogen-only pill – Missed pill rules: traditional POP vs Cerazette
concepts.content: Traditional POPs (Micronor, Noriday, Nogeston, Femulen): if less than 3 hours late, no action required; if more than 3 hours late (>27 hours since last pill), action needed. Cerazette (desogestrel): if less than 12 hours late, no action required; if more than 12 hours late (>36 hours since last pill), action needed. Action required: take the missed pill as soon as possible (one pill only even if multiple missed); continue rest of pack; use extra precautions (condoms) until pill-taking re-established for 48 hours.

concepts.title: Progestogen-only pill – Types: second and third generation
concepts.content: Second generation POPs: norethisterone, levonorgestrel, ethynodiol diacetate. Third generation POP: desogestrel (Cerazette). Cerazette differs from traditional POPs in that it inhibits ovulation in the majority of women (traditional POPs do not reliably inhibit ovulation) and allows a 12-hour window for missed pills (rather than 3 hours for traditional POPs).

concepts.title: Quick starting contraception – When pregnancy can be excluded
concepts.content: Quick starting (starting contraception outside the recommended time in the menstrual cycle) may require additional contraceptive precautions depending on the method and day of cycle: COCP (not Zoely or Qlaira) from day 6 onwards requires 7 days of additional contraception; POP (traditional/desogestrel) from day 6 onwards requires 2 days; progestogen-only injectable and implant from day 6 onwards require 7 days; LNG-IUS from day 8 onwards requires 7 days; copper IUD on any start day requires 0 additional days.

concepts.title: Quick starting contraception – When pregnancy cannot be excluded
concepts.content: If pregnancy cannot be excluded (negative pregnancy test but at risk from recent UPSI): assess and offer emergency contraception first. If levonorgestrel EC given: COCP, POP, or implant can commence immediately. If ulipristal EC given: delay quick-starting progestogen-containing contraception for 5 days (ulipristal effectiveness may be reduced by progestogen). Intrauterine contraception should not be offered unless pregnancy is reasonably excluded. A pregnancy test must be taken 21 days after the last UPSI.

concepts.title: Contraception for transgender and non-binary people – General principles
concepts.content: Contraceptive choices and sexual health guidance applies to any individual engaging in vaginal sex where there is a risk of pregnancy and/or STIs, regardless of gender identity. Sensitive communication and personalised options are essential. Condoms and dental dams are recommended for STI prevention. Cervical screening should be offered to all sexually active individuals with a uterus. HPV vaccination should be offered to all sexually active individuals.

concepts.title: Contraception for transgender and non-binary people – Contraceptive choices for trans men
concepts.content: For patients assigned female at birth with a uterus: testosterone therapy does not provide protection against pregnancy; if pregnancy occurs, testosterone is contraindicated (teratogenic). Oestrogen-containing regimes are not recommended during testosterone therapy (antagonise testosterone effects). Progestogen-only contraceptives are not considered to have a detrimental effect on testosterone therapy; IUS and injections may also suspend menstruation. Non-hormonal IUDs do not interact with hormonal regimes but may exacerbate menstrual bleeding. Either oral emergency contraceptive option may be used as neither is believed to interact with testosterone therapy.

concepts.title: Contraception for young people – Legal and ethical framework
concepts.content: The age of consent for sexual activity in the UK is 16 years. Practitioners may provide contraception to those under 16 if the young person is assessed as 'competent' using the Fraser Guidelines. Children under 13 cannot consent to sexual intercourse; consultations involving this age group must automatically trigger child protection measures. Fraser Guidelines require all of the following: the young person understands the advice; cannot be persuaded to inform parents; is likely to have sex with or without treatment; their health would suffer without treatment; and their best interests require receiving contraception.

concepts.title: Contraception for young people – Choice of method
concepts.content: Long-acting reversible contraceptive methods (LARCs) have advantages in young people due to less reliance on daily adherence. Concerns about Depo-Provera in young people: potential effect on bone mineral density. The UKMEC category for the IUS and IUD is 2 for women under 20 years, meaning they may not be the best choice. The progestogen-only implant (Nexplanon) is therefore the LARC of choice in young people. Young people should be advised to have STI tests 2 and 12 weeks after an incident of unprotected sexual intercourse.

concepts.title: Metastatic disease – Definition of bone metastases
concepts.content: Bone metastases occur when cancer cells from a primary tumour spread to the bone, most commonly via the blood or lymphatic system. Up to 50% of patients who die from cancer are found to have bone metastases.

concepts.title: Metastatic disease – Epidemiology of bone metastases
concepts.content: The incidence of bone metastases is approximately 100 cases per 100,000 person-years, with a peak incidence in individuals aged 70 years and older. The sex ratio is equal (1:1).

concepts.title: Metastatic disease – Classification of bone metastases
concepts.content: Bone metastases are classified as osteoblastic (new bone deposition, e.g., prostate cancer, Hodgkin's lymphoma), osteolytic (bone destruction, e.g., renal cell cancer, melanoma), or mixed (both processes, e.g., breast and GI cancers).

concepts.title: Metastatic disease – Common primary cancers causing bone metastases
concepts.content: The most common primary cancers that metastasise to bone are breast, bronchus (lung), thyroid, prostate, and kidney cancer.

concepts.title: Metastatic disease – Pain characteristics in bone metastases
concepts.content: Pain from bone metastases is characteristically severe, often described as a 'gnawing' pain similar to a toothache, and frequently wakes the patient from sleep. In one study, 91.6% of patients with metastatic bone disease experienced pain.

concepts.title: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy – Clinical features
concepts.content: Symptoms of hypercalcaemia, which can be a feature of bone metastases, include bone pain, muscle weakness, thirst, excessive urination, confusion, and malaise. When hypercalcaemia is found, 80% of patients are found to have metastases.

concepts.title: Pathological fracture – Presentation in bone metastases
concepts.content: Bone metastases can lead to pathological fractures, which are fractures that occur in a bone weakened by disease with little or no preceding trauma. An increase in pain intensity may occur shortly before the fracture.

concepts.title: Metastatic disease – Investigations with bone scintigraphy
concepts.content: Whole-body bone scintigraphy using Technetium-99m is used to visualize areas of increased bone turnover (osteoblastic activity). Asymmetrical or increased uptake can indicate pathological processes like malignancy. Absence of kidney and bladder uptake is a worrying sign suggesting diffuse bone disease.

concepts.title: Metastatic disease – Role of CT and MRI in bone metastases
concepts.content: CT or MRI scans are the preferred imaging modalities for suspected bone metastases when there are features of nerve involvement, such as weakness or paralysis, as they provide better visualization of soft tissues and nerve compression.

concepts.title: Metastatic disease – Blood tests in suspected bone metastases
concepts.content: Blood tests for suspected bone metastases include FBC (may show anaemia), U&Es, LFTs, and CRP. A raised Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) is very likely as it is released during bone breakdown, but an isolated rise is not diagnostic.

concepts.title: Spinal cord compression – Definition
concepts.content: Neoplastic spinal cord compression is an oncological emergency affecting up to 5% of cancer patients. It is most commonly caused by extradural compression from vertebral body metastases, particularly from lung, breast, and prostate cancer.

concepts.title: Spinal cord compression – Epidemiology
concepts.content: The incidence of neoplastic spinal cord compression is approximately 10 cases per 100,000 person-years. The peak incidence occurs between 60-70 years of age, with an equal male-to-female ratio.

concepts.title: Spinal cord compression – Aetiology from metastatic deposits
concepts.content: Metastatic deposits account for up to 90% of masses on spinal imaging in neoplastic cord compression. The most common primary cancers are breast (21%), lung (19%), and prostate (8%).

concepts.title: Spinal cord compression – Aetiology from haematological cancers
concepts.content: Haematological cancers can cause cord compression. Myeloma leads to bone resorption and vertebral collapse. A plasmacytoma (a collection of plasma cells) can also form in vertebrae or soft tissues, causing compression. CNS Lymphoma can also cause cord compression.

concepts.title: Spinal cord compression – Pathophysiology of metastatic spread to spine
concepts.content: Metastases usually spread to the spine via the blood (haematogenous). For prostate and breast cancer, this is often via the paravertebral venous plexus. In contrast, lung cancers typically spread via the arterial system.

concepts.title: Spinal cord compression – Clinical feature of back pain
concepts.content: Back pain is the earliest and most common symptom of neoplastic spinal cord compression. The pain may be worse on lying down and coughing.

concepts.title: Spinal cord compression – Neurological signs by lesion level
concepts.content: In neoplastic spinal cord compression, neurological signs depend on the lesion level. Lesions above L1 typically cause upper motor neuron (UMN) signs in the legs and a sensory level. Lesions below L1 usually cause lower motor neuron (LMN) signs and perianal numbness.

concepts.title: Spinal cord compression – Gold standard investigation
concepts.content: The 2019 NICE guidelines recommend a whole spine MRI within 24 hours of presentation as the gold standard investigation for suspected neoplastic spinal cord compression. MRI has a sensitivity of 44-93% and specificity of 90-98% for this condition.

concepts.title: Spinal cord compression – Initial management with corticosteroids
concepts.content: Patients with suspected neoplastic spinal cord compression should be started on high-dose oral dexamethasone immediately to reduce cord oedema. Blood glucose monitoring is required due to the risk of steroid-induced diabetes.

concepts.title: Spinal cord compression – Definitive treatment options
concepts.content: Definitive treatment for neoplastic cord compression should begin within 24 hours. Options include surgical decompression and stabilisation (for patients with >3 months expected survival) and radiotherapy (sole treatment or post-operative).

concepts.title: Spinal cord compression – Prognosis
concepts.content: Neoplastic spinal cord compression generally indicates advanced disease and has a poor prognosis, with a median life expectancy of 2-3 months post-diagnosis. The neurological outcome is heavily determined by the deficit at presentation; only 7% of patients who are non-ambulatory at diagnosis regain the ability to walk.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Superior Vena Cava Obstruction definition
