concepts.content: Superior vena cava obstruction (SVCO) is an oncological emergency caused by the partial or complete blockage of the superior vena cava, impairing venous return from the upper body. It is most commonly caused by malignancies like bronchogenic carcinoma (lung cancer) and lymphomas.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Aetiology of Superior Vena Cava Obstruction
concepts.content: The majority of SVCO cases are secondary to malignancy. Lung cancer, particularly small cell and non-small cell lung carcinoma, is the most common cause. Other causes include lymphomas, metastatic cancers, thrombosis (e.g., from central lines), and rare causes like mediastinal fibrosis or infections.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Clinical features of Superior Vena Cava Obstruction
concepts.content: The most common symptom of SVCO is dyspnoea, which may be worse when lying down (orthopnoea). Other features include swelling of the face, neck, and arms (with conjunctival and periorbital oedema), headache (often worse in the mornings), and pulseless jugular venous distension.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Compressive symptoms in Superior Vena Cava Obstruction
concepts.content: Direct compression from SVCO can cause specific symptoms depending on the structure affected: tracheal compression can cause stridor, oesophageal compression can cause dysphagia, and recurrent laryngeal nerve compression can lead to hoarseness.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Investigations for Superior Vena Cava Obstruction
concepts.content: The most useful imaging test for SVCO is a CT of the thorax with intravenous contrast. This helps establish the diagnosis, shows the location and severity of the obstruction, and can identify the underlying pathology. It can also be used to guide a biopsy.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Management of Superior Vena Cava Obstruction
concepts.content: Management of SVCO involves relieving symptoms (e.g., head elevation, oxygen) and treating the cause. Endovascular stenting is often used for rapid symptom relief. For malignant causes, treatment depends on the tumour type, with radiotherapy and chemotherapy being common options.

concepts.title: Cancer – Carcinogen associations
concepts.content: Specific carcinogens are linked to particular cancers: Aflatoxin (Aspergillus) to liver cancer; aniline dyes to bladder cancer; asbestos to mesothelioma and bronchial carcinoma; nitrosamines to oesophageal and gastric cancer; and vinyl chloride to hepatic angiosarcoma.

concepts.title: Cervical cancer – Role of Human Papilloma Virus (HPV)
concepts.content: Human papilloma virus (HPV) infection is the most significant risk factor for developing cervical cancer. Subtypes 16, 18, and 33 are particularly carcinogenic, while subtypes 6 and 11 are non-carcinogenic and associated with genital warts.

concepts.title: Cervical cancer – Koilocyte characteristics
concepts.content: Koilocytes are cells that have undergone changes due to HPV infection. Their characteristics include an enlarged nucleus, an irregular nuclear membrane contour, a nucleus that stains darker than normal (hyperchromasia), and a potential perinuclear halo.

concepts.title: Cancer – Management of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting
concepts.content: For patients at low risk of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, metoclopramide may be used first-line. For high-risk patients (e.g., age < 50, anxiety, certain chemo types), 5HT3 receptor antagonists like ondansetron, often combined with dexamethasone, are effective.

concepts.title: Cancer – Cyclophosphamide mechanism and adverse effects
concepts.content: Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent that causes cross-linking in DNA. Its adverse effects include haemorrhagic cystitis (risk reduced by hydration and mesna), myelosuppression, and an increased risk of transitional cell carcinoma.

concepts.title: Cancer – Bleomycin mechanism and adverse effects
concepts.content: Bleomycin is a cytotoxic antibiotic that works by degrading preformed DNA. Its major dose-limiting side effect is lung fibrosis.

concepts.title: Cancer – Anthracyclines (Doxorubicin) mechanism and adverse effects
concepts.content: Anthracyclines, such as doxorubicin, stabilize the DNA-topoisomerase II complex, which inhibits DNA and RNA synthesis. Their main adverse effect is cardiomyopathy.

concepts.title: Cancer – Methotrexate mechanism and adverse effects
concepts.content: Methotrexate is an antimetabolite that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and thymidylate synthesis. Its adverse effects include myelosuppression, mucositis, liver fibrosis, and lung fibrosis.

concepts.title: Cancer – Vinca alkaloids (Vincristine, Vinblastine) mechanism and adverse effects
concepts.content: Vinca alkaloids, such as vincristine and vinblastine, inhibit the formation of microtubules. Vincristine typically causes reversible peripheral neuropathy and paralytic ileus, whereas vinblastine is more associated with myelosuppression.

concepts.title: Cancer – Cisplatin mechanism and adverse effects
concepts.content: Cisplatin is a platinum-based chemotherapy agent that causes cross-linking in DNA. Its primary dose-limiting side effect is nephrotoxicity. Other notable adverse effects include ototoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, and hypomagnesaemia.

concepts.title: Cancer – Li-Fraumeni Syndrome
concepts.content: Li-Fraumeni Syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition resulting from germline mutations in the p53 tumour suppressor gene. It is associated with a high incidence of malignancies, particularly sarcomas and leukaemias.

concepts.title: Breast cancer – BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene mutations
concepts.content: BRCA1 (chromosome 17) and BRCA2 (chromosome 13) are tumour suppressor genes. Mutations are linked to a 60% lifetime risk of breast cancer. They also increase the risk of ovarian cancer (55% with BRCA1, 25% with BRCA2). BRCA2 mutations are also associated with prostate cancer in men.

concepts.title: Colorectal tumours – Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC)
concepts.content: Lynch Syndrome, or Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC), is an autosomal dominant condition that confers a high risk of developing colorectal and endometrial cancer at a young age. Approximately 80% of affected individuals will develop one of these cancers.

concepts.title: Colorectal tumours – Gardner's Syndrome
concepts.content: Gardner's syndrome is an autosomal dominant variant of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) caused by a mutation in the APC gene. It is characterized by multiple colonic polyps and extra-colonic diseases including skull osteomas, thyroid cancer, and epidermoid cysts.

concepts.title: Metastatic disease – Investigations for unknown primary
concepts.content: For metastatic disease of unknown primary, NICE recommends initial investigations for all patients including FBC, U&E, LFTs, calcium, LDH, urinalysis, chest X-ray, and a CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. AFP and hCG should also be checked.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Squamous cell carcinoma features
concepts.content: Squamous cell lung cancer is typically central and is associated with the secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP), leading to hypercalcaemia. It is also strongly associated with finger clubbing and may show cavitating lesions.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Adenocarcinoma features
concepts.content: Adenocarcinoma of the lung is typically located in the periphery of the lungs. It is the most common type of lung cancer found in non-smokers, although the majority of patients who develop it are smokers.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – Large cell carcinoma features
concepts.content: Large cell lung carcinoma is a typically peripheral, anaplastic, and poorly differentiated tumour with a poor prognosis. It may secrete β-hCG.

concepts.title: Cancer – Positron Emission Tomography (PET) principle and use
concepts.content: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a nuclear imaging technique using fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) to create a 3D image of metabolic activity, with glucose uptake as a proxy. It is combined with CT to determine if lesions are metabolically active, primarily for evaluating primary and metastatic disease.

concepts.title: Cancer – Tumour marker associations (Monoclonal antibodies)
concepts.content: Certain monoclonal antibody tumour markers are associated with specific cancers: CA 125 with ovarian cancer, CA 19-9 with pancreatic cancer, and CA 15-3 with breast cancer. It is important to note that tumour markers generally have low specificity.

concepts.title: Cancer – Tumour marker associations (Tumour antigens)
concepts.content: Common tumour antigen markers include: Prostate specific antigen (PSA) for prostatic carcinoma; Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) for hepatocellular carcinoma and teratomas (e.g., testicular cancer); and Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) for colorectal cancer.

concepts.title: Malignant melanoma – S-100 tumour marker
concepts.content: The S-100 protein is a tumour marker associated with melanoma and schwannomas.

concepts.title: Metastatic disease – Causes of raised Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)
concepts.content: In an oncology context, a raised alkaline phosphatase (ALP) can be caused by liver neoplasia (primary or metastatic) or bone metastases. Other causes include cholestasis, Paget's disease, and physiological states like pregnancy or healing fractures.

concepts.title: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy – Management
concepts.content: The initial management of hypercalcaemia is aggressive rehydration with normal saline (e.g., 3-4 litres/day). Following rehydration, intravenous bisphosphonates are used; they take 2-3 days to work, with a maximal effect at 7 days. Calcitonin has a quicker effect.

concepts.title: Lung cancer – SIADH as a paraneoplastic syndrome
concepts.content: The Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH Secretion (SIADH) can be a paraneoplastic syndrome. The most common malignant cause is small cell lung cancer. Other associated cancers include pancreatic and prostate cancer. It leads to a euvolemic hyponatraemia.

concepts.title: Acute glaucoma – Definition
concepts.content: Glaucoma is a group of disorders characterised by optic neuropathy, mostly due to raised intraocular pressure (IOP), though some patients with raised IOP do not have glaucoma and vice versa.

concepts.content: Acute angle-closure glaucoma occurs due to impaired aqueous humour outflow causing raised IOP. Predisposing factors include hypermetropia, pupillary dilatation, and age-related lens growth.

concepts.content: AACG presents with severe ocular or headache pain, decreased visual acuity, hard red eye, haloes around lights, semi-dilated non-reactive pupil, corneal oedema causing hazy cornea, and systemic symptoms like nausea and vomiting.

concepts.title: Macular degeneration – Definition
concepts.content: Age-related macular degeneration (ARMD) is the most common cause of blindness in the UK, characterised by degeneration of the central retina (macula), usually bilateral, with retinal photoreceptor loss and drusen formation.

concepts.title: Macular degeneration – Epidemiology
concepts.content: ARMD is more common with advancing age, especially over 75 years, and is more prevalent in females. It is the leading cause of blindness in the UK.

concepts.title: Macular degeneration – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Advancing age is the greatest risk factor for ARMD, with a threefold increase over age 75. Smoking doubles risk, family history quadruples risk, and cardiovascular risk factors like hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and diabetes also increase risk.

concepts.title: Macular degeneration – Classification
concepts.content: ARMD is classified into dry (atrophic, 90%) with drusen deposits and wet (exudative, 10%) with choroidal neovascularisation causing fluid leakage and rapid vision loss. Early ARMD shows drusen and RPE changes; late ARMD involves neovascularisation.

concepts.title: Macular degeneration – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients present with subacute visual loss, worse centrally, affecting near vision, with gradual loss in dry ARMD and subacute in wet ARMD. Symptoms include difficulty reading, dark adaptation problems, photopsia, glare, and possible Charles-Bonnet visual hallucinations.

concepts.content: Amsler grid testing shows line distortion. Fundoscopy reveals drusen as yellow pigment deposits in the macula, which may coalesce into scars. Wet ARMD shows red patches from intra- or sub-retinal fluid leakage or haemorrhage.

concepts.content: Slit-lamp microscopy with colour fundus photography is first-line to identify pigmentary, exudative, or haemorrhagic retinal changes. Fluorescein angiography and indocyanine green angiography assess neovascular ARMD. Optical coherence tomography visualises retinal structure in 3D.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Definition
concepts.content: Allergic conjunctivitis is an inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by an allergic reaction, often occurring alone or in association with hay fever.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Allergic conjunctivitis may be seasonal, triggered by pollen, or perennial, caused by allergens such as dust mites or washing powder; it is often associated with a history of atopy.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Allergic conjunctivitis typically presents with bilateral conjunctival erythema and swelling (chemosis), prominent itching, and possible eyelid swelling.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Management
concepts.content: Management of allergic conjunctivitis includes topical antihistamines and topical mast-cell stabilisers such as sodium cromoglicate and nedocromil to reduce allergic inflammation.

concepts.title: Uveitis – Definition
concepts.content: Anterior uveitis, also known as iritis, is inflammation of the anterior uvea, specifically the iris and ciliary body.

concepts.title: Uveitis – Clinical features: Onset and pain
concepts.content: Anterior uveitis typically presents with acute onset ocular discomfort and pain, which may worsen with eye movement or use.

concepts.title: Uveitis – Clinical features: Pupil changes
concepts.content: The pupil in anterior uveitis may be small and irregular due to sphincter muscle contraction.

concepts.title: Uveitis – Clinical features: Photophobia
concepts.content: Photophobia is often intense in anterior uveitis, causing discomfort in bright light.

concepts.title: Uveitis – Clinical features: Vision changes
concepts.content: Blurred vision occurs in anterior uveitis; visual acuity is initially normal but may become impaired as inflammation progresses.

concepts.title: Uveitis – Clinical features: Red eye and lacrimation
concepts.content: Anterior uveitis presents with a red eye and lacrimation, often accompanied by a ciliary flush, a ring of redness spreading outwards from the cornea.

concepts.title: Uveitis – Clinical features: Hypopyon
concepts.content: Hypopyon, the presence of pus and inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber, may be seen in anterior uveitis and can produce a visible fluid level.

concepts.title: Uveitis – Aetiology/Risk factors: HLA-B27 association
concepts.content: Anterior uveitis is associated with the HLA-B27 antigen and may occur in conjunction with other HLA-B27 linked conditions.

concepts.title: Uveitis – Associated conditions
concepts.content: Anterior uveitis may be associated with ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, Behcet's disease, and sarcoidosis (which may cause bilateral disease).

concepts.title: Uveitis – Management: Urgent ophthalmology review
concepts.content: Anterior uveitis requires urgent review by an ophthalmologist to prevent complications and initiate appropriate treatment.

concepts.title: Uveitis – Management: Cycloplegics
concepts.content: Cycloplegic agents such as atropine or cyclopentolate are used in anterior uveitis to dilate the pupil, relieving pain and photophobia.

concepts.title: Uveitis – Management: Steroid eye drops
concepts.content: Topical steroid eye drops are used to reduce inflammation in anterior uveitis.

concepts.title: Blepharitis – Definition
concepts.content: Blepharitis is inflammation of the eyelid margins, caused by meibomian gland dysfunction (posterior blepharitis) or seborrhoeic dermatitis/staphylococcal infection (anterior blepharitis).

concepts.title: Blepharitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Blepharitis is more common in patients with rosacea and may be caused by meibomian gland dysfunction or seborrhoeic dermatitis and staphylococcal infection.

concepts.title: Blepharitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Meibomian glands secrete oil to prevent tear film evaporation; dysfunction leads to dry eyes causing irritation and inflammation of eyelid margins in blepharitis.

concepts.title: Blepharitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Symptoms are usually bilateral with eyelid margin grittiness, discomfort, redness, sticky eyes in the morning; swollen eyelids in staphylococcal blepharitis; styes, chalazions, and secondary conjunctivitis may occur.

concepts.title: Blepharitis – Management
concepts.content: Management includes hot compresses twice daily to soften lid margins, mechanical lid hygiene using cotton wool buds with cooled boiled water and baby shampoo or sodium bicarbonate solution, and artificial tears for dry eyes.

concepts.title: Cataracts – Definition
concepts.content: A cataract is a common eye condition characterised by gradual opacification (cloudiness) of the lens, reducing light reaching the retina and causing blurred vision.

concepts.title: Cataracts – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Cataracts are more common in women than men and incidence increases with age; about 30% of people aged 65+ have visually-impairing cataracts in one or both eyes.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Definition
concepts.content: Corneal abrasions are defects of the corneal epithelium, commonly caused by recent local trauma such as fingernails or branches.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Corneal abrasion presents with eye pain, lacrimation, photophobia, foreign body sensation, conjunctival injection, and decreased visual acuity in the affected eye.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Investigations
concepts.content: Fluorescein staining highlights corneal abrasions as yellow-stained areas visible to the naked eye, with enhanced visualization using a cobalt blue filter or Wood's lamp.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Management
concepts.content: Topical antibiotics are recommended for corneal abrasions to prevent secondary bacterial infection.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Corneal foreign body typically presents with eye pain, foreign body sensation, photophobia, watering eye, and red eye.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Indications for referral to ophthalmology
concepts.content: Referral is indicated for suspected penetrating eye injury from high-velocity or sharp objects, significant orbital or peri-ocular trauma, chemical injury after irrigation, organic material foreign bodies, central corneal foreign bodies, or any red flags such as severe pain, abnormal pupils, or reduced visual acuity.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Risk factors for complications
concepts.content: Foreign bodies composed of organic material such as seeds or soil carry a higher risk of infection and complications, necessitating referral to ophthalmology.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Definition
concepts.content: A corneal ulcer is a defect in the cornea, usually caused by an infection. Corneal abrasion refers to corneal defects caused by physical trauma, distinguishing it from infective causes.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Risk factors
concepts.content: Contact lens use is a significant risk factor for infective keratitis. Vitamin A deficiency, especially prevalent in developing countries, also increases susceptibility to corneal ulcers.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Infective keratitis can be caused by bacteria, fungi, viruses (herpes simplex and herpes zoster causing dendritic ulcers), and Acanthamoeba, which is linked to contact lens use.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients with infective keratitis typically present with eye pain, photophobia, watering of the eye, and focal fluorescein staining of the cornea on examination.

concepts.title: Blepharitis – Clinical features of dry eye syndrome
concepts.content: Dry eye syndrome presents with dryness, grittiness, or soreness in both eyes, worsening through the day, and watering, especially when exposed to wind.

concepts.title: Blepharitis – Clinical features of Meibomian gland dysfunction
concepts.content: Symptoms worse on waking, eyelids sticking together on waking, and redness of eyelids suggest dry eye syndrome caused by Meibomian gland dysfunction.

concepts.title: Blepharitis – Complications of dry eye syndrome
concepts.content: Complications of dry eye syndrome include conjunctivitis or corneal ulceration, indicated by severe pain, photophobia, marked redness, and loss of visual acuity.

concepts.title: Blepharitis – Management of dry eye syndrome
concepts.content: Eyelid hygiene is the most appropriate management step for dry eye syndrome and helps control blepharitis.

concepts.title: Blepharitis – Association with dry eye syndrome
concepts.content: Most people with dry eye syndrome have blepharitis, indicating a strong association between the two conditions.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Definition
concepts.content: Episcleritis is the acute onset of inflammation in the episclera of one or both eyes, often presenting with redness and mild symptoms.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Most episcleritis cases are idiopathic; associated systemic conditions include inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Episcleritis presents with red eye, typically mild pain or irritation (less than scleritis), watering, and mild photophobia; about 50% of cases are bilateral.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Clinical features
concepts.content: In episcleritis, injected vessels are mobile with gentle pressure on the sclera, unlike scleritis where vessels are deeper and immobile.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Investigations
concepts.content: Phenylephrine eye drops can differentiate episcleritis from scleritis by blanching conjunctival and episcleral vessels but not scleral vessels; improvement in redness supports episcleritis diagnosis.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Management
concepts.content: Episcleritis is managed conservatively, often requiring no treatment; artificial tears may be used to relieve symptoms.

concepts.title: Benign eyelid disorders – Common types
concepts.content: Common benign eyelid disorders include blepharitis (inflammation of eyelid margins causing red eye), stye (infection of eyelid glands), chalazion (Meibomian cyst), entropion (in-turning of eyelids), and ectropion (out-turning of eyelids).

concepts.title: Benign eyelid disorders – Blepharitis
concepts.content: Blepharitis is inflammation of the eyelid margins that typically leads to a red eye due to irritation and inflammation around the eyelid edges.

concepts.title: Benign eyelid disorders – Stye definition
concepts.content: A stye is an infection of the glands of the eyelids, commonly caused by staphylococcal bacteria, affecting either the glands of Zeis or Moll externally or the Meibomian glands internally.

concepts.title: Benign eyelid disorders – External stye (hordeolum externum)
concepts.content: External stye is an infection, usually staphylococcal, of the glands of Zeis (sebum producing) or glands of Moll (sweat glands) located at the eyelid margin.

concepts.title: Benign eyelid disorders – Internal stye (hordeolum internum)
concepts.content: Internal stye is an infection of the Meibomian glands within the eyelid and may leave a residual chalazion (Meibomian cyst) after resolution.

concepts.title: Benign eyelid disorders – Stye management
concepts.content: Management of stye includes hot compresses and analgesia; topical antibiotics are recommended only if there is associated conjunctivitis.

concepts.title: Benign eyelid disorders – Chalazion definition
concepts.content: A chalazion (Meibomian cyst) is a retention cyst of the Meibomian gland presenting as a firm, painless lump in the eyelid.

concepts.title: Benign eyelid disorders – Chalazion clinical course
concepts.content: Most chalazions resolve spontaneously without treatment, but some cases require surgical drainage if persistent or symptomatic.

concepts.title: Benign eyelid disorders – Entropion
concepts.content: Entropion is the inward turning of the eyelids, which can cause irritation and damage to the ocular surface.

concepts.title: Benign eyelid disorders – Ectropion
concepts.content: Ectropion is the outward turning of the eyelids, which can lead to exposure and dryness of the ocular surface.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Herpes simplex keratitis typically presents with a red, painful eye accompanied by photophobia and epiphora. Visual acuity may be decreased due to corneal involvement.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Definition
concepts.content: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) is the reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, causing shingles in the eye area and accounting for about 10% of shingles cases.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: HZO presents with a vesicular rash around the eye which may or may not involve the eye itself, and Hutchinson's sign, a rash on the tip or side of the nose indicating nasociliary nerve involvement and increased risk of ocular complications.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Management
concepts.content: Treatment of HZO involves oral antivirals for 7-10 days, ideally started within 72 hours of rash onset; intravenous antivirals may be used in severe or immunocompromised cases; topical antivirals are not used; topical corticosteroids may treat secondary ocular inflammation.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Complications
concepts.content: Ocular complications of HZO include conjunctivitis, keratitis, episcleritis, and anterior uveitis; other complications include ptosis and post-herpetic neuralgia.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Urgent referral
concepts.content: Ocular involvement in herpes zoster ophthalmicus requires urgent ophthalmology review to prevent vision-threatening complications.

concepts.title: Diabetic eye disease – Hypertensive retinopathy stage I
concepts.content: Stage I hypertensive retinopathy is characterised by arteriolar narrowing and tortuosity, with increased light reflex known as silver wiring.

concepts.title: Diabetic eye disease – Hypertensive retinopathy stage II
concepts.content: Stage II hypertensive retinopathy is characterised by arteriovenous nipping, where arterioles compress venules at crossing points.

concepts.title: Diabetic eye disease – Hypertensive retinopathy stage III
concepts.content: Stage III hypertensive retinopathy features cotton-wool spots, flame-shaped and blot haemorrhages, which may collect around the fovea forming a macular star.

concepts.title: Diabetic eye disease – Hypertensive retinopathy stage IV
concepts.content: Stage IV hypertensive retinopathy is characterised by papilloedema, indicating severe retinal and optic nerve head swelling.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Definition
concepts.content: Conjunctivitis is the most common eye problem in primary care, characterised by sore, red eyes with a sticky discharge.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Bacterial conjunctivitis features
concepts.content: Bacterial conjunctivitis presents with purulent discharge and eyes may be stuck together in the morning.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Viral conjunctivitis features
concepts.content: Viral conjunctivitis presents with serous discharge, recent upper respiratory tract infection, and preauricular lymphadenopathy.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Natural history
concepts.content: Infective conjunctivitis is normally self-limiting and usually resolves without treatment within 1-2 weeks.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Topical antibiotic treatment
concepts.content: Topical antibiotics such as chloramphenicol drops (2-3 hourly) or ointment (four times daily) are commonly used to treat bacterial conjunctivitis.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Alternative antibiotic for pregnancy
concepts.content: Topical fusidic acid is an alternative antibiotic for infective conjunctivitis and should be used twice daily in pregnant women.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Contact lens users management
concepts.content: Contact lens users with conjunctivitis should have topical fluorescein staining to check for corneal involvement and should not wear lenses during infection.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Infection control advice
concepts.content: Patients with infective conjunctivitis should be advised not to share towels to prevent spread of infection.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – School exclusion policy
concepts.content: School exclusion is not necessary for children with infective conjunctivitis.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Definition
concepts.content: Keratitis is inflammation of the cornea. Microbial keratitis is a sight-threatening condition that requires urgent evaluation and treatment, unlike conjunctivitis.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Aetiology Bacterial causes
concepts.content: Bacterial keratitis is commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus; Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a frequent cause in contact lens wearers.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Aetiology Fungal causes
concepts.content: Fungal keratitis is a cause of microbial keratitis, often associated with eye exposure to soil or contaminated water.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Aetiology Amoebic causes
concepts.content: Acanthamoebic keratitis accounts for around 5% of cases and is more common with eye exposure to soil or contaminated water; pain is often out of proportion to clinical findings.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Aetiology Parasitic causes
concepts.content: Onchocercal keratitis, also known as 'river blindness', is a parasitic cause of keratitis.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Aetiology Viral and environmental causes
concepts.content: Other causes of keratitis include viral infections such as herpes simplex keratitis and environmental causes like photokeratitis (e.g., welder's arc eye) and exposure keratitis.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Clinical features of infective keratitis include red eye with pain and erythema, photophobia, foreign body or gritty sensation, and sometimes hypopyon.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Referral criteria
concepts.content: Contact lens wearers presenting with a painful red eye require same-day referral to an eye specialist for slit-lamp examination to exclude microbial keratitis.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Management general
concepts.content: Management includes stopping contact lens use until symptoms resolve, topical antibiotics (usually quinolones first-line), and cycloplegics such as cyclopentolate for pain relief.

concepts.title: Infective keratitis – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of infective keratitis include corneal scarring, corneal perforation, endophthalmitis, and visual loss.

concepts.title: Optic neuritis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Multiple sclerosis is the most common disease associated with optic neuritis, with other causes including diabetes and syphilis.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Definition
concepts.content: Orbital cellulitis is an infection of fat and muscles posterior to the orbital septum within the orbit, sparing the globe. Periorbital cellulitis is a superficial infection anterior to the septum.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Orbital cellulitis usually results from spreading upper respiratory tract infection from the sinuses. Risk factors include childhood (mean age 7-12), previous sinus infection, lack of Hib vaccination, recent eyelid infection or insect bite, and ear or facial infection.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Orbital cellulitis presents with redness and swelling around the eye, severe ocular pain, visual disturbance, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia or pain with eye movements, eyelid oedema and ptosis, and sometimes drowsiness or nausea if meningeal involvement occurs.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Differentiation from preseptal cellulitis
concepts.content: Reduced visual acuity, proptosis, and ophthalmoplegia or pain with eye movements are features of orbital cellulitis and are not consistent with preseptal cellulitis.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations include full blood count showing elevated WBC and inflammatory markers, clinical ophthalmological assessment for vision, pupillary defects, proptosis, dysmotility, oedema, erythema, CT with contrast showing orbital inflammation and sinusitis, and blood cultures to identify causative organisms.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Common causative organisms
concepts.content: The most common bacterial causes of orbital cellulitis are Streptococcus species, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae type B.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Management
concepts.content: Orbital cellulitis is a medical emergency requiring hospital admission and urgent senior review, with treatment consisting of intravenous antibiotics.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Definition
concepts.content: Preseptal cellulitis, also called periorbital cellulitis, is an infection of soft tissues anterior to the orbital septum, including eyelids, skin, and subcutaneous facial tissue, excluding orbital contents.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Definition
concepts.content: Orbital cellulitis is an infection of soft tissues behind the orbital septum and is more serious than preseptal cellulitis.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Infection usually spreads from nearby sites such as breaks in skin, sinusitis, or respiratory tract infections to the tissues surrounding the orbit.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causative organisms include Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, streptococci, and anaerobic bacteria.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Preseptal cellulitis most commonly affects children; 80% are under 10 years old with a median age of 21 months, and incidence is higher in winter due to respiratory infections.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients present with acute onset of red, swollen, painful eye often accompanied by fever.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Signs include erythema and oedema of eyelids spreading to surrounding skin and partial or complete ptosis due to swelling.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Absence of orbital signs such as pain on eye movement, restricted eye movements, proptosis, visual disturbance, chemosis, or relative afferent pupillary defect distinguishes preseptal cellulitis from orbital cellulitis.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Important differentials include orbital cellulitis and allergic reactions.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Investigations
concepts.content: Blood tests show raised inflammatory markers; swabs of any discharge should be taken; contrast CT orbit helps differentiate preseptal from orbital cellulitis and is indicated if orbital cellulitis is suspected.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Management
concepts.content: All cases require referral to secondary care; oral antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav are usually sufficient; children may need admission for observation.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Complications
concepts.content: Bacterial infection can spread posteriorly into the orbit, causing orbital cellulitis, a more serious condition.

concepts.title: Chronic glaucoma – Definition
concepts.content: Chronic glaucoma is an optic neuropathy associated with raised intraocular pressure (IOP) due to increased resistance to aqueous humour outflow through the trabecular meshwork, despite the peripheral iris being clear of the meshwork.

concepts.title: Chronic glaucoma – Definition
concepts.content: Glaucomas are optic neuropathies associated with raised intraocular pressure (IOP), leading to progressive optic nerve damage and visual field loss.

concepts.title: Chronic glaucoma – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: In primary open-angle glaucoma, the peripheral iris does not cover the trabecular meshwork, but increased resistance in the trabecular network reduces aqueous humour outflow, causing raised intraocular pressure.

concepts.title: Chronic glaucoma – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Primary open-angle glaucoma affects less than 1.5% of individuals under 55 years but up to 10% of those over 80 years of age.

concepts.title: Chronic glaucoma – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for primary open-angle glaucoma include increasing age, Afro-Caribbean ethnicity, family history, myopia, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and corticosteroid use.

concepts.title: Chronic glaucoma – Clinical features
concepts.content: Primary open-angle glaucoma often presents insidiously with peripheral visual field loss (nasal scotomas progressing to tunnel vision), decreased visual acuity, and optic disc cupping.

concepts.title: Visual field defects – Associated diseases

concepts.title: Scleritis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Ocular manifestations occur in 25% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis, indicating a significant prevalence of eye problems in this population.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Scleritis in rheumatoid arthritis presents with erythema and pain, distinguishing it from episcleritis which presents with erythema but no pain.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca is the most common ocular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis, causing dry eyes due to decreased tear production.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Corneal ulceration and keratitis are additional ocular complications of rheumatoid arthritis, potentially leading to corneal damage and vision impairment.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Complications
concepts.content: Steroid treatment for rheumatoid arthritis can cause iatrogenic cataracts, contributing to lens opacity and visual impairment.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Definition
concepts.content: Scleritis is a full-thickness inflammation of the sclera, usually caused by non-infective processes, leading to a red, painful eye.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Scleritis is commonly associated with autoimmune diseases including rheumatoid arthritis (most common), systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, and granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Scleritis presents with a red eye that may have a violet-bluish hue due to scleral oedema and vessel dilatation; it is classically painful but can sometimes cause only mild discomfort.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients with scleritis commonly experience watering and photophobia, along with a gradual decrease in vision.

concepts.title: Scleritis – Management
concepts.content: Scleritis requires same-day ophthalmology assessment; first-line treatment is oral NSAIDs, with oral glucocorticoids for severe cases and immunosuppressants for resistant disease or underlying systemic conditions.

concepts.title: Retinal detachment – Definition
concepts.content: Vitreous haemorrhage is bleeding into the vitreous humour, causing sudden painless loss of vision ranging from floaters to complete visual loss.

concepts.title: Retinal detachment – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Spontaneous vitreous haemorrhage incidence is around 7 cases per 100,000 patient-years, varying by age and sex according to underlying causes.

concepts.title: Retinal detachment – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of vitreous haemorrhage include proliferative diabetic retinopathy (>50%), posterior vitreous detachment, and ocular trauma, especially in children and young adults.

concepts.title: Retinal detachment – Clinical features
concepts.content: Patients present with acute or subacute painless visual loss or haze, red hue in vision, and floaters or shadows/dark spots; visual acuity and field defects vary with haemorrhage severity.

concepts.title: Retinal detachment – Investigations
concepts.content: Dilated fundoscopy may reveal vitreous cavity haemorrhage; slit-lamp exam shows red blood cells in anterior vitreous; ultrasound rules out retinal tear/detachment if view obscured; fluorescein angiography identifies neovascularisation.

concepts.title: Retinal detachment – Investigations
concepts.content: Orbital CT is used if open globe injury is suspected in vitreous haemorrhage cases.

concepts.title: Retinal detachment – Management
concepts.content: Urgent ophthalmology referral is required; manage underlying causes such as optimising diabetes control and laser therapy; consider pars plana vitrectomy if haemorrhage does not clear spontaneously.

concepts.title: Retinal detachment – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Bleeding into the vitreous humour arises from disruption of retinal vessels or extension through the retina from other areas, with blood clearing at approximately 1% per day after bleeding stops.

concepts.title: Asthma – Severe Attack Criteria in Children
concepts.content: A severe asthma attack in children is indicated by SpO2 < 92%, PEF 33-50% of best or predicted, being too breathless to talk or feed, heart rate >125 bpm (>5 years) or >140 bpm (1-5 years), respiratory rate >30 breaths/min (>5 years) or >40 breaths/min (1-5 years), and use of accessory neck muscles.

concepts.title: Asthma – Life-Threatening Attack Criteria in Children
concepts.content: A life-threatening asthma attack in children is indicated by SpO2 < 92%, PEF < 33% of best or predicted, silent chest, poor respiratory effort, agitation, altered consciousness, or cyanosis.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management of Moderate Attack in Children (2-5 years)
concepts.content: In children aged 2-5 years with a moderate asthma attack (SpO2 > 92% and no clinical features of severe asthma), management involves bronchodilator therapy with a beta-2 agonist via a spacer (1 puff every 30-60 seconds up to 10 puffs) and steroid therapy (prednisolone for 3-5 days).

concepts.title: Asthma – Management of Severe Attack in Children (2-5 years)
concepts.content: Children aged 2-5 years with a severe asthma attack (SpO2 < 92%, too breathless to talk or feed, heart rate > 140/min, respiratory rate > 40/min, use of accessory neck muscles) should be transferred immediately to hospital.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management of Life-Threatening Attack in Children (2-5 years)
concepts.content: Children aged 2-5 years with a life-threatening asthma attack (SpO2 < 92%, silent chest, poor respiratory effort, agitation, altered consciousness, cyanosis) require immediate hospital transfer.

concepts.title: Asthma – Management of Moderate Attack in Children (>5 years)
concepts.content: In children over 5 years with a moderate asthma attack (SpO2 > 92%, PEF > 50% best or predicted, no clinical features of severe asthma), management involves bronchodilator therapy and steroid therapy.

concepts.title: Asthma – 2024 NICE/BTS/SIGN Guideline Changes
concepts.content: In 2024, joint guidelines from NICE, the British Thoracic Society, and SIGN advocated for using combined inhalers (ICS + long-acting beta-2 agonist) as either reliever therapy or for regular use, a change from the previous standard of starting with a short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) inhaler.

concepts.title: Asthma – Maintenance and Reliever Therapy (MART)
concepts.content: Maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) involves using a single inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)/formoterol combination inhaler for both daily maintenance therapy and for the relief of symptoms as needed.

concepts.title: Asthma – Initial Management in Children (5-11 years)
concepts.content: The first step in managing asthma in children aged 5 to 11 is a twice-daily paediatric low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) plus a short-acting beta2 agonist (SABA) as needed.

concepts.title: Biliary atresia – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Biliary atresia is a condition in children involving the obliteration or discontinuity of the extrahepatic biliary system, leading to an obstruction in bile flow and resulting in neonatal cholestasis.

concepts.title: Biliary atresia – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Biliary atresia is more common in females and occurs in 1 in every 10,000-15,000 live births. The perinatal form presents in the first two weeks of life, and the postnatal form presents within the first 2-8 weeks.

concepts.title: Biliary atresia – Classification
concepts.content: Biliary atresia is classified into three types. Type 1: common duct is obliterated. Type 2: atresia of the cystic duct. Type 3: atresia of the left and right ducts to the level of the porta hepatis, accounting for over 90% of cases.

concepts.title: Biliary atresia – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Patients with biliary atresia typically present in the first few weeks of life with jaundice extending beyond two weeks, dark urine, pale stools, and potentially appetite and growth disturbance.

concepts.title: Biliary atresia – Signs
concepts.content: Signs of biliary atresia include jaundice, hepatomegaly with splenomegaly, abnormal growth, and cardiac murmurs if associated cardiac abnormalities are present.

concepts.title: Biliary atresia – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations for biliary atresia include serum bilirubin (conjugated will be high), LFTs, serum alpha 1-antitrypsin, sweat chloride test, ultrasound of the biliary tree, and a percutaneous liver biopsy with intraoperative cholangioscopy.

concepts.title: Biliary atresia – Management
concepts.content: The only definitive treatment for biliary atresia is surgical intervention, such as a Kasai procedure. Medical management includes post-operative antibiotics and bile acid enhancers.

concepts.title: Biliary atresia – Complications and Prognosis
concepts.content: Complications of biliary atresia include unsuccessful anastomosis, progressive liver disease, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. The prognosis is good if surgery is successful; otherwise, a liver transplant may be required within the first two years of life.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Bronchiolitis is an acute inflammation of the bronchioles, most commonly caused by Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in 75-80% of cases.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Bronchiolitis is the most common cause of serious lower respiratory tract infection in children under 1 year old, with a peak incidence between 3-6 months. It is more common in winter.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Aetiology and Risk Factors
concepts.content: The most common cause of bronchiolitis is Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV). Other causes include mycoplasma and adenoviruses. The condition is more serious in children with bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease, or cystic fibrosis.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Bronchiolitis typically presents with coryzal symptoms followed by a dry cough, increasing breathlessness, wheezing, and fine inspiratory crackles. Feeding difficulties due to dyspnoea are a common reason for hospital admission.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Indications for Immediate Hospital Referral
concepts.content: Immediate hospital referral for a child with bronchiolitis is recommended for apnoea, appearing seriously unwell, severe respiratory distress (grunting, marked chest recession, RR > 70), central cyanosis, or persistent oxygen saturation < 92%.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Indications for Considering Hospital Referral
concepts.content: Consider hospital referral for a child with bronchiolitis if they have a respiratory rate over 60 breaths/minute, difficulty with breastfeeding or inadequate oral fluid intake (50-75% of usual volume), or clinical dehydration.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis of bronchiolitis is primarily clinical. Immunofluorescence of nasopharyngeal secretions may be used to detect RSV.

concepts.title: Bronchiolitis – Management
concepts.content: Management of bronchiolitis is largely supportive, including humidified oxygen via a head box if saturations are persistently < 92%, nasogastric feeding if oral intake is inadequate, and suction for excessive upper airway secretions.

concepts.title: Croup – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Croup is an upper respiratory tract infection in infants and toddlers, characterized by stridor from laryngeal oedema and secretions. Parainfluenza viruses are the most common cause.

concepts.title: Croup – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Croup has a peak incidence between 6 months and 3 years of age and is more common in the autumn.

concepts.title: Croup – Clinical Features
concepts.content: The clinical features of croup include stridor, a barking cough that is worse at night, fever, and coryzal symptoms.

concepts.title: Croup – Admission Criteria
concepts.content: Admission for a child with croup should be considered if they are under 6 months of age, have known upper airway abnormalities (e.g., Laryngomalacia, Down's syndrome), or if there is uncertainty about the diagnosis.

concepts.title: Croup – Management
concepts.content: All children with croup, regardless of severity, should receive a single dose of oral dexamethasone (0.15mg/kg). Prednisolone is an alternative if dexamethasone is unavailable.

concepts.title: Croup – Emergency Management
concepts.content: Emergency treatment for severe croup includes high-flow oxygen and nebulised adrenaline.

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene, leading to increased viscosity of secretions.

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Genetics and Epidemiology
concepts.content: In the UK, 80% of cystic fibrosis cases are due to the delta F508 mutation on chromosome 7. The condition affects 1 in 2,500 births, with a carrier rate of approximately 1 in 25.

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Common Colonising Organisms
concepts.content: Organisms that commonly colonise the respiratory tract of patients with cystic fibrosis include Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Burkholderia cepacia, and Aspergillus.

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Diagnosis (Sweat Test)
concepts.content: The sweat test is used to diagnose cystic fibrosis. A sweat chloride level greater than 60 mEq/l is indicative of the condition. False positives can occur due to malnutrition, adrenal insufficiency, and other conditions.

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Presenting Features
concepts.content: Cystic fibrosis can present in the neonatal period with meconium ileus or prolonged jaundice (20%), with recurrent chest infections (40%), or with malabsorption and failure to thrive (30%).

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Other Clinical Features
concepts.content: Other features of cystic fibrosis include short stature, diabetes mellitus, delayed puberty, rectal prolapse, nasal polyps, male infertility, and female subfertility.

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Management
concepts.content: Management of cystic fibrosis involves regular chest physiotherapy, a high-calorie diet, vitamin supplementation, and pancreatic enzyme supplements. Lung transplantation may be considered in severe cases.

concepts.title: Cystic fibrosis – Lumacaftor/Ivacaftor (Orkambi)
concepts.content: Lumacaftor/ivacaftor (Orkambi) is a combination therapy used to treat cystic fibrosis patients who are homozygous for the delta F508 mutation. Lumacaftor increases the number of CFTR proteins transported to the cell surface, while ivacaftor potentiates the function of the defective channel.

concepts.title: Epiglottitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Acute epiglottitis is a serious infection caused by Haemophilus influenzae type B, which can lead to life-threatening airway obstruction. Its incidence has decreased due to the Hib immunisation programme.

concepts.title: Epiglottitis – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Clinical features of acute epiglottitis include a rapid onset, high temperature, stridor, drooling of saliva, and the patient adopting a 'tripod' position (leaning forward, neck extended).

concepts.title: Epiglottitis – Diagnosis
concepts.content: Diagnosis of acute epiglottitis is made by direct visualisation of a swollen epiglottis, which should only be performed by senior staff able to intubate. A lateral neck X-ray may show the 'thumb sign'.

concepts.title: Epiglottitis – Management
concepts.content: Management of acute epiglottitis requires immediate senior involvement (anaesthetics, ENT). Endotracheal intubation may be necessary to protect the airway. Intravenous antibiotics and oxygen should be administered.

concepts.title: Epiglottitis – Contraindicated Action
concepts.content: If acute epiglottitis is suspected, the throat must NOT be examined due to the high risk of precipitating acute airway obstruction.

concepts.title: Febrile convulsion – Definition
concepts.content: Febrile convulsions are seizures provoked by fever in otherwise normal children, typically occurring between the ages of 6 months and 5 years. They are seen in approximately 3% of children.

concepts.title: Febrile convulsion – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Febrile convulsions usually occur early in a viral infection as the temperature rises rapidly. The seizures are typically brief, lasting less than 5 minutes, and are most commonly tonic-clonic.

concepts.title: Febrile convulsion – Simple vs. Complex
concepts.content: A simple febrile convulsion lasts less than 15 minutes, is generalized, and does not recur within 24 hours. A complex febrile convulsion lasts 15-30 minutes, is focal, and may have repeat seizures within 24 hours.

concepts.title: Febrile convulsion – Febrile Status Epilepticus
concepts.content: Febrile status epilepticus is defined as a febrile convulsion lasting longer than 30 minutes.

concepts.title: Febrile convulsion – Management
concepts.content: Children who have had a first febrile seizure or any features of a complex seizure should be admitted to a paediatrics ward for further assessment.

concepts.title: Kawasaki disease – Definition
concepts.content: Kawasaki disease is a vasculitis that predominantly affects children and can lead to serious complications, including coronary artery aneurysms.

concepts.title: Kawasaki disease – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Kawasaki disease is characterized by a high-grade fever lasting more than 5 days, conjunctival injection, bright red cracked lips, a 'strawberry' tongue, cervical lymphadenopathy, and red palms and soles that later peel.

concepts.title: Kawasaki disease – Diagnosis
concepts.content: The diagnosis of Kawasaki disease is clinical, as there is no specific diagnostic test.

concepts.title: Kawasaki disease – Management
concepts.content: Management of Kawasaki disease includes high-dose aspirin and intravenous immunoglobulin. An echocardiogram is used as the initial screening test for coronary artery aneurysms.

concepts.title: Kawasaki disease – Complications
concepts.content: The main complication of Kawasaki disease is the development of coronary artery aneurysms.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Causative Organisms (Neonatal to 3 months)
concepts.content: In neonates up to 3 months old, the common causative organisms for meningitis are Group B Streptococcus (usually acquired from the mother), E. coli and other Gram-negative organisms, and Listeria monocytogenes.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Causative Organisms (1 month to 6 years)
concepts.content: In children aged 1 month to 6 years, the common causative organisms for meningitis are Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus), Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus), and Haemophilus influenzae.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Causative Organisms (>6 years)
concepts.content: In children older than 6 years, the common causative organisms for meningitis are Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus) and Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus).

concepts.title: Meningitis – Contraindications to Lumbar Puncture
concepts.content: Contraindications to performing a lumbar puncture in a child with suspected meningitis include signs of raised intracranial pressure such as focal neurological signs, papilloedema, significant bulging of the fontanelle, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and signs of cerebral herniation.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Management (<3 months)
concepts.content: The antibiotic management for meningitis in children under 3 months of age is intravenous amoxicillin plus intravenous cefotaxime.

concepts.title: Meningitis – Management (>3 months)
concepts.content: The antibiotic management for meningitis in children over 3 months of age is intravenous cefotaxime.

concepts.title: Acute kidney injury – Definition
concepts.content: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is characterized by a reversible increase in the blood concentration of creatinine and nitrogenous waste products and by the inability of the kidney to regulate fluid and electrolyte homeostasis appropriately.

concepts.title: Acute kidney injury – Aetiology
concepts.content: The etiology of AKI in children has shifted from primary renal disease to multifactorial causes, including pre-renal injury (decreased intravascular volume), intrinsic renal disease (e.g., acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, vascular lesions), and obstructive uropathy.

concepts.title: Acute kidney injury – Pathophysiology of Hypoxic/Ischemic Injury
concepts.content: The pathophysiology of hypoxia/ischemia-induced AKI is complex and involves cellular, biochemical, and molecular events that are not yet fully understood.

concepts.title: Acute kidney injury – Diagnosis
concepts.content: The diagnosis of AKI is established through history, physical examination, and laboratory studies, including urinalysis and radiographic studies. The serum creatinine level is an insensitive and delayed measure of decreased kidney function.

concepts.title: Acute kidney injury – Management
concepts.content: Many interventions, such as ‘renal-dose dopamine’ and diuretic therapy, have not been shown to alter the course of AKI. Management is largely supportive and focused on the underlying cause.

concepts.title: Acute kidney injury – Prognosis and Long-Term Risks
concepts.content: The prognosis of AKI is highly dependent on the underlying etiology. Children who have had AKI are at risk for the late development of chronic kidney disease several years after the initial insult.

concepts.title: Muscular dystrophies – Definition
concepts.content: Muscular dystrophy (MD) is a group of more than 30 genetic diseases that cause progressive weakness and degeneration of skeletal muscles. All forms of MD worsen over time as muscles progressively degenerate and weaken.

concepts.title: Muscular dystrophies – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: In muscular dystrophy, defects in the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex in the muscle fiber membrane lead to muscle fiber damage, leakage of creatine kinase, and excess calcium entry, ultimately causing muscle fiber death and progressive degeneration.

concepts.title: Muscular dystrophies – Inheritance Patterns
concepts.content: Muscular dystrophies can be inherited in three ways: autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked recessive.

concepts.title: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), the most common childhood form, primarily affects boys and becomes apparent in the toddler years. It presents with progressive weakness and muscle wasting, a waddling gait, frequent falls, and difficulty rising from a sitting position.

concepts.title: Becker Muscular Dystrophy – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Becker muscular dystrophy is less severe than DMD and usually appears around age 11. It is characterized by muscle weakness in the upper arms, shoulders, upper legs, and pelvis, with toe-walking and frequent falls as early symptoms.

concepts.title: Congenital Muscular Dystrophy – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Congenital muscular dystrophy is present at birth or evident before age 2. Most children with this type are unable to sit or stand without support, and some may never learn to walk. It can also cause contractures, scoliosis, and breathing difficulties.

concepts.title: Non-accidental injury – Definition
concepts.content: Non-accidental injury (NAI) or physical abuse is any bodily injury that is deliberately inflicted on a vulnerable person. It can include hitting, kicking, burning, biting, or choking.

concepts.title: Non-accidental injury – Suspicious History
concepts.content: Suspicion of non-accidental injury should be raised by factors such as a delay in seeking medical attention, an implausible or changing history of the injury, a lack of concern from the caregiver, or abnormal behaviour from the child.

concepts.title: Non-accidental injury – Bruising Patterns
concepts.content: In non-accidental injury, bruises are often multiple, in different stages of healing, and located on soft tissues like the thighs, abdomen, buttocks, and cheeks. They may also have a pattern indicative of the object used, such as a handprint or belt buckle.

concepts.title: Non-accidental injury – Burn Patterns
concepts.content: Cigarette burns often appear as rounded ulcers or erosions. Immersion burns from scalding water have a sharp demarcation in a 'glove and stocking' distribution. Branding injuries may represent the shape of the heated object used.

concepts.title: Non-accidental injury – Bite Marks
concepts.content: Human bites tend to cause a crush injury. If the distance between the canine marks is greater than 3 cm, the perpetrator is likely an adult. Animal bites have narrower puncture marks and different spacing.

concepts.title: Non-accidental injury – Signs of Neglect
concepts.content: Physical neglect can present with poor hygiene, malnutrition, and untreated illnesses such as dermatitis, scabies, or head lice. A lack of immunizations may also be a sign.

concepts.title: Obesity in children – Definition and Assessment
concepts.content: Defining obesity in children is complex as BMI varies with age. UK 1990 BMI percentile charts are used for accurate assessment. A BMI at or above the 91st centile suggests a need for tailored clinical intervention.

concepts.title: Obesity in children – Comorbidity Assessment
concepts.content: NICE recommends considering an assessment for comorbidities in children with a BMI at or above the 98th centile.

concepts.title: Obesity in children – Causes and Associations
concepts.content: The most common cause of childhood obesity is lifestyle factors. Other associations include being of Asian ethnicity, female, and taller than average. Medical causes include growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism, Down's syndrome, and Cushing's syndrome.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Definition
concepts.content: Pneumothorax is the accumulation of air in the pleural space, the area between the lungs and the chest wall. It can occur spontaneously or be associated with trauma or pre-existing pulmonary conditions.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Clinical Features
concepts.content: The symptoms of a pneumothorax develop suddenly and include sharp chest pain and shortness of breath. On examination, there may be decreased breath sounds on the affected side.

concepts.title: Tension Pneumothorax – Clinical Features
concepts.content: A tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening emergency that presents with more severe symptoms and respiratory distress than a simple pneumothorax. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are crucial.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Diagnosis
concepts.content: A pneumothorax is confirmed with an upright inspiratory chest radiograph. A CT scan may be recommended for unusual cases or to evaluate for recurrence.

concepts.title: Pneumothorax – Management
concepts.content: Many spontaneous pneumothoraces resolve with conservative therapy, such as the administration of high-concentration oxygen. Large, complicated, or tension pneumothoraces require decompression and chest tube placement.

concepts.title: Septic arthritis in children – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Septic arthritis has an incidence of around 4-5 per 100,000 children and is more common in boys (M:F ratio = 2:1). The most commonly affected joints are the hip, knee, and ankle.

concepts.title: Septic arthritis in children – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Septic arthritis in children presents with joint pain, limp, fever, and systemic signs of illness such as lethargy. The affected joint is typically swollen and red, with minimal movement possible.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis in children – Definition
concepts.content: Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It usually affects the lungs but can also affect other parts of the body like the brain, kidneys, or spine.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis in children – Latent vs. Active Disease
concepts.content: Children can have latent TB infection, where they have TB germs but are not sick and cannot spread them, or active TB disease, where the germs are multiplying, causing illness, and can be spread to others.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis in children – Clinical Features
concepts.content: Symptoms of active TB disease in children include cough, weakness, lethargy, weight loss or failure to thrive, fever, and night sweats. TB meningitis can cause sleepiness, headache, irritability, and seizures.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis in children – Risk Factors
concepts.content: Children are at higher risk for TB if they live with adults with TB risk factors, were born in or travel to high-prevalence countries, live in congregate settings, have been exposed to someone with active TB, or have a weakened immune system.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis in children – Diagnosis
concepts.content: Diagnosis of TB in children involves a medical history, physical exam, TB test (skin or blood), chest x-ray, and laboratory tests on sputum or other samples. Diagnosis can be challenging as it is often difficult to collect sputum from children.

concepts.title: Tuberculosis in children – Treatment
concepts.content: Treatment is recommended for children with latent TB to prevent active disease. Active TB disease requires a multi-drug regimen for 4, 6, or more months. Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) is the best way to ensure adherence.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Definition
concepts.content: Anaemia in paediatrics is defined as a haemoglobin concentration below the age-specific lower limit: for children aged 6 months to 5 years, Hb < 110 g/L; for 5 to 12 years, Hb < 115 g/L; and for 12 to 15 years, Hb < 120 g/L.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Anaemia affects approximately 25% of children worldwide, with higher prevalence in low-income settings; in the UK, iron deficiency anaemia is the most common cause in paediatric populations.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Aetiology/Risk factors: Iron deficiency
concepts.content: Iron deficiency is the leading cause of anaemia in UK children, commonly due to inadequate dietary intake, increased requirements during growth, or chronic blood loss; risk factors include prematurity, exclusive breastfeeding beyond 6 months without supplementation, and poor weaning practices.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Aetiology/Risk factors: Haemolytic anaemia
concepts.content: Haemolytic anaemia in children can be caused by hereditary conditions such as sickle cell disease or thalassaemia, or acquired causes like autoimmune haemolytic anaemia; these conditions lead to premature red blood cell destruction.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Anaemia results from decreased red blood cell production, increased destruction, or blood loss, leading to reduced oxygen-carrying capacity and tissue hypoxia; compensatory mechanisms include increased cardiac output and erythropoietin production.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Clinical features: Pallor
concepts.content: Pallor, especially of the conjunctivae, palms, and nail beds, is a common clinical feature of anaemia in children and may be the earliest visible sign.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Clinical features: Breathlessness
concepts.content: Children with moderate to severe anaemia may present with breathlessness on exertion due to reduced oxygen delivery to tissues.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Clinical features: Fatigue and irritability
concepts.content: Fatigue and irritability are common non-specific symptoms in paediatric anaemia due to decreased oxygen delivery and resultant tissue hypoxia.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Investigations: Full blood count
concepts.content: Full blood count (FBC) is essential for diagnosis, showing low haemoglobin, haematocrit, and red cell indices; microcytic hypochromic anaemia suggests iron deficiency, while macrocytic anaemia suggests B12 or folate deficiency.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Investigations: Iron studies
concepts.content: Serum ferritin is the most specific test for iron deficiency anaemia; ferritin < 12 µg/L in children indicates depleted iron stores; serum iron, total iron-binding capacity, and transferrin saturation assist in diagnosis.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Management: Iron supplementation
concepts.content: First-line treatment for iron deficiency anaemia in children is oral ferrous sulphate at 3 mg/kg elemental iron twice daily for at least 3 months; vitamin C enhances absorption and should be given with iron supplements.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Management: Blood transfusion
concepts.content: Blood transfusion is indicated in paediatric anaemia when haemoglobin is < 70 g/L with symptoms or < 50 g/L regardless of symptoms; transfuse 10-15 mL/kg of packed red cells slowly with monitoring for transfusion reactions.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Complications
concepts.content: Severe or chronic anaemia in children can lead to cardiac complications such as left ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure, developmental delay, and increased susceptibility to infections.

concepts.title: Anaemia – Prognosis
concepts.content: With timely diagnosis and appropriate management, prognosis of paediatric anaemia is excellent; iron deficiency anaemia typically resolves with supplementation, though untreated cases may cause long-term developmental impairment.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis – Definition
concepts.content: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterised by rapid onset and involving multiple organ systems, typically mediated by IgE antibodies.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: In the UK, the incidence of anaphylaxis in children is approximately 1-3 per 10,000 per year, with food allergies being the most common trigger in paediatric populations.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common triggers of paediatric anaphylaxis in the UK include foods (peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs), insect stings, medications (e.g. penicillin), and latex; risk factors include previous anaphylaxis, asthma, and atopy.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Anaphylaxis results from IgE-mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation releasing histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins causing vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, bronchospasm, and mucous secretion.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis – Clinical features: Skin and mucosal signs
concepts.content: In paediatric anaphylaxis, skin signs such as urticaria, flushing, and angioedema occur in over 80% of cases and are often the earliest manifestations.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis – Clinical features: Respiratory symptoms
concepts.content: Respiratory involvement in paediatric anaphylaxis includes stridor, wheeze, cough, and breathlessness, occurring in approximately 70% of cases and may rapidly progress to airway obstruction.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis – Clinical features: Cardiovascular symptoms
concepts.content: Cardiovascular signs in paediatric anaphylaxis include hypotension, tachycardia, dizziness, and shock; hypotension is defined as systolic BP <70 + (2 × age in years) mmHg in children.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis – Clinical features: Gastrointestinal symptoms
concepts.content: Gastrointestinal manifestations in paediatric anaphylaxis include abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhoea, present in up to 45% of cases.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis – Investigations
concepts.content: Serum tryptase measurement within 1-3 hours of symptom onset can support diagnosis but is not required for acute management; baseline tryptase may be elevated in mastocytosis.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis – Management: First-line treatment
concepts.content: Intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) is the first-line treatment for paediatric anaphylaxis; dose is 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) administered into the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5-15 minutes as needed.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis – Management: Adjunctive treatments
concepts.content: Adjunctive treatments include high-flow oxygen, intravenous fluids (20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus), antihistamines (chlorphenamine 0.1 mg/kg IV max 10 mg), and corticosteroids (hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg IV max 100 mg), although steroids have no immediate effect.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis – Management: Observation and referral
concepts.content: Children treated for anaphylaxis should be observed for at least 4-6 hours due to risk of biphasic reactions; referral to allergy services for assessment and provision of adrenaline auto-injectors is essential.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of paediatric anaphylaxis include biphasic reactions occurring in up to 20% of cases, airway obstruction, hypoxic brain injury, and rarely death if untreated.

concepts.title: Anaphylaxis – Prognosis
concepts.content: With prompt recognition and treatment, paediatric anaphylaxis has an excellent prognosis; however, risk of recurrence exists, necessitating education and avoidance strategies.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Definition
concepts.content: Appendicitis is inflammation of the vermiform appendix, typically caused by obstruction of the appendiceal lumen leading to bacterial infection and inflammation.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency in children, with peak incidence between 10 and 19 years of age. It affects approximately 70,000 children annually in the UK.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Aetiology and Risk Factors
concepts.content: Common causes include luminal obstruction by faecoliths, lymphoid hyperplasia (especially post-viral), foreign bodies, or rarely tumours. Risk factors include male sex, age 10-19 years, and family history.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen leads to increased intraluminal pressure, venous congestion, bacterial overgrowth, ischemia, and eventual inflammation and necrosis of the appendix wall.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
concepts.content: Initial periumbilical pain that later localises to the right lower quadrant (McBurney’s point) is characteristic in paediatric appendicitis.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Low-grade fever (37.5-38.5°C) is common in paediatric appendicitis, with higher temperatures suggesting perforation or abscess formation.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Clinical features: Nausea and vomiting
concepts.content: Nausea and vomiting typically follow the onset of abdominal pain in paediatric appendicitis and are present in approximately 80% of cases.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Clinical features: Tenderness and signs
concepts.content: Tenderness at McBurney’s point, rebound tenderness, guarding, and Rovsing’s sign are common physical examination findings in paediatric appendicitis.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Investigations: Blood tests
concepts.content: Blood tests often show leukocytosis with neutrophilia (white cell count >12 x10^9/L) and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) in paediatric appendicitis.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Investigations: Imaging
concepts.content: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality in paediatric appendicitis, showing a non-compressible, enlarged appendix >6 mm diameter. CT scan is reserved for equivocal cases.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Differential diagnoses in children include mesenteric adenitis, gastroenteritis, Meckel’s diverticulitis, intussusception, urinary tract infection, and ovarian torsion in females.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Management: Initial treatment
concepts.content: Initial management includes nil by mouth, intravenous fluids, analgesia with paracetamol and/or ibuprofen, and intravenous antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav 30 mg/kg every 8 hours.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Management: Surgical treatment
concepts.content: Definitive treatment is appendicectomy, preferably laparoscopic, performed urgently to prevent perforation and complications.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include perforation, peritonitis, abscess formation, sepsis, and bowel obstruction. Perforation risk is higher in children under 5 years.

concepts.title: Appendicitis – Prognosis
concepts.content: With prompt diagnosis and treatment, prognosis is excellent; mortality is rare in the UK. Delayed treatment increases risk of complications and longer hospital stay.

concepts.title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Definition
concepts.content: Atopic dermatitis and eczema is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin condition characterised by dry, itchy, and inflamed skin, commonly affecting children and often associated with other atopic diseases such as asthma and allergic rhinitis.

concepts.title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Epidemiology
