concepts.content: Atopic dermatitis affects approximately 15-20% of children in the UK, with onset commonly before 5 years of age; prevalence has increased over recent decades.

concepts.title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors include family history of atopy, filaggrin gene mutations, environmental triggers such as allergens and irritants, and impaired skin barrier function.

concepts.title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Atopic dermatitis involves a defective skin barrier with reduced ceramide levels and filaggrin deficiency, leading to increased transepidermal water loss and enhanced allergen penetration, triggering a Th2-mediated immune response.

concepts.title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Clinical features: Acute rash
concepts.content: Acute flares present with intensely pruritic, erythematous, weeping, and crusted plaques commonly on the face, scalp, and extensor surfaces in infants, and flexural areas in older children.

concepts.title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Clinical features: Chronic rash
concepts.content: Chronic eczema is characterised by lichenification, scaling, and thickened skin due to repeated scratching, often affecting flexural areas such as the antecubital and popliteal fossae.

concepts.title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis is clinical; skin swabs may be taken if secondary bacterial infection is suspected, commonly Staphylococcus aureus. Patch testing may be used in chronic or refractory cases to identify contact allergens.

concepts.title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Management
concepts.content: Management includes regular use of emollients (e.g., aqueous cream or emulsifying ointment applied liberally at least twice daily), topical corticosteroids (e.g., hydrocortisone 1% cream for mild flares, potent steroids like betamethasone valerate 0.1% for severe flares) applied once or twice daily for 1-2 weeks, and avoidance of triggers. Antihistamines may be used for severe pruritus. Infected eczema requires topical or oral antibiotics (e.g., flucloxacillin 25-50 mg/kg/day divided into 3-4 doses for 7 days).

concepts.title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include secondary bacterial infection (commonly Staphylococcus aureus), eczema herpeticum caused by herpes simplex virus, and chronic skin changes such as lichenification and pigmentary changes.

concepts.title: Atopic dermatitis and eczema – Prognosis
concepts.content: Most children experience improvement or resolution by late childhood or adolescence; however, some may have persistent or relapsing disease into adulthood.

concepts.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Definition
concepts.content: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by a persistent pattern of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development, typically diagnosed in childhood.

concepts.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Epidemiology
concepts.content: ADHD affects approximately 5% of children in the UK, with a higher prevalence in boys (male to female ratio of about 3:1). Symptoms typically present before the age of 12 years.

concepts.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: ADHD is multifactorial with genetic factors accounting for up to 75% of risk. Environmental risk factors include prenatal exposure to tobacco smoke, alcohol, low birth weight, and psychosocial adversity.

concepts.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: ADHD is associated with dysregulation of dopaminergic and noradrenergic neurotransmission in the prefrontal cortex, leading to impaired attention, executive function, and behavioural control.

concepts.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Clinical features: Inattention
concepts.content: Children with ADHD often show inattention characterised by difficulty sustaining focus, careless mistakes, poor organisational skills, and forgetfulness in daily activities.

concepts.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Clinical features: Hyperactivity and impulsivity
concepts.content: Hyperactivity presents as excessive fidgeting, inability to remain seated, running or climbing in inappropriate situations, and impulsivity includes interrupting others, difficulty waiting turn, and acting without thinking.

concepts.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis of ADHD is clinical based on DSM-5 or ICD-10 criteria; no specific laboratory or imaging tests are required. Assessment includes detailed history, behaviour rating scales (e.g., Conners’), and exclusion of other causes.

concepts.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Management: Pharmacological treatment
concepts.content: First-line pharmacological treatment in the UK for children over 5 years with moderate to severe ADHD is methylphenidate, starting at 5 mg once or twice daily, titrated up to a maximum of 60 mg daily. Alternatives include lisdexamfetamine and atomoxetine.

concepts.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Management: Non-pharmacological treatment
concepts.content: Non-pharmacological management includes behavioural therapy, parent training programmes, educational support, and school-based interventions to improve attention and reduce disruptive behaviour.

concepts.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of untreated ADHD include poor academic performance, low self-esteem, increased risk of substance misuse, conduct disorders, and higher rates of accidental injury.

concepts.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder – Prognosis
concepts.content: ADHD symptoms persist into adulthood in approximately 60% of cases. Early diagnosis and treatment improve long-term outcomes including academic achievement and social functioning.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Definition
concepts.content: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterised by persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, alongside restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests, or activities.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Epidemiology
concepts.content: The prevalence of autism spectrum disorder in the UK is approximately 1 in 100 children, with a male to female ratio of around 4:1. Diagnosis typically occurs in early childhood, often by age 3 years.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: ASD has a multifactorial aetiology including genetic factors such as mutations in genes like SHANK3 and environmental risk factors including advanced parental age, prenatal exposure to valproate, and low birth weight.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: ASD is associated with atypical brain development including altered synaptic connectivity and neurotransmitter imbalances, particularly involving glutamate and GABA pathways, leading to impaired social cognition and repetitive behaviours.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Clinical features: Social communication deficits
concepts.content: Children with ASD often present with impaired social interaction including poor eye contact, difficulty understanding social cues, lack of shared enjoyment, and delayed or absent speech development.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Clinical features: Restricted and repetitive behaviours
concepts.content: ASD is characterised by repetitive motor movements, insistence on sameness, inflexible adherence to routines, and highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Clinical features: Associated conditions
concepts.content: Common comorbidities in ASD include intellectual disability (present in approximately 30-50% of cases), epilepsy (20-30%), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and anxiety disorders.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis of ASD is clinical based on DSM-5 or ICD-11 criteria; investigations include developmental assessments, Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS), and Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R). Genetic testing and metabolic screening may be considered in selected cases.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Management
concepts.content: Management of ASD involves early intensive behavioural interventions such as Applied Behaviour Analysis (ABA), speech and language therapy, occupational therapy, and educational support. Pharmacological treatment with risperidone or aripiprazole may be used for irritability or behavioural problems at doses of 0.5-3 mg/day and 2-15 mg/day respectively.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of ASD include social isolation, increased risk of anxiety and depression, self-injurious behaviours, and increased risk of premature mortality due to accidents or comorbid epilepsy.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis varies widely; early diagnosis and intervention improve outcomes. Many individuals achieve varying degrees of independence, though some require lifelong support. Intellectual disability and comorbidities worsen prognosis.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Definition
concepts.content: Bronchiectasis is a chronic paediatric respiratory condition characterised by permanent dilatation and destruction of the bronchial walls, leading to impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent respiratory infections.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Bronchiectasis is an uncommon but important cause of chronic respiratory morbidity in UK paediatric populations, with higher prevalence in children with underlying conditions such as cystic fibrosis or immunodeficiency.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common aetiological factors for paediatric bronchiectasis in the UK include post-infectious causes (e.g. severe or recurrent pneumonia), cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, immunodeficiency, and aspiration syndromes.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Bronchiectasis results from a cycle of airway inflammation, infection, and impaired mucociliary clearance causing permanent bronchial wall damage and dilation, which predisposes to further infection and inflammation.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Clinical features: Chronic productive cough
concepts.content: The most common presentation of paediatric bronchiectasis is a chronic productive cough lasting more than 8 weeks, often with purulent sputum.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Clinical features: Recurrent chest infections
concepts.content: Children with bronchiectasis frequently experience recurrent chest infections characterised by increased cough, sputum production, fever, and malaise.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Clinical features: Digital clubbing
concepts.content: Digital clubbing is a common physical sign in children with bronchiectasis, indicating chronic hypoxia and lung disease.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Investigations: Chest X-ray
concepts.content: Chest X-ray in bronchiectasis may show tram-track lines, ring shadows, and areas of lung hyperinflation but has limited sensitivity compared to CT.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Investigations: High-resolution CT chest
concepts.content: High-resolution CT (HRCT) chest is the gold standard investigation for bronchiectasis, showing bronchial wall thickening, bronchial dilation (signet ring sign), and lack of bronchial tapering.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Investigations: Microbiological sputum analysis
concepts.content: Sputum culture in bronchiectasis often grows pathogens such as Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, guiding antibiotic therapy.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Management: Airway clearance physiotherapy
concepts.content: Regular airway clearance physiotherapy is essential in managing paediatric bronchiectasis to improve mucus clearance and reduce infection risk; techniques include active cycle of breathing and postural drainage.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Management: Antibiotic therapy
concepts.content: Acute exacerbations of bronchiectasis are treated with targeted antibiotics based on sputum culture; common choices include amoxicillin 25-50 mg/kg/day orally in three divided doses or co-amoxiclav 25-45 mg/kg/day, with intravenous therapy for severe cases.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Management: Immunisations
concepts.content: Children with bronchiectasis should receive routine UK immunisations including annual influenza vaccine and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine to reduce respiratory infection risk.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Complications
concepts.content: Potential complications of paediatric bronchiectasis include recurrent respiratory infections, haemoptysis, respiratory failure, and cor pulmonale due to chronic hypoxia.

concepts.title: Bronchiectasis – Prognosis
concepts.content: With early diagnosis and appropriate management including airway clearance and infection control, many children with bronchiectasis can maintain good lung function and quality of life; however, untreated disease may progress to irreversible lung damage.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Definition
concepts.content: Candidiasis is a fungal infection caused by Candida species, most commonly Candida albicans, affecting mucosal surfaces, skin, and occasionally systemic sites in paediatric patients.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Candidiasis is a common fungal infection in paediatric populations, particularly in neonates and immunocompromised children; Candida albicans accounts for over 70% of cases in the UK.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Aetiology and Risk Factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for paediatric candidiasis include prematurity, broad-spectrum antibiotic use, immunosuppression, indwelling catheters, and prolonged hospitalisation.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Candida species colonise mucosal surfaces and can invade epithelial tissues when host immunity is compromised, leading to superficial or systemic infection in children.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Clinical features: Oral thrush
concepts.content: Oral thrush presents with white, curd-like plaques on the buccal mucosa, tongue, and palate in infants, which can be wiped off to reveal erythematous mucosa; associated with difficulty with breast feeding.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Clinical features: Diaper dermatitis
concepts.content: Candidal diaper dermatitis presents as a bright red rash with satellite pustules and papules in the diaper area, typically in infants with prolonged exposure to moisture.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Clinical features: Oesophageal candidiasis
concepts.content: Oesophageal candidiasis in children presents with odynophagia, dysphagia, and retrosternal pain, often in immunocompromised patients.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis of candidiasis is confirmed by microscopic examination and culture of samples from affected sites; blood cultures are required for suspected systemic infection.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Management: Oral thrush
concepts.content: Oral thrush in paediatric patients is treated with topical antifungals such as nystatin oral suspension 100,000 units/mL, 1 mL four times daily for 7–14 days.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Management: Systemic infection
concepts.content: Systemic candidiasis in children requires intravenous antifungal therapy with agents such as liposomal amphotericin B 3–5 mg/kg/day or intravenous fluconazole 6–12 mg/kg/day, adjusted according to clinical response.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of paediatric candidiasis include systemic dissemination causing candidemia, endocarditis, meningitis, and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis in immunodeficient children.

concepts.title: Candidiasis – Prognosis
concepts.content: The prognosis of paediatric candidiasis is generally good with prompt antifungal treatment; however, systemic infection in immunocompromised children carries a higher risk of morbidity and mortality.

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest – Definition
concepts.content: Cardiac arrest in paediatrics is defined as the sudden cessation of effective cardiac mechanical activity, resulting in the absence of a palpable central pulse, unresponsiveness, and apnea or agonal breathing.

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Paediatric cardiac arrest has an incidence of approximately 8 per 100,000 children per year in the UK, with higher rates in infants under 1 year. Survival to hospital discharge is around 10-20%, varying by cause and setting.

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of paediatric cardiac arrest include respiratory failure, shock, congenital heart disease, arrhythmias, trauma, sepsis, and drowning. Risk factors include prematurity, chronic illness, and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Paediatric cardiac arrest typically results from hypoxia-induced bradycardia progressing to asystole or pulseless electrical activity, unlike adults where ventricular fibrillation is more common.

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
concepts.content: Paediatric cardiac arrest presents with sudden loss of consciousness and unresponsiveness, with absence of normal breathing or presence of agonal gasping.

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest – Clinical features: Shock
concepts.content: Signs of shock such as pallor, cool extremities, weak pulses, and delayed capillary refill may precede or accompany paediatric cardiac arrest.

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest – Investigations
concepts.content: Initial investigations include ECG monitoring to identify rhythm, pulse oximetry, capnography with end-tidal CO2 monitoring during resuscitation, blood gases, glucose, electrolytes, and chest X-ray post-resuscitation.

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest – Management
concepts.content: Management follows the UK Resuscitation Council paediatric advanced life support guidelines: immediate recognition, call for help, high-quality chest compressions at 100-120/min with depth of one-third chest diameter, 15:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio for two rescuers, airway management, ventilation with 100% oxygen, and administration of adrenaline 10 mcg/kg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes during resuscitation.

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest – Complications
concepts.content: Potential complications include hypoxic brain injury, multi-organ failure, rib fractures from chest compressions, and post-resuscitation myocardial dysfunction.

concepts.title: Cardiac arrest – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis depends on cause, duration of arrest, and quality of resuscitation; survival to hospital discharge is approximately 10-20% with many survivors suffering neurological impairment.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Definition
concepts.content: Cellulitis is a common bacterial skin infection characterised by inflammation of the dermis and subcutaneous tissues, typically caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Cellulitis is a common paediatric infection, with an incidence of approximately 1.5 to 4 cases per 1000 children annually in the UK, more frequent in children under 5 years old.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Aetiology and Risk Factors
concepts.content: Cellulitis in children is most commonly caused by Group A Streptococcus and Staphylococcus aureus; risk factors include skin barrier disruption (e.g., eczema, insect bites, trauma), immunodeficiency, and lymphatic obstruction.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Cellulitis results from bacterial invasion of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, leading to localised inflammation, oedema, erythema, and pain due to host immune response and bacterial toxins.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Clinical Features: Local Signs
concepts.content: Typical local signs of cellulitis include erythema, warmth, swelling, tenderness, and poorly demarcated borders; affected skin may be shiny and stretched.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Clinical Features: Systemic Signs
concepts.content: Systemic features may include fever, malaise, and regional lymphadenopathy; in severe cases, children may appear unwell with tachycardia and hypotension.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis of cellulitis is primarily clinical; blood tests such as full blood count and C-reactive protein may show raised inflammatory markers; blood cultures are reserved for severe or systemic cases.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Differential Diagnosis
concepts.content: Differential diagnoses include erysipelas, abscess, necrotising fasciitis, insect bite reactions, and deep vein thrombosis; necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency and must be excluded.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Management: Antibiotic Therapy
concepts.content: First-line treatment for uncomplicated paediatric cellulitis in the UK is oral flucloxacillin 25-50 mg/kg/day divided into 4 doses (max 2 g/day) for 5 days; for penicillin allergy, clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg/dose twice daily is used.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Management: Supportive Care
concepts.content: Supportive care includes elevation of the affected limb to reduce swelling, analgesia with paracetamol or ibuprofen, and ensuring adequate hydration and nutrition.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Complications
concepts.content: Potential complications include abscess formation, lymphangitis, sepsis, necrotising fasciitis, and chronic lymphoedema; early recognition and treatment reduce risk.

concepts.title: Cellulitis – Prognosis
concepts.content: With prompt antibiotic treatment, the prognosis of paediatric cellulitis is excellent, with most children recovering fully within 7 to 10 days without sequelae.

concepts.title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Definition
concepts.content: Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of permanent disorders of the development of movement and posture, causing activity limitation, attributed to non-progressive disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain. Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE) is brain dysfunction caused by a reduction in oxygen (hypoxia) and blood flow (ischaemia) to the brain around the time of birth.

concepts.title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Cerebral palsy affects approximately 2 per 1000 live births in the UK. Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy occurs in 1 to 3 per 1000 live births and is a leading cause of neonatal encephalopathy and subsequent cerebral palsy.

concepts.title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for HIE include perinatal asphyxia, placental abruption, umbilical cord prolapse, maternal hypotension, and prolonged labour. Prematurity and low birth weight increase risk of cerebral palsy.

concepts.title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: HIE results from impaired cerebral blood flow and oxygen delivery leading to energy failure, excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, and neuronal death. This brain injury during the perinatal period causes the motor and cognitive impairments seen in cerebral palsy.

concepts.title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Clinical features: Neonatal seizures
concepts.content: Neonatal seizures are a common presentation of HIE, occurring within the first 24 to 48 hours of life. Seizures may be subtle (e.g., lip smacking, eye deviation) or tonic-clonic.

concepts.title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Clinical features: Abnormal muscle tone
concepts.content: Children with cerebral palsy typically present with abnormal muscle tone, which may be spasticity (increased tone), dystonia, or hypotonia, often evident in the first year of life.

concepts.title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Clinical features: Developmental delay
concepts.content: Developmental delay, including delayed motor milestones and speech and language problems, is common in children with cerebral palsy secondary to HIE.

concepts.title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Investigations: Neuroimaging
concepts.content: MRI brain is the investigation of choice for assessing HIE and cerebral palsy, typically performed between days 4 and 14 of life. It shows patterns of injury such as watershed infarcts or basal ganglia/thalamic lesions.

concepts.title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Management: Therapeutic hypothermia
concepts.content: Therapeutic hypothermia (cooling to 33.5°C for 72 hours) initiated within 6 hours of birth reduces death and disability in term infants with moderate to severe HIE and is standard care in UK neonatal units.

concepts.title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Management: Supportive care
concepts.content: Supportive care includes maintaining adequate ventilation and oxygenation, managing seizures with phenobarbital (loading dose 20 mg/kg IV, maintenance 3-5 mg/kg/day), and ensuring normoglycaemia and normothermia.

concepts.title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of HIE and cerebral palsy include epilepsy, intellectual disability, feeding difficulties, musculoskeletal deformities such as hip dislocation and scoliosis, and respiratory problems.

concepts.title: Cerebral palsy and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis depends on severity of initial brain injury; mild HIE may have normal outcomes, while severe HIE has high mortality and risk of severe cerebral palsy and neurodevelopmental impairment. Early therapeutic hypothermia improves outcomes.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Definition
concepts.content: Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated systemic disorder elicited by gluten and related prolamines in genetically susceptible individuals, characterised by a variable combination of gluten-dependent clinical manifestations, specific antibodies, HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 haplotypes, and enteropathy.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Coeliac disease affects approximately 1% of the paediatric population in the UK, with a higher prevalence in females and individuals with a first-degree relative affected by the condition.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for coeliac disease include carrying HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 haplotypes, having a first-degree relative with coeliac disease, type 1 diabetes mellitus, autoimmune thyroid disease, and Down syndrome.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: In coeliac disease, ingestion of gluten leads to an inappropriate T-cell mediated immune response causing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis in the small intestine, resulting in malabsorption.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Clinical features: Diarrhoea
concepts.content: Chronic diarrhoea is a common presenting feature in paediatric coeliac disease, often accompanied by steatorrhoea due to malabsorption.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
concepts.content: Children with coeliac disease may present with chronic abdominal pain, often colicky in nature, related to intestinal inflammation and malabsorption.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Clinical features: Failure to thrive
concepts.content: Failure to thrive and poor weight gain are common in infants and young children with untreated coeliac disease due to malabsorption and nutritional deficiencies.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Clinical features: Anaemia
concepts.content: Iron deficiency anaemia refractory to oral iron therapy is a frequent feature in paediatric coeliac disease due to impaired iron absorption in the proximal small intestine.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Investigations: Serology
concepts.content: Initial screening for coeliac disease includes serological tests such as tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA) and total serum IgA to exclude IgA deficiency; tTG-IgA has a sensitivity and specificity >90%.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Investigations: Small bowel biopsy
concepts.content: Definitive diagnosis of coeliac disease is confirmed by duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (Marsh classification), performed while the child is on a gluten-containing diet.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Management
concepts.content: The mainstay of treatment for paediatric coeliac disease is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet, eliminating all sources of wheat, barley, and rye, with dietetic support to ensure nutritional adequacy.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Complications
concepts.content: Untreated coeliac disease in children can lead to complications including growth failure, osteoporosis, iron deficiency anaemia, and rarely, enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma.

concepts.title: Coeliac disease – Prognosis
concepts.content: With adherence to a strict gluten-free diet, children with coeliac disease typically have an excellent prognosis with resolution of symptoms, mucosal healing within 6-12 months, and normal growth and development.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Definition
concepts.content: Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the mucous membrane covering the white part of the eye and the inner surface of the eyelids, commonly presenting with redness, discharge, and irritation in paediatric patients.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Conjunctivitis is a common paediatric condition, accounting for approximately 1-2% of general practice consultations in the UK, with viral causes being the most frequent, especially in children under 5 years old.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of paediatric conjunctivitis include viral infections (adenovirus), bacterial infections (Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae), allergic reactions, and irritants such as smoke or chlorine.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Conjunctivitis results from inflammation of the conjunctival epithelium due to infection, allergy, or irritation, leading to vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and mucous or purulent discharge.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Clinical features: Redness and irritation
concepts.content: Children with conjunctivitis typically present with redness of the conjunctiva, a gritty or burning sensation, and mild eye discomfort without significant pain.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Clinical features: Discharge type
concepts.content: Viral conjunctivitis usually produces a watery discharge, whereas bacterial conjunctivitis causes purulent, sticky discharge often leading to eyelids sticking together, especially in the morning.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Clinical features: Associated symptoms
concepts.content: Other symptoms may include eyelid swelling, mild photophobia, and regional preauricular lymphadenopathy, particularly in viral conjunctivitis.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; however, conjunctival swabs for bacterial culture may be considered in severe, recurrent, or non-resolving cases to guide antibiotic therapy.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Management: Viral conjunctivitis
concepts.content: Management of viral conjunctivitis is supportive, including maintaining eye hygiene, using cold compresses, and lubricating eye drops; antibiotics are not indicated.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Management: Bacterial conjunctivitis
concepts.content: Topical antibiotics such as chloramphenicol 1% eye drops, 1 drop every 2 hours while awake for the first 2 days, then 4 times daily for 5 days, are recommended for bacterial conjunctivitis in children.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Management: Allergic conjunctivitis
concepts.content: Treatment includes avoidance of allergens and use of topical antihistamines or mast cell stabilisers such as olopatadine eye drops, 1 drop twice daily, to reduce symptoms.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Complications
concepts.content: Complications are rare but can include keratitis, corneal ulceration, and rarely, chronic conjunctivitis leading to scarring or visual impairment if untreated.

concepts.title: Conjunctivitis – Prognosis
concepts.content: The prognosis for paediatric conjunctivitis is excellent, with most cases resolving within 1-2 weeks without long-term sequelae when appropriately managed.

concepts.title: Constipation – Definition
concepts.content: Constipation in paediatrics is defined as infrequent, hard, painful stools or difficulty passing stools, typically fewer than three bowel movements per week.

concepts.title: Constipation – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Constipation affects approximately 3% of children worldwide and is one of the most common paediatric gastrointestinal complaints presenting in primary care in the UK.

concepts.title: Constipation – Aetiology and Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of paediatric constipation include low dietary fibre intake, inadequate fluid intake, withholding behaviour, toilet training issues, and secondary causes such as hypothyroidism, Hirschsprung disease, and medication side effects (e.g., anticholinergics).

concepts.title: Constipation – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Constipation results from slowed colonic transit or outlet obstruction due to voluntary withholding of stool, leading to faecal impaction and decreased rectal sensation.

concepts.title: Constipation – Clinical features: Infrequent and hard stools
concepts.content: Children with constipation typically present with fewer than three bowel movements per week and pass hard, pellet-like or large stools that may be painful to pass.

concepts.title: Constipation – Clinical features: Abdominal pain and distension
concepts.content: Constipated children may complain of intermittent or chronic abdominal pain and visible abdominal distension due to faecal loading.

concepts.title: Constipation – Clinical features: Faecal incontinence
concepts.content: Overflow soiling or faecal incontinence occurs in up to 30% of children with chronic constipation due to leakage around impacted stool.

concepts.title: Constipation – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis is clinical; investigations such as abdominal X-ray may be used to assess faecal loading in complex cases. Thyroid function tests and calcium levels may be checked if secondary causes are suspected.

concepts.title: Constipation – Management: Lifestyle and dietary advice
concepts.content: Initial management includes increasing dietary fibre intake to 10-15 g/day for toddlers and 20-30 g/day for older children, ensuring adequate hydration, and encouraging regular toilet habits with positive reinforcement.

concepts.title: Constipation – Management: Pharmacological treatment
concepts.content: Oral osmotic laxatives such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) are first-line pharmacological treatment. The typical dose is 0.4-0.8 g/kg/day, adjusted according to response, with treatment duration of at least 2 months to prevent relapse.

concepts.title: Constipation – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include faecal impaction, anal fissures, rectal prolapse, urinary tract infections due to bladder compression, and psychological distress.

concepts.title: Constipation – Prognosis
concepts.content: With appropriate management, most children with constipation improve within weeks to months. However, relapse is common, and some children may require prolonged treatment and follow-up.

concepts.title: Dehydration – Definition
concepts.content: Dehydration in paediatrics is a clinical condition characterised by a deficit of total body water, leading to impaired cellular and organ function. It is commonly classified by severity based on percentage of body weight lost: mild (<5%), moderate (5-10%), and severe (>10%).

concepts.title: Dehydration – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Dehydration is a common paediatric condition, particularly in children under 5 years old. It is a leading cause of hospital admission and mortality worldwide, especially in low-income settings. In the UK, viral gastroenteritis is the most frequent cause.

concepts.title: Dehydration – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of dehydration in children include acute gastroenteritis (viral or bacterial), inadequate fluid intake, excessive sweating, diabetic ketoacidosis, and heat exposure. Risk factors include young age (<2 years), prematurity, and underlying chronic illnesses.

concepts.title: Dehydration – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Dehydration results from a net loss of water exceeding intake, causing hypovolaemia and hyperosmolarity. This leads to reduced tissue perfusion and cellular dysfunction. In children, extracellular fluid volume depletion occurs rapidly due to higher body water content and metabolic rate.

concepts.title: Dehydration – Clinical features: General signs
concepts.content: Signs of dehydration in children include dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, decreased skin turgor, delayed capillary refill (>2 seconds), tachycardia, hypotension in severe cases, and reduced urine output (oliguria).

concepts.title: Dehydration – Clinical features: Severity classification
concepts.content: Mild dehydration presents with thirst and dry mouth; moderate dehydration includes additional signs such as sunken eyes, reduced urine output, and lethargy; severe dehydration is characterised by signs of shock including tachycardia, hypotension, cold extremities, and decreased consciousness.

concepts.title: Dehydration – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations include blood tests (serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine, blood glucose), blood gas analysis to assess acid-base status, urine analysis, and assessment of weight loss compared to baseline. In severe cases, capillary blood lactate may be measured.

concepts.title: Dehydration – Management: Oral rehydration therapy
concepts.content: Mild to moderate dehydration is managed with oral rehydration therapy (ORT) using oral rehydration salts (ORS) solution containing 75 mmol/L sodium, 75 mmol/L glucose, 20 mmol/L potassium, and 10 mmol/L citrate. The WHO recommends 50-100 ml/kg over 3-4 hours.

concepts.title: Dehydration – Management: Intravenous fluid therapy
concepts.content: Severe dehydration or shock requires intravenous fluid resuscitation with isotonic fluids such as 0.9% sodium chloride or Hartmann's solution. Initial bolus dose is 20 ml/kg over 15-30 minutes, repeated as needed. Subsequent maintenance fluids are calculated using Holliday-Segar method.

concepts.title: Dehydration – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of dehydration include hypovolaemic shock, acute kidney injury, electrolyte imbalances (hyponatraemia, hypernatraemia, hypokalaemia), seizures, and in severe cases, death.

concepts.title: Dehydration – Prognosis
concepts.content: With prompt recognition and appropriate management, the prognosis of dehydration in children is excellent. Delayed treatment or severe dehydration increases risk of morbidity and mortality, particularly in infants and children with comorbidities.

concepts.title: Developmental delay – Definition
concepts.content: Developmental delay is defined as a significant lag in one or more areas of development including gross/fine motor skills, speech and language, cognitive, social, and adaptive skills, compared to normative age expectations in paediatric patients.

concepts.title: Developmental delay – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Developmental delay affects approximately 5-10% of children in the UK, with higher prevalence in those born prematurely or with low birth weight.

concepts.title: Developmental delay – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of developmental delay include genetic disorders (e.g., Down syndrome), perinatal insults (e.g., hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy), infections (e.g., congenital CMV), metabolic conditions, and environmental factors such as neglect or deprivation.

concepts.title: Developmental delay – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Developmental delay results from disruptions in normal brain development or function affecting neuronal migration, synaptogenesis, or myelination, leading to impaired acquisition of developmental milestones.

concepts.title: Developmental delay – Clinical features: Gross and fine motor delay
concepts.content: Children with developmental delay may present with delayed milestones such as sitting unsupported beyond 9 months, walking independently beyond 18 months, or poor hand-eye coordination.

concepts.title: Developmental delay – Clinical features: Speech and language problems
concepts.content: Speech delay is common, with children failing to babble by 12 months or speak single words by 18 months, often accompanied by difficulties in language comprehension.

concepts.title: Developmental delay – Clinical features: Behavioural difficulties
concepts.content: Some children with developmental delay exhibit behavioural difficulties including hyperactivity, inattention, or autistic features.

concepts.title: Developmental delay – Investigations
concepts.content: Initial investigations include developmental screening tools (e.g., Ages and Stages Questionnaire), hearing and vision assessments, and targeted blood tests such as thyroid function, metabolic screen, and genetic testing as indicated.

concepts.title: Developmental delay – Management
concepts.content: Management includes early intervention with multidisciplinary input from speech and language therapists, occupational therapists, physiotherapists, and educational support; addressing underlying causes where possible.

concepts.title: Developmental delay – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include increased risk of learning disabilities, social isolation, behavioural problems, and reduced independence in adulthood.

concepts.title: Developmental delay – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis varies widely depending on the underlying cause and severity; early intervention improves outcomes, but some children may have persistent disabilities requiring lifelong support.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Definition
concepts.content: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a serious acute complication of diabetes mellitus characterised by hyperglycaemia (blood glucose >11 mmol/L), metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L), and ketonaemia or ketonuria.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: DKA is the most common presentation of new-onset type 1 diabetes in children in the UK, occurring in approximately 25-30% of cases at diagnosis. It also occurs in children with known diabetes due to insulin omission or intercurrent illness.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: DKA is caused by absolute or relative insulin deficiency combined with increased counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, cortisol, catecholamines). Risk factors include new diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, infection, missed insulin doses, and physiological stress.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Insulin deficiency leads to decreased glucose utilisation and increased lipolysis, resulting in free fatty acid release and hepatic ketogenesis. Accumulation of ketone bodies causes metabolic acidosis. Hyperglycaemia induces osmotic diuresis causing dehydration and electrolyte imbalances.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Clinical features: Dehydration
concepts.content: Children with DKA commonly present with signs of dehydration including dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, and hypotension in severe cases.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Clinical features: Vomiting
concepts.content: Vomiting is a common presenting symptom in paediatric DKA due to metabolic acidosis and gastric irritation.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
concepts.content: Abdominal pain occurs frequently in children with DKA, often mimicking an acute abdomen but typically resolving with treatment of ketoacidosis.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Clinical features: Kussmaul breathing
concepts.content: Kussmaul breathing, a deep and laboured respiratory pattern, is a compensatory mechanism for metabolic acidosis seen in DKA.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Clinical features: Altered consciousness
concepts.content: Severe DKA may present with decreased or loss of consciousness due to cerebral oedema or severe acidosis.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Investigations: Blood glucose and ketones
concepts.content: Diagnosis requires blood glucose >11 mmol/L and presence of ketones in blood (>3 mmol/L) or urine (ketonuria).

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Investigations: Blood gas analysis
concepts.content: Arterial or venous blood gas shows metabolic acidosis with pH <7.3 and bicarbonate <15 mmol/L in DKA.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Investigations: Electrolytes and renal function
concepts.content: Serum electrolytes typically show hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia (masked by acidosis), and elevated urea and creatinine due to dehydration.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Management: Fluid resuscitation
concepts.content: Initial management includes cautious intravenous fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride at 10-20 mL/kg over 1-2 hours to restore circulatory volume, avoiding rapid correction to prevent cerebral oedema.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Management: Insulin therapy
concepts.content: Start intravenous insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour after initial fluid resuscitation; do not give insulin as bolus. Continue until acidosis resolves (pH >7.3, bicarbonate >15 mmol/L).

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Management: Electrolyte monitoring and replacement
concepts.content: Monitor serum potassium closely; replace potassium once urine output is confirmed and serum potassium <5.5 mmol/L, typically adding 40 mmol potassium chloride per litre of IV fluids.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Management: Avoidance of cerebral oedema
concepts.content: Prevent cerebral oedema by avoiding rapid fluid administration and rapid correction of hyperglycaemia; monitor neurological status closely during treatment.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Complications
concepts.content: Potential complications include cerebral oedema (most common cause of mortality), hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, thrombosis, and acute kidney injury.

concepts.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis – Prognosis
concepts.content: With prompt recognition and appropriate management, mortality from paediatric DKA in the UK is low (<1%). Neurological sequelae may occur if cerebral oedema develops.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Definition
concepts.content: Diabetes mellitus type 1 is an autoimmune condition characterised by destruction of pancreatic beta cells leading to absolute insulin deficiency. Type 2 diabetes mellitus involves insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Type 1 diabetes is the most common form of diabetes in children in the UK, with an incidence of approximately 25 per 100,000 children per year. Type 2 diabetes is increasing in prevalence among adolescents, particularly in those with obesity and ethnic minority backgrounds.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Type 1 diabetes is associated with genetic susceptibility (HLA-DR3 and DR4) and environmental triggers such as viral infections. Type 2 diabetes risk factors include obesity, family history, sedentary lifestyle, and certain ethnicities (South Asian, African-Caribbean).

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: In type 1 diabetes, autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causes absolute insulin deficiency. In type 2 diabetes, peripheral insulin resistance leads to compensatory hyperinsulinaemia and eventual beta cell dysfunction.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Clinical features: Polydipsia
concepts.content: Polydipsia (excessive thirst) is a common presenting symptom in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes due to osmotic diuresis caused by hyperglycaemia.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Clinical features: Polyuria and enuresis
concepts.content: Polyuria and secondary nocturnal enuresis occur due to osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia in children with diabetes mellitus.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Clinical features: Weight loss
concepts.content: Unintentional weight loss is a common feature in type 1 diabetes due to catabolism from insulin deficiency.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Clinical features: Fatigue
concepts.content: Fatigue is commonly reported in children with uncontrolled diabetes due to hyperglycaemia and metabolic derangements.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Clinical features: Diabetic ketoacidosis presentation
concepts.content: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) presents with dehydration, vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, and decreased consciousness in children with type 1 diabetes.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Investigations: Blood glucose
concepts.content: Diagnosis is confirmed by a fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L or random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms. HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%) supports diagnosis.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Investigations: Autoantibodies
concepts.content: Type 1 diabetes is associated with positive pancreatic autoantibodies including anti-GAD, anti-IA2, and islet cell antibodies.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Management: Insulin therapy
concepts.content: Type 1 diabetes requires lifelong insulin therapy. Basal-bolus regimens use long-acting insulin (e.g., insulin detemir) once or twice daily and rapid-acting insulin (e.g., insulin aspart) before meals. Doses are individualised based on blood glucose monitoring.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Management: Lifestyle and oral therapy in type 2
concepts.content: Type 2 diabetes management in children includes lifestyle modification (diet and exercise) and metformin as first-line oral therapy, starting at 500 mg once daily, titrated to 1 g twice daily as tolerated.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Complications: Acute diabetic ketoacidosis
concepts.content: DKA is a life-threatening complication characterised by hyperglycaemia, metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3), ketonaemia (>3 mmol/L), dehydration, and electrolyte disturbances requiring urgent treatment.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Complications: Long-term microvascular complications
concepts.content: Long-term complications include retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy. Annual screening for microalbuminuria and retinal examination is recommended from age 12 or 5 years after diagnosis.

concepts.title: Diabetes mellitus type 1 and 2 – Prognosis
concepts.content: With optimal glycaemic control, children with diabetes can have a normal lifespan; however, poor control increases risk of acute and chronic complications reducing life expectancy by up to 10 years.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Definition
concepts.content: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a pathological process characterised by systemic activation of coagulation pathways leading to widespread microvascular thrombosis and consumption of platelets and coagulation factors, resulting in bleeding and organ dysfunction.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Epidemiology
concepts.content: DIC occurs in paediatric patients as a complication of various underlying conditions such as sepsis, trauma, malignancy, and severe burns. The incidence varies depending on the underlying cause, with neonatal DIC being more common in premature infants and those with perinatal asphyxia.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of DIC in paediatric patients include severe bacterial sepsis (especially meningococcal septicaemia), viral infections, malignancies such as acute promyelocytic leukaemia, severe trauma, burns, and complications of prematurity.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: DIC results from excessive thrombin generation causing fibrin deposition in microvasculature, consumption of platelets and clotting factors, activation of fibrinolysis, and secondary bleeding. This leads to microvascular thrombosis, multi-organ ischaemia, and haemorrhagic manifestations.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Clinical features: Bruising
concepts.content: Paediatric patients with DIC commonly present with bruising due to thrombocytopenia and consumption of clotting factors.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Clinical features: Shock
concepts.content: Shock may develop in paediatric patients with DIC secondary to underlying sepsis or massive bleeding.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Clinical features: The sick child
concepts.content: Children with DIC often appear acutely unwell with signs of systemic illness including fever, pallor, tachycardia, and altered consciousness.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Investigations
concepts.content: Laboratory findings in DIC include prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), low fibrinogen (<1.0 g/L), thrombocytopenia (platelets <100 x10^9/L), elevated D-dimer and fibrin degradation products, and evidence of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia on blood film.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Management
concepts.content: Management of paediatric DIC focuses on treating the underlying cause, supportive care including blood product replacement (platelets if <50 x10^9/L with bleeding, fresh frozen plasma 15-20 mL/kg to replace clotting factors, cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen <1.0 g/L), and maintaining organ perfusion. Heparin is rarely used and only considered in chronic DIC with predominant thrombosis.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of DIC in children include multi-organ failure due to microvascular thrombosis, severe bleeding, shock, and death if untreated or underlying cause is not controlled.

concepts.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause and severity of DIC. Early recognition and treatment improve outcomes; however, mortality remains high in severe cases, especially in neonates and children with sepsis.

concepts.title: Drug overdose – Definition
concepts.content: Drug overdose in paediatrics refers to the ingestion or administration of a medication in quantities greater than recommended, leading to toxic effects or poisoning.

concepts.title: Drug overdose – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Paediatric drug overdose is a common cause of emergency hospital admissions in the UK, with accidental ingestions most frequent in children under 5 years and intentional overdoses more common in adolescents.

concepts.title: Drug overdose – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of paediatric drug overdose include accidental ingestion of adult medications such as paracetamol, ibuprofen, and opioids, as well as intentional overdose in adolescents often associated with self-harm or substance misuse.

concepts.title: Drug overdose – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Toxic effects in paediatric drug overdose occur due to excessive plasma concentrations of the drug leading to cellular toxicity, organ dysfunction, and metabolic disturbances depending on the drug involved.

concepts.title: Drug overdose – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
concepts.content: Paediatric patients with drug overdose may present with decreased level of consciousness or coma, depending on the drug and dose ingested.

concepts.title: Drug overdose – Clinical features: Fits/seizures
concepts.content: Seizures may occur in paediatric drug overdose, particularly with agents such as tricyclic antidepressants, theophylline, or isoniazid.

concepts.title: Drug overdose – Clinical features: Vomiting
concepts.content: Vomiting is a common early symptom in paediatric drug overdose and may be induced by the toxic effects of the drug or as a protective response.

concepts.title: Drug overdose – Clinical features: Overdose
concepts.content: Clinical signs of overdose vary by drug but may include altered mental status, respiratory depression, hypotension, arrhythmias, and metabolic abnormalities.

concepts.title: Drug overdose – Investigations
concepts.content: Initial investigations include blood glucose, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, blood gas analysis, ECG, and specific drug levels such as paracetamol and salicylate concentrations.

concepts.title: Drug overdose – Management
concepts.content: Management includes stabilisation of airway, breathing, and circulation, administration of activated charcoal if within 1 hour of ingestion, specific antidotes such as N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol overdose, and supportive care in a paediatric intensive care setting if required.

concepts.title: Drug overdose – Complications
concepts.content: Potential complications include respiratory failure, cardiac arrhythmias, hepatic failure (notably with paracetamol overdose), renal failure, and neurological damage.

concepts.title: Drug overdose – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis depends on the drug involved, dose, time to treatment, and presence of complications; early recognition and treatment generally result in good outcomes in paediatric patients.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Definition
concepts.content: Eating disorders in paediatrics are a group of mental health conditions characterised by abnormal eating behaviours and preoccupation with body weight or shape, including anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge-eating disorder.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Eating disorders affect approximately 1-3% of adolescents in the UK, with a higher prevalence in females (up to 10 times more common) and peak incidence between ages 12 and 18 years.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for paediatric eating disorders include genetic predisposition, female sex, adolescence, family history of psychiatric illness, societal pressure for thinness, low self-esteem, and comorbid mental health disorders such as anxiety and depression.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Eating disorders involve complex interactions between neurobiological, psychological, and environmental factors leading to dysregulation of appetite, reward pathways, and cognitive distortions about body image and food.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Clinical features: Behavioural difficulties in childhood
concepts.content: Children with eating disorders often present with behavioural difficulties including food restriction, excessive exercise, secretive eating, and social withdrawal.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Clinical features: Dehydration
concepts.content: Dehydration may occur in paediatric eating disorders due to vomiting, laxative abuse, or inadequate fluid intake.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Clinical features: Self-harm
concepts.content: Self-harm and suicidal thoughts are common in paediatric patients with eating disorders, occurring in up to 30% of cases, necessitating careful mental health assessment.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
concepts.content: Severe malnutrition in eating disorders can lead to hypoglycaemia and electrolyte imbalances causing decreased consciousness or coma.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Investigations
concepts.content: Initial investigations include full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests, thyroid function, glucose, ECG to assess bradycardia or QT prolongation, and bone density scans if indicated.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Management
concepts.content: Management includes a multidisciplinary approach with medical stabilisation, nutritional rehabilitation aiming for gradual weight gain of 0.5-1 kg/week, psychological therapies such as family-based treatment, and pharmacotherapy only for comorbid conditions.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include cardiac arrhythmias, electrolyte disturbances (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia), osteoporosis, growth retardation, amenorrhoea, and increased risk of suicide.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis varies; approximately 50% of paediatric patients recover fully with treatment, 30% have a chronic course, and mortality rates are around 5-10%, mainly due to medical complications or suicide.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Definition
concepts.content: Epididymitis and orchitis refer to inflammation of the epididymis and testis respectively, commonly presenting with scrotal pain and swelling in paediatric patients.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Epididymitis and orchitis are uncommon in prepubertal boys but more frequent in adolescents, with a peak incidence in boys aged 15-19 years. Viral orchitis, particularly mumps orchitis, is a notable cause in the paediatric population.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of epididymitis and orchitis in children include viral infections such as mumps virus, bacterial infections often associated with urinary tract infections or sexually transmitted infections in adolescents, and trauma. Risk factors include recent urinary tract instrumentation, congenital urinary tract abnormalities, and unprotected sexual activity in adolescents.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Inflammation of the epididymis and/or testis occurs due to infection or immune response, leading to increased blood flow, oedema, and infiltration of inflammatory cells. This results in scrotal pain, swelling, and sometimes systemic symptoms such as fever.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Clinical features: Scrotal/testicular pain and swelling
concepts.content: The most common presentation is acute onset of unilateral scrotal or testicular pain and swelling, often accompanied by erythema and tenderness on examination.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Fever is commonly present in paediatric patients with epididymitis and orchitis, reflecting systemic inflammatory response.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Clinical features: Urinary symptoms
concepts.content: Some children may present with urinary symptoms such as dysuria, frequency, or urgency, especially if bacterial infection is the underlying cause.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations include urine dipstick and microscopy to detect infection, urethral swabs for sexually transmitted infections in adolescents, scrotal ultrasound with Doppler to differentiate from testicular torsion, and blood tests including full blood count and inflammatory markers.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Management
concepts.content: Management includes analgesia with paracetamol and NSAIDs, scrotal support, and antibiotics if bacterial infection is suspected. Empirical antibiotic therapy in children over 15 years includes ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10 days, adjusted for age and weight. Viral orchitis requires supportive care only.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Complications
concepts.content: Potential complications include abscess formation, testicular infarction, infertility due to impaired spermatogenesis, and chronic epididymitis.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Prognosis
concepts.content: With prompt diagnosis and appropriate treatment, prognosis is generally good with resolution of symptoms. Delayed treatment increases risk of complications including infertility.

concepts.title: Epilepsy – Definition
concepts.content: Epilepsy is a neurological disorder characterised by a predisposition to generate epileptic seizures, defined by at least two unprovoked seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart.

concepts.title: Epilepsy – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Epilepsy affects approximately 5 per 1000 children in the UK, with the highest incidence in the first year of life and during adolescence.

concepts.title: Epilepsy – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of epilepsy in children include genetic factors, structural brain abnormalities (e.g. cortical dysplasia), perinatal brain injury, central nervous system infections, and metabolic disorders.

concepts.title: Epilepsy – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Epileptic seizures result from abnormal, excessive, and synchronous neuronal activity in the brain, often due to an imbalance between excitatory glutamate and inhibitory GABA neurotransmission.

concepts.title: Epilepsy – Clinical features: Fits/seizures
concepts.content: Seizures in paediatric epilepsy can present as focal (with or without impaired awareness) or generalised seizures, including tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic, or atonic seizures.

concepts.title: Epilepsy – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
concepts.content: Generalised tonic-clonic seizures typically present with sudden loss of consciousness, tonic stiffening followed by clonic jerking, lasting 1-2 minutes, often followed by post-ictal drowsiness.

concepts.title: Epilepsy – Investigations
concepts.content: Initial investigations include EEG to detect epileptiform activity, brain MRI to identify structural abnormalities, and metabolic and genetic testing if indicated by clinical features.

concepts.title: Epilepsy – Management
concepts.content: First-line treatment for paediatric epilepsy is monotherapy with antiepileptic drugs such as sodium valproate (initial dose 10-15 mg/kg/day) or carbamazepine (5 mg/kg/day), titrated to seizure control and tolerability.

concepts.title: Epilepsy – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include status epilepticus, cognitive impairment, psychosocial difficulties, and increased risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP), which occurs in approximately 1 in 1000 children per year.

concepts.title: Epilepsy – Prognosis
concepts.content: Approximately 70% of children with epilepsy achieve seizure remission with appropriate treatment; prognosis is poorer in those with symptomatic epilepsy or developmental delay.

concepts.title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Definition
concepts.content: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) in paediatrics is the pathological retrograde flow of gastric contents into the oesophagus causing troublesome symptoms or complications.

concepts.title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Epidemiology
concepts.content: GORD affects up to 50% of infants under 3 months, with most cases resolving by 12-18 months; prevalence decreases with age.

concepts.title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for paediatric GORD include prematurity, neurological impairment, congenital oesophageal abnormalities (e.g., oesophageal atresia), and obesity.

concepts.title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: GORD results from transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations, impaired oesophageal clearance, delayed gastric emptying, or anatomical abnormalities leading to reflux of acidic gastric contents.

concepts.title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Clinical features: Vomiting
concepts.content: Frequent regurgitation or vomiting of feeds, often non-projectile and occurring after meals, is a common presentation in infants with GORD.

concepts.title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Clinical features: Infant feeding problems
concepts.content: Infants with GORD may exhibit feeding difficulties including refusal to feed, irritability during feeds, and poor weight gain.

concepts.title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Clinical features: Chronic cough and wheeze
concepts.content: Chronic cough and wheeze may occur due to aspiration of refluxed gastric contents causing airway irritation or reactive airway disease.

concepts.title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations are not routinely required but may include 24-hour oesophageal pH monitoring, oesophageal impedance, and upper GI contrast studies in complicated or atypical cases.

concepts.title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Management: Conservative measures
concepts.content: Initial management includes positional therapy (elevating the head of the cot), smaller frequent feeds, and thickening feeds with infant formula thickeners.

concepts.title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Management: Pharmacological treatment
concepts.content: If conservative measures fail, acid suppression with proton pump inhibitors (e.g., omeprazole 1 mg/kg once daily) or H2 receptor antagonists may be used, typically for 4-8 weeks.

concepts.title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Management: Surgical treatment
concepts.content: Surgical intervention (e.g., Nissen fundoplication) is reserved for severe, refractory cases with complications such as failure to thrive or recurrent aspiration pneumonia.

concepts.title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include oesophagitis, strictures, Barrett's oesophagus (rare in children), aspiration pneumonia, and failure to thrive.

concepts.title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease – Prognosis
concepts.content: Most infants with GORD improve spontaneously by 12-18 months; long-term prognosis is excellent with appropriate management.

concepts.title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Definition
concepts.content: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP) is a small vessel vasculitis characterised by IgA immune complex deposition, primarily affecting children and causing palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal involvement.

concepts.title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is the most common vasculitis in children, with an incidence of approximately 20 per 100,000 children per year, typically affecting those aged 3 to 15 years, with a slight male predominance.

concepts.title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is often preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection, commonly streptococcal or viral, which triggers IgA immune complex deposition; other risk factors include recent vaccinations and certain medications.

concepts.title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Henoch-Schonlein purpura results from IgA1-dominant immune complex deposition in small vessels, leading to leukocytoclastic vasculitis with inflammation and damage to vessel walls, causing purpura, arthritis, and renal involvement.

concepts.title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Clinical features: Acute rash
concepts.content: The characteristic rash of Henoch-Schonlein purpura is palpable purpura predominantly on the lower limbs and buttocks, occurring in nearly 100% of cases.

concepts.title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Clinical features: Acute joint pain/swelling
concepts.content: Arthritis or arthralgia occurs in approximately 80% of children with Henoch-Schonlein purpura, typically affecting knees and ankles with transient, non-erosive joint swelling and pain.

concepts.title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Clinical features: Acute abdominal pain
concepts.content: Abdominal pain occurs in up to 50% of children with Henoch-Schonlein purpura and may be colicky due to bowel vasculitis; it can be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and gastrointestinal bleeding.

concepts.title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Clinical features: Haematuria
concepts.content: Renal involvement in Henoch-Schonlein purpura occurs in 20-50% of cases, presenting as haematuria and/or proteinuria; microscopic haematuria is common, and nephritic syndrome may develop in severe cases.

concepts.title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis of Henoch-Schonlein purpura is clinical; investigations include urinalysis for haematuria and proteinuria, full blood count, renal function tests, and skin biopsy showing leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposition if diagnosis is uncertain.

concepts.title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Management
concepts.content: Management of Henoch-Schonlein purpura is mainly supportive including analgesia with paracetamol or NSAIDs; corticosteroids such as oral prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day may be used for severe abdominal pain or renal involvement; monitoring of renal function is essential.

concepts.title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of Henoch-Schonlein purpura include chronic kidney disease from persistent nephritis, intussusception due to bowel vasculitis, and rare severe gastrointestinal haemorrhage or perforation.

concepts.title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Prognosis
concepts.content: The prognosis of Henoch-Schonlein purpura in children is generally excellent, with over 90% achieving full recovery; however, 1-2% may develop chronic renal impairment requiring long-term follow-up.

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Definition
concepts.content: Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver, which in paediatric patients can be caused by infectious agents, autoimmune conditions, metabolic diseases, or toxins.

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: In the UK, paediatric hepatitis is most commonly caused by viral infections, with hepatitis A and B vaccination programmes reducing incidence; hepatitis C remains rare but significant in children born to infected mothers.

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of paediatric hepatitis in the UK include viral infections (hepatitis A, B, C, E, and rarely D), autoimmune hepatitis, metabolic disorders such as Wilson’s disease, and drug-induced liver injury from paracetamol overdose.

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Hepatitis causes liver inflammation due to immune-mediated hepatocyte injury triggered by viral infection, autoimmune attack, or toxic/metabolic insults, leading to hepatocyte necrosis and impaired liver function.

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Clinical features: Jaundice
concepts.content: Paediatric hepatitis commonly presents with jaundice characterised by yellowing of the skin and sclera due to elevated serum bilirubin levels, often >34 µmol/L (2 mg/dL).

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Children with acute viral hepatitis may present with fever, often low-grade, reflecting systemic viral infection.

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
concepts.content: Right upper quadrant or epigastric abdominal pain is a common symptom in paediatric hepatitis due to liver capsule inflammation.

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Clinical features: Fatigue and malaise
concepts.content: Children with hepatitis often experience fatigue and malaise due to systemic illness and impaired liver function.

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Investigations: Liver function tests
concepts.content: Liver function tests in paediatric hepatitis typically show elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), often >500 IU/L in acute viral hepatitis, with raised bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase.

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Investigations: Viral serology
concepts.content: Diagnosis of viral hepatitis in children involves serological testing for hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), hepatitis B core IgM antibody, and hepatitis C antibody with PCR for viral RNA if positive.

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Management: Supportive care
concepts.content: Management of paediatric hepatitis is primarily supportive including adequate hydration, nutrition, and avoidance of hepatotoxic drugs; hospital admission is required for severe cases or acute liver failure.

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Management: Antiviral therapy
concepts.content: In chronic hepatitis B infection in children, antiviral treatment with entecavir (0.015 mg/kg once daily, max 0.5 mg) or tenofovir may be indicated to reduce viral replication and liver damage.

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of paediatric hepatitis include acute liver failure, chronic liver disease with fibrosis and cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma particularly in chronic hepatitis B and C.

concepts.title: Hepatitis – Prognosis
concepts.content: The prognosis of paediatric hepatitis varies by cause; acute viral hepatitis A usually resolves completely with full recovery, while chronic hepatitis B or C may lead to long-term liver damage requiring specialist follow-up.

concepts.title: Hernias – Definition
concepts.content: A hernia is the protrusion of an organ or tissue through an abnormal opening in the surrounding muscle or connective tissue, commonly occurring in the abdominal wall in paediatric patients.

concepts.title: Hernias – Epidemiology
concepts.content: In the UK, paediatric inguinal hernias occur in approximately 1-5% of full-term infants and up to 30% of premature infants, with a male to female ratio of about 6:1.

concepts.title: Hernias – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for paediatric hernias include prematurity, low birth weight, male sex, family history of hernias, and conditions increasing intra-abdominal pressure such as chronic cough or constipation.

concepts.title: Hernias – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Paediatric hernias commonly result from a persistent processus vaginalis, allowing abdominal contents to protrude through the inguinal canal, or from weakness in the abdominal wall muscles.

concepts.title: Hernias – Clinical features: Abdominal mass
