concepts.content: Paediatric hernias typically present as a painless, reducible swelling in the groin or scrotum, which may become more prominent on crying or straining.

concepts.title: Hernias – Clinical features: Acute abdominal pain
concepts.content: Incarcerated or strangulated hernias present with acute, severe pain, tenderness, erythema over the swelling, and systemic signs such as vomiting and irritability.

concepts.title: Hernias – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis of paediatric hernias is primarily clinical; ultrasound may be used to confirm diagnosis or assess complications like incarceration, especially in atypical cases.

concepts.title: Hernias – Management
concepts.content: Elective surgical repair is recommended for paediatric inguinal hernias to prevent incarceration; timing depends on age and symptoms, with emergency surgery indicated for incarcerated hernias.

concepts.title: Hernias – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include incarceration, strangulation leading to bowel ischaemia, testicular ischaemia in males, and recurrence after surgical repair.

concepts.title: Hernias – Prognosis
concepts.content: With timely surgical repair, the prognosis for paediatric hernias is excellent, with low rates of recurrence and minimal long-term morbidity.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Definition
concepts.content: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is a double-stranded DNA virus causing infections primarily of the skin, mucous membranes, and central nervous system in paediatric patients. There are two types: HSV-1, commonly causing orolabial infections, and HSV-2, typically associated with genital infections.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Epidemiology
concepts.content: HSV infection is common in the UK paediatric population, with HSV-1 seroprevalence reaching 60-70% by adolescence. Neonatal herpes occurs in approximately 1 in 10,000 live births, often due to maternal primary infection near delivery.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Primary risk factors for paediatric HSV infection include close contact with infected individuals, maternal primary HSV infection during pregnancy, prematurity, and immunosuppression. Neonatal infection risk is highest with maternal primary genital HSV infection near delivery.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: HSV infects epithelial cells causing cytolysis and vesicular lesions; it establishes latency in sensory nerve ganglia with potential for reactivation. In neonates, HSV can disseminate causing severe systemic illness including encephalitis.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Paediatric HSV infection often presents with fever, which may be high-grade and persistent, especially in neonatal herpes and HSV encephalitis.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features: Acute rash
concepts.content: HSV causes painful grouped vesicular lesions on an erythematous base, commonly affecting the orolabial area in children (cold sores) and occasionally genital regions.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
concepts.content: HSV encephalitis in paediatric patients can present with altered mental status, decreased level of consciousness, seizures, and focal neurological signs.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis is confirmed by PCR testing of vesicle fluid, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), or blood. CSF analysis in HSV encephalitis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and normal glucose. MRI brain may show temporal lobe abnormalities.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Management
concepts.content: First-line treatment for paediatric HSV infection is intravenous aciclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 hours for 14-21 days in neonatal or CNS disease. Oral aciclovir or valaciclovir may be used for mucocutaneous disease. Supportive care includes hydration and analgesia.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of paediatric HSV infection include neonatal disseminated disease, HSV encephalitis causing long-term neurological impairment, keratitis leading to vision loss, and secondary bacterial infection of skin lesions.

concepts.title: Herpes simplex virus – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis depends on disease severity; neonatal HSV and HSV encephalitis have high morbidity and mortality despite treatment. Early aciclovir therapy improves outcomes, but neurological sequelae occur in up to 50% of encephalitis cases.

concepts.title: Human papilloma virus infection – Definition
concepts.content: Human papilloma virus (HPV) infection is a viral infection caused by human papillomaviruses, a group of DNA viruses that infect epithelial cells, leading to warts and potentially malignant lesions.

concepts.title: Human papilloma virus infection – Epidemiology
concepts.content: HPV infection is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections in the UK, with peak prevalence in adolescents and young adults. The UK HPV vaccination programme targets children aged 12-13 years to reduce infection rates.

concepts.title: Human papilloma virus infection – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for HPV infection in paediatric populations include early onset of sexual activity, multiple sexual partners, immunosuppression, and vertical transmission during childbirth.

concepts.title: Human papilloma virus infection – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: HPV infects basal epithelial cells through micro-abrasions, integrating viral DNA into host cells, causing epithelial proliferation and potential dysplasia, which may progress to malignancy in high-risk HPV types.

concepts.title: Human papilloma virus infection – Clinical features: Cutaneous warts
concepts.content: Cutaneous warts present as hyperkeratotic papules commonly on hands and feet in children, caused by HPV types 1, 2, and 4, often asymptomatic but may cause discomfort or cosmetic concern.

concepts.title: Human papilloma virus infection – Clinical features: Anogenital warts
concepts.content: Anogenital warts in paediatric patients may present as soft, flesh-coloured papules or cauliflower-like lesions around the genital or perianal area, caused mainly by HPV types 6 and 11.

concepts.title: Human papilloma virus infection – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; HPV DNA testing via PCR is used in specialised settings. Biopsy may be required for atypical lesions or suspected malignancy. Cytology screening is part of cervical screening in older adolescents.

concepts.title: Human papilloma virus infection – Management
concepts.content: Management includes watchful waiting for spontaneous resolution, topical treatments such as salicylic acid for cutaneous warts, cryotherapy, and surgical removal for persistent or symptomatic lesions. The UK HPV vaccination programme uses the quadrivalent or nonavalent vaccine at 12-13 years to prevent infection.

concepts.title: Human papilloma virus infection – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include persistent warts causing discomfort, psychological distress, and in rare cases, progression to malignancies such as cervical, vulvar, penile, or oropharyngeal cancers, especially with high-risk HPV types 16 and 18.

concepts.title: Human papilloma virus infection – Prognosis
concepts.content: Most HPV infections in children resolve spontaneously within 1-2 years without intervention. Vaccination significantly reduces the risk of persistent infection and HPV-related malignancies, improving long-term prognosis.

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Definition
concepts.content: Hypoglycaemia in paediatrics is defined as a plasma glucose concentration less than 2.6 mmol/L (47 mg/dL).

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Neonatal hypoglycaemia affects approximately 1 to 5 per 1000 live births in the UK, with higher incidence in preterm infants and those with low birth weight.

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of hypoglycaemia in children include hyperinsulinism, inborn errors of metabolism, endocrine deficiencies such as hypopituitarism or adrenal insufficiency, and prolonged fasting.

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Hypoglycaemia results from an imbalance between glucose utilisation and production, often due to excessive insulin or impaired gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis.

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Clinical features: Neurogenic symptoms
concepts.content: Neurogenic symptoms of hypoglycaemia in children include sweating, tremor, pallor, tachycardia, irritability, and hunger.

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Clinical features: Neuroglycopenic symptoms
concepts.content: Neuroglycopenic symptoms include lethargy, irritability, seizures (fits/seizures), decreased level of consciousness, and coma in severe hypoglycaemia.

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Investigations: Blood glucose measurement
concepts.content: Confirm hypoglycaemia by measuring plasma glucose; a level below 2.6 mmol/L in symptomatic children requires urgent treatment.

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Investigations: Critical sample
concepts.content: During hypoglycaemia, obtain a critical sample including insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, beta-hydroxybutyrate, free fatty acids, and lactate to aid diagnosis.

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Management: Initial treatment
concepts.content: Immediate treatment of hypoglycaemia involves administering 200 mg/kg of oral glucose (equivalent to 2 mL/kg of 10% glucose) if the child is conscious; if unconscious, give intravenous 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose over 5 minutes.

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Management: Maintenance therapy
concepts.content: After initial correction, maintain normoglycaemia with intravenous dextrose infusion (e.g., 10% dextrose at 6-8 mg/kg/min) and frequent feeds; monitor blood glucose regularly.

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Complications
concepts.content: Severe or prolonged hypoglycaemia may cause permanent neurological damage including developmental delay, seizures, and cerebral palsy.

concepts.title: Hypoglycaemia – Prognosis
concepts.content: The prognosis depends on the cause, severity, and duration of hypoglycaemia; early recognition and treatment improve neurological outcomes.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Definition
concepts.content: Hyposplenism refers to reduced splenic function, while splenectomy is the surgical removal of the spleen. Both conditions result in impaired immune function, particularly affecting the clearance of encapsulated bacteria.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Hyposplenism and splenectomy are uncommon in the paediatric population but occur in children with conditions such as sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, or following trauma or surgery. The prevalence of hyposplenism in sickle cell disease is high due to autosplenectomy.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of hyposplenism in children include sickle cell disease leading to autosplenectomy, thalassaemia, coeliac disease, and post-splenectomy status following trauma or haematological malignancy.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Loss of splenic function impairs clearance of encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis, increasing risk of severe infections. There is also reduced opsonisation and impaired antibody production.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Children with hyposplenism or splenectomy are at increased risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI), which commonly presents with sudden onset fever and rapid clinical deterioration.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
concepts.content: Post-splenectomy children may present with acute abdominal pain due to complications such as splenic remnant infarction or infection.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Investigations
concepts.content: Blood film may show Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells, and thrombocytosis. Immunological tests include pneumococcal antibody titres. Imaging may be used to confirm absence of splenic tissue post-splenectomy.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Management
concepts.content: Management includes lifelong prophylactic oral penicillin V (250 mg twice daily for children aged 5 years and older; 125 mg twice daily for younger children), vaccination against pneumococcus (PCV13 and PPSV23), Haemophilus influenzae type b, meningococcus (MenACWY and MenB), and annual influenza vaccination. Parents should be educated on seeking urgent medical attention for fever.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Complications
concepts.content: The major complication is overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI), a rapidly progressive sepsis with high mortality caused by encapsulated organisms, especially Streptococcus pneumoniae.

concepts.title: Hyposplenism/splenectomy – Prognosis
concepts.content: With appropriate vaccination, antibiotic prophylaxis, and education, children with hyposplenism or splenectomy have a significantly reduced risk of severe infection and good long-term prognosis.

concepts.title: Idiopathic arthritis – Definition
concepts.content: Idiopathic arthritis in paediatrics, also known as juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), is a heterogeneous group of autoimmune disorders characterised by persistent arthritis of unknown cause lasting for at least 6 weeks in children under 16 years of age.

concepts.title: Idiopathic arthritis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis affects approximately 1 in 1,000 children in the UK, with a slight female predominance. The peak age of onset is between 1 and 3 years, but it can present at any age before 16 years.

concepts.title: Idiopathic arthritis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: The exact cause of juvenile idiopathic arthritis is unknown, but it is believed to involve a combination of genetic predisposition (e.g., HLA-DRB1 alleles) and environmental triggers such as infections.

concepts.title: Idiopathic arthritis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is characterised by chronic synovial inflammation due to autoimmune mechanisms, leading to synovial hypertrophy, joint effusion, cartilage destruction, and potential joint deformity.

concepts.title: Idiopathic arthritis – Clinical features: Acute joint pain/swelling
concepts.content: Children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis typically present with persistent joint swelling, pain, and stiffness lasting more than 6 weeks, often affecting the knees, wrists, and ankles; morning stiffness is common.

concepts.title: Idiopathic arthritis – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis may present with quotidian high spiking fevers often exceeding 39°C, accompanied by a salmon-pink macular rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and serositis.

concepts.title: Idiopathic arthritis – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations include raised inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), normocytic anaemia, thrombocytosis, and negative rheumatoid factor in most cases; ANA positivity is common in oligoarticular JIA. Joint ultrasound or MRI may show synovitis.

concepts.title: Idiopathic arthritis – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Differential diagnoses include septic arthritis, reactive arthritis, haemarthrosis, malignancy (e.g., leukaemia), and other connective tissue diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus.

concepts.title: Idiopathic arthritis – Management
concepts.content: Management includes NSAIDs such as naproxen 10-15 mg/kg/day in divided doses, intra-articular corticosteroid injections, and disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) like methotrexate 10-15 mg/m2 weekly. Biologic agents (e.g., etanercept) are used for refractory cases. Regular physiotherapy is essential.

concepts.title: Idiopathic arthritis – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include joint damage and deformity, growth disturbances, uveitis (especially in ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA), and macrophage activation syndrome in systemic JIA.

concepts.title: Idiopathic arthritis – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis varies by subtype; oligoarticular JIA often has a good prognosis with remission in 50-70% of cases, whereas polyarticular and systemic forms may have a more chronic course with persistent disability.

concepts.title: Impetigo – Definition
concepts.content: Impetigo is a common, superficial bacterial skin infection primarily affecting children, characterised by honey-coloured crusted lesions typically around the nose and mouth.

concepts.title: Impetigo – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Impetigo is most common in children aged 2 to 5 years, with higher incidence in summer months and in areas of overcrowding or poor hygiene.

concepts.title: Impetigo – Aetiology and Risk factors
concepts.content: Impetigo is caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes infection of superficial skin; risk factors include minor skin trauma, insect bites, eczema, and close contact with infected individuals.

concepts.title: Impetigo – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Bacterial colonisation of superficial epidermis leads to localised skin inflammation, vesicle formation, rupture, and characteristic honey-coloured crusting; exfoliative toxins from S. aureus may cause bullous impetigo.

concepts.title: Impetigo – Clinical features: Non-bullous impetigo
concepts.content: Presents with erythematous macules progressing to vesicles and pustules that rupture to form characteristic thick, honey-coloured crusts, commonly around the nose and mouth.

concepts.title: Impetigo – Clinical features: Bullous impetigo
concepts.content: Characterised by fragile, fluid-filled bullae that rupture easily leaving a thin brown crust, often caused by exfoliative toxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus.

concepts.title: Impetigo – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis is clinical; bacterial swab for culture and sensitivity may be taken if lesions are extensive, recurrent, or not responding to treatment.

concepts.title: Impetigo – Management: Topical antibiotics
concepts.content: Mild cases are treated with topical fusidic acid 2% ointment applied three times daily for 5 days.

concepts.title: Impetigo – Management: Systemic antibiotics
concepts.content: Extensive or bullous impetigo requires oral antibiotics such as flucloxacillin 25-50 mg/kg/day divided into 4 doses for 7 days; erythromycin 30-50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses is an alternative if penicillin allergy is present.

concepts.title: Impetigo – Management: Supportive care
concepts.content: Advise good hygiene, regular handwashing, and keeping nails short to reduce spread; lesions should be gently cleaned with soap and water.

concepts.title: Impetigo – Complications
concepts.content: Potential complications include cellulitis, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and rarely, bacteraemia or scarring.

concepts.title: Impetigo – Prognosis
concepts.content: With appropriate treatment, impetigo usually resolves within 7-10 days without scarring; recurrence is common if hygiene measures are not maintained.

concepts.title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Definition
concepts.content: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) in paediatrics refers to a group of chronic inflammatory conditions of the gastrointestinal tract, primarily including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, characterised by relapsing and remitting inflammation leading to symptoms such as diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and growth failure.

concepts.title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Epidemiology
concepts.content: The incidence of paediatric inflammatory bowel disease in the UK is approximately 5.2 per 100,000 children per year, with a rising trend especially in children under 10 years old. It affects males and females equally and is more common in Caucasian populations.

concepts.title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Paediatric IBD aetiology is multifactorial involving genetic predisposition (e.g., NOD2 mutations), environmental factors such as smoking exposure, diet, and alterations in gut microbiota, as well as immune dysregulation leading to chronic intestinal inflammation.

concepts.title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: IBD pathophysiology involves an inappropriate immune response to intestinal microbiota in genetically susceptible children, resulting in chronic mucosal inflammation, epithelial barrier disruption, and tissue damage in the gastrointestinal tract.

concepts.title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Clinical features: Diarrhoea
concepts.content: Chronic diarrhoea is a common presenting symptom in paediatric IBD, often bloody in ulcerative colitis and may be non-bloody in Crohn's disease, lasting for more than four weeks and associated with urgency and tenesmus.

concepts.title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
concepts.content: Children with IBD frequently present with chronic or intermittent abdominal pain, which may be colicky or constant, often localised to the right lower quadrant in Crohn's disease or more diffuse in ulcerative colitis.

concepts.title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Clinical features: Growth failure and delayed puberty
concepts.content: Growth failure occurs in up to 30% of children with IBD due to chronic inflammation, malnutrition, and corticosteroid use; delayed puberty is also common, requiring regular monitoring of height, weight, and pubertal staging.

concepts.title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Clinical features: Extraintestinal manifestations
concepts.content: Extraintestinal manifestations in paediatric IBD include arthritis (acute joint pain/swelling), erythema nodosum, uveitis, and primary sclerosing cholangitis, occurring in up to 25% of cases and requiring multidisciplinary management.

concepts.title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Investigations: Blood tests
concepts.content: Blood tests in paediatric IBD typically show raised inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR), anaemia (often microcytic or normocytic), hypoalbuminaemia, and elevated faecal calprotectin (>250 µg/g) indicating intestinal inflammation.

concepts.title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Investigations: Endoscopy and biopsy
concepts.content: Definitive diagnosis of paediatric IBD requires ileocolonoscopy with biopsy demonstrating characteristic histological features: transmural inflammation and granulomas in Crohn's disease, and continuous mucosal inflammation in ulcerative colitis.

concepts.title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Management: Induction of remission
concepts.content: Induction of remission in paediatric IBD commonly involves corticosteroids such as oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg/day (max 40 mg/day) for 4-6 weeks, with tapering thereafter; exclusive enteral nutrition is an alternative first-line therapy in Crohn's disease.

concepts.title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Management: Maintenance therapy
concepts.content: Maintenance therapy includes immunomodulators such as azathioprine (2-2.5 mg/kg/day) or methotrexate (15 mg/m2 weekly), and biologics like infliximab (5 mg/kg at 0, 2, and 6 weeks then every 8 weeks) for moderate to severe paediatric IBD.

concepts.title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of paediatric IBD include strictures, fistulae, growth retardation, colorectal cancer (rare in children), toxic megacolon, and increased risk of osteoporosis due to chronic inflammation and corticosteroid use.

concepts.title: Inflammatory bowel disease – Prognosis
concepts.content: Paediatric IBD is a lifelong condition with variable prognosis; early diagnosis and treatment improve growth outcomes and quality of life. Approximately 20-30% of children require surgery within 10 years of diagnosis, especially in Crohn's disease.

concepts.title: Influenza – Definition
concepts.content: Influenza is an acute viral respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses A and B, characterised by sudden onset of fever, cough, and systemic symptoms.

concepts.title: Influenza – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Influenza affects all age groups but is particularly common in children under 5 years in the UK, with seasonal epidemics occurring mainly in winter months (December to March).

concepts.title: Influenza – Aetiology and Risk factors
concepts.content: Influenza is caused by influenza A and B viruses transmitted via respiratory droplets; risk factors in children include age under 5 years, chronic respiratory disease, immunosuppression, and lack of vaccination.

concepts.title: Influenza – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Influenza virus infects respiratory epithelial cells causing cell death and inflammation, leading to airway epithelial damage, increased mucus production, and systemic cytokine release responsible for fever and malaise.

concepts.title: Influenza – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Children with influenza typically present with sudden onset high fever, often >38.5°C, lasting 3-4 days.

concepts.title: Influenza – Clinical features: Cough and respiratory symptoms
concepts.content: A dry cough and sore throat are common in paediatric influenza, often accompanied by nasal congestion and rhinorrhoea.

concepts.title: Influenza – Clinical features: Systemic symptoms
concepts.content: Children often experience myalgia, headache, lethargy, and anorexia during influenza infection.

concepts.title: Influenza – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; nasopharyngeal swab PCR testing confirms influenza virus; blood tests are usually not required unless complications suspected.

concepts.title: Influenza – Management
concepts.content: Supportive care includes hydration and antipyretics such as paracetamol (15 mg/kg every 4-6 hours, max 60 mg/kg/day) or ibuprofen (10 mg/kg every 6-8 hours, max 30 mg/kg/day). Oseltamivir is recommended for children at high risk or with severe disease at 3 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days.

concepts.title: Influenza – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include secondary bacterial pneumonia, otitis media, febrile seizures, and exacerbation of asthma or chronic respiratory disease.

concepts.title: Influenza – Prognosis
concepts.content: Most children recover fully within 1-2 weeks without sequelae; prognosis is excellent in healthy children but worse in those with comorbidities.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Definition
concepts.content: Intestinal obstruction is a blockage that prevents the normal passage of intestinal contents, while ileus is a functional impairment of intestinal motility without mechanical obstruction, both causing abdominal distension and vomiting in paediatric patients.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Intestinal obstruction is a common surgical emergency in paediatrics, with causes varying by age; neonatal causes include atresia and malrotation, while older children commonly present with intussusception or adhesions. Ileus is frequently seen postoperatively or with systemic illness.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of paediatric intestinal obstruction include congenital anomalies (e.g. atresia, malrotation with volvulus), intussusception, Hirschsprung disease, and postoperative adhesions; ileus risk factors include abdominal surgery, peritonitis, electrolyte imbalances, and certain medications.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Mechanical intestinal obstruction causes proximal bowel dilation, increased intraluminal pressure, and impaired venous return leading to bowel wall oedema and ischaemia; ileus results from disruption of normal enteric nervous system signalling causing decreased peristalsis without physical blockage.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Clinical features: Vomiting
concepts.content: Vomiting is an early and common symptom of intestinal obstruction in children; bilious vomiting suggests distal obstruction and requires urgent assessment.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Clinical features: Abdominal distension
concepts.content: Abdominal distension is a key clinical sign in paediatric intestinal obstruction and ileus, often progressive and associated with tympanic bowel loops on palpation.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
concepts.content: Acute colicky abdominal pain is typical in mechanical intestinal obstruction due to intermittent peristalsis against the blockage; ileus usually causes less severe, diffuse discomfort.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Clinical features: Constipation and failure to pass flatus
concepts.content: In intestinal obstruction, children often present with constipation and failure to pass flatus, indicating distal bowel blockage.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Investigations: Abdominal X-ray
concepts.content: Abdominal X-ray in paediatric intestinal obstruction typically shows dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels and absence of gas distal to the obstruction; in ileus, diffuse bowel dilation without a transition point is seen.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Investigations: Ultrasound
concepts.content: Ultrasound is useful in paediatric intestinal obstruction to identify intussusception, assess bowel viability, and detect free fluid; it is non-invasive and preferred in children.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Management: Initial resuscitation
concepts.content: Initial management includes fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloid (e.g. 0.9% saline), correction of electrolyte imbalances, nasogastric decompression, and nil by mouth status in paediatric intestinal obstruction and ileus.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Management: Surgical intervention
concepts.content: Surgical intervention is indicated in paediatric intestinal obstruction caused by volvulus, atresia, or failed conservative management; timing depends on clinical stability and risk of bowel ischaemia.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include bowel ischaemia, perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, electrolyte disturbances, and shock, which can be life-threatening in paediatric intestinal obstruction and ileus.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction and ileus – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis depends on cause, timeliness of diagnosis, and treatment; early intervention in mechanical obstruction generally results in good outcomes, whereas delayed treatment increases morbidity and mortality.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Definition
concepts.content: Intussusception is a condition where a segment of the intestine telescopes into an adjacent distal segment, causing bowel obstruction and potential ischaemia.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children aged 6 months to 3 years, with an incidence of approximately 1 to 4 per 1,000 live births in the UK.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Most cases of intussusception in infants are idiopathic; however, risk factors include viral infections such as adenovirus, Meckel's diverticulum, polyps, and lymphoid hyperplasia.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Telescoping of the proximal bowel segment into the distal bowel causes venous congestion, bowel wall oedema, and can progress to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation if untreated.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Clinical features: Acute abdominal pain
concepts.content: Children typically present with sudden onset intermittent severe colicky abdominal pain, often causing the child to draw their knees up and cry inconsolably.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Clinical features: Vomiting
concepts.content: Vomiting is a common symptom and may initially be non-bilious but can progress to bilious vomiting as obstruction worsens.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Clinical features: Red currant jelly stools
concepts.content: A classic late sign is the passage of red currant jelly stools, caused by intestinal mucosal sloughing and blood mixing with mucus.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Clinical features: Abdominal mass
concepts.content: A palpable, sausage-shaped, tender abdominal mass is often felt in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium during physical examination.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Investigations: Ultrasound
concepts.content: Abdominal ultrasound is the diagnostic investigation of choice, showing the characteristic 'target' or 'doughnut' sign representing the intussuscepted bowel.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Investigations: Contrast enema
concepts.content: A therapeutic and diagnostic air or contrast (barium) enema can confirm intussusception and may reduce it by hydrostatic pressure; success rates are approximately 75-90%.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Management: Initial resuscitation
concepts.content: Initial management includes fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline to correct dehydration and electrolyte imbalances, and nasogastric decompression if vomiting is severe.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Management: Non-surgical reduction
concepts.content: Non-surgical reduction using pneumatic (air) or hydrostatic (contrast) enema under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance is first-line treatment in stable patients without signs of perforation.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Management: Surgical treatment
concepts.content: Surgical intervention is required if non-surgical reduction fails, if there is evidence of bowel perforation or peritonitis, or if the patient is unstable; surgery involves manual reduction or bowel resection.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include bowel necrosis, perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, and recurrence of intussusception which occurs in approximately 10% of cases after successful reduction.

concepts.title: Intussusception – Prognosis
concepts.content: With prompt diagnosis and treatment, prognosis is excellent with low mortality; delayed treatment increases risk of bowel necrosis and mortality.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Definition
concepts.content: Leukaemia is a malignant neoplasm of haematopoietic stem cells characterised by uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal white blood cells in the bone marrow and peripheral blood.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Leukaemia is the most common childhood cancer in the UK, accounting for approximately 30% of all paediatric malignancies, with an incidence of around 4 per 100,000 children per year.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Aetiology and Risk Factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for paediatric leukaemia include genetic conditions such as Down syndrome, exposure to ionising radiation, previous chemotherapy, and certain inherited bone marrow failure syndromes.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Leukaemia arises from clonal proliferation of immature lymphoid or myeloid precursors in the bone marrow, leading to marrow failure and infiltration of other organs.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Clinical features: Pallor
concepts.content: Pallor is a common presenting feature due to anaemia caused by marrow infiltration and reduced red cell production.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Clinical features: Bruising
concepts.content: Bruising and petechiae occur due to thrombocytopenia from bone marrow failure.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Fever is frequently present due to neutropenia and increased susceptibility to infection.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Clinical features: Lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: Lymphadenopathy may be present due to infiltration of lymph nodes by leukaemic cells.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Clinical features: Abdominal mass
concepts.content: An abdominal mass may be palpable due to hepatosplenomegaly from leukaemic infiltration.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Investigations: Full blood count
concepts.content: Full blood count typically shows anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and variable white cell count with presence of blasts in peripheral blood.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Investigations: Bone marrow biopsy
concepts.content: Bone marrow biopsy confirms diagnosis by demonstrating >20% blasts in marrow aspirate or biopsy sample.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Management: Chemotherapy
concepts.content: Treatment involves multi-agent chemotherapy protocols such as the UKALL regimen, including induction with vincristine, corticosteroids (prednisolone 60 mg/m2/day), and asparaginase, followed by consolidation and maintenance phases.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Management: Supportive care
concepts.content: Supportive care includes transfusions for anaemia and thrombocytopenia, antimicrobial prophylaxis, and management of tumour lysis syndrome with hydration and allopurinol.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Complications: Infection
concepts.content: Neutropenia during treatment increases risk of severe infections including sepsis, requiring prompt antibiotic therapy.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Complications: Tumour lysis syndrome
concepts.content: Tumour lysis syndrome can cause hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia, and acute kidney injury, typically within 48 hours of chemotherapy initiation.

concepts.title: Leukaemia – Prognosis
concepts.content: The 5-year survival rate for paediatric acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in the UK exceeds 90% with current treatment protocols.

concepts.title: Lymphoma – Definition
concepts.content: Lymphoma is a malignant neoplasm of lymphoid tissue characterised by the clonal proliferation of lymphocytes. It is broadly classified into Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, both of which can occur in paediatric patients.

concepts.title: Lymphoma – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Lymphoma is the third most common paediatric malignancy after leukaemia and brain tumours, accounting for approximately 10-15% of childhood cancers in the UK. Hodgkin lymphoma peaks in adolescence, while non-Hodgkin lymphoma is more common in younger children.

concepts.title: Lymphoma – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for paediatric lymphoma include immunodeficiency states (e.g. HIV infection, post-transplant immunosuppression), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, family history of lymphoma, and certain genetic syndromes such as ataxia-telangiectasia.

concepts.title: Lymphoma – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Lymphoma arises from malignant transformation of lymphocytes, leading to uncontrolled proliferation and accumulation in lymph nodes and extranodal sites. Hodgkin lymphoma is characterised by Reed-Sternberg cells, while non-Hodgkin lymphoma includes diverse subtypes such as Burkitt lymphoma and lymphoblastic lymphoma.

concepts.title: Lymphoma – Clinical features: Lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: The most common presentation of paediatric lymphoma is painless, firm lymphadenopathy, often cervical or supraclavicular. Nodes may be rubbery and non-tender, and persist for more than 2 weeks.

concepts.title: Lymphoma – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: B symptoms including unexplained fever >38°C lasting more than 1 week are common in paediatric lymphoma and indicate systemic involvement.

concepts.title: Lymphoma – Clinical features: Abdominal mass
concepts.content: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma in children often presents with an abdominal mass due to involvement of mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymph nodes or extranodal sites such as the bowel.

concepts.title: Lymphoma – Clinical features: Breathlessness
concepts.content: Mediastinal lymphadenopathy in paediatric lymphoma can cause compression of airways or large vessels, leading to breathlessness and superior vena cava syndrome.

concepts.title: Lymphoma – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis of paediatric lymphoma involves excisional lymph node biopsy for histopathology and immunophenotyping. Staging includes chest X-ray, CT scan of chest, abdomen and pelvis, and bone marrow biopsy. LDH is often elevated and can be used as a tumour marker.

concepts.title: Lymphoma – Management
concepts.content: Treatment of paediatric lymphoma depends on subtype and stage. Hodgkin lymphoma is treated with combination chemotherapy (e.g. ABVD regimen: doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) and sometimes radiotherapy. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma requires intensive multi-agent chemotherapy protocols such as the UK Children's Cancer Study Group regimens.

concepts.title: Lymphoma – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of paediatric lymphoma and its treatment include tumour lysis syndrome, infection due to immunosuppression, secondary malignancies, and long-term effects such as cardiotoxicity from anthracyclines and infertility.

concepts.title: Lymphoma – Prognosis
concepts.content: Paediatric lymphoma generally has a favourable prognosis with current treatment, with 5-year survival rates exceeding 85% for Hodgkin lymphoma and 70-90% for non-Hodgkin lymphoma depending on subtype and stage.

concepts.title: Malaria – Definition
concepts.content: Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by Plasmodium species, transmitted by the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes, leading to cyclical febrile illness primarily affecting red blood cells.

concepts.title: Malaria – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Malaria is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, with the highest burden in sub-Saharan Africa; children under 5 years are most at risk of severe disease and mortality.

concepts.title: Malaria – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for paediatric malaria include living in or travelling to endemic areas, lack of insecticide-treated bed nets, poor socioeconomic status, and absence of prior immunity.

concepts.title: Malaria – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Plasmodium parasites invade hepatocytes and then erythrocytes, causing haemolysis and microvascular obstruction, leading to anaemia, hypoxia, and organ dysfunction.

concepts.title: Malaria – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Children with malaria typically present with intermittent fever, often with a cyclical pattern every 48–72 hours depending on Plasmodium species.

concepts.title: Malaria – Clinical features: Anaemia and pallor
concepts.content: Haemolysis of infected red blood cells causes anaemia, presenting as pallor and fatigue in paediatric patients with malaria.

concepts.title: Malaria – Clinical features: Jaundice
concepts.content: Severe malaria may cause jaundice due to haemolysis and hepatic dysfunction, evident as yellowing of the sclera and skin.

concepts.title: Malaria – Clinical features: Fits/seizures
concepts.content: Cerebral malaria can present with neurological symptoms including seizures, altered consciousness, and coma in children.

concepts.title: Malaria – Investigations: Blood film microscopy
concepts.content: Definitive diagnosis is by thick and thin blood film microscopy demonstrating Plasmodium parasites; species identification guides treatment.

concepts.title: Malaria – Investigations: Rapid diagnostic tests
concepts.content: Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) detect Plasmodium antigens and provide quick diagnosis when microscopy is unavailable.

concepts.title: Malaria – Management: Uncomplicated malaria
concepts.content: First-line treatment for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in children is artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), e.g., artemether-lumefantrine dosed by weight for 3 days.

concepts.title: Malaria – Management: Severe malaria
concepts.content: Severe malaria requires intravenous artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, and 24 hours, then daily until oral therapy is possible; supportive care includes fluid management and treatment of complications.

concepts.title: Malaria – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of paediatric malaria include cerebral malaria, severe anaemia, hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis, acute kidney injury, and respiratory distress.

concepts.title: Malaria – Prognosis
concepts.content: With prompt diagnosis and treatment, prognosis is good; however, cerebral malaria and severe anaemia carry significant mortality risk, especially in children under 5 years.

concepts.title: Measles – Definition
concepts.content: Measles is a highly contagious viral infection caused by the measles virus, characterised by fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a characteristic maculopapular rash.

concepts.title: Measles – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Measles primarily affects children under 5 years old in the UK, with outbreaks occurring mainly in unvaccinated populations. The incidence has decreased significantly due to the MMR vaccine, but sporadic cases and outbreaks still occur.

concepts.title: Measles – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Measles is caused by the measles virus, transmitted via respiratory droplets. Risk factors include lack of vaccination with MMR, immunodeficiency, and close contact with infected individuals.

concepts.title: Measles – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: The measles virus infects respiratory epithelial cells, then spreads via lymphatics causing viremia. It leads to immune suppression and characteristic epithelial damage causing rash and Koplik spots.

concepts.title: Measles – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: High fever typically begins 3-5 days after exposure, often exceeding 39°C and lasting 4-7 days.

concepts.title: Measles – Clinical features: Cough
concepts.content: A dry, hacking cough is common during the prodromal phase and may persist throughout the illness.

concepts.title: Measles – Clinical features: Coryza
concepts.content: Nasal congestion and runny nose (coryza) occur early in the illness, contributing to respiratory symptoms.

concepts.title: Measles – Clinical features: Conjunctivitis
concepts.content: Bilateral conjunctivitis with photophobia and watery eyes is common during the prodromal phase.

concepts.title: Measles – Clinical features: Koplik spots
concepts.content: Koplik spots are small, white lesions on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars, appearing 1-2 days before rash onset and lasting 1-3 days.

concepts.title: Measles – Clinical features: Rash
concepts.content: A maculopapular rash appears 3-5 days after prodrome onset, starting at the hairline and spreading cephalocaudally and centrifugally, lasting 5-6 days.

concepts.title: Measles – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis is clinical but can be confirmed by detection of measles-specific IgM antibodies in serum or by PCR testing of throat swabs or urine.

concepts.title: Measles – Management
concepts.content: Management is supportive: ensure adequate hydration, antipyretics such as paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever and discomfort. Vitamin A supplementation (200,000 IU orally on diagnosis and the next day for children >12 months) reduces morbidity and mortality.

concepts.title: Measles – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include otitis media (7-9%), pneumonia (1-6%), diarrhoea, encephalitis (1 in 1000 cases), and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (rare, delayed).

concepts.title: Measles – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis is generally good in immunocompetent children with supportive care; mortality is rare in the UK but higher in malnourished or immunocompromised children.

concepts.title: Migraine – Definition
concepts.content: Migraine in paediatrics is a primary headache disorder characterised by recurrent episodes of moderate to severe headache, often unilateral, pulsating in nature, lasting 1 to 72 hours, and associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia.

concepts.title: Migraine – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Migraine affects approximately 10% of children and adolescents in the UK, with prevalence increasing with age; it is more common in females after puberty.

concepts.title: Migraine – Aetiology and Risk factors
concepts.content: Common triggers for paediatric migraine include stress, sleep deprivation, certain foods (e.g. chocolate, caffeine), dehydration, and hormonal changes; family history is a significant risk factor.

concepts.title: Migraine – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Paediatric migraine pathophysiology involves neuronal hyperexcitability, cortical spreading depression, and activation of the trigeminovascular system causing release of vasoactive neuropeptides leading to inflammation and pain.

concepts.title: Migraine – Clinical features: Headache
concepts.content: Paediatric migraine headache is typically moderate to severe, unilateral or bilateral, pulsating, worsened by physical activity, lasting 1 to 72 hours.

concepts.title: Migraine – Clinical features: Associated symptoms
concepts.content: Associated symptoms in paediatric migraine include nausea (up to 80%), vomiting (up to 50%), photophobia, phonophobia, and occasionally aura such as visual disturbances lasting less than 60 minutes.

concepts.title: Migraine – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis of paediatric migraine is clinical; neuroimaging (MRI) is reserved for atypical features such as abnormal neurological signs, sudden onset, or progressive symptoms.

concepts.title: Migraine – Management: Acute treatment
concepts.content: First-line acute treatment for paediatric migraine includes weight-based dosing of ibuprofen (10 mg/kg per dose) or paracetamol (15 mg/kg per dose) given early in the headache; antiemetics such as domperidone may be used if vomiting occurs.

concepts.title: Migraine – Management: Preventive treatment
concepts.content: Preventive treatment is considered if migraines occur more than 4 times per month or significantly impair quality of life; options include propranolol starting at 0.5 mg/kg/day up to 2 mg/kg/day, or topiramate 1–3 mg/kg/day, under specialist supervision.

concepts.title: Migraine – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of paediatric migraine include chronic migraine (headache on 15 or more days per month for over 3 months) and medication overuse headache from frequent analgesic use.

concepts.title: Migraine – Prognosis
concepts.content: Paediatric migraine often improves with age; approximately 50% of children experience significant reduction or resolution of symptoms by late adolescence.

concepts.title: Mumps – Definition
concepts.content: Mumps is an acute viral infection caused by the mumps virus, a paramyxovirus, primarily affecting the salivary glands, especially the parotid glands, leading to painful swelling.

concepts.title: Mumps – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Mumps incidence has declined significantly in the UK due to the MMR vaccine; however, outbreaks still occur, particularly in unvaccinated children and adolescents.

concepts.title: Mumps – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Mumps is caused by the mumps virus transmitted via respiratory droplets or direct contact with saliva; risk factors include lack of MMR vaccination and close contact in school or household settings.

concepts.title: Mumps – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: The mumps virus infects the respiratory epithelium, then spreads via the bloodstream to the salivary glands causing inflammation and swelling, predominantly affecting the parotid glands.

concepts.title: Mumps – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Fever is a common early symptom in mumps, typically low-grade to moderate, occurring 1-2 days before parotid swelling.

concepts.title: Mumps – Clinical features: Parotid gland swelling
concepts.content: Painful unilateral or bilateral parotid gland swelling occurs 16-18 days after exposure, lasting 7-10 days, causing characteristic facial swelling below and in front of the ears.

concepts.title: Mumps – Clinical features: Lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: Tender regional lymphadenopathy, particularly of the submandibular and cervical nodes, may accompany parotid swelling.

concepts.title: Mumps – Clinical features: Orchitis
concepts.content: Orchitis occurs in approximately 20-30% of post-pubertal males with mumps, presenting with unilateral testicular pain and swelling typically 4-8 days after parotitis onset.

concepts.title: Mumps – Clinical features: Meningitis
concepts.content: Aseptic meningitis occurs in up to 10% of mumps cases, presenting with headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and vomiting, usually within the first week of illness.

concepts.title: Mumps – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis is clinical but can be confirmed by detecting mumps-specific IgM antibodies in serum or mumps RNA by PCR from saliva or cerebrospinal fluid; full blood count may show lymphocytosis.

concepts.title: Mumps – Management
concepts.content: Management of mumps is supportive: analgesia with paracetamol or ibuprofen, adequate hydration, and isolation for 5 days after parotid swelling onset to reduce transmission; no specific antiviral treatment is available.

concepts.title: Mumps – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include orchitis, oophoritis, aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis, hearing loss, and rarely encephalitis; orchitis can lead to testicular atrophy and infertility in post-pubertal males.

concepts.title: Mumps – Prognosis
concepts.content: The prognosis for mumps in children is generally excellent with full recovery; complications are uncommon, and mortality is rare in the UK with appropriate supportive care.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Definition
concepts.content: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) in paediatrics is characterised by repeated episodes of partial or complete upper airway obstruction during sleep, leading to disrupted sleep patterns and intermittent hypoxia.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea affects approximately 1-5% of children aged 2 to 8 years, with peak incidence between 2 and 6 years, often related to adenotonsillar hypertrophy.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Common risk factors for paediatric OSA include adenotonsillar hypertrophy, obesity, craniofacial abnormalities (e.g., micrognathia), neuromuscular disorders, and Down syndrome.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: In paediatric OSA, upper airway obstruction during sleep results from adenotonsillar hypertrophy causing airway narrowing, leading to intermittent hypoxia, hypercapnia, and sleep fragmentation.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Clinical features: nocturnal symptoms
concepts.content: Children with OSA commonly present with habitual loud snoring (≥3 nights/week), witnessed apnoeas, restless sleep, and nocturnal sweating.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Clinical features: daytime symptoms
concepts.content: Daytime features of paediatric OSA include behavioural difficulties, hyperactivity, poor concentration, and excessive daytime sleepiness.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Investigations
concepts.content: The gold standard investigation for paediatric OSA is overnight polysomnography, which measures apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI); an AHI >1 event/hour is diagnostic in children.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Management: first-line treatment
concepts.content: First-line treatment for paediatric OSA is adenotonsillectomy, especially in children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy; surgery improves symptoms in approximately 80% of cases.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Management: medical therapy
concepts.content: Intranasal corticosteroids (e.g., mometasone 100 mcg once daily) and montelukast may be used in mild paediatric OSA or when surgery is contraindicated.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Management: continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
concepts.content: CPAP therapy is indicated for children with persistent OSA after adenotonsillectomy or those unsuitable for surgery; pressure settings are titrated during sleep studies.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Complications
concepts.content: Untreated paediatric OSA can lead to cardiovascular complications (e.g., pulmonary hypertension), growth failure, behavioural problems, and neurocognitive impairment.

concepts.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – Prognosis
concepts.content: With appropriate treatment, most children with OSA have an excellent prognosis; however, residual symptoms may persist in obese children or those with craniofacial anomalies.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Definition
concepts.content: Otitis media is an inflammation or infection of the middle ear, commonly occurring in children aged 6 months to 3 years, characterised by ear pain, fever, and sometimes hearing loss.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Otitis media affects up to 80% of children by the age of 3 years in the UK, making it one of the most common paediatric infections.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Common causative organisms include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis; risk factors include young age, attendance at daycare, exposure to tobacco smoke, and recent upper respiratory tract infection.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Eustachian tube dysfunction leads to fluid accumulation in the middle ear, creating an environment for bacterial or viral infection and inflammation.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Children with otitis media commonly present with a fever, often ranging from 38°C to 39°C.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Clinical features: Ear pain
concepts.content: Otalgia is a hallmark symptom of otitis media, often described as moderate to severe ear pain, which may cause irritability or crying in young children.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Clinical features: Hearing loss
concepts.content: Temporary conductive hearing loss may occur due to middle ear effusion in otitis media, potentially affecting speech development if recurrent or persistent.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; otoscopy reveals a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane with loss of normal landmarks; tympanometry and audiometry may be used in recurrent or chronic cases.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Management: Analgesia
concepts.content: First-line management includes analgesia with paracetamol (15 mg/kg every 4-6 hours, max 60 mg/kg/day) or ibuprofen (5-10 mg/kg every 6-8 hours, max 40 mg/kg/day) to relieve pain and fever.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Management: Antibiotic use
concepts.content: Antibiotics are recommended for children under 2 years with bilateral otitis media or those with severe symptoms (moderate/severe otalgia or fever ≥39°C); first-line is amoxicillin 25 mg/kg orally every 8 hours for 5 days.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Management: Watchful waiting
concepts.content: In children over 2 years with mild symptoms, a watchful waiting approach for 48-72 hours is advised before starting antibiotics, as many cases resolve spontaneously.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Complications
concepts.content: Potential complications include tympanic membrane perforation, mastoiditis, hearing loss, and rarely intracranial infections such as meningitis or brain abscess.

concepts.title: Otitis media – Prognosis
concepts.content: Most children recover fully within 3 days with appropriate management; recurrent otitis media may affect hearing and speech development but usually resolves by school age.

concepts.title: Pancytopenia – Definition
concepts.content: Pancytopenia is defined as a reduction in all three blood cell lines: haemoglobin <11 g/dL, white blood cells <4 x10^9/L, and platelets <150 x10^9/L in paediatric patients.

concepts.title: Pancytopenia – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Pancytopenia is a rare haematological condition in paediatrics, with an incidence of approximately 2-5 cases per 100,000 children per year in the UK.

concepts.title: Pancytopenia – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of pancytopenia in paediatric patients include aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, myelodysplastic syndromes, infections such as parvovirus B19, and nutritional deficiencies like vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

concepts.title: Pancytopenia – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Pancytopenia results from bone marrow failure or infiltration leading to decreased production of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets in paediatric patients.

concepts.title: Pancytopenia – Clinical features: Pallor
concepts.content: Pallor due to anaemia is a common clinical feature in paediatric pancytopenia, often presenting with fatigue and lethargy.

concepts.title: Pancytopenia – Clinical features: Bruising
concepts.content: Bruising and petechiae occur in paediatric pancytopenia due to thrombocytopenia, with platelet counts often below 50 x10^9/L.

concepts.title: Pancytopenia – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Fever in paediatric pancytopenia may indicate neutropenia-related infection, with neutrophil counts often <0.5 x10^9/L.

concepts.title: Pancytopenia – Investigations
concepts.content: Initial investigations for paediatric pancytopenia include a full blood count showing reductions in haemoglobin, white blood cells, and platelets, blood film, reticulocyte count, and bone marrow aspiration and biopsy for definitive diagnosis.

concepts.title: Pancytopenia – Management
concepts.content: Management of paediatric pancytopenia depends on the underlying cause; supportive care includes transfusions of red cells and platelets, infection prophylaxis with antibiotics, and immunosuppressive therapy such as ciclosporin 3-5 mg/kg/day or bone marrow transplantation in aplastic anaemia.

concepts.title: Pancytopenia – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of paediatric pancytopenia include severe infections due to neutropenia, bleeding from thrombocytopenia, and heart failure secondary to severe anaemia.

concepts.title: Pancytopenia – Prognosis
concepts.content: The prognosis of paediatric pancytopenia varies with cause; aplastic anaemia has a 5-year survival of approximately 70% with bone marrow transplantation, while untreated leukaemia has a poor prognosis.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Definition
concepts.content: Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) in paediatrics refers to mucosal erosions equal to or greater than 5 mm in the stomach or duodenum, caused by an imbalance between mucosal protective factors and aggressive factors such as gastric acid. Gastritis is inflammation of the gastric mucosa, which may be acute or chronic.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Peptic ulcer disease affects approximately 1-2% of children, with duodenal ulcers more common than gastric ulcers. Helicobacter pylori infection prevalence in UK children is estimated at 5-10%, higher in socioeconomically deprived populations.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Aetiology/Risk factors: Helicobacter pylori infection
concepts.content: Helicobacter pylori infection is the leading cause of peptic ulcer disease and chronic gastritis in children, transmitted via oral-oral or faecal-oral routes. Infection prevalence is higher in children from lower socioeconomic backgrounds.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Aetiology/Risk factors: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
concepts.content: Use of NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can cause mucosal injury leading to gastritis and peptic ulcer disease in children by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, reducing mucosal protection.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Aetiology/Risk factors: Other causes
concepts.content: Other causes include stress-related mucosal damage in critically ill children, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma), Crohn’s disease, and rare infections such as cytomegalovirus or fungal gastritis.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Peptic ulcer disease results from an imbalance between aggressive factors (gastric acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) and mucosal defence mechanisms (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins, mucosal blood flow). Gastritis involves inflammation of the gastric mucosa, which may progress to mucosal erosion and ulceration.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Clinical features: Abdominal pain
concepts.content: Children with peptic ulcer disease typically present with epigastric or upper abdominal pain, often described as burning or gnawing, which may be relieved by food or antacids. Pain may be nocturnal or occur several hours after meals.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Clinical features: Vomiting
concepts.content: Vomiting may occur in children with peptic ulcer disease or gastritis, sometimes containing blood (haematemesis) if there is mucosal bleeding.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Clinical features: Gastrointestinal bleeding
concepts.content: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding may present as haematemesis or melaena in children with peptic ulcer disease, indicating mucosal ulceration and erosion into blood vessels.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Investigations: Helicobacter pylori testing
concepts.content: Non-invasive tests for H. pylori include the urea breath test and stool antigen test, both with sensitivity and specificity >90%. Serology is less useful in children due to poor specificity. Endoscopic biopsy with rapid urease test or histology is the gold standard.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Investigations: Endoscopy
concepts.content: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is indicated in children with suspected peptic ulcer disease to visualise ulcers, obtain biopsies for H. pylori, and exclude malignancy or other causes. It allows direct assessment of mucosal damage.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Management: Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy
concepts.content: First-line eradication therapy in children includes a 14-day triple therapy regimen: amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day divided twice daily (max 1 g twice daily), clarithromycin 15 mg/kg/day divided twice daily (max 500 mg twice daily), and a proton pump inhibitor (e.g., omeprazole 1 mg/kg/day divided twice daily, max 40 mg/day).

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Management: Acid suppression therapy
concepts.content: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) such as omeprazole (1 mg/kg/day in two divided doses, max 40 mg/day) or H2 receptor antagonists like ranitidine (4-8 mg/kg/day divided twice daily) are used to reduce gastric acid secretion and promote ulcer healing.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Management: Avoidance of NSAIDs and supportive care
concepts.content: Discontinuation of NSAIDs and avoidance of irritant foods (spicy, acidic) are advised. Supportive care includes adequate hydration and nutritional support.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include upper gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, gastric outlet obstruction, and rarely gastric malignancy. In children, bleeding is the most common serious complication requiring urgent management.

concepts.title: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis – Prognosis
concepts.content: With appropriate treatment including H. pylori eradication and acid suppression, most children achieve complete healing with low recurrence rates. Untreated ulcers may lead to chronic symptoms and complications.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Definition
concepts.content: Periorbital cellulitis is an infection of the eyelid and surrounding skin anterior to the orbital septum, whereas orbital cellulitis involves infection of the tissues posterior to the orbital septum, including the fat and muscles within the orbit.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Periorbital cellulitis is more common in children under 5 years old, with orbital cellulitis being less common but more severe. The incidence of orbital cellulitis is approximately 3.5 cases per 100,000 children per year in the UK.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causative organisms include Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae type b (rare since vaccination). Risk factors include recent upper respiratory tract infection, sinusitis (especially ethmoid), trauma, insect bites, and dacryocystitis.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Infection spreads via contiguous spread from adjacent structures such as the paranasal sinuses or through local trauma. Periorbital cellulitis is limited anterior to the orbital septum, while orbital cellulitis involves the orbit posteriorly, risking complications such as abscess formation and intracranial spread.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Children with periorbital or orbital cellulitis commonly present with fever, often above 38°C, indicating systemic infection.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Clinical features: Eyelid swelling and erythema
concepts.content: Periorbital cellulitis presents with unilateral eyelid swelling, erythema, and tenderness without proptosis or ophthalmoplegia.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Clinical features: Proptosis and ophthalmoplegia
concepts.content: Orbital cellulitis is characterised by proptosis, painful and restricted eye movements (ophthalmoplegia), decreased visual acuity, and chemosis, indicating involvement of orbital tissues.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Investigations: Blood tests
concepts.content: Blood tests typically show raised inflammatory markers including C-reactive protein (CRP) and white cell count (WCC). Blood cultures may be positive in severe cases.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Investigations: Imaging
concepts.content: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the orbits and sinuses is the imaging modality of choice to differentiate periorbital from orbital cellulitis and to identify abscess formation or sinusitis.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Differential diagnoses include allergic reaction, insect bite, dacryocystitis, trauma with haematoma, and neoplasms such as rhabdomyosarcoma.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Management: Antibiotic therapy
concepts.content: Initial management includes intravenous antibiotics targeting common pathogens: intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg every 6 hours plus ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily. If MRSA is suspected, add intravenous vancomycin dosed according to weight and renal function. Switch to oral antibiotics when clinically improved, typically for a total of 10-14 days.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Management: Surgical intervention
concepts.content: Surgical drainage is indicated for orbital abscesses, subperiosteal abscesses, or if there is no improvement after 48 hours of intravenous antibiotics. Sinus surgery may be required if sinusitis is the source.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Complications
concepts.content: Potential complications include subperiosteal or orbital abscess, vision loss, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess, and sepsis.

concepts.title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Prognosis
concepts.content: With prompt diagnosis and appropriate antibiotic treatment, prognosis is excellent with full recovery. Delayed treatment increases risk of serious complications and permanent visual impairment.

concepts.title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Definition
concepts.content: Peripheral nerve injuries or palsies in paediatrics refer to damage or dysfunction of the peripheral nerves resulting in motor, sensory, or autonomic deficits. These injuries can be caused by trauma, compression, or iatrogenic factors affecting nerves outside the central nervous system.

concepts.title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Peripheral nerve injuries in children are relatively uncommon but important causes of motor and sensory deficits. Neonatal brachial plexus palsy occurs in approximately 1-2 per 1000 live births in the UK, often associated with difficult deliveries.

concepts.title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of peripheral nerve injuries in paediatrics include birth trauma (e.g., shoulder dystocia causing brachial plexus injury), fractures, penetrating injuries, iatrogenic nerve damage during surgery, and compression neuropathies such as carpal tunnel syndrome.

concepts.title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Peripheral nerve injury results in disruption of axonal conduction and Wallerian degeneration distal to the site of injury. The degree of injury ranges from neurapraxia (temporary conduction block) to axonotmesis and neurotmesis (complete nerve transection), affecting motor and sensory function.

concepts.title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Clinical features: Motor deficits
concepts.content: Peripheral nerve injuries in children commonly present with weakness or paralysis of muscles supplied by the affected nerve. For example, Erb's palsy (upper brachial plexus injury) causes weakness of shoulder abduction, external rotation, and elbow flexion.

concepts.title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Clinical features: Sensory deficits
concepts.content: Sensory loss or altered sensation such as numbness or paraesthesia may be present in the distribution of the injured peripheral nerve. For example, median nerve injury can cause sensory loss over the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger.

concepts.title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis is primarily clinical but can be supported by nerve conduction studies and electromyography (EMG) to assess the extent and location of nerve injury. Ultrasound or MRI may be used to visualise nerve continuity or compression.

concepts.title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Management
concepts.content: Initial management includes physiotherapy to maintain joint mobility and muscle strength. Analgesia with paracetamol or ibuprofen is used for pain. Surgical nerve repair or grafting may be indicated in severe cases or if no recovery occurs after 3-6 months.

concepts.title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include permanent motor and sensory deficits, muscle atrophy, joint contractures, and chronic pain syndromes such as neuropathic pain. Early intervention reduces the risk of long-term disability.

concepts.title: Peripheral nerve injuries/palsies – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis depends on the severity and type of nerve injury. Neurapraxia often recovers fully within weeks to months. More severe injuries may have incomplete recovery despite surgical intervention. Early diagnosis and rehabilitation improve outcomes.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Definition
concepts.content: Peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum, the serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering the viscera, often due to infection or chemical irritation.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Peritonitis in paediatrics is most commonly secondary to appendicitis, bowel perforation, or peritoneal dialysis, with higher incidence in neonates and infants due to immature immune response.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of paediatric peritonitis include perforated appendicitis, intestinal perforation (e.g. necrotising enterocolitis in neonates), trauma, peritoneal dialysis infection, and intra-abdominal abscess rupture.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Peritonitis results from bacterial invasion or chemical irritation of the peritoneum causing an inflammatory response with exudate formation, increased vascular permeability, and recruitment of neutrophils leading to pain and systemic illness.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Clinical features: Acute abdominal pain
concepts.content: Children with peritonitis typically present with severe, constant abdominal pain that worsens with movement and coughing, often localised initially then becoming generalised.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Fever is a common presenting feature in paediatric peritonitis, often exceeding 38°C, reflecting systemic inflammatory response to infection.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Clinical features: Vomiting
concepts.content: Vomiting is frequently observed in paediatric peritonitis due to bowel irritation and ileus.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Clinical features: Dehydration
concepts.content: Dehydration may develop secondary to vomiting, fever, and reduced oral intake in children with peritonitis.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations include blood tests (FBC showing raised WCC, CRP elevated), blood cultures, abdominal ultrasound to detect fluid collections or abscess, and abdominal X-ray to identify free air under diaphragm indicating perforation.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Management
concepts.content: Initial management includes fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloid (e.g. 20 mL/kg boluses), correction of electrolyte imbalances, analgesia with paracetamol and opioids if required, and empiric intravenous antibiotics such as cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 8 hours plus metronidazole 7.5 mg/kg every 8 hours. Surgical intervention is often required for source control.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include sepsis, septic shock, abscess formation, adhesions causing bowel obstruction, and multi-organ failure.

concepts.title: Peritonitis – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis depends on prompt diagnosis and treatment; with early intervention, mortality is low in children, but delayed treatment increases risk of morbidity and mortality.

concepts.title: Pyloric stenosis – Definition
concepts.content: Pyloric stenosis is a condition characterised by hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the pyloric muscle, leading to gastric outlet obstruction in infants, typically presenting within the first 2 to 8 weeks of life.

concepts.title: Pyloric stenosis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Pyloric stenosis occurs in approximately 2 to 4 per 1000 live births in the UK, with a higher incidence in first-born male infants and a male-to-female ratio of about 4:1.
