concepts.title: Pyloric stenosis – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for pyloric stenosis include male sex, first-born status, family history of the condition, exposure to erythromycin in the first two weeks of life, and bottle feeding.

concepts.title: Pyloric stenosis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the circular muscle of the pylorus cause progressive narrowing of the pyloric canal, resulting in gastric outlet obstruction and subsequent projectile non-bilious vomiting.

concepts.title: Pyloric stenosis – Clinical features: Vomiting
concepts.content: Infants with pyloric stenosis typically present with progressive, projectile, non-bilious vomiting occurring after feeds, usually starting between 2 and 8 weeks of age.

concepts.title: Pyloric stenosis – Clinical features: Palpable abdominal mass
concepts.content: A palpable, firm, mobile 'olive-shaped' mass is often felt in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium during abdominal examination in infants with pyloric stenosis.

concepts.title: Pyloric stenosis – Clinical features: Dehydration
concepts.content: Due to persistent vomiting, infants may develop signs of dehydration including dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, and tachycardia.

concepts.title: Pyloric stenosis – Investigations: Ultrasound
concepts.content: Abdominal ultrasound is the diagnostic investigation of choice, showing an elongated pyloric canal >17 mm in length and a pyloric muscle thickness >3 mm.

concepts.title: Pyloric stenosis – Investigations: Blood tests
concepts.content: Blood tests typically reveal hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis due to loss of gastric acid from vomiting.

concepts.title: Pyloric stenosis – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Differential diagnoses include gastro-oesophageal reflux, gastroenteritis, milk protein allergy, intestinal malrotation with volvulus, and other causes of vomiting in infants.

concepts.title: Pyloric stenosis – Management: Preoperative care
concepts.content: Initial management involves correcting dehydration and electrolyte imbalances with intravenous fluids, typically 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium chloride added once urine output is adequate.

concepts.title: Pyloric stenosis – Management: Surgical treatment
concepts.content: Definitive treatment is a Ramstedt pyloromyotomy, a surgical procedure that splits the hypertrophied pyloric muscle to relieve obstruction, usually performed once the infant is stable.

concepts.title: Pyloric stenosis – Complications
concepts.content: Potential complications include persistent vomiting postoperatively, wound infection, mucosal perforation during surgery, and metabolic disturbances if untreated.

concepts.title: Pyloric stenosis – Prognosis
concepts.content: With timely diagnosis and surgical treatment, prognosis is excellent; most infants recover fully with normal feeding and growth.

concepts.title: Reactive arthritis – Definition
concepts.content: Reactive arthritis is an aseptic inflammatory arthritis that occurs following an infection, typically affecting children and young adults. It is characterised by the triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis, although not all features are always present.

concepts.title: Reactive arthritis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Reactive arthritis is uncommon in the paediatric population but can occur at any age, with a peak incidence in late childhood and adolescence. It is more common in males and is associated with HLA-B27 positivity in approximately 60-80% of cases.

concepts.title: Reactive arthritis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Reactive arthritis in children is typically triggered by a preceding gastrointestinal infection (e.g., Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter) or genitourinary infection (e.g., Chlamydia trachomatis). The interval between infection and arthritis onset is usually 1-4 weeks.

concepts.title: Reactive arthritis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Reactive arthritis is an autoimmune response triggered by bacterial antigens from a distant infection site. It involves immune complex deposition and T-cell mediated inflammation in joints, entheses, and other tissues, often in genetically predisposed individuals (HLA-B27 positive).

concepts.title: Reactive arthritis – Clinical features: Acute joint pain/swelling
concepts.content: Children with reactive arthritis typically present with acute onset of asymmetric oligoarthritis, predominantly affecting the lower limb large joints such as knees and ankles. Joint swelling, pain, and limited range of movement are common.

concepts.title: Reactive arthritis – Clinical features: Acute rash
concepts.content: Some children develop keratoderma blennorrhagicum, a hyperkeratotic rash on the palms and soles, or circinate balanitis, a painless erythematous rash on the glans penis, as part of reactive arthritis.

concepts.title: Reactive arthritis – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Low-grade fever is common in children with reactive arthritis, often accompanying joint inflammation and systemic symptoms.

concepts.title: Reactive arthritis – Clinical features: Conjunctivitis
concepts.content: Conjunctivitis occurs in approximately 30-50% of paediatric reactive arthritis cases, presenting as a mild, bilateral, non-purulent inflammation of the conjunctiva.

concepts.title: Reactive arthritis – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations include raised inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR), sterile joint aspirate with elevated white cells, negative bacterial cultures, HLA-B27 testing, and evidence of preceding infection via stool cultures or urethral swabs. Imaging may show joint effusion and enthesitis.

concepts.title: Reactive arthritis – Management
concepts.content: Management includes NSAIDs such as ibuprofen 20-30 mg/kg/day divided into 3-4 doses for symptom relief. Intra-articular corticosteroids may be used for persistent monoarthritis. Antibiotics are indicated only if active infection is present. Physical therapy supports joint function.

concepts.title: Reactive arthritis – Complications
concepts.content: Chronic arthritis may develop in a minority of children, leading to joint damage and functional impairment. Rare complications include uveitis and secondary amyloidosis.

concepts.title: Reactive arthritis – Prognosis
concepts.content: The prognosis in paediatric reactive arthritis is generally good, with most children experiencing resolution within 6 months. Approximately 15-20% may develop chronic symptoms requiring long-term management.

concepts.title: Respiratory arrest – Definition
concepts.content: Respiratory arrest in paediatrics is the complete cessation of effective breathing, resulting in inadequate oxygenation and ventilation, requiring immediate intervention to prevent hypoxic injury and death.

concepts.title: Respiratory arrest – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Respiratory arrest is a rare but life-threatening event in paediatrics, often occurring secondary to respiratory failure, airway obstruction, or severe neurological impairment; it is a leading cause of paediatric cardiac arrest in the UK.

concepts.title: Respiratory arrest – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of respiratory arrest in paediatric patients include severe asthma exacerbation, bronchiolitis, foreign body airway obstruction, neuromuscular disorders, trauma, central nervous system infections, and drug overdose.

concepts.title: Respiratory arrest – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Respiratory arrest results from failure of the respiratory centre or airway obstruction leading to cessation of effective ventilation, causing hypoxia, hypercapnia, and subsequent respiratory acidosis, which can rapidly progress to cardiac arrest if untreated.

concepts.title: Respiratory arrest – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
concepts.content: Paediatric patients in respiratory arrest typically present with decreased or complete loss of consciousness due to hypoxia and hypercapnia affecting cerebral function.

concepts.title: Respiratory arrest – Clinical features: Cyanosis
concepts.content: Central cyanosis is a key clinical feature in paediatric respiratory arrest, indicating significant hypoxaemia due to inadequate oxygenation of haemoglobin.

concepts.title: Respiratory arrest – Clinical features: Absence of respiratory effort
concepts.content: In respiratory arrest, there is a complete absence of spontaneous respiratory effort, with no chest wall movement or airflow detected on auscultation or observation.

concepts.title: Respiratory arrest – Investigations
concepts.content: Initial investigations in paediatric respiratory arrest include pulse oximetry, arterial blood gas analysis showing hypoxaemia and hypercapnia, chest X-ray to identify underlying causes, and capnography during resuscitation to confirm airway placement.

concepts.title: Respiratory arrest – Management
concepts.content: Management of paediatric respiratory arrest involves immediate airway opening using head tilt-chin lift or jaw thrust, bag-valve-mask ventilation with 100% oxygen, advanced airway placement if necessary, and adherence to paediatric advanced life support (PALS) guidelines; adrenaline (epinephrine) 10 mcg/kg IV/IO may be administered during resuscitation.

concepts.title: Respiratory arrest – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of paediatric respiratory arrest include hypoxic brain injury, cardiac arrest, multi-organ failure, and death if not promptly recognised and treated.

concepts.title: Respiratory arrest – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis following paediatric respiratory arrest depends on the duration of hypoxia and timeliness of resuscitation; early intervention can result in full recovery, whereas prolonged arrest often leads to permanent neurological impairment or death.

concepts.title: Rubella – Definition
concepts.content: Rubella is a contagious viral infection caused by the rubella virus, characterised by a mild febrile illness and a maculopapular rash, primarily affecting children and young adults.

concepts.title: Rubella – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Rubella incidence has significantly declined in the UK due to the MMR vaccination programme; however, outbreaks can still occur, particularly in unvaccinated populations and susceptible pregnant women.

concepts.title: Rubella – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Rubella is caused by the rubella virus, transmitted via respiratory droplets; risk factors include lack of immunisation, close contact with infected individuals, and pregnancy due to risk of congenital rubella syndrome.

concepts.title: Rubella – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Rubella virus infects the upper respiratory tract, replicates in nasopharyngeal mucosa and regional lymph nodes, causing viraemia and dissemination leading to characteristic rash and systemic symptoms.

concepts.title: Rubella – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Low-grade fever is typically present for 1–5 days before rash onset in paediatric rubella cases.

concepts.title: Rubella – Clinical features: Rash
concepts.content: A pink maculopapular rash typically appears 14–21 days after exposure, starting on the face and spreading to the trunk and limbs, lasting approximately 3 days.

concepts.title: Rubella – Clinical features: Lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: Tender, bilateral postauricular, occipital, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy is common in paediatric rubella.

concepts.title: Rubella – Clinical features: Arthralgia
concepts.content: Arthralgia or arthritis, especially in adolescent females, may occur and typically affects small joints such as wrists, fingers, and knees.

concepts.title: Rubella – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis is confirmed by rubella-specific IgM antibodies in serum or by rubella RNA detection using RT-PCR from throat swabs or urine; serology is the mainstay in the UK.

concepts.title: Rubella – Management
concepts.content: Management is supportive with antipyretics such as paracetamol (dose 10–15 mg/kg every 4–6 hours, max 60 mg/kg/day) and isolation to prevent spread; no specific antiviral treatment exists.

concepts.title: Rubella – Complications
concepts.content: Congenital rubella syndrome occurs if maternal infection happens during the first trimester, causing sensorineural deafness, cataracts, cardiac defects (e.g., patent ductus arteriosus), and developmental delay.

concepts.title: Rubella – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis in immunocompetent children is excellent with full recovery; however, congenital rubella syndrome has significant morbidity and mortality.

concepts.title: Self-harm – Definition
concepts.content: Self-harm is defined as the intentional self-poisoning or self-injury irrespective of the apparent purpose of the act, commonly seen in paediatric populations as a coping mechanism for emotional distress.

concepts.title: Self-harm – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Self-harm affects approximately 10-15% of adolescents in the UK, with higher prevalence in females and peak incidence between ages 12 and 16 years.

concepts.title: Self-harm – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for self-harm in paediatric patients include a history of mental health disorders (e.g., depression, anxiety), family dysfunction, bullying, abuse, substance misuse, and social isolation.

concepts.title: Self-harm – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Self-harm is thought to result from complex interactions between psychological distress, impaired emotional regulation, and neurobiological factors including altered serotonin pathways.

concepts.title: Self-harm – Clinical features: Presentation with self-inflicted cuts or lacerations
concepts.content: Paediatric patients may present with superficial or deep cuts, often on the forearms, wrists, thighs, or abdomen, sometimes concealed by clothing; scars from previous episodes may also be evident.

concepts.title: Self-harm – Clinical features: Presentation with self-poisoning or overdose
concepts.content: Presentation may include ingestion of medications such as paracetamol, ibuprofen, or prescribed psychotropic drugs, with symptoms ranging from nausea and vomiting to altered consciousness and metabolic disturbances.

concepts.title: Self-harm – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations include blood tests such as full blood count, liver function tests, coagulation profile, and toxicology screening; ECG is indicated if cardiotoxic drug overdose is suspected.

concepts.title: Self-harm – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Differential diagnoses include accidental injury, dermatological conditions causing skin lesions, factitious disorder, and suicidal attempts requiring psychiatric assessment.

concepts.title: Self-harm – Management: Immediate care
concepts.content: Immediate management includes assessment of airway, breathing, and circulation; wound care with cleaning and dressing; administration of antidotes such as N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol overdose as per UK guidelines (150 mg/kg over 15 minutes, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours).

concepts.title: Self-harm – Management: Psychiatric assessment and follow-up
concepts.content: All paediatric patients presenting with self-harm require urgent mental health assessment, risk stratification for suicide, and referral to child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) for ongoing support and therapy.

concepts.title: Self-harm – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include infection, scarring, permanent tissue damage, accidental severe overdose leading to organ failure, and increased risk of completed suicide.

concepts.title: Self-harm – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis varies; many adolescents recover with appropriate psychological intervention, but there is a significant risk of recurrence and increased suicide risk, necessitating long-term follow-up.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Definition
concepts.content: Sickle cell disease is an inherited autosomal recessive haematological disorder characterised by the presence of abnormal haemoglobin S, leading to chronic haemolytic anaemia and vaso-occlusive phenomena.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Sickle cell disease affects approximately 1 in 2000 live births in the UK, predominantly in children of African, Caribbean, Middle Eastern, and South Asian descent.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Sickle cell disease is caused by a point mutation in the beta-globin gene resulting in haemoglobin S; risk factors include having two copies of the mutated gene (homozygous HbSS) or compound heterozygous states such as HbSC or HbSβ-thalassaemia.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Polymerisation of deoxygenated haemoglobin S causes red blood cells to sickle, leading to vaso-occlusion, chronic haemolysis, endothelial damage, and increased risk of thrombosis.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Clinical features: Anaemia and pallor
concepts.content: Children with sickle cell disease often present with chronic haemolytic anaemia causing pallor and fatigue; haemoglobin levels typically range from 6 to 9 g/dL.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Clinical features: Acute painful crises
concepts.content: Vaso-occlusive crises present as acute joint pain and swelling, commonly affecting long bones, ribs, and back; pain episodes may require opioid analgesia for management.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Clinical features: Acute chest syndrome
concepts.content: Acute chest syndrome is characterised by new pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray, fever, chest pain, cough, and hypoxia; it is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in paediatric sickle cell patients.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Clinical features: Splenic sequestration
concepts.content: Splenic sequestration presents with sudden enlargement of the spleen, severe anaemia, pallor, and hypovolaemic shock; it is a paediatric emergency requiring urgent blood transfusion.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Investigations: Haemoglobin electrophoresis
concepts.content: Haemoglobin electrophoresis is the diagnostic test of choice, demonstrating predominantly haemoglobin S in homozygous sickle cell disease; newborn screening is standard in the UK.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Investigations: Blood tests
concepts.content: Blood tests typically show normocytic anaemia, reticulocytosis, raised bilirubin, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase reflecting haemolysis.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Management: Penicillin prophylaxis
concepts.content: Oral penicillin V prophylaxis (125 mg twice daily for children under 3 years, 250 mg twice daily for children over 3 years) is recommended from diagnosis until at least 5 years old to prevent pneumococcal infections.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Management: Hydroxycarbamide therapy
concepts.content: Hydroxycarbamide (hydroxyurea) is used in children with frequent vaso-occlusive crises or severe disease; typical dosing starts at 15 mg/kg/day orally, titrated up to a maximum of 35 mg/kg/day under haematology supervision.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Management: Acute pain crisis treatment
concepts.content: Management of acute pain crises includes adequate hydration, analgesia with paracetamol and NSAIDs, and opioids such as oral morphine starting at 0.3-0.5 mg/kg every 4 hours as needed, with careful monitoring.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Management: Blood transfusion
concepts.content: Blood transfusions are indicated for severe anaemia, acute chest syndrome, stroke, and splenic sequestration; exchange transfusion may be required in severe cases to reduce HbS levels below 30%.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Complications: Stroke
concepts.content: Children with sickle cell disease are at increased risk of ischaemic stroke, especially between ages 2 and 16; transcranial Doppler screening is recommended to identify high-risk patients for regular transfusion therapy.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Complications: Infection
concepts.content: Functional asplenia increases susceptibility to encapsulated organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae; prompt treatment of fever with empirical intravenous antibiotics is essential.

concepts.title: Sickle cell disease – Prognosis
concepts.content: With early diagnosis, penicillin prophylaxis, vaccination, and specialist care, children with sickle cell disease in the UK have improved life expectancy, with many surviving into adulthood; however, complications may reduce quality of life.

concepts.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Definition
concepts.content: Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is bleeding into the subarachnoid space, the area between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater surrounding the brain, leading to increased intracranial pressure and potential brain injury.

concepts.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Subarachnoid haemorrhage is rare in paediatric populations, accounting for less than 5% of all strokes in children. The incidence is approximately 0.5 to 1 per 100,000 children per year in the UK.

concepts.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: In children, common causes of subarachnoid haemorrhage include arteriovenous malformations (AVMs), cerebral aneurysms, trauma, bleeding disorders such as haemophilia, and less commonly, infections or vasculitis.

concepts.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Bleeding into the subarachnoid space causes increased intracranial pressure, cerebral vasospasm, and irritation of meninges, leading to headache, neurological deficits, and risk of secondary brain injury.

concepts.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Clinical features: Headache
concepts.content: The most common presenting symptom in paediatric subarachnoid haemorrhage is a sudden, severe headache often described as 'the worst headache of life'.

concepts.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
concepts.content: Children with subarachnoid haemorrhage may present with decreased level of consciousness or coma due to raised intracranial pressure or brain injury.

concepts.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Clinical features: Fits/seizures
concepts.content: Seizures may occur in paediatric patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage due to cortical irritation from blood in the subarachnoid space.

concepts.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Investigations
concepts.content: Initial investigation includes non-contrast CT head which detects acute blood in over 95% of cases within 24 hours. If CT is negative but suspicion remains, lumbar puncture is performed to detect xanthochromia. MRI and cerebral angiography are used to identify underlying vascular abnormalities.

concepts.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Management
concepts.content: Management includes stabilisation with airway, breathing, and circulation support. Nimodipine 1 mg/kg orally every 4 hours is used to reduce cerebral vasospasm in children. Neurosurgical intervention such as clipping or endovascular coiling of aneurysms or AVMs is indicated. Supportive care includes analgesia, seizure control with anticonvulsants like levetiracetam, and monitoring in a paediatric intensive care unit.

concepts.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include cerebral vasospasm leading to ischaemic stroke, hydrocephalus, rebleeding, seizures, and long-term neurological deficits.

concepts.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis depends on the severity of haemorrhage and promptness of treatment. Mortality in paediatric SAH is lower than adults but significant morbidity including cognitive impairment and neurological deficits occurs in up to 30% of survivors.

concepts.title: Subdural haemorrhage – Definition
concepts.content: Subdural haemorrhage (SDH) is a collection of blood between the dura mater and the arachnoid membrane of the brain, often resulting from tearing of bridging veins.

concepts.title: Subdural haemorrhage – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Subdural haemorrhage is more common in infants and young children, particularly under 2 years of age, and is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in paediatric head trauma.

concepts.title: Subdural haemorrhage – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of paediatric subdural haemorrhage include non-accidental injury (child abuse), accidental head trauma such as falls or road traffic accidents, and bleeding disorders like haemophilia.

concepts.title: Subdural haemorrhage – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Subdural haemorrhage occurs due to rupture of bridging veins between the cerebral cortex and dural sinuses, leading to blood accumulation that increases intracranial pressure and causes brain compression.

concepts.title: Subdural haemorrhage – Clinical features: Decreased/loss of consciousness
concepts.content: Children with subdural haemorrhage often present with decreased level of consciousness or coma depending on the severity of brain injury.

concepts.title: Subdural haemorrhage – Clinical features: Fits/seizures
concepts.content: Seizures are a common presentation in paediatric subdural haemorrhage and may be focal or generalised.

concepts.title: Subdural haemorrhage – Clinical features: Trauma
concepts.content: A history of head trauma, including falls or suspected non-accidental injury, is often present in children with subdural haemorrhage.

concepts.title: Subdural haemorrhage – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis is confirmed by neuroimaging; non-contrast CT head is the first-line investigation showing crescent-shaped hyperdense collection over the cerebral hemisphere. MRI may be used for further characterisation.

concepts.title: Subdural haemorrhage – Management
concepts.content: Management depends on severity; mild cases may be observed with supportive care, while significant haemorrhages require neurosurgical intervention such as burr hole drainage. Intracranial pressure monitoring and seizure control with anticonvulsants like levetiracetam may be necessary.

concepts.title: Subdural haemorrhage – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include raised intracranial pressure, brain herniation, persistent neurological deficits, developmental delay, and death.

concepts.title: Subdural haemorrhage – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis depends on severity and promptness of treatment; mild cases have good outcomes, but severe haemorrhages, especially those associated with non-accidental injury, have higher rates of mortality and long-term neurological impairment.

concepts.title: Substance use disorder – Definition
concepts.content: Substance use disorder in paediatrics is characterised by a pattern of harmful use of substances such as alcohol, cannabis, opioids, or stimulants leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, as defined by DSM-5 criteria.

concepts.title: Substance use disorder – Epidemiology
concepts.content: In the UK, approximately 14% of 11-15 year olds report having used an illicit drug at least once, with cannabis being the most commonly used substance among adolescents.

concepts.title: Substance use disorder – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for paediatric substance use disorder include family history of substance misuse, peer pressure, mental health disorders such as depression or ADHD, social deprivation, and early exposure to substances.

concepts.title: Substance use disorder – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Substance use disorder involves neuroadaptations in the brain's reward pathways, particularly affecting dopaminergic circuits in the mesolimbic system, leading to tolerance, dependence, and compulsive drug-seeking behaviour.

concepts.title: Substance use disorder – Clinical features: Behavioural difficulties in childhood
concepts.content: Children and adolescents with substance use disorder often present with behavioural difficulties including irritability, aggression, truancy, and decline in academic performance.

concepts.title: Substance use disorder – Clinical features: Substance misuse
concepts.content: Presentation may include signs of intoxication or withdrawal from substances such as alcohol, cannabis, opioids, or stimulants, with symptoms like slurred speech, impaired coordination, or agitation.

concepts.title: Substance use disorder – Clinical features: Overdose
concepts.content: Overdose presentations in paediatric substance use disorder can include respiratory depression, altered consciousness, seizures, or cardiac arrhythmias depending on the substance involved.

concepts.title: Substance use disorder – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations include urine drug screening, blood tests for liver function and full blood count, and assessment for coexisting mental health disorders; no single test confirms diagnosis.

concepts.title: Substance use disorder – Management
concepts.content: Management includes psychosocial interventions such as cognitive behavioural therapy and family therapy; pharmacological treatments like methadone or buprenorphine are used for opioid dependence under specialist supervision.

concepts.title: Substance use disorder – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include increased risk of accidents, mental health disorders such as depression and anxiety, social problems, and long-term cognitive impairment.

concepts.title: Substance use disorder – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis varies; early intervention improves outcomes, but untreated substance use disorder in paediatric patients is associated with chronic substance dependence and increased morbidity into adulthood.

concepts.title: Tension headache – Definition
concepts.content: Tension headache is a common primary headache disorder characterised by bilateral, pressing or tightening pain of mild to moderate intensity, not aggravated by routine physical activity, and without nausea or vomiting. It is the most frequent type of headache in children and adolescents.

concepts.title: Tension headache – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Tension headache affects up to 30% of school-aged children in the UK, with prevalence increasing during adolescence. It is slightly more common in females than males after puberty.

concepts.title: Tension headache – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for tension headache in children include psychological stress, poor posture, sleep disturbances, and family history of headache disorders. Environmental triggers such as screen time and dehydration may also contribute.

concepts.title: Tension headache – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Tension headache pathophysiology involves increased pericranial muscle tenderness and heightened sensitivity of pain pathways in the central nervous system, resulting in a sensitised response to normal stimuli.

concepts.title: Tension headache – Clinical features: Headache characteristics
concepts.content: Tension headache presents with bilateral, pressing or tightening headache of mild to moderate intensity, lasting from 30 minutes to several hours, typically without associated nausea or vomiting.

concepts.title: Tension headache – Clinical features: Associated symptoms
concepts.content: Unlike migraine, tension headache in children usually lacks photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, or vomiting, and is not worsened by routine physical activity.

concepts.title: Tension headache – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis of tension headache is clinical; neuroimaging is not routinely indicated unless red flags such as neurological deficits, altered consciousness, or signs of raised intracranial pressure are present.

concepts.title: Tension headache – Management: Acute treatment
concepts.content: First-line acute treatment for paediatric tension headache includes paracetamol (15 mg/kg per dose, maximum 60 mg/kg/day) or ibuprofen (10 mg/kg per dose, maximum 40 mg/kg/day), administered at onset of headache.

concepts.title: Tension headache – Management: Preventative strategies
concepts.content: Preventative management includes addressing triggers such as stress reduction, improving sleep hygiene, regular physical activity, and ergonomic posture correction. Cognitive behavioural therapy may be considered for recurrent headaches.

concepts.title: Tension headache – Complications
concepts.content: Chronic tension-type headache may develop if acute headaches become frequent and persistent, potentially impacting school attendance and quality of life.

concepts.title: Tension headache – Prognosis
concepts.content: The prognosis for paediatric tension headache is generally good with appropriate management; many children experience resolution or significant improvement during adolescence.

concepts.title: Testicular torsion – Definition
concepts.content: Testicular torsion is a urological emergency characterised by the twisting of the spermatic cord leading to ischaemia of the testis.

concepts.title: Testicular torsion – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Testicular torsion most commonly occurs in males aged 12-18 years, with an incidence of approximately 4.5 per 100,000 males under 25 years annually in the UK.

concepts.title: Testicular torsion – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for testicular torsion include a congenital 'bell clapper' deformity, previous torsion episodes, trauma, and rapid testicular growth during puberty.

concepts.title: Testicular torsion – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Testicular torsion occurs when the spermatic cord twists, obstructing venous outflow and arterial inflow, causing ischaemia and potential infarction of the testis.

concepts.title: Testicular torsion – Clinical features: Scrotal/testicular pain and/or lump/swelling
concepts.content: Acute onset of severe unilateral scrotal pain and swelling is the hallmark presentation of testicular torsion in paediatric patients.

concepts.title: Testicular torsion – Clinical features: Absent cremasteric reflex
concepts.content: An absent cremasteric reflex on the affected side is a key clinical sign suggestive of testicular torsion.

concepts.title: Testicular torsion – Clinical features: Nausea and vomiting
concepts.content: Nausea and vomiting may accompany the acute scrotal pain in paediatric patients with testicular torsion.

concepts.title: Testicular torsion – Investigations: Doppler ultrasound
concepts.content: Doppler ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice to confirm testicular torsion, demonstrating reduced or absent blood flow to the affected testis.

concepts.title: Testicular torsion – Management: Emergency surgical detorsion and orchidopexy
concepts.content: Immediate surgical exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchidopexy is the definitive treatment for testicular torsion and should be performed ideally within 6 hours of symptom onset to optimise testicular salvage.

concepts.title: Testicular torsion – Management: Analgesia
concepts.content: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg orally or intravenously every 4-6 hours (maximum 60 mg/kg/day) is recommended for pain relief in paediatric patients with testicular torsion.

concepts.title: Testicular torsion – Complications
concepts.content: Delayed treatment of testicular torsion can result in testicular infarction, atrophy, infertility, and rarely, sepsis.

concepts.title: Testicular torsion – Prognosis
concepts.content: Testicular salvage rates are approximately 90-100% if surgery occurs within 6 hours of symptom onset, decreasing to less than 50% after 12 hours.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Definition
concepts.content: Thyrotoxicosis in paediatrics is a clinical syndrome caused by excess circulating thyroid hormones, resulting in a hypermetabolic state. It is most commonly due to Graves' disease in children.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Paediatric thyrotoxicosis is rare, with an incidence of approximately 0.9 per 100,000 children per year in the UK. It is more common in girls, with a peak incidence in adolescence.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: The most common cause of paediatric thyrotoxicosis is Graves' disease, an autoimmune disorder characterised by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins. Other causes include toxic multinodular goitre, thyroiditis, and iodine excess.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: In paediatric thyrotoxicosis, excess thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) increase basal metabolic rate, enhance beta-adrenergic receptor sensitivity, and cause multisystem effects including increased cardiac output and heat intolerance.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Clinical features: Weight loss
concepts.content: Children with thyrotoxicosis often present with unexplained weight loss despite an increased appetite.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Clinical features: Tachycardia and palpitations
concepts.content: Tachycardia is common in paediatric thyrotoxicosis, often exceeding 100 beats per minute at rest, and may be accompanied by palpitations and arrhythmias.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Clinical features: Heat intolerance and sweating
concepts.content: Affected children frequently experience heat intolerance and excessive sweating due to increased metabolic rate.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Clinical features: Goitre
concepts.content: A diffuse, smooth, and sometimes tender goitre is often present in children with Graves' disease causing thyrotoxicosis.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Clinical features: Eye signs
concepts.content: Paediatric Graves' disease may present with ophthalmopathy including lid lag, lid retraction, and proptosis, although less common than in adults.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Clinical features: Behavioural difficulties
concepts.content: Children with thyrotoxicosis may exhibit behavioural difficulties including irritability, hyperactivity, and poor concentration.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Investigations: Thyroid function tests
concepts.content: Diagnosis is confirmed by suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH <0.01 mU/L) with elevated free thyroxine (FT4) and free triiodothyronine (FT3) levels.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Investigations: Thyroid autoantibodies
concepts.content: Positive thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) or TSH receptor antibodies support the diagnosis of Graves' disease in paediatric thyrotoxicosis.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Investigations: Radioactive iodine uptake scan
concepts.content: A radioactive iodine uptake scan shows diffusely increased uptake in Graves' disease, but is rarely used in children due to radiation exposure.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Management: Antithyroid drugs
concepts.content: First-line treatment is carbimazole, starting at 0.5 to 0.75 mg/kg/day divided into two doses, adjusted according to thyroid function tests every 4-6 weeks.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Management: Beta-blockers
concepts.content: Propranolol is used to control adrenergic symptoms at 0.5 to 2 mg/kg/day divided into 3-4 doses, particularly in the initial phase of treatment.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Management: Definitive treatment
concepts.content: Definitive treatment options for refractory or relapsing paediatric thyrotoxicosis include thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine ablation, with specialist paediatric endocrinology input.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Complications: Thyroid storm
concepts.content: Thyroid storm is a rare but life-threatening complication characterised by fever, tachycardia, altered consciousness, and heart failure requiring urgent intensive care.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Complications: Growth and development delay
concepts.content: Untreated thyrotoxicosis in children can cause delayed growth and pubertal development due to metabolic disturbances.

concepts.title: Thyrotoxicosis – Prognosis
concepts.content: With appropriate treatment, most children with thyrotoxicosis achieve remission; however, relapse occurs in up to 50% within 2 years, necessitating long-term follow-up.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Definition
concepts.content: Tonsillitis is inflammation of the palatine tonsils, commonly caused by viral or bacterial infections, leading to sore throat, fever, and difficulty swallowing in paediatric patients.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Tonsillitis is most common in children aged 5 to 15 years and accounts for a significant proportion of paediatric sore throat presentations in the UK, with viral causes predominating.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Aetiology and Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of tonsillitis in children include viral infections such as adenovirus, rhinovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus, and bacterial infections predominantly Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus (GABHS). Risk factors include close contact in school settings and immunodeficiency.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Tonsillitis results from infection-induced inflammation of the tonsillar lymphoid tissue, leading to oedema, erythema, and exudate formation, which causes pain and difficulty swallowing.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Clinical features: Sore throat and fever
concepts.content: Children with tonsillitis typically present with a sore throat and fever, often above 38°C, which may be accompanied by malaise and headache.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Clinical features: Tonsillar erythema and exudate
concepts.content: On examination, tonsils are enlarged, erythematous, and may have white or yellow exudate; this is more common in bacterial tonsillitis.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Clinical features: Cervical lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: Tender, enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes are commonly palpable in paediatric tonsillitis.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Clinical features: Difficulty swallowing and drooling
concepts.content: Children may have odynophagia causing difficulty swallowing and in severe cases drooling due to pain.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Investigations: Throat swab and rapid antigen test
concepts.content: A throat swab for bacterial culture or rapid antigen detection test may be performed to identify Group A Streptococcus in children with suspected bacterial tonsillitis.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Investigations: Blood tests
concepts.content: Blood tests such as full blood count may show raised white cell count with neutrophilia in bacterial tonsillitis or lymphocytosis in viral causes like infectious mononucleosis.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Management: Supportive care
concepts.content: Supportive management includes analgesia with paracetamol (15 mg/kg every 4-6 hours, max 60 mg/kg/day) or ibuprofen (5-10 mg/kg every 6-8 hours, max 40 mg/kg/day), adequate hydration, and rest.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Management: Antibiotic therapy
concepts.content: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin is first-line for bacterial tonsillitis in children: 250 mg twice daily for under 10 years, 500 mg twice daily for over 10 years, for 10 days. Alternatives include erythromycin if penicillin-allergic.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Management: Indications for tonsillectomy
concepts.content: Tonsillectomy may be considered in children with recurrent tonsillitis defined as 7 or more episodes in one year, 5 or more episodes per year for two consecutive years, or 3 or more episodes per year for three consecutive years.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Complications: Peritonsillar abscess
concepts.content: A peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is a serious complication characterised by severe unilateral throat pain, trismus, muffled voice, and uvular deviation; it requires urgent ENT referral and drainage.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Complications: Rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis
concepts.content: Untreated Group A Streptococcal tonsillitis can lead to immune-mediated complications such as acute rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, although these are rare in the UK due to widespread antibiotic use.

concepts.title: Tonsillitis – Prognosis
concepts.content: Most cases of paediatric tonsillitis resolve within 7 to 10 days with appropriate supportive care; bacterial tonsillitis responds well to antibiotics with low risk of complications.

concepts.title: Toxic shock syndrome – Definition
concepts.content: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a rare, acute, life-threatening condition caused by toxin-producing strains of Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, characterised by sudden high fever, rash, hypotension, and multi-organ involvement.

concepts.title: Toxic shock syndrome – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Toxic shock syndrome is rare in the UK paediatric population, with an incidence estimated at 0.5 to 1.0 cases per 100,000 children annually; it predominantly affects children aged 5 to 15 years.

concepts.title: Toxic shock syndrome – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for paediatric toxic shock syndrome include recent skin or soft tissue infections, surgical wounds, burns, tampon use in adolescent girls, and varicella infection.

concepts.title: Toxic shock syndrome – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Toxic shock syndrome results from superantigen exotoxins (TSST-1 from Staphylococcus aureus or pyrogenic exotoxins from Streptococcus pyogenes) causing massive T-cell activation and cytokine release leading to systemic inflammation and shock.

concepts.title: Toxic shock syndrome – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Children with toxic shock syndrome typically present with a sudden onset of high fever, often ≥39°C.

concepts.title: Toxic shock syndrome – Clinical features: Acute rash
concepts.content: A diffuse, erythematous macular rash resembling sunburn is characteristic, often involving the trunk and extremities, which may desquamate after 1-2 weeks.

concepts.title: Toxic shock syndrome – Clinical features: Shock
concepts.content: Hypotension is a key feature, defined as systolic blood pressure <5th percentile for age or signs of poor perfusion, often progressing to shock requiring fluid resuscitation.

concepts.title: Toxic shock syndrome – Clinical features: Multi-organ involvement
concepts.content: Clinical signs may include vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion or altered consciousness, conjunctival hyperaemia without exudate, mucous membrane erythema, and elevated liver enzymes or renal impairment.

concepts.title: Toxic shock syndrome – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations include blood cultures, wound or mucosal site cultures, full blood count showing leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated C-reactive protein, renal and liver function tests, coagulation profile, and chest X-ray if respiratory symptoms present.

concepts.title: Toxic shock syndrome – Management
concepts.content: Management includes urgent supportive care with aggressive fluid resuscitation, vasopressors if needed, empirical intravenous antibiotics such as clindamycin 10 mg/kg every 6-8 hours plus flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg every 6 hours, and surgical debridement of infected foci if present.

concepts.title: Toxic shock syndrome – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include multi-organ failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and death if untreated or delayed treatment.

concepts.title: Toxic shock syndrome – Prognosis
concepts.content: With prompt recognition and treatment, paediatric toxic shock syndrome has a mortality rate of less than 5%, but delayed diagnosis significantly increases risk of death and long-term morbidity.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Definition
concepts.content: A urinary tract infection (UTI) in paediatrics is an infection involving any part of the urinary system, including the urethra, bladder, ureters, and kidneys, caused predominantly by bacteria such as Escherichia coli.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Epidemiology
concepts.content: UTIs affect approximately 5% of children under 5 years in the UK, with a higher incidence in females and uncircumcised males under 1 year of age.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Aetiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Common risk factors for paediatric UTI include urinary tract malformations (e.g., vesicoureteric reflux), constipation, poor perineal hygiene, bladder dysfunction, and female sex.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: UTIs occur when uropathogenic bacteria colonise the periurethral area and ascend the urethra to infect the bladder (cystitis) or kidneys (pyelonephritis), causing inflammation and tissue damage.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Fever is a common presenting feature of UTI in children, often the only symptom in infants and young children.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Urinary symptoms
concepts.content: Older children with UTI may present with dysuria, frequency, urgency, and urinary incontinence.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Clinical features: Vomiting and abdominal pain
concepts.content: Vomiting and acute abdominal pain may occur in children with pyelonephritis or severe UTI.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Investigations: Urine dipstick and microscopy
concepts.content: Urine dipstick testing for leukocyte esterase and nitrites is used for initial UTI screening; microscopy may show pyuria and bacteriuria.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Investigations: Urine culture
concepts.content: Urine culture is the gold standard for diagnosing UTI; a significant growth is defined as ≥10^5 colony-forming units/mL of a single uropathogen.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Management: Antibiotic treatment
concepts.content: First-line oral antibiotics for uncomplicated UTI in children include trimethoprim 2 mg/kg once daily or nitrofurantoin 1-2 mg/kg/dose four times daily for 3 days; intravenous antibiotics such as cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 8 hours are used for severe cases or pyelonephritis.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Management: Supportive care
concepts.content: Supportive care includes adequate hydration, antipyretics such as paracetamol (15 mg/kg every 4-6 hours, max 60 mg/kg/day), and monitoring for clinical improvement.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of paediatric UTI include renal scarring, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and recurrent infections.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Prognosis
concepts.content: With prompt diagnosis and appropriate treatment, most children recover fully from UTI without long-term sequelae; however, delayed treatment increases risk of renal damage.

concepts.title: Urticaria – Definition
concepts.content: Urticaria is a common paediatric condition characterised by transient, pruritic, raised wheals (hives) on the skin, often accompanied by angioedema. Lesions typically last less than 24 hours and resolve without scarring.

concepts.title: Urticaria – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Urticaria affects up to 15-20% of children at some point in childhood. Acute urticaria is more common than chronic urticaria in paediatric populations, with chronic urticaria affecting approximately 0.5-1% of children.

concepts.title: Urticaria – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common triggers for paediatric urticaria include viral infections, food allergens (e.g. nuts, eggs, milk), medications (e.g. penicillin, NSAIDs), insect stings, and physical stimuli such as cold or pressure. Family history of atopy increases risk.

concepts.title: Urticaria – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Urticaria results from mast cell degranulation in the skin, releasing histamine and other mediators causing increased vascular permeability, leading to wheal formation and angioedema.

concepts.title: Urticaria – Clinical features: Acute rash
concepts.content: Children with urticaria present with sudden onset of pruritic, erythematous wheals that blanch on pressure. Individual lesions last less than 24 hours but new lesions may appear continuously.

concepts.title: Urticaria – Clinical features: Angioedema
concepts.content: Approximately 40% of children with urticaria also develop angioedema, characterised by deeper swelling of the lips, eyelids, or extremities, which may be painful but is usually non-pruritic.

concepts.title: Urticaria – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis of urticaria is clinical. Routine blood tests are not required unless chronic urticaria persists beyond 6 weeks. Specific IgE testing or skin prick tests may be considered if an allergic trigger is suspected.

concepts.title: Urticaria – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Differential diagnoses include erythema multiforme, viral exanthems, mastocytosis, and vasculitis such as urticarial vasculitis. Lesion duration over 24 hours and systemic symptoms suggest alternative diagnoses.

concepts.title: Urticaria – Management
concepts.content: First-line treatment is non-sedating H1-antihistamines such as cetirizine (0.25 mg/kg twice daily, max 10 mg twice daily) or loratadine. Avoid known triggers. Severe cases may require short courses of oral corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for 3-5 days).

concepts.title: Urticaria – Complications
concepts.content: Complications are rare but may include anaphylaxis, especially if urticaria is part of an allergic reaction. Chronic urticaria can impact quality of life due to persistent itching and sleep disturbance.

concepts.title: Urticaria – Prognosis
concepts.content: Acute urticaria in children usually resolves within days to weeks with complete recovery. Chronic urticaria may persist for months to years but often improves by adolescence.

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Definition
concepts.content: Viral exanthema refers to a widespread rash occurring in children, typically caused by viral infections. It is characterised by erythematous maculopapular lesions that may be accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever.

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Viral exanthems are common in paediatric populations, particularly in children aged 6 months to 10 years. Incidence peaks in early childhood due to exposure to common viruses such as measles, rubella, and parvovirus B19.

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common viral causes of viral exanthema in children include measles virus, rubella virus, parvovirus B19, human herpesvirus 6 (roseola), and enteroviruses. Risk factors include lack of vaccination, recent exposure to infected individuals, and immunocompromised status.

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Viral exanthems result from immune-mediated responses to viral infections, causing inflammation and damage to dermal blood vessels and skin cells, leading to characteristic erythematous maculopapular rashes.

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Fever is a common presenting feature in viral exanthema, often preceding the rash by 1 to 2 days. Temperatures typically range from 38°C to 40°C in paediatric patients.

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Clinical features: Rash
concepts.content: The rash in viral exanthema typically presents as a widespread erythematous maculopapular eruption, starting on the face or trunk and spreading centrifugally. The rash is usually non-pruritic and resolves within 3 to 7 days.

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Clinical features: Lymphadenopathy
concepts.content: Cervical and postauricular lymphadenopathy may be present in viral exanthema, particularly in rubella infection, and is usually tender and bilateral.

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis of viral exanthema is primarily clinical. Laboratory investigations may include viral serology (e.g., measles IgM, rubella IgM), PCR testing from throat swabs or blood, and full blood count showing lymphocytosis.

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Management
concepts.content: Management of viral exanthema is supportive, including antipyretics such as paracetamol (15 mg/kg every 4-6 hours, max 60 mg/kg/day) and adequate hydration. Isolation is recommended to prevent spread. Specific antiviral treatment is rarely indicated.

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of viral exanthema can include secondary bacterial infection of the skin, post-infectious arthritis (notably with parvovirus B19), and, rarely, encephalitis in measles infection.

concepts.title: Viral exanthema – Prognosis
concepts.content: The prognosis for viral exanthema in children is generally excellent, with most rashes resolving spontaneously without sequelae within 1 week. Serious complications are uncommon in immunocompetent children.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Definition
concepts.content: Viral gastroenteritis is an inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract caused by viral infection, leading to symptoms such as diarrhoea and vomiting in paediatric patients.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Viral gastroenteritis is a common cause of acute diarrhoea in children under 5 years old in the UK, with rotavirus being the most frequent pathogen before the introduction of the rotavirus vaccine in 2013.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common viral causes of paediatric viral gastroenteritis in the UK include rotavirus, norovirus, adenovirus (types 40 and 41), and astrovirus; risk factors include poor hand hygiene, close contact in childcare settings, and lack of rotavirus vaccination.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Viral gastroenteritis causes inflammation and damage to the small intestinal mucosa, leading to malabsorption and secretory diarrhoea due to disruption of enterocytes and increased intestinal motility.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Clinical features: Diarrhoea
concepts.content: Paediatric viral gastroenteritis typically presents with acute onset of watery diarrhoea, which may be frequent and without blood or mucus.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Clinical features: Vomiting
concepts.content: Vomiting is a common symptom in paediatric viral gastroenteritis, often preceding diarrhoea and lasting 1-3 days.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Clinical features: Fever
concepts.content: Mild to moderate fever (up to 38.5°C) may be present in children with viral gastroenteritis.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Clinical features: Dehydration
concepts.content: Signs of dehydration in paediatric viral gastroenteritis include dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes, lethargy, and decreased urine output.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Investigations
concepts.content: Diagnosis is usually clinical; stool PCR testing may be used in severe or prolonged cases to identify viral pathogens; blood tests are not routinely required unless dehydration or complications are suspected.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Management: Oral rehydration therapy
concepts.content: First-line management of paediatric viral gastroenteritis is oral rehydration therapy using WHO-recommended oral rehydration solution (ORS) to prevent or treat dehydration.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Management: Antiemetics
concepts.content: Ondansetron may be used in children over 6 months with persistent vomiting to facilitate oral rehydration; typical dose is 0.15 mg/kg orally once.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Management: Hospital admission criteria
concepts.content: Hospital admission is indicated for children with severe dehydration, inability to tolerate oral fluids, shock, or other complications requiring intravenous fluids and monitoring.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of viral gastroenteritis include severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, metabolic acidosis, and in rare cases, intussusception or secondary bacterial infection.

concepts.title: Viral gastroenteritis – Prognosis
concepts.content: The prognosis of paediatric viral gastroenteritis is generally excellent with appropriate rehydration; symptoms usually resolve within 3-7 days without long-term sequelae.

concepts.title: Visual field defects – Definition
concepts.content: Visual field defects in paediatrics refer to areas of lost or reduced vision within the visual field, caused by damage or dysfunction along the visual pathway from the retina to the visual cortex.

concepts.title: Visual field defects – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Visual field defects in children are relatively uncommon but can occur due to congenital, traumatic, neoplastic, or neurological causes. The prevalence varies depending on the underlying aetiology, with congenital causes being more frequent in early childhood.

concepts.title: Visual field defects – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Common causes of visual field defects in paediatrics include congenital optic nerve hypoplasia, brain tumours (e.g. craniopharyngioma), trauma, stroke, infections such as meningitis, and demyelinating diseases like multiple sclerosis.

concepts.title: Visual field defects – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Visual field defects result from interruption or damage to the visual pathway, which includes the retina, optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiations, and visual cortex. The location of the lesion determines the pattern of visual field loss.

concepts.title: Visual field defects – Clinical features: Presentation
concepts.content: Children with visual field defects may present with difficulty seeing objects to one side, bumping into objects, squint, or behavioural difficulties related to impaired vision. Visual field loss may be detected during routine vision screening or following neurological symptoms.

concepts.title: Visual field defects – Clinical features: Types of visual field loss
concepts.content: Common visual field defects include bitemporal hemianopia (lesion at optic chiasm), homonymous hemianopia (lesion posterior to optic chiasm), quadrantanopia (lesion in optic radiations), and central scotomas (lesion affecting macular fibres).

concepts.title: Visual field defects – Investigations
concepts.content: Assessment includes formal visual field testing adapted for children (e.g. confrontation testing, automated perimetry if possible), fundoscopic examination, neuroimaging with MRI brain and orbits to identify structural lesions, and visual evoked potentials if optic nerve dysfunction is suspected.

concepts.title: Visual field defects – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Differential diagnoses include ocular causes such as retinal dystrophies, amblyopia, refractive errors, and neurological causes like cortical visual impairment or optic neuritis.

concepts.title: Visual field defects – Management
concepts.content: Management depends on the underlying cause. For example, brain tumours may require neurosurgical intervention and oncology input. Supportive measures include referral to paediatric ophthalmology and low vision services, and educational support for children with persistent visual impairment.

concepts.title: Visual field defects – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include permanent visual impairment, increased risk of injury due to impaired peripheral vision, and psychosocial impact including learning difficulties and behavioural problems.

concepts.title: Visual field defects – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis depends on the cause and extent of visual pathway damage. Some defects may improve with treatment (e.g. inflammation), but many visual field defects are permanent. Early diagnosis and intervention improve functional outcomes and quality of life.

concepts.title: Volvulus – Definition
concepts.content: Volvulus is a paediatric surgical emergency characterised by twisting of a loop of intestine around its mesenteric attachment, leading to bowel obstruction and potential ischaemia.

concepts.title: Volvulus – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Volvulus most commonly presents in neonates and infants, particularly within the first month of life, with an incidence of approximately 1 in 6000 live births in the UK.

concepts.title: Volvulus – Aetiology/Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for volvulus in paediatric patients include malrotation of the intestine, Hirschsprung disease, intestinal atresia, and previous abdominal surgery.

concepts.title: Volvulus – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Volvulus causes twisting of the bowel around its mesentery, leading to obstruction of the intestinal lumen and vascular compromise, which can result in bowel ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation if untreated.

concepts.title: Volvulus – Clinical features: Acute abdominal pain
concepts.content: Presentation typically includes sudden onset of severe, colicky abdominal pain in infants or children, often accompanied by irritability and inconsolable crying.

concepts.title: Volvulus – Clinical features: Vomiting
concepts.content: Bilious vomiting is a key clinical feature in paediatric volvulus and should be considered a surgical emergency until proven otherwise.

concepts.title: Volvulus – Clinical features: Abdominal distension
concepts.content: Abdominal distension is commonly observed in infants with volvulus due to bowel obstruction and accumulation of gas and fluid proximal to the twist.

concepts.title: Volvulus – Clinical features: Shock
concepts.content: Signs of shock such as tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, and poor peripheral perfusion may develop rapidly in volvulus due to bowel ischaemia and systemic inflammatory response.

concepts.title: Volvulus – Investigations
concepts.content: Initial investigations include erect abdominal X-ray showing a 'double bubble' sign or dilated bowel loops; upper gastrointestinal contrast study is the gold standard to diagnose malrotation and volvulus.

concepts.title: Volvulus – Differential diagnosis
concepts.content: Differential diagnoses include midgut malrotation without volvulus, intussusception, necrotising enterocolitis, Hirschsprung disease, and other causes of neonatal intestinal obstruction.

concepts.title: Volvulus – Management
concepts.content: Management requires urgent surgical intervention with laparotomy and detorsion of the volvulus; intravenous fluid resuscitation, correction of electrolyte imbalances, and broad-spectrum antibiotics such as intravenous amoxicillin 30 mg/kg every 8 hours plus gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg once daily are administered preoperatively.

concepts.title: Volvulus – Complications
concepts.content: Complications include bowel ischaemia, necrosis, perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, short bowel syndrome following extensive resection, and death if untreated.

concepts.title: Volvulus – Prognosis
concepts.content: Prognosis depends on prompt diagnosis and treatment; early surgical intervention leads to good outcomes, but delayed treatment increases mortality rates up to 30% in neonates.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa definition
concepts.content: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a severe psychiatric disorder characterised by self-induced starvation, excessive weight loss, and distorted body image. It typically manifests during adolescence and predominantly affects females. It is the most common cause of admissions to child and adolescent psychiatric wards.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa epidemiology
concepts.content: Incidence: 37 cases per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 20–30 years. Sex ratio: more common in females 5:1. Approximately 90% of patients are female. Prevalence is between 1:100 and 1:200.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa genetic and biological aetiology
concepts.content: Family studies indicate increased risk for first-degree relatives, suggesting a heritable component. Twin studies show higher concordance in monozygotic than dizygotic twins. Certain gene polymorphisms, particularly those involved in serotonin regulation and energy homeostasis, are associated with AN. Endocrine disturbances (hypercortisolaemia, altered leptin levels) and neuroimaging changes (reduced grey matter volume, altered reward system) have been observed.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa psychological and sociocultural aetiology
concepts.content: Psychological risk factors include perfectionism, rigidity, harm avoidance, low self-esteem, and obsessive-compulsive tendencies. Prior exposure to traumatic events or adverse childhood experiences is linked to AN. Sociocultural factors include cultural idealisation of thinness, peer and family pressure, media promoting thin ideals, and participation in activities emphasising leanness (e.g. ballet, gymnastics).

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa pathophysiology
concepts.content: Pathogenesis involves genetic predisposition (polygenic), neurobiological alterations (serotonin and dopamine dysregulation affecting mood and appetite; HPA axis hyperactivity causing hypercortisolaemia and amenorrhoea), psychological factors (perfectionism, cognitive inflexibility), and sociocultural pressures. Starvation induces neuroendocrine and metabolic changes that perpetuate the disorder in a vicious cycle.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa physical clinical features
concepts.content: Physical signs include reduced body mass index, bradycardia, hypotension, and enlarged salivary glands.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa physiological abnormalities
concepts.content: Physiological abnormalities include hypokalaemia, low FSH, LH, oestrogens and testosterone, raised cortisol and growth hormone, impaired glucose tolerance, hypercholesterolaemia, hypercarotinaemia, and low T3.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa DSM-5 diagnostic criteria
concepts.content: Diagnosis is based on DSM-5 criteria (BMI and amenorrhoea are no longer specifically mentioned): (1) Restriction of energy intake relative to requirements leading to significantly low body weight. (2) Intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, even though underweight. (3) Disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced, undue influence on self-evaluation, or denial of the seriousness of the current low body weight.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa vs bulimia nervosa differential
concepts.content: Both AN and bulimia nervosa (BN) involve preoccupation with body weight/shape and abnormal eating behaviours. Unlike AN, BN is characterised by recurrent binge eating followed by compensatory behaviours (self-induced vomiting, laxatives, diuretics). Patients with BN typically maintain normal or slightly above-normal weight, whereas AN patients are significantly underweight.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa vs major depressive disorder differential
concepts.content: Both AN and MDD can present with weight loss, poor appetite, social withdrawal, and mood disturbances. In MDD, weight loss is unintentional and not associated with distorted body image or fear of weight gain. The primary focus in MDD is pervasive depressive mood and loss of interest, whereas in AN the primary focus is on weight and body image.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa vs hyperthyroidism differential
concepts.content: Both AN and hyperthyroidism can cause significant weight loss and increased physical activity. Hyperthyroidism is distinguished by increased heart rate, heat intolerance, and tremors, with elevated thyroid hormones on blood tests. In AN, thyroid function tests are typically normal or show low-normal function due to the body's adaptive response to starvation.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa management in adults
concepts.content: For adults with anorexia nervosa, NICE recommend considering one of: individual eating-disorder-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT-ED), Maudsley Anorexia Nervosa Treatment for Adults (MANTRA), or specialist supportive clinical management (SSCM).

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa management in children and young people
concepts.content: In children and young people, NICE recommend anorexia-focused family therapy as the first-line treatment. The second-line treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT).

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa cardiovascular complications
concepts.content: Cardiovascular complications include bradycardia, hypotension, and prolonged QT interval, increasing the risk of sudden cardiac death. Mitral valve prolapse may also occur.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa endocrine complications
concepts.content: Endocrine complications include amenorrhoea (due to hypothalamic dysfunction), thyroid dysfunction (hypothyroidism), growth hormone resistance, cortisol excess, and insulin resistance.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa gastrointestinal and bone complications
concepts.content: Gastrointestinal complications include gastroparesis, constipation, liver dysfunction, and superior mesenteric artery syndrome. Bone complications include osteopenia or osteoporosis due to decreased bone mineral density from low oestrogen levels.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa haematological and nutritional complications
concepts.content: Haematological complications include leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and anaemia. Nutritional deficiencies can lead to pellagra (niacin deficiency), scurvy (vitamin C deficiency), and Wernicke's encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency). Secondary complications from purging include electrolyte imbalances, dental issues, and Russell's sign (calluses on knuckles).

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa psychiatric complications
concepts.content: Patients with AN frequently have comorbid psychiatric conditions including depression, anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and an increased risk of suicide.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa prognosis and mortality
concepts.content: AN has the highest mortality rate among psychiatric disorders. The standardised mortality ratio is approximately 5.86, meaning individuals with AN are almost six times more likely to die prematurely. Up to 10% of patients will eventually die because of the disorder. Most deaths occur due to complications from severe malnutrition or suicide.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Anorexia nervosa treatment outcomes
concepts.content: Approximately 50% of individuals with AN achieve full recovery, while around 20–30% remain chronically ill. The remaining patients may experience partial recovery but continue to struggle with body image issues or disordered eating. Early intervention improves outcomes significantly.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Bulimia nervosa definition
concepts.content: Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder characterised by recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by intentional compensatory behaviours such as self-induced vomiting, use of laxatives or diuretics, or excessive exercise.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Bulimia nervosa DSM-5 diagnostic criteria
concepts.content: DSM-5 criteria: (1) Recurrent binge eating (larger amount than most people would eat in similar circumstances). (2) Sense of lack of control during the episode. (3) Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviour (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, fasting, excessive exercise). (4) Binge eating and compensatory behaviours occur on average at least once a week for three months. (5) Self-evaluation unduly influenced by body shape and weight. (6) Disturbance does not occur exclusively during episodes of anorexia nervosa.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Bulimia nervosa physical signs
concepts.content: Recurrent vomiting may lead to erosion of teeth and Russell's sign — calluses on the knuckles or back of the hand due to repeated self-induced vomiting.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Bulimia nervosa management in adults
concepts.content: Referral for specialist care is appropriate in all cases. NICE recommend bulimia-nervosa-focused guided self-help for adults as first-line. If unacceptable, contraindicated, or ineffective after 4 weeks, NICE recommend individual eating-disorder-focused CBT (CBT-ED). Pharmacological treatment: high-dose fluoxetine is currently licensed for bulimia, though long-term data is lacking.

concepts.title: Eating disorders – Bulimia nervosa management in children
concepts.content: Children with bulimia nervosa should be offered bulimia-nervosa-focused family therapy (FT-BN).

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Definition and terminology
concepts.content: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterised by qualitative impairment in social interaction and communication, and repetitive stereotyped behaviour, interests, and activities. DSM-5 uses the term 'autism spectrum disorder' (ASD); ICD-10 uses 'pervasive developmental disorder' (PDD). Symptoms are usually present during early childhood but may manifest later.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Genetic aetiology
concepts.content: Genetic causes including gene defects and chromosomal anomalies are seen in 25% of cases. Sibling recurrence risk is approximately 10%. Concordance in monozygotic twins is 36–60%. Advanced maternal age (≥40 years) and paternal age (≥50 years) are independently associated with ASD risk. Genetic diagnoses associated with ASD include tuberous sclerosis complex, fragile X syndrome, chromosome 15q11-13 duplication syndrome, Angelman syndrome, Rett's syndrome, and Down syndrome.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Immunisation and ASD
concepts.content: The available evidence does not support any association between immunisations and ASD.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: The pathogenesis is not completely understood. Genetic, perinatal, and environmental factors may alter brain development. ASD may result from abnormal function in the hippocampal/amygdala regions and other brain areas. Altered cytokine levels affecting neuronal cell proliferation, neuron death, and synaptic pruning, as well as altered microglia affecting phagocytosis of neurons, may contribute.

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – DSM-5 classification and severity levels
concepts.content: DSM-5 includes autism, Asperger's syndrome, and PDD-NOS under ASD. Severity is rated separately for social communication and restricted/repetitive behaviours: Level 1 (requiring support), Level 2 (requiring substantial support), Level 3 (requiring very substantial support).

concepts.title: Autism spectrum disorder – Clinical features: social communication impairments
concepts.content: Children and adults with ASD show persistent deficits in social communication and interaction: failure to regulate social interaction with nonverbal cues (eye gaze, facial expression, gestures); failure to form and maintain appropriate relationships; social isolation; and deficits in social-emotional reciprocity.
