concepts.content: BPH is a common condition in older men. Around 50% of 50-year-old men have evidence of BPH and 30% have symptoms. Around 80% of 80-year-old men have evidence of BPH. Ethnicity risk: black > white > Asian.

concepts.title: Benign prostatic hyperplasia – Voiding (obstructive) symptoms
concepts.content: BPH voiding (obstructive) symptoms include: weak or intermittent urinary flow, straining, hesitancy, terminal dribbling, and incomplete emptying.

concepts.title: Benign prostatic hyperplasia – Storage (irritative) symptoms
concepts.content: BPH storage (irritative) symptoms include: urgency, frequency, urgency incontinence, and nocturia.

concepts.title: Benign prostatic hyperplasia – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of BPH include: urinary tract infection, urinary retention, and obstructive uropathy.

concepts.title: Benign prostatic hyperplasia – Assessment
concepts.content: Assessment of BPH includes: urine dipstick, U&Es (especially if chronic retention suspected), PSA (if obstructive symptoms or concern about prostate cancer), urinary frequency-volume chart (≥3 days), and International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS). IPSS: 0–7 mildly symptomatic; 8–19 moderately symptomatic; 20–35 severely symptomatic.

concepts.title: Benign prostatic hyperplasia – Alpha-1 antagonist treatment
concepts.content: Alpha-1 antagonists (e.g. tamsulosin, alfuzosin) decrease smooth muscle tone of the prostate and bladder. They are considered first-line by NICE for moderate-to-severe voiding symptoms (IPSS ≥8) and improve symptoms in around 70% of men. Adverse effects include dizziness, postural hypotension, dry mouth, and depression.

concepts.title: Benign prostatic hyperplasia – 5-alpha reductase inhibitor treatment
concepts.content: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (e.g. finasteride) block conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which induces BPH. They are indicated for significantly enlarged prostate with high risk of progression. Unlike alpha-1 antagonists, they reduce prostate volume and may slow disease progression, but symptoms may not improve for 6 months. They may decrease PSA by up to 50%. Adverse effects: erectile dysfunction, reduced libido, ejaculation problems, gynaecomastia.

concepts.title: Benign prostatic hyperplasia – Combination therapy and antimuscarinics
concepts.content: Combination therapy (alpha-1 antagonist + 5-alpha reductase inhibitor) is supported by the MTOPS trial and NICE for men with bothersome moderate-to-severe voiding symptoms and prostatic enlargement. If storage symptoms persist after alpha-blocker alone, an antimuscarinic (e.g. tolterodine, darifenacin) may be added. Surgery (TURP) is the main surgical option.

concepts.title: Benign prostatic hyperplasia – TURP syndrome
concepts.content: TURP syndrome is a rare, life-threatening complication of TURP surgery. It is caused by systemic absorption of large volumes of hypo-osmolar glycine irrigation fluid when prostatic venous sinuses are opened. This causes hyponatraemia and, when glycine is metabolised to ammonia by the liver, hyperammonaemia and visual disturbances. Risk factors include: surgical time >1 hour, bag height >70 cm, resected tissue >60 g, large blood loss, perforation, large fluid volume used, and poorly controlled cardiac failure.

concepts.title: Bladder cancer – Epidemiology and histological types
concepts.content: Bladder cancer is the second most common urological cancer, most commonly affecting males aged 50–80 years. Histological types: urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma >90% of cases; squamous cell carcinoma 1–7% (more common in schistosomiasis-endemic regions); adenocarcinoma 2%.

concepts.title: Bladder cancer – Risk factors for TCC
concepts.content: Risk factors for urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma of the bladder: smoking (most important in Western countries, accounting for ~50% of cases; hazard ratio ~4); exposure to aniline dyes (e.g. 2-naphthylamine, benzidine; printing and textile industry); rubber manufacture; cyclophosphamide.

concepts.title: Bladder cancer – Risk factors for SCC
concepts.content: Risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder include schistosomiasis (most important cause of SCC globally) and smoking.

concepts.title: Bladder cancer – TNM staging
concepts.content: TNM staging of bladder cancer: T0 = no evidence of tumour; Ta = non-invasive papillary carcinoma; T1 = tumour invades sub-epithelial connective tissue; T2a = invades superficial muscularis propria (inner half); T2b = invades deep muscularis propria (outer half); T3 = tumour extends beyond muscularis propria; T4 = invades adjacent structures. Those with T3 disease or worse have ≥30% risk of regional or distant lymph node metastasis.

concepts.title: Bladder cancer – Prognosis by stage
concepts.content: Five-year survival rates for bladder cancer by stage: T1: 90%; T2: 60%; T3: 35%; T4a: 10–25%; any T with N1–N2: 30%.

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – Common causes
concepts.content: Common causes of chronic kidney disease include: diabetic nephropathy, chronic glomerulonephritis, chronic pyelonephritis, hypertension, and adult polycystic kidney disease.

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – eGFR estimation
concepts.content: Serum creatinine alone does not accurately reflect renal function due to differences in muscle mass. The MDRD equation estimates GFR using serum creatinine, age, gender and ethnicity. Factors affecting eGFR accuracy include pregnancy, muscle mass extremes (amputees, bodybuilders), and eating red meat within 12 hours of sampling.

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – eGFR staging
concepts.content: CKD staging by eGFR: Stage 1: >90 ml/min with kidney damage signs; Stage 2: 60–90 ml/min with kidney damage signs; Stage 3a: 45–59 ml/min; Stage 3b: 30–44 ml/min; Stage 4: 15–29 ml/min (severe reduction); Stage 5: <15 ml/min (established kidney failure — dialysis or transplant may be needed).

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – Clinical features
concepts.content: CKD is usually asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally on abnormal U&Es. Late-stage features include: oedema (ankle swelling, weight gain), polyuria, lethargy, pruritus (secondary to uraemia), anorexia/weight loss, insomnia, nausea and vomiting, and hypertension.

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – Hypertension management
concepts.content: Most CKD patients require more than two antihypertensive drugs. ACE inhibitors are first-line, particularly in proteinuric renal disease. An eGFR fall of up to 25% or creatinine rise of up to 30% is acceptable; greater rises may indicate renovascular disease. Furosemide is useful when GFR falls below 45 ml/min (NKF K/DOQI suggests <30 ml/min) — it lowers serum potassium but should be withheld if dehydration risk.

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – Anaemia: causes
concepts.content: Anaemia in CKD is usually normochromic normocytic and becomes apparent when GFR <35 ml/min. Causes include: reduced erythropoietin production (most significant); reduced iron absorption (elevated hepcidin levels in CKD impair gut iron absorption and macrophage iron release); uraemia toxicity on bone marrow; anorexia/nausea; reduced RBC survival (especially on haemodialysis); blood loss from capillary fragility and poor platelet function; and stress ulceration. Anaemia in CKD predisposes to left ventricular hypertrophy — associated with a threefold increase in mortality.

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – Anaemia: management
concepts.content: NICE 2011 guidelines suggest a target haemoglobin of 10–12 g/dl. Iron status should be optimised before starting erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs). Oral iron is offered to patients not on ESAs or haemodialysis; if target Hb not reached within 3 months, switch to IV iron. Patients on ESAs or haemodialysis generally require IV iron. ESAs (erythropoietin, darbepoetin) are used in those likely to benefit in terms of quality of life and physical function.

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – Bone disease: pathophysiology
concepts.content: In CKD: reduced 1-alpha hydroxylation → low vitamin D; reduced phosphate excretion → high phosphate. High phosphate drags calcium from bones (renal osteodystrophy); low calcium results from lack of vitamin D and high phosphate (phosphate binds free calcium). Secondary hyperparathyroidism develops due to low calcium, high phosphate and low vitamin D, leading to bone resorption and vascular calcification.

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – Bone disease: clinical manifestations
concepts.content: Clinical manifestations of CKD-related bone disease include: osteitis fibrosa cystica (hyperparathyroid bone disease); adynamic bone disease (reduced osteoblast/osteoclast activity, may be due to over-treatment with vitamin D); osteomalacia (due to low vitamin D); osteosclerosis; and osteoporosis.

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – Bone disease: phosphate binders
concepts.content: Phosphate binders used in CKD: calcium-based binders are first-line if serum calcium is normal or low with no significant vascular calcification risk (risk of hypercalcaemia). Sevelamer (non-calcium based) is used if hypercalcaemic or vascular calcification risk — it also reduces uric acid and improves lipid profiles. Other non-calcium options include lanthanum carbonate and ferric citrate. Aluminium-based binders are less commonly used.

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – Bone disease: vitamin D therapy
concepts.content: In early CKD (stages 1–3), native vitamin D (ergocalciferol/cholecalciferol) is used first to correct deficiency, as some renal 1-alpha hydroxylase activity remains. In advanced CKD (stages 4–5), active analogues alfacalcidol or calcitriol are used to suppress PTH in secondary hyperparathyroidism, as the kidneys can no longer activate vitamin D. Doses should be titrated to minimise hypercalcaemia and adynamic bone disease.

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – Bone disease: parathyroidectomy
concepts.content: Parathyroidectomy may be considered in patients with refractory secondary hyperparathyroidism despite optimal medical management, typically when PTH remains persistently elevated with associated symptoms or complications.

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – Proteinuria: ACR measurement
concepts.content: NICE recommend the albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) over protein:creatinine ratio (PCR) for identifying proteinuria, as it has greater sensitivity. ACR should be a first-pass morning urine specimen. If initial ACR is 3–70 mg/mmol, confirm with a subsequent early morning sample. If ≥70 mg/mmol, repeat is not needed. A confirmed ACR ≥3 mg/mmol is clinically important proteinuria. Approximate equivalents: ACR 30 ≈ PCR 50 ≈ 0.5 g/24h; ACR 70 ≈ PCR 100 ≈ 1 g/24h.

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – Proteinuria: referral criteria
concepts.content: NICE referral criteria to nephrologist for proteinuria: ACR ≥70 mg/mmol (unless caused by diabetes and already treated); ACR ≥30 mg/mmol with persistent haematuria (2/3 dipstick tests showing 1+ blood after UTI excluded); consider referral for ACR 3–29 mg/mmol with persistent haematuria and other risk factors (declining eGFR, cardiovascular disease).

concepts.title: Chronic kidney disease – Proteinuria: management with ACE inhibitors and SGLT-2 inhibitors
concepts.content: ACE inhibitors (or ARBs) are key in proteinuria management: first-line in CKD with hypertension if ACR >30 mg/mmol; indicated regardless of blood pressure if ACR >70 mg/mmol. SGLT-2 inhibitors benefit patients with proteinuric CKD (with or without diabetes) by blocking proximal tubule glucose reabsorption → glycosuria, reducing sodium reabsorption → natriuresis, and normalising tubuloglomerular feedback to reduce intraglomerular pressure.

concepts.title: ADPKD – Genetics and epidemiology
concepts.content: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common inherited kidney disease, affecting 1 in 1,000 Caucasians. Two disease loci: PKD1 (chromosome 16, polycystin-1) accounts for 85% of cases and presents with renal failure earlier; PKD2 (chromosome 4, polycystin-2) accounts for 15% of cases.

concepts.title: ADPKD – Ultrasound diagnostic criteria
concepts.content: Ultrasound diagnostic criteria for ADPKD in patients with positive family history: aged <30 years: ≥2 cysts (unilateral or bilateral); aged 30–59 years: ≥2 cysts in both kidneys; aged >60 years: ≥4 cysts in both kidneys.

concepts.title: ADPKD – Management with tolvaptan
concepts.content: Tolvaptan (vasopressin receptor 2 antagonist) may slow cyst development and renal insufficiency in ADPKD. NICE recommend it only if: CKD stage 2 or 3 at start of treatment; evidence of rapidly progressing disease; and the company provides it with the agreed patient access scheme discount.

concepts.title: Diabetic nephropathy – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Diabetic nephropathy is the commonest cause of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in the western world. 33% of patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus have diabetic nephropathy by age 40 years. Approximately 5–10% of patients with type 1 DM develop ESRD.

concepts.title: Diabetic nephropathy – Pathophysiology and histology
concepts.content: Pathophysiology involves haemodynamic changes in the glomerulus leading to increased glomerular capillary pressure, and non-enzymatic glycosylation of the basement membrane. Histological changes include: basement membrane thickening, capillary obliteration, mesangial widening, and nodular hyaline areas (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules).

concepts.title: Diabetic nephropathy – Risk factors
concepts.content: Modifiable risk factors for diabetic nephropathy: hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, smoking, poor glycaemic control, raised dietary protein. Non-modifiable risk factors: male sex, duration of diabetes, genetic predisposition (e.g. ACE gene polymorphisms).

concepts.title: Diabetic nephropathy – Stages 1–5
concepts.content: Stage 1: hyperfiltration (increased GFR), may be reversible. Stage 2 (silent/latent): most patients do not develop microalbuminuria for 10 years; GFR remains elevated. Stage 3 (incipient nephropathy): microalbuminuria (albumin excretion 30–300 mg/day, dipstick negative). Stage 4 (overt nephropathy): persistent proteinuria (>300 mg/day, dipstick positive); hypertension in most; diffuse and focal glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules). Stage 5: ESRD, GFR typically <10 ml/min; renal replacement therapy needed.

concepts.title: Diabetic nephropathy – Screening
concepts.content: All patients with diabetes should be screened annually using urinary ACR (early morning specimen). ACR ≥3.0 mg/mmol indicates clinically significant albuminuria. ACR >2.5 mg/mmol in men or >3.5 mg/mmol in women suggests abnormal excretion and should be confirmed with repeat testing.

concepts.title: Diabetic nephropathy – Management
concepts.content: Management of diabetic nephropathy: tight glycaemic control to slow progression; BP target <130/80 mmHg if ACR ≥3.0 mg/mmol, or <140/90 mmHg if ACR <3.0 mg/mmol; ACE inhibitor or ARB if urinary ACR ≥3.0 mg/mmol regardless of blood pressure (dual RAS blockade should NOT be used); statin therapy for dyslipidaemia; dietary protein restriction not routinely recommended.

concepts.title: Diabetes insipidus – Definition and types
concepts.content: Diabetes insipidus (DI) is characterised by a deficiency in the action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH/AVP). Cranial (central) DI (AVP-D) results from deficient ADH secretion. Nephrogenic DI (AVP-R) results from renal insensitivity to ADH. ADH is synthesised in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary.

concepts.title: Diabetes insipidus – Causes of cranial DI
concepts.content: Causes of cranial DI include: idiopathic, post head injury, pituitary surgery, craniopharyngiomas, infiltrative disease (histiocytosis X, sarcoidosis). DIDMOAD (Wolfram's syndrome) is the association of cranial Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy and Deafness.

concepts.title: Diabetes insipidus – Causes of nephrogenic DI
concepts.content: Causes of nephrogenic DI: genetic (more common form: ADH receptor mutation; less common: aquaporin-2 channel mutation); electrolyte disturbances (hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia); lithium (desensitises collecting duct response to ADH); demeclocycline; tubulo-interstitial disease (obstruction, sickle-cell, pyelonephritis); haemochromatosis.

concepts.title: Diabetes insipidus – Clinical features
concepts.content: Clinical features of diabetes insipidus are polyuria and polydipsia.

concepts.title: Diabetes insipidus – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations for DI: high plasma osmolality (often >295 mOsm/kg) with low urine osmolality (often <300 mOsm/kg); urine osmolality >700 mOsm/kg generally excludes DI. Water deprivation test is used to confirm diagnosis. A desmopressin test differentiates cranial from nephrogenic DI — an increase in urine osmolality after desmopressin suggests cranial DI.

concepts.title: Diabetes insipidus – Management
concepts.content: Management of nephrogenic DI: thiazide diuretics and low salt/protein diet. Management of cranial DI: desmopressin (synthetic ADH analogue).

concepts.title: Dehydration – Clinical features
concepts.content: Dehydration is a common presentation in the elderly. Examination findings have poor sensitivity and specificity. Features include: dry mucous membranes, loss of skin turgor, sunken eyes; in severe dehydration: tachycardia, hypotension and delirium.

concepts.title: Dehydration – Adult IV fluid maintenance requirements
concepts.content: NICE 2013 maintenance fluid requirements for adults: 25–30 ml/kg/day of water; approximately 1 mmol/kg/day of potassium, sodium and chloride; approximately 50–100 g/day of glucose (to limit starvation ketosis). For a 80 kg patient this equates to approximately 2 litres of water and 80 mmol potassium per 24 hours.

concepts.title: Dehydration – IV fluid types and electrolyte composition
concepts.content: Electrolyte concentrations (mmol/L): Plasma: Na+ 135–145, Cl- 98–105, K+ 3.5–5, HCO3- 22–28. 0.9% saline: Na+ 154, Cl- 154. 5% glucose: glucose 50 g/L. 0.18% saline with 4% glucose: Na+ 30, Cl- 30, glucose 40 g/L. Hartmann's solution: Na+ 131, Cl- 111, K+ 5, HCO3- 29. Large volumes of 0.9% saline increase risk of hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis.

concepts.title: Dehydration – Paediatric IV fluid indications and requirements
concepts.content: IV fluids in children are required if >10% dehydrated, or 5–10% dehydrated with oral/enteral rehydration not tolerated. Fluid requirements (Holliday-Segar): <10 kg: 100 ml/kg/24h; 10–20 kg: 100 ml/kg for first 10 kg + 50 ml/kg for each kg over 10 kg; >20 kg: 100 + 50 + 20 ml/kg for each kg over 20 kg (max 2 L in females, 2.5 L in males). Fluid type: 0.9% NaCl + 5% dextrose, with potassium added as required.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Definition and causes
concepts.content: Epididymo-orchitis is an infection of the epididymis +/- testes. In sexually active younger adults, it is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (local spread from genital tract). In older adults with low-risk sexual history, E. coli (spread from bladder) is the typical cause.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Clinical features
concepts.content: Features of epididymo-orchitis: unilateral testicular pain and swelling; urethral discharge may be present but urethritis is often asymptomatic. The most important differential is testicular torsion, which should be excluded urgently. Features suggesting torsion: age <20 years, severe pain, acute onset.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Management: STI cause
concepts.content: If STI is the most likely cause, urgent referral to a sexual health clinic is advised. If organism unknown, BASHH recommend: ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly as a single dose, plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10–14 days.

concepts.title: Epididymitis and orchitis – Management: enteric cause
concepts.content: If enteric organisms are the most likely cause (older adults, low-risk sexual history), send a mid-stream urine (MSU) for microscopy and culture, and treat empirically with an oral quinolone for 2 weeks (e.g. ofloxacin). Further investigations following treatment may be recommended to exclude structural abnormalities.

concepts.title: Multiple myeloma – Definition and epidemiology
concepts.content: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a haematological malignancy characterised by plasma cell proliferation arising from genetic mutations during B-lymphocyte differentiation. It is the second most common haematological malignancy. Median age at presentation is 70 years.

concepts.title: Multiple myeloma – CRABBI features: Calcium
concepts.content: Hypercalcaemia in myeloma is primarily due to increased osteoclastic bone resorption caused by local cytokines (IL-1, TNF) released by myeloma cells. Less common contributing factors include impaired renal function, increased renal tubular calcium reabsorption and elevated PTH-rP. Symptoms: constipation, nausea, anorexia and confusion.

concepts.title: Multiple myeloma – CRABBI features: Renal
concepts.content: Renal involvement in myeloma results from monoclonal immunoglobulin light chain deposition within renal tubules, causing renal damage presenting as dehydration and increasing thirst. Other causes of renal impairment in myeloma include amyloidosis, nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis.

concepts.title: Multiple myeloma – CRABBI features: Anaemia, Bleeding, Bones, Infection
concepts.content: Anaemia: bone marrow crowding suppresses erythropoiesis → fatigue, pallor. Bleeding: thrombocytopenia from bone marrow crowding → increased bruising/bleeding risk. Bones: lytic lesions from plasma cell infiltration and cytokine-mediated osteoclast overactivity → back pain, pathological fractures. Infection: reduced normal immunoglobulin production → increased susceptibility to infection.

concepts.title: Multiple myeloma – Other clinical features
concepts.content: Other features of myeloma include: amyloidosis (e.g. macroglossia), carpal tunnel syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, and hyperviscosity.

concepts.title: Multiple myeloma – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations for myeloma: FBC (anaemia); peripheral blood film (rouleaux formation); U&E (renal failure); bone profile (hypercalcaemia); protein electrophoresis (monoclonal IgA/IgG in serum; Bence Jones proteins in urine); bone marrow aspiration (significantly raised plasma cells confirms diagnosis); imaging: whole-body MRI (recommended by 2016 NICE guidelines); X-ray: 'raindrop skull'.

concepts.title: Multiple myeloma – Diagnostic criteria
concepts.content: Diagnostic criteria for myeloma require one major and one minor criterion, or three minor criteria, in a symptomatic patient. Major criteria: plasmacytoma on biopsy; ≥30% plasma cells in bone marrow; elevated M protein in blood or urine. Minor criteria: 10–30% plasma cells in bone marrow; minor M protein elevation; osteolytic lesions on imaging; low levels of normal antibodies in blood.

concepts.title: Multiple myeloma – Induction therapy
concepts.content: Myeloma is currently incurable; management aims to control symptoms, reduce complications and prolong survival. Induction therapy uses a combination of: targeted drugs (thalidomide, lenalidomide, bortezomib, daratumumab); chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide or melphalan); and steroids (prednisolone or dexamethasone). The combination depends on suitability for autologous haematopoietic cell transplantation.

concepts.title: Multiple myeloma – Autologous HSCT
concepts.content: Autologous haematopoietic cell transplantation (HSCT) involves removal of the patient's own stem cells prior to chemotherapy, then replacement after chemotherapy. It prolongs both event-free and overall survival compared to non-transplant strategies. It is typically offered to younger, healthier patients. Allogenic HSCT is not commonly used due to high overall mortality and graft-versus-host disease; currently only used in clinical trials.

concepts.title: Multiple myeloma – Complications management
concepts.content: Complications management in myeloma: pain: WHO analgesic ladder; pathological fractures: zoledronic acid to prevent/manage osteoporosis and fragility fractures; infection: annual influenza vaccination, immunoglobulin replacement therapy; VTE prophylaxis; fatigue: treat underlying causes, consider erythropoietin analogue if symptoms persist.

concepts.title: Nephrotic syndrome – Definition and causes
concepts.content: Nephrotic syndrome is characterised by a triad of: proteinuria (>3 g/24hr), hypoalbuminaemia (<30 g/L), and oedema. Primary causes include minimal change disease, FSGS, and membranous nephropathy. Secondary causes include diabetes mellitus, SLE, amyloidosis, infections (HIV, hepatitis B and C), and drugs (NSAIDs, gold therapy).

concepts.title: Nephrotic syndrome – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Nephrotic syndrome pathophysiology: damage to the glomerular basement membrane and podocytes → increased protein permeability → proteinuria → hypoalbuminaemia → reduced plasma oncotic pressure → oedema. Loss of antithrombin-III, proteins C and S, and rise in fibrinogen → thrombosis risk. Loss of thyroxine-binding globulin → low total (but not free) thyroxine.

concepts.title: Nephrotic syndrome – Investigations
concepts.content: Initial investigations in nephrotic syndrome: urine dipstick (proteinuria; check for microscopic haematuria); MSU to exclude UTI; quantify proteinuria using early morning protein:creatinine ratio or ACR; FBC and coagulation screen; urea and electrolytes.

concepts.title: Nephrotic syndrome – Complications
concepts.content: Complications of nephrotic syndrome: thromboembolism (DVT, PE, renal vein thrombosis) due to loss of antithrombin III and plasminogen; hyperlipidaemia (increased risk of ACS, stroke); chronic kidney disease; increased infection risk (urinary immunoglobulin loss); hypocalcaemia (vitamin D and binding protein lost in urine).

concepts.title: Minimal change disease – Epidemiology and causes
concepts.content: Minimal change disease accounts for 75% of nephrotic syndrome in children and 25% in adults. The majority of cases are idiopathic. In around 10–20% a cause is found: drugs (NSAIDs, rifampicin), Hodgkin's lymphoma, thymoma, or infectious mononucleosis.

concepts.title: Minimal change disease – Pathophysiology
concepts.content: Minimal change disease pathophysiology: T-cell and cytokine-mediated damage to the glomerular basement membrane → polyanion loss → reduced electrostatic charge → increased glomerular permeability to serum albumin.

concepts.title: Minimal change disease – Features and biopsy findings
concepts.content: Features: nephrotic syndrome; normotension (hypertension is rare); highly selective proteinuria (only albumin and transferrin leak). Renal biopsy: normal glomeruli on light microscopy; electron microscopy shows fusion of podocytes and effacement of foot processes.

concepts.title: Minimal change disease – Management and prognosis
concepts.content: Management: oral corticosteroids (80% of cases are steroid-responsive); cyclophosphamide is the next step for steroid-resistant cases. Prognosis is overall good but relapse is common: approximately 1/3 have one episode; 1/3 have infrequent relapses; 1/3 have frequent relapses that stop before adulthood.

concepts.title: Prostate cancer – Epidemiology
concepts.content: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in adult males in the UK and the second most common cause of cancer death in men after lung cancer. Up to 30,000 men are diagnosed each year; up to 9,000 die from the condition per year in the UK.

concepts.title: Prostate cancer – Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for prostate cancer: increasing age, obesity, Afro-Caribbean ethnicity, family history (around 5–10% of cases have a strong family history), and BRCA mutations.

concepts.title: Prostate cancer – Clinical features
concepts.content: Localised prostate cancer is often asymptomatic (cancers develop in the peripheral zone and do not cause early obstructive symptoms). Features may include: bladder outlet obstruction (hesitancy, urinary retention); haematuria, haematospermia; back, perineal or testicular pain; DRE: asymmetrical, hard, nodular enlargement with loss of median sulcus. Metastatic disease may present as bone pain.

concepts.title: Prostate cancer – PSA and pathology
concepts.content: Normal upper limit for PSA is 4 ng/ml. False positives: prostatitis, UTI, BPH, vigorous DRE. Free:total PSA <20% is suggestive of cancer and biopsy is advised. Pathology: 95% adenocarcinoma; often multifocal; 70% lie in the peripheral zone. Graded using Gleason score (sum of two grades, each 1–5; score 2 = best prognosis, 10 = worst). Lymphatic spread occurs first to obturator nodes.

concepts.title: Prostate cancer – Active surveillance criteria
concepts.content: NICE recommends active surveillance as the preferred option for low-risk prostate cancer. Suitable for: clinical stage T1c, Gleason score 3+3, PSA density <0.15 ng/ml/ml, cancer in <50% of biopsy cores, <10 mm of any core involved. Candidates should have ≥10 biopsy cores taken and ≥1 re-biopsy. If disease progression is evident, offer radical treatment.

concepts.title: Prostate cancer – Treatment options
concepts.content: Treatment options for prostate cancer: watchful waiting (elderly, multiple comorbidities, low Gleason score); external beam radiotherapy (curative and palliative; similar survival to surgery; radiation proctitis risk; brachytherapy); radical prostatectomy (robotic preferred; obturator lymph nodes removed; erectile dysfunction common complication); hormonal therapy (testosterone dependence; bilateral orchidectomy; LHRH analogues; anti-androgens; used in metastatic disease or as neoadjuvant therapy).

concepts.title: Testicular cancer – Epidemiology and types
concepts.content: Testicular cancer is the most common malignancy in men aged 20–30 years. 95% of testicular tumours are germ cell tumours (GCTs). Types: seminomas; non-seminomas (embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumour, teratoma, choriocarcinoma); non-germ cell tumours (Leydig cell tumours, sarcomas). Peak incidence: teratomas at 25 years; seminomas at 35 years.

concepts.title: Testicular cancer – Risk factors
concepts.content: Risk factors for testicular cancer: infertility (3× increased risk); cryptorchidism (undescended testes); family history; Klinefelter's syndrome; mumps orchitis.

concepts.title: Testicular cancer – Clinical features
concepts.content: Most common presentation is a painless lump. Pain is present in a minority. Hydrocele may be present. Gynaecomastia may occur due to an increased oestrogen:androgen ratio — germ cell tumours produce hCG, which stimulates Leydig cells and disrupts the normal testosterone:oestrogen balance.

concepts.title: Testicular cancer – Tumour markers
concepts.content: Tumour markers in testicular cancer: seminomas: hCG elevated in ~20% (AFP is NOT elevated in pure seminomas); non-seminomas: AFP and/or beta-hCG elevated in 80–85%; LDH elevated in ~40% of all GCTs (marker of tumour bulk). Ultrasound is the first-line investigation.

concepts.title: Testicular cancer – Management and prognosis
concepts.content: Management: orchidectomy is the primary treatment; chemotherapy (BEP: bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin) and/or radiotherapy depending on stage and histological type. Prognosis: seminoma Stage I: 95% 5-year survival; teratoma Stage I: 85% 5-year survival.

concepts.title: Urinary incontinence – Epidemiology and risk factors
concepts.content: Urinary incontinence affects 4–5% of the population and is more common in elderly females. Risk factors: advancing age, pregnancy and childbirth, high BMI, hysterectomy, and family history.

concepts.title: Urinary incontinence – Classification
concepts.content: Classification of urinary incontinence: overactive bladder (OAB)/urge incontinence (involuntary detrusor contractions); stress incontinence (leakage with increased intra-abdominal pressure, e.g. coughing, sneezing); mixed incontinence (both urge and stress); overflow incontinence (bladder over-distension, e.g. BPH, neurological disease); functional incontinence (physical/cognitive impairment preventing timely toileting).

concepts.title: Urinary incontinence – Investigations
concepts.content: Investigations for urinary incontinence: bladder diaries (minimum 3 days); vaginal examination; urine dipstick and culture (to exclude UTI); urodynamic studies (if diagnosis unclear or prior to surgery).

concepts.title: Urinary incontinence – Management of urge incontinence
concepts.content: Management of urge incontinence: first-line: bladder retraining for ≥6 weeks; antimuscarinics: oxybutynin (immediate-release; avoid in frail elderly due to CNS side effects), tolterodine (immediate-release), darifenacin, solifenacin; mirabegron (beta-3 agonist, alternative to antimuscarinics); desmopressin for nocturia; botulinum toxin injection for refractory cases.

concepts.title: Urinary incontinence – Management of stress incontinence
concepts.content: Management of stress incontinence: lifestyle modifications (weight loss, reduce caffeine); pelvic floor muscle training (≥8 contractions, 3 sets per day, for ≥3 months); surgical options: mid-urethral tape (tension-free vaginal tape), colposuspension, urethral bulking agents; duloxetine (SNRI) increases noradrenaline and serotonin at the pudendal nerve motor nucleus → urethral sphincter contraction.

concepts.title: Urinary tract calculi – Types and radiographic appearance
concepts.content: Types and frequency of urinary tract calculi: calcium oxalate 40%; mixed calcium oxalate/phosphate 25%; triple phosphate (struvite) 10%; calcium phosphate 10%; urate 5–10%; cystine 1%; xanthine <1%. Radiographic appearance: calcium-based stones: radio-opaque; urate and xanthine stones: radiolucent; cystine stones: semi-opaque (ground-glass appearance).

concepts.title: Urinary tract calculi – Staghorn calculi
concepts.content: Staghorn calculi are triple phosphate (struvite) stones that form in alkaline urine, typically in the context of infection with urease-producing organisms such as Ureaplasma urealyticum and Proteus mirabilis. They involve the renal pelvis and at least two calyces.

concepts.title: Urinary tract calculi – Risk factors for calcium stones
concepts.content: Risk factors for calcium stones: dehydration, hypercalciuria, hyperparathyroidism, hypercalcaemia, cystinuria, high dietary oxalate, renal tubular acidosis, medullary sponge kidney, polycystic kidney disease, beryllium and cadmium exposure. Drugs promoting calcium stones: loop diuretics, steroids, acetazolamide, theophylline. Thiazide diuretics reduce calcium stone risk.

concepts.title: Urinary tract calculi – Risk factors for urate stones
concepts.content: Risk factors for urate stones: gout and ileostomy (increased uric acid excretion).

concepts.title: Haematuria – Terminology and epidemiology
concepts.content: Haematuria terminology: non-visible (microscopic) haematuria = blood detected on dipstick or microscopy but not visible to the naked eye; visible (macroscopic/frank) haematuria = blood visible to the naked eye. Non-visible haematuria is found in approximately 2.5% of the population.

concepts.title: Haematuria – Causes of transient non-visible haematuria
concepts.content: Common causes of transient or spurious non-visible haematuria: urinary tract infection, menstruation, vigorous exercise, and recent sexual intercourse.

concepts.title: Haematuria – Causes of persistent non-visible haematuria
concepts.content: Causes of persistent non-visible haematuria: malignancy (bladder, renal, prostate cancer), urinary tract calculi, BPH, prostatitis, urethritis, IgA nephropathy, and thin basement membrane disease.

concepts.title: Haematuria – Thin basement membrane disease
concepts.content: Thin basement membrane disease is a hereditary condition characterised by diffuse thinning of the glomerular basement membrane. It is autosomal dominant and affects approximately 1–5% of the population. It is an important cause of persistent non-visible haematuria and carries an excellent prognosis.

concepts.title: Haematuria – Spurious red/orange urine
concepts.content: Causes of red or orange urine that are not haematuria: foods (beetroot, rhubarb); drugs (rifampicin, doxorubicin). These will be negative on urine dipstick for blood.

concepts.title: Haematuria – Investigation and NICE referral criteria
concepts.content: Persistent non-visible haematuria is defined as blood detected on 2 out of 3 dipstick tests, 2–3 weeks apart, with UTI excluded. Investigations: renal function, ACR/PCR, blood pressure. NICE urgent referral (2-week wait): age ≥45 with unexplained visible haematuria without UTI, or visible haematuria that persists after UTI treatment; age ≥60 with non-visible haematuria plus dysuria or raised WBC on urinalysis. Non-urgent referral: age ≥60 with recurrent or persistent unexplained UTI.

concepts.title: Hyperkalaemia – Staging and ECG changes
concepts.content: Hyperkalaemia staging: mild 5.5–5.9 mmol/L; moderate 6.0–6.4 mmol/L; severe ≥6.5 mmol/L. ECG changes in order of severity: peaked T waves (first change); loss of P waves; broad QRS complex; sinusoidal pattern (pre-cardiac arrest). Hyperkalaemia is a medical emergency when severe or associated with ECG changes.

concepts.title: Hyperkalaemia – Management
concepts.content: Management of hyperkalaemia: (1) Cardiac membrane stabilisation: IV calcium gluconate 10 ml of 10% over 5–10 minutes (onset immediate; duration 30–60 min). (2) Shift K+ into cells: combined insulin/dextrose infusion (e.g. 10 units actrapid in 50 ml of 50% glucose over 30 min); nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg. (3) Remove K+ from body: calcium resonium (oral or enema); loop diuretics; dialysis. Newer agents: sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (selective K+ trapper; better tolerability than resonium).

concepts.title: Hypokalaemia – Features and ECG changes
concepts.content: Features of hypokalaemia: muscle weakness, hypotonia, cardiac arrhythmias, increased risk of digoxin toxicity. ECG changes: U waves (most characteristic), small or absent T waves, prolonged PR interval, ST depression.

concepts.title: Hypokalaemia – Causes with alkalosis vs. acidosis
concepts.content: Hypokalaemia with alkalosis: vomiting, thiazide/loop diuretics, Cushing's syndrome, Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism). Hypokalaemia with acidosis: diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis (types 1 and 2), acetazolamide, partially treated DKA.

concepts.title: Hypokalaemia – Causes with and without hypertension
concepts.content: Hypokalaemia with hypertension: Cushing's syndrome, Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism), Liddle's syndrome, 11-beta hydroxylase deficiency. Hypokalaemia without hypertension: diuretics, GI loss, renal tubular acidosis (types 1 and 2), Bartter's syndrome, Gitelman's syndrome.

concepts.title: Hyponatraemia – Causes and classification
concepts.content: Hyponatraemia causes by urinary sodium: urinary Na >20 mmol/L: diuretics, Addison's disease, SIADH, hypothyroidism. Urinary Na <20 mmol/L: GI loss (vomiting/diarrhoea), heart failure, liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome. Severity: mild 130–134 mmol/L; moderate 120–129 mmol/L; severe <120 mmol/L.

concepts.title: Hyponatraemia – Clinical features
concepts.content: Early symptoms of hyponatraemia: headache, lethargy, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, confusion, muscle cramps. Late/severe symptoms: seizures, coma, respiratory arrest.

concepts.title: Hyponatraemia – Management
concepts.content: Management by volume status: hypovolaemic hyponatraemia: 0.9% NaCl IV. Euvolaemic hyponatraemia (e.g. SIADH): fluid restriction 500–1000 ml/day; demeclocycline (ADH antagonist); vaptans (V2 receptor antagonists). Hypervolaemic hyponatraemia (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome): fluid restriction; loop diuretics; vaptans. Acute severe hyponatraemia (<120 mmol/L with severe symptoms): hypertonic saline (3% NaCl) in HDU setting.

concepts.title: Hyponatraemia – Osmotic demyelination syndrome
concepts.content: Osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS) occurs when hyponatraemia is corrected too rapidly. Rapid correction causes osmotic stress in astrocytes and oligodendrocytes → apoptosis → demyelination. Sodium should be raised by no more than 4–6 mmol/L per 24 hours. Symptoms of ODS: dysarthria, dysphagia, paraparesis, seizures, and locked-in syndrome.

concepts.title: Hypocalcaemia – Causes, features and management
concepts.content: Causes of hypocalcaemia: vitamin D deficiency, CKD, hypoparathyroidism, pseudohypoparathyroidism, rhabdomyolysis, magnesium deficiency, massive blood transfusion, acute pancreatitis. Features: tetany, perioral paraesthesia, depression, cataracts; ECG: prolonged QT interval; Trousseau's sign (95% sensitive); Chvostek's sign (70% sensitive). Management of severe hypocalcaemia: IV calcium gluconate 10 ml of 10% solution over 10 minutes with ECG monitoring.

concepts.title: Hypophosphataemia – Causes and consequences
concepts.content: Causes of hypophosphataemia: alcohol excess, acute liver failure, DKA, refeeding syndrome, primary hyperparathyroidism, osteomalacia. Consequences: RBC haemolysis, WBC and platelet dysfunction, muscle weakness and rhabdomyolysis, CNS dysfunction.

concepts.title: Metabolic acidosis – Anion gap classification
concepts.content: Anion gap = Na+ + K+ − Cl− − HCO3−; normal range 10–18 mmol/L. Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) causes: GI bicarbonate loss (diarrhoea, ureterosigmoidostomy, fistula), renal tubular acidosis, acetazolamide, ammonium chloride, Addison's disease. Raised anion gap causes: lactic acidosis (shock, sepsis, hypoxia, burns; metformin), ketoacidosis (DKA, alcoholic), uraemia (renal failure), acid poisoning (salicylates, methanol).

concepts.title: Renal tubular acidosis – Overview and types
concepts.content: All types of renal tubular acidosis (RTA) cause hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap. Type 1 (distal): inability to secrete H+ in the distal tubule; hypokalaemia; nephrocalcinosis and renal stones; causes: idiopathic, RA, SLE, Sjogren's, amphotericin B, analgesic nephropathy. Type 2 (proximal): decreased HCO3- reabsorption; hypokalaemia; osteomalacia; causes: idiopathic, Fanconi syndrome, Wilson's disease, cystinosis, outdated tetracyclines, acetazolamide/topiramate. Type 3 (mixed): extremely rare; carbonic anhydrase II deficiency; hypokalaemia. Type 4 (hyperkalaemic): reduced aldosterone → reduced ammonium excretion; hyperkalaemia; causes: hypoaldosteronism, diabetes.

concepts.title: IgA nephropathy – Epidemiology, features and pathophysiology
concepts.content: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) is the most common glomerulonephritis worldwide. It typically presents in a young male with macroscopic haematuria occurring concurrently with (not after) an upper respiratory tract infection. Nephrotic-range proteinuria is rare. Pathophysiology: mesangial deposition of IgA immune complexes; overlaps with Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP). Histology: mesangial hypercellularity; IgA and C3 on immunofluorescence.

concepts.title: IgA nephropathy – Differentiation from post-streptococcal GN
concepts.content: Key differences between IgA nephropathy and post-streptococcal GN: IgA nephropathy: haematuria concurrent with URTI; normal complement; haematuria predominant. Post-streptococcal GN: haematuria 7–14 days after Group A Strep infection; low C3 complement; proteinuria predominant; raised ASOT.

concepts.title: IgA nephropathy – Management and prognosis
concepts.content: Management of IgA nephropathy: isolated haematuria with normal renal function: no treatment, monitor; persistent proteinuria: ACE inhibitors/ARBs; active disease or failure of ACE inhibitors: corticosteroids. Prognosis: 25% develop end-stage renal failure. Poor prognostic factors: male sex, proteinuria >2 g/day, hypertension, smoking, hyperlipidaemia, ACE DD genotype.

concepts.title: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis – Features and investigations
concepts.content: Post-streptococcal GN occurs 7–14 days after Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) infection. Most commonly affects young children. Features: headache, malaise, visible haematuria, proteinuria, oedema, hypertension, oliguria; raised ASOT; low C3 complement. Renal biopsy: acute diffuse proliferative GN; endothelial proliferation with neutrophils; subepithelial 'humps' on electron microscopy; granular 'starry sky' on immunofluorescence (IgG, IgM, C3).

concepts.title: Membranous nephropathy – Epidemiology, causes and diagnosis
concepts.content: Membranous nephropathy is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults and the third most common cause of ESRD. Causes: idiopathic (anti-PLA2R antibodies in ~70–80%); infections (hepatitis B, malaria, syphilis); malignancy (5–20% of adult cases); drugs (gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs); autoimmune (SLE, thyroiditis, RA). Renal biopsy: 'spike and dome' appearance on electron microscopy (subepithelial immune deposits).

concepts.title: Membranous nephropathy – Management and prognosis
concepts.content: Management: ACE inhibitor/ARB for proteinuria; immunosuppression for severe/progressive disease (corticosteroid + cyclophosphamide); anticoagulation for high-risk patients. Prognosis follows the 'rule of thirds': 1/3 spontaneous remission; 1/3 remain proteinuric but stable; 1/3 develop ESRD.

concepts.title: FSGS – Features and prognosis
concepts.content: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) causes nephrotic syndrome. Secondary causes include IgA nephropathy, reflux nephropathy, HIV, heroin use, Alport's syndrome, and sickle-cell disease. Renal biopsy: focal and segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis on light microscopy; foot process effacement on electron microscopy. Prognosis: <10% chance of spontaneous remission; high recurrence rate in renal transplants.

concepts.title: MPGN – Types and features
concepts.content: Membranoproliferative (mesangiocapillary) GN (MPGN) presents with nephrotic syndrome, haematuria and proteinuria and has a poor prognosis. Type 1 (90%): associated with cryoglobulinaemia and hepatitis C; tram-track appearance on electron microscopy. Type 2 (dense deposit disease): associated with partial lipodystrophy, factor H deficiency, and alternative complement pathway activation; low C3; C3b nephritic factor in 70%; dense deposits on EM. Type 3: associated with hepatitis B and C. Steroids may be effective.

concepts.title: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome – Triad, causes and investigations
concepts.content: HUS is characterised by the triad of: AKI, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA), and thrombocytopenia. Typical HUS (>90% of childhood cases): Shiga-toxin producing E. coli (STEC) O157:H7; also pneumococcal, HIV, SLE, drugs, cancer. Atypical HUS: complement dysregulation. Investigations: blood film (schistocytes); Hb <8 g/dL; thrombocytopenia; U&E (AKI); stool culture; PCR for Shiga toxins.

concepts.title: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome – Management
concepts.content: Management of HUS: supportive care (IV fluids, blood transfusion, dialysis); antibiotics should NOT be given (may increase Shiga toxin release); plasma exchange for severe non-diarrhoeal HUS; eculizumab (complement inhibitor) for atypical HUS.

concepts.title: Henoch-Schonlein purpura – Features and management
concepts.content: HSP is an IgA-mediated small vessel vasculitis that overlaps with IgA nephropathy. It typically follows infection in children. Features: palpable purpuric rash on buttocks and extensor surfaces; abdominal pain; polyarthritis; haematuria and renal failure. Treatment: analgesia; supportive nephropathy management; evidence for steroids and immunosuppressants is inconsistent. Prognosis: usually excellent and self-limiting; 1/3 relapse; monitor BP and urinalysis.

concepts.title: Contrast nephrotoxicity – Definition, risk factors and prevention
concepts.content: Contrast-induced nephropathy is defined as a 25% rise in serum creatinine within 3 days of intravascular contrast administration (typically occurs 2–5 days after). Risk factors: renal impairment (especially diabetic nephropathy), age >70, dehydration, cardiac failure, nephrotoxic drugs. Prevention: IV 0.9% NaCl at 1 ml/kg/hr for 12 hours before and after procedure; isotonic sodium bicarbonate is an alternative; N-acetylcysteine is NOT effective (no benefit in trials); withhold metformin for ≥48 hours after contrast.

concepts.title: Peritoneal dialysis – Overview and peritonitis management
concepts.content: Continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) involves four 2-litre exchanges per day. The most common complication is peritonitis. Most common causative organism: coagulase-negative Staphylococcus; also S. aureus. Treatment: vancomycin or teicoplanin plus ceftazidime in dialysis fluid; OR vancomycin in dialysis fluid plus ciprofloxacin orally. Aminoglycosides are an alternative for Gram-negative organisms. Sclerosing peritonitis is a rare but serious complication.

concepts.title: Erythropoietin – Uses, side effects and failure to respond
concepts.content: Erythropoietin (EPO) is a haematopoietic growth factor secreted by the kidney in response to hypoxia. Uses: anaemia of CKD; anaemia secondary to cytotoxic therapy. Side effects: accelerated hypertension (25% of patients), bone aches, flu-like symptoms, skin rashes, pure red cell aplasia (rare; darbepoetin has greatly reduced this risk), raised PCV (thrombosis risk), iron deficiency. Failure to respond to EPO: iron deficiency (most common), inadequate dose, infection/inflammation, hyperparathyroid bone disease, aluminium toxicity.

concepts.title: Fanconi syndrome – Definition, features and causes
concepts.content: Fanconi syndrome is a generalised reabsorptive disorder of the proximal convoluted tubule. Features: type 2 renal tubular acidosis, polyuria, aminoaciduria, glycosuria, phosphaturia, and osteomalacia. Causes: cystinosis (most common in children), Sjogren's syndrome, multiple myeloma, nephrotic syndrome, Wilson's disease.

concepts.title: Fibromuscular dysplasia – Features and management
concepts.content: Fibromuscular dysplasia accounts for 10% of renal vascular disease and affects 90% females. Features: hypertension, CKD or acute renal failure, flash pulmonary oedema. Investigations: renal function; Doppler ultrasound (first-line); CT or MR angiography for confirmation. Management: antihypertensives (ACE inhibitors/ARBs); revascularisation (percutaneous angioplasty ± stenting).

concepts.title: Erectile dysfunction – Overview
concepts.content: Erectile dysfunction (ED) is the inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual performance. It is a presentation within the renal and urology system and may be associated with conditions such as BPH, prostate cancer treatment, diabetes, hypertension, and vascular disease.

concepts.title: Urinary tract infection – Overview and context
concepts.content: Urinary tract infection (UTI) is a common cause of urinary symptoms and haematuria. It is a complication of BPH and may cause transient non-visible haematuria. UTI should be excluded before diagnosing persistent haematuria. In older adults, E. coli is the most common causative organism in epididymo-orchitis.

concepts.title: Polyuria – Causes by frequency
concepts.content: Causes of polyuria by frequency: Common: diuretics, caffeine, alcohol, diabetes mellitus, lithium, heart failure. Infrequent: hypercalcaemia, hyperthyroidism. Rare: CKD, primary polydipsia, hypokalaemia. Very rare: diabetes insipidus.

concepts.title: Body fluid compartments
concepts.content: Distribution of body fluid: intracellular fluid 28 L (60–65% of total body water); extracellular fluid 14 L (35–40%): plasma 3 L (5%), interstitial fluid 10 L (24%), transcellular fluid 1 L (3%).

concepts.title: Hyperuricaemia – Causes
concepts.content: Hyperuricaemia may be asymptomatic and is associated with hyperlipidaemia, hypertension and metabolic syndrome. Causes of increased uric acid synthesis: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, myeloproliferative disorders, purine-rich diet, exercise, psoriasis, cytotoxic drugs. Causes of decreased uric acid excretion: low-dose aspirin, diuretics, pyrazinamide, pre-eclampsia, alcohol, renal failure, lead toxicity.

concepts.title: Vaptans – Mechanism, uses and cautions
concepts.content: Vaptans are vasopressin (V2) receptor antagonists that cause selective water diuresis (aquaresis) without sodium loss. Uses: euvolaemic hyponatraemia (SIADH) and hypervolaemic hyponatraemia (heart failure, cirrhosis). Cautions: avoid in hypovolaemic hyponatraemia (worsens volume depletion); hepatotoxic; stimulate thirst (may counteract benefit).
